That almost broke Zoe's heart; but she strove to hide her wounds from him, and especially from her tormentor.

The storm kept Edward in the house: at another time that would have been a joy to Zoe, but now it only added to her troubles, affording constant opportunity to the wily foe to carry out her evil designs.

On the evening of the second day from the setting in of the storm, Miss Deane challenged Edward to a game of chess. He accepted at once, and with an air of quiet satisfaction brought out the board, and placed the men.

He was fond of the game; but Zoe had never fancied it, and he had played but seldom since their marriage.

Miss Deane was a more than ordinarily skilful player, and so was he; indeed, so well matched were they, that neither found it an easy matter to checkmate the other: and that first game proved a long one,--so long that Zoe, who had watched its progress with some interest in the beginning, eager to see Edward win, at length grew so weary as to find it difficult to keep her eyes open, or refrain from yawning.

But Edward, usually so tenderly careful of her, took no notice,--indeed, as she said bitterly to herself, seemed to have forgotten her existence.

Still, it was with a thrill of delight that she at length perceived that he had come off victorious.

Miss Deane took her defeat with very good grace, and smilingly challenged him to another contest.

"Rather late, isn't it?" he said with a glance at the clock, whose hands pointed to half-past eleven. "Suppose we sign a truce until to-morrow?"

"Certainly: that will be decidedly best," she promptly replied, following the direction of his glance. "I feel so fresh, and have enjoyed myself so much, that I had no idea of the hour, and am quite ashamed of having kept my youthful hostess up so late," she added, looking sweetly at Zoe. "Very young people need a large amount of sleep, and can't keep up health and strength without it."

"You are most kind," said Zoe, a touch of sarcasm in her tones: "it must be a very sympathetic nature that has enabled you to remember so long how young people feel."

A twinkle of fun shone in Edward's eyes at that.

Miss Deane colored furiously, bade a hasty good-night, and departed to her own room.

"That was a rather hard thrust, my dear," remarked Edward, laughing, as he led the way into their dressing-room; "not quite polite, I'm afraid."

"I don't care if it wasn't!" said Zoe. "She is always twitting me on my extreme youth."

"Sour grapes," he said lightly: "she will never see twenty-five again, and would give a great deal for your youth. And since you are exactly the age to suit me, why should you care a fig for her sneers?"

"I don't, when I seem to suit you in all respects," returned Zoe with tears in her voice.

Her back was toward him; but he caught sight of her face in a mirror, and saw that tears were also glistening in her eyes.

Putting his arm round her waist, and drawing her to him, "I don't want a piece of perfection for my wife," he said; "she would be decidedly too great a contrast to her husband: and I have never yet seen the woman or girl I should be willing to take in exchange for the one belonging to me. And I'm very sure such a one doesn't exist."

The sun had retired, leaving behind a soft twilight, an array of pastels bleeding harmoniously into the heavens. Old Jolyon leaned against the balustrade of the terrace, his gaze tracing the fading hues as they danced upon the edges of the garden, a sanctuary of life nestled beneath the sprawling arms of the old oak. A gentle breeze stirred the leaves, whispering secrets only the trees could comprehend. It was within this tranquility that he found his thoughts returning to Irene, her presence as vivid in his mind as the colors now waning in the sky.

Her laughter resonated still, suffusing the very air around him with warmth, a stark contrast to the cool indifference of his twenty-four years. He recalled her question, posed so lightly: "Is beauty but the reflection of love?” A beauty susceptible to time's relentless river, yet eternal in its essence. Jolyon chided himself for his previous notions; indeed, love seemed to drape itself over the dull contours of existence, binding together the fragmented shards of life.

He turned suddenly at the sound of footsteps, his heart inexplicably quickening. It was Irene, enveloped in a diaphanous gown that caught the dimming light. She stepped with careful grace, each footfall a delicate caress against the stone. Jolyon’s heart swelled at the sight, her beauty undiminished by the shadows of her past or the burdens she carried. Here was a woman forged in trials yet unyielding, an emboldened spirit weaving her way through the thorny underbrush of life.

“I find the evening so enchanting,” she mused, looking past him to the horizon, her voice a silken thread stitching the fabrics of their conversation. “Do you ever think of how the sunset mirrors our spirits? Each flicker of light, a gentle reminder of what we endure.”

“Quite astute, my dear,” Old Jolyon replied, crossing his arms against the chill that lingered in the air. “There is much suffering endured beneath such beauty. I sometimes wonder if that’s the price of love—a burden we carry silently.”

“I have borne my share of burdens,” Irene confessed, her gaze now directed towards him, intense and searching. “Yet each was tempered by kindness, perhaps one of the greatest gifts of all. Do you remember the woman who offered me shelter during my tumultuous time? She was but a stranger yet offered a hand in darkness.”

The mention of the past stirred within him an ache, a tender regret that she had not sought refuge in him. “I would have lent you my hand, had I known,” he said earnestly, his heart naked as the evening fell around them. “To think you weathered those storms alone, it stirs my very soul.”

“Your presence is the light I sought but did not recognize until now,” she replied quietly, her eyes glistening with unshed tears. “We are often blind to comfort, you see. Yet it is in the moments of despair that we grow despite ourselves.”

He reached out, tentatively placing a caring hand upon her arm, feeling the warmth beneath its fabric. “Then let us make new memories anchored in kindness. A tea upon the morrow? Or perhaps a stroll through the gardens where we may indulge in the trivialities of life?”

“Ah, and the beauty of these trivialities,” she laughed softly, a sound that lifted Jolyon's spirits as if they had taken wing. “In their simplicity, you remind me that love holds the mightiest compass.”

“Irene,” he began softly, “do you think one can navigate brambles without the aid of another? Forgive me, but I wonder, in all your endeavors to uplift others, have you not considered that perhaps it is time to lift yourself?”

“Ah, but I draw strength from them,” she said, a hint of mischief in her smile as she regarded him. “In every soul I offer sanctuary, I find fragments of my own. It is a circular dance, or so I dare hope. Do you question the heart in its endeavors?”

“Not question, my dear. I marvel!” He smiled, warmth enveloping him at the very notion. “Each flicker of love, each act of kindness, wrests us from the abyss.”

Just then, the door creaked open, and a shadow emerged—a figure indistinct yet compelling. It lingered in the half-light before stepping fully into view. The presence seemed aware, drawn to these two kindred souls, perhaps another soul seeking warmth amid the cooling night. Old Jolyon raised an eyebrow, a silent question passing between them, prompting an understanding that they were hardly alone in their charitable pursuits.

Gaige Grosskreutz Admits Pointing Gun at Rittenhouse Before Being Shot, Testifies at Trial; Survivor of Kenosha Protests Shooting Previously Filed $10M Lawsuit Against Law Enforcement

KENOSHA – Gaige Grosskreutz, the lone survivor of Kyle Rittenhouse's shooting during the 2020 Kenosha protests, admitted in court that he pointed his gun at Rittenhouse before being shot. Grosskreutz, a trained paramedic, testified that he was not intending to kill Rittenhouse but rather trying to preserve his own life, providing testimony that appeared to bolster Rittenhouse's self-defense claim while acknowledging he believed Rittenhouse was being chased with intent to harm.

Grosskreutz, who organized a medical corps at the protests and was carrying a gun and providing first aid during the demonstrations, obtained his firearm through proper channels and was certified as an EMT. Unlike Rittenhouse, Grosskreutz was not participating in the protests but was there in a medical and protective capacity.

"I thought that the defendant was an active shooter," Grosskreutz said while testifying. He accused Rittenhouse of "murdering" another individual, Anthony Huber, but the judge instructed the jury to disregard the comment.

Although Grosskreutz had a legal permit for the gun, his testimony revealed that he might have unintentionally pointed his gun at Rittenhouse at the time of the shooting. Grosskreutz underwent several surgeries after the shooting, losing sensation below the elbow of the injured arm.

Grosskreutz, who survived the incident, filed a $10 million lawsuit against Kenosha law enforcement, claiming they shared blame for Rittenhouse's actions due to their encouragement of armed volunteers in the city.

In a tense exchange during the trial, Assistant District Attorney Thomas Binger suggested Grosskreutz's actions might have been reckless. Grosskreutz replied, "I was trying to preserve the life of the individual I believed was an active shooter."

Grosskreutz's testimony, which lasted for four hours, provided Rittenhouse's defense team with key insights into the mindset of both Rittenhouse and the people around him on the night of the protests. While Grosskreutz claimed he was not threatening Rittenhouse when he pulled out his gun, his ability to make rational decisions at the time came into question due to the fact that he had been drinking that evening and, in his own words, "wasn't sober enough to be handling a firearm."

The incident began when Rittenhouse shot and killed Joseph Rosenbaum and Anthony Huber and injured Grosskreutz during protests following the shooting of Jacob Blake by Kenosha police. Blake, a 29-year-old Black man, was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot seven times in the back by police officer Rusten Sheskey, who was subsequently placed on administrative leave.

The protests that followed drew hundreds of people to the streets, resulting in widespread unrest and property damage. Rittenhouse, who was 17 at the time, and Grosskreutz, then 26, both found themselves in the midst of the chaos, each armed and with different intentions.

Grosskreutz, who arrived in Kenosha on August 24, 2020, the day before the shooting, was there as part of a group of volunteer medics, aiding those injured during the protests. He also carried a pistol, which he obtained legally, and had been certified as an EMT.

The confrontation between Rittenhouse and Grosskreutz followed a series of events that led Rittenhouse to shoot three individuals in a span of less than five minutes. After shooting Rosenbaum, Rittenhouse was chased by a crowd, and when Grosskreutz caught up to him, he pointed his gun at Rittenhouse.

In the wake of the shootings, the Kenosha community has been left reeling, struggling to make sense of the chaos and violence that unfolded in their city that night. The trial of Kyle Rittenhouse, who faces first-degree intentional homicide charges for the killings, has captivated the nation and brought the issues of gun violence, racial justice, and vigilantism to the forefront of public discourse.

In their pursuit of justice, the families of the victims, along with law enforcement and the legal system, must navigate the delicate balance between personal responsibility, the consequences of actions taken under extreme duress, and the role that systemic issues play in the escalation of events leading to tragic outcomes.

Never as long as Ella Winter lives will she forget the picture that imprinted itself on her brain, as instantaneously as though it had been photographed there, at the moment when, startled by Aaron Stone's cry, she stepped out of the window of the sitting-room. On the borders of the lawn, at the foot of a large holly-bush, the leaves of which glistened brightly in the morning sun, knelt Aaron, his rugged features working convulsively, his trembling arms twined round the unconscious form of him who lay there in all the moveless majesty of death. One glance at the white set face, and Ella knew that the wanderer, whose absence had caused so much speculation, had come back at last, but that whatever secrets he might have in his keeping would remain secrets still, and would never be whispered in mortal ear. The pulses of her life stood still as she gazed in her shock of bewilderment.

The old man's voice broke the spell: he saw her standing there.

"Oh, ma'am, my dear young mistress, it is my boy! My boy come back to me--dead. There has been murder done here!"

A shudder ran through Ella. Murder! Was it true?--or was old Aaron demented?

She rushed indoors to the sitting-room, ringing its bells as they had never been rung before; and then she sank into a chair. Never had Ella Winter been so near fainting.

The servants came running in, and she strove to collect her thoughts. Some one ran to the huge bell that rang in the stable-yard, and sounded a peal upon it. It brought forth the coachman, Barnet. John Tilney came up with one of his men.

Barnet satisfied himself that Hubert Stone was really dead, also that he had in all probability been murdered; he then sped back to his stable-yard, and saddled a horse to ride forth in search of a doctor. "Fetch the nearest doctor you can find," had been Miss Winter's gasping order to him, and he hastened to obey it. By Barnet's orders the groom rode forth on another horse to summon the chief-constable from his office at Nullington.

The frightened maids had gathered round Miss Winter, when Dorothy Stone appeared in the doorway, tying her cap-strings with trembling fingers. The bells and the commotion had startled her, but she did not know what had happened. At sight of the patient, furrowed face and the dim blue eyes, just now full of anxious wonder, a great pity took the heart of Miss Winter, and the tears filled her own eyes as she went up to the old woman and led her away. No need for her to know the terrible news just yet.

Mrs. Toynbee next appeared upon the scene; she had waited to dress. Her first act was to order the white-faced servants away to their duties; her second to speak with John Tilney. It was by her directions that he and his two men--for the other man had come up now--carried the ill-fated young fellow into a room on the ground-floor. Then, with much tact and gentleness, Mrs. Toynbee succeeded in persuading Aaron, who seemed half-stupefied with grief and horror, to allow himself to be got into his own apartments by Tilney. Nothing more could be done till the arrival of the doctor and the police.

Dr. Spreckley and Mr. Chief-Constable Wade reached Heron Dyke together, driving over in a gig from the Rose and Crown. The first thing they did was to look at the dead. That Hubert Stone had been murdered a very slight examination sufficed to prove. He had been stabbed through the heart with a stiletto or some other sharp instrument. The disordered state of his attire, as well as the condition of the trimly-kept gravel walk, showed that he had not met his fate without a struggle; some desperate encounter must have taken place.

The years passed, each one etching deeper the peculiar bond between Balaam and young Master Berrien. The boy, once small enough for Balaam to carry on his shoulders, now towered over him, his frame lean and wiry, his face handsome in a sharp, untamed way. But the look in his eyes, the flash of temper that could erupt with the suddenness of a summer storm, that remained unchanged.

Only Balaam seemed to possess the key to those turbulent depths. He could quell a tantrum with a look, a word, a gentle hand on Berrien’s arm. He knew the boy’s moods as surely as a sailor knows the tides, sensing the gathering storm clouds and steering him clear of danger with a wisdom born of years spent navigating the treacherous waters of Berrien’s volatile nature.

Their days were spent in a familiar rhythm, woven from the threads of plantation life. Mornings found them in the stables, the air thick with the scent of hay and horseflesh, Berrien impatient to be astride his favorite mount, a spirited chestnut mare named Dixie. Balaam, ever watchful, would check the girth, adjust a stirrup, his hands moving with the practiced ease of long habit. He’d murmur a word of caution, his voice barely audible above the restless stamping of hooves, but Berrien would hear it, his gaze meeting Balaam’s with a flicker of begrudging respect.

Afternoons were for lessons, a trial that tested both student and observer. Berrien chafed under the constraints of formal education, his mind as restless as a caged bird. Books held little appeal for him, his gaze drifting towards the open window, the lure of the woods beyond proving far more potent than any Latin declension. It was Balaam, his presence a calming influence in the stifling air of the schoolroom, who kept Berrien anchored, however tenuously, to his studies.

He’d sit quietly in a corner, his hands busy with some mending or carving, his presence a silent promise of respite once the ordeal was over. And Berrien, for all his outward disdain, drew strength from that unspoken promise, his gaze seeking Balaam’s from time to time, as if drawing reassurance from the steady brown eyes that watched him with unwavering loyalty.

But it was in the evenings, when the shadows lengthened and the day’s heat finally relented, that the true depth of their bond was revealed. With the other slaves gathered on the porch, their voices rising and falling in the mournful sweetness of spirituals, Berrien and Balaam would find themselves drawn together, as if by an invisible thread, to the relative coolness of the veranda.

Here, under the soft glow of the oil lamps, Berrien would shed the mantle of the young master, his arrogance and impatience fading away, replaced by a vulnerability he seldom allowed himself to show to others. He’d talk to Balaam, pouring out his thoughts and dreams, his frustrations and fears, confiding in him in a way he never could with his own family.

Balaam listened, as he always did, with a patience that bordered on the infinite. He offered no judgments, no platitudes, only the solace of his quiet presence and the occasional insightful comment that spoke volumes without ever needing to raise its voice. He was, to Berrien, more than just a servant, more even than a friend. He was a confidant, a counselor, a mirror reflecting back not the young man Berrien showed the world, but the one he kept hidden deep within himself.

One such evening, as fireflies winked in the gathering darkness and the scent of honeysuckle hung heavy in the air, Berrien spoke of his growing unease. The talk among the plantation owners had turned increasingly to matters that filled him with a nameless dread—talk of secession, of war, of a future that seemed balanced precariously on a knife’s edge.

“What do you make of it all, Balaam?” he asked, his voice unusually subdued.

Balaam, his gaze fixed on some distant point beyond the veranda, took his time answering. When he finally spoke, his voice was low and grave, tinged with an ancient sorrow. “The wind is changin’, Master Berrien,” he said, “and it ain’t gonna be a gentle breeze, neither. It’s gonna be a storm, a mighty storm, and ain’t nobody, not even the likes of you and me, gonna be able to stop it.”

Vice President Kamala Harris: We must 'speak truth' about history of racism in America

Vice President Kamala Harris said Thursday in an exclusive interview with ABC's "Good Morning America" that she did not think the United States was a "racist country" but that it was important to "speak the truth" about the role racism has played in the nation's history.

Harris, the first Black vice president, was responding to GOP Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who on Wednesday night delivered the Republican response to President Joe Biden's address to a joint session of Congress.

Scott, the only Black Republican senator, said "America is not a racist country" and took issue with what he called fighting "discrimination with different types of discrimination" and trying "to use our painful past to dishonestly shut down debates in the present."

"No, I don't think America is a racist country," Harris told "Good Morning America" co-anchor George Stephanopoulos. "But we also do have to speak truth about the history of racism in our country and its existence today."

The vice president said that "we want to unify the country, but not without speaking truth and requiring accountability, as appropriate."

"These are issues that we must confront, and it doesn't--it does not help to heal our country to unify us as a people to ignore the realities of that," she said.

The vice president praised Biden for calling white supremacy terrorism in his speech and noting U.S. intelligence agencies have determined it to be "the most lethal terrorist threat to the homeland today."

During her interview with "Good Morning America," Harris also addressed the Biden administration's $2.3 trillion infrastructure plan.

Asked by Stephanopoulos how much the White House was willing to compromise with Republicans, who are widely opposed to Biden's expansive package and the president's ideas about how to pay for it, Harris would not say.

But she did say the administration was "very serious" and "very sincere in our hope that we can reflect the bipartisan nature of the American people on these issues."

"We have been in many meetings in the Oval Office with Republicans and Democrats together, talking about all of these issues and inviting their feedback, inviting their ideas," Harris said. "We're very serious about that -- and very sincere in our hope that we can reflect the bipartisan nature of the American people on these issues, and come together in a way that is about, again, investing in families, investing in job creation, investing in the competitiveness of our country, vis-a-vis the world."

On Wednesday night, Biden laid out the components of his plan, including expanding broadband internet access, then said, "I am asking the vice president to lead this effort."

It was widely reported that the president had tasked Harris with shepherding the entire infrastructure proposal through Congress, but Thursday morning, Harris's office said that Biden was only talking about Harris "taking a lead on expanding broadband access" -- not the whole plan.

Biden had also previously asked Harris to lead the diplomatic effort to stem the flow of migration from Central America, to which he referred in his speech. The president did not address the situation on the southern border, though.

When pressed by "Good Morning America" co-anchor Robin Roberts about why Biden omitted any mention of the situation there, Harris would not say.

Instead, she laid out her work to address the lack of opportunity and threats causing many to flee the region.

“The way that we are then dealing with this," she said, "is to say, 'Hey, let's, one, understand these are our neighbors in the Western Hemisphere, and let's do what we can to give the folks there some hope, that if they stay, help is on the way.'"

Harris explained she has been working with Cabinet secretaries, including Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo and Agriculture Secretary Tom Vilsack, as well as working with other world leaders to recommit to helping the region.

“It's not a new issue but we are prepared to make the investment and to get in there for the long haul to do what is necessary to address the reasons people flee,” Harris added.

But when a young lady is to be a heroine, the perverseness of forty surrounding families cannot prevent her. Something must and will happen to throw a hero in her way.

Mr. Allen, who owned the chief of the property about Fullerton, the village in Wiltshire where the Morlands lived, was ordered to Bath for the benefit of a gouty constitutio–nd his lady, a good-humoured woman, fond of Miss Morland, and probably aware that if adventures will not befall a young lady in her own village, she must seek them abroad, invited her to go with them. Mr. and Mrs. Morland were all compliance, and Catherine all happiness.

In addition to what has been already said of Catherine Morland's personal and mental endowments, when about to be launched into all the difficulties and dangers of a six weeks' residence in Bath, it may be stated, for the reader's more certain information, lest the following pages should otherwise fail of giving any idea of what her character is meant to be, that her heart was affectionate; her disposition cheerful and open, without conceit or affectation of any kin–er manners just removed from the awkwardness and shyness of a girl; her person pleasing, and, when in good looks, prett–nd her mind about as ignorant and uninformed as the female mind at seventeen usually is.

When the hour of departure drew near, the maternal anxiety of Mrs. Morland will be naturally supposed to be most severe. A thousand alarming presentiments of evil to her beloved Catherine from this terrific separation must oppress her heart with sadness, and drown her in tears for the last day or two of their being together; and advice of the most important and applicable nature must of course flow from her wise lips in their parting conference in her closet. Cautions against the violence of such noblemen and baronets as delight in forcing young ladies away to some remote farm-house, must, at such a moment, relieve the fulness of her heart. Who would not think so? But Mrs. Morland knew so little of lords and baronets, that she entertained no notion of their general mischievousness, and was wholly unsuspicious of danger to her daughter from their machinations. Her cautions were confined to the following points. “I beg, Catherine, you will always wrap yourself up very warm about the throat, when you come from the rooms at night; and I wish you would try to keep some account of the money you spend; I will give you this little book on purpose.”

Sally, or rather Sarah (for what young lady of common gentility will reach the age of sixteen without altering her name as far as she can?), must from situation be at this time the intimate friend and confidante of her sister. It is remarkable, however, that she neither insisted on Catherine's writing by every post, nor exacted her promise of transmitting the character of every new acquaintance, nor a detail of every interesting conversation that Bath might produce. Everything indeed relative to this important journey was done, on the part of the Morlands, with a degree of moderation and composure, which seemed rather consistent with the common feelings of common life, than with the refined susceptibilities, the tender emotions which the first separation of a heroine from her family ought always to excite. Her father, instead of giving her an unlimited order on his banker, or even putting an hundred pounds bank-bill into her hands, gave her only ten guineas, and promised her more when she wanted it.

Under these unpromising auspices, the parting took place, and the journey began. It was performed with suitable quietness and uneventful safety. Neither robbers nor tempests befriended them, nor one lucky overturn to introduce them to the hero. Nothing more alarming occurred than a fear, on Mrs. Allen's side, of having once left her clogs behind her at an inn, and that fortunately proved to be groundless.

Sir, 'tis a strange turn of fortune that befalls us in this humble village, where the shadows of the past seem to linger and whisper tales of defiance and rebirth. 'Tis but the day following our discourse with Mr. Pepperill, and the whispers grow louder still.

The landlord’s public-house now stands as a beacon of prosperity, its windows glinting with the promise of a hearty meal and warm conversation. 'Twas the tramp, an unfortunate wretch of unsteady gait, who lit the spark that set ablaze the old edifice. Ha, but 'twas providence, perchance, that the landlord stood as blessed with insurance against such calamities. 'Twas a fire that wrought destruction, yet sowed the seeds of a new beginning.

The changed landscape of the village gossips with the story, and the tale of renewal spreads like wildfire. What once was a dwelling of meager repute now flourishes in the finest timber and stone. The landlord surveys his domain with a content smile, the very image of success.

"An uncommon sight, indeed," murmurs Mr. Pasco Pepperill as he surveys the renovated inn, his mind turned to considerations darker than the smoke of the fire that was.

"Mark you, sir," whispered his wife, her voice a whisper laced with worry, "Our woes are many, and your mind turns too often towards thoughts of ruin. Do not let despair cloak itself in the guise of hope."

Mr. Pepperill, absorbed in his contemplation, scarcely heard his wife's cautionary words. His heart was heavy with the burden of his debts, and the specter of fire danced before his eyes, as potent a solution as 'twas sinister.

"Heigh-ho," he sighed, "The coal merchant's threat looms large, and the specter of the courts casts a long shadow."

Meanwhile, Miss Kate Quarm finds solace in the embrace of the moors, where she retreats to seek respite from the tumult of her thoughts. The landscape offers her a balm—the sun's golden caress upon her face and the piercing bite of the wind, which serves to cleave through her worries. The hills shelter her from the world and fortify her spirit, much as the sturdy walls of the landlord's establishment shield the village from its troubles.

The day, like a dutiful servant, turns from morn to eve, and the brief moments of respite are numbered. Miss Quarm sits upon a crag, her thoughts coalescing as she gazes upon the horizon, where the setting sun paints a vivid tapestry upon the sky. Her heart swells with a peculiar joy—the contentment of one who, though buffeted by life’s tempests, finds refuge in the unyielding arms of nature.

“It is as if the very elements conspire to soothe my soul,” she murmurs, her fingers tracing patterns upon the rough bark of a tree, a solitary sentinel amidst the rolling hills.

The village, bucolic and teeming with life despite its trials, whispers of the landlord’s newfound fortune, and the hint of it catches in the ears of Mr. Pepperill. The notion that one might rise from ashes to bask in the warmth of prosperity is an alluring one, yet the unspoken question lingers: Can such a miracle be wrought for him?

The fire that rekindled the landlord's dreams casts its glow across the village, beckoning to the hopeful hearts within. And Miss Quarm, who finds peace in the wilderness, serves as a reminder that, even in the face of adversity, the spirit may find renewal.

Yet, amidst the tales of rebirth and whispered hopes, there lies the creeping shadow of discontent. For every hopeful whisper of fortune, there echoes a faint murmur of doubt—a reminder that the path to prosperity is fraught with peril and that the winds of chance may shift at any moment.

Thus, the village continues its quiet existence, each soul bound by the threads of their fates, weaving a tapestry of dreams and regrets. And as the sun dips below the horizon, painting the sky with hues of twilight, the people pause to contemplate the day that has passed and the tomorrow that awaits—a tomorrow filled with both promise and uncertainty.

As night descends, the village drifts into slumber, its denizens lulled by the gentle lullabies of the firelit inn and the distant cries of the wild creatures that roam the moors. And Miss Quarm, content in her solitude, surrenders to the tranquility of the night, her spirit fortified by the day's simple pleasures.

The wind stirs the leaves—a soft symphony that lulls the village into forgetfulness, and the fires that once threatened to consume all hope now serve as beacons of renewal. In this land of shadows and sunlight, the story of rebirth continues to unfold, a testament to the resilience of the human spirit.

Wilfrid Athel went down invalided a few days after the beginning of Trinity term. The event was not unanticipated. At Christmas it had been clear enough that he was overtaxing himself; his father remarked on the fact with anxiety, and urged moderation, his own peculiar virtue. Wilfrid, whose battle with circumstances was all before him, declined to believe that the body was anything but the very humble servant of the will. So the body took its revenge.

He had been delicate in childhood, and the stage of hardy naturalism which interposes itself between tender juvenility and the birth of self-consciousness did not in his case last long enough to establish his frame in the vigour to which it was tending. There was nothing sickly about him; it was only an excess of nervous vitality that would not allow body to keep pace with mind. He was a boy to be, intellectually, held in leash, said the doctors. But that was easier said than done. What system of sedatives could one apply to a youngster whose imagination wrought him to a fever during a simple walk by the seashore, who if books were forcibly withheld consoled himself with the composition of five-act tragedies, interspersed with lyrics to which he supplied original strains? Mr. Athel conceived a theory that such exuberance of emotionality might be counterbalanced by studies of a strictly positive nature; a tutor was engaged to ground young Wilfrid in mathematics and the physical sciences. The result was that the tutor's enthusiasm for these pursuits communicated itself after a brief repugnance to the versatile pupil; instincts of mastery became as vivid in the study of Euclid and the chemical elements as formerly in the humaner paths of learning; the plan had failed. In the upshot Wilfrid was sent to school; if that did not develop the animal in him, nothing would.

He was not quite three-and-twenty when the break-down removed him from Oxford. Going to Balliol with a scholarship, he had from the first been marked for great things, at all events by the measure of the schools. Removal from the system of home education had in truth seemed to answer in some degree the ends aimed at; the lad took his fair share of cricket and football, and kept clear of nervous crises. At the same time he made extraordinary progress with his books. He acquired with extreme facility, and his ambition never allowed him to find content in a second place; conquest became his habit; he grew to deem it the order of nature that Wilfrid Athel's name should come first in the list. Hence a reputation to support. During his early terms at Balliol he fagged as hard as the mere dullard whose dear life depended upon a first class and a subsequent tutorship. What he would make of himself in the end was uncertain; university distinctions would probably be of small moment to him as soon as they were achieved, for already he spent the greater portion of his strength in lines of study quite apart from the curriculum, and fate had blessed him with exemption from sordid cares. He led in a set devoted to what were called advanced ideas; without flattering himself that he was on the way to solve the problem of the universe, he had satisfaction in reviewing the milestones which removed him from the unconscious man, and already clutched at a measure of positive wisdom in the suspicion that lie might shortly have to lay aside his school-books and recommence his education under other teachers. As yet he was whole-hearted in the pursuit of learning. The intellectual audacity which was wont to be the key-note of his conversation did not, as his detractors held, indicate mere bumptiousness and defect of self-measurement; it was simply the florid redundancy of a young mind which glories in its strength, and plays at victory in anticipation. It was true that he could not brook the semblance of inferiority; if it were only five minutes' chat in the Quad, he must come off with a phrase or an epigram; so those duller heads who called Athel affected were not wholly without their justification. Those who shrugged their shoulders with the remark that he was overdoing it, and would not last out to the end of the race, enjoyed a more indisputable triumph. One evening, when Athel was taking the brilliant lead in an argument on 'Fate, free-will, foreknowledge absolute,' his brain began to whirl, tobacco-smoke seemed to have dulled all the lights before his eyes, and he fell from his chair in a fainting-fit.

The afternoon sun slanted low over the rolling dunes, casting long shadows across the deserted beach. Harrie waded out into the icy water, the waves lapping gently at her ankles. She held her breath, submerging herself, and felt the chill seep into her bones. As she emerged, the frigid water sent a shock through her system, invigorating her senses. She imagined the years melting away with each plunge, her skin becoming taut and smooth, her features regaining their youthful glow.

Coming ashore, she wrapped herself in a thick woolen shawl. Her teeth chattered, and her skin tingled as the warmth of the shawl slowly replaced the ocean's bite. Turning towards the distant house perched on the cliff, she saw Myron standing on the verandah, his silhouette stark against the darkening sky. His gaze was fixed on her, and she felt a pang of guilt. His disapproval lingered in his earlier words – a woman her age should not expose herself to such frigid waters.

His lips moved, the distance muffling his words. But she saw the frown etched between his brows, a mirror of his displeasure. She knew this was not about the cold. It was about her age, her fading beauty, her persistent attempts to recapture the vibrancy of her youth.

Harrie returned to the house, her head hung low. The warmth of the fireplace in the drawing-room did little to dispel the chill that had settled within her. Myron was engrossed in the newspaper, an unread book lying open on his lap. He glanced up as she entered, a fleeting glint in his eyes before he returned to his reading.

"Miss Dallas was most gracious this morning," he remarked, folding the paper and laying it carefully on the table next to the book. "She volunteered to accompany me on a fishing trip tomorrow. Such a lively young woman – a breath of fresh air."

Harrie swallowed, forcing a smile. "Indeed, she is quite delightful. I am glad she found you agreeable company."

"Agreeable and capable," Myron added, a hint of amusement in his voice. "She can handle a fishing rod with the best of them, and she even knows which bait to use for the afternoon catch."

Harrie felt a wave of jealousy wash over her. She recalled the times they had gone fishing together, when she was younger and Myron's eyes seemed to sparkle just for her. Now, with Miss Dallas in the picture, their shared moments felt distant, like whispers of a half-forgotten dream.

She excused herself and retreated to her room, the image of Myron and Miss Dallas laughing together on a fishing boat burning in her mind. She walked to the window, her reflection staring back at her – a tired, worn visage, etched with the lines of time and burdened by loneliness.

In the darkness of her room, Harrie decided she would not let it end like this. She would not surrender her husband's affections to a younger woman without a fight. She would regain his admiration, recapture his gaze, revive the love that seemed to have dwindled with the passage of time.

But how? Harrie stood before the mirror, studying her reflection. She needed to reignite the spark, the joy that Myron had found in her once. She needed to rediscover herself, the woman he fell in love with all those years ago.

A thought struck her, a mischievous glint appearing in her eyes. She wouldn't let age define her, nor would she allow Miss Dallas to eclipse her. She would prove to her husband that she could still be the vibrant, captivating woman he married.

"If Miss McCroke could hear you!"

"She does, often. You can't imagine the wild things I say to her. But I love her--fondly."

A great bell clanged out with a vigorous peal, that seemed to shake the old stable.

"There's the first bell. I must run and dress. Come to the drawing-room and see mamma."

"But, Vixen, how can I sit down to dinner in such a costume," remonstrated Rorie, looking down at his brown shooting-suit, leather gaiters, and tremendous boots--boots which, instead of being beautified with blacking, were suppled with tallow; "I can't do it, really."

"Nonsense," cried Vixen, "what does it matter? Papa seldom dresses for dinner. I believe he considers it a sacrifice to mamma's sense of propriety when he washes his hands after coming in from the home farm. And you are only a boy--I beg pardon--an undergraduate. So come along."

"But upon my word, Vixen, I feel too much ashamed of myself."

"I've asked you to dinner, and you've accepted," cried Vixen, pulling him out of the stable by the lapel of his shooting-jacket.

He seemed to relish that mode of locomotion, for he allowed himself to be pulled all the way to the hall-door, and into the glow of the great beech-wood fire; a ruddy light which shone upon many a sporting trophy, and reflected itself on many a gleaming pike and cuirass, belonging to days of old, when gentlemanly sport for the most part meant man-hunting.

It was a fine old vaulted hall, a place to love and remember lovingly when far away. The walls were all of darkly bright oak panelling, save where here and there a square of tapestry hung before a door, or a painted window let in the moonlight. At one end there was a great arched fireplace, the arch surmounted with Squire Tempest's armorial bearings, roughly cut in freestone. A mailed figure of the usual stumpy build, in helm and hauberk, stood on each side of the hearth; a large three-cornered chair covered with stamped and gilded leather was drawn up to the fireside, the Squire's favourite seat on an autumn or winter afternoon. The chair was empty now, but, stretched at full length before the blazing logs, lay the Squire's chosen companion, Nip, a powerful liver-coloured pointer; and beside him in equally luxurious rest, reclined Argus, Vixen's mastiff. There was a story about Vixen and the mastiff, involving the only incident in that young lady's life the recollection whereof could make her blush.

The dog, apparently coiled in deepest slumber, heard the light footsteps on the hall floor, pricked up his tawny ears, sprang to his feet, and bounded over to his young mistress, whom he nearly knocked down in the warmth of his welcome. Nip, the pointer, blinked at the intruders, yawned desperately, stretched himself a trifle longer, and relapsed into slumber.

"How fond that brute is of you," said Rorie; "but it's no wonder, when one considers what you did for him."

"If you say another word I shall hate you," cried Vixen savagely.

"Well, but you know when a fellow fights another fellow's battles, the other fellow's bound to be fond of him; and when a young lady pitches into a bird-boy with her riding-whip to save a mastiff pup from ill-usage, that mastiff pup is bound----"

"Mamma," cried Vixen, flinging aside a tapestry portière, and bouncing into the drawing-room, "here's Roderick, and he's come to dinner, and you must excuse his shooting-dress, please. I'm sure pa will."

"Certainly, my dear Violet," replied a gentle, traînante voice from the fire-lit dimness near the velvet-curtained hearth. "Of course I am always glad to see Mr. Vawdrey when your papa asks him. Where did you meet the Squire, Roderick?"

I walk through the exhibition at the Cleveland Museum of Art, marveling at how 17th and 18th-century art from Europe and Great Britain encapsulates the cultural evolution of its time. I stand before Rubens’s Portrait of Isabella Brant, where I am immediately struck by the liveliness and technical finesse with which Rubens brings his subject to life. The delicate interplay of light and shadow, coupled with an almost tangible depth of emotion, testifies to an era that prized grand humanistic expression through art. In striking contrast, I examine the gilt bronze microscope, a dazzling example of 18th-century luxury and craftsmanship. Its intricate designs and sumptuous metallic sheen speak not to the vibrancy of human portraiture, but rather to a celebration of material opulence and scientific curiosity. This juxtaposition between Rubens’s emotionally charged portrait and the opulent, meticulously crafted microscope reveals a shift in cultural values from the admiration of raw technical prowess to an appreciation for the fusion of artistic elegance with artisanal skill.

As I continue my journey, I encounter La Tour’s Saint Peter Repentant, a work that offers both a visual feast and a call for deeper intellectual engagement. The painting’s sophisticated use of lighting creates a dramatic yet sensitive depiction of repentance, while the inclusion of symbolic elements like the rooster invites me to ponder larger moral and theological themes. Compared to Rubens’s exuberant celebration of human character, La Tour’s restrained yet profound narrative challenges me to reflect on the interplay of spirituality and human fallibility. Meanwhile, a gilt bronze clock on display subtly reinforces these themes by embodying the era’s fascination with precision and the passage of time, serving as a reminder of the temporal journey from vibrant emotional expression to measured scientific and artistic inquiry. In my view, the contrast between the portrait and the microscope is especially striking: the portrait captivates with its dynamic representation of life and personality, whereas the microscope encapsulates a period when art began to engage with the mechanical and scientific revolutions. The differing entertainment values—where Rubens’s work indulges the senses and the clock and microscope invite contemplation—highlight a broader shift in cultural interests that spans generations. As I stroll among these masterpieces, I appreciate how the careful curation not only celebrates individual artistic achievements but also offers insight into the sweeping transformations in societal values and intellectual pursuits over the centuries.

Crumbleys Plead Not Guilty in Michigan School Shooting

OXFORD TOWNSHIP, Mich. – James and Jennifer Crumbley, the parents of Ethan Crumbley, the 15-year-old charged with murder and other crimes in the Michigan high school shooting, pleaded not guilty to involuntary manslaughter charges on Friday.

The charges stem from the November 30 shooting at Oxford High School that killed four students and injured seven others. Ethan Crumbley is accused of carrying out the attack with a gun his father had purchased just days before.

A timeline of events leading up to the shooting reveals a series of concerning behaviors and missed warnings.

Disturbing Social Media Posts and Note

In the days leading up to the shooting, Ethan Crumbley posted disturbing messages on social media, including a photo of a gun with the caption "Just got my new beauty today." He also posted a video of himself shooting at a target.

On the morning of the shooting, a teacher found Ethan searching for ammunition online at school. The teacher reported the incident to school officials, but no action was taken.

Later that morning, another teacher discovered a note Ethan had drawn on his math homework. The note contained drawings of a handgun and phrases indicating distress and violence.

Parents Refuse to Take Son Home

School counselors evaluated Ethan's behavior and responses and did not believe he posed a threat. However, they called his parents and asked them to take him home.

James and Jennifer Crumbley refused, saying they would take him to a doctor after school. They left the school without Ethan, who went on to shoot and wound students and a teacher shortly after.

Manhunt and Arrests

Following a manhunt, the Crumbleys were arrested and charged with involuntary manslaughter. A third-party review of the events leading up to the shooting has been announced.

Prosecutor: Parents 'Had a Duty to Intervene'

Oakland County Prosecutor Karen McDonald said the Crumbleys "had a duty to intervene" when they saw their son's disturbing behavior.

"They failed to do so, and as a result, four students are dead and seven others are injured," McDonald said.

Superintendent: 'We Failed Our Students'

Oxford Community Schools Superintendent Tim Throne said the district "failed our students" by not taking appropriate action after Ethan Crumbley's note was discovered.

"We should have done more to protect our students," Throne said.

Sheriff: 'Missed Opportunities'

Sheriff's Lieutenant Tim Willis said there were "missed opportunities" to prevent the shooting.

"We could have done more to connect the dots and prevent this tragedy," Willis said.

Parents' Attorney: 'They're Not Guilty'

The Crumbleys' attorney, Shannon Smith, said his clients are "not guilty" of involuntary manslaughter.

"They did not know their son was going to commit this terrible crime," Smith said.

The trial for the Crumbleys is scheduled to begin on January 17, 2023.

It’s 2021 in America, so go give blood for school shooting victims in the parking lot of a gun store

Saturday brings a unique opportunity to give blood for shooting victims in the parking lot of a gun store.

I shit you not, this Saturday you can give blood to help victims of gun violence, and pick up supplies to perpetrate your very own gun violence, all in one stop.

The Arkansas Blood Institute is hosting a blood drive this Saturday in response to this week’s shooting murders of four Michigan high school students. It’s a lovely gesture for the touch-and-go students and a teacher who are still fighting to survive their bullet wounds, although obviously too late to help the four who already succumbed. The location for the blood drive is the Bass Pro Shop parking lot, where if you like, you can purchase a 9 mm semiautomatic Sig Sauer pistol just like the one the 15-year-old sophomore used to murder and maim.

A press release about the blood drive arrived in the newsroom today, a trumpeting announcement inviting do-gooders to come out and do some good. And while we’re happy to help get the word out, one can’t help but wonder how nobody saw the irony here. Or maybe they did and just didn’t care? To be fair, ironies like this one are impossible to escape in the United States circa 2021, where we love our kids, but love our guns more.

Basic logistics suggest Arkansas blood is unlikely to make it into the veins of injured Michiganders. Still, the sentiment is nice. The need for blood usually goes up around the holidays, in Michigan and everywhere else. Plus, here’s a great opportunity to pretend you’re doing something about gun violence without actually doing anything about gun violence at all. Expect to see some NRA-endorsed Republican politicians there with sleeves rolled up. School shootings have become America’s signature move, and no amount of junior-sized body bags seem to convince these NRA-owned lawmakers that maybe giving the gun lobby and gun manufacturers free rein isn’t a healthy idea.

The school shooting in Michigan on Tuesday has a few unique traits. The gun used was a brand new one, a Black Friday purchase by the dad of the shooter. We don’t yet know much about the gunman. But his name hasn’t yet been released and he’s reportedly on suicide watch in a juvenile detention facility, which means we can safely assume he’s white. Black kids who shoot other kids tend to get publicly named and charged as adults right off the bat.

Gun violence rates, and school shooting rates especially, have been spiking up in recent years, as chest-thumping Trumpublicans arm themselves for civil war or whatever, and cunning lobbyists push through stand your ground laws to help white men get away with murder. This year is on pace to be the worst for gun violence in decades.

The vast majority of Americans, Republican and Democrat alike, oppose our insane menu of laws that put our children in the crosshairs by making guns available anytime, anywhere, for pretty much anyone. But the majority of lawmakers clearly think our laws are fine. And doing the unglamorous grassroots work of fighting the NRA’s bought-and-paid-for operatives in Congress and state houses is a slog. An exhausting, heartbreaking slog.

It would be cool if voters would call their representatives today and ask for meaningful gun safety legislation, like universal background checks and safe storage requirements so 15-year-olds can’t just pick up dad’s new gun and pick off their classmates.

Or you can just go give some blood from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Saturday at the Bass Pro Shop parking lot if it makes you feel better.

Buddhism in Sri Lanka has long been intertwined with the country's colonial history, shaping the social and religious landscape of the nation. The essence of Buddhism lies in the Noble Eightfold Path, which outlines the way to overcome suffering and attain enlightenment. This path includes right beliefs, intention, speech, action, job, effect, awareness, and mental state. However, achieving this enlightenment is hindered by ten fetters, which prevent individuals from reaching spiritual liberation.

Understanding the social structure in Sri Lanka involves recognizing the roles of monks (Bhikkus and Bhikkunis) and laypeople (Upasakas and Upasikas). Monks adhere to strict monastic rules, dedicating their lives to spiritual practice and study, while laypeople follow simpler precepts as they navigate their daily lives. This distinction plays a significant role in the practice of Buddhism in Sri Lankan society.

The colonial history of Sri Lanka is marked by various foreign powers, with the British Empire emerging as the last colonial ruler. British colonialism brought about significant changes in Sri Lanka, leading to the collapse of the caste system and the introduction of race consciousness in the country. Unlike earlier colonial powers that were hostile to Buddhism, the British were relatively lenient towards the religion.

The 1815 Kandyan Convention serves as a pivotal moment in British colonial rule in Sri Lanka, highlighting their intentions to protect Buddhist practices in the region. This event demonstrated a shift in colonial attitudes towards Buddhism compared to previous powers. The Portuguese, for example, aligned with Catholic interests, were critical of Buddhism, creating tension within Sri Lankan society. The contrast between the attitudes of different colonial powers towards Buddhism has had a lasting impact on the religious and social fabric of Sri Lanka.

Here's What We Understand About the Michigan High School Shooting Suspect

In a devastating turn of events, police sirens echoed through the surroundings of Michigan's Oxford High School last Tuesday, marking the somber day that saw four students tragically lose their lives.

An additional six students and a teacher suffered injuries from gunfire. In connection with the harrowing incident, a 15-year-old individual has been apprehended and faces charges as an adult, confirmed by officials.

Following the incident, the suspect's parents faced charges of involuntary manslaughter on Friday due to their alleged connection to their child's actions. They were captured in Detroit on Saturday after evading authorities for hours, state officials.

This fatal occurrence has been identified as the deadliest school shooting in the U.S. since the May 2018 tragedy at Texas' Santa Fe High School, which resulted in ten fatalities. For this year alone, educational campuses have witnessed 48 shootings, with a notable 32 of these instances occurring since August 1, as per a CNN report.

Details Surrounding the Incident

Upon reports of the shooting, deputies arrived at the scene by 12:52 p.m., with Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard detailing an overwhelming response of over 100 911 calls.

The rapid intervention of law enforcement led to the swift detention of the suspect within three minutes of their arrival, with the individual surrendering and being disarmed by officers.

Sheriff Bouchard noted that the weapon, a 9 mm Sig Sauer SP2022 semiautomatic pistol, was obtained by the suspect's father just days before the incident. At the scene, deputies discovered three 15-round magazines and recovered over 30 shell casings, suggesting that the suspect had discharged at least 30 rounds during the event. Impressively, the suspect had 18 rounds remaining, underscoring the potential for further tragedy had the response not been as swift.

Victim Information

The lives lost in this senseless act were Madisyn Baldwin (17), Tate Myre (16), Hana St. Juliana (14), and Justin Shilling (17), with Tate Myre succumbing to his injuries en route to the hospital and Justin Shilling passing away the following morning. Additionally, seven others, including six students and a teacher, sustained injuries, with conditions ranging from critical to discharged, as updated by officials.

Suspect Profile

Authorities have identified the suspect as Ethan Crumbley, a 15-year-old sophomore at Oxford High School. He currently resides in Oakland County Jail, facing multiple charges including terrorism causing death, first-degree murder, assault with intent to murder, and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony.

Due to Michigan laws regarding the interrogation of juveniles, Ethan Crumbley has had no police interaction, barred by his parents' refusal for consent and their request for legal representation.

With the investigation ongoing, additional charges against Ethan Crumbley are a possibility, according to Oakland County Prosecutor Karen D. McDonald. Ethan's parents, James and Jennifer Crumbley, also faced charges of involuntary manslaughter and became subjects of a law enforcement manhunt before their arrest in a Detroit warehouse, prompted by a tip-off about their vehicle's location.

President-elect Joe Biden's inauguration this week is set to be a historic one, marked by circumstances vastly different from past ceremonies due to the COVID-19 pandemic and heightened security concerns following the recent insurrection in Washington, D.C.

Traditionally, the inauguration includes the swearing-in at the U.S. Capitol, a practice that will continue. However, the usual large gatherings and in-person celebrations have been significantly reduced. Instead, a blend of virtual events and heavy security measures, including the deployment of 25,000 National Guard soldiers, will characterize this year’s inauguration.

Tourists have been advised to avoid traveling to the capital, and the customary inaugural balls will be substituted with a virtual concert led by Tom Hanks, which will be streamed live across major networks. Added to the week's events is a memorial dedicated to the lives lost to the coronavirus pandemic.

As we approach Wednesday, the inauguration of the 46th president is preceded by virtual events and volunteer activities championed by Biden's inaugural committee, emphasizing service, especially on Martin Luther King Day. Despite the pivot to virtual engagement, the spirit of community service remains a focal point, with Americans encouraged to contribute through the bideninaugural.org/day-of-service.

A poignant moment dedicated to COVID-19 victims is planned for Tuesday evening at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. This nationwide event of remembrance and unity will also invite communities to participate by lighting buildings and ringing church bells.

While it was initially reported that Biden might travel to D.C. via Amtrak, security concerns have led to adjustments in travel plans, which remain unspecified. Biden has accepted the invitation to stay at the Blair House, the president's official guesthouse, before the inauguration, though specifics about his stay are not fully disclosed.

Security adjustments extend to the postponement of the inauguration rehearsal and an increased focus on potential threats, underscored by FBI warnings of concerning online chatter about armed protests. In response, extensive security measures, including the closure of the National Mall, are being implemented to ensure safety.

This inauguration's focus will notably divert from crowd size, a typically highlighted aspect, to adapt to the unique challenges of the current moment, emphasizing safety, unity, and remembrance.

John Neihardt’s work, Black Elk Speaks, remains widely read and influential in understanding Native American narrative despite its late surge in popularity. Neihardt, who holds the distinction of having served as Nebraska’s Poet Laureate until his death in 1973, approaches Black Elk’s life with an evident commitment to capturing a historic and lyrical narrative. Although he is neither a trained journalist nor historian, his collaboration with Black Elk is seen as a seminal scholarly work that bridges oral tradition and academic discourse. Supporters of Neihardt assert that his work "transcends mere storytelling to establish a historical document," thus affirming its scholarly value. His methodology, which melds poetic expression with historical transcription, situates Black Elk’s personal testimony within a broader cultural and political context, reflecting an assimilationist yet respectful perspective toward Sioux traditions. This framework has, however, drawn critique for its Euro-American biases and the privileging of mainstream aesthetic values in recounting indigenous spirituality and resistance.

In contrast, Julian Rice, an English professor with a committed interest in Sioux spirituality and culture, adopts a markedly different approach in his reinterpretation of Black Elk’s narrative. Lacking direct access to Black Elk due to the generational gap, Rice constructs his version from a foundation markedly focused on spiritual elements, diverging from Neihardt’s broader narrative. Rice’s Black Elk’s Story concentrates on elucidating Black Elk’s inner life and spiritual insights, presenting a counter-narrative that criticizes the perceived limitations of Neihardt’s work. He argues that Neihardt’s portrayal "perpetuates misconceptions of Native Americans by endorsing assimilationist views," a stance that finds its roots in what Rice perceives as an "Euro-American arrogance" underlying Neihardt’s philosophy. His analysis not only highlights differences in focus—spiritual versus comprehensive historical reconstruction—but also mirrors the tension between retelling indigenous narratives in ways that either resonate with attraction to mythic abstraction or fidelity to cultural autonomy.

A comparative reading of Neihardt and Rice reveals contrasting interpretative frameworks driven by divergent visions of Native American identity. While Neihardt’s synthesis of historical narrative and poetic license results in a work that has both historical significance and literary appeal, Rice’s critique centers on disavowing what he considers to be the inherent ideological compromises of Neihardt’s method. Rice’s tendency to engage in personal critique—attacking Neihardt for his assimilationist and superficially Eurocentric perspectives—detracts from a broader discussion of societal attitudes toward Native Americans. As one scholar notes, "the debate between narrative authenticity and cultural reinterpretation lies at the heart of Black Elk’s legacy." Both authors, in their distinct methodologies, expose the challenges inherent in mediating indigenous voice through Western interpretative lenses, ultimately illuminating the persistent negotiation between historical documentation and ideological contamination.

The atmosphere in the drawing room hung heavy with unsaid words and the echo of the song that lingered, its whimsical notes weaving through the tension like a mischievous specter. Wyley sat near the flickering glow of the fireplace, his fingers idly tapping against the arm of the chair as he surveyed the faces of those gathered. Each seemed a tableau of restrained curiosity and veiled trepidation. The room was an elaborate stage set for a drama yet to unfold.

Knightley, standing by the window with his back to the company, appeared deep in thought, the weight of his contemplation visible in the rigid line of his shoulders. Outside, the evening cloaked the world in indigo, with lamplights casting flickering shadows across his resolute stance. There was nothing of frivolity in his posture, no hint of nostalgia in the solemn focus of his gaze.

Scrope was ensconced in a settee by the opposite wall, his airs that of a man feigning ease whilst entangled in a web of his own weaving. A furtive glance would escape him now and again, darting from Wyley to Knightley, the former's implacable calm in juxtaposition to the tension riddling his own demeanor. His hands, though clasped before him, fidgeted, each movement betraying the discord within.

Wyley's thoughts circled back to the tune – that foolish, innocuous melody – now imbued with an uncanny significance. It was a refrain that danced through his mind with uncanny persistence, weaving its simple, repetitive notes into the very fabric of the evening's burgeoning mystery. What power did such mere trifles hold over these seasoned men, knighted by the fires of experience?

"Sir Wyley," Knightley’s voice cut through the room, smooth yet carrying a hint of rough, unhealed edges. "Is there wisdom in supposing that a melody, so harmless in its guise, might signal truths unspoken?" His gaze remained fixed on the world teetering on the edge of night, yet his words reached out, binding the circle of intrigue tighter around them all.

Wyley met the question with contemplative grace, knowing well that the path they treaded was one fraught with perilous revelations. "A melody," he began, choosing his words with the precision of a swordsman, "though slender, may unravel more than its own threadbare notes. It may, indeed, lay bare the tapestry of human endeavor." His words hung in the air, moments before the crackle of the fire swallowed them whole.

Scrope shifted, the settee creaking beneath him, as if it too sought relief from the tension coiled within its occupant. "Knightley," he said, his voice carefully modulated, "that song—" he managed, his sentence trailing off as Knightley turned abruptly, his face now illuminated by the lamplight’s dim halo. There was an indefinable glint in his eyes, a subtle spark that spoke of decisions made and confidences sealed.

"I shall not press where the truth ought best to lie shrouded," Knightley declared, the authority of his manner precluding any further inquiry just yet. He moved towards Scrope, seating himself opposite with an elegance that belied the tumult under their exchanges. "Yet," he continued, "we must unravel this tale as comrades, without rising enmity."

Scrope inclined his head, acknowledging both the olive branch and the boundary thus delineated. Yet beneath his studied demeanor lurked a curiosity too eager to be easily placated. "Then speak," he urged, his voice possessing a shade more urgency, "of your captivity. For surely, therein lies the crux of this matter, the piece of this infernal musical puzzle we lack."

A soft sigh, nearly inaudible, escaped Wyley, as if the effort to weave such complexities into clarity was an endeavor of Herculean proportion. Yet it was not his tale to unveil. He reclined further into his chair, content to act the observer until such time intervention was required.

Now it was Knightley’s turn to face the company, the firelight accentuating the sharp planes of his face, lending him an aspect both noble and haunted. "Upon those foreign shores, I was visited not only by the enemies' lash and steel, but also by doubts, whispering with the coy insistence of a lover's lilting bedside confession."

Wyley's eyes remained steady upon Knightley, but his mind was a tumult of speculation. The chapter of a man's life informed by captivity often held deeper caverns than any might guess; this he did not doubt, and yet it was Knightley's own pen that must compose its own account.

"As comrades, we seek but the truth," Wyley murmured at last, his voice low, almost swept away by the embers’ dance in the hearth. His words were an echo of the code they collectively strove to observe, a guiding light amid the gathering shadows.

In the heart of Edinburgh, where the cobblestones whispered tales of a bygone era, there resided an aloof critic, known only as Macgregor. His house was a worn-out relic, like a weathered novel, filled with the ghosts of pens and inkpots. Macgregor, a man of keen intellect and insatiable curiosity, was a connoisseur of words and a connoisseur of humanity, a dual passion that often intertwined in his critical examinations.

A candle flickered in the study, casting dancing shadows upon the leather-bound tomes that lined the walls. The clock ticked softly, like the heartbeat of a slumbering great creature. Macgregor was engrossed in a novel by one of the New Scottish writers, a young man who seeks to carve out his own niche in the literary landscape. He had heard murmurs about this young man, whispers of a new type of storytelling, a blend of adventure and reflection. Yet, these whispers were drowned in a deluge of praise, a chorus of critics claiming him to be the inheritor of Sir Walter Scott's mantle, the master of romance, the sage of Scottish lore. Macgregor, however, was not so easily swayed by such hyperbole. He turned the pages swiftly, his eyes scanning the text like a hawk on the hunt, searching for any sign of truth amongst the adulation.

A sudden knock at the door broke his concentration. He sighed, putting aside the novel and squinting at the darkened window. The knock came again, more insistent this time. Macgregor opened the door to find a young woman, her face flushed with excitement and her eyes sparkling with a passion only youth can ignite. "Mister Macgregor," she began, out of breath, "I'm a reader, a passionate one, and I've just finished the latest novel by the young author. It's... it's marvelous!" she exclaimed, her voice barely holding back her enthusiasm. Macgregor raised an eyebrow, "Indeed? And pray, what other words would you use to describe it?" The young woman hesitated for a moment before continuing, "It's like... it's like Mr. Scott, but... different. It's better!" Macgregor chuckled softly, "Ah, the same old song, sung by a different bird. The New Scottish novelists, they yearn for Scott's influence, but I fear many of them only mimic his style. They forget, or perhaps they never knew, that true artistry lies not in the echoes, but in the original riffs." The young woman looked taken aback, her earlier enthusiasm faltering. "But..." she began, her voice trailing off. Macgregor leaned against the doorframe, his expression grave. "My dear young lady, the New Scottish novelists are not the heirs to Sir Walter. They are the renovators of his legacy. They take his themes, his settings, his very essence, and mold it into something new. But they must be careful. They must not let the praise turn their heads, must not let the critics skew the balance. After all, as much as Scott's influence is great, his legacy must not be burdened with inflated praise. It's like trying to feed a hungry man with a feast from the past, instead of a hearty meal of their own making." The young woman nodded, her expression thoughtful. "Thank you, Mister Macgregor," she said, a hint of resolution in her voice. "You've given me much to ponder." And with that, she turned and walked away, leaving Macgregor alone with his thoughts and his candles. The clock continued to tick, the dance of shadows on the wall a silent testament to the enduring power of a great critic.

It was not a satisfactory situation. Mr. Wilkins had given his son an education and tastes beyond his position. He could not associate with either profit or pleasure with the doctor or the brewer of Hamley; the vicar was old and deaf, the curate a raw young man, half frightened at the sound of his own voice. Then, as to matrimony--for the idea of his marriage was hardly more present in Edward's mind than in that of his father--he could scarcely fancy bringing home any one of the young ladies of Hamley to the elegant mansion, so full of suggestion and association to an educated person, so inappropriate a dwelling for an ignorant, uncouth, ill-brought-up girl. Yet Edward was fully aware, if his fond father was not, that of all the young ladies who were glad enough of him as a partner at the Hamley assemblies, there was not of them but would have considered herself affronted by an offer of marriage from an attorney, the son and grandson of attorneys. The young man had perhaps received many a slight and mortification pretty quietly during these years, which yet told upon his character in after life. Even at this very time they were having their effect. He was of too sweet a disposition to show resentment, as many men would have done. But nevertheless he took a secret pleasure in the power which his father's money gave him. He would buy an expensive horse after five minutes' conversation as to the price, about which a needy heir of one of the proud county families had been haggling for three weeks. His dogs were from the best kennels in England, no matter at what cost; his guns were the newest and most improved make; and all these were expenses on objects which were among those of daily envy to the squires and squires' sons around. They did not much care for the treasures of art, which report said were being accumulated in Mr. Wilkins's house. But they did covet the horses and hounds he possessed, and the young man knew that they coveted, and rejoiced in it.

By-and-by he formed a marriage, which went as near as marriages ever do towards pleasing everybody. He was desperately in love with Miss Lamotte, so he was delighted when she consented to be his wife. His father was delighted in his delight, and, besides, was charmed to remember that Miss Lamotte's mother had been Sir Frank Holster's younger sister, and that, although her marriage had been disowned by her family, as beneath her in rank, yet no one could efface her name out of the Baronetage, where Lettice, youngest daughter of Sir Mark Holster, born 1772, married H. Lamotte, 1799, died 1810, was duly chronicled. She had left two children, a boy and a girl, of whom their uncle, Sir Frank, took charge, as their father was worse than dead--an outlaw whose name was never mentioned. Mark Lamotte was in the army; Lettice had a dependent position in her uncle's family; not intentionally made more dependent than was rendered necessary by circumstances, but still dependent enough to grate on the feelings of a sensitive girl, whose natural susceptibilty to slights was redoubled by the constant recollection of her father's disgrace. As Mr. Wilkins well knew, Sir Frank was considerably involved; but it was with very mixed feelings that he listened to the suit which would provide his penniless niece with a comfortable, not to say luxurious, home, and with a handsome, accomplished young man of unblemished character for a husband. He said one or two bitter and insolent things to Mr. Wilkins, even while he was giving his consent to the match; that was his temper, his proud, evil temper; but he really and permanently was satisfied with the connection, though he would occasionally turn round on his nephew-in-law, and sting him with a covert insult, as to his want of birth, and the inferior position which he held, forgetting, apparently, that his own brother-in-law and Lettice's father might be at any moment brought to the bar of justice if he attempted to re-enter his native country.

As my reader has divined, Rosa was preparing the comedy of a cool reception; but looking up, she saw his pale cheek tinted with a lover's beautiful joy at the bare sight of her, and his soft eye so divine with love, that she had not the heart to chill him. She gave him her hand kindly, and smiled brightly on him instead of remonstrating. She lost nothing by it, for the very first thing he did was to excuse himself eagerly. “I am behind time: the fact is, just as I was mounting my horse, a poor man came to the gate to consult me. He had a terrible disorder I have sometimes succeeded in arresting--I attack the cause instead of the symptoms, which is the old practice--and so that detained me. You forgive me?”

“Of course. Poor man!--only you said you wanted to see papa, and he always goes out at two.”

When she had been betrayed into saying this, she drew in suddenly, and blushed with a pretty consciousness.

“Then don't let me lose another minute,” said the lover. “Have you prepared him for--for--what I am going to have the audacity to say?”

Rosa answered, with some hesitation, “I MUST have--a little. When I refused Colonel Bright--you need not devour my hand quite--he is forty.”

Her sentence ended, and away went the original topic, and grammatical sequence along with it. Christopher Staines recaptured them both. “Yes, dear, when you refused Colonel Bright”--

“Well, papa was astonished; for everybody says the colonel is a most eligible match. Don't you hate that expression? I do. Eligible!”

Christopher made due haste, and recaptured her. “Yes, love, your papa said”--

“I don't think I will tell you. He asked me was there anybody else; and of course I said 'No.'”

“Oh!”

“Oh, that is nothing; I had not time to make up my mind to tell the truth. I was taken by surprise; and you know one's first impulse is to fib--about THAT.”

“But did you really deceive him?”

“No, I blushed; and he caught me; so he said, 'Come, now, there was.'”

“And you said, 'Yes, there is,' like a brave girl as you are.”

“What, plump like that? No, I was frightened out of my wits, like a brave girl as I am not, and said I should never marry any one he could disapprove; and then--oh, then I believe I began to cry. Christopher, I'll tell you something; I find people leave off teasing you when you cry--gentlemen, I mean. Ladies go on all the more. So then dear papa kissed me, and told me I must not be imprudent, and throw myself away, that was all; and I promised him I never would. I said he would be sure to approve my choice; and he said he hoped so. And so he will.”

Dr. Staines looked thoughtful, and said he hoped so too. “But now it comes to the point of asking him for such a treasure, I feel my deficiencies.”

“Why, what deficiencies? You are young, and handsome, and good, and ever so much cleverer than other people. You have only to ask for me, and insist on having me. Come, dear, go and get it over.” She added, mighty coolly, “There is nothing so DREADFUL as suspense.”

“I'll go this minute,” said he, and took a step towards the door; but he turned, and in a moment was at her knees. He took both her hands in his, and pressed them to his beating bosom, while his beautiful eyes poured love into hers point-blank. “May I tell him you love me? Oh, I know you cannot love me as I love you; but I may say you love me a little, may I not?--that will go farther with him than anything else. May I, Rosa, may I?--a little?”
