His passion mastered her. She dropped her head sweetly on his shoulder, and murmured, “You know you may, my own. Who would not love you?”

As Van Bibber closed the door behind him, the sound echoed through the empty hallway, a solemn punctuation mark to the tense exchange that had just transpired in Mr. Caruthers' office. Still under the weight of the heavy conversation, Van Bibber descended the stairs, each step a deliberate echo of the turbulent emotions churning within him.

He had entered Mr. Caruthers' office with the intention of a friendly visit, a light-hearted respite from the monotonous routine of his day. Little did he anticipate the whirlwind of emotions he would encounter, the glimpse into a life so vastly different from his own. Mr. Caruthers' tale had laid bare a vulnerability he rarely witnessed in the upper echelons of society, a raw honesty that simultaneously repelled and attracted.

Emerging onto the bustling street, Van Bibber felt a disorientation, as if the world had shifted on its axis while he was trapped in the confines of Mr. Caruthers' office. The carefree banter of the passersby, the clatter of carriages, the rhythmic cries of the vendors, all seemed incongruous with the weight of the story he carried within him.

He hailed a hansom cab, sinking into the plush leather seat with a sigh. The rhythmic clip-clop of the horse's hooves against the cobblestones became a lullaby, lulling his mind into a state of introspection. Mr. Caruthers' words echoed in his ears, painting vivid pictures of a life lived in defiance of societal norms, a life marked by both defiance and despair.

The image of Mrs. Caruthers, a woman thrust into a world she didn't quite understand, haunted him. He imagined her uncertainty, her vulnerability, her longing for acceptance. He saw her not as a fallen woman, but as a human being caught in the crossfire of societal judgment.

Van Bibber, a man of privilege and conformity, found himself grappling with the complexities of Mr. Caruthers' situation. He questioned his own prejudices, his ingrained assumptions about the world. Could he, in Mr. Caruthers' shoes, have stood against the tide of disapproval, have fought for his love with such unwavering conviction?

The cab came to a halt in front of his apartment building, jolting him back to the present. He stepped out, the weight of the conversation still clinging to him like a shadow. As he ascended the stairs to his apartment, he knew that this encounter had irrevocably altered him. He had glimpsed a world beyond the gilded cage of his own existence, a world where love and defiance danced a precarious waltz in the face of societal judgment.

He reached his apartment, the familiar surroundings offering a semblance of comfort. Yet, the echoes of Mr. Caruthers' story lingered, a persistent reminder of the human drama that unfolded beyond the confines of his privileged life. He knew that he could not simply dismiss it, could not retreat into the comfortable oblivion of his routine. He had to find a way to reconcile this newfound understanding with his own comfortable existence.

Sleep eluded him that night. He tossed and turned, the images of Mr. and Mrs. Caruthers playing out in his mind's eye. He saw their struggles, their triumphs, their ultimate defeat. He saw a reflection of his own potential for both empathy and judgment.

As the first rays of dawn crept through the window, Van Bibber made a decision. He would not allow this encounter to fade into a distant memory. He would use it as a catalyst for change, a lens through which to view the world with newfound compassion and understanding. He would seek out those who lived on the fringes of society, those whose stories were rarely heard, whose struggles were often ignored. He would become a voice for the voiceless, a champion for the marginalized.

With a newfound purpose, Van Bibber rose from his bed, his heart filled with a mixture of trepidation and anticipation. He knew the path ahead would not be easy, but he was determined to walk it, to use his voice and his privilege to make a difference in the world. The encounter with Mr. Caruthers had opened his eyes, and he would not let them close again. He would embrace the complexities of human experience, the beauty and the ugliness, the light and the darkness. He would become a witness to the world, a storyteller for the forgotten, a champion for the downtrodden.

The sun rose higher in the sky, casting a golden glow upon the city below. Van Bibber stood at his window, a new chapter unfolding before him, a chapter filled with both promise and uncertainty. He took a deep breath, the air crisp and invigorating, and stepped out into the world, ready to embrace the challenges and opportunities that lay ahead. His journey had just begun.

It was on a gilded autumn afternoon that I first began to feel the inexorable pull of destiny, a summons from that nebulous border between memory and regret. The mandated passage of time had rendered the agony of my trial ever more profound, while the echoes of Beljames’s dying confession reverberated ceaselessly in the recesses of my troubled mind.

In those long months since that fateful encounter, when the venerable landlady had once again advanced with grim tidings, I had found no relief from the oppressive shadows of my past—a spectre of guilt compounded by misfortune, debt, and the daunting expression of law. The cursed cipher note, entrusted to my care in dire circumstances, now lay unopened in a battered drawer as if to mock my inaction.

My dearest Mrs. Westerfield, whose steadfast heart had borne the burden of my many missteps, had become increasingly absorbed in meditations both sombre and profound. I observed, with the quiet anguish of one condemned by time itself, that her grief had delicately mingled with a resolute determination to set right the wrongs of our shared history.

I remember, with a visceral chill, the moment when Beljames—languishing on his deathbed—revealed his misdeeds: his whispered confession of altering a ship’s course and expropriating a glittering hoard of diamonds. He thrust into my trembling hand not only the fateful cipher but also the heavy knowledge that his illicit act might indeed serve to exonerate me, if only its secrets could be laid bare.

This mysterious note, inscribed in a code known only to a few, held the promise of redemption and the threat of further peril. Its cryptic lines seemed to embody both the hope of vindication and a curse upon those who might dare unravel its mysteries. Every time I beheld it under the flickering light of a wan candle, I was reminded of my desperate and uncertain course.

Several learned men, well versed in the arcane study of cryptography, had been summoned to decipher this enigma; yet, despite their most earnest efforts and the application of modern science, the puzzle remained obstinately opaque. Their silence then, as now, served only to deepen the chasm of despair into which I had been forced to plummet.

The matter was rendered yet more hopeless by the unyielding lattice of legal strictures—a labyrinth of statutes and decrees which forbade me to utilize Beljames’s confession as any form of evidence to clear my sullied name. Thus, the dead man’s secrets were thieved not only from the law but from the reach of justice itself, leaving me entangled in the web of my own past misdeeds.

Every night I found myself haunted by visions of courtrooms and guillotined men, recalling with a paralyzing clarity the burden of errors long past and debts unpaid. I pleaded inwardly for a miracle, for the recovery of those stolen diamonds that might yet prove my innocence and finally dispel the stain upon my reputation.

In a fevered delirium born of despair and solitude, I had once entreated that the precious stones be found, to serve as the final arbiter of my redemption and to clear away the tarnish of my former life. Yet fate had dictated that my entreaties should fall on deaf ears even as the law itself was held in thrall to responsibilities beyond a single man’s power.

Now, as one year since that infamous trial had drawn to a close, a subtle transformation had taken place in the nature of our sorrow. Mrs. Westerfield, having endured an ordeal not solely of heart but of spirit, now regarded the cipher note with an enigmatic calm. It lay, almost as if by fate, at her side—a silent witness to our shared tribulations.

In the early hours of a wintry morning, her countenance became imbued with an uncanny resolve. Within the quiet confines of our modest chamber, her eyes shimmered with a light that betrayed neither mourning nor despair, but rather a measured determination to use the secrets held within the cryptic inscription for a noble purpose.

Ever since I had first received the note, I had felt that it carried within it not merely the seeds of my restoration, but the latent promise of justice—a promise that now, under my dear wife’s quiet stewardship, might yet be fulfilled. Her methodical perusal of its arcane lines seemed to forge a fragile bridge between our troubled past and a future unburdened by the stain of legal iniquity.

I cannot help but confess that, in observing this transformation, I have experienced a tentative reprieve from the perpetual anxiety that once gripped my soul. The prospect that these very diamonds might, in time, restore not only my honor but also the sanctity of our family name now appears less a flight of fancy than a tangible hope.

Thus, as the pale light of dawn ushered in yet another day, I remained seated in quiet contemplation, awaiting the moment when Mrs. Westerfield shall declare that she has unraveled the secrets of that dark cipher. In that delicate balance between redemption and perdition, there resides, for us, the final measure of our salvation.

Tom Brady's Seven Super Bowl Wins: An Unparalleled Statistical Marvel

In the realm of professional sports, few accomplishments resonate as powerfully as Tom Brady’s remarkable feat of winning seven Super Bowl championships. Drafted as the 199th overall pick in the 2000 NFL Draft, Brady’s journey from near obscurity to football immortality is not just a tale of determination, but also a staggering testament to the rarity of such an achievement in the National Football League (NFL).

The overarching narrative surrounding Brady’s career raises an intriguing question: what are the actual chances of a player winning seven or more Super Bowls? Statistically, the odds can be illustrated in dramatic fashion, likened to winning the Powerball jackpot after purchasing five or six tickets—a daunting pipeline of probability that few would be willing to engage in.

According to the Pro Football Reference database, the observed probability of a player achieving such an unprecedented milestone is roughly 1 in 26,683. “That’s a jaw-dropping figure that underscores just how special Brady’s success really is,” remarked Vince Jansen, a self-proclaimed stats whiz, who emphasizes the rarity of superlative athletic performances.

Digging deeper, the theoretical probability of a random player selected from the 2000 NFL Draft winning at least seven Super Bowls is estimated at a staggering 1 in 51.8 million. “This level of achievement transcends chance; it's a combination of unparalleled skill, strategic gameplay, and perhaps an element of the unpredictable,” stated Thomas Severini, a statistics professor at Northwestern University.

As one peels back layers of Brady’s success, it becomes evident that the complexity and improbability of his accomplishments invite scrutiny from experts in mathematical modeling. “You have to consider not only the skill involved but also the structure of the NFL, team dynamics, and the fluctuation of player performance across seasons,” remarked Mark Glickman, a statistics professor at Harvard. “Brady's consistency over two decades makes his seven Super Bowls not just impressive, but statistically revolutionary.”

Even for an athlete guaranteed a 21-year career, the odds of achieving seven Super Bowl victories rests at 1 in 435,119. “These figures indicate that even with access to a long career, it’s still a rarity to achieve such sustained excellence over time,” Glickman proclaimed, echoing a sentiment that resonates deeply within statistical circles.

When narrowing the focus strictly to quarterbacks—a role that typically holds a stronger correlation with winning titles—the probabilities improve marginally. “For quarterbacks alone, the likelihood of claiming seven or more championships drops to 1 in 12.8 million,” noted Abraham Wyner, a stats professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business. “However, even with a more manageable probability, the odds remain daunting.”

Analysts must tread cautiously, as fundamental assumptions in these calculations can necessitate adjustments. While a player’s odds of clinching a Super Bowl title in any given season are typically suggested as 1 in 32—reflecting the league’s team structure—this figure may not accurately reflect team strength variations or the impact of injuries over a season.

Considering the future, estimations on whether any player might reach or surpass Brady’s record by the year 2075 are sobering. Current predictions land the likelihood at a mere 0.01%. “That means the chances are exceedingly thin, essentially disqualifying the average player. Tom Brady’s record may stand unchallenged for generations,” Severini elaborated.

As Brady’s legacy continues to evolve, his seven championships are regularly placed among the most improbable feats in sports history. “In the grander scheme of athletic performance, it’s right up there with the most extraordinary achievements we’ve seen,” Wyner remarked. “It’s hard to envision another player doing what he’s done.”

With each Super Bowl victory illuminating his unmatched prowess, Brady prompts new levels of fandom and analysis. His career, characterized by resilience, hard work, and continued evolution, serves as both motivation and a quantitative case study.

Embracing the intricacies of statistical analysis, Brady’s story is one that challenges conventional understanding of talent in sports. “He has managed to remain relevant and perform at elite levels well into the late phase of what is traditionally considered a quarterback's prime. That's something the numbers just aren't prepared for,” Jansen shared.

The triumphs of Tom Brady not only alter our perspectives on sporting excellence but also create a narrative rich with statistics, dreams, and probabilities. As fans and statisticians alike revel in his incredible accomplishments, it becomes increasingly clear that Brady is not just a player—he is a phenomenon that will remain etched in history.

Brady’s success serves as a reminder that within the world of sports, extraordinary feats can emerge from the most improbable circumstances. It’s a narrative adorned with unyielding statistics, delivering a happiness only witnessed by those fortunate enough to watch a player who rewrote the very rules of possibility.

Tom Brady, with his seven Super Bowl victories, has firmly positioned himself not only as a dominant athlete but also a statistical marvel—an icon of what happens when tremendous skill marries the rarest of opportunities. His legacy, bolstered by impossibly high achievements, promises to intrigue both analysts and casual fans for many years to come.

Born in the north of Ireland, the child of a Scottish-Ulster mother and a Connaught father, she had ingeniously contrived to combine in her own person the vices of two distinct races, and exclude the virtues of both.

Her accent was the most fearful which could be imagined. She had the brogue of the West grafted on the accent of the North. And yet there was a variety about her even in this respect. One never could tell, from visit to visit, whether she proposed to pronounce "written" as "wrutten" or "wretten";[Footnote: The wife of a celebrated Indian officer stated that she once, in the north of Ireland, heard Job's utterance thus rendered--"Oh! that my words were wrutten, that they were prented in a buke."] whether she would elect to style her parents, to whom she made frequent reference, her "pawpaw and mawmaw," or her "pepai and memai."

It all depended with whom Miss Blake had lately been most intimate. If she had been "hand and glove" with a "nob" from her own country--she was in no way reticent about thus styling her grander acquaintances, only she wrote the word "knob"--who thought to conceal his nationality by "awing" and "hawing," she spoke about people being "morried" and wearing "sockcloth and oshes." If, on the contrary, she had been thrown into the society of a lady who so far honoured England as to talk as some people do in England, we had every A turned into E, and every U into O, while she minced her words as if she had been saying "niminy piminy" since she first began to talk, and honestly believed no human being could ever have told she had been born west of St. George's Channel.

But not merely in accent did Miss Blake evidence the fact that her birth had been the result of an injudicious cross; the more one knew of her, the more clearly one saw the wrong points she threw out.

Extravagant to a fault, like her Connaught father, she was in no respect generous, either from impulse or calculation.

Mean about minor details, a turn of character probably inherited from the Ulster mother, she was utterly destitute of that careful and honest economy which is an admirable trait in the natives of the north of Ireland, and which enables them so frequently, after being strictly just, to be much more than liberal.

Honest, Miss Blake was not--or, for that matter, honourable either. Her indebtedness to our firm could not be considered other than a matter of honour, and yet she never dreamt of paying her debt to Mr. Craven.

Indeed, to do Miss Blake strict justice, she never thought of paying the debts she owed to anyone, unless she was obliged to do so.

Nowadays, I fear it would fare hard with her were she to try her old tactics with the British tradesman; but, in the time of which I am writing, co-operative societies were not, and then the British tradesman had no objection, I fancy, to be gulled.

Perhaps, like the lawyer and the unprofitable client, he set-off being gulled on one side his ledger against being fleeced on the other.

Be this as it may, we were always compounding some liability for Miss Blake, as well as letting her house and fighting with the tenants.

At first, as I have said, we found Miss Blake an awful bore, but we generally ended by deciding we could better spare a better man. Indeed, the months when she did not come to our office seemed to want flavour.

Of gratitude--popularly supposed to be essentially characteristic of the Irish--Miss Blake was utterly destitute. I never did know--I have never known since, so ungrateful a woman.

He sat on the veranda of his friend’s villa, the warm Mediterranean breeze caressing his face. The air was filled with the scent of orange blossoms and the distant hum of cicadas. Below him, the blue expanse of the bay shimmered under the midday sun, while the distant mountains, cloaked in a haze of purple and gold, seemed to touch the heavens. Yet, amidst this idyllic scene, a shadow lingered in his heart—a shadow cast by memories of another world, far removed from the Riviera’s charms.

It was the memory of her, his wife, that troubled him. She sat now in their London drawing-room, the dim light of a London winter filtering through the fog-veiled windows. Bloomsbury was a world away from this paradise, a place of gray skies and damp streets, where the fog crept into the bones as insidiously as the smoke from the city’s chimneys. He could see her now, by the fire, the light from the flames casting long shadows across her face as she read by the hearth. Her presence in that gloomy room seemed both solitary and serene, a contrast to the lively chatter and laughter that surrounded him here.

He had received her letter that morning, a missive that had found its way across the miles with the unwavering determination of love. Her words, though simple, were filled with a warmth that no London winter could diminish. She spoke of the quiet joys of their home, of Bertie’s latest escapades, and of the small comforts that filled their days. Yet, as he read, he felt a pang of guilt, for he knew that this life she described was one she had chosen for him, not for herself. She remained in Bloomsbury, content in her role as wife and mother, while he wandered the world, seeking pleasure and distraction in the company of others.

The company of others—that was what had led him here. He was not alone in the villa; the house was filled with the laughter and conversation of friends, their voices carrying the carefree abandon of those who had little to trouble them. They spoke of politics, art, and the latest fashions, their talk filled with the facile charm that came so easily to them. Yet, amidst their lively banter, he found himself growing more isolated, for he knew that his wife was not among them. She was not wanted here, he told himself, for her quiet nature and plain ways did not suit the vibrant energy of this place. But was that truly the case, or was it simply that her presence was deemed less desirable than the sparkling wit of Society’s daughters?

He looked down at the letter again, the ink still fresh upon the page. Her words were those of a woman who had found contentment in the simplicity of her life, yet he could not help but wonder if she sometimes longed for the world he inhabited. Had he ever truly considered her desires, or had he assumed that her sacrifices were made solely for his benefit? The thought pierced him like a dagger, for he realized that he had come to take her presence for granted, her strength and resilience overlooked in favor of the fleeting fascinations of Society.

As the afternoon sun dipped lower in the sky, casting long shadows across the veranda, he found himself reflecting on their marriage. They had been happy once, their love a quiet, steady flame that had burned brightly through the years. Yet, as the years had passed, he had found himself drawn more and more to the distractions of Society, to the allure of conversation that sparkled like diamonds, and to the admiration of those who found him charming and witty. His wife, on the other hand, had remained content in her role, her presence a constant source of comfort and stability in his life. But had he, in his pursuit of pleasure, failed to appreciate the depth of her character, the strength of her spirit?

The evening brought with it a cool breeze, carrying the scent of salt and the distant cries of fishermen returning to port. He sat alone, the letter still clutched in his hand, his thoughts turning to the life he had left behind. In London, the fog would be thickening now, the gas lamps flickering to life in the dim streets. His wife would be preparing for bed, the fire dying in the grate as she settled into the quiet solitude of her room. Yet, even in that solitude, she found peace, her mind occupied with thoughts of their son, of their home, and of him. He had always marveled at her ability to find joy in the simplest of things, her contentment never dependent on the trappings of Society or the approving glances of others.

As the stars began to appear in the darkening sky, he felt a deep sense of regret settle over him. He had allowed himself to be swayed by the opinions of others, to measure his wife’s worth by the standards of a world that valued superficiality above substance. In doing so, he had failed to see the true depth of her character, the quiet strength that had sustained her through the years. He had come to take her for granted, her presence a comforting but unremarkable fixture in his life, until now, when the distance between them had forced him to confront the truth of what he had lost.

The thought of returning to London filled him with a strange mixture of dread and anticipation. He knew that he could not continue to live this life of endless distractions, of hollow pleasures that left him empty and unfulfilled. His wife deserved more than the occasional letter and the distant thoughts of a man who had forgotten the true importance of his home. She deserved to be cherished, to be appreciated for the remarkable woman she was, and to share in the joys of a life that had been too long defined by absence and neglect.

As the night deepened, he made a decision. He would return to London, to the foggy streets and the dimly lit rooms, to the woman who had always been his true companion. He would seek to rebuild the connection that had been allowed to fade, to rediscover the love that had once been the foundation of their marriage. The Riviera and its distractions would have to wait, for he had realized that the greatest treasure of his life was not to be found in the glittering society of the South, but in the quiet, enduring love of the woman who had always been his true home.

"I wonder how he likes the dusty days, and the crowded rooms, the classical music, and high-art exhibitions?" thought Vixen savagely. "I wonder how he likes being led about like a Pomeranian terrier? I don't think I could endure it if I were a man. But I suppose when one is in love----"

And then Vixen thought of their last talk together, and how little of the lover's enthusiasm there was in Roderick's mention of his cousin.

"In the bottom of my heart I know that he is going to marry her for the sake of her estate, or because his mother wished it and urged it, and he was too weak-minded to go on saying No. I would not say it for the world, or let anyone else say it in my hearing, but, in my heart of hearts, I know he does not love her."

And then, after a thoughtful silence, she cried to the mute unresponsive woods:

"Oh, it is wicked, abominable, mad, to marry without love!"

The woods spoke to her of Roderick Vawdrey. How often she had ridden by his side beneath these spreading beech-boughs, dipping her childish head, just as she dipped it to-day, under the low branches, steering her pony carefully between the prickly holly-bushes, plunging deep into the hollows where the dry leaves crackled under his hoofs.

"I fancied Rorie and I were to spend our lives together--somehow," she said to herself. "It seems very strange for us to be quite parted."

She saw Mr. Vawdrey's name in the fashionable newspapers, in the lists of guests at dinners and drums. London life suited him very well, no doubt. She heard that he was a member of the Four-in-hand Club, and turned out in splendid style at Hyde Park Corner. There was no talk yet of his going into Parliament. That was an affair of the future.

Since that evening on which Mrs. Tempest announced her intention of taking a second husband, Violet and Captain Winstanley had only met in the presence of other people. The Captain had tried to infuse a certain fatherly familiarity into his manner; but Vixen had met every attempt at friendliness with a sullen disdain, which kept even Captain Winstanley at arm's length.

"We shall understand each other better by-and-by," he said to himself, galled by this coldness. "It would be a pity to disturb these halcyon days by anything in the way of a scene. I shall know how to manage Miss Tempest--afterwards."

He spoke of her, and to her, always as Miss Tempest. He had never called her Violet since that night in the Pavilion garden.

These days before her wedding were indeed a halcyon season for Mrs. Tempest. She existed in an atmosphere of millinery and pretty speeches. Her attention was called away from a ribbon by the sweet distraction of a compliment, and oscillated between tender whispers and honiton lace. Conrad Winstanley was a delightful lover. His enemies would have said that he had done the same kind of thing so often, that it would have been strange if he had not done it well. His was assuredly no 'prentice hand in the art. Poor Mrs. Tempest lived in a state of mild intoxication, as dreamily delicious as the effects of opium. She was enchanted with her lover, and still better pleased with herself. At nine-and-thirty it was very sweet to find herself exercising so potent an influence over the Captain's strong nature. She could not help comparing herself to Cleopatra, and her lover to Antony. If he had not thrown away a world for her sake, he was at least ready to abandon the busy career which a man loves, and to devote his future existence to rural domesticity. He confessed that he had been hardened by much contact with the world, that he did not love now for the first time; but he told his betrothed that her influence had awakened feelings which had never before been called into life, that this love which he felt for her was to all intents and purposes a first love, the first pure and perfect affection that had subjugated and elevated his soul.

In the pleasant drawing-room of the milliner's shop, sunlight filtered through lace curtains, casting dappled shadows on the polished floor. Above the counter, "ROBINSON & SONS - Milliners and Founders of Gentlemanly Occasions" adorned the glass window, a relic of a bygone era. Here, Tom Robinson stood, his broad shoulders hunched over ledgers, his brow furrowed in thought. The once esteemed Cambridge graduate now found solace in the humblest of tasks.

The polite chiming of the bell overhead announced the entrance of Miss Dorothea Sterling, a woman of high spirits and unwavering opinions. She approached the counter, her green eyes narrowing as she surveyed Tom, still bent over his records. "Tom," she greeted, her voice a blend of icy frost and forced honey. "I see you remain immersed in your... duties. How very heartening."

Tom looked up, his expression softening at the sight of her. "Dora, it's good to see you. Have you come to browse? We've received some new bonnets from Paris."

Dora scoffed, her lips curling in disdain. "hardly, Tom. I'd rather wade through a bog than enter your shop. It's beneath my dignity."

Tom's smile faded, but he kept his voice steady. "I'm afraid business is business, Dora. And it seems to be in need of my attention, now more than ever."

On the street, a group of young men, including Cyril Carey and Ned Hewett, huddled together, their laughter echoing through the quiet square. Among them was Charles Millar, his eyes scanning the milliner's shop with a morbid fascination. He turned to his friends, his voice barely audible. "That's how Tom chooses to spend his days now? Behind the counter in a shop? It's a disgrace."

"Indeed," Ned concurred, "But old Millerton's shop has been in ruins for years. Someone had to take up the reins."

"But Tom," Cyril interjected, his tone earnest, "He could have pursued a proper career. He was well-educated, like us. Yet, here he is, like a common tradesman."

Charles sneered. "Exactly. And we all know what common tradesmen are like. They're... crude, uncultured."

Dora, overhearing the exchange, met Charles' gaze with a challenge. "You're too kind, Charles. Tom's not merely crude; he's beneath me."

Tom, hearing Dora's dismissal, stepped out from behind the counter, his jaw set. "Dora, will you please not speak of me that way? I value your friendship."

Dora's eyes flashed. "Your friendship? Tom, how can we maintain such a thing when you've given up on your prospects? You're a laughing stock in town now."

Tom sighed, running a hand through his hair. "I'm sorry, Dora. I only wish to maintain my family's legacy. That's all."

In the back of the shop, Mrs. Robinson, Tom's mother, stood silently, her hands steepled against her chest. She watched this spectacle, her eyes reflecting a mix of pride and worry. Her son's choices, once a source of pride, now caused her sleepless nights.

Meanwhile, the younger men of Redcross continued their deliberations, their voices growing louder. "We should speak to him, make him see sense," Charles declared.

Cyril shook his head. "And cause a scene? No, let him have his delusions. Besides, we have our own battles. The shop isn't the only business in trouble."

Ned nodded in agreement. "Aye, the Rectory's funds are dwindling too. We must focus on that."

As the men dispersed, Tom stepped back inside his shop, a grim determination in his eyes. He knew he faced an uphill battle, not just against the disapproving whispers, but also against the shrinking profits, the dwindling respect, and the relentless judgment of his peers. But he was not one to falter. He was Tom Robinson, and he would stand by his choices, no matter the adversity.

Frustration Mounts as Louisiana Grapples with Power Outages Post-Ida

LaPLACE, La. – Tens of thousands of Louisiana residents remain in the dark as the state continues to grapple with the aftermath of Hurricane Ida, which hit the state over a week ago. More than nine days after the devastating storm, power restoration efforts continue, with a glaring disparity in progress between New Orleans and other heavily affected communities.

Frustration has been mounting among residents who feel neglected in the state's restoration priorities. "It seems like some areas are getting power back quickly while others are being left behind," said State Rep. Tanner Magee, expressing the concerns of residents who are fed up with the delays in returning to normal life.

Entergy Louisiana, the state's largest electric utility, has been striving to speed up the restoration process. "While we are making significant progress, it's likely some areas will not have power until the end of September," said Phillip May, Entergy Louisiana President and CEO. More than 159,000 household applications for disaster assistance have been approved by FEMA, highlighting the widespread need for support across the state.

In a tragic development, the state has revoked the licenses of seven nursing homes after seven residents died in post-Ida conditions. Warner Thomas, President and CEO of Ochsner Health, emphasized the strain on healthcare facilities, noting how Ochsner Health's two hospitals in the hardest-hit parishes are operating emergency rooms but are not fully open due to the extensive damage. "We've faced enormous challenges in keeping our facilities operational in these conditions," Thomas said.

In an effort to aid recovery efforts, the Carnival Glory has docked in New Orleans to temporarily house first responders assisting with the relief efforts. The state, however, is struggling with widespread fuel shortages, water service intermittency, and countless homes left uninhabitable by the storm.

Many residents are still seeking shelter, with about 3,200 people staying in mass shelters and around 25,000 in FEMA hotel rooms for transitional accommodation. "It’s difficult not knowing when we’ll be able to go back to living safely at home," said Kim Bass, a resident of St. John the Baptist Parish. According to the latest reports, the death toll from Ida has risen to 15 in Louisiana, with additional fatalities attributed to storm-related injuries and a lack of oxygen during power outages.

For Michael Lathers, a resident of LaPlace, coping with the slow pace of recovery adds to the burden. "The waiting game feels endless," he remarked. The road to recovery appears lengthy as the community braves the hardships left in Ida’s wake, yearning for a semblance of normalcy.

The state and utility companies are called to address the immediate needs of all affected regions equitably while also planning for long-term resilience in the face of future storms. For now, the priority remains restoring power and essential services to the hundreds of thousands still waiting for relief.

Vaccine Hesitancy Among Parents: A Closer Look at the Dividing Lines

Despite the widespread availability of COVID-19 vaccines for children and teenagers, a noticeable division in vaccination rates and perspectives has emerged among parents in the United States. Surveys reveal a significant portion of parents remain hesitant or outright opposed to vaccinating their children against COVID-19, highlighting the challenge public health officials face in bolstering vaccine uptake amongst the younger population.

The vaccination rates among teenagers, specifically within the 12-17 age group, have observed a standstill, with approximately half of the parents reporting their teen has been vaccinated. The scenario appears even more pronounced in children aged 5 to 11, where only about 16% of parents report their child has received the vaccine. An additional 13% of these parents claim they intend to vaccinate their child 'right away,' thus indicating a slow but hopeful inclination towards higher vaccination rates in the near future. However, a significant hurdle remains as three in ten parents of both teens and younger children firmly state they will 'definitely not' vaccinate their children against COVID-19.

Central to the hesitancy observed among parents are concerns surrounding the safety and potential side effects of the COVID-19 vaccines in children. These apprehensions have understandably caused a pause among parents, pondering whether the benefits of vaccination outweigh the risks. Additionally, access barriers to vaccination have been more prominently voiced by Hispanic, Black, and lower-income parents, underscoring the disparities in vaccine accessibility and the additional hurdles marginalized communities face in protecting their children from COVID-19.

Interestingly, pediatricians have emerged as the most trusted source of information on COVID-19 vaccines for many parents, though less than half of the surveyed parents have had discussions about COVID-19 vaccinations with their child's healthcare provider. Schools have also played a pivotal role in vaccination efforts, with nearly half of the parents indicating that their child's school provided information or encouraged COVID-19 vaccination. As it turns out, encouragement from schools correlates with a higher likelihood of children being vaccinated, underscoring the influence of educational institutions in public health initiatives.

However, when it comes to mandating COVID-19 vaccines for eligible students, a majority of parents of 5-17 year-olds express opposition, favoring personal choice over collective responsibility. This sentiment reflects a broader societal debate over vaccine mandates and individual freedoms, which has intensified during the pandemic.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on families has been profound, with parents reporting negative effects on their mental health, financial stability, and children's education. These challenges have disproportionately impacted lower-income and minority groups, further exacerbating existing inequalities and underscoring the widespread consequences of the pandemic beyond public health.

As America navigates the next phases of the pandemic, the divide in parental perspectives on vaccinating children presents a multifaceted challenge. Addressing concerns around vaccine safety, ensuring equitable access, and fostering trust in public health guidelines will be critical in achieving higher vaccination rates and protecting communities against COVID-19.

John Barty drew deeply upon his pipe, the pungent smoke curling about his grizzled face in a most distracting fashion. He regarded his son, Barnaby, with eyes narrowed almost to slits, as if trying to pierce the very soul of him.

"Seven hundred thousand pounds, ye say?" he rumbled at length, the words seeming to rumble up from some deep cavern within his chest.

Barnaby, standing straighter now, though still a flicker of uncertainty danced in his gaze, inclined his head. "Aye, Father. Uncle Thomas… he left it all to me."

Natty Bell, who had been shifting from one foot to the other like a restless colt, suddenly smacked his thigh with a resounding thwack.

"Why, blast me if the lad ain't set for life!" he exclaimed, his eyes wide with a mixture of awe and disbelief. "Seven hundred thousand! Enough to buy half of Kent, I reckon!"

John Barty, however, remained unimpressed. He took another long pull on his pipe, the bowl glowing a fierce red in the dim light of the cottage.

"And what, pray tell," he said, his voice thick with suspicion, "do ye intend to do with all this… this coin?"

Barnaby cleared his throat, his gaze drifting towards the worn, wooden floor. "I… I wish to travel, Father. To see the world, perhaps. To learn… to improve myself."

John Barty snorted, a sound like the bellows of a forge. "Improve yourself? Ye're already stronger than any man in these parts! What more improvement do ye need?"

Natty Bell, eager to avert a brewing argument, chimed in. "Why, John, a bit of travel never hurt nobody! Broadens the mind, it does!"

John Barty shot him a withering glance. "Broadens the pockets of those what prey on innocents, more like. London is a den of vipers, Barnaby. Ye'll be fleeced before ye can say Jack Robinson."

Barnaby, however, stood his ground. "I shall be careful, Father. I am not a fool."

John Barty puffed furiously on his pipe, his silence heavy with disapproval. He knew his son. He knew the stubborn streak that ran through him, as deep and unyielding as the granite hills of their homeland.

At length, he spoke, his voice softer now, tinged with a reluctant resignation. "And what of… what of the fighting, Barnaby? Will ye abandon the ring?"

Barnaby hesitated, a shadow of regret passing over his face. "I… I do not know, Father. I have not yet decided."

Natty Bell, ever the optimist, clapped Barnaby on the back. "Why, lad, ye can do both! Be a gentleman by day, and a bruiser by night! A regular Corinthian, ye'll be!"

John Barty glared at Natty, his eyes flashing with a spark of the old fire. "A Corinthian, is it? More like a fool! A fancy waistcoat and a silver-handled cane won't save him from a broken nose."

Barnaby sighed, running a hand through his thick, dark hair. "I understand your concerns, Father. But I must follow my own path. I must see what lies beyond these hills."

John Barty fell silent again, his gaze fixed on the swirling smoke rising from his pipe. He knew he could not stop his son. Barnaby had a will of his own, and a fortune besides.

He only hoped that the world would treat him kindly, that it would not break the spirit of the boy he had raised. He finished his pipe, and a long silence descended upon the small cottage.

Among the new arrivals, of whom thousands flocked into the township every day, were some dozen men and women, who came in dusty and weary with the toils of the road. They had travelled more than a hundred and fifty miles, being attracted to Silver Creek township by the news of its wonderful prosperity. They were a common-enough troop in outward appearance, and did not look like traders or gold-miners. They had with them a dray drawn by one horse--a poor weak-kneed creature, to whom existence seemed to be a burden as he toiled painfully along with his load behind him. What this load was could not be seen, for the dray had a tarpaulin over it. Upon the tarpaulin were seated three women. The first who calls for notice by virtue of her position was a stately person, probably about thirty-five years of age; her complexion was dark, and in her face was an expression, which might be said to be stamped upon it, and which represented all the tragic passions in little; she bore herself loftily in more senses than one. Her mind was a storehouse, filled with tragedy queens, intermixed with heroines of tenderer sentiment--which latter, however, were somewhat out of place; but you would have roused her to great indignation had you said so in her hearing. The second, about twenty-three years of age, was a nice-looking saucy widow, with a pretty baby in her arms. The third was a beautiful girl, of some eighteen or nineteen summers. The men, who were all much sunburnt, walked along by the side and in the rear of the dray, and when they entered High Street, peered curiously about them, and then at each other, with an air of "This will do." The eyes of one of the party, the eldest, a man of over sixty years of age, were expressive of something more than curiosity: anxiety was plainly there, but presently this vanished, and bright twinkles took their place. He rubbed his hands joyously, and smiled upon one and another.

"It looks well," he said.

He was the chief of the party, which was nothing less than a company of actors and actresses come to open the first theatre at Silver Creek. Before they started from Melbourne, they had formed themselves into a joint stock company, and agreed to divide profits in proportion to their abilities. There were twelve in the party, not reckoning the baby, and the number of shares were thirty-six. These, after much anxious discussion and deliberation, and some display of the peacock's chief attribute, were distributed as follows:--

Shares. 1. Tragedian, light comedian, and stage-manager, playing the lead in everything. 4½ 2. Heavy man. 3 3. First old man. 2½ 4. Second old man. 1½ 5. First low comedy. 3 6. Second low comedy. 2 7. Walking gentleman and treasurer. 3 8. Supernumerary. 1 9. Juvenile lead and general utility, scene painter, acting-manager, and general director. 4½ 10. Leading lady. 4½ 11. First old woman. 3 (There was no second.) 12. Chambermaid (who could sing and dance). 2½

These proportions being settled, they jogged along comfortably, dreaming of full purses; but on the second day the First Old Man drew attention to the circumstance that although there were thirty-six shares in the company, only thirty-five had been allotted. The Walking Gentleman, who, as treasurer, was looked upon as the arithmetician of the company, and was, therefore, the great authority in figures, instantly began to reckon up, for the fifty-seventh time, and made the number of shares thirty-seven: he tried again and made them thirty-four; tried again, and made them thirty-eight. Then, in desperation, he said that the First Old Man had "discovered a mare's nest," and that the figures were right--thirty-six shares in the company, and thirty-six allotted. Hurt in a tender point, the First Old Man began again to pencil and reckon, and after achieving a dozen different results, came back to his original discovery, and stuck to his guns like a man. Thereupon high words ensued between the Walking Gentleman and the First Old Man, and the matter was referred to the arbitration of the other ten, who immediately set to work to settle the dispute. The results they produced were extraordinary, varying from seventeen to fifty-two, the highest and the lowest totals being accomplished by the First Old Woman (who, to prove the general fitness of things, should have been the First Old Man's wife, but in proof of the general unfitness of things, wasn't) and the singing and dancing Chambermaid.

The air in Crimsworth Hall, though thick with the scent of beeswax and old damask, did little to sweeten my humor. Indeed, the very grandeur of the place, its silent testament to generations of Crimsworths who had lived and died within its stone embrace, seemed only to amplify the gnawing discontent that had taken root in my breast. I had hoped, upon discovering those portraits of my parents, to feel a sense of belonging, a connection to this place that was, by right of birth, partially mine. Instead, I felt like an interloper, a distant cousin who had arrived uninvited to a family gathering, dressed in clothes too plain and bearing gifts too meager.

My aunt, Miss Crimsworth, remained an enigma. She treated me with a politeness so studied, so meticulously measured, that it felt more like a performance than genuine affection. Her questions were precise and carefully chosen, her answers, when she deigned to offer them, were similarly guarded. I suspected she knew far more about my circumstances, about my past, than she let on, and this suspicion only deepened the sense of unease that pervaded my days. The servants, too, were a source of perpetual observation, their glances darting and furtive, their whispers hushed and conspiratorial. I was, without a doubt, an object of intense scrutiny, a puzzle they were all attempting to solve.

Yesterday, I had attempted to break through the icy reserve that surrounded my aunt, to engage her in a more personal conversation. I had spoken of my father, of his kindness and his untimely death, hoping to evoke some shared memory, some flicker of familial warmth. But her response was chillingly detached. She acknowledged my father’s existence, of course, but spoke of him as one might speak of a distant acquaintance, with a cool, impersonal objectivity that bordered on indifference. I was left with the distinct impression that she regarded my father’s choice to marry outside the Crimsworth family, to embrace a life beyond the confines of Crimsworth Hall, as a betrayal, a stain upon the family name.

And then there was the matter of the letter. I had written to Charles, my oldest and dearest friend, detailing my arrival at Crimsworth Hall, my encounters with my aunt and cousin, my impressions of the surrounding landscape. I had poured out my heart to him, as I had done a hundred times before, seeking his counsel, his reassurance, his unwavering support. But days had turned into weeks, and still no reply. I could only assume, with a sinking heart, that he was still ensconced in his new colonial post, the distance and demands of his new station having already begun to erode the bonds of our long-standing friendship.

I spent much of my time wandering the grounds of Crimsworth Hall, seeking solace in the solitude of the surrounding woods. The ancient trees, their gnarled branches reaching skyward like supplicating arms, seemed to offer a silent understanding, a comforting presence in the midst of my growing isolation. I would sit for hours beneath their leafy canopy, lost in thought, attempting to make sense of my present circumstances, to chart a course for my future.

The town of X-, with its belching chimneys and grimy streets, held little appeal. The factories, with their ceaseless din and suffocating atmosphere, were a constant reminder of the trade I had so reluctantly embraced. I felt suffocated by the predictability of my existence, by the relentless pursuit of profit that seemed to be the sole driving force behind the lives of those around me.

I yearned for something more, something beyond the accumulation of wealth, something that would ignite my passion and give purpose to my days. Perhaps, I thought, I could dedicate myself to some noble cause, some work of public benefit that would alleviate the suffering of others. Or perhaps I could devote myself to the pursuit of knowledge, to the study of literature and philosophy, to the exploration of the human condition.

Such thoughts occupied my mind as I strolled through the gardens late one afternoon, the air fragrant with the scent of roses and honeysuckle. I paused before a sundial, its bronze face tarnished with age, and watched as the shadow slowly crept across its surface. Time, I reflected, was a precious commodity, and I could not afford to waste it on idle discontent. I must find a way to make my mark upon the world, to leave behind something of lasting value.

“She has no right to be a princess,” said the mother, overwrought and irritable, “and duty is better than ease surely. You, I know, think so.”

“For the like of me, yes,” said the curate; “for her, I don’t know.”

“I was once very much like her, though you would not think it,” said the mother, with the slightest tinge of bitterness, “but that is not the question--no, no, we must not trouble you.”

“When I tell you the mornings hang on my hands! I don’t know what to do with my mornings. There’s Tuesday I’m due at the schools, but the rest of the week I do nothing but idle. And idling’s a great temptation. A cigar comes natural when you’ve nothing to do. You don’t like a man smoking in the morning; I’ve heard you say so. So you see the young ones will save me from a--no, I won’t say cigar; worse than that; cigars are too dear for a curate, me dear lady--from a pipe.”

“Mr. Nolan, you are too good for this world,” said poor Mrs. Damerel, affected to tears; “but I must first try what can be done at home,” she added after a pause; “no, no, you weigh me down under your kindness. What would the parish be but for you?”

“It would be just the same if I were dead and buried,” said the curate, shrugging his shoulders. “Ah, that’s the worst of it: try for a little bit of a corner of work like a child’s lessons, and you may be of service; but try to mend the world, even a bit of a parish, and you’re nowhere. They don’t think half as much of me as they do of the rector?” he added, with a curious smile, which the rector’s wife only half understood. Was it satirical? or could it be possible that the curate was surprised that the people thought more of the rector than of himself? Mrs. Damerel was aware, no one better, of her husband’s faults. Many a time she was ready to say in bitterness (to herself) that he was wearing her to death; but nevertheless she looked at long, loosely-built, snub-nosed Mr. Nolan, with mingled amusement and surprise. Was it possible that he could entertain any hopes of rivalling her husband? Of course a visit from the rector was an honor to any one, for Mr. Damerel was a man who, notwithstanding a little human weakness, was the very picture and model of a gentleman; and the idea of comparing him with good Mr. Nolan was too absurd.

“Yes, no doubt they are pleased to see him,” she said: “poor people are very quick to recognize high breeding; but I am sure, my dear Mr. Nolan, that they are all very fond of you.”

The curate made no immediate answer. I am not sure that he had not in his private heart something of the same feeling with which his present companion had been thinking of her daughter, a feeling less intense in so far as it was much more indifferent to him, yet in a way stronger because untempered by affection. The rector was of his own kind, the ornamental and useless specimen, while he was the worker whom nobody thought of; but these secret feelings neither of the two confided to the other. Mr. Nolan would have been horrified had he detected in Mrs. Damerel that slight bitterness about Rose, which indeed would have shocked herself as deeply had she paused to identity the sentiment, and she would have been, and was, to some slight extent--suspecting the existence of the feeling--contemptuous and indignant of Nolan’s “jealousy,” as I fear she would have called it. They returned, however, to the educational question, which did not involve anything painful, and after considerable discussion it was settled that he should give the elder children lessons in the morning “if their papa approved.” It is impossible to say what a relief this decision was to the mother, who had felt these lessons to be the last straw which proverbially breaks the camel’s back. She was glad of the chat with a sympathizing friend, who understood, without saying anything about, her troubles--and doubly glad of the holiday exacted from her by his means--and gladder still to get rid of him and return to her many other occupations; for it was Monday, as has already been mentioned, and there was the laundress to look after, and a thousand other things awaiting her. The curate went out by the garden door when he left her, out upon the lawn, where he paused to look at as charming a scene as could be found in England: a fair country spreading out for miles its trees and fields and soft undulations under a summer sky, which was pale with excess of light, and ran into faint lines of misty distance almost colorless in heat and haze. Here and there the sunshine caught in a bend of the river, and brought out a startling gleam as from a piece of silver. The world was still with noon and distance, no sound in the air but the rustle of the leaves, the hum of insects; the landscape was all the sweeter that there was no remarkable feature in it, nothing but breadth and space, and undulating lines, and light, everywhere light; and to make up for its broad, soft vagueness, how distinct, like a picture, was the little group in the foreground--the lime-trees in their silken green, the soft rippling shadows on the grass, the picturesque figure in the chair, and the beautiful girl!

Amidst the somber confines of the jail, an air of desolation clung heavy to the stone walls, draping the dimly-lit chambers in shades of melancholy. A man, whose name echoed less frequently in better days than the fleeting fancies of time, lay cast upon the grimy floor, his once noble demeanor rendered into a mere specter of squalor. Beneath the flickering light of a sputtering lamp, his skin, pallid and gaunt, bore testament to the toll exacted by his long dalliance with vice, now manifest visibly upon his besotted visage.

The old jailer, a man of many seasons whose heart had grown calloused through years of witnessing human frailty, peered down upon the prostrate figure with a mingling of sorrow and resignation. He shook his head slowly, the gesture more poignant than any words could convey, as though mourning not merely the wretched man before him, but also the ambitions and dreams that now lay buried beneath the weight of whiskey bottles and shattered resolve. The notion that hope might yet sprout once more was a notion the jailer reserved for children or the foolishly optimistic; for the likes of Tom Swiggs, no such reprieve could be found within these walls, nor indeed without.

Just then, as luck would have it—though perhaps more accurately misfortune—a figure emerged from the shadows, clad in a crimson shirt so bold it seemed to mock the very elegy of despair that permeated the air. Mr. Mingle, a rough-hewn man with a roll of contempt curling upon his lips, strode forth, his gait betraying the swagger of one well-acquainted with the hardships of life on the streets, and the insatiable thirst that rendered him a frequent guest at this institution in moments of political fervor. “Look at ’im!” he bellowed, with a sneer that amplified the compunction of the surroundings. “No finer example of how the bottle has turned a man to muck! Tom Swiggs, once a gentleman! Now consorting with rats!”

The scorn in Mr. Mingle’s voice was palpable, a vindictive melody that danced in the air, igniting splinters of laughter from some unseen corners of the jail, where shadows seemed to conspire with contempt. Yet, as derisive as his tone might have been, it stretched the truth beyond its pallor. Tom had not always been so reviled; he had been cherished once in the warm embrace of familiar faces. Yet, as Mr. Mingle continued his lament, it became clear that the ties of fellowship had grown tenuous with the brittle threads of time, fraying beneath the strain of vanities past.

Yet amidst the scorn, fate was not entirely unkind. A figure of gentle stature soon materialized from the dismal ether, emerging like a pearlescent ray from a storm-laden sky. Spunyarn, whose rustic countenance bore marks of the sea—the kindest shard of fortune in an unforgiving realm—approached with a caring tenderness that seemed to momentarily abate the tempestuous atmosphere. “Hush now, Tom,” he coaxed, kneeling beside the fallen man whose endearing spirit lingered, albeit faintly, beneath layers of misfortune. “You’ve weathered worse seas, me lad.”

With hands calloused by rough toil yet tender and warm as a spring breeze, Spunyarn gently rested a hand upon Tom’s shoulder, hoping to instill a flicker of hope in the darkened heart of his friend. “Remember the times on the dock? The laughter, the tales we spun like fine yarn on a loom,” he said, his voice a soothing balm against the harsh reality encasing them. The sincerity imbued in Spunyarn’s words enveloped them both, forging a bridge towards recollections of camaraderie that transcended the present shadows.

Around them, the warmth of loyalty began to take root, a flicker of light amidst the oppressive gloom. The jailer, once merely a silent observer, felt his heart soften at the sight of this unexpected alliance. It paved a path toward a semblance of grace, even in such dire straits. Carefully, he joined Spunyarn in aiding Tom to his cell, an act that evoked a rare harmony among them, transcending the weight of societal judgment and scorn.

In the silence that followed, as they settled Tom upon the cold cot, Spunyarn remained steadfast, his vigilance unwavering. “Rest now, my old friend,” he whispered tenderly, smoothing the damp hair from Tom’s brow, an act infused with all the love of brotherhood. “I shall keep watch through the night, for true friends endure even in the valley of despair.” With those words, Spunyarn imbued the space with a warmth that promised to glean shards of hope from the darkness, a fleeting glimpse of faith reborn amongst the ruins of a life adrift. As Tom yielded to the embrace of sleep, the shadows dimmed, leaving only the enduring light of friendship to illuminate the path ahead.

The butterfly was gone, but the bee still hummed about them. The hot afternoon air was unstirred by any breeze.

'How glad I am,' Wilfrid exclaimed when he had brooded for a few moments, 'that I happened to see you as I rode past! I should have wandered restlessly about the house in vain, seeking for some one to talk to. And you listen so patiently. What a snowy crown!'

'That is a pretty spray,' he added, holding to her one that he had plucked.

She looked at it; then, as he still held it out, took it from him. The exquisite fingers touched his own redder and coarser ones.

'Have you friends in Dunfield?' he asked.

'Friends?'

'Any real friend, I mean--any girl who gives you real companionship?'

'Scarcely that.'

'How shall you spend your time when you are not deep in electrics? What do you mean to read these holidays?'

'Chiefly German, I think. I have only just begun to read it.'

'And I can't read it at all. Now and then I make a shot at the meaning of a note in a German edition of some classical author, every time fretting at my ignorance. But there is so endlessly much to do, and a day is so short.'

'Isn't it hateful,' he broke forth, 'this enforced idleness of mine? To think that weeks and weeks go by and I remain just where I was, when the loss of an hour used to seem to me an irreparable misfortune. I have such an appetite for knowledge, surely the unhappiest gift a man can be endowed with; it leads to nothing but frustration. Perhaps the appetite weakens as one grows in years; perhaps the sphere of one's keener interests contracts; I hope it may be so. At times I cannot work--I mean, I could not--for a sense of the vastness of the field before me. I should like you to see my rooms at Balliol. Shelves have long since refused to take another volume; floor, tables, chairs, every spot is heaped. And there they lie; hosts I have scarcely looked into, many I shall never have time to take up to the end of my days.'

'You have the satisfaction of being able to give your whole time to study.'

'There is precisely the source of dissatisfaction. My whole time, and that wholly insufficient. I have a friend, a man I envy intensely; he has taken up the subject of Celtic literature; gives himself to it with single-heartedness, cares for nothing that does not connect itself therewith; will pursue it throughout his life; will know more of it than any man living. My despair is the universality of my interests. I can think of no branch of study to which I could not surrender myself with enthusiasm; of course I shall never master one. My subject is the history of humanity; I would know everything that man has done or thought or felt. I cannot separate lines of study. Philology is a passion with me, but how shall I part the history of speech from the history of thought? The etymology of any single word will hold me for hours; to follow it up I must traverse centuries of human culture. They tell me I have a faculty for philosophy, in the narrow sense of the word; alas! that narrow sense implies an exhaustive knowledge of speculation in the past and of every result of science born in our own time. Think of the sunny spaces in the world's history, in each of which one could linger for ever. Athens at her fairest, Rome at her grandest, the glorious savagery of Merovingian courts, the kingdom of Frederick II., the Moors in Spain, the magic of Renaissance Italy--to become a citizen of any one age means a lifetime of endeavour. It is easy to fill one's head with names and years, but that only sharpens my hunger. Then there is the world of art; I would know every subtlest melody of verse in every tongue, enjoy with perfectly instructed taste every form that man has carved or painted. I fear to enter museums and galleries; I am distracted by the numberless desires that seize upon me, depressed by the hopelessness of satisfying them. I cannot even enjoy music from the mere feeling that I do not enjoy it enough, that I have not had time to study it, that I shall never get at its secret.... And when is one to live? I cannot lose myself in other men's activity and enjoyments. I must have a life of my own, outside the walls of a library. It would be easy to give up all ambition of knowledge, to forget all the joy and sorrow that has been and passed into nothingness; to know only the eternity of a present hour. Might one not learn more in one instant of unreflecting happiness than by toiling on to a mummied age, only to know in the end the despair of never having lived?'

While she was thinking and praying, tears stole down her face; Fanny saw them, and stopped her work, and looked sorrowfully at her--

"Now you are crying again, grandmother, she said," and that's what makes me break the tenth commandment, for I can't help wishing the gentleman had given me that half-sovereign. But I will say the verses again to-day about the lilies and birds; for you know I said that morning--

'Mortals fly from doubt and sorrow, God provideth for the morrow,'

and when I came back with my three sixpences, you said God had provided for the morrow, for you had only two or three pennies in the house when I went out."

"And how many pennies, pray, have you in the house to-day?" said a rather gruff voice at the door.

Mrs. Newton and Fanny started; but there, standing at the door, Fanny saw the fat gentleman who had given her the half-sovereign.

"So you have been wishing for my gold, you little rogue," he said, looking as if he meant to frighten her. "Never mind," he added, smiling, "you are a good child, and did what was right; and I always meant to bring it back to you, but I have been kept rather busy these few days past. There it is for you, and try not to break the tenth commandment again." Then turning to Mrs. Newton, he said, "We should not expect rewards, ma'am, for doing our duty, but if children do not meet with approbation when they do right, they may be discouraged, and perhaps think there is no use in being good: for they are silly little creatures, you know, and do not always recollect that God will reward the just one day if men do not."

"Oh! sir!" said poor Mrs. Newton, but the tears streamed down, and she could not say a word more. And there Fanny sat gazing on the half-sovereign, as if she was half stupefied.

"Well, take up that bit of gold, and do what you like with it," said the fat gentleman; "and then run off to sell your flowers, for we must not be idle because we have got enough for to-day. But do what you like with that money."

Fanny rose up from her seat, and looking very much as if she was moving in her sleep, with her wondering eyes fixed on the shining piece that lay in her hand, she walked slowly over to Mrs. Newton, and putting it into hers, said,--

"May I go to the grocer's now, grandmother, and get you the tea for your breakfast?"

"Yes, my love," said Mrs. Newton, kissing her, "and take care of this, and bring back the change carefully." Then turning to the gentleman, she said, "I am not young, sir, and I am very, very poorly; I find it hard to go without my tea, but it is a luxury I have been obliged latterly to forego."

"But could you not get tea on credit, from the grocer?" said the gentleman.

"Oh! yes, I believe so; but there would be no use in getting credit;" said Mrs. Newton, "for I am not certain of being better able to pay next week than I am this week; and when I have not the money to pay for what I wish to get, it is better to do without it, than to add to one's anxieties by running in debt. Do you not think so, sir?"

"Ma'am," said the old gentleman, sitting down, and resting his large silver-topped stick between his knees, "it is of very little consequence what I think; but if you wish to know this, I will tell you that I think very well both of you and your little girl, who, as I have heard, for I have made inquiries about you both, is a dependant on your bounty. You have trained her up well, though I wouldn't praise the child to her face; and so take as much tea as you like till you hear from me again, and your grocer need be in no trouble about his bill."

How did Evergreen's ship get stuck in the Suez Canal and create the world's heaviest traffic jam?

The skyscraper-size ship blocking the Suez Canal was freed today, five days after wedging itself sideways into the banks of one of the world's busiest waterways.

The 1,312-foot, 220,000 ton Ever Given, nearly a quarter-mile long, created a shipper's nightmare and captured the public's imagination when it blocked the canal on March 23. It created a traffic jam of more than 360 ships as of Sunday and is costing billions in delayed shipments.

Teams of dredgers and tugboats were able to free the ship's stern on Sunday, moving 330 feet from the western bank. The bow was pulled loose today.

Workers were aided by high tides helped by a full moon. The full moon offers a spring tide, or king tide, in which high tides are higher and the low tides are lower because of the effects of gravity during a straight-line alignment of the Earth, the moon and the sun, USA TODAY reported.

Tugboats are pulling the Ever Given to the canal's Great Bitter Lake, where it will be inspected.

How did it happen?

The Ever Given was stuck near the Egyptian city of Suez, about 3.7 miles north of the canal's southern entrance. It was in a single-lane section of the canal, about 985 feet wide.

Its owners originally said high winds in a sandstorm pushed the ship sideways, wedging it into both banks of the waterway. Containers stacked on deck may have acted as a sail.

However, the chairman of Egypt's Suez Canal Authority said Saturday, without giving details, that weather conditions "were not the main reasons" for the grounding, and that "there may have been technical or human reasons," the BBC reported. An investigation is ongoing.

How many ships are waiting?

At least 360 ships, carrying everything from cars to oil to grain, wait at the canal’s northern and southern entrances. The AP said an analysis by data firm Refinitiv showed an additional 300 ships were en route to the canal over the next two weeks. Some ships have already diverted to the African route.

CNN said the U.S. Navy offered dredging experts to assist.

Authorities originally disagree on how long the canal will be blocked. The ship’s owner, Shoei Kisen, said its goal was to free the vessel by the night of March 27.

An Egyptian presidential adviser told Agence France Presse on March 26 that traffic would resume within 48 to 72 hours. However, the CEO of a dredging company has said the operation could take weeks.

The uncertainty has forced some shippers to alter course and take the longer, alternate route around the Cape of Good Hope in Africa, adding weeks to their destinations and increasing fears of piracy. Some have contacted the U.S. Navy about increased security.

Officials were under great pressure to remove the ship.

The canal is a 120-mile-long shipping link between the Mediterranean and Red seas that carries 10% to 12% of commercial shipping and about 2.5% of the world’s oil. A German insurer said delays could cost global trade $6 billion to $10 billion a week, Reuters reported.

USA TODAY said the blockage could worsen shipping delays and cause shortages of toilet paper, coffee and other goods.

GlobalSecurity.org calls the canal “strategically and economically one of the most important waterways in the world.”

Who owns the canal?

The Suez Canal is operated by Egypt, through its state-owned Suez Canal Authority. Canal revenue for Egypt was $5.6 billion in 2020, according to Arab News. On average, about 50 ships pass through the canal daily.

The canal took 10 years to build and opened in 1869. It's a sea-level canal, without locks, connecting major bodies of water at different altitudes. It normally takes a ship 13 to 15 hours to cross from one end to the other. It's been widened over the years, with the latest project in 2015 at a cost of $8 billion.

The Panama-flagged Ever Given was built in 2018 and is operated by Evergreen Marine of Taiwan. It can carry 20,000 20-foot containers, according to Reuters, and transports cargo between Asia and Europe. It has a crew of 25.

The 1,312-foot ship is often compared to the Empire State Building, which is 1,454 feet tall, including its spire and antenna.

Despite the serious implications of the jam, some on social media have been making light of the situation including a popular comic and a parody account for a digger at the center of the action.

"Dick!" said the farmer, in a peremptory voice, giving the rein a quick jerk as he spoke.

But Dick moved not a step.

"Dick! you vagabond! get up." And the farmer's whip cracked sharply by the pony's ear.

It availed not, however, this second appeal. Dick stood firmly disobedient. Next the whip was brought down upon him, with an impatient hand; but the pony only reared up a little. Fast and sharp the strokes were next dealt to the number of a half-dozen. The man might as well have beaten his wagon, for all his end was gained.

A stout lad now came out into the road, and catching Dick by the bridle, jerked him forward, using, at the same time, the customary language on such occasions, but Dick met this new ally with increased stubbornness, planting his forefeet more firmly, and at a sharper angle with the ground. The impatient boy now struck the pony on the side of his head with his clenched hand, and jerked cruelly at his bridle. It availed nothing, however; Dick was not to be wrought upon by any such arguments.

"Don't do so, John!" I turned my head as the maiden's sweet voice reached my ear. She was passing through the gate into the road, and, in the next moment, had taken hold of the lad and drawn him away from the animal. No strength was exerted in this; she took hold of his arm, and he obeyed her wish as readily as if he had no thought beyond her gratification.

And now that soft hand was laid gently on the pony's neck, and a single low word spoken. How instantly were the tense muscles relaxed--how quickly the stubborn air vanished.

"Poor Dick!" said the maiden, as she stroked his neck lightly, or softly patted it with a child-like hand.

"Now, go along, you provoking fellow!" she added, in a half-chiding, yet affectionate voice, as she drew upon the bridle. The pony turned toward her, and rubbed his head against her arm for an instant or two; then, pricking up his ears, he started off at a light, cheerful trot, and went on his way as freely as if no silly crotchet had ever entered his stubborn brain.

"What a wonderful power that hand possesses!" said I, speaking to my companion, as we rode away.

He looked at me for a moment as if my remark had occasioned surprise. Then a light came into his countenance, and he said, briefly--

"She's good! Everybody and every thing loves her."

Was that, indeed, the secret of her power? Was the quality of her soul perceived in the impression of her hand, even by brute beasts! The father's explanation was, doubtless, the true one. Yet have I ever since wondered, and still do wonder, at the potency which lay in that maiden's magic touch. I have seen something of the same power, showing itself in the loving and the good, but never to the extent as instanced in her, whom, for a better name, I must still call "Gentle Hand."

A gentle touch, a soft word. Ah! how few of us, when the will is strong with its purpose, can believe in the power of agencies so apparently insignificant! And yet all great influences effect their ends silently, unobtrusively, and with a force that seems at first glance to be altogether inadequate. Is there not a lesson for us all in this?
