"Come, Barbara, sit beside me under this ancient oak, and listen well," said Deta softly, though a tremor of earnestness lay in her tone. "For it is time I divulge that which we have long concealed in secret. The man whom you know as the Alm-Uncle, though oft spoken of in fearful whispers, bears a past of triumph and lament we dare not speak aloud elsewhere."

Barbara leaned forward, her eyes aglow with a mixture of curiosity and apprehension. "Tell me, dear Deta, what is it that ties our kin to this solitary soul? My mind conjures images of a man shrouded in disgrace and haunted by harsh retribution, yet I sense that there is more hidden beneath the villagers’ tales."

Deta nodded, her gaze drifting momentarily to the distant mountains. "Long ago, he was a man of great fortune, bestowed with a vast and verdant farm that flourished under his care. However, pride and folly ensnared him. He sought solace in goblets of wine and the lure of gambling rather than in the honest sweat of his brow. In that pursuit, he lost not only his wealth, but also the affections of his kin, who found his ways intolerable and forsook him."

As a cool breeze swept over the hillside, Barbara interjected with gentle urgency, "But what of his duty now? How is it that he bears responsibility for the care of the child? I had thought his heart hardened by bitter regrets, his soul closed against the world. How does he come to safeguard the well-being of another?"

A faint, sardonic smile touched Deta's lips. "Ah, dear Barbara, it is not merely duty that binds him to that little one. An unspoken bond—a remnant of unacknowledged kinship—ties us all together. Though the path he trod led him astray, circumstances now demand he subsume his past misdeeds beneath a mantle of care. His apparent severity belies a tenderness reserved for those who depend upon him, a truth overlooked by quick judgments."

Just then, Deta’s gaze shifted, and she noted the goatherd Peter guiding the child within a safe range of the hillside. "See there," she whispered, "where young Peter wheels the child to the pasture? Thus does providence allow me to recount these matters without fear that our innocent charge may be led into the entanglements of our lore."

Barbara folded her hands, her countenance reflecting concern intermingled with wonder. "Yet, Deta, a secret such as this weighs heavy upon my conscience. How might I, a simple listener, bear such a truth without tarnishing the love I hold for this child and for the land that nurtures our spirits?"

"Promise me, then, that you shall hold this confession as sacred as your heart's own desires," Deta answered, her voice rising in a tone both firm and imploring. "Let not the idle prattle of the village or the prejudices of the unknowing contaminate our shared past. The Alm-Uncle, though barred from our commonplace discourse, remains a man ensnared by fate. While his fortunes crumbled in a haze of iniquity, a spark of redemption yet flickers within him, a spark that now guides his every act towards earning forgiveness."

Barbara’s eyes glistened with those unspoken secrets of sorrow and hope. "I pledge, dear Deta, that I shall keep your words within my bosom, as one carries a cherished relic from a bygone age. For though the tale be marred by missteps of the past, I sense the promise of eventual atonement—an unfolding drama written by destiny itself."

Deta’s countenance softened with relief and resolve as she resumed her narrative. "Upon losing all that was dear to him, the Alm-Uncle withdrew into isolation upon a solitary peak, far from the bustling hamlets below. In this silent refuge, amid the echoing whispers of winds and the gentle murmur of the valley, he began to rebuild not his fortune, but his honor. No longer shall the remnants of his past transgressions dictate his future, for each day he labors in quiet penitence."

Thus, as the dusk deepened into the serene embrace of twilight, the two friends remained vested in a covenant of trust. Deta’s confession, imbued with both regret and hope, mingled with the rustling of mountain leaves. And while distant echoes of the village tales persisted, there now shone a fragile light of understanding—a light that promised to guide not only the solitary Alm-Uncle in his journey towards redemption but also those who, like Barbara and Deta, dared to see beyond the veil of scandal into the heart of human fallibility.

Beatrice Avon took no part in the tableaux--the other girls had not absolutely insisted on her appearing beside them on the stage that had been fitted up; they had an+ informal council together, Miss Craven being stage-manager, and they had come to the conclusion that they could get along very nicely without her assistance.

Some of them said that Beatrice preferred flirting with the men. However this may have been, the fact remained that Harold, when he had washed the paint off his face--he had been the ill-tempered lover, Miss Craven being the young woman with whom he was supposed to have quarrelled, requiring the interposition of a sweet Peacemaker in the person of Miss Innisfail--went round by a corridor to the back of the hall, and stood for a few minutes behind a ‘portiere that took the place of a door at one of the entrances. The hall was, of course, dimly lighted to make the contrast with the stage the greater, so that he could not see the features of the man who was sitting on the chair at the end of the row nearest the portiere; but the applause that greeted a reproduction of the picture of a monk shaving himself, having previously used no other soap than was supplied by a particular maker, had scarcely died away before Harold heard the voice of Edmund Airey say, in a low and earnest tone, to someone who was seated beside him, “I do hope that before you go away, you will let me know where you will next pitch your tent. I don’t want to lose sight of you.”

“If you wish I shall let you know when I learn it from my father,” was the reply that Harold heard, clearly spoken in the voice of Beatrice Avon.

Harold went back into the billowy folds of the tapestry curtain, and then into the corridor. The words that he had overheard had startled him. Not merely were the words spoken by Edmund Airey the same as he himself had employed a few days before to Beatrice, but her reply was practically the same as the reply which she had made to him.

When the last of the figurantes had disappeared from the stage, and when the buzz of congratulations was sounding through the hall, now fully lighted, Harold was nowhere to be seen.

Only a few of the most earnest of the smokers were still in the hall when, long past midnight, he appeared at the door leading to the outer hall or porch. His shoes were muddy and his shirt front was pulpy, for the night was a wet one.

He explained to his astonished friends that it was invariably the case that putting paint and other auxiliaries to “making up” on his face, brought on a headache, which he had learned by experience could only be banished by a long walk in the open air.

Well, he had just had such a walk.

He did not expect that his explanation would carry any weight with it; and the way he was looked at by his friends made him aware of the fact that, in giving them credit for more sense than to believe him, he was doing them no more than the merest justice.

No one who was present on his return placed the smallest amount of credence in his story. What many of them did believe was of no consequence.

THE boats were scattered like milestones--as was stated by Brian--through the sinuous length of Lough Suangorm. The cutter yacht Acushla was leading the fleet out to the Atlantic, with two reefs in her mainsail, and although she towed a large punt, and was by no means a fast boat, she had no difficulty in maintaining her place, the fact being that the half-dozen boats that lumbered after her were mainly fishing craft hailing from the village of Cairndhu, and, as all the world knows, these are not built for speed but endurance. They are half-decked and each carries a lug sail. One of the legends of the coast is that when a lug sail is new its colour is brown, and as a new sail is never seen at Cairndhu there are no means of finding out if the story is true or false. The sails, as they exist, are kaleidoscopic in their patchwork. It is understood that anything will serve as a patch for a lug sail. Sometimes the centre-piece of an old coat has been used for this purpose; but if so, it is only fair to state that it is on record that the centre-piece of an old sail has been shaped into a jacket for the ordinary wearing of a lad.

DarkSide Ransomware Group's "Double Extortion" Tactics: Stealing Data Before Encrypting and Threatening Public Disclosure

The DarkSide ransomware group, known for its "double extortion" tactics, operated as a "ransomware-as-a-service" (RaaS) model, recruiting affiliates to launch attacks on unsuspecting organizations since its emergence in August 2020. According to Christopher Ballod, Associate Managing Director for Cyber Risk at Kroll, "DarkSide represents a significant threat due to their advanced techniques and financial acumen."

DarkSide's "double extortion" strategy involves stealing sensitive data before encrypting files, giving the group leverage to demand larger ransoms or sell the stolen information to third parties. Phil Wittmann, an attorney at Stone Pigman Walther Wittmann, explained, "The theft of data before encryption increases the pressure on organizations to pay the ransom to prevent the public exposure of their confidential information."

DarkSide carefully selected its targets based on financial analysis and information gleaned from corporate emails. Michael Walshe Jr., Chair of the Management Committee at Stone Pigman Walther Wittmann, stated, "DarkSide's targeted approach to selecting victims demonstrates a high level of sophistication and planning."

To infiltrate target networks, DarkSide employed advanced techniques like "zero-day exploits," which exploit vulnerabilities in software for which no patch is yet available. Ballod noted, "Zero-day exploits give attackers a significant advantage, as they can bypass security measures that rely on known vulnerabilities."

Once inside a target's network, DarkSide moved swiftly to encrypt files and exfiltrate data. They also investigated victims' cyber insurance policies to tailor ransom demands effectively. Wittmann commented, "DarkSide's understanding of cyber insurance policies is a testament to their research capabilities and knowledge of the cyber threat landscape."

DarkSide's quick attack window and demands on the high end, typically $5 million or more, put pressure on organizations to respond rapidly. Ballod cautioned, "The window of opportunity for organizations to prevent a ransomware attack is shrinking, making it essential for them to invest in robust cybersecurity measures and incident response plans."

DarkSide threatened to share stolen information with short-sellers if publicly traded companies refused to pay the ransom. Wittmann warned, "The potential for public disclosure of sensitive information can lead to significant reputational damage and financial losses for organizations."

After DarkSide's shutdown by law enforcement, affiliates complained on a forum that they had not been paid their share of the ransoms. Walshe Jr. commented, "The lack of transparency in ransomware-as-a-service operations can lead to mistrust among affiliates and potential legal repercussions."

Seven of Tantleff's clients paid ransoms ranging from $1.25 million to $6 million after negotiations from higher initial demands. Wittmann emphasized, "Paying the ransom is not an ideal solution, but it may be the most effective way to mitigate the damage caused by a ransomware attack and prevent the public disclosure of sensitive information."

If the city child goes through the arithmetic once, it is as much as ever. In the Old Red School-house those who hadn't gone through the arithmetic at least six times, were little thought of. In town, the last subject in the book was “Permutation,” to which you gave the mere look its essentially frivolous nature deserved. It was: “End of the line. They make a big fuss about the psychology of the child's mind nowadays. Well, I tell you they couldn't teach the man that got up that arithmetic a thing about the operation of the child's mind. He knew what was what. He didn't put down the answers. He knew that if he did, weak, erring human nature, tortured by suspense, determined to have the agony over, would multiply by four and divide by thirteen, and subtract 127--didn't, either. I didn't say “substract.” I guess I know they'd get the answer somehow, it didn't matter much how.

In the country they ciphered through this part, and handed in their sums to Teacher, who said she'd take 'em home and look 'em over; she didn't have time just then. As if that fooled anybody! She had a key! And when you had done the very last one on the very last page, and there wasn't anything more except the blank pages, where you had written, “Joe Geiger loves Molly Meyers,” and, “If my name you wish to see, look on page 103,” and all such stuff, then you turned over to the beginning, where it says, “Arithmetic is the science of numbers, and the art of computing by them,” and once more considered, “Ann had four apples and her brother gave her two more. How many did she then have?” There were the four apples in a row, and the two apples, and you that had worried over meadows so long and so wide, and men mowing them in so many days and a half, had to think how many apples Ann really did have. Some of the fellows with forked hairs on their chins and uncertain voices--the big fellows in the back seats, where the apple-cores and the spit-balls come from knew every example in the book by heart.

And there is yet another reason why the country school has brought forth men of whom we do well to be proud. At the county-seat, every so often, the school commissioners held an examination. Thither resorted many, for the most part anxious to determine if they really knew as much as they thought they did. If you took that examination and got a “stiff kit” for eighteen months, you had good cause to hold your head up and step as high as a blind horse. A “stiff kit” for eighteen months is no small thing, let me tell you. I don't know if there is anything corresponding to a doctor's hood for such as win a certificate to teach school for two years hand-running; but there ought to be. A fellow ought not to be obliged to resort to such tactics as taking out a folded paper and perusing it in the hope that some one will ask him: “What you got there, Calvin?” so as to give you a chance to say, carelessly, “Oh, jist a 'stiff-kit' for two years.”

(When you get as far along as that, you simply have to take a term in the junior Prep. Department at college, not because there is anything left for you to learn, but for the sake of putting a gloss on your education, finishing it off neatly.)

And then if you were going to read law with Mr. Parker, or study medicine with old Doc. Harbaugh, and you kind of run out of clothes, you took that certificate and hunted up a school and taught it. Sometimes they paid you as high as $20 a month and board, lots of board, real buckwheat cakes (“riz” buckwheat, not the prepared kind), and real maple syrup, and real sausage, the kind that has sage in it; the kind that you can't coax your butcher to sell you. The pale, tasteless stuff he gives you for sausage I wouldn't throw out to the chickens. Twenty dollars a month and board! That's $4 a month more than a hired man gets.

Kamala Harris and Doug Emhoff Still Living Out of Suitcases at Blair House Due to Vice President's Residence Renovations

CNN – More than two months after her inauguration, Vice President Kamala Harris and her husband, Douglas Emhoff, are still living out of suitcases at Blair House due to ongoing renovations at the vice president's official residence.

"We're just making it work," Harris told reporters during a recent event, with a small smile. Her husband added, "We're just taking it one day at a time."

Harris, the first woman and the first woman of color to hold the office of vice president in the United States, is facing a unique challenge as she settles into her new role. The reason behind the prolonged renovation period at the 9,000-plus square feet mansion built in 1893 is unclear, leading to frustration for the new vice president.

Sabrina Singh, Harris' deputy press secretary, said in a statement, "The Vice President and Second Gentleman are grateful for the hospitality of Blair House during this time, but they look forward to moving into their permanent residence soon."

Historically, new vice presidents have often delayed moving into the official residence to allow for maintenance and upgrades. Elizabeth Haenle, former Vice President Residence Manager and Social Secretary for Former Vice President Dick Cheney, noted, "It's not uncommon for renovations to take some time. The residence is a historical building, and there are always updates and improvements to be made."

While Blair House offers luxury accommodations, it does not provide the casual, informal atmosphere Harris and Emhoff prefer. The vice president's residence, on the other hand, offers more privacy, fewer staff, and less formality compared to the White House.

Previous vice presidents have personalized the residence with unique features such as a heated pool and a horseshoe pit. Harris, who values fitness and cooking, looks forward to utilizing the residence's outdoor space and potentially personalizing it.

However, according to Singh, no work is currently being conducted on the kitchen. "The Vice President has not requested any renovations to the kitchen at this time," she clarified.

Renovations and upkeep of the vice president's residence come with substantial government contracts for various works. The exact cost and scope of the current renovations have not been disclosed to the public.

In the meantime, Harris and Emhoff continue to make the most of their temporary accommodations at Blair House while they wait for their permanent residence to be ready.

The Abbe sat alone in his study, the late afternoon sun casting long shadows across the worn rug and well-loved books. The air was thick with the scent of old paper and pipe tobacco, a familiar comfort that did little to soothe the unease that had taken root in his heart. The rhythmic ticking of the grandfather clock, usually a reassuring presence, now seemed to underscore the swift passage of time, each tick another moment closer to the unknown.

He thought of the auction, the brisk pronouncements of the auctioneer echoing in the grand hall of Longueval, a place that had once thrummed with life, with laughter and music, now filled with the hushed whispers of strangers and the clink of coins. Two million, five hundred thousand francs - a king's ransom, and yet a pittance compared to the legacy of Longueval, the weight of generations etched into its very stones.

The thought of the estate being carved up, divided amongst strangers who would never understand its true worth, filled him with a profound sadness. The new owners would walk the halls where the Marquise once graced, their footsteps echoing in the silence where her laughter should have been. They would tend the gardens she had so lovingly cultivated, oblivious to the memories blooming alongside the roses.

And what of Pierre, Helene, and Camille? The Abbe sighed, his heart heavy with concern. They were like his own grandchildren, their laughter echoing in his memory, their faces a testament to the Marquise's kindness and spirit. He had watched them grow, had shared their joys and sorrows, and now they were scattered, their inheritance a burden rather than a blessing.

Pierre, burdened by debts and unwise choices, had been forced to relinquish his birthright. The weight of responsibility, so different from the carefree mantle he had assumed in his youth, had aged him beyond his years. His youthful exuberance was replaced by a weary resignation, his eyes reflecting a sadness that mirrored the Abbe's own.

Helene, her spirit as fiery as her auburn hair, had borne the ordeal with a stoicism that belied her tender years. Yet, the Abbe detected a flicker of fear in her eyes, a vulnerability that tugged at his heartstrings. She had always been the protector, the fierce defender of her siblings, and now she faced an uncertain future, adrift in a world that seemed determined to test her resilience.

And then there was Camille, the youngest, her innocence a poignant counterpoint to the unfolding drama. The Abbe could still picture her, flitting through the gardens like a butterfly, her laughter as bright and carefree as the summer sunshine. He prayed that the harsh realities of the world would not dim her spirit, that she would find solace and strength in the memories they all shared.

The clock chimed five, its resonant tones jolting the Abbe from his reverie. He rose from his chair, his joints protesting the prolonged stillness. As he moved to the window, his gaze fell upon the familiar path leading to Longueval, the path he had walked countless times over the years, his steps lightened by the promise of companionship and the satisfaction of shared purpose.

The path was empty now, a silent testament to the changing tides. Yet, as the Abbe looked out at the familiar landscape, he felt a surge of determination. He may not have had the power to alter the course of events, but he could offer solace, could be a beacon of hope in the gathering darkness.

ISIS-K: A Terror Group Emerging from Chaos

In the wake of the deadly Kabul airport attack, the world's attention has turned to ISIS-K, the terror group claiming responsibility. This affiliate of the Islamic State has leveraged Afghanistan's instability to become a formidable force in the region.

A Deadly Legacy:

The August 2021 attack, which killed 13 US troops and over 90 Afghans, marked ISIS-K's most significant global action to date. This brutality drew a promise of retribution from President Biden, highlighting the group's growing threat.

Origins and Ideology:

Formed in 2015, ISIS-K operates in Central Asia, taking its name from its designation for the region encompassing Afghanistan and Pakistan. Despite sharing ideology and tactics with its parent group, ISIS, the extent of their organizational and command-and-control connection remains unclear.

From Defectors to Fighters:

Early members included Pakistani militants who emerged in Afghanistan's Nangarhar province, many of whom defected from other terror groups. Current estimates suggest a strength of 1,500-2,000 fighters, potentially bolstered by the release of captured ISIS-K members from Kabul prisons during the Taliban takeover.

Radical Ambitions:

Unlike the Taliban, ISIS-K has little interest in governance. Their goal is to establish a caliphate governed by strict Sharia law, extending beyond Afghanistan and Pakistan to encompass South and Central Asia. This extreme vision attracts individuals with even more radical views than the Taliban.

Capitalizing on Uncertainty:

ISIS-K has capitalized on the recent turmoil in Afghanistan, launching brutal attacks and exploiting the impending US troop withdrawal to regain strength. Their presence poses a significant threat to regional stability and underscores the complex challenges facing Afghanistan's future.

John Taylor of Caroline, a prominent figure in early American political thought, ardently championed the principles of Republicanism and an agrarian economy. His vision was deeply rooted in the belief that personal freedom must be preserved, necessitating minimal government intervention in the lives of individuals. Taylor perceived the United States, lacking in native tradition, as uniquely positioned to establish self-governing systems that respected the natural rights of their citizens. These rights, in his view, were not merely to be acknowledged but protected from encroaching governmental authority, underscoring the inherent interdependence of such rights.

Central to Taylor's philosophy was the notion that a society must be fashioned to accommodate both the good and evil intrinsic to human nature. He expounded on the significance of good government, which he defined as institutions designed to safeguard private property, enhance agricultural productivity, and eschew the temptations of capitalist excess. Taylor's support for strict constructionism of the Constitution stemmed from his conviction that a limited Federal government would be better equipped to honor these principles. His warnings against an expansive Federal entity were grounded in the fear that unchecked growth would lead to extravagance and despotism, undermining the very foundations of liberty and justice he so fervently upheld.

Taylor's interpretation of the Declaration of Independence diverged from the prevailing federalist view, emphasizing the sovereignty of individual states rather than a consolidated national identity. He advocated for constitutional interpretation that referenced the original intent of its framers, a practice he believed would shield the document from the ravages of corruption and misinterpretation over time. This commitment to historical fidelity was emblematic of his broader political ideology, which sought to preserve the integrity of individual liberties against the tide of encroaching governmental power. Through his writings and speeches, Taylor effectively articulated a vision of American governance that celebrated the virtues of simplicity, natural right, and state-centric sovereignty, leaving an indelible mark on the discourse surrounding Republicanism and the role of government in American society.

The day following our contest was one painted with the soft brush strokes of early spring, the earth still trembling from the fierce grip of winter. As I moved about the yard of my father's homestead, the scent of freshly turned soil mingled with the crisp air, awakening within me a sense of renewal. Yet my mind, unsettled still after the match, wandered back to that singular struggle; a dance of strength that had captivated my spirit like the rarest ballet upon the stage.

There lingered in my veins the thrill of having been bested by such a formidable adversary. The events of the day before played over and over in my mind, unspooling like the unraveling yarn of a forgotten tale. How could I have been so easily undone by a man whose countenance had struck me as benign, yet whose sinewy strength had nearly cast me down? My musings drew me to the grand barn nearby, its once-splendid walls now dull from neglect but still possessing a charm of rustic fortitude.

Inside, the soft peals of hay rustled beneath my boots as I moved with purpose toward an ancient oak beam, its grain polished by hard labor and seasoned with the passage of time. As I ran my fingers over its surface, I felt the pride of my lineage housed within its timbers, and yet a nagging realization whispered through the corners of my mind—a need to understand that wily art of grappling which had momentarily cast me into the abyss of defeat.

Intent on my enlightenment, I set about simulating the movements we had performed in our altercation. First, I rehearsed the strides of a confident conqueror as I wrestled bravely with the ghosts of the past, attempting to capture the grace and agility that had eluded me during our bout. Yet, with every feigned hold and escape, I felt the weight of my own immobility—a reminder that I had assumed manhood too abruptly, that victory was a jewel requiring the polishing of skill and experience.

As I strained against the imagined opponent, a sudden rustle disturbed the veil of my solitude. I turned to see a figure approaching—none other than my recent combatant, the man whose strength had so startled me. His expression was one of friendly amusement, and I could not help but return his smile, a recognition of camaraderie that transcended our earlier exchange.

“Ah, it seems my dance partner has taken to the floor in solitary practice,” he declared, eyes glinting with the delight of shared memory. “I cannot fault you for the desire to harness the wisdom of our moments gone by. There are teaches in loss that even victory cannot bestow.”

His words, full of a good-natured bravery, sparked within me a stirring acknowledgment of our shared memento mori, for destiny had kissed us both in that fleeting instance on the earthen floor. I gestured to the space around us, a silent invitation to join me in a more playful engagement, with the lurking promise of further insight hidden within.

At once he took my invitation, and together we danced a second round, though this time it was not a matter of conquest but one of mutual endeavor. We shifted and twisted, our bodies moving in synchrony as we navigated the space with caution and respect. I could feel the tension ebbing; each grip an exchange, focused not on besting one another but on exploring the tangible strength of man’s spirit combined. In this subtle ballet, I began to discern the nuanced distinctions between our styles, each rise and fall a brushstroke painting the canvas of tradition and innovation.

Before long, laughter echoed through the barn; it rang out against wooden beams and hay-strewn floors, a mirth born of respect and burgeoning friendship. At last, we sank breathlessly to the ground, muscles taut yet unyielding, the intimacy of our sport renewing the bonds of our kindred spirits. He clapped his hands upon his knees and nodded at me with profound respect.

“Today,” he said, his voice softened by comradeship, “was but a gathering of the old and the new—an exchange knitted with history.” My heart warmed at the revelation and I knew, at that moment, I had been gifted an insight far richer than victory itself, for I had glimpsed the heart of a tradition that transcended mere strength, binding men in an eternal dance of respect and valor.

Fordham, who had been standing by him all the time, came a little closer.

'Come, Hugh, let's get out of this, you and I, and talk over things quietly together.'

Again Chisholm kept him from him with his outstretched hand.

'In your tone, Fordham, more even than in your words, there is suggestion. Of what? that I am mad? You have known me all my life. Have I struck you as being of the stuff which makes for madness? As a victim of hysteria? As a subject of hallucinations? As a liar? I am as sane as you, as clear-headed, as matter-of-fact, as truthful. I tell you, in very truth and very deed, that to-night I have seen Christ hard by here in the square.'

'My dear fellow, these people have come here to dine.'

'Is, then, dinner more than Christ?'

Smiling his easy, tolerant smile, Fordham touched Chisholm lightly with his fingers on the arm.

'My very dear old chap, this sort of thing is so awfully unlike you, don't you know?'

'You, also, will be changed when you have seen Christ. Fordham, I have seen Christ!'

The intensity of his utterance seemed to strike his hearers a blow. The women shivered, turning pale--even those who were painted. Mr. Warton leaned across the table towards Mrs. Amplett.

'I really think that you ladies had better retire. Our friend seems to be in a curious mood.'

The hostess nodded. She rose from her seat, looking very queerly at Mr. Chisholm, for whom her penchant is well known. The other women followed her example. The rustling concourse fluttered from the room, the Incumbent of St. Ethelburga holding the door open to let them pass, and himself bringing up the rear. The laymen were left alone together, Chisholm and Fordham standing at the head of the table with, on their faces, such very different expressions.

The host seemed snappish.

'You see what you've done? I offer you my congratulations, Mr. Chisholm. I don't know if you call the sort of thing with which you have been favouring us good form.'

'Is good form more than Christ?'

Amplett made an impatient sound with his lips. He stood up.

'Upon my word of honour, Mr. Chisholm, you must be either drunk or mad. I trust, for your own sake, that you are merely mad. Come, gentlemen, let's join the ladies.'

The men quitted the room in a body. Only Clement Fordham stayed with his friend. Chisholm watched them as they went. Then, when the last had gone and the door was closed, he turned to his companion.

'Yet it is the truth that this night I have seen Christ!'

The other laughed.

'Then, in that case, let's hope that you won't see much more of Him-- no impiety intended, I assure you. Now let you and me take our two selves away.'

He slipped his arm through his friend's. As they were about to move, the door opened and a servant entered. It was the man who had dropped the dish. He approached Chisholm with stuttering tongue.

'Pardon me, sir, if I seem to take a liberty, but might I ask if the Second Coming has really come at last? As a Seventh-Day Christian it's a subject in which I take an interest, and the fact is that there's a difference of opinion between my wife and me as to whether it's to be this year or next.'

The man bore ignorance on his countenance written large, and worse. Hugh Chisholm turned from him with repugnance.

'He's your brother,' whispered Fordham in his ear, as they moved towards the door.

The expression of Hugh Chisholm's face was stern.

Missing in Plain Sight: The Unequal Narrative of Gabby Petito’s Case

Gabby Petito’s tragic disappearance and the subsequent confirmation of her death as a homicide have captivated media outlets and the public alike. Images of the young woman, her Instagram photos, and the wrenching details of her story have dominated headlines for weeks. While any case of a missing person is undeniably heartbreaking, Petito's experience illustrates the grotesque phenomenon known as "missing white woman syndrome." This unsettling trend sheds light on the glaring racial and class disparities within the media's treatment of missing persons cases, raising important questions about the value placed on different lives in society.

Petito was not just a missing person; she was a social media influencer with a substantial online following, which undoubtedly fueled the virality of her story on platforms like Instagram and TikTok. Her case erupted into a viral sensation, causing an avalanche of media coverage that is rarely seen for other demographics. In contrast, women of color, particularly Black and Indigenous women, face a grim reality where their disappearances attract significantly less attention and urgency. The implications of this are profound, affecting the allocation of resources by officials during search and investigation efforts.

The stark differences in how cases are handled can be seen in the extensive resources deployed in the search for Petito. Authorities scoured national parks and mobilized an impressive network of volunteers and law enforcement. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indigenous people continue to go missing in Wyoming, often with little to no media coverage and far fewer resources dedicated to finding them. Underreporting and insufficient coordination in these communities contribute to the lack of urgent action, resulting in a painful and all-too-familiar pattern of invisibility for marginalized groups.

The media's disproportionate focus on Petito’s case raises troubling concerns about racial biases in coverage. Algorithmic bias on social media platforms further compounds this issue, as systems that prioritize trending content can inadvertently perpetuate disparities. If Petito had been a Black woman, it is difficult to fathom that her case would have garnered even a fraction of the attention it now enjoys. Every hour that goes by without justice for missing women of color reinforces the idea that their stories are considered less valuable, less tragic, than those of their white counterparts.

As we reflect on the societal implications of Petito's case, we must recognize it as a microcosm of broader issues—violence against women, systemic racism, and the commodification of certain narratives over others. The collective outrage surrounding her plight is undoubtedly justified, but it serves as a painful reminder of the countless others whose stories remain buried in silence, hidden away by an inequitable media landscape. The glaring disparities in coverage demand not just awareness, but a urgent call to action—so that we may begin to rectify the systemic biases that undervalue the lives of women of color.

The artist, intrigued by the unusual request and the unusual clientele, found himself in a state of perplexed curiosity. As the sun dipped lower, casting elongated shadows across the room, he sat at his drafting table, shading in the sketch he had begun earlier. His mind meandered through the mystifying conversation he had just shared with the Monarchs. He imagined the couple, still in their fine attire, standing outside his studio door, as if a pair of unusual birds had found their way into his nest.

Mr. Monarch, a gentleman of quiet dignity, and Mrs. Monarch, a lady of poise and elegance—both possessed an air of distinction that seemed at odds with the notion of posing for illustrations. The idea alone was so startling that the artist could hardly bring himself to complete the sketch. He paused, dipping his pencil in the inkwell and contemplating the situation.

The notion of their wanting to work as models had been suggested by Claude Rivet, the artist's own cousin and a wine-soaked man with a keen eye for the dramatic and the extreme of human situation. Claude, always with a story or two of his own making, had wandered into the artist's studio that very morning, showering him with a deluge of 'news' about the Monarchs. He had described them as an interesting case of fortune's caprices, and their circumstances, alas, quite dire. The Major had left the army, leaving behind a life of comfort and respect, and the subsequent dealings of his finances had not fared any better. The couple was now left with the daunting task of supporting themselves, and the thought of employing their considerable physical advantages, as Claude so elegantly put it, had fallen on fertile ground.

The artist, however, was not entirely convinced. Claude's stories were often a mixture of truth and embellishment, and he could not help but feel that there was more to the tale than meets the eye. Yet, he could not deny the sincerity of their plight, and the humility with which they had presented it. He knew that many a great artist had risen to prominence on the backs of those who had less, and the thought that the Monarchs might be willing to contribute to his own rising fame did not go unnoticed. Moreover, there was an element of curiosity, a desire to test the waters of his own creative prowess, that caught him off guard.

The next morning, the artist found himself walking to the Monarchs' residence. He had decided that a visit was in order, a chance to see them in their natural habitat and perhaps gain a better understanding of their predicament. The house was a grand affair, a testament to past prosperity, and it was clear that the stately mansion was in dire need of repair. The artist was struck by the stark contrast between the grandeur within and the tattered elegance of its inhabitants.

Upon entering the house, he was greeted by Mrs. Monarch, her eyes weary but her smile warm. She showed him into a sitting room, where Mr. Monarch was already seated, his hands clasped together, as if in prayer. The artist was struck by the measure of patience and quiet dignity they both exuded, a stark contrast to the chaos he was expecting. They spoke of their situation, their voices steady and calm, as if they were mere acquaintances discussing the weather.

The artist listened intently, trying to decipher the motives behind their offer. He could not ignore the romance of the situation, the improperness of it all, and the potential scandal that could erupt should their true intention be uncovered. He found himself drawn to their plight, their desperation, and their quiet grace. Yet, he also felt a sense of discomfort, a prickling awareness that this was not their world, that they were out of their depth.

The conversation turned to the specifics of their arrangement, and the artist found himself launching into an impassioned speech about the art of illustration. He spoke of the artistry involved, the need for accuracy, and the subtleties of shading and line. He saw the looks exchange between the Monarchs, saw their eyes glaze over, and realized that perhaps he was talking over their heads. He faltered, the words caught in his throat, and the silence that followed was palpable.

Mrs. Monarch, however, was the first to break the silence. She cleared her throat, and in her voice, the artist heard a note of determination. "We understand," she said, her eyes meeting his. "We understand that this is not just about posing, but about capturing something that is uniquely us. Something that, though it may not be in our nature, we are willing to put our trust in you to do."

The artist was struck by her words, the vulnerability they conveyed, and the strength they hid beneath. He saw in her gaze a reflection of his own struggle, the desire to create something true and lasting. He felt a stirring within him, a sense of purpose, and a sudden, profound understanding of this peculiar job they were about to undertake together.

He nodded, a slow, deliberate nod, and felt a smile spread across his face.

ZZ Top Bassist Dusty Hill Dies at 72

The music world mourns the loss of legendary bassist Dusty Hill, a founding member of the iconic rock band ZZ Top. Hill passed away peacefully in his sleep at his Houston home at the age of 72.

The news was confirmed by his bandmates, Billy Gibbons and Frank Beard, in a heartfelt Facebook post. "We, along with legions of ZZ Top fans around the world, will miss your steadfast presence, your good nature and enduring commitment to providing that monumental bottom to the 'Top,'" they wrote.

Hill's cause of death remains undisclosed. He had recently been recovering from a hip injury at his home, forcing the band to cancel several shows on their "Celebration With ZZ Top" tour. Guitar tech Elwood Francis filled in for Hill during his absence.

Born Joe Michael Hill in Dallas, Hill moved to Houston in 1970 and joined forces with Gibbons and Beard to form ZZ Top. The trio's unique blend of blues and rock propelled them to international fame, with a career spanning nearly 50 years and 15 studio albums.

Their 1984 masterpiece, "Eliminator," featuring the smash hits "Gimme All Your Lovin'", "Sharp Dressed Man", and "Legs," sold over 10 million copies and achieved Diamond certification by the Recording Industry Association of America. ZZ Top also boasted four Platinum albums, including the five-times Platinum "Afterburner," and four Gold records with Hill on bass and backing vocals.

In 2003, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted ZZ Top, with Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards bestowing the honor.

Beyond their musical achievements, ZZ Top was renowned for their signature style, most notably the long beards and black sunglasses sported by Hill and Gibbons. The iconic look originated in the 1970s when the duo returned from a vacation sporting newly grown facial hair. They decided to keep it, and the rest is history.

In 1984, razor company Gillette reportedly offered a cool $1 million to the pair in exchange for shaving off their famous beards. ZZ Top, staying true to their image, politely declined.

Dusty Hill's legacy as a talented musician and a cornerstone of ZZ Top's success will forever be etched in the annals of rock and roll history. He will be deeply missed by his bandmates, fans, and the music community at large.

In an era where ransomware attacks are becoming an escalating menace, one corporation stood firm against cybercriminals' extortion efforts. At a time when businesses frequently find themselves at the mercy of hackers encrypting their data and demanding hefty ransoms, this company chose a path less traveled.

The landscape of cyber threats has dramatically evolved, with incidents like the massive global attack over the Fourth of July weekend, the spring attack on Colonial Pipeline, and the 2017 WannaCry virus only highlighting the increasing frequency and financial demands of these breaches. The past five years, in particular, have seen a surge in such attacks, with pivotal infrastructure and corporate systems being prime targets for digital hostage-taking.

The attack on Colonial Pipeline in early May 2021 underscored the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the ease with which essential services could be disrupted and coerced into paying large sums. Following the attack, Colonial Pipeline handed over $4.4 million to the perpetrators, a decision followed by fuel shortages across the East Coast.

However, the narrative shifted when Norsk Hydro, a Norwegian company specializing in renewable energy and aluminum manufacturing, faced a ransomware attack. In contrast to the usual response, they resolved not to pay the ransom and aimed to eradicate the virus on their own.

The challenge arrived unexpectedly on the day Hilde Merete Aasheim assumed her role as CEO of Norsk Hydro. A 4 a.m. phone call disrupted any normalcy, delivering news of a severe cyberattack. The company quickly realized that their operations, spanning across a large network of servers and PCs and essential to powering nearly 900,000 homes in Norway, were under siege.

Choosing not to negotiate with the attackers, Norsk Hydro embarked on a journey to reclaim control and integrity of their systems. This decision stemmed from a belief that succumbing to the ransom would only invite future attacks. As a result, they halted network access and shifted to manual operations where possible, a move that froze nearly all digital activity and placed immense pressure on maintaining essential functions without the aid of technology.

The aftermath saw the company navigating unprecedented territory – running a manufacturing enterprise devoid of modern digital conveniences. For weeks, operations hinged on paper-based methods and manual labor, an approach unfathomable in today's tech-driven industry. Manufacturing precision components and managing smelters at extreme temperatures suddenly relied on hands-on techniques and the knowledge of retired employees acquainted with pre-digital methods.

Norsk Hydro's stand against paying a ransom in the face of a crippling cyberattack not only highlights the evolving nature of cybersecurity threats but also showcases the resilience and innovative problem-solving businesses must adopt in such scenarios. Through a blend of old-school methodologies and expert intervention, the company demonstrated that it is possible to overcome even the most daunting digital challenges without yielding to the demands of cybercriminals.

"I dare say she will be a great comfort to you, love," said Lady Wetheral, in a sleepy tone, "but, suppose the nurse is summoned for Miss Christobel--I am inclined to sleep."

The child was soon taken from Lady Wetheral's arms, and consigned to the distant apartment which constituted the nursery. Sir John also rose to depart, but his lady's languid voice detained him.

"Sir John!"

"Yes, dear."

"I think I shall require change of air after all this."

"Certainly; where would you like to move? Shall we go to the sea-side?"

"No, love, the sea air is too keen; but I half promised the Tyndals to pay them a visit after my confinement."

"The infant will inconvenience them in their present house, Gertrude."

"I do not mean to take the infant, Sir John, on that account; besides, my nights would be dreadfully disturbed; no, I shall leave Christobel with you, love, and only take Anna Maria with me for a fortnight."

"I am not included in your 'arrangements', then?"

"My love, you know I require great quiet, and at the Tyndals every thing is so agreeably methodical and peaceful, I shall recover my strength quickly; then, you know, dear, the Pynsents live within a short drive; I shall, perhaps, see a great deal of the Pynsents."

"That will be a nuisance, certainly, as you do not like Mrs. Pynsent, but you will not be disturbed by her frequent visits, for the disinclination is mutual."

"You are so obtuse, love. I am going to the Tyndals on purpose to renew my acquaintance with Mrs. Pynsent, and I trust we shall be very intimate."

"What, with the woman you denounce as vulgar, and contradictory?"

"I have argued these things with you, Sir John, till my patience is nearly exhausted, and you are still benighted on a subject so closely interwoven with my happiness. I tell you I am going on purpose to effect a scheme, and I take Anna Maria with me, to prepossess Mrs. Pynsent in her favour."

"And what the deuce, Gertrude, makes you wish to prepossess a woman so disagreeable as you describe Mrs. Pynsent to be? Why can't you keep away?"

"My love, I tell you Anna Maria is destined for Tom."

"And what has Tom to do with his mother? He is at Eton. You had better take lodgings near Eton, if you want to catch Tom."

"I can argue with you no more, Sir John. Your ideas are so very limited, it is impossible to graft a plan upon them. It is well your daughters have a mother who is anxious to establish them in life, since their father would effect nothing. If I was on my death-bed, my last hours would be horrified by visions of my daughters' pairing off with curates or lieutenants."

"And pray, where do you look for future bishops and Wellingtons, but among curates and lieutenants?" cried Sir John, warmly.

"Indeed, Sir John, you make me sick with your levelling principles," retorted Lady Wetheral, rising in her bed; "my health is far from strong; you have given me a severe headache, and I do request you will never again breathe the word 'curate;' it puts such wretched thoughts into my mind. Fancy Anna Maria shuffling after a fat country curate, smelling of onions, and bawling at a row of charity-children! or, Julia married to your friend Leslie, handing her basket upon a baggage-waggon! Pray, my love, send Thompson to me with some tea, and never let this disagreeable subject be renewed between us. I think I am very poorly."

Sir John was long habituated to resign his opinions when they affected his lady's health; and, on this occasion, he renounced them with his usual good humour.

"Well, Gertrude, get rid of your aches and pains, and you shall become intimate with Mrs. Pynsent, and catch her son Tom, if it will give you pleasure. I don't like to see you nervous and ill."

It is neither to the Roman Prince, nor to the representative of the illustrious house of Cajetani, which has given more than one Pope to the Christian Church, that I dedicate this short portion of a long history; it is to the learned commentator of Dante.

It was you who led me to understand the marvelous framework of ideas on which the great Italian poet built his poem, the only work which the moderns can place by that of Homer. Till I heard you, the Divine Comedy was to me a vast enigma to which none had found the clu–he commentators least of all. Thus, to understand Dante is to be as great as he; but every form of greatness is familiar to you.

A French savant could make a reputation, earn a professor's chair, and a dozen decorations, by publishing in a dogmatic volume the improvised lecture by which you lent enchantment to one of those evenings which are rest after seeing Rome. You do not know, perhaps, that most of our professors live on Germany, on England, on the East, or on the North, as an insect lives on a tree; and, like the insect, become an integral part of it, borrowing their merit from that of what they feed on. Now, Italy hitherto has not yet been worked out in public lectures. No one will ever give me credit for my literary honesty. Merely by plundering you I might have been as learned as three Schlegels in one, whereas I mean to remain a humble Doctor of the Faculty of Social Medicine, a veterinary surgeon for incurable maladies. Were it only to lay a token of gratitude at the feet of my cicerone, I would fain add your illustrious name to those of Porcia, of San-Severino, of Pareto, of di Negro, and of Belgiojoso, who will represent in this "Human Comedy" the close and constant alliance between Italy and France, to which Bandello did honor in the same way in the sixteenth centur–andello, the bishop and author of some strange tales indeed, who left us the splendid collection of romances whence Shakespeare derived many of his plots and even complete characters, word for word.

The two sketches I dedicate to you are the two eternal aspects of one and the same fact. Homo duplex, said the great Buffon: why not add Res duplex? Everything has two sides, even virtue. Hence Moliere always shows us both sides of every human problem; and Diderot, imitating him, once wrote, "This is not a mere tale"--in what is perhaps Diderot's masterpiece, where he shows us the beautiful picture of Mademoiselle de Lachaux sacrificed by Gardanne, side by side with that of a perfect lover dying for his mistress.

In the same way, these two romances form a pair, like twins of opposite sexes. This is a literary vagary to which a writer may for once give way, especially as part of a work in which I am endeavoring to depict every form that can serve as a garb to mind.

Most human quarrels arise from the fact that both wise men and dunces exist who are so constituted as to be incapable of seeing more than one side of any fact or idea, while each asserts that the side he sees is the only true and right one. Thus it is written in the Holy Book, "God will deliver the world over to divisions." I must confess that this passage of Scripture alone should persuade the Papal See to give you the control of the two Chambers to carry out the text which found its commentary in 1814, in the decree of Louis XVIII.

May your wit and the poetry that is in you extend a protecting hand over these two histories of "The Poor Relations"

Body Found in Wyoming Believed to be Gabby Petito

MOOSE, Wyo. (AP) – In a somber development, a body discovered in Wyoming's Bridger-Teton National Forest is believed to be that of 22-year-old Gabrielle "Gabby" Petito, the young woman who vanished while on a cross-country road trip with her boyfriend, Brian Laundrie. The FBI confirmed the grim news after an extensive two-day search of campgrounds in the area.

The discovery marks a tragic turn in the case that has captivated the nation, with many following Petito's journey and expressing concern for her well-being. FBI Supervisory Special Agent Charles Jones shared the news during a press conference, stating, "We believe we have found the remains of Gabrielle Petito."

The cause of death remains undetermined at this time, as the investigation continues. According to Jones, a full forensic identification of the body is still pending. Nevertheless, the Petito family has been notified of the discovery, though they understandably request privacy during this difficult time.

Richard Benson Stafford, an attorney representing the Petito family, expressed gratitude to the law enforcement agencies involved in the search. He stated, "The Petito family is grateful for the support of the FBI and other law enforcement agencies. We ask that you respect their privacy as they grieve the loss of their beautiful daughter."

In light of the ongoing investigation, certain areas within Grand Teton National Park and its vicinity have been temporarily closed to the public. Authorities are urging anyone who may have seen Petito or Laundrie near the Spread Creek Dispersed Camping Area between August 27 and August 30 to come forward with any relevant information.

Laundrie, who is considered a person of interest in the case, returned to his parents' home in North Port, Florida, on September 1 without Petito. He has since disappeared, prompting a massive search involving over 50 law enforcement officers in the Carlton Reserve, Sarasota County, Florida.

The search for Laundrie continues, and authorities are appealing to the public for any information that could assist in locating him. Anyone with relevant details is encouraged to contact the FBI or local law enforcement agencies.

The Petito family's attorney, Stafford, reiterated the importance of respecting the family's privacy during this challenging time. He emphasized, "The Petito family has suffered an unimaginable loss, and they ask for privacy as they mourn the death of their daughter."

As the investigation unfolds, the nation stands united in offering support and prayers to the Petito family. The search for Laundrie remains a top priority, and law enforcement agencies are committed to bringing justice in this heartbreaking case.

In the brightness of this morning, the lovers went out to look at the storm-wrecks that lay scattered around. Here a tree had been twisted off where the tough wood measured by feet instead of inches; there stood the white and shivered trunk of another sylvan lord, blasted in an instant by a lightning stroke; and there lay, prone upon the ground, giant limbs, which, but the day before, spread themselves abroad in proud defiance of the storm. Vines were torn from their fastenings; flower-beds destroyed; choice shrubbery, tended with care for years, shorn of its beauty. Even the solid earth had been invaded by floods of water, which ploughed deep furrows along its surface. And, saddest of all, two human lives had gone out while the mad tempest raged in uncontrollable fury.

As the lover and maiden stood looking at the signs of violence so thickly scattered around, the former said, in a cheerful tone--

"For all his wild, desolating power, the tempest is vassal to the sun and dew. He may spread his sad trophies around in brief, blind rage; but they soon obliterate all traces of his path, and make beautiful what he has scarred with wounds or disfigured by the tramp of his iron heel."

"Not so, my children," said the calm voice of the maiden's father, to whose ears the remark had come. "Not so, my children. The sun and dew never fully restore what the storm has broken and trampled upon. They may hide disfiguring marks, and cover with new forms of life and beauty the ruins which time can never restore. This is something, and we may take the blessing thankfully, and try to forget what is lost, or so changed as to be no longer desirable. Look at this fallen and shattered elm, my children. Is there any hope for that in the dew, the rain and sunshine? Can these build it up again, and spread out its arms as of old, bringing back to me, as it has done daily, the image of my early years? No, my children. After every storm are ruins which can never be repaired. Is it not so with that lightning-stricken oak? And what art can restore to its exquisite loveliness this statue of Hope, thrown down by the ruthless hand of the unsparing tempest? Moreover, is there human vitality in the sunshine and fructifying dew? Can they put life into the dead?

"No--no--my children. And take the lesson to heart. Outward tempests but typify and represent the fiercer tempests that too often desolate the human soul. In either case something is lost that can never be restored. Beware, then, of storms, for wreck and ruin follow as surely as the passions rage."

THE LOVERS.

IRENE DELANCY was a girl of quick, strong feelings, and an undisciplined will. Her mother died before she reached her tenth year. From that time she was either at home under the care of domestics, or within the scarcely more favorable surroundings of a boarding-school. She grew up beautiful and accomplished, but capricious and with a natural impatience of control, that unwise reactions on the part of those who attempted to govern her in no degree tempered.

Hartley Emerson, as a boy, was self-willed and passionate, but possessed many fine qualities. A weak mother yielded to his resolute struggles to have his own way, and so he acquired, at an early age, control over his own movements. He went to college, studied hard, because he was ambitious, and graduated with honor. Law he chose as a profession; and, in order to secure the highest advantages, entered the office of a distinguished attorney in the city of New York, and gave to its study the best efforts of a clear, acute and logical mind. Self-reliant, proud, and in the habit of reaching his ends by the nearest ways, he took his place at the bar with a promise of success rarely exceeded. From his widowed mother, who died before he reached his majority, Hartley Emerson inherited a moderate fortune with which to begin the world. Few young men started forward on their life-journey with so small a number of vices, or with so spotless a moral character. The fine intellectual cast of his mind, and his devotion to study, lifted him above the baser allurements of sense and kept his garments pure.

Trump impeached after Capitol riot in historic second charge

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump was impeached by the U.S. House for a historic second time Wednesday, charged with “incitement of insurrection” over the deadly mob siege of the Capitol in a swift and stunning collapse of his final days in office.

With the Capitol secured by armed National Guard troops inside and out, the House voted 232-197 to impeach Trump. The proceedings moved at lightning speed, with lawmakers voting just one week after violent pro-Trump loyalists stormed the U.S. Capitol, egged on by the president’s calls for them to “fight like hell” against the election results.

Ten Republicans fled Trump, joining Democrats who said he needed to be held accountable and warned ominously of a “clear and present danger” if Congress should leave him unchecked before Democrat Joe Biden’s inauguration Jan. 20.

Trump is the only U.S. president to be twice impeached. It was the most bipartisan presidential impeachment in modern times, more so than against Bill Clinton in 1998.

The Capitol insurrection stunned and angered lawmakers, who were sent scrambling for safety as the mob descended, and it revealed the fragility of the nation’s history of peaceful transfers of power. The riot also forced a reckoning among some Republicans, who have stood by Trump throughout his presidency and largely allowed him to spread false attacks against the integrity of the 2020 election.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi invoked Abraham Lincoln and the Bible, imploring lawmakers to uphold their oath to defend the Constitution from all enemies, foreign “and domestic.”

She said of Trump: “He must go, he is a clear and present danger to the nation that we all love.”

Holed up at the White House, watching the proceedings on TV, Trump later released a video statement in which he made no mention at all of the impeachment but appealed to his supporters to refrain from any further violence or disruption of Biden’s inauguration.

“Like all of you, I was shocked and deeply saddened by the calamity at the Capitol last week,” he said, his first condemnation of the attack. He appealed for unity “to move forward” and said, “Mob violence goes against everything I believe in and everything our movement stands for. ... No true supporter of mine could ever disrespect law enforcement.”

Trump was first impeached by the House in 2019 over his dealings with Ukraine, but the Senate voted in 2020 acquit. He is the first president to be impeached twice. None has been convicted by the Senate, but Republicans said Wednesday that could change in the rapidly shifting political environment as officeholders, donors, big business and others peel away from the defeated president.

Biden said in a statement after the vote that it was his hope the Senate leadership “will find a way to deal with their Constitutional responsibilities on impeachment while also working on the other urgent business of this nation.”

The soonest Republican Senate leader Mitch McConnell would start an impeachment trial is next Tuesday, the day before Trump is already set to leave the White House, McConnell’s office said. The legislation is also intended to prevent Trump from ever running again.

McConnell believes Trump committed impeachable offenses and considers the Democrats’ impeachment drive an opportunity to reduce the divisive, chaotic president’s hold on the GOP, a Republican strategist told The Associated Press on Wednesday.

McConnell told major donors over the weekend that he was through with Trump, said the strategist, who demanded anonymity to describe McConnell’s conversations.

In a note to colleagues Wednesday, McConnell said he had “not made a final decision on how I will vote.”

Unlike his first time, Trump faces this impeachment as a weakened leader, having lost his own reelection as well as the Senate Republican majority.

Even Trump ally Kevin McCarthy, the House Republican leader, shifted his position and said Wednesday the president bears responsibility for the horrifying day at the Capitol.

In making a case for the “high crimes and misdemeanors” demanded in the Constitution, the four-page impeachment resolution approved Wednesday relies on Trump’s own incendiary rhetoric and the falsehoods he spread about Biden’s election victory, including at a rally near the White House on the day of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

A Capitol Police officer died from injuries suffered in the riot, and police shot and killed a woman during the siege. Three other people died in what authorities said were medical emergencies. The riot delayed the tally of Electoral College votes that was the last step in finalizing Biden’s victory.

Ten Republican lawmakers, including third-ranking House GOP leader Liz Cheney of Wyoming, voted to impeach Trump, cleaving the Republican leadership, and the party itself.

Cheney, whose father is the former Republican vice president, said of Trump’s actions summoning the mob that “there has never been a greater betrayal by a President” of his office.

Trump was said to be livid with perceived disloyalty from McConnell and Cheney.

With the team around Trump hollowed out and his Twitter account silenced by the social media company, the president was deeply frustrated that he could not hit back, according to White House officials and Republicans close to the West Wing who weren’t authorized to speak publicly about private conversations.

From the White House, Trump leaned on Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina to push Republican senators to resist, while chief of staff Mark Meadows called some of his former colleagues on Capitol Hill.

The president’s sturdy popularity with the GOP lawmakers’ constituents still had some sway, and most House Republicans voted not to impeach.

Security was exceptionally tight at the Capitol, with tall fences around the complex. Metal-detector screenings were required for lawmakers entering the House chamber, where a week earlier lawmakers huddled inside as police, guns drawn, barricaded the door from rioters.

“We are debating this historic measure at a crime scene,” said Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass.

During the debate, some Republicans repeated the falsehoods spread by Trump about the election and argued that the president has been treated unfairly by Democrats from the day he took office.

Other Republicans argued the impeachment was a rushed sham and complained about a double standard applied to his supporters but not to the liberal left. Some simply appealed for the nation to move on.

Rep. Tom McClintock of California said, “Every movement has a lunatic fringe.”

Yet Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo. and others recounted the harrowing day as rioters pounded on the chamber door trying to break in. Some called it a “coup” attempt.

Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., contended that Trump was “capable of starting a civil war.”

Conviction and removal of Trump would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, which will be evenly divided. Republican Sen. Pat Toomey of Pennsylvania joined Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska over the weekend in calling for Trump to “go away as soon as possible.”

Fending off concerns that an impeachment trial would bog down his first days in office, Biden is encouraging senators to divide their time between taking taking up his priorities of confirming his nominees and approving COVID-19 relief while also conducting the trial.

The impeachment bill draws from Trump’s own false statements about his election defeat to Biden. Judges across the country, including some nominated by Trump, have repeatedly dismissed cases challenging the election results, and former Attorney General William Barr, a Trump ally, has said there was no sign of widespread fraud.

The House had first tried to persuade Vice President Mike Pence and the Cabinet to invoke their authority under the 25th Amendment to remove Trump from office. Pence declined to do so, but the House passed the resolution anyway.

The impeachment bill also details Trump’s pressure on state officials in Georgia to “find” him more votes.

While some have questioned impeaching the president so close to the end of his term, there is precedent. In 1876, during the Ulysses Grant administration, War Secretary William Belknap was impeached by the House the day he resigned, and the Senate convened a trial months later. He was acquitted.

The following morning brought with it a pall of unease that hung over the village like the fog that clung to the moor at dawn. Conversations, when they occurred, were hushed and furtive, as though the very空气 itself had become a witness to the uncanny events of the previous night. Old Mrs. Durgan, though her son and daughter-in-law had tried to dismiss her tale as the ramblings of age, insisted that the peculiar golden glare had been accompanied by a sound—something like distant singing, but not of children, she said, but of voices older, deeper, and more sorrowful than any human throat could manage. She spoke of it with a trembling lip and wide, unblinking eyes, her gnarled hands clutching the edge of her chair as though the very floor might give way beneath her.

In the village pub, the Red Lion, the landlord, a burly man named Tomkins, had overheard snippets of the tale from a traveler who had passed through on the road to Iping. The traveler spoke of a creature, large and shadowy, with wings that seemed to shimmer in the moonlight. He described it as something between a bird and a shadow, yet with an aura of misplaced familiarity, as though it should have been a part of the natural world but had been torn from its proper place. The landlord, though skeptical, found himself glancing nervously at the rafters above, as though the creature might yet linger there, unseen but ever-watchful.

For Sandy Bright, the memory of the Strange Bird lingered like a splinter beneath his skin. He had returned home that night, his thoughts a jumble of fear and something else—something he dared not name, even to himself. But as the days passed, the vision of that vast,Spread of wings and the golden glow it had carried began to take on a certain ... clarity. He found himself poring over old tomes in the village library, his fingers brushing over illustrations of mythical beasts and ancient birds, each one faintly reminiscent of the creature he had encountered. He spoke of it to no one, but the weight of it pressed upon him like a shrouded burden, making sleep a fitful thing and his waking hours a restless search for answers.

Meanwhile, the solicitor's clerk at Iping Hanger found himself the subject of whispered speculation. His account of the Strange Bird had been met with a mix of disbelief and awe, for he was not a man given to flights of fancy. But there was something in his description—of the bird's colours, shifting and impossible, of the way it seemed to move not through the air but alongside it—that gave his words a strange weight. The solicitor himself, a pragmatic man with little patience for the supernatural, found himself compulsively revisiting the clerk's report, as though the truth might leap from the page if he stared long enough.

Word of the golden glare and the Strange Bird had begun to spread beyond the immediate vicinity, carried by travelers and traders who found the tale both eerie and compelling. In the neighboring villages, the stories were embellished and exaggerated, each retelling adding new details—of spectral children dancing at the edge of the moor, of voices that called from the shadows, of a light that seemed to hold within it the promise of both revelation and doom. The villagers of Sidderford, for their part, found themselves caught between pride and unease, as though the world at large might soon discover that their quiet little corner of England was no longer so quiet, no longer so ordinary.

And yet, for all the talk and speculation, there remained a persistent silence at the heart of these events—a refusal to be fully understood, to be reduced to mere words or explanations. The golden glare had come and gone, leaving behind only the faintest trace of its passage, like the imprint of a hand on mist. The Strange Bird, too, had vanished into the darkness, its colours fading into the night as though it had never been. And yet, to those who had seen or heard of it, there remained a sense that it had not truly departed—that it lingered still, somewhere beyond the reach of mortal eyes, waiting.

As the days turned into weeks, the villagers of Sidderford began to experience strange, disconnected phenomena. Objects would be found misplaced, as though moved by unseen hands. The sound of laughter, soft and distant, would drift through the streets at odd hours, only to fade away when investigated.
