“True. It is for the Reverend Father Superior of San Jose Mission. I'll give it to him.”

Juanita was becoming alarmed, first at this prospect, second at the power the stranger seemed to be gaining over her. She recalled Francisco's description of him with something like superstitious awe.

“But it concerns Francisco. It contains a secret he should know.”

“Then you can tell him it. Perhaps it would come easier from you.”

Juanita blushed again. “Why?” she asked, half dreading his reply.

“Because,” said the American, quietly, “you are old playmates; you are attached to each other.”

Juanita bit her lips. “Why don't you read it yourself?” she asked bluntly.

“Because I don't read other people's letters, and if it concerns me you'll tell me.”

“What if I don't?”

“Then the Father Superior will.”

“I believe you know Francisco's secret already,” said the girl, boldly.

“Perhaps.”

“Then, Mother of God! Senor Crancho, what do you want?”

“I do not want to separate two such good friends as you and Francisco.”

“Perhaps you'd like to claim us both,” said the girl, with a sneer that was not devoid of coquetry.

“I should be delighted.”

“Then here is your occasion, Senor, for here comes my adopted father, Don Juan, and your friend, Senor Br--r--own, the American alcalde.”

Two men appeared in the garden path below them. The stiff, glazed, broad-brimmed black hat, surmounting a dark face of Quixotic gravity and romantic rectitude, indicated Don Juan Briones. His companion, lazy, specious, and red-faced, was Senor Brown, the American alcalde.

“Well, I reckon we kin about call the thing fixed,” said Senor Brown, with a large wave of the hand, suggesting a sweeping away of all trivial details. “Ez I was saying to the Don yer, when two high-toned gents like you and him come together in a delicate matter of this kind, it ain't no hoss trade nor sharp practice. The Don is that lofty in principle that he's willin' to sacrifice his affections for the good of the gal; and you, on your hand, kalkilate to see all he's done for her, and go your whole pile better. You'll make the legal formalities good. I reckon that old Injin woman who can swear to the finding of the baby on the shore will set things all right yet. For the matter o' that, if you want anything in the way of a certificate, I'm on hand always.”

“Juanita and myself are at your disposition, caballeros,” said Don Juan, with a grave exaltation. “Never let it be said that the Mexican nation was outdone by the great Americanos in deeds of courtesy and affection. Let it rather stand that Juanita was a sacred trust put into my hands years ago by the goddess of American liberty, and nurtured in the Mexican eagle's nest. Is it not so, my soul?” he added, more humanly, to the girl, when he had quite recovered from the intoxication of his own speech. “We love thee, little one, but we keep our honor.”

“There's nothing mean about the old man,” said Brown, admiringly, with a slight dropping of his left eyelid; “his head is level, and he goes with his party.”

“Thou takest my daughter, Senor Cranch,” continued the old man, carried away by his emotion; “but the American nation gives me a son.”

“You know not what you say, father,” said the young girl, angrily, exasperated by a slight twinkle in the American's eye.

“Not so,” said Cranch. “Perhaps one of the American nation may take him at his word.”

“Then, caballeros, you will, for the moment at least, possess yourselves of the house and its poor hospitality,” said Don Juan, with time-honored courtesy, producing the rustic key of the gate of the patio. “It is at your disposition, caballeros,” he repeated, leading the way as his guests passed into the corridor.

There are few joys so profound as those which accompany the discovery of a new treasure among the well-fingered tomes of an antiquarian bookshop, a place where the very air seems steeped in echoes of the past. One such day, while the autumnal sun hung low, casting elongated shadows mingled with the chill of a waning season, I chanced upon a hallowed corner of my beloved second-hand emporium. The proprietor, a wizened gentleman whose spectacles perched precariously upon his nose, seemed to detect my keen interest the moment I trespassed beyond the threshold, as though I were an incautious moth drawn to the flickering flames of his literary wares. Amid the morass of leather-bound volumes and yellowing paperbacks, I espied a small book, its spine battered yet regal, whispering tales of yore through its humble exterior. It was a copy of Virgil, my old friend, that had once brought solace during the query of my youth.

As I cradled the delicate book in my hands, a rush of reminiscence enveloped me. I was transported to the summer evenings spent beneath the lustrous branches of the great elm in my grandfather's garden, where the world melted away amidst verses of pastoral beauty and tributes to unearthly love. The scent of aged parchment caught a breeze, ushering forth the ghost of my grandfather, his familiar voice resonating in the aether: “You see, my boy, literature is far more than mere words. It is the heartbeat of those who dared to dream before us.” Could he have fathomed the delightful paradox that lay in my heart—the prizing of such light, lamentable reads while my stomach grumbled for the earth’s more miserable offerings? It was a time when I would barter a meal to sate my insatiable hunger for words, embodying a peculiar calculus of passion over punishment, a sweet trade made in the name of burgeoning intellect.

But such sacrifices, while rich with sentiment, rarely translated into financial peace; I often found myself lingering in the dusky shops that snaked through the quieter lanes of our modest town, hands trembling in anticipation as I thumbed through dog-eared pages. I had long since learned that there was a language in the scents of my volumes, each musty musk or faint whiff of rosemary acting as portals to uncharted territories of memory. I do not understand those who claim to prefer pristine copies, untouched by the eager hands of kindred spirits; to me, a book’s character lies in its very wear, the scuffs that bespeak a life well lived, and the frayed edges that echo with unspoken journeys. In this, even the most oft-visited volumes in my humble collection, like the tattered pages of my Milton or the once-resplendent editions of Thucydides, became akin to cherished friends, accompanied by laughter and perhaps a few tears.

It was on this gilded afternoon of serendipity, sorrows past and vanished laughter flowing like a brook through a forest glen, that I opened my newly-acquired Virgil. A thin leaf fluttered from its confines, landing delicately on the floor. I picked it up to discover fraying quill-written lines penned in a hand both elegant and fatigued, invoking a historical note from some forgotten soul of ages past—'To Anna, who loved like the July sun, but whose spirit waned, forever longing.' I felt an inexplicable kinship to this nameless reader and her elusive sorrows, as if we shared an interstitial thread through time. How curious that she, in the depths of her own quiet despair, had turned to Virgil’s words to salvage her essence, just as I had done countless nights in candlelight hemmed by shadows. I pondered, did she too wander the byways of life, trading sustenance for the nectar of words, her heart forever entwined with the pulse of her beloved books? Or, was she merely a wayward child of circumstance—one more to add to the risible roster of those who succumb to the charms of classic literature?

Thus within the pages of a simple book, I unearthed the entirety of an unseen saga. The tendrils of her existence intertwined with my own, borne upon the backs of our cherished authors—a sensibility forlorn yet enchanting. I cradled the volume a moment longer, inhaling the sweet bouquet of must and hope, allowing my imagination to paint silken images of Anna’s past wandering through a world both cold and inviting, just as I had been often drawn. Therein lay the romance of connection that transcends both time and space, and I vowed, silently, that this Virgil would not merely fulfill a place upon my shelf, but would serve as a testament to that eternal dialogue—the romantic, relentless pursuit of beauty, a bond forged in the unyielding passion for the written word.

Chandler's fiscal report for this year raises some intriguing points and leaves me wanting a clearer picture of the city's financial health. The most glaring figure is the $149 million allocated to public safety, a significant leap from the previous year and the largest expenditure by far. While it's reassuring to see Chandler boasts a lower crime rate than neighboring cities, it makes me wonder if such a substantial increase was entirely necessary and if it truly reflects increased safety or simply higher spending. Overall, expenses have ballooned to $495 million, resulting in a $6 million deficit. This raises concerns about short-term fiscal challenges, even as the city benefits from long-term population growth.

My analysis of Chandler's Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) deepens my concerns. The lack of comparative data from the previous year regarding assets and liabilities is a significant oversight. Without this context, it becomes difficult to accurately assess Chandler's true fiscal standing. Are we building a strong financial foundation, or are we neglecting crucial areas? The difference between the city's assets and liabilities could illuminate this, but the current CAFR stops short of providing that clarity.

Furthermore, the lack of detailed breakdowns in the CAFR, particularly compared to a Form 990, is frustrating. I would like to see more transparency in areas like the highest-paid employee salaries and a comprehensive breakdown of the transportation budget. Similarly, a detailed account of service charges would be invaluable in understanding the true cost of running city services versus business expenditures. Without this granular data, it's challenging to gain a complete understanding of Chandler's financial priorities and decision-making process.

“But,” says Abel, “it would look dretful odd to the neighbors if she didn’t dress in black.” Says he, in a skairful tone, and in his intense way,—

“I would ruther resk my life than to have her fail in duty in this way: it would make talk!” And says he, “What is life worth when folks talk?”

I turned around the crazed block, and tackled it in a new place (more luny than ever it seemed to me), and says I, mekanickly,—

“It is pretty hard work to keep folks from talkin’, to keep ’em from sayin’ sunthin’.”

But I see from their looks it wouldn’t do to say anything more, so I had to set still and see it go on.

At that time of year flowers wuz dretful high, but S. Annie and Abel had made up their minds that they must have several flower-pieces from the city nighest to Loontown.

One wuz goin’ to be a gate ajar, and one wuz to be a gate wide open. And one wuz to be a big book. Abel asked me what book I thought would be prefferable to represent. And I mentioned the Bible.

But Abel says, “No, he didn’t think he would have a Bible; he didn’t think it would be appropriate, seein’ the deceased wuz a lawyer.” He said “he hadn’t quite made up his mind what book to have. But anyway it wuz to be in flowers,—beautiful flowers.” Another piece wuz to be his name in white flowers on a purple background of pansies. His name wuz William Henry Harrison Rockyfeller. And I says to Abel,—

“To save expense, you will probable have the moneygram W. H. H. R.?”

“Oh, no,” says he.

Says I, “Then the initials of his given names, and the last name in full.”

“Oh, no,” he said; “it wuz S. Annie’s wish, and hisen, that the hull name should be put on. They thought it would show more respect.”

I says, “Where Harrison is now, that hain’t a-goin’ to make any difference;” and, says I, “Abel, flowers are dretful high this time of year, and it is a long name.”

But Abel said ag’in that he didn’t care for expense, so long as respect wuz done to the memory of the deceased. He said that he and S. Annie both felt that it wuz their wish to have the funeral go ahead of any other that had ever took place in Loontown or Jonesville. He said that S. Annie felt that it wuz all that wuz left her now in life, the memory of such a funeral as he deserved.

Says I, “There is his children left for her to live for,” says I,—“three little bits of his own life, for her to nourish, and cherish, and look out for.”

“Yes,” says Abel. “And she will do that nobly, and I will help her. They are all goin’ to the funeral, too, in deep-black dresses.” He said “they wuz too little to realize it now, but in later and maturer years it would be a comfort to ’em to know they had took part in such a funeral as that wuz goin’ to be, and wuz dressed in black.”

“Wall,” says I (in a quite onassumin’ way I would gin little hints of my mind on the subject), “I am afraid that will be about all the comforts of life the poor little children will ever have,” says I. “It will if you buy many more flower-pieces and crape dresses.”

Abel said “it wouldn’t take much crape for the children’s dresses, they wuz so little, only the baby’s: that would have to be long.”

Says I, “The baby would look better in white, and it will take sights of crape for a long baby dress.”

“Yes, but S. Annie can use it afterwards for veils. She is very economical; she takes it from me. And she feels jest as I do, that the baby must wear it in respect to her father’s memory.”

Says I, “The baby don’t know crape from a clothes-pin.”

“No,” says Abel, “but in after-years the thought of the respect she showed will sustain her.”

“I was saying, Monsieur l’Abbe,” he went on, “that you are wrong to take things so seriously. Shall I tell you what I think? This is a very fortunate affair.”

“Very fortunate?”

“Yes, very fortunate. I would rather see the Scotts at Longueval than the Gallards. Did you not hear Monsieur de Larnac reproach these Americans with spending their money foolishly. It is never foolish to spend money. The folly lies in keeping it. Your poor for I am perfectly sure that it is your poor of whom you are thinking--your poor have made a good thing of it to-day. That is my opinion. The religion? Well, they will not go to mass, and that will be a grief to you, that is only natural; but they will send you money, plenty of money, and you will take it, and you will be quite right in doing so. You will see that you will not say no. There will be gold raining over the whole place; a movement, a bustle, carriages with four horses, postilions, powdered footmen, paper chases, hunting parties, balls, fireworks, and here in this very spot I shall perhaps find Paris again before long. I shall see once more the two riders, and the two little grooms of whom I was speaking just now. If you only knew how well those two sisters look on horseback! One morning I went right round the Bois de Boulogne behind them; I fancy I can see them still. They had high hats, and little black veils drawn very tightly over their faces, and long riding-habits made in the princess form, with a single seam right down the back; and a woman must be awfully well made to wear a riding-habit like that, because you see, Monsieur l’Abbe, with a habit of that cut no deception is possible.”

For some moments the Cure had not been listening to Paul’s discourse. They had entered a long, perfectly straight avenue, and at the end of this avenue the Cure saw a horseman galloping along.

“Look,” said the Cure to Paul, “your eyes are better than mine. Is not that Jean?”

“Yes, it is jean. I know his gray mare.”

Paul loved horses, and before looking at the rider looked at the horse. It was indeed Jean, who, when he saw in the distance the Cure and Paul de Lavardens, waved in the air his kepi adorned with two golden stripes. Jean was lieutenant in the regiment of artillery quartered at Souvigny.

Some moments after he stopped by the little carriage, and, addressing the Cure, said:

“I have just been to your house, ‘mon parrain’. Pauline told me that you had gone to Souvigny about the sale. Well, who has bought the castle?”

“An American, Mrs. Scott.”

“And Blanche-Couronne?”

“The same, Mrs. Scott.”

“And La Rozeraie?”

“Mrs. Scott again.”

“And the forest? Mrs. Scott again?”

“You have said it,” replied Paul, “and I know Mrs. Scott, and I can promise you that there will be something going on at Longueval. I will introduce you. Only it is distressing to Monsieur l’Abbe because she is an American--a Protestant.”

“Ah! that is true,” said Jean, sympathizingly. “However, we will talk about it to-morrow. I am going to dine with you, godfather; I have warned Pauline of my visit; no time to stop to-day. I am on duty, and must be in quarters at three o’clock.”

“Stables?” asked Paul.

“Yes. Good-by, Paul. To-morrow, godfather.”

The lieutenant galloped away. Paul de Lavardens gave his little horse her head.

“What a capital fellow Jean is!” said Paul.

“Oh, yes, indeed!”

“There is no one on earth better than Jean.”

“No, no one.”

The Cure turned round to take another look at Jean, who was almost lost in the depths of the forest.

“Oh, yes, there is you, Monsieur le Cure.”

Concho was vexed, Concho was bruised, Concho was, to put it mildly, indignant. The untoward incident with the recalcitrant mule had not improved his humor, already soured by the deceptive liquor. The sun, a fiery orb in the cerulean heavens, seemed to mock his predicament, baking the very stones underfoot with relentless fervor.

He disentangled himself from the chaotic embrace of blankets, cooking pots, and sundry gear, casting a baleful glance at the prone animal. "¡Caramba!" he muttered, more to himself than to the offending creature. "This is a pretty pass, indeed. A plague upon all four-legged beasts and the trails they presume to traverse!"

He spat, a dry, dusty expectoration that landed harmlessly upon the parched earth. He considered his options, which seemed distressingly limited. He could remain where he was, a helpless supplicant to the whims of fate. Or, he could attempt to right the mule himself, a task that appeared, at best, fraught with peril, and at worst, likely to result in further injury.

He approached the mule cautiously, murmuring soothing words in a voice that belied his inner turmoil. "Come now, mi burra," he cajoled. "Get up, get up! There's sweet grass and cool water waiting at the top of the pass."

The mule remained stubbornly unresponsive, its eyes closed, its ears drooping. Concho sighed. He was beginning to suspect that the Americano’s diagnosis was more accurate than he had initially hoped. A slipped shoulder was no trifling matter, especially in this forsaken wilderness.

He rummaged through his pack, extracting a length of rope. With infinite patience, he fashioned a makeshift harness, attempting to support the injured shoulder. It was a clumsy affair, but it was the best he could manage under the circumstances.

He strained against the rope, pulling with all his might. The mule groaned, but remained resolutely earthbound. Concho grunted, his muscles screaming in protest.

"Mother of God, grant me strength!" he implored, the heathens did not seem to be helping.

Another heave, another groan from the mule, and then, with a sudden, disconcerting lurch, the animal was on its feet. Concho staggered backward, nearly losing his balance.

The mule stood trembling, its injured leg dangling awkwardly. It regarded Concho with a doleful expression, as if to say, "Is this truly necessary?"

Concho ignored the implied reproach. He tightened the makeshift harness, securing it as best he could. "There, there," he soothed. "We'll take it slow and easy."

And so, they began their ascent once more, Concho leading the hobbled mule with painstaking care. Every step was a trial, every inch gained a victory. The sun beat down mercilessly, the dust swirled around them in choking clouds, and the silence of the wilderness was broken only by the rasping breath of man and beast.

Hours passed, marked only by the slow, relentless progress up the mountain. Concho's body ached, his throat was parched, and his spirit was weary. But he pressed on, driven by a stubborn determination to overcome the obstacles that fate had placed in his path.

As the sun began its descent, casting long shadows across the landscape, they reached the crest of the pass. Before them lay a vista of breathtaking beauty: rolling hills, verdant valleys, and the shimmering expanse of the Pacific Ocean.

Concho paused, gazing at the scene with a sense of profound gratitude. He had faced adversity and overcome it. He had endured hardship and emerged stronger. And now, he stood on the precipice of a new beginning.

He smiled, a weary but genuine smile. "¡Gracias a Dios!" he whispered. "We made it." He then, with a renewed sense of purpose, began his descent into the valley below, the injured mule limping bravely beside him.

$2,000 Monthly Stimulus Checks Until the End of the Pandemic: A Growing Call Among Some Democrats in Congress

Some Democrats in Congress are pushing for monthly $2,000 stimulus checks until the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, arguing that recurring payments are essential to supporting struggling American families. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) and other Members of Congress recently sent a letter to President Joe Biden urging for recurring direct cash assistance. A similar push is underway in the Senate, where a group of Democratic lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), plan to send a letter to the president advocating for recurring stimulus checks and automatic unemployment insurance extensions tied to economic conditions.

"As Covid-19 continues to spread in the United States and the economic fallout endures, we urge you to include recurring direct cash assistance and automatic unemployment insurance extensions in your Build Back Better long-term economic plan," Omar and her colleagues wrote in their letter to Biden.

Senate Democrats' upcoming letter will not specify a dollar amount or frequency for the stimulus checks, leaving those details to be determined as part of ongoing negotiations in Congress. However, the proposal is expected to call for direct payments and the automatic extension of unemployment insurance benefits during periods of economic downturn.

"This crisis is far from over, and families deserve certainty that they can put food on the table and keep a roof over their heads," Sanders tells Forbes. "That's why Sen. Warren, Rep. Omar, and I are calling on President Biden to include recurring direct payments and automatic unemployment insurance extensions in his long-term economic plan."

The push for recurring stimulus checks comes as the U.S. Senate considers President Biden's stimulus package, which includes a one-time, $1,400 stimulus check for eligible individuals. However, the proposal for monthly $2,000 stimulus checks faces an uphill battle in the Senate, where Republicans and some moderate Democrats, including Sen. Joe Manchin (D-WV), are unlikely to support the measure.

Manchin, who has expressed concerns about the cost of President Biden's stimulus package, tells Forbes that he does not support the idea of recurring stimulus checks. "I don't think we need to be sending money out monthly," Manchin says. "We need to get people back to work."

Despite this opposition, supporters of the recurring payments argue that the measure is necessary to support struggling families and prevent further economic hardship. According to a recent analysis by the Urban Institute, a one-time $1,200 stimulus check and enhanced unemployment insurance could prevent 12 million people from falling into poverty.

President Biden, a moderate Democrat, is seen as unlikely to support the proposal for recurring checks. However, supporters argue that the idea has broad support among the American public, with a recent survey by Data for Progress finding that 65% of Americans, including majorities of Republicans and independents, favor monthly $2,000 stimulus checks.

"This is not a partisan issue; it's an American issue," Warren tells Forbes. "We need to make sure that every family in this country has the financial resources they need to get through this crisis and build a strong, stable future."

Florence was deeply moved. She was not prepared for so decisive a step as this on the part of her uncle.

She had supposed that he would storm a little, and then, finding that she was fixed in her resolution, would gradually become reconciled to the idea of her disobedience.

Now she found herself suddenly brought face to face with a serious problem. Was it right to sacrifice her whole future happiness for the sake of retaining a luxurious home? That was the question she had to answer.

"I will give you twenty-four hours to consider," said her uncle, abruptly. "At twelve o'clock tomorrow I will see you again. If you then decide to accept my proposition I will receive you in this room. If not, consider yourself no longer an inmate of this house. You can go to your room now."

Florence rose, and without a word, left the library.

"I have offended him past forgiveness," she thought, sadly. "But I cannot, cannot marry Curtis, even to please him."

Left to herself, Florence burst into a passion of tears. It was hard to leave the home where she had spent so many pleasant years.

Yet she did not waver in her resolution. She felt that she could not love Curtis, that she could never be happy as his wife, and this decided her.

She was aroused from her reflections by a knock at the door.

"Come in!" she said, mechanically.

The door opened, and a young man of twenty-three, with an effeminate air and a foppish manner, sauntered into the room.

"Ah, Miss Linden," he said, "I am charmed to see you looking so well. I heard you had a slight headache, and I thought I would drop in and offer my condolences."

This was Mr. Percy de Brabazon, a young man of fortune, who spent his time chiefly in paying attention to the ladies. He was reputed to be a great admirer of beauty, and Florence, who was very beautiful, he considered one of his greatest conquests.

"You are very kind, Mr. de Brabazon," said Florence, coldly. "My headache is quite insignificant."

"I am very glad to hear it," said Mr. de Brabazon, seating himself on the sofa by her side. "And how are you getting on with your little affair of the heart?"

"My affair of the heart?" repeated Florence, interrogatively.

"Yes, your marriage with your cousin, you know. It is quite the talk of the town."

"Indeed! I was not aware that it had become a matter of public comment."

"Oh, these things always will get out, you know," said Mr. de Brabazon, complacently. "But I must say, Miss Linden, that I think you are very wise to secure a good husband while you can."

"You do?"

"Yes, indeed. Marriage is an excellent institution, but it is well to be on the safe side, you know. There is nothing like a good settlement to make a woman happy."

Florence could not help smiling at this remark, though it was made at her expense.

"You seem to have a high opinion of matrimony, Mr. de Brabazon," she said.

"Oh, yes, indeed. But then, you know, I belong to one of the oldest families in England. We always make a point of marrying well in our family."

"I have heard that the English nobility pride themselves on their antiquity," said Florence, sarcastically.

"Yes, indeed," said Mr. de Brabazon, innocently unconscious of her sarcasm. "We think a great deal of blood in England, you know."

"So I have been led to believe," said Florence. "But I fear you will find little to interest you in our plebeian society."

"Oh, I don't know," said Mr. de Brabazon. "I find some very pleasant people in America. But then, you know, one must make allowances for a new country. You can't expect everything to be as it is in England."

"No, of course not," said Florence. "We must be content with our humble lot."

"Exactly," said Mr. de Brabazon. "But I am keeping you with my chatter. I must be going. Good-morning, Miss Linden. Pray give my regards to your uncle."

And Mr. Percy de Brabazon took his departure, highly pleased with himself and his visit.

The lady said, “An orphan’s fate Is sad and hard to bear.”--Scott.

“Mother, you could do a great kindness.”

“Well, Joe?”

“If you would have the little teacher at the Miss Heath’s here for the holidays. After all the rest, she has had the measles last and worst, and they don’t know what to do with her, for she came from the asylum for officers’ daughters, and has no home at all, and they must go away to have the house purified. They can’t take her with them, for their sister has children, and she will have to roam from room to room before the whitewashers, which is not what I should wish in the critical state of chest left by measles.”

“What is her name?”

“Allen. The cry was always for Miss Allen when the sick girls wanted to be amused.”

“Allen! I wonder if it can be the same child as the one Robert was interested about. You don’t remember, my dear. It was the year you were at Vienna, when one of Robert’s brother-officers died on the voyage out to China, and he sent home urgent letters for me to canvass right and left for the orphan’s election. You know Robert writes much better than he speaks, and I copied over and over again his account of the poor young man to go with the cards. ‘Caroline Otway Allen, aged seven years, whole orphan, daughter of Captain Allen, l07th Regiment;’ yes, that’s the way it ran.”

“The year I was at Vienna, and Robert went out to China. That was eleven years ago. She must be the very child, for she is only eighteen. They sent her to Miss Heath’s to grow a little older, for though she was at the head of everything at the asylum, she looks so childish that they can’t send her out as a governess. Did you see her, mother?”

“Oh, no! I never had anything to do with her; but if she is daughter to a friend of Robert’s--”

Mother and son looked at each other in congratulation. Robert was the stepson, older by several years, and was viewed as the representative of sober common sense in the family. Joe and his mother did like to feel a plan quite free from Robert’s condemnation for enthusiasm or impracticability, and it was not the worse for his influence, that he had been generally with his regiment, and when visiting them was a good deal at the United Service Club. He had lately married an heiress in a small way, retired from the army, and settled in a house of hers in a country town, and thus he could give his dicta with added weight.

Only a parent or elder brother would, however, have looked on “Joe” as a youth, for he was some years over thirty, with a mingled air of keenness, refinement, and alacrity about his slight but active form, altogether with the air of some implement, not meant for ornament but for use, and yet absolutely beautiful, through perfection of polish, finish, applicability, and a sharpness never meant to wound, but deserving to be cherished in a velvet case.

This case might be the pretty drawing-room, full of the choice artistic curiosities of a man of cultivation, and presided over by his mother, a woman of much the same bright, keen, alert sweetness of air and countenance: still under sixty, and in perfect health and spirits--as well she might be, having preserved, as well as deserved, the exclusive devotion of her only child during all the years in which her early widowhood had made them all in all to each other. Ten years ago, on his election to a lectureship at one of the London hospitals, the son had set up his name on the brass plate of the door of a comfortable house in a once fashionable quarter of London; she had joined him there, and they had been as happy as affection and fair success could make them. He became lecturer at a hospital, did much for the poor, both within and without its walls, and had besides a fair practice, both among the tradespeople, and also among the literary, scientific, and artistic world, where their society was valued as much as his skill. Mrs. Brownlow was well used to being called on to do the many services suggested by a kind heart in the course of a medical man’s practice, and there was very little within, or beyond, reason that she would not have done at her Joe’s bidding. So she made the arrangement, exciting much gratitude in the heads of the Pomfret House Establishment for Young Ladies; though without seeing little Miss Allen, till, from the Doctor’s own brougham, but escorted only by an elderly maid-servant, there came climbing up the stairs a little heap of shawls and cloaks, surmounted by a big brown mushroom hat.

East Coast Fuel Crisis: Long Lines, Price Hikes as Colonial Pipeline Hack Disrupts Supply

CLEMMONS, N.C. (AP) – A cyberattack on the Colonial Pipeline, which delivers approximately 45% of the East Coast's fuel, has caused panic-buying and long lines at gas stations, prompting concerns over fuel supply and leading to price hikes. Jeanette McGee, spokeswoman for the American Automobile Association (AAA) auto club, expressed her concerns, saying, "With Memorial Day weekend just around the corner, this is not the news drivers wanted to hear."

The Colonial Pipeline was shut down due to the cyberattack on May 7, 2021. According to Jamar Gatison, a construction worker and Uber Eats driver in Clemmons, "I've been seeing long lines at gas stations for days now. People are really worried." However, government officials and energy analysts have clarified that there is no gasoline shortage, but a distribution issue due to the pipeline shutdown.

Mair Martinez, a landscaper in Raleigh-Durham, reported that 28% of gas stations in North Carolina were out of fuel, with some areas experiencing much higher numbers, such as 72% in the Raleigh-Durham region. In response, North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper declared a state of emergency on May 10, 2021, to ease fuel transportation into the state.

The national average price for a gallon of gasoline rose above $3 for the first time since 2016, according to AAA. With over 37 million Americans expected to travel during the Memorial Day weekend, anticipating a significant increase in fuel demand, officials are seeking alternative transportation routes for fuel to mitigate the disruption.

Johnathan King, an employee at a towing company in Greensboro, NC, stated, "We've been receiving a lot of calls about cars running out of gas on the side of the road. It's been a busy few days."

Jen Psaki, White House press secretary, announced that the U.S. government is coordinating efforts to prevent fuel shortages, including allowing certain states to transport overweight loads of fuel. The Department of Homeland Security is prepared to review Jones Act waiver requests to alleviate fuel shortages.

Psaki emphasized, "We want to reassure the American people that there is no fuel shortage in this country. We have ample supply, and we're working to ensure that it gets to where it needs to go as quickly as possible."

McGee from AAA noted, "We're encouraging drivers to conserve fuel as much as possible during this time. Simple steps like carpooling, combining errands, and staying home if you don't need to travel can help ease the strain on fuel supplies."

Cooper expressed his concern, stating, "This situation is serious, and we need to take swift action to get fuel moving again. That's why I've declared a state of emergency to help expedite the transportation of fuel into North Carolina."

Martinez, the landscaper, added, "I just hope this gets resolved soon. I need gas to get to my job sites and keep my business running."

Gatison, the construction worker and Uber Eats driver, shared, "I've had to cancel a few rides because I ran out of gas myself. It's a tough situation for a lot of people."

As the situation continues to unfold, the East Coast grapples with the uncertainty of when the Colonial Pipeline will be back online and when fuel supplies will return to normal. The AAA, government officials, and energy analysts urge patience and conservation as efforts are made to mitigate the disruption caused by the cyberattack.

“Why should I listen to you?” she had said more than once. “I do not love you. You do not please me. When you wish to marry me, I hate you. Go away, and speak to some one else.”

“I will never marry any one,” she said to José. “I will stay with you and be happy. Girls who marry grow ugly and are wretched. Their husbands do not love them after they are married. They must work and slave and take care of the house and the children. Look at Tessa! Her husband used to be wild about her. She could make him pale with misery if she turned away from him; he used to follow her about everywhere. Now he makes eyes at Juanita, and beats Tessa if she complains. And don’t we both remember how it was with our mother? I will never love any one, and never be married. Let them love me if they are so stupid, but I will be left alone. I care nothing for any of them.”

The truth is that José knew it was what she remembered of her mother’s unhappiness and what Jovita had told her, which was the foundation of all this. Did he not remember it himself, and remember, with a shudder, those first miserable years of their childhood--the great, beautiful, wretched eyes of their mother, their gay, handsome father, and his careless cruelty and frequent brutality? Had not Pepita and himself clung together hidden in the loft at night, listening to their mother’s sobs, and often to the sound of blows and curses rained down upon her because she was no longer a beauty, and there were beauties who had smiles to bestow on handsome fellows who were free, and even upon those who were not? It was enough to irritate any handsome fellow--this one had thought--to come home to a squalid place after enjoyment, and be forced to face poverty and children and a haggard wife with large staring eyes, red with weeping. Yes, Pepita and José remembered all this, and upon Pepita’s character it had left curious traces. Young as she was, she had awakened quite grand passions in more than one heart, and on two or three occasions the suitors had been of far better fortune than herself--one of them, indeed, being the only son of a rich farmer, who might have chosen a wife of much greater importance than this pretty, scornful child, and whose family rebelled bitterly against his folly, and at last sent him away to Seville, but not before Pepita herself had coolly trodden him under her small feet.

“I like you less than any of them,” she said, fixing her great, direct eyes upon him when he revealed his frenzy. “Go and marry that girl your father chose for you--if she will have you. They have no need to be afraid and speak ill of me. I don’t want you. I can’t bear to have you stand near me.”

To José it never occurred to complain of her, but Jovita’s sense of worldly advantage was outraged at this time, and she did not hesitate to express herself with much freedom and grumbling.

“God knows, I want no haste,” she said; “but this is a chance for any girl. And see what a fool she is. But that is as it always happens. There will come along some worthless fellow, and she will be fooled like the rest, and be ready enough to run after him.”

“I!” said Pepita, who stood in the doorway. “I!” And she opened her dark eyes in genuine anger and amazement.

“Yes, you,” answered Jovita. “And you will be worse than any of them. Girls who think themselves too good to be spoken to are always easiest to coax when they find their match. Let him come, and you’ll drop like a ripe grape.”

“He will never come,” said Pepita. “Never!” And there was not a shade of doubt in her look--nothing but cold indignation at Jovita’s ill-humor. “I am not afraid of men. They are all stupid. They think they can have anything they want, and they can have nothing. They have to ask, and it is the girls who can say ‘No;’ and then they are miserable, and beg and beg until one detests them. If any one said ‘No’ to me, I would not let them see it hurt me. They should think I did not care.”

The morning sun filtered through the heavy draperies, casting a golden pattern across the Turkoman rug, which harmonized with the rich mahogany of the furniture that seemed almost to converse in their own silent language. Our protagonist, now resolved, or so he believed, sat with a determination that was only slightly undermined by the habitual inclinations of a gentleman who hardly ever rose before noon without some internal battle. Candle-sticks were still aglow on the mantelpiece, denoting the late hour he had kept company with himself and his inward deliberations. No sooner had the first flush of dawn adorned the horizon than the sober reality of his decision began to settle upon him like a well-worn cloak.

Market Harborough! He rolled the name over his tongue as if tasting the bouquet of a fine claret, a slight furrow creasing his brow in concentration. The prospect seemed agreeable, almost idyllic, devoid of the ostentation that plagued Melton or the boisterous assemblies of Leamington. Fox-hunting would be unfettered, free from the encumbrances of fashion and social rivalry, granting him the liberty to devote his days to the meditative solitude of the chase. Yet no resolution comes without its snags; the social elite would surely judge his choice inferior. Those same acquaintances, who favoured conversation over cognac at old city clubs and considered their own societal grandeur as indispensable as their finely tailored jackets, would surely raise their eyebrows and purse their lips in delicate disapproval. However, not even the disdainful glances of his social contemporaries could dissuade him now; indeed, their opinions, much like the remnants of smoked cigars lingering in an emptied room, seemed inconsequential to the liberation he anticipated.

With that matter firmly behind him, he began to think on the preparations for his departure, considering with meticulous care the wardrobe requisite for such an endeavor—a collection of serviceable tweeds and riding boots well-burnished, yet neither too new nor too worn, striking that fine balance between practical and presentable. It would not do to appear anything less than a gentleman fully aware of his station, even amidst a community less renowned for its finery. Then there was the choosing of the mounts, each of which ought to be capable, sound, and, of course, discreetly handsome; they must be born to the hunt, keen in scent and sure of foot, but without inciting envy or scorn among his future companions of the field.

A gentle knock at the chamber door disturbed his reverie, revealing the familiar face of his manservant, whose patience and tact had long served as an indispensable complement to his own lack of both. A letter awaited on the silver tray carried with the ser

vant's customary air of unobtrusive efficiency. He recognized the seal immediately—a friend from the days at Eton, now living a life of purported leisure in Market Harborough, speaking of social seasons and the fine details of provincial living in ink and paper almost as vivid as conversation over a brandy. A timely correspondence, perhaps. Breaking the seal, he surveyed its contents with a growing sense of pleasure.

His friend extolled the virtues of their rural congregation, the ease with which propriety intermingled with congeniality, a lauded balance absent elsewhere, like the blending of gentian and vernal notes in a particularly fine port. The sporting days were highlighted as mere adjuncts to evenings enlivened with ribaldry and tales of derring-do whispered through curling smoke as firelight danced in the hearth. There would be straightforward folk—the salt of the earth, uncomplicated in their mirth and woes alike, offering no less than a full embrace of camaraderie and sport.

Thus it was settled, his heart and mind conclusively aligned; he would send a wire posthaste, ensuring lodgings prepared and arrangements finalized. But first, he allowed himself the luxury of a long, thoughtful gaze out of the window, the vista offering a prequel to the adventure soon to unfold over fields unfettered by the scandalous artifice of society that so often tainted his urban sphere. The gleam of the morning sun's advance across pasture and steadfast stone walls promised new discourse, new friendships, and a chapter yet untold—fresh canvases for mundane and noble pursuits alike, not unlike the moment when one encounters a blank page, pen poised for storytelling erudition. And so he lingered, poised, almost caught between himself and the anticipation of his newly appointed fate, until the breakfast bell drew him to the more immediate concern of intake and sustenance.

WHO Designates New SARS-CoV-2 Variant B.1.1.529 as a Variant of Concern, Named Omicron

Geneva, Switzerland - The World Health Organization (WHO) Technical Advisory Group on SARS-CoV-2 Virus Evolution (TAG-VE) met on 26 November 2021 to evaluate the recently identified B.1.1.529 variant of the virus responsible for COVID-19. This variant was first reported to the WHO by South Africa on 24 November, with the earliest known infection dating back to 9 November 2021.

The B.1.1.529 variant, now designated as a Variant of Concern (VOC) and named Omicron, has drawn global attention due to its significant number of mutations. Preliminary evidence indicates that this variant may pose an increased risk of reinfection compared to other circulating variants.

South Africa has witnessed a rapid rise in Omicron cases across most of its provinces, highlighting the potential for increased transmissibility. However, current SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) diagnostic tests remain effective in detecting the Omicron variant. A notable feature is the S gene target failure in one PCR test, which can serve as an indicator of this specific variant.

Based on the available evidence, the TAG-VE recommended the classification of B.1.1.529 as a VOC. The WHO has promptly communicated this decision to its member states and will continue to provide updates as new information becomes available.

In response to the emergence of Omicron, the WHO is urging countries to enhance their surveillance and sequencing efforts to identify and report cases associated with this VOC. Public health measures, such as mask-wearing, physical distancing, hand hygiene, and ventilation, remain critical in controlling the spread of the virus. Vaccination against COVID-19 is also essential, as it continues to provide protection against severe disease and death.

The WHO defines a Variant of Interest (VOI) as a SARS-CoV-2 variant with specific genetic changes that are suspected to affect transmissibility, disease severity, immunity, or diagnostic or therapeutic tools. A Variant of Concern (VOC), like Omicron, is a VOI that has been demonstrated to have increased transmissibility, more severe disease, decreased effectiveness of treatments or vaccines, or difficulty in detection.

Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, the WHO's COVID-19 Technical Lead, emphasized the importance of global collaboration in monitoring and responding to new variants. "We must work together to understand the potential implications of this variant and ensure that all countries have access to the tools and resources needed to detect, sequence, and respond effectively," she stated.

As the world continues to grapple with the ongoing pandemic, the WHO's classification of Omicron as a VOC underscores the need for continued vigilance, research, and global cooperation in the fight against COVID-19.

Chauvin's Knee Remained on Floyd's Neck Throughout Restraint, Expert Testifies

In a pivotal moment at Derek Chauvin's murder trial, a use-of-force expert testified that Chauvin kept his knee on George Floyd's neck or neck area for the entire 9 1/2 minutes Floyd lay prone with his hands cuffed behind his back.

Los Angeles Police Department Sergeant Jody Stiger, serving as a prosecution witness, analyzed video evidence and concluded that Chauvin applied continuous pressure to Floyd's neck from the moment officers pinned him down until paramedics moved him onto a stretcher.

Prosecutor Steve Schleicher presented the jury with a composite of five still images, asking, "That particular force did not change during the entire restraint period?"

"Correct," replied Stiger, who had previously testified that the force used against Floyd was excessive.

Defense attorney Eric Nelson challenged Stiger, pointing to moments in the video where Chauvin's knee appeared to be on Floyd's shoulder blade area or the base of his neck. Stiger conceded that the officer's knee might have shifted at times but maintained that it remained in proximity to Floyd's neck in the contested images.

Earlier, lead Minnesota state investigator James Reyerson initially agreed with Nelson that Floyd seemed to say "I ate too many drugs" in a police body-camera video. However, upon reviewing a longer clip, Reyerson revised his interpretation, believing Floyd actually said "I ain't do no drugs."

Chauvin, 45, faces murder and manslaughter charges in connection with Floyd's death on May 25, 2020. Floyd, 46, was arrested outside a convenience store after allegedly attempting to pass a counterfeit $20 bill. During the arrest, Floyd struggled and claimed to be claustrophobic, prompting officers to pin him to the ground.

Bystander video capturing Floyd's cries of "I can't breathe" while onlookers pleaded with Chauvin to release him sparked widespread protests and scattered violence across the U.S.

Nelson argues that Chauvin, a now-fired white officer, acted in accordance with his 19 years of training. He suggests that Floyd's drug use and underlying health conditions, not Chauvin's knee, caused his death. Toxicology reports confirmed the presence of fentanyl and methamphetamine in Floyd's system.

Forensic experts Breahna Giles and Susan Meith testified that pills found in Floyd's SUV and the police squad car contained methamphetamine and fentanyl. One pill, found in the back of the squad car, contained DNA from Floyd's saliva.

Earlier, Nelson questioned Stiger about "lawful but awful" uses of force, acknowledging that actions may appear brutal to the public but remain legal under certain circumstances. Nelson also emphasized the distracting presence of a growing crowd of onlookers during the incident.

The philosophical landscape of Western thought is markedly shaped by the contributions of two towering figures: Plato and Aristotle. Both philosophers significantly influence human understanding of ethics, metaphysics, and epistemology. While both engage deeply with the nature of morality, they diverge in essential ways, reflecting their distinct methodologies and underlying assumptions. All major religions posit that sincere morality is intrinsically rewarded, often correlating ethical behavior with ultimate existential validation. However, the philosophical inquiry into morality suggests that true moral action cannot be exclusively motivated by self-interest or the pursuit of reward. This fundamental premise serves as a backdrop for the exploration of Plato's and Aristotle's theories of Forms and their implications for moral philosophy.

Plato articulates a vision of morality deeply entwined with his metaphysical framework, particularly evident in his theory of Forms. He posits that the realm of Forms constitutes a domain of abstract, perfect versions of perceivable objects, such as beauty, justice, and goodness. These Forms exist independently of the material world, transcending the limitations of space and time. Plato's distinction between the sensible world, characterized by imperfection and temporal existence, and the intelligible realm of Forms underscores his belief that true wisdom arises from understanding these eternal essences. As he famously states in "The Republic," “the philosopher, when he sees the truth of the things, turns away from the world of appearances and ascends to the knowledge of the real.”

In contrast, Aristotle emerges as a critical voice to Plato's idealism, offering an empirical approach that seeks to ground philosophy in observable reality. He challenges Plato's theory of Forms through rigorous inquiry, questioning the existence of abstract entities divorced from the particulars of the material world. Aristotle’s empirical investigations lead him to assert that the essence of a thing cannot exist independently of it; instead, he argues that substance and form are intrinsically connected. In his work "Metaphysics," Aristotle emphasizes, “the essence of a thing does not reside in a separate realm of existence,” thus employing an ontology that is bound to the particulars of the world rather than an abstract plane of ideal forms.

The philosophical rift between Plato and Aristotle extends beyond metaphysics into ethical theory. Plato's belief in the Forms leads him to argue that moral truths exist as objective realities, accessible through philosophical contemplation. For him, the knowledge of the Good is paramount, elevating the moral agent to a higher state of being. Conversely, Aristotle's ethical framework, articulated in the "Nicomachean Ethics," advocates for a more pragmatic approach to virtue. He posits that ethical behavior is achieved through the cultivation of habits, highlighting the importance of character and context in moral decision-making. Aristotle contends that virtue lies in achieving a mean between extremes—a nuanced perspective that underscores the complexities of human behavior.

The debates between Plato and Aristotle continue to resonate within contemporary discussions of ethics and metaphysics. Their contrasting philosophies invite scholars to navigate the delicate interplay between abstract ideals and concrete realities. Plato’s metaphysical idealism espouses a world where perfect forms offer guidance to moral agents, whereas Aristotle’s grounded realism suggests that understanding morality requires engagement with the material world and the nuances of human experience. In essence, these philosophical giants present two distinct paths for the exploration of knowledge and ethics, one that reaches for transcendent truths and another that grapples with the immanent struggles of human life. Their dialogues not only enrich the field of philosophy but also illuminate enduring questions about the nature of morality, knowledge, and human existence.

Tiger Woods Faces Long Road to Recovery After Serious Car Accident

Tiger Woods, one of the greatest golfers of all time, is facing a long and uncertain recovery after sustaining serious leg injuries in a car accident. The 45-year-old golfer, who has won 82 PGA Tour events and 15 major championships, may be hospitalized for several weeks and could require a stabilizing frame for his leg, according to Gian Corrado, Northeastern's head team physician and Associate Director of the Sports Medicine Fellowship Program at Boston Children's Hospital.

Corrado, who has not treated Woods personally but has experience working with athletes who have suffered similar injuries, warned that Woods's recovery could be a long and difficult process. "It's not just about the physical healing, but also the mental and emotional toll that being away from golf will take on him," Corrado said.

Dan Boothby, who oversees Northeastern's athletic trainers, physical therapists, and strength-and-conditioning coaches, echoed Corrado's concerns. "The focus should be on Tiger's survival and healing, rather than a return to golf," Boothby said. "Emotional healing is just as important as physical healing in this case."

Woods's history of substance abuse also poses a risk for his mental health during recovery. Law enforcement officials found no signs of substance influence at the crash scene, but Corrado noted that past substance abuse can still have a negative impact on mental health.

The recovery process for Woods is expected to be long and grueling. Rehabilitation will likely start with gentle exercises, but setbacks are a possibility. "It's important to remember that every injury is different, and Tiger's recovery will be unique to him," Corrado said.

Despite the challenges ahead, Woods has a strong support system in place. His girlfriend, Erica Herman, has been by his side throughout the ordeal, and his team of medical professionals is committed to helping him recover fully.

Woods's accident has sent shockwaves through the golf world, with many of his fellow golfers expressing their support and concern for his well-being. The golf community is rallying around Woods, and fans are eagerly awaiting his return to the course.

However, Corrado and Boothby caution that a return to championship golf form may not be in the cards for Woods. "It's important to focus on Tiger's overall health and well-being, rather than his return to golf," Boothby said. "The road to recovery will be long and difficult, but with the right support and care, Tiger can overcome this challenge."

As Woods begins his journey to recovery, the golf world will be watching with bated breath. His determination and resilience have carried him through many challenges throughout his career, and fans are hopeful that he will overcome this setback as well.

In conclusion, Tiger Woods faces a long and uncertain road to recovery after his serious car accident. His physical injuries are significant, and the mental and emotional toll of being away from golf could be just as challenging. However, with the support of his medical team, loved ones, and the golf community, Woods has the strength and determination to overcome this setback and emerge stronger than ever.

I think that the reader will agree with me that my mother showed in her conduct great strength of character. She had been compelled to marry a man whom she despised, and to whom she felt herself superior in every respect; she had done so to save her reputation. That she had been in error is true but situation and opportunity had conspired against her; and when she found out the pride and selfishness of the man to whom she was devoted, and for whom she had sacrificed so much,--when her ears were wounded by proposals from his lips that she should take such a step to avoid the scandal arising from their intimacy--when at the moment that he made such a proposition, and the veil fell down and revealed the heart of man in its selfishness, it is not to be wondered that, with bitter tears, arising from wounded love, anger, and despair at her hopeless position, she consented. After having lost all she valued, what did she care for the future? It was but one sacrifice more to make, one more proof of her devotion and obedience. But there are few women who, like my mother, would have recovered her position to the extent that she did. Had she not shown such determination, had she consented to have accompanied her husband to the barracks, and have mixed up with the other wives of the men, she would have gradually sunk down to their level; to this she could not consent. Having once freed herself from her thraldom, he immediately sunk down to his level, as she rose up to a position in which, if she could not ensure more than civility and protection, she was at all events secure from insult and ill-treatment.

Such was the state of affairs when I had arrived at the important age of six years, a comic-looking, laughing urchin, petted by the officers, and as fall of mischief as a tree full of monkeys. My mother's business had so much increased, that, about a year previous to this date, she had found it necessary to have some one to assist her, and had decided upon sending for her sister Amelia to live with her. It was, however, necessary to obtain her mother's consent. My grandmother had never seen my mother since the interview which she had had with her at Madeline Hall shortly after her marriage with Ben the marine. Latterly, however, they had corresponded; for my mother, who was too independent to seek her mother when she was merely the wife of a private marine, now that she was in flourishing circumstances had first tendered the olive branch, which had been accepted, as soon as my grandmother found that she was virtually separated from her husband. As my grandmother found it rather lonely at the isolated house in which she resided, and Amelia declared herself bored to death, it was at last agreed that my grandmother and my aunt Amelia should both come and take up their residence with my mother, and in due time they arrived. Milly, as my aunt was called, was three years younger than my mother, very pretty and as smart as her sister, perhaps a little more demure in her look, but with more mischief in her disposition. My grandmother was a cross, spiteful old woman; she was very large in her person, but very respectable in her appearance. I need not say that Miss Amelia did not lessen the attraction at the circulating library, which after her arrival was even more frequented by the officers than before.

My aunt Milly was very soon as fond of me as I was of mischief; indeed it is not to be wondered at, for I was a type of the latter. I soon loved her better than my mother, for she encouraged me in all my tricks. My mother looked grave, and occasionally scolded me; my grandmother slapped me hard and rated me continually; but reproof or correction from the two latter were of no avail; and the former, when she wished to play any trick which she dared not do herself, employed me as her agent; so that I obtained the whole credit for what were her inventions, and I may safely add, underwent the whole blame and punishment; but that I cared nothing for; her caresses, cakes, and sugar-plums, added to my natural propensity, more than repaid me for the occasional severe rebukes of my mother, and the vindictive blows I received from the long fingers of my worthy grandmother. Moreover, the officers took much notice of me, and it must be admitted, that, although I positively refused to learn my letters, I was a very forward child. My great patron was a Captain Bridgeman, a very thin, elegantly-made man, who was continually performing feats of address and activity; occasionally I would escape with him and go down to the mess, remain at dinner, drink toasts, and, standing on the mess-table, sing two or three comic songs which he had taught me. I sometimes returned a little merry with the bumpers, which made my mother very angry, my old grandmother to hold up her hands, and look at the ceiling through her spectacles, and my aunt Milly as merry as myself. Before I was eight years old, I had become so notorious, that any prank played in the town, any trick undiscovered, was invariably laid to my account; and many were the applications made to my mother for indemnification for broken windows and other damage done, too often, I grant, with good reason, but very often when I had been perfectly innocent of the misdemeanour. At last I was voted a common nuisance, and every one, except my mother and my aunt Milly, declared that it was high time that I went to school.

The sun had sunk low behind the horizon, and the long shadows of the parlor stretched across the carpet like the fingers of some unseen presence. Mrs. Waring sat by the window, a lace shawl draped over her shoulders, her hands folded in her lap. The ticking of the ormolu clock on the mantelpiece seemed to echo the steady, relentless march of time, a reminder of the years that had passed since her wedding day, yet the memory of that morning remained as vivid as if it had been yesterday. She could still see the white dress, the delicate lace, the_SCOREheartbeat of anticipation as she walked down the aisle. But now, as she glanced at Henry’s portrait above the mantel, a faint shadow crossed her face. The passage of time had not dimmed her affection, but it had tempered it, like a flame that burns steadily but no longer blazes with the same fierce intensity.

The baby, little Henry, slept soundly in his cradle, his breath coming in soft, regular puffs. Beesy, the nurse-maid, was busy with her sewing, her needle moving deftly through the fabric as she hummed a tune beneath her breath. Mrs. Waring watched her for a moment, then her gaze drifted to the door. She could hear the faint sound of footsteps in the hallway, the creak of a stair, and a moment later, Henry himself entered the room, his tall frame casting a shadow that fell across the hearth.

“How tired you look,” he said, coming to stand beside her. His voice was gentle, but there was a weariness in it that she did not miss. He placed a hand on her shoulder, and she leaned into it slightly, though she could not summon the warmth she once would have felt at his touch.

“Perhaps I am,” she replied, her tone cooler than she intended. “The day has been long with the baby.”

Henry smiled, but it did not reach his eyes. “It is a trying age,” he said. “But I suppose he will sleep better soon, won’t he?”

Mrs. Waring nodded, but her mind was elsewhere. She had been waiting for this moment, the moment when Henry would turn to her and—she did not know quite what, but something. A word, a glance, a gesture that would bridge the growing gap between them. But instead, he had come in to speak of trivialities, as he so often did, as though the weight of their circumstance did not press upon him as it did upon her.

The silence between them lengthened, heavy with unspoken words. Beesy, sensing the tension, lowered her needlework and glanced up, her dark eyes betraying her unease. Mrs. Waring gave her a imperceptible nod, and the girl dipped her head, returning to her sewing with renewed concentration.

“Ethel,” Henry said at last, his voice hesitant, “there is something I must tell you.” He turned to face her, his hands clasped behind his back. “I have received a letter from my brother. He and his family are coming to visit next week. It will be a fortnight at least.”

Mrs. Waring’s heart sank. She had hoped, vaguely, for something else, though she could not have said what. A word of affection, perhaps, or a promise of change. But this—this news of a family visit—seemed to confirm her worst fears. Her face fell, and Henry, noticing, frowned.

“What is it?” he asked. “You look as though I have told you something dreadful.”

“It is dreadful,” she replied, her voice trembling slightly. “A fortnight with your family? Henry, I have not seen you in days without the children interrupting us, and now—”

He raised an eyebrow. “Ethel, I beg your pardon, but you are not making much sense. A fortnight with my family is not dreadful. It is an opportunity for us to socialize, to have a little diversion—”

“No, Henry, I cannot abide it,” she interrupted, her voice rising. “I have had enough of diversion. What I want—what I need—is—” She paused, her throat tight.

“Ethel?” Henry prompted, his tone softening. “What is it you require?”

Mrs. Waring turned to him, her eyes tearing. “I require your understanding,” she said. “I require—”

“Ethel,” he interrupted, his patience fraying, “you must not speak to me in this way. I have done nothing to deserve such—”

“You have done nothing?” she cried, her voice breaking. “You have done everything! You call me Ethel when you are angry, and ‘Doll’ when you are not. You presume to know my thoughts, to understand my feelings, when you have not a notion of what it is to be me!”

“‘Doll’?” Henry repeated, his expression one of genuine surprise. “Where did you get that notion, Ethel? I have never—”

“Yes, you have!” she exclaimed, her voice shaking with emotion. “You have called me ‘Doll’ a thousand times, as though I am nothing more than a child’s plaything, a trinket to be tossed aside when you are weary of it!”

Henry’s face darkened. “Ethel, I have never meant—”

“Do not ‘Ethel’ me!” she interrupted, leaping to her feet, her hands clenched into fists. “I am not a child, Henry. I am your wife, and I deserve to be treated as such!”

The room seemed to hold its breath, the tension crackling like a live wire. Beesy, sensing the storm, had long since departed with the baby, leaving the two of them alone. Henry’s hand tightened on the edge of the chair, his knuckles white.

“Ethel,” he said at last, his voice low and dangerous, “you must calm yourself.”

“Do not tell me to calm myself!” she cried. “How dare you presume to instruct me on how to behave, when you—”

“Ethel,” he interrupted again, his tone sharp. “Sit down.”

She froze, her eyes narrowing. “No,” she said. “I will not. Not until you understand—”

“Ethel, I am your husband,” he said, his voice rising. “You will do as I say.”

Mrs. Waring stared at him, her chest heaving. There was a moment of pure, crystalline clarity, a moment when she saw him as he was, not as she had once imagined him. He was not the man she had married, not the man she had fallen in love with. He was a stranger, a shadow of the man he had once been.

She turned away from him, her shoulders shaking. “Go,” she said, her voice trembling. “I cannot bear to look at you.”

Henry stood for a moment, his face a mask of disbelief, then he turned on his heel and left the room, the door slamming behind him. Mrs. Waring sank to her knees, her hands covering her face. For a long time, she sat there, the silence of the room pressing down upon her, the weight of her loneliness heavier than she could bear.

“You persist, Fernand,” said the dark-eyed Mercédès, her voice barely a whisper above the mournful cry of a seagull circling overhead, “in a pursuit that wounds us both. Must I reiterate, yet again, what lies etched within my very soul?”

“But Mercédès,” Fernand pleaded, his hands outstretched as if to grasp not only her person but also the very air that surrounded her, “consider, I implore you. Is a life of solitude and unanswered affection truly preferable to the solace of a devoted husband? A man who would lay down his very life for your happiness?”

“Solitude?” she questioned, a wry smile playing upon her lips. “Am I truly alone when every waking moment is filled with the image of another? When the very name you utter – Fernand – serves only to conjure the memory of he who possesses my heart?”

Fernand’s face clouded with a mixture of pain and frustration. “And this phantom, this dream, this…” he searched for the appropriate word, “…fantasy! Is he capable of offering you the security, the comfort, that I can? Does he understand the ways of our people, the bonds of kinship that tie us together?”

“Our kinship, Fernand, is one of shared childhood, of familiar faces and sun-drenched days spent upon the shore. It is not a kinship of the heart. And as for security… security purchased at the cost of one’s very soul is a gilded cage, not a sanctuary.”

“But poverty, Mercédès! Look around you. We are but humble fisherfolk, scraping a meagre existence from the unforgiving sea. Can you truly envision a life of hardship with this… this other man?”

Mercédès turned her gaze towards the shimmering expanse of the Mediterranean, her dark eyes reflecting the endless horizon. “Hardship I can endure, Fernand, with a heart filled with love. Hardship without love is a barren desert, a life devoid of all joy.”

Fernand stepped closer, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “Rumours reach even these humble ears, Mercédès. Whispers of Parisian gentlemen, of fortunes squandered and promises broken. Is this the path you choose? To be swept away by a charming rogue, only to be abandoned to a life of destitution and regret?”

A flicker of something akin to anger flashed in Mercédès’ eyes. “You presume too much, Fernand. You paint a portrait of a man you do not know, of a life you cannot comprehend. His heart is as true as the North Star, his intentions as pure as the driven snow.”

“And yet,” Fernand persisted, his voice laced with a desperate plea, “you remain here, bound by tradition, by circumstance. Are you not even tempted to accept a life, a future, with a man who has loved you since boyhood? A man who would reshape himself, remold his very being, to become the husband you desire?”

Mercédès reached out and gently touched Fernand’s cheek, her expression filled with a sorrowful tenderness. “Do not speak of reshaping yourself, Fernand. You are who you are: a strong, capable, and loyal man. But your heart belongs elsewhere, though you refuse to see it. And mine… mine is forever lost.”

She paused, her gaze softening. “Remain a fisherman, Fernand. It is in your blood, in your very soul. It is a noble profession, a life of honest toil. Do not sacrifice your true calling in pursuit of a love that can never be.”

Fernand stood silently, his shoulders slumped in defeat. The sea gulls continued their mournful cries, a fitting soundtrack to the unspoken tragedy unfolding between them. The sun began its descent, casting long shadows across the beach, as Mercédès turned and walked away, leaving Fernand alone with his unrequited love and the bitter taste of rejection. The chapter that was about to start would be one of resentment, but the readers were unaware of it.

The moment is perhaps not the most auspicious, but yet we will make use of it, in order to give a slight sketch of the two contending persons.

Harald Bergman had speaking, somewhat sharp features, in which an expression of great gravity could easily be exchanged for one of equal waggery. The dark hair fell in graceful waves over a brow in which one saw that clear thought was entertained. His figure was finely proportioned, and his movements showed great freedom and vigour.

He had been brought up in a respectable family, had enjoyed a careful education, and was regarded by friends and acquaintances as a young man of extraordinary promise. Just as he had left the S. seminary, and was intending a journey into foreign countries, in order to increase still more his knowledge of agriculture, chance brought him acquainted with the widow of Colonel Hjelm, at the time in which she was returning to her native country, and in consequence thereof he altered his plans. In a letter to his sister, he expresses himself on this subject in the following manner:

"I cannot properly describe to you, Alette, the impression which she made upon me. I might describe to you her tall growth, her noble bearing, her countenance, where, spite of many wrinkles and a pale-yellow complexion, traces of great beauty are incontrovertible; the lofty forehead, around which black locks sprinkled with grey, press forth from beneath her simple cap. I might tell of her deep, serious eyes, of her low and yet solemn voice; and yet thou couldst form to thyself no representation of that which makes her so uncommon. I have been told that her life has been as much distinguished by exemplary virtue as by sufferin–nd virtue and suffering have called forth in her a quiet greatness, a greatness which is never attained to by the favourites of fortune and of nature, which stamps her whole being. She seemed to me as if all the frivolities of the world passed by her unremarked. I felt for her an involuntary reverence, such as I had never felt before for any human being; and at the same time a great desire to approach her more nearly, to be useful to her, to deserve, and to win her estee–t seemed to me that I should thereby become somewhat greater, or at least better; and as I was informed that she sought for a clever and experienced steward for her sorely decayed estate, I offered myself as such, in all modesty, or rather without any; and when accepted, I felt an almost childish joy, and set off immediately to her estate, that I might make myself at home there, and have everything in readiness to receive her."

Thus much for Harald, now for Susanna.

Barbara Susanna Björk was not handsome, could not be even called pretty (for that, she was too large and strong), but she was good-looking. The blue eyes looked so honestly and openly into the world; the round and full face testified health, kindness, and good spirits; and when Susanna was merry, when the rosy lips opened themselves for a hearty laugh, it made any one right glad only to look at her. But true is it, that she was very often in an ill humour, and then she did not look at all charming. She was a tall, well-made girl, too powerful in movement ever to be called graceful, and her whole being betrayed a certain want of refinement.

Poor child! how could she have obtained this in the home abounding in disorder, poverty, and vanity, in which the greater part of her life had been passed.

Her father was the Burgomaster of Uddevalla; her mother died in the infancy of her daughter. Soon afterwards an aunt came into the house, who troubled herself only about the housekeeping and her coffee-drinking acquaintance, left her brother himself to seek for his pleasures at the club, and the child to take care of herself. The education of the little Susanna consisted in this, that she learned of necessity to read, and that when she was naughty they said to her, "Is Barbra there again? Fie, for shame, Barbra! Get out, Barbra!" and when she was good again, it was, "See now, Sanna is here again! Welcome, sweet Sanna!" A method which certainly was not without its good points, if it had only been wisely applied. But often was the little girl talked to as "Barbra" when there was no occasion for it, and this had often the effect of calling forth the said personage. In the mean time, she was accustomed as a child to go out as Barbra, and to come in again as Sanna, and this gave her early an idea of the two natures which existed in her, as they exist in every person. This idea attained to perfect clearness in Susanna's religious instruction,--the only instruction which poor Susanna ever had. But how infinitely rich is such instruction for an ingenuous mind, when it is instilled by a good teacher. Susanna was fortunate enough to have such a one, and she now became acquainted in Barbra with the earthly demon which should be overcome in Sanna, the child of heaven, which makes free and enlightens; and from this time there began between Barbra and Sanna an open strife, which daily occurred, and in which the latter, for the most part, got the upper hand, if Susanna was not too suddenly surprised by a naturally proud and violent temper.
