Miss Martha Compton, and Miss Sophia Compton, were, some five-and-twenty years ago, the leading beauties of the pretty town of Silverton in Devonshire.

The elder of these ladies is the person I propose to present to my readers as the heroine of my story; but, ere she is placed before them in the station assigned her in my title-page, it will be necessary to give some slight sketch of her early youth, and also such brief notice of her family as may suffice to make the subsequent events of her life, and the persons connected with them, more clearly understood.

The Reverend Josiah Compton, the father of my heroine and her sister, was an exceedingly worthy man, though more distinguished for the imperturbable tranquillity of his temper, than either for the brilliance of his talents or the profundity of his learning. He was the son of a small landed proprietor at no great distance from Silverton, who farmed his own long-descended patrimony of three hundred acres with skilful and unwearied industry, and whose chief ambition in life had been to see his only son Josiah privileged to assume the prefix of reverend before his name. After three trials, and two failures, this blessing was at last accorded, and his son ordained, by the help of a very good-natured examining chaplain of the then Bishop of Exeter.

This rustic, laborious, and very happy Squire lived to see his son installed Curate of Silverton, and blessed with the hand of the dashing Miss Martha Wisett, who, if her pedigree was not of such respectable antiquity as that of her bridegroom, had the glory of being accounted the handsomest girl at the Silverton balls; and if her race could not count themselves among the landed gentry, she enjoyed all the consideration that a fortune of one thousand pounds could give, to atone for any mortification which the accident of having a ci-devant tallow-chandler for her parent might possibly occasion.

But, notwithstanding all the pride and pleasure which the Squire took in the prosperity of this successful son, the old man could never be prevailed upon by all Mrs. Josiah's admirable reasonings on the rights of primogeniture, to do otherwise than divide his three hundred acres of freehold in equal portions between the Reverend Josiah Compton his son, and Elizabeth Compton, spinster, his daughter.

It is highly probable, that had this daughter been handsome, or even healthy, the proud old yeoman might have been tempted to reduce her portion to the charge of a couple of thousand pounds or so upon the estate; but she was sickly, deformed, and motherless; and the tenderness of the father's heart conquered the desire which might otherwise have been strong within him, to keep together the fields which for so many generations had given credit and independence to his race. To leave his poor little Betsy in any degree dependent upon her fine sister-in-law, was, in short, beyond his strength; so the home croft, and the long fourteen, the three linny crofts, the five worthies, and the ten-acre clover bit, together with the farm-house and all its plenishing, and one half of the live and dead farming stock, were bequeathed to Elizabeth Compton and her heirs for ever--not perhaps without some hope, on the part of her good father, that her heirs would be those of her reverend brother, also; and so he died, with as easy a conscience as ever rocked a father to sleep.

But Mrs. Josiah Compton, when she became Mrs. Compton, with just one half of the property she anticipated, waxed exceeding wroth; and though her firm persuasion, that "the hideous little crook-back could not live for ever," greatly tended to console and soothe her, it was not without very constant reflections on the necessity of keeping on good terms with her, lest she might make as "unnatural a will as her father did before her," that she was enabled to resist the temptation of abusing her openly every time they met; a temptation increased, perhaps, by the consciousness that Miss Betsy held her and all her race in the most sovereign contempt.

As I continue to reflect upon my time among the mind-readers, I find myself captivated by the artifice to which we cling in our customary societies—the masks that we wear unknowingly, the well-practiced smiles, and the layers of artful dance around unspoken thoughts. Here was a place where none of that mattered, where the soul's nakedness was an accepted inevitability and regarded as the natural state of being. Each mind, laid open like a book on a shelf, was not a cause for alarm or scandal but a testament to the unhurried sincerity that knit the society together. The barriers we so diligently maintain, the veils and curtains of our innermost sanctuaries, were avenues here, pathways rather than partitions. In my early days, shadows of old habits would rise within me, tugging at the corners of my consciousness—a reflex born of generations taught that some thoughts were best left unspoken, some feelings too raw for the light of others’ eyes. Yet, the longer I lingered, the more natural the condition became. I began to understand that thoughts, unchecked and free as birds in a vast sky, found both their flight and fulfillment among those similarly untethered.

It was thus that I came to appreciate a sentiment I had never before entertained: the sweet freedom of no longer being weighed by the ponderous chains of secrets. Indeed, the cravings for isolation, for the gulfs we erect of faux privacy, seemed to me a curious relic of another world. I marveled at the candor with which one could lay bare the heart's desires and despairs, confident that the truth, shorn of guile and pretense, would meet comprehension, not condemnation. No whisper of malevolence or deceit marred this atmosphere, for what use had they where there were no barriers to breach? Instead, each revelation brought with it the balm of understanding and the strength of shared experience. It seemed to me as though I had been granted a reprieve from the melodrama of guarded existences; the clarity that emerged from such transparency was as a brisk river current, washing away the residues of an old and crumbling world. Observing the harmony born of their openness, the simplicity yet profoundness therein, I came to harbor the belief that such nakedness of mind was not just the aberration of a secluded people, but a glimmer—a foreshadowing, perhaps—of a world not yet realized, wherein humanity, unshackled by the iron clasp of its own insecurities, might find the truest form of paradise.

Richards sees a gap in the luggage market: a carry-on that effectively prevents clothing wrinkles. His product idea, O-Fold, is born from the increasing frustration travelers face with airline baggage fees and the inevitable wrinkling of packed clothes. While the concept holds promise, Richards' journey to launch O-Fold and achieve profitability is paved with challenges. He lacks experience in the industry, has limited capital, and faces a daunting competitive landscape dominated by giants like Samsonite and Louis Vuitton, brands with established reputations and vast resources. Additionally, building a team, marketing the product, and scaling operations all present significant hurdles.

A strategic, multi-pronged approach is essential for O-Fold to succeed. Given the limited resources, a 'crawl, walk, run' business model is recommended. This model emphasizes minimizing initial overhead and gradually scaling operations as revenue grows. Instead of directly competing with established brands in the mass market, Richards could explore a licensing agreement with a company already established in the luggage industry. This approach bypasses the need for large upfront investments in manufacturing and distribution, allowing him to leverage the licensee's existing infrastructure and market reach. Imagine a scenario where O-Fold's innovative wrinkle-free design is incorporated into a Samsonite carry-on line. This partnership could give O-Fold instant credibility and access to a global customer base.

Simultaneously, Richards needs to build brand awareness and generate initial sales. This can be achieved through a lean team focused on digital marketing. The team's primary responsibilities include building a user-friendly website with high-quality product photography, creating engaging tutorial videos demonstrating O-Fold's unique features and benefits, and managing low-cost online advertising campaigns targeting travelers frustrated with wrinkled clothes. Word-of-mouth marketing, incentivized through referral programs, can further amplify reach. Early operations can be managed from Richards' home, minimizing overhead. Securing a patent for O-Fold's unique design is crucial and should be pursued within the U.S. government's one-year grace period. This patent protection safeguards O-Fold's intellectual property and strengthens its market position, whether Richards chooses to license the product or build his own brand.

“Of course, Positivism claiming to be a creed of demonstration, not of faith, Régnier did not ask me to receive this proposition as his mere statement, but proceeded to establish its reasonableness by logic. I am going to give you what I remember of his argument, because I believe still, as I did when I heard it, that it is the only philosophical explanation of the instinctive reverence of man for woman which we have been talking about to-night. It was given to me, of course, as a doctrine peculiar to Positivism; but I don’t know of any form of religious belief, inconsistent with the recognition of the sacred quality of womanhood on the grounds given by Régnier. Indeed, I am by no means sure whether the doctrine as I received it is orthodox Positivism at all. I have reason to think that Régnier was quite too original a character for a very good interpreter, and should be interested to know how far his ideas were his own and how far his master’s.

“First he pointed out to me as matter of fact that there was no more striking feature of the modern and humane as compared with the ancient and barbaric world than the constantly growing tendency of the most civilized races to apotheosize womanhood. The virgin ideal had been set up by the larger part of Christendom as the object of divine honors. The age of chivalry had translated for all time the language of love into that of worship. Art had personified under the feminine form every noble and affecting ideal of the race, till now it was in the name of woman that man’s better part adjured his baser in every sort of strife towards the divine. Is it alleged that it is man’s passion for woman that has moved him thus in a sort to deify the sex? Passion is no teacher of reverence. Moreover, it is as the race outgrows the dominion of passion that it recognizes the worshipfulness of woman. The gross and sensual recognize in her no element of sacredness. It is the clear soul of the boy, the poet, and the seer which is most surely aware of it. Equally vain is it to seek the explanation in any general superiority of woman to man, either moral or mental. Her qualities are indeed in engaging contrast with his, but on the whole no such superiority has ever been maintained. How, then, were we to account for a phenomenon so great in its proportions that either it indicates a world-wide madness infecting the noblest nations while sparing the basest, or else must be the outcome of some profound monition of nature, which, in proportion as man’s upward evolution progresses, he becomes capable of apprehending? Why this impassioned exaltation by him of his tender companion? What is the secret spring that makes her the ceaseless fountain of lofty inspiration she is to him? What is the hint of divinity in her gentle mien that brings him to his knees? Who is this goddess veiled in woman whom men instinctively reverence yet cannot name?

“The adoration of woman, which may almost be called the natural religion of the modern man, springs from his recognition, instinctive when not conscious, that she is in an express sense, as he is not, the type, the representative, and the symbol of the race from which he springs, of that immortal and mystical life in which the secret of his own is hid. She is this by virtue, not of her personal qualities, but of the mother-sex, which, overbearing in part her individuality, consecrates her to the interests of the race, and makes her the channel of those irresistible attractions by which humanity exists and men are made to serve it. As compared with woman’s peculiar identification with the race, man’s relation to it is an exterior one. By his constitution he is above all an individual, and that is the natural line of his development. The love of woman is the centripetal attraction which in due time brings him back from the individual tangent to blend him again with mankind. In returning to woman he returns to humanity. All that there is in man’s sentiment for woman which is higher than passion and larger than personal tenderness--all, that is to say, which makes his love for her the grand passion which in noble hearts it is--is the fact that under this form his passion for the race finds expression. Mysterious ties, subtending consciousness, bind him, though seemingly separate, to the mighty life of humanity, his greater self, and these are the chords which, when ‘Love took up the harp of life,’... ‘passed in music out of sight.’ In woman humanity is enshrined and made concrete for the homage of man. This is the mighty indwelling which causes her to suggest something more august than herself, and invests her with an impersonal majesty commanding reverence.

“An odd fish!” commented March mentally. “Why should a civilized family haul him after them like a badly made kite tail? And they are not vulgarians, either!”

His eyes strayed discreetly back to the table set for seven. The mistress of ceremonies sat at the head, and was studying the printed menu. It lay flat on the cloth that the crippled girl at her right might read it with her. Their heads were close together, and the gravity upon the countenance of the elder was reflected by the shrewd elfin face. Presently they began to whisper, the bare, thin finger of the younger of the two tracing the lines to the extreme right of the carte. It was plainly a question of comparative expense, March perceived with a pang of his kind heart. For he had been a boy himself, and the children were hungry.

“Hurry up—won’t you, Hetty,” called the redheaded twin impatiently. “Give us the first thing you come to so long as it isn’t corned beef, pork and beans, or rice pudding. I’m starved!”

“Me, too!” echoed his fellow.

“You needn’t make mincemeat of your English on that account!” piped the crippled sister tartly. “It is no little matter to order just the right things for such a host. Mamma, you must have a cup of tea, I suppose?”

The young lady interposed, writing while she talked:

“Of course! And all of us will be the better for some good, hot soup. This is luncheon, not dinner, recollect. We only need something to stay our appetites until six o’clock,” she added, putting the paper in the waiter’s hand.

She did not look like one who did things for effect, yet there was meaning in her manner of saying it. If she was obliged to cut her coat according to her cloth, she would just now make the scantiness of the pattern seem a matter of choice and carry out the seaming gallantly.

“How much further have we to go?” queried eight-year-old, somewhat ruefully.

Six o’clock was to her apprehension a long time ahead.

“We are within half an hour of home. We might have been there by now, but we thought it better to wait over a train to rest and get rid of the dust we brought off the cars.”

“And to let him get shaved and barbered and prinked up generally!” shrilled the cripple malevolently.

“Hester!” The mother’s voice was heard for the first time.

“Well, mamma?”

“That is not respectful, my love. You are tired, I am afraid.”

The shrewd face jerked fretfully, and the lips were opened for a retort, checked by a gloved hand laid upon the forward child’s. There was only a murmur, accompanied by a pettish shrug.

March was ashamed of the impulse that made him steal a look at the tray bearing the result of the whispered consultation. Three tureens, each containing two generous portions of excellent English gravy soup with barley in it, a pot of tea, bread and milk for the baby and plenty of bread and butter were duly deposited upon the board.

“I’ll take the rest of your order now,” said the waiter, civilly suggestive.

“This is all. Thank you!” in a matter-of-course tone that was not resentfully positive.

The “courier” understood herself, and having taken ground, how to hold it. This was luncheon. March caught himself speculating as to the dinner bill of fare.

As soon as Vixen had withdrawn from Captain Winstanley's study, her heart swelled with a strange mixture of trepidation and exultation. The idea of leaving the Abbey House, of escaping the stifling confines of its bleak corridors and echoing halls, filled her with an eagerness she could scarcely contain. Yet, amid this yearning for freedom, there lingered a heaviness in her chest - a disquietude that gnawed at her resolve.

She paced through the rooms of the Abbey House, her footsteps echoing like a questioning echo through the vast halls. The very walls seemed to press upon her, whispering tales of sorrow and solitude. It was as if the house, with its endless rooms and gilded ennui, had ensnared her spirit, demanding its tribute in tears.

Vixen sought solace in the vast, sunlit garden, where the scent of roses mingled with the crisp morning air. The sun cast long shadows across the dew-drenched lawn, and for a fleeting moment, she draped herself against the cool stone of the arbor, feeling the soothing caress of the ivy. Here, among the fragrant blooms, she allowed her thoughts to wander.

Yet, happiness was a fleeting visitor in Vixen's garden of dreams. The memory of Captain Winstanley's agreement to her departure weighed heavily upon her heart. It was a captive bird's acceptance of the cage's door being open - relieved yet apprehensive. The decision to depart left her suspended between hope and dread, torn between the promise of new horizons and the fear of the unknown.

It was not long before Captain Winstanley called upon her once more. "Miss Tempest," he said, his voice as mild as the morning air, "I have arranged for your departure to Jersey. Aunt Fournier awaits your arrival, and she shall take great care of you."

Vixen's breath caught in her throat. Jersey was a distant promise, an island of refuge, yet it was far away from the only home she had known. The name of the place carried the weight of both comfort and exile, a beacon of safety against a storm and a gateway to irrevocable change.

As the days passed, Vixen prepared for her journey, her resolve hardening with each passing moment. The Abbey House receded into the distance, its stories and secrets folding around it like a shroud. She packed her belongings, each item carrying with it memories - some cherished, others regretted.

The day of her departure came, shrouded in the uncertain brightness of the early evening. Captain Winstanley escorted her to the dock, his demeanor unreadable. Vixen's carriage stood ready, the horses impatient to be on their way, eager to leave the confines of the land.

"You'll find Aunt Fournier a most considerate hostess," Captain Winstanley said, his words trailing off as he watched the ship pull away. Vixen nodded, her gaze fixed on the receding shore.

As the Abbey House slipped beneath the horizon, Vixen felt a peculiar jubilation mix with her sorrow. The sea, vast and unending, symbolized both her freedom and her loss. She turned her face to the wind, tasting the salty promise of adventure, and whispered a silent farewell to the life she had known.

And so, with the sun dipping below the waves, Vixen embarked on her journey, leaving behind the confines of the Abbey House and stepping onto a path fraught with uncertainty. Yet, within her, something stirred - a dormant spirit awakening to the promise of a new world.

In the solitude of her cabin aboard the ship, Vixen reflected on the journey she had undertaken. She was leaving behind not just a place, but a chapter that had been written in tears and longing. Ahead lay an unknown future, one where she would forge her own story, untethered by the constraints of the past.

The ocean's embrace was both comforting and vast, a testament to the endless possibilities that awaited her. And as the stars twinkled overhead, a whisper of hope fluttered in her heart - a quiet determination to find happiness beyond the walls of the Abbey House.

In the days and nights that followed, Vixen explored the contours of her new life. The rhythm of the sea became her heartbeat, and the islands around her, with their ancient tales and vibrant cultures, whispered secrets of resilience and survival.

The journey to Jersey was not merely a physical voyage; it was a transformative odyssey that would shape Vixen's destiny. And as she finally disembarked, the ground beneath her feet was that of a new beginning, where the weight of the past was left behind, and the promise of a future, filled with untapped dreams and possibilities, lay ahead.

In the end, Vixen Tempest was not just leaving the Abbey House; she was bidding farewell to a chapter defined by sorrow and constraint. As she stepped into the unknown, she carried with her the resolve to write a new story, one where happiness was not a fleeting visitor but a steadfast companion.

Twitter Suspends Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene Over Election Fraud Claims

Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene has found herself at the center of a social media storm after her Twitter account was temporarily suspended for violating the platform's integrity policy. The suspension came after she posted a series of tweets containing baseless allegations of election fraud in relation to the Georgia Senate elections.

Greene, an ardent supporter of former President Donald Trump and a proponent of the QAnon conspiracy theory, lashed out at Twitter, labeling the suspension as censorship. "Twitter is an enemy to free speech and Americans' rights are being stripped away," she said. "Conservatives are being targeted by the internet police for our political opinions."

QAnon, a far-right conspiracy theory, alleges that Trump was engaged in a secret war against a global cabal of Satan-worshipping paedophiles, a claim with no credible evidence. Greene's embrace of these theories has drawn criticism from both sides of the political aisle.

Twitter flagged at least two of Greene's tweets as "disputed" and limited their distribution, citing concerns about the "risk of violence." The move follows the platform's permanent ban on Trump's account and the mass removal of over 70,000 accounts linked to QAnon, actions that have ignited a firestorm among Republicans.

In the aftermath of the January 6 Capitol attack, for which Trump was impeached for a second time on charges of incitement, tech companies have come under scrutiny for their role in moderating content and limiting the spread of misinformation. Greene's suspension is the latest in a series of actions taken by social media giants to curb the spread of false information and potential incitement to violence.

"Free speech is under attack! Censorship is happening like never before!" Greene tweeted before her account was locked. "I will never back down. America is worth it."

The suspension of Greene's account has reignited the debate over the balance between freedom of expression and the responsibility of social media platforms to prevent the spread of harmful content. Critics argue that these actions amount to silencing conservative voices, while proponents of the moderation argue that it is necessary to maintain the integrity of the platforms and protect public safety.

As tensions between tech companies and conservative politicians continue to escalate, the future of online discourse and the role of social media in shaping public opinion remain at the forefront of the national conversation.

'It was wild': Tugboat crew rides out Hurricane Ida near landfall at Port Fourchon

What began as a routine job last week for the tugboat Brittany Lynn became a frightening struggle against Hurricane Ida.

Shannon Dryden, the 40-year-old relief captain of the Brittany Lynn, received his assignment Aug. 25 to pull a barge down from Bourg to Port Fourchon. The disturbance in the Gulf of Mexico that would morph into Hurricane Ida was days away from landfall.

“We were supposed to bring a barge down here to Port Fourchon to get loaded and get back out,” Dryden said during a phone interview Tuesday. “We were trying to get loaded and tried to get back out before the storm hit. Well, we got down here and it was raining and there were thunderstorms. We just didn’t have enough time to get out.”

Ida strengthened to a Category 4 hurricane as it churned toward Louisiana’s southeast coast. The storm swept ashore near Port Fourchon about 11:55 a.m. Sunday packing 150-mph winds and a storm surge forecasters and local officials estimated was at least 12 feet.

There was nothing the Brittany Lynn’s three-member crew could do except batten down the hatches and hope for the best, said Dryden, who is from Deridder.

“I definitely didn’t want to be down here because I knew this area was close to getting a direct hit,” he said. “You couldn’t see the debris flying through the air. We were tied up against a dock. There was a trailer of offices out there about 600 feet from us and you couldn’t see it during the storm. When the winds died down you could see right through that trailer. The walls were gone.”

As the boat rocked against Ida’s ferocious 150 mph winds, the unthinkable happened, Dryden said.

“At one point there when the eye was just about to come over us, there were some boats that got loose and hit our barges that we were tied to, which broke us loose,” he said. “I was looking at my chart system and could tell we were starting to move. I said to the head captain, ‘We broke loose, man. Those boats behind us done hit us and broke us loose.’ ”

It was the only time during the harrowing ordeal that Dryden said he was scared.

“The only time I got really worried was when we broke loose,” he said. “When it broke our barges loose and we went across the canal, I couldn’t tell which way we were going. All I could tell is that we were moving. I didn’t know if we were going to have to abandon the ship or what was fixing to happen.”

Ida’s winds tapered about 30 minutes later, which gave the crew just enough time to move the barges back to the dock and get secured, Dryden said.

But Ida wasn’t through with Port Fourchon just yet.

“No sooner than we got them secured, the back side of the eye came and we were in for another ride for about three or four hours,” Dryden said. “The back end was way worse. I was concerned, but at least it was blowing us to the dock and not away from it. It was wild.”

There were about 40 boats carrying around 300 people combined at Port Fourchon when Ida made landfall Sunday, said Chett Chiasson, executive director of the Greater Lafourche Port Commission.

The port, at the southern tip of Lafourche Parish, serves as the service hub for almost all of the Gulf of Mexico oilfield.

“There were no injuries for our employees and family and to my knowledge no major injuries in this area,” Chiasson said. “There will not be movement in the port until we can assess the navigable waterways for obstructions.”

As for Dryden, he said he will never ride out a storm on a boat again.

“That’s the first time and the last time for sure,” he said.

Harry and Meghan visit with Afghan refugees at Task Force Liberty

CNN — Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, visited a military base Thursday where they met Afghan refugees who had made it to the United States.

The couple spoke with women recently arrived at Task Force Liberty, on Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, New Jersey, which is home to more than 10,000 Afghan refugees, a spokesperson for them said. The royals asked to spend time with young children who were in daily schooling and stopped by a classroom of children learning conversational English.

Harry and Meghan talked with the kids, many of them practicing their English by saying phrases like, “Nice to meet you,” the spokesperson said. The couple asked staff about common terms in Dari – Persian dialects spoken in Afghanistan – and left every interaction with children and adults saying “Tashakur,” or “thank you.”

The teachers had been leading the song “Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes,” the spokesperson added. The Duke and Duchess “happily” led the children in singing the song, and said it’s a favorite of their son, Archie.

They thanked the teachers for their efforts, and reminded them to take care of themselves and their own mental health.

The couple join the children in singing the song "Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes." SSgt Jake Carter/Task Force Liberty Public Affairs

Harry and Meghan speak to some of the Afghan refugees who recently arrived in the US. SSgt Jake Carter/Task Force Liberty Public Affairs

Harry and Meghan are known for speaking openly about their mental health and for encouraging others to do the same.

According to the US Air Force Expeditionary Center website, “Task Force Liberty initiated in August in line with the withdrawal of American troops from Afghanistan. Active duty, guard and reserve service members from across the force came together with outside agencies to create a space that could provide support to over 10,000 Afghan guests as they immigrated into the United States.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Latest on Joe Biden’s presidential inauguration (all times local):

Joe Biden is making his return to the Washington area on the eve of his inauguration as the nation’s 46th president.

Biden touched down at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Tuesday afternoon, taking a brief flight from his home state of Delaware down to the District of Columbia. Born to the parched soil of a discontented country, Miss Blake was nourished on a diet of contradiction, a creature of such peculiar heritage that it might be said she wore her lineage like a garish cloak. Her mother, a daughter of the Scottish-Ulster hills, was renowned for her sharp tongue and sharper gaze; her father, a Connaught man of soft manners, bore an unwarranted affection for fanciful tales, often spinning them as finely as the cobwebs of a neglected attic. In this curious amalgamation of tempers and tendencies, my dear reader, Miss Blake stood a solitary monument to the caprices of fortune, embodying all the ire of her mother's ancestors while inheriting naught but romantic folly from her sire.

In company, her voice darted and curled, a chameleon’s adaptation to the shifting sands of social influence. One moment, it bore the crisp accent of Belfast; the next, it sported the dulcet tones of Galway, seducing her audience, yet diverting and disquieting those who sensed the dissonance lurking beneath her charming façade. It was as though the very air around her conspired to reflect the discordant nature of her spirit. Those unassuming souls who dared inquire about her origins would hear her deliver an unconsidered answer, as though rehearsing a monologue in a play for which she could never recall the lines.

“Such a delight to see you, Mrs. Murphy,” Miss Blake would simper, her words slick with feigned affection, every deep vowel marked by an ecstatic flourish that faded as swiftly as summer rain. Yet, beneath this preposterous artifice waned the unmistakable shavings of discontent. Like the unfortunate allocation of unripe fruit, she was an extravagance rendered meaningless by the lack of any contributing virtue.

As for her disposition, it leaned towards a mystifying paradox, an extravagant display devoid of generosity. For every extravagant gown she donned, with its flouncy ruffles and cascading laces, echoed a glimmer of her keen ability to extract without recompense—a voracious appetite for elegance tempered only by her mean tendency to clutch at purse strings whenever charitable impulses surfaced. Indeed, few knew the struggles she waged against the enticing grasp of parsimonious habits, waging clandestine battles in her mind, that Elysium of profligacy against the spectre of fiscal responsibility.

To encounter Miss Blake at the marketplace was to witness the theatre of her complicated character. Onlookers might marvel at her resplendent attire, each fabric chosen not merely for the sake of fashion but attuned to the whims of those around her. She filched admiration from her peers, yet offered them the currency of disdain in return. Bargaining sharply for the finest produce, she would ride roughshod over those who offered her too little respect; her words dipped in perfumed malice, leaving a bitter taste upon the lips of those unfortunate enough to cross her path.

And lo, to speak of her debts was to invite a tempest. Bills remained unpaid not through any prolonged bout of poverty, but due to a twisted sense of honor, or the lack thereof. Only when the shadows of imminent necessity loomed large did she grace the baker or the butcher with a coin, accompanied by protestations that echoed with a hollow conviction: “Aye, I shall prosper soon, but the affairs of the heart take precedence, you see.” Indeed, each repetitive plea belied her veracity, for, however tender their claims, the debts lingered as ghosts left to haunt her reputation.

In a peculiar twist of fate, her presence acted as both a burden and a boon to those who circled her sphere. Her absence was palpably lamented, for in the absence of her peculiar mischief one felt an unsettling void, a siren’s song transformed into silence. She became a stark reminder that even those wreathed in disdain could elicit longing. Thus, Miss Blake thrived upon this paradox of being a source of both vexation and nostalgia, her laughter as sharp as the candlelight was dim, forever flickering amid the currents of her controversial existence.

Such was the essence of Miss Blake: a creature remarkable for the very reasons one might deem unremarkable, a testament to the power of perception, and the contradictions that lay therein, lurking like leaves beneath the surface of a quiet pond.

The shadows deepened their grip on Hadleyburg and Mrs. Richards's heart remained an eager drum, pulsing with the echoes of the night's possibilities. She stood by the lamp, her fingers trembling as they grazed the edges of the newspaper. It was not just the sack of unknown riches lent by the foreigner's generosity that made her anxious. It was the thought of which local benefactor she might be honoring unknowingly. Could it be the kind Mr. Richards? The thought was bittersweet, for he was a man of earnestness, always content with his modest earnings and seldom touched by luck's capricious hand.

She unknotted the strings binding the letter and unfolded it, her eyes taking in each word with deliberate care. The foreigner's gratitude was palpable, and his tale of ascending fortune was enough to make one's mind teem with wild fantasies. The very thought of such wealth changing their lives stirred a whirlwind of emotions within her. Yet, alongside this hope, loomed the moral quandary. What of the moral implications? Accepting such funds, earned through chance and hazard, was far from the virtuous path she had always aspired to.

The room was silent save for the ticking of the clock, a melancholic reminder of the passage of time. Mrs. Richards weighed the dilemma on the delicate scales of her conscience. She glanced again at the paper, the light from the lamp casting shadows that seemed to dance with the sentiments she could barely voice. If only they could be deserving of such bounty, if only the benefactor could be her steadfast Mr. Richards. But to what ends would fortune be put, if not used to uplift the spirits of the good men of Hadleyburg?

And then, as if the very air held an answer, she recalled a tale her husband had once told of a similar windfall, only to see it slip through their fingers, squandered by those who doubted their integrity. A chill touched her spine at the remembrance. Could this be her husband's opportunity to prove his worthiness to himself and to her? Or would the coin be as treacherous as those that had come before?

The decision was a burden too heavy for her alone. She yearned for counsel, for wisdom that could untangle this web of right and wrong. But there was no one to turn to, no one who could truly understand the depth of her concerns. As the night deepened and the shadows grew, Mrs. Richards pressed her lips together, the resolution hardening within her like stone. She would trust in the goodness of man, in the purity of motives, and in the hope that fortune, when it shall come, will be as steadfast as the love she held for Mr. Richards, and as steadfast as the moral fiber of the benefactor, whose identity remained yet a mystery.

And thus, with the lamp burning steadily and the room cloaked in the quiet of night, Mrs. Richards awaited the dawn, pondering the enigmatic letter and the secrets it held, her heart a silent sanctuary for the dreams of a fortune found.

El Paso Emerged Unscathed from Winter Storm by Heeding Past Lessons

In El Paso, while residents of other Texas cities queued for groceries amidst barren shelves, Robert Gomez entered an Albertsons with ease on Wednesday. The store was not only well-stocked but also warm and brightly lit. A similar situation awaited him at Food King. The fifty-year-old graphic designer and his fellow El Pasoans encountered minimal disruption from a historic winter storm, despite having to navigate through remaining patches of snow and ice. The city had experienced subfreezing temperatures and three inches of snow and ice, yet life was largely unaffected.

On the same day, as Gomez scrolled through Twitter, the dire situations faced by Texans elsewhere—burst pipes, collapsing ceilings, and homes succumbing to the cold—prompted a compassionate response from him. He tweeted an invitation to those suffering in the cold: “TEXAS! Head west, far west. Our grid is up in El Paso, and we welcome anyone needing respite from this frigid chaos. Hotels, shelters, and hope.”

When the winter storms hit El Paso on February 14, the impact was markedly less severe than in the rest of Texas. Only about 3,000 residents experienced power outages, with power being swiftly restored for the majority within five minutes. Unlike millions in other parts of the state, no El Pasoan had to endure prolonged periods without power or heat. The city’s better fortune can be attributed to the lessons learned from a devastating storm in February 2011 and its connection to a different electric grid from the rest of Texas.

Separated by considerable distance from Texas's other major cities and serving customers in parts of southern New Mexico, El Paso's public utility is connected to the Western Interconnection grid, encompassing fourteen Western states, Canada, and Mexico. This setup allowed El Paso Electric to source additional power from the Palo Verde Nuclear Generating Station in Arizona when demand spiked, a luxury not afforded to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT)-managed grid that serves about 90% of Texas and is designed to avoid federal energy regulation.

ERCOT's grid, contained within Texas to eschew federal oversight, found itself unable to tap into external energy supplies when the winter storm disrupted its wind, nuclear, and natural gas sources. Steve Buraczyk, El Paso Electric’s senior vice president of operations, noted the significant supply disruptions facing ERCOT, describing the challenges of managing the crisis without external support.

A vital difference for El Paso Electric was the winterization of its power plants, a lesson learned after the 2011 storm left many customers without power. The utility has since invested millions in preparing for extreme winter conditions, spending $4.5 million to adapt its facilities to operate in freezing temperatures. This preparation involves insulating valves, transmitters, and pipelines, and installing heat lamps where needed, similar to winter-proofing a home but on a much grander scale. This foresight and investment ensured that El Paso stood resilient in the face of winter’s wrath, sparing its residents from the hardships faced by many Texans.

The Toll of Bolsonaro’s Disastrous Covid-19 Response

Click to expand Image Brazil's President Jair Bolsonaro holds a drug he recommended to treat Covid-19 during a Facebook live event in April 2020. That drug has no proven effect against the virus. © The image is a screenshot of a video posted on President Bolsonaro's Facebook account

A Brazilian Senate committee yesterday approved on a 1,100-page report that lays bare what happens when a country’s president adopts policies with utter disregard for human rights during a pandemic.

The report was the result of months of hearings and investigation by the committee into the government’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic. It portrays a president who turned his back on science and endangered the health and lives of Brazilians.

Covid-19 has killed more than 600,000 Brazilians, but thousands of those deaths could have been avoided, evidence presented in the report indicates.

President Jair Bolsonaro spread false information about Covid-19, opposed social distancing, refused to wear masks, and routinely shook hands with crowds of supporters. His ultimate goal, the report concluded, was rapid contagion so that Brazil would reach herd immunity.

He not only refused to follow World Health Organization recommendations to protect public health, but he sought to block Congress and local officials from following guidelines. For instance, in July 2020, he vetoed legal provisions to make mask wearing mandatory in churches and in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

An episode in Amazonas state in January 2021 encapsulates the tragic consequences of those policies. In late 2020, local officials had warned the federal government of an impending shortage of oxygen, but instead of securing supply, the Bolsonaro administration sent drugs that have no proven effect against the virus, the report said. When the oxygen ran out, dozens of Covid-19 patients died.

The government sent the same unproven drugs to Indigenous people, the investigative committee found. It drafted a plan to protect them from Covid-19 only after repeated orders by the Supreme Court.

The report showed that the Bolsonaro administration did not respond to several offers of vaccines from the Butantan Institute – a research center owned by the São Paulo state government. The report also included testimony showing that Bolsonaro was presented with some evidence of corruption in one vaccine procurement contract. A witness said Bolsonaro committed to report the case to federal police, “but that did not happen,” the report said.

The report recommended a variety of criminal charges against Bolsonaro and other officials, as well as his impeachment. The attorney general, who was appointed by Bolsonaro and has been widely criticized for allegedly taking decisions favoring the president, should examine the strong evidence uncovered by the committee very seriously.

"That is my own darling child," said he, returning her caress, "your ready obedience deserved a reward. Now put on your hat, and we will take our walk."

Mr. Travilla joined them in the avenue, and his kind heart rejoiced to see how the clouds of care and sorrow had all passed away from his little friend's face, leaving it bright and beaming, as usual. Her father had one hand, and Mr. Travilla soon possessed himself of the other.

"Bravo! I shall be delighted to be of the party, if the ladies don't object; eh! Elsie, what do you think?" with a questioning look down into her glad face, "will they want me?"

"You needn't be a bit afraid, Mr. Travilla," laughed the little girl; "I like you next to papa, and I believe Lucy and the rest like you better."

"Oh! take care, Elsie; are you not afraid of hurting his feelings?"

"No danger, as long as she puts me first," Mr. Dinsmore said, bestowing a smile and loving glance on her.

Caroline Howard was in Elsie's room, waiting to show her bracelet, which had just been handed to her by her maid; Pomp having brought it from the city late the night before.

"Oh! Elsie, I am so glad you have come at last. I have been waiting for half an hour, I should think, to show you these," she said, as Elsie came in from her walk. "But how bright and merry you look; so different from last night! what ailed you then?"

"Never mind," replied Elsie, taking the bracelet from her hand, and examining it. "Oh! this is very pretty, Carry! the clasp is so beautiful, and they have braided the hair so nicely."

"Yes, I'm sure mamma will like it. But now that Christmas is gone, I think I will keep it for a New Year's gift. Wouldn't you, Elsie?"

"Yes, perhap–ut I want to tell you, Carry, what papa says. He and Mr. Travilla are going to take you, and Lucy, and Mary, and me, riding on horseback this afternoon. Don't you think it will be pleasant?"

"Elsie, I think now that your papa is very kind; and do you know I like him very much, indeed; quite as well as I do Mr. Travilla, and I always liked him--he's so pleasant, and so funny, too, sometimes. Elsie opened a drawer and laid it carefully in, and they ran off to the nursery.

Tragedy on Set: 'Rust' Production Suspended After Fatal Shooting, Legal and Financial Implications Abound

The tragic shooting of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins on the set of Alec Baldwin's movie "Rust" has sent shockwaves through the film industry, raising questions about safety on set and the potential legal and financial consequences for those involved. The production has been suspended, and speculation is rife about the possibility of criminal charges and civil lawsuits.

Santa Fe District Attorney Mary Carmack-Altwies has confirmed that her office is investigating the incident, stating, "We are looking into all aspects of this incident, including the possibility of criminal charges." (Variety)

As the investigation unfolds, the decision to finish or abandon the film carries significant implications for both legal and financial outcomes. Counsel Michael Davis of DTO Law notes, "If the production decides to finish the film, they'll need to weigh the costs of doing so against the potential revenue. If they abandon the project, they'll need to consider the financial hit and potential legal liabilities." (The Hollywood Reporter)

Insurance may cover some costs related to the shutdown and legal defenses, but there's a limit to the coverage. Andrew Hurwitz, co-chair of the entertainment group at Frankfurt Kurnit, explains, "Insurance policies typically have a cap on the amount of coverage for negligent acts, and it's possible that the costs associated with this incident could exceed that cap." (The Hollywood Reporter)

Rust reportedly had difficulty obtaining a completion bond, which is crucial for financial security in film production. The absence of a completion bond complicates financial recovery and legal defense strategies for the production. Hurwitz adds, "A completion bond provides assurance to investors and distributors that the film will be completed, and without it, the production may struggle to secure funding or distribution." (The Hollywood Reporter)

Bankruptcy is being considered as a potential path forward for the production, to manage lawsuits and financial liabilities. Davis notes, "Bankruptcy could provide a way for the production to protect its assets and manage its liabilities, but it's a complex process that requires careful consideration." (The Hollywood Reporter)

The tragedy has prompted reconsideration of the use of guns on film sets and the necessity of completion guarantees. Carmack-Altwies comments, "This incident highlights the need for safety protocols and accountability on set. We need to take a closer look at the use of firearms in film production and ensure that proper safety measures are in place." (Variety)

Completion bond premiums and insurance costs may rise, impacting larger studios less than independent filmmakers. And so saying, he wheeled round upon the music-stool, and played a queer piece of dance music, which, he said, was called “Go to the Devil and shake yourself.”

We passed the rest of the evening pleasantly, in hearing Conny sing, or listening to uncle Dick’s stories, or arguing good-humouredly on a variety of topics until ten o’clock struck, when uncle Dick said he must go to bed; he had to be up early to catch the train for London, and wanted to fortify himself for a hot and fatiguing day. He shook my hand very warmly after bidding the others good-night, and said, “I shall expect you on Monday. I daresay Teazer will meet you, if you let her know what train you arrive by. If not, our house isn’t a mile from the station, and you won’t be able to miss it after getting into the high road.”

I now thought it about time that I should be making my way home: but uncle Tom, seeing me prepare to leave, came up to me, and said, “What’s your hurry? I have something to say to you. The night is fine, and the longer you stay, the more brightly the moon will light you home.”

He then turned to his wife, who was watching us, and said, “My dear, I have something of importance to talk over with Charlie, and we mean to shut ourselves up in the library. You need not sit up. Send us in the whiskey, and we’ll strive our utmost to console ourselves for your absence.”

“What a quantity of talking you will have had before you go to bed!” exclaimed his wife. “Pray what is all this mighty mystery about?”

“Some of these days you shall hear,” replied her husband, with a good-natured laugh. “Now then, Charlie, bid your aunt and Conny good-night, and follow me.”

On entering the library, whither he had preceded me by some minutes, as I had chosen to linger a little whilst I wished Conny good-night, I found the lamp lighted, glasses upon the table, and my uncle seated in an arm-chair near the open window. High overhead rode the brilliant moon; the soft night-wind rustled the leaves of the trees; and the wide grounds lay mottled with moonshine, and the shadows of bush and plant. I drew a chair to the window, lighted a cigar, and, as I felt the cool air breathing upon my face, exclaimed, “A Turk would call this paradise.”

“And so might a Christian,” answered my uncle. “We ought to be happy. We ought to be grateful. I hope, I believe, I am. Few men have better reason to be satisfied with life than myself. I enjoy good health; my wife is the best of women; my girl is dutiful and loving; my brothers are spared to delight me with their society whenever they choose to see me, and,” he added, leaning forward and grasping my hand, “I have a nephew who is a thoroughly good fellow, and to whom I am as much attached as if he were my son.”

I thanked him in warm and affectionate terms.

“And now what do you think of Dick?” he asked.

“I think him a very fine fellow, and a very fine gentleman, which I did not think him this morning.”

“Ay, truly, he’s a gentleman in a much higher sense than mere behaviour and the power of talking well imply. He is charitable to a fault; so soft-hearted that he refused to be a magistrate because he said the position would cost him more than he was worth, as he never could agree to a conviction without endowing the families of the men he helped to send to gaol. He and I have been having a long talk about you, and I am delighted to say that he thinks well of my scheme.”

“I hope,” said I, “that I didn’t offend him by my somewhat cool reception of him at the bank this morning?”

FDA Authorizes Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine for Children Aged 5 to 11, Promising New Protection for Young Americans

In a significant step toward safeguarding the health of younger populations, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted emergency use authorization for the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine in children aged 5 through 11. This decision marks a pivotal expansion of the nation's arsenal in combating the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly as cases surge among younger cohorts.

Clinical trials have shown the vaccine to be highly effective for this age group, with a notable efficacy rate of 90.7% in preventing COVID-19. The trials included approximately 3,100 children, providing reassuring safety data, as no serious side effects were detected. These findings underscore the vaccine's critical role in both curbing the spread of COVID-19 and protecting children from severe illness.

The newly authorized vaccine for children in this age bracket is administered as a two-dose regimen, akin to the vaccination process for those aged 12 and older. However, it features a lower dosage tailored specifically for children, designed to elicit a robust immune response while minimizing potential side effects.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices will convene next week to deliberate on further recommendations for the implementation of this vaccine within the pediatric population. This pending guidance will detail best practices for the distribution and administration of the vaccine, ensuring that healthcare providers across the nation can effectively deliver it to children in need.

COVID-19 continues to exert a profound impact on younger age groups, with children aged 5 through 11 accounting for approximately 39% of COVID-19 cases among those under 18 years of age in the United States. This demographic has faced increased vulnerability to the virus, often resulting in significant disruptions to their educational and social activities. Vaccination provides a promising avenue to restore a sense of normalcy while guarding against potential health complications.

Janet Woodcock, M.D., Acting FDA Commissioner, highlighted the extensive evaluation process undertaken prior to granting this authorization. Dr. Woodcock stated, "Vaccinating younger children against COVID-19 will bring us closer to returning to a sense of normalcy and ease the worry many parents have as a result of the pandemic. Our team has worked tirelessly to ensure that the vaccine meets our rigorous standards for safety, effectiveness, and manufacturing quality."

The authorization also includes a new formulation of the vaccine, which employs a Tris buffer. This innovation serves to enhance the vaccine's stability and storage conditions, facilitating broader distribution across diverse environments, particularly those with limited resources.

In light of concerns raised in recent months regarding myocarditis and pericarditis, particularly in younger populations receiving mRNA vaccines, Pfizer Inc. has updated its safety monitoring plan. This comprehensive evaluation strategy will closely monitor these conditions, among other safety measures, ensuring swift action and transparency should any issues arise.

Peter Marks, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, emphasized the commitment to maintaining high standards of oversight throughout this process. "As with all of our decisions pertaining to COVID-19 vaccines, the FDA conducted a rigorous and comprehensive evaluation of the data available in this case. We are confident in the safety and efficacy of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine for this younger age group, as our findings mirror the stringent benchmarks set for adults and older children."

The FDA, in collaboration with the CDC, has employed a sophisticated suite of systems to continuously monitor the safety of COVID-19 vaccines post-authorization. These robust frameworks ensure that any potential adverse effects are rapidly identified and addressed, reinforcing public trust in the vaccine process.

This emergency use authorization represents a critical advance in public health, addressing an acute need for protective measures within a highly susceptible group. As vaccination efforts broaden to include younger children, it is expected that transmission rates may decrease significantly, stemming the tide of emerging COVID-19 variants.

Healthcare providers across the country are preparing for the imminent rollout, coordinating logistics to administer vaccines promptly and efficiently to eligible children. Parents and guardians are urged to consult with their healthcare providers to understand the benefits and potential risks associated with vaccinating their children against COVID-19.

The Biden administration, along with state and local health departments, has developed strategic plans to support an equitable vaccine distribution, focusing on underserved areas and communities disproportionately affected by the pandemic. This comprehensive approach is crucial to ensuring that all children have access to this life-saving intervention.

The authorization for the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine in children aged 5 through 11 is a significant milestone in the ongoing battle against the pandemic. It is a testament to the tireless work of scientists, healthcare professionals, and regulatory agencies striving to protect public health and enhance the well-being of future generations.

In the weeks ahead, the public is encouraged to stay informed about further developments and recommendations from federal health agencies. As America takes this decisive step forward, collaboration between parents, educators, and healthcare providers will be vital in ensuring a seamless and successful vaccination campaign for young children.

For additional information, parents and caregivers are advised to stay tuned to updates from the FDA and CDC, as these agencies continue to provide comprehensive guidance to assist the public in making informed decisions regarding COVID-19 vaccination for their children.

This authorization not only represents a promising new chapter in the fight against COVID-19 but also epitomizes the rigorous scientific inquiry and thoughtful planning essential to safeguarding health across all demographics. Together, through shared commitment and vigilance, a brighter, healthier future for our nation’s children is within reach.

In Kabul, Afghanistan, a tragic incident occurred as at least seven individuals lost their lives in a desperate scramble to enter the city's international airport, according to the British military. This event happened amidst the frenzied attempts of thousands trying to depart the nation following the Taliban's rapid takeover, which saw nearly all of Afghanistan fall under their control just days earlier.

As the first whispers of armed opposition to the Taliban began to surface, anti-Taliban fighters claimed to have taken control of three mountainous districts. Meanwhile, a leading militia commander in the sole province not yet subdued by the Taliban vowed to resist if confronted with an attack.

Sunday saw the British military confirm the death of at least seven individuals in the vicinity of the airport, where the crush may have led to people being trampled, suffocating, or suffering from heart attacks while Taliban forces fired into the air in an attempt to disperse the gathering crowds. The dead were covered with white cloths by soldiers, who also sought to pacify the amassed crowds from atop concrete barriers.

With the Taliban's entry into Kabul on August 15, the airport has been besieged by chaos, transforming it into one of the few remaining exits from Afghanistan. The horrifying scenes included Afghans falling to their deaths after clinging to a departing U.S. military cargo plane, highlighting the desperate measures some are willing to take.

Despite the Taliban's assurances of amnesty for those affiliated with the U.S., NATO, and the toppled Afghan government, fear of retribution has driven many Afghans to flee. Reports have emerged of the Taliban actively searching for former adversaries, raising questions about the sincerity of their promises or whether their fighters are acting independently.

On Saturday, western military personnel were seen struggling to manage the enormous crowds outside the airport, their efforts visible from satellite imagery. They provided assistance to those overcome by the heat and distributed water as temperatures soared to 34 degrees Celsius (93 F).

A NATO official described the situation at Kabul airport as "extremely challenging and unpredictable," unable to confirm the exact number of casualties. Meanwhile, the U.S. Embassy, now operating from the airport's military side, cautioned American citizens and others against attempting to reach the airport without specific instructions.

Jake Sullivan, U.S. National Security Adviser, stated that 3,900 individuals had been airlifted from Kabul on U.S. flights within a 24-hour period, a significant increase from the day before. This number was complemented by approximately 3,900 people flown out on non-U.S. military flights, though it still falls short of the military's daily airlift capacity.

The British government reported having airlifted over 5,000 persons, including 1,000 in just the past 14 hours. In response to the ongoing crisis, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin activated the Civil Reserve Air Fleet program, enlisting 18 aircraft from U.S. carriers to aid in transporting Afghan refugees following their evacuation.

President Joe Biden has committed to evacuating all Americans from Afghanistan as well as Afghans who supported the U.S. war effort. Efforts have included utilizing U.S. military helicopters to rescue 169 Americans from areas beyond the airport. Nevertheless, tens of thousands remain in hope of evacuation amid concerns of a potential attack on the airport by an Islamic State affiliate.

The U.S. military has employed defensive maneuvers, such as corkscrew landings and flare discharges during takeoff, to mitigate missile threats. The Taliban have pointed to the U.S. military's management of the evacuation as the root of the chaos, asserting that Afghans have no reason to fear them despite their forcible methods of crowd control at the airport.

Senior Taliban official Amir Khan Motaqi criticized the American handling of the situation, urging the U.S. not to tarnish its image globally by portraying the Taliban as hostile.

"Now then, Faquita, don’t you git so upset, gal!" She was wailing aloud, making no effort to wipe away the tears running down her cheeks. "Johnny, what kinda game you tryin’? You know these kids are straight; them an’ their ol’ man’s come to work th’ Range for wild ones on Rennie’s own askin’. Takin’ a quirt to th’ kid, eh?" Kells’ voice slid up the scale. "You sure have yourself a snootful tonight! Now you jus’ walk yourself outta here on th’ bounce. I’m doin’ th’ sayin’ of what goes on, on my own property."

"You do a lotta sayin’, Kells." The scowl was gone; Shannon’s battered mouth was actually smiling. But, Drew decided, he liked the scowl better than the smile and the tone of the voice accompanying it. "Some men oughtta put a hobble on their tongues. Sure, I know these young whelps an’ their pa too. Sniffin’ round where they ain’t wanted. An’ mustangers ain’t above throwin’ a sticky loop when they see a hoss worth it. We ain’t blind on th’ Range." His head swung a little so he was looking at the girl. "You’d better hold that in mind, gal. Double R hosses have come up missin’ lately. It’s easy to run a few prime head south to do some moonlight tradin’ at th’ border. An’ we don’t take kindly to losin’ good stock!"

The boy lunged against Drew’s pinioning arm. "Now he says we are horse thieves! Tell that to us before the Don Cazar!"

Shannon curled the quirt lash about his wrist. "Don’t think I won’t, Mex! He don’t like havin’ his colt crop whittled down. You—" Those blue eyes, brilliant, yet oddly shallow and curtained, met Drew’s for the second time. "Don’t know who you are, stranger, but you had no call to mix in. I’ll be seein’ you. Kinda free with a gun, leastwise at showin’ it. As quick to back up your play?"

"Try me!" The words came out of Drew before he thought.

Why had he said that? He had never been one to pick a fight or take up a challenge. What was there about Shannon that prodded Drew this way? He’d met the gamecock breed before and had never known the need to bristle at their crowing. Now he was disturbed that Shannon could prick him so.

Odd, the other had been successfully turned from his purpose here. Yet now as he swung around and walked away down the alley Drew was left with a nagging doubt, a feeling that in some way or other Shannon had come off even in this encounter.... But how and why?

Teodoro spat. His sister tugged at Kells’ sleeve. "It is not true what he said. Why does he wish to make trouble?"

"Lissen, gal, an’ you, too, Teodoro—jus’ keep clear of Johnny Shannon when he’s on th’ prod that way. I’ve knowed that kid since he didn’t have muscle enough to pull a gun ’less he took both hands to th’ job. But he’s not needin’ any two hands to unholster now. An’ he’s drinkin’ a lot—mean, ugly drunk, he is. Somethin’ must have riled him good tonight—"

"In the cantina there was a soldier from the camp," Faquita volunteered. "They call names. He and Señor Juanito fight. Don Reese, he put them both out in the street. Señor Juanito he falls, drops purse. Teodoro picks it up, and we follow. When we try to give it back Señor Juanito yell, ’spy,’ hit with whip. That is the truth, por Dios, the truth!"

"Yeah, sounds jus’ like Johnny these days. Him with a snootful an’ somebody yellin’ Reb and Yank. Some men can’t forgit an’ don’t seem to want to. Johnny sure takes it hard bein’ on th’ losin’ side—turned him dirt mean. Now, you kids, you stayin’ in town?"

"Sí." Faquita nodded vigorously. "With Tía María."

"Then you git there an’ stay clear of Johnny Shannon, sabe? No more trouble."
