Henri Rousseau’s The Dream stands as a potent testament to the artist’s unwavering dedication, a quality which resonates even in today's design landscape. The painting, completed in 1910, showcases Rousseau's unique artistic voice, deliberately diverging from established academic norms. The inclusion of wild, exotic cats within the lush, imagined jungle serves as a signature flourish, a symbolic assertion of his ambition to transcend the label of a naive artist and achieve recognition alongside his more formally trained contemporaries. These felines, powerful and untamed, mirror Rousseau’s own artistic spirit, striving to break free from the constraints of conventional technique.

The symbolic weight of these animals extends beyond mere stylistic distinction. They represent Rousseau’s profound desire to be considered a painter of significance, a creator of works that command attention and inspire awe. This aspiration is further underscored by the presence of the sinuous creature lurking in the undergrowth, heavily implied to be a snake. This evokes a direct link to his earlier painting, The Snake Charmer (1907), revealing a consistent preoccupation with themes of primal power and exotic allure. Comparing these works suggests a developing iconography within Rousseau's oeuvre, where specific motifs recur to reinforce his artistic vision.

Examining the technical aspects of The Dream reveals a relentless, albeit imperfect, pursuit of perfection. Certain sections of the canvas appear overworked, betraying Rousseau’s struggle to achieve the desired level of detail and refinement. This is understandable given his lack of formal training, yet it highlights his commitment to his craft. Although he may fall short of technical prowess in the conventional sense, his sincerity and palpable passion are undeniable. As Robert Hughes argues, "Authenticity can be faked, but passionate belief cannot" (Hughes, 1991, Nothing If Not Critical). This "passionate belief" is precisely what elevates Rousseau's art beyond mere imitation or naive rendering.

For Rousseau, art functions as a refuge, a sanctuary from the perceived mediocrity of the everyday world. The Dream, with its escapist imagery and idealized vision of nature, embodies this sentiment. It is a testament to the transformative power of artistic creation, a means of forging an alternative reality imbued with beauty and wonder. This dedication finds echoes in the world of design, a field that, at its core, seeks to shape and improve the human experience.

Design, like art, is a powerful tool for persuasion and expression. Throughout history, from the rudimentary cave drawings of our ancestors to the sophisticated websites of today, design has served as a means of communication, influence, and even control. A successful design strategy, however, is contingent upon its intended purpose. A design geared towards revenue generation will necessarily differ from one aimed at fostering user engagement or conveying a specific message.

This dichotomy is particularly evident in contemporary web design, where we witness a growing polarization between two distinct approaches. On one hand, there are dynamic, data-driven designs optimized for conversion rates and advertising revenue. These designs prioritize functionality and profitability, often at the expense of aesthetic considerations. On the other hand, there are minimalist, user-centric designs that emphasize clarity, simplicity, and intuitive navigation. These prioritize user experience and brand identity, potentially sacrificing short-term revenue gains for long-term loyalty. This divergence in design philosophies, mirroring Rousseau's own struggle between technical perfection and authentic expression, represents an ongoing and increasingly visible trend in the digital age.

The Western genre underwent significant evolution over the past few decades, transforming from its early emphasis on racism against Native Americans and hypermasculinity to a more contemporary focus on ultraviolence. Initial portrayals often glorified rugged individualism while reinforcing racial stereotypes, but modern interpretations have leaned heavily into graphic violence that sometimes lacks meaning. Yet, in this landscape, films like 'Open Range,' produced in 2003 and starring Robert Duvall and Kevin Costner, successfully revisited the genre's roots. This film combined traditional Western elements, balancing violence with a nuanced portrayal of masculinity, and was praised for its authentic representation. Although the changes in the genre reflect societal shifts, they also highlight a tension between nostalgia and modern sensibilities.

Broncos Fans Stuck Between a Rock and a Hard Place for Super Bowl LV

As Super Bowl LV approaches, Broncos fans find themselves facing an unenviable decision: root for the Kansas City Chiefs, their most despised AFC West adversary, or the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, led by their longtime arch-nemesis, Tom Brady. It's a conundrum that leaves fans grappling with a choice between, as some might say, the lesser of two evils.

For years, Broncos fans have nurtured an intense rivalry with the Kansas City Chiefs. Divisional games have consistently stoked emotions and fostered an unwavering sense of animosity. If there's any team that Broncos fans relish defeating, it's the Chiefs. And yet, here they are, watching them contend for a Super Bowl title, with the potential to eclipse the Broncos' historical success within the AFC West.

At the opposing end of the Super Bowl spectrum stands Tom Brady, a player who has haunted the Broncos' narrative for decades. Known for his incredible NFL career and numerous Super Bowl victories with the New England Patriots, Brady has been a formidable rival to the Broncos on many occasions. His startling move to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was an unwelcome surprise for many, further solidifying his status as a perennial antagonist to Broncos fans everywhere.

A recent Twitter poll revealed that about a third of Broncos fans adamantly refuse to root for either the Chiefs or Tom Brady in this year's Super Bowl, illustrating the deep-seated frustration that has taken hold. It paints a vivid picture of a fan base caught in a bind, unable to support either team and finding themselves wondering who, if anyone, they should lend their cheers to this weekend.

Julie Thuis, a diehard Broncos fan, echoes this widespread sentiment, "Honestly, this is a nightmare scenario. How am I supposed to choose between the Chiefs and Brady? It's like asking me to pick between two of my worst nightmares!" Her frustration unfurls a line shared by many fans who view both options with palpable disdain.

On the other hand, Christine Voss, another devoted fan of the Broncos, feels a sense of obligation to prioritize the divisional rivalry over personal dislike. When discussing her support for Tampa Bay, she exclaims, “Rooting for Brady over the Chiefs just makes more sense. I've despised the Chiefs since day one; I refuse to see them celebrate another win in our division.”

However, not every fan can overlook their animosity for the infamous quarterback. A good number of Broncos fans consider Tom Brady as the NFL's 'Voldemort,' the somber specter who has haunted their dreams too long to ignore. With his attempt to trademark 'Tompa Bay,' the moniker meant to meld his name with his current team’s, Brady managed to draw even more ire from Bronco country, confirming that some resentments run deeper.

While Dave DeNovellis, another staunch Broncos fan, admits he’s struggling with this year’s Super Bowl predicament, he proposes a little levity as a solution, "I just might root for the commercials this year. There's always some good ones to look forward to, and let's be honest, who doesn't appreciate a clever ad in the middle of the game?" It’s a sentiment shared by those yearning for a neutral option, an escape from the emotional turmoil of choosing what feels like an inevitable loss.

Former State Rep. Cole Wist expresses his perplexity, saying, "As a Broncos fan, there's no win here. I'll just have to flip a coin or watch the game for the love of football. It’s not the end of the world, but it sure feels like it." The reality of unprecedented times calls for unexpected choices, and humor often paves the way to easing the decision-making process for many fans who simply don't want to choose.

For fans feeling increasingly alienated from both Super Bowl contenders, contrasting criteria may open new avenues of support. Some fans may find it more favorable to lend their backing to teams with strong connections to Colorado, either through players, coaches, or even cities involved in historic games. Others might simply choose to support the team perceived as the underdog, hoping to witness an enthralling victory against all odds.

But at the heart of this complex decision lies a profound sense of alienation, deepened by the seasonal absence of the Denver Broncos from the championships, only to be further burdened by an unenviable choice. Fans are tossed into the choppy seas of choice, left with an ironic predicament that tests their fandom in new and bewildering ways.

Historical natural antagonism toward the Chiefs collides head-on with the long-standing personal grievance against Brady in a mashup that appears only when stars misalign in this unlucky scenario for Broncos fans. In essence, the Super Bowl LV contest invites Broncos supporters to ponder what it really means to be a fan amidst a thorny reality.

For those unable to root for the commercial breaks or split loyalties, look to the fundamental reasons that Broncos fans tune into football: thrill, unpredictability, and the love of the game. The very spirit of sport is illuminated in contests wrought with contention and invocations of biblical rivalries when unanticipated paths merge.

In conclusion, this Super Bowl LV serves as a stark reminder of football’s beautiful nature – messy rivalry, classic battles, and the possibilities that arise out of uncertainty. Broncos fans, meanwhile, find humor in their hiatus from cheerful support, arguing whether choosing between Brady and the Chiefs might just be the strongest indication yet of a world led astray.

While some have jokingly suggested questioning the existence of a higher power when faced with supporting their most loathed rivals, this predicament, though unwelcome, invites reflections on the core of sporting spirit. Broncos fans, remain heartened; football endures as a testament to resilience, proving that even the polarizing matchups, like choosing among Super Bowl LV's two unwanted contenders, urge us to treasure its dynamic unpredictability.

Update on Omicron

On 26 November 2021, WHO designated the variant B.1.1.529 a variant of concern, named Omicron, on the advice of WHO’s Technical Advisory Group on Virus Evolution (TAG-VE). This decision was based on the evidence presented to the TAG-VE that Omicron has several mutations that may have an impact on how it behaves, for example, on how easily it spreads or the severity of illness it causes. Here is a summary of what is currently known.

Current knowledge about Omicron

Researchers in South Africa and around the world are conducting studies to better understand many aspects of Omicron and will continue to share the findings of these studies as they become available.

Transmissibility: It is not yet clear whether Omicron is more transmissible (e.g., more easily spread from person to person) compared to other variants, including Delta. The number of people testing positive has risen in areas of South Africa affected by this variant, but epidemiologic studies are underway to understand if it is because of Omicron or other factors.

Severity of disease: It is not yet clear whether infection with Omicron causes more severe disease compared to infections with other variants, including Delta. Preliminary data suggests that there are increasing rates of hospitalization in South Africa, but this may be due to increasing overall numbers of people becoming infected, rather than a result of specific infection with Omicron. There is currently no information to suggest that symptoms associated with Omicron are different from those from other variants. Initial reported infections were among university students—younger individuals who tend to have more mild disease—but understanding the level of severity of the Omicron variant will take days to several weeks. All variants of COVID-19, including the Delta variant that is dominant worldwide, can cause severe disease or death, in particular for the most vulnerable people, and thus prevention is always key.

Effectiveness of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection

Preliminary evidence suggests there may be an increased risk of reinfection with Omicron (ie, people who have previously had COVID-19 could become reinfected more easily with Omicron), as compared to other variants of concern, but information is limited. More information on this will become available in the coming days and weeks.

Effectiveness of vaccines: WHO is working with technical partners to understand the potential impact of this variant on our existing countermeasures, including vaccines. Vaccines remain critical to reducing severe disease and death, including against the dominant circulating variant, Delta. Current vaccines remain effective against severe disease and death.

Effectiveness of current tests: The widely used PCR tests continue to detect infection, including infection with Omicron, as we have seen with other variants as well. Studies are ongoing to determine whether there is any impact on other types of tests, including rapid antigen detection tests.

Effectiveness of current treatments: Corticosteroids and IL6 Receptor Blockers will still be effective for managing patients with severe COVID-19. Other treatments will be assessed to see if they are still as effective given the changes to parts of the virus in the Omicron variant.

Studies underway

At the present time, WHO is coordinating with a large number of researchers around the world to better understand Omicron. Studies currently underway or underway shortly include assessments of transmissibility, severity of infection (including symptoms), performance of vaccines and diagnostic tests, and effectiveness of treatments.

WHO encourages countries to contribute the collection and sharing of hospitalized patient data through the WHO COVID-19 Clinical Data Platform to rapidly describe clinical characteristics and patient outcomes.

More information will emerge in the coming days and weeks. WHO’s TAG-VE will continue to monitor and evaluate the data as it becomes available and assess how mutations in Omicron alter the behaviour of the virus.

Recommended actions for countries

As Omicron has been designated a Variant of Concern, there are several actions WHO recommends countries to undertake, including enhancing surveillance and sequencing of cases; sharing genome sequences on publicly available databases, such as GISAID; reporting initial cases or clusters to WHO; performing field investigations and laboratory assessments to better understand if Omicron has different transmission or disease characteristics, or impacts effectiveness of vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics or public health and social measures. More detail in the announcement from 26 November.

Countries should continue to implement the effective public health measures to reduce COVID-19 circulation overall, using a risk analysis and science-based approach. They should increase some public health and medical capacities to manage an increase in cases. WHO is providing countries with support and guidance for both readiness and response.

In addition, it is vitally important that inequities in access to COVID-19 vaccines are urgently addressed to ensure that vulnerable groups everywhere, including health workers and older persons, receive their first and second doses, alongside equitable access to treatment and diagnostics.

Recommended actions for people

The most effective steps individuals can take to reduce the spread of the COVID-19 virus is to keep a physical distance of at least 1 metre from others; wear a well-fitting mask; open windows to improve ventilation; avoid poorly ventilated or crowded spaces; keep hands clean; cough or sneeze into a bent elbow or tissue; and get vaccinated when it’s their turn.

WHO will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available, including following meetings of the TAG-VE. In addition, information will be available on WHO’s digital and social media platforms.

Trump's Lawyers Defend Impeachment Dismissal, Citing First Amendment and Due Process Concerns

Washington, D.C. - Former President Donald Trump's legal team presented their case before the Senate on Tuesday, arguing that the impeachment charge against him should be dismissed on grounds of free speech protection and lack of due process. The lawyers, Bruce Castor and David Schoen, asserted that Trump's speech on January 6, which preceded the Capitol riot, is protected by the First Amendment and does not constitute incitement of insurrection.

First Amendment Defense and Lack of Due Process

Castor emphasized that Trump's speech was "figurative" and "rhetorical hyperbole," protected by the First Amendment. He argued that the impeachment effort is an attempt to "criminalize political speech" and sets a dangerous precedent for future political discourse. Schoen echoed this sentiment, stating that the impeachment is "political theater" and "an effort to disenfranchise President Trump and his supporters."

The legal team also challenged the constitutionality of the impeachment, arguing that it lacks due process because Trump is no longer in office. They contend that the Senate does not have jurisdiction to try a former president and that the impeachment violates the separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches.

Timeline for Impeachment Trial and Potential Witnesses

Senate leaders have agreed on a timeline for the impeachment trial, allowing four days for opening arguments from both the House impeachment managers and Trump's defense team. The decision on whether to call witnesses, including potentially Trump himself, will be made early next week.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) stated that the agreed-upon timeline "ensures a fair and thorough trial" and allows both sides to present their cases effectively. Republican Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) expressed support for the timeline, saying it "preserves due process for both the prosecution and the defense."

Preplanned Capitol Riot and Trump's Speech

Trump's legal brief suggests that the Capitol riot was preplanned, citing law enforcement reports of potential attacks. The brief argues that Trump's speech did not directly incite the violence and that he had no knowledge of any planned violence.

Reactions and Implications

The impeachment trial has drawn significant attention and polarized opinions, with Democrats largely supporting the impeachment and Republicans mostly opposing it. The outcome of the trial could have implications for future political discourse and the accountability of public figures for their statements and actions.

In conclusion, Trump's lawyers presented their defense against the impeachment charge, arguing that his speech is protected by the First Amendment and that the impeachment lacks due process. The Senate trial will unfold over the coming days, with the decision on calling witnesses and the final verdict yet to be determined.

"Ruined my constitution, you did!" cried Nestley, striking the table with his clenched fist. "And for what? For your own amusement, I suppose."

Beaumont watched him through a haze of cigarette smoke, a supercilious smile playing upon his lips. "My dear fellow," he drawled, "you do exaggerate so. A few nights on the town never hurt anyone."

"A few nights!" Nestley sprang to his feet, his voice shaking with barely suppressed fury. "It was every night, for months on end! You, with your endless thirst for brandy and late hours, dragging me along with you like a damned puppet!"

He paced the room, his hands clenching and unclenching at his sides. The other occupants, sensing a scene, had discreetly withdrawn to the furthest corners, leaving the two men in a tense bubble of isolation.

"You knew I couldn't handle it," Nestley continued, his voice thick with emotion. "You knew my health was delicate. But did you care? Not you! You were having too much fun, leading me down the primrose path to ruin."

Beaumont flicked a speck of ash from his impeccably tailored waistcoat, his expression one of languid amusement. "Come now, Doctor," he purred, "don't tell me you've gone and turned into a teetotaler. Why, I remember the nights you could outdrink even me, and I flatter myself I have a rather strong head for liquor."

"That was before," Nestley spat, his voice raw. "Before I realized the hold it had on me, before I woke up one morning staring into the abyss. It took me five years, five long years to climb out of that hole you helped dig for me."

He stopped his pacing and stood before Beaumont, his chest heaving. "Five years of discipline, of denying myself every indulgence, to rebuild what you so carelessly destroyed."

Beaumont raised an eyebrow, a flicker of something akin to admiration flitting across his features. "Well, well, Doctor," he murmured, "it seems you possess a stronger will than I gave you credit for. Most commendable."

But the compliment, if indeed it was one, rang hollow in Nestley's ears. It did nothing to erase the bitterness, the resentment that festered within him.

"You find it amusing, do you?" he asked, his voice low and dangerous.

Beaumont shrugged, his indifference like a slap in the face. "Life is rather amusing, don't you think? All these twists and turns, these little dramas we create for ourselves. Keeps things interesting, wouldn't you say?"

Nestley stared at him, his anger warring with a profound weariness. Beaumont would never understand, never comprehend the true cost of his actions. He was like a child playing with fire, oblivious to the potential for destruction.

"I suppose it is," Nestley said finally, his voice devoid of inflection. "For some."

Cruz Acknowledges Mistake in Mexico Trip During Texas Storm

DALLAS (AP) – Texas Senator Ted Cruz has admitted that his decision to travel to Mexico with his family during the devastating winter storm in Texas was a mistake. Cruz, a Republican, faced heavy criticism from both Democrats and members of his own party for leaving the state while millions of Texans were struggling without electricity or water.

The Senator explained that he initially flew to Cancun because his daughters asked to go and he intended to stay through the weekend. However, the backlash and the severity of the crisis in his home state prompted Cruz to return early, stating the need to focus on the issues facing Texas.

The incident has raised questions about Cruz's political future, particularly his rumored interest in a 2024 presidential run. Texas GOP Chair Allen West did not come to Cruz's defense, instead emphasizing the importance of supporting those affected by the storm.

Over 7 million Texans were advised to boil water before consuming it due to damage to the state's infrastructure caused by the storm. Cruz's absence during the crisis and the government's overall response were met with criticism from Texas residents and politicians alike.

White House Press Secretary Jen Psaki mentioned Cruz's actions, stating, "I don't have any updates on the exact location of Senator Ted Cruz, nor does anyone at the White House, but our focus is on working directly with leadership in Texas on addressing the winter storm and the crisis at hand."

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez also weighed in on Cruz's trip, calling it "unfortunately predictable" and criticizing his decision to leave his constituents at a time of urgent need.

Following his return to Texas, Cruz's office reportedly contacted the Houston Police Department. Department spokesperson Jodi Silva confirmed this but did not clarify if this was a routine procedure for the Senator's arrivals.

As Texas continues to recover from the aftermath of the winter storm, attention remains on providing assistance to those grappling with the fallout of power outages, burst pipes, and other challenges. The controversy surrounding Cruz's trip serves as a reminder of the public's expectations from their elected officials during times of crisis.

In the exploration of artificial life simulation, a project was undertaken to model organisms that could move, consume, hunt, and exhibit rudimentary thinking capabilities. The foundation for the simulation was carefully laid out through the creation of pseudo-code, meticulously breaking the program into a series of distinct functions. This structured approach facilitated modular development, ensuring each component of the simulation, from the organism's movement to its cognitive processes, could be independently designed and refined. The environment within which these organisms operated was endowed with randomly distributed food items, each possessing varying energy levels, thus mirroring real-world ecological diversity.

The organisms themselves were imbued with fundamental functionalities, such as basic navigation and energy management. The integration of a genetic algorithm into the simulation allowed these organisms to evolve, optimizing their behaviors through successive iterations. Each organism's actions and outcomes were recorded, serving as data for shaping the genetic makeup of future generations. This continuous cycle of evaluation and adaptation mirrored natural selection, effectively enabling the simulation to progress toward increasingly efficient organisms.

A graphical user interface (GUI) was developed to visually represent the simulation and provide users with a main menu, facilitating the selection of various simulation functions. An initial outline and flowchart were essential tools in guiding the programming process, ensuring a coherent and logical progression from concept to implementation. With Bloodshed Dev-C++ 4.9.9.2 serving as the project development environment, the software was compiled as a console application, leveraging the language's capabilities for efficient computation and interaction.

Key functionalities, including 'create_environment()','main_menu()', and'main()', played pivotal roles in structuring the program's architecture. These functions orchestrated the simulation's operation, managing the environment's setup, user interaction, and overall execution. Through this methodical process, the simulation successfully integrated biological principles with computational techniques, offering insights into evolutionary strategies and the dynamics of artificial ecosystems.

It was a dreary autumn afternoon, and the sleepy town of T---- lay shrouded in a dismal mist, its narrow streets and crumbling houses seeming to slumber beneath a damp and sullen veil. The monotony of its existence was a palpable thing, and the town's inhabitants, a listless and apathetic lot, went about their daily routine with a listlessness that bordered on despair. The officers of the regiment, quartered in the town's rambling barracks, were no exception, and their evenings were often spent in seeking distraction from the dullness that lay without.

It was on one such evening, as Charles Lovell sat in the warm and smoke-filled confines of the mess, that he chanced upon a group of his comrades, deep in conversation and laughter. The clinking of glasses and the murmur of their voices served as a poignant reminder of the gulf that separated him from the life he had once known. And yet, as he listened to their words, he felt a pang of jealousy, a reminder that he was still an outsider, a stranger in a world that seemed to be passing him by. For, despite his outward appearance of confidence, Charles Lovell was a man beset by doubts and uncertainties, and the uncertainty of his future gnawed at his very soul.

As the evening wore on, the conversation turned to the subject of the forthcoming dinner at the mess, where the regiment's young officers would gather to dine and socialize. It was to be a grand occasion, with plenty of wine and good company, and the officers were eager to attend, if only to pass the time and dull the edge of their disappointment. And so, as Charles sat down at the table, he felt a sense of trepidation, a fear that he might be recognized, that someone might see through the mask he wore and discover the vulnerable and uncertain man beneath. For he knew that his reputation as a gambler was beginning to precede him, and he feared that the officers would not take kindly to his company.

The dinner was a sumptuous affair, with plenty of roast meat and fine wine, and the officers, flushed with drink and good company, laughed and chatted with abandon. Charles, however, was cool and reserved, watching the proceedings with a detached and calculating air, his mind already turning to the possibilities of the night ahead. For he knew that the officers would soon be gathering in the mess, their pockets heavy with gold and their spirits high, and he saw an opportunity to strike, to make a kill, as it were, in the gambler's parlance. And so, as the evening wore on, and the wine flowed freely, Charles Lovell's thoughts turned to the cards, and the possibilities of the night, his heart pounding with anticipation, his senses alert, and his spirit afire with the thrill of the gamble.

"But why must you always be reading, Edward?" asked Maggie, her voice tinged with a familiar note of exasperation. She stood in the doorway of the small parlour, her hands on her hips, her gaze fixed upon her brother, who sat comfortably ensconced in their father's old armchair.

Edward, for his part, did not even bother to lift his eyes from the pages of his Latin grammar. "Why must you always be bustling about, Maggie?" he countered, his tone a touch sharper than he perhaps intended. "Can a fellow not have a moment's peace in his own home?"

Maggie crossed the room, her footsteps muffled by the worn rug, and perched herself upon the edge of the settee opposite Edward. The silence stretched between them, punctuated only by the rustle of turning pages and the gentle ticking of the grandfather clock in the corner.

"It is not bustling, Edward," Maggie said at length, her voice quieter now. "It is called keeping a home." She gestured vaguely at the room around them, at the dust motes dancing in the afternoon sunbeams, at the stack of mending piled high upon the table. "These things do not see to themselves, you know."

Edward finally lowered his book, but his expression remained distant, his thoughts still seemingly lost in the intricacies of Latin declensions. "Yes, yes, I know," he murmured, a hint of impatience creeping into his voice. "But surely there is someone else who could attend to such matters. Mrs. Jenkins, perhaps?"

Maggie let out a small sigh. "Mrs. Jenkins has her own tasks to see to, Edward. Besides, it is not seemly for a young lady of good family to shirk her domestic duties."

"Seemly?" Edward scoffed, tossing his book onto the nearby table with a thud that made Maggie wince. "Since when have you cared about what is 'seemly', Maggie? You spend more time in the garden with your hands in the dirt than any lady I know."

Maggie's cheeks flushed pink at his words. It was true, she felt most at peace amongst the flowers and vegetables, her hands stained with earth, the sun warm upon her face. But Edward, with his books and his studies and his grand ambitions of becoming a clergyman, could not be expected to understand such simple pleasures.

"Gardening is honest work, Edward," she said quietly, picking at a loose thread on her skirt. "And someone must tend to the vegetables if we are to eat."

Edward sighed, his earlier impatience giving way to a weary sort of resignation. "You know I do not mean to be unkind, Maggie," he said, rising from his chair and crossing the room to stand by the window. "It is just that...well, I have my studies, my future to consider. A clergyman must be a scholar, a gentleman. He cannot be expected to concern himself with the mundane details of running a household."

"And what of a clergyman's wife, Edward?" Maggie challenged, her chin lifting a fraction. "Is she not also expected to be a lady? And yet, I wager she knows her way around a kitchen and a mending basket just as well as any housemaid."

Edward turned back to face her, a flicker of amusement dancing in his eyes. "Ah, so that is it, is it? You fancy yourself the future wife of a clergyman, do you?"

Maggie felt her cheeks flush even warmer now. "Do not be absurd, Edward," she retorted, though a small smile played at the corners of her lips. "I am merely pointing out that there is more to life than books and sermons."

Edward chuckled, the tension between them easing somewhat. "Perhaps you are right, little sister," he conceded, reaching out to ruffle her hair in a rare display of affection. "Perhaps you are right."

New York City, a vibrant mosaic touted for its diversity, often concentrates that diversity into specific pockets. We see it bustling on the subway, filling lecture halls, yet the reality is, these spaces don't always mirror the nuanced racial landscape of the city's neighborhoods. As a resident of Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, I witness this complexity daily. My neighborhood, once predominantly Italian-American, is now experiencing a significant demographic shift, with a rapidly growing Chinese immigrant population. Recent estimates suggest that the Chinese population has increased by roughly 30% in the last decade, now comprising nearly half the neighborhood’s residents. This change inevitably reshapes the racial dynamics, prompting me to examine how different races perceive the Chinese community and, equally importantly, how these perceptions are reciprocated. My investigation delves into the lived experiences of Bensonhurst residents, using cultural materialism as a framework to understand the connection between material conditions, human behavior, and racial perceptions.

Understanding culture, as I am learning, necessitates a boots-on-the-ground approach. Observing people’s living conditions, their interactions, their daily routines, provides invaluable insight. Ethnography, however, is not without its pitfalls. As I navigate this study, I am acutely aware of the potential for labeling and stereotyping based on perceived racial characteristics. It is crucial to remain conscious of the dangers of essentializing individuals based on group affiliation. This requires a constant self-assessment and a willingness to challenge my own biases. Singh’s work resonates here: “Language is never neutral; it is always laden with histories, power relations, and social meanings.” These words serve as a constant reminder of the weight and complexity of the language I use to describe the interactions I observe. Similarly, Hill’s analysis of language, race, and public perception underscores the power of linguistic choices in shaping racial attitudes. My own experience living here informs my observations; I, too, am implicated in the very dynamics I am trying to understand.

My primary method is participant observation. I spend hours in Seth Low Park, a central gathering place for Bensonhurst residents. On a typical afternoon, I observe groups of Chinese elders practicing Tai Chi while children of different racial backgrounds play basketball nearby. Interactions are often stilted, marked by language barriers. I notice, however, a curious phenomenon: non-Chinese youths often engage in what I term "mock-Chinese," attempting to communicate with Chinese residents by mimicking tones and phrases they believe represent the language. This behavior, while seemingly lighthearted, reveals underlying assumptions and a clear demarcation of "us" versus "them." The act of mimicking, however well-intentioned, highlights the existing language barrier and potentially perpetuates stereotypes, unintentionally creating distance instead of bridging the gap.

This investigation connects directly to cultural materialism, the theory that material conditions shape human behavior and beliefs. In Bensonhurst, the influx of Chinese immigrants has altered the material landscape. Businesses have changed, reflecting the needs and tastes of the new population. The availability of specific foods, the prominence of Chinese characters on storefronts, and the sound of Mandarin spoken on the streets – all contribute to a new material reality. This reality, in turn, influences how different groups perceive each other. I consider Du Bois’ concept of "double-consciousness," the feeling of looking at oneself through the eyes of others, a relevant framework here. Chinese immigrants, I suspect, experience a similar sense of being constantly observed and judged based on their perceived racial identity. They navigate Bensonhurst aware of how they are seen by their neighbors, a constant negotiation between their own self-perception and the expectations of the dominant culture.

My research is ongoing. I am still grappling with the complexities of racial perception in Bensonhurst. But one thing is clear: understanding the nuances of race requires a multifaceted approach, one that acknowledges the power of language, the influence of material conditions, and the importance of personal experience. As I continue my observations, I strive to remain aware of my own positionality, constantly questioning my assumptions and seeking to understand the perspectives of all Bensonhurst residents. The shifting demographics of my neighborhood offer a unique opportunity to examine the evolving landscape of race in New York City, a city that perpetually reinvents itself, neighborhood by neighborhood.

And so it came to pass that the very next morn, the morning succeeding that dark and chilly evening when Percival Keene had been christened with all the solemnity that the salt-stained hall could muster, and where Ben Keene had earned the speechless respect of every man, woman, and child within earshot, the wind did blow from the east with a keenness that cut to the bone, and rattled the windows of our humble abode like the foremast of a ship in a tempest. It was a day ill-suited for the stroll, yet it found Percival Keene and his mother afoot, for she had resolved to brave the hard elements in order to make inquiries regarding the availability of a modest chamber in the quaint district of Chatham. Her confidant in this venture was Ben, who, having once been a man of few words, was now a paragon of taciturn determination.

The streets of our fair town were empty, save for the bustling of our neighbors within their dwellings, and the occasional passing of a carriage or a footman upon an urgent errand. The brisk air did little to diminish the warm glow of affection that Percival felt towards his mother, for he knew that the trials they had weathered together had forged a bond stronger than the stoutest oak. As they passed the market square, where the aroma of freshly baked bread mingled with the scent of hay and leather, Percival could not help but notice the curious glances bestowed upon the pair by the townsfolk. Their diminished status was evident, and yet, Percival felt no shame in his station; for he bore no ill will towards those who might whisper behind their hands.

Upon their arrival at the lodgings, Percival's mother, ever the diplomat, engaged the landlord in polite discourse, inquiring about the availability of a suitable chamber. The man, a grizzled fellow with weathered features, eyed them with a keenness that suggested he was no fool. "A fine little chamber, this," he said, gesturing to an unadorned room that overlooked a cobbled alleyway. "Furnished to your satisfaction? Though, mind you, not to the fashion of the Hall."

"Indeed," Percival's mother replied with a grace that belied the grace of their diminished circumstances. "We seek no grandeur, but a warm hearth and a place to lay our heads. And, if it might please you, a discreet silence from the servants, for we understand the importance of maintaining discretion."

The landlord, seemingly mollified by her request, nodded sagely and led them to the chamber. As Percival gazed around the room, he felt a burgeoning sense of peace; for herein lay a sanctuary from the prying eyes and malicious tongues of their former acquaintances. It was a home, small as it may be, yet rich with the promise of security and respite.

As the days passed, Percival, with the patience of a veteran and the wisdom of one thrice his years, found solace in the brisk ordinariness of life at Chatham. The barracks were a place of order and discipline, where the clanging of bayonets and the cadence of marching boots offered a comforting familiarity. And every evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, casting the sky in hues of orange and purple, Percival would walk by the riverside, his mind at ease and his heart alight with the promise of new beginnings. For he carried with him the knowledge that, amidst the trials and tribulations of life, there is always a beacon of hope, guiding one towards the dawn of a brighter tomorrow.

Six months passed—six long, delightful months of sun, and summer, and smiles, without a cloud to darken, without a care to trouble them. No thought of dividing us crossed my mother's mind; the doctor's advice was too seriously considered, his authority too implicitly obeyed, to admit of the idea of my going to school being so much as entertained. And, on my side, to whom were my thoughts given, but to Mary?

We lived for each other—we breathed for each other—we thought for each other. If I was away from her for more than five minutes together, I began to be fretful and uneasy; and if she was away from me, she came back with her sweet little face all flushed and excited, and threw her arms round my neck in a quiet, pretty, tantalizing way, which was perfectly irresistible. "Oh, George, I am so happy to see you again! It is so long since I saw you last. I thought you were never coming back!" That is what she said to me, with her plump, youthful arms round my neck, and her warm, young breath on my cheek—and how, I should like to know, was a fellow of thirteen to resist such a sister as that?

For I was a fellow of thirteen, please to remember; and Mary was a child of ten; and we were both, as I have already said, without father or mother to care for us, and without brother or sister to come between us. Is it wonderful, then, I ask—is it not, on the contrary, quite natural and likely—that our childish thoughts of each other should have taken the form of sweetheart and lover?

The summer holidays were over; and still I did not go back to school. No; the doctor said it was of no use my going back to school yet awhile. My mother opened her eyes wider than usual at this, and said she thought it very strange. The doctor only shook his head, and told her she would see, if she would only wait; and that was all. So I, of course, saw nothing at all, and waited accordingly.

My time being so very much at my own disposal, I determined to improve it by beginning to teach Mary everything I knew myself. The idea no sooner occurred to me than I put it into execution.

Our studies—if studies they could be called—were carried on entirely in the open air. My class-room was a little green slope in the garden, at the back of the bailiff's cottage; my pupils' seat was a root of an elm tree, which grew at the bottom of the slope; the sky above, and the fresh air all about us, was my class-room ceiling and walls; and the only teaching implement I employed was my own voice. It is useless to inquire how long these lessons lasted, or what they were about. Sometimes I invented stories for Mary, and related them with the most wonderful energy and feeling; sometimes I acted whole plays—tragedy, comedy, and opera—all by myself; sometimes I was a school-master, and Mary was a class, and I asked her dreadful sums, and she answered them all right, directly; sometimes we were gipsies in the wood, and I taught Mary to tell fortunes by the lines in her hand—oh, what a soft little hand it was! I used to think I could have gone on holding it, and looking at the pretty pink palm of it, for the rest of my life!

One day—it was just at the time when my lessons to Mary were in the most flourishing condition—I was sitting, as usual, on the grass by the elm-tree root, waiting for my pupil to come to me. She was later than usual that morning; and I began to wonder very much what it was that kept her away from me so long. My wondering, however, was put an end to, though not very satisfactorily, in a minute or two more. I heard footsteps behind me; and, looking round, saw a servant-girl, who immediately dropped a very elaborate curtsey, and said,

"If you please, sir, my mistress's compliments, and would I be so kind as to step round to the house, as she wished to speak to me particularly."

The sun had sought to rise above the horizon, a pale shade of gold sending threads of warmth across the moody waters; but alas, my spirit, burdened by the weight of last night’s revelries, held fast to the vestiges of the dark. A withdrawal from the tide of memories, I found myself in a skiff, casting ripples upon the long-neglected Thames, the very river that seemed to mutter familiar secrets with each light swell. Though my vessel rocked with rhythmic discord—the boatman’s groaning paddle reminded me of that devil-may-care future, wherein one might dream too audaciously—the serene beauty was, to be honest, almost unendurable. Always, I had it against me: the fountains of nature sang a lilting refrain, yet my heart hung like a gossamer curtain, torn and ragged in the winds of sobriety.

For hours I floated like a wayward ghost, ebbing and flowing in my reedy craft, caressed by willows that mourned over the riverbank. My mind, a tempestuous cauldron, leapt and danced about images of yeasted spirits and the raucous laughter of yestereve. How I had come to revel in their embrace! Yet, shadows stretched long along the water’s edge, and the name of Billy Devine echoed in the rafters of my brain—not forgotten, mind you, but dulled to the hue of a worn remembrance. He, the gentleman of the night and the arbiter of dreamy conviviality, seemed lost within the shimmering cascades of that twilight—an image fleeting, like a syllable from a fading song.

The boat glided to a halt, and I—having discarded thoughts of last night’s intoxication—looked up to behold the first light marked upon my destiny. There, lo! A verdant inn, rising before me like a spire from the sea, where very life seemed to be stitched into the fabric of the ivy-clothed walls. "The Sculling Goose" it was called, and my stomach, a treacherous ally in moments such as these, rumbled with unhappy demand for sustenance. But it was not just food I sought; nay, it was the sweet solace of storytelling, the kind that flourishes only within the company of men who have too much to drink and become far more eloquent than their temperance would ever permit.

As I docked with modest clumsiness, the door swung open to reveal figures clad in fine linen and the trappings of careless wealth. Amongst them appeared Bob Darbishire, that wayward scion of fortune, emerging like a benevolent spirit from his own extravagant tomb of vice. His laughter rang out, rippling horizons with the tones of careless abandon. As I approached the gathering of laughter, I noted the blue satin cravat tied loosely about his throat and the tilt of his waistcoat, snug and boastful as he swaggered into the sunlit realm. “Come, my dear friend!” he called, with an exuberant grin that flickered with the promise of mischief. “You look as if you’ve seen a phantom—have you returned to haunt us all?”

Earlier, his kind was bred to lead; yet here they lay like spent coins amidst the bills, with no guidance other than their own scarcely learned lessons. Bob draped a brawny arm around my shoulders, and I felt the breath of mischief swirling close. “What tales of folly and chase shall we share this fine morn?” he inquired, eyes sparkling like indolent stars barely awake to the day. I could scarcely resist, though caution nagged at the edges of my mind—a truth most clear emerged: within the crest of youth lies the somber echo of decay, and too many of our merry fellows had taken the plunge into the abyss of unwarranted extravagance, each joy a step toward a reckoning unwelcome.

Over mugs of foamy ale, stories unfolded like delicate petals splayed wide for bounteous inspection. Bob spun yarns of glorious escapades: rugby, betting, gambling games played in the velvet-cloaked corners of clandestine salons—each brief, raucous thrall, a note suspended in a dissonant tune. As he recounted his most recent dalliance with a thoroughbred at Newmarket, I caught the bitter wine of disappointment as it slipped down my throat. The young men at his side, eager acolytes to his grandiose tales, mirrored him and sought to infect their own lives with a splash of his dazzling lifestyle. But I observed yet another truth—a mirror held to their exuberance revealed the visages of decadence’s rookies, perfumed with ignorance and bloated with dreams.

As the sun hung higher in the sky, illuminating the wrestling shadows of the occluded pasts, realization dawned upon me with striking clarity: while these figures danced gleefully on the sanguine edge of wealth’s waltz, the lineage they had inherited faltered—once hallowed promises became tattered and stained remembrances, mocking their foolish endeavors. Ah, the charm of extravagance was indeed beguiling, yoking its followers to ambitions so grand yet so hollow. And as I sat, a silent observer ensnared by prose’s chains while regaling my old friend, I sensed the unseen shadows looming over their revelry, their fates entangled like the very waters beneath us, churning incessantly into a drearier abyss of longing and lost fortune.

California Set to Release Third Batch of Golden State Stimulus Checks on Oct. 5

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — As part of the Golden State Stimulus program, California is preparing to send out another round of direct payments to eligible residents starting on Oct. 5. Third stimulus check: Here's how to know if you'll get the $1,400 payments

Washington CNN — A third round of stimulus payments is expected to be on the way later this month.

The payments are included in a sweeping $1.9 trillion Covid relief package that was approved by the Senate on Saturday and could be signed by President Joe Biden soon after the House takes a final vote, now expected to be on Wednesday.

“Once the rescue plan is signed, we’ll be able to start getting payments out this month. Treasury and IRS are working tirelessly to make that happen,” White House press secretary Jen Psaki said on Tuesday.

Roughly 90% of American households will be eligible, according to an estimate from the Penn Wharton Budget Model.

Here’s what you need to know:

How much will you get?

The payments are worth up to $1,400 per person, including dependents. So a couple with two children could receive up to $5,600. Unlike prior rounds, families will now receive the additional money for adult dependents over the age of 17.

The full amount goes to individuals earning less than $75,000 of adjusted gross income, heads of households (like single parents) earning less than $112,500 and married couples earning less than $150,000. But then the payments gradually phase out as income goes up.

Do you make too much money to be eligible?

Individuals who earn at least $80,000 a year of adjusted gross income, heads of households who earn at least $120,000 and married couples who earn at least $160,000 will be completely cut off from the third round of stimulus payments – regardless of how many children they have.

On what year are the income limits based?

The income thresholds will be based on a taxpayer’s most recent return. If they’ve already filed a 2020 return by the time the payment is sent, the IRS will base eligibility on their 2020 adjusted gross income. If not, it will be based on the 2019 return or the information submitted through an online portal set up last year for people who don’t usually file tax returns.

When can you expect the money?

People could start seeing the payments hit their bank accounts within days of Biden signing the bill – which is expected to happen soon after the House votes on Wednesday on the $1.9 trillion Covid relief package.

For the previous pandemic stimulus bill, the IRS started sending out the second round of payments three days after then-President Donald Trump signed that legislation in late December. But it’s possible that tax filing season, which is underway, could slow down the process this time.

The payments do not all go out at once. Those whose bank information is on file with the IRS would likely get the money first, because it would be directly deposited into their accounts. Others may receive paper checks or prepaid debit cards in the mail.

The IRS is “building on lessons learned from previous rounds to increase the households that will get electronic payments, which are substantially faster than checks,” Psaki said.

You got the last stimulus check. Will you get this one?

Not necessarily. While the same people who received the full amounts in the previous two rounds of stimulus payments will likely get the full amount this time, the checks will phase out faster now – cutting off people at a lower income level.

The first round, which was worth up to $1,200, excluded individuals who earned at least $99,000, head of household filers with one child who earned more than $136,500 and married couples without children earning more than $198,000 – but families earning a little more were still eligible if they had children. About 160 million payments were delivered, with 94% of families receiving the money.

The second round, which was worth up to $600, also phased out a little faster because the full amount was smaller. It phased out entirely at $87,000 for single filers without children and $174,000 for those married filing jointly without children. Again, those earning a little more were still eligible if they had children. About 158 million payments went out, with 92% of families receiving them.

The payments have been based on a taxpayer’s most recent tax return. So those who have filed new returns since last March could fall into or out of eligibility if their incomes changed.

Who else isn’t eligible?

Undocumented immigrants who don’t have Social Security numbers remain ineligible for the payments. But their spouses and children are eligible as long as they have Social Security numbers. They were excluded from the first round.

Will you owe back some money to the IRS if you earned more in 2020?

No. If your 2019 income was less than your pay in 2020 you will not owe back any money.

But if your income fell in 2020, filing your tax return now – before the payments go out – may mean you’ll get a bigger check.

What if you never got the last payment but believe you’re eligible?

Most people receive the payments automatically, but there are many who missed out – for a variety of reasons. An estimated 8 million eligible people didn’t get the first round of payments that were delivered last year.

Many of these people have very low incomes and are not normally required to file tax returns. Last year, the IRS set up an online portal where they could register for the money. It’s not yet clear whether the agency will open up the portal again for the third round of payments.

People who have moved or changed bank accounts since the last time they filed tax returns may have also missed out.

Those who were due money during the first two rounds of payments and did not receive it can claim it as a tax credit, known as the Recovery Rebate Credit, on their 2020 tax returns.

Trump's Social Media Silence: Mentions Plummet 91% Since Ban

Donald Trump's social media presence has dwindled dramatically since his ban from Twitter and Facebook in January 2021. Mentions of the former president across social media platforms have plummeted by a staggering 91%, highlighting the significant impact of his removal from these influential platforms.

The ban, implemented following the Capitol riot in Washington D.C., aimed to curb the potential for further violence incited by Trump's online activity. Both Facebook and Twitter cited concerns about his posts' ability to incite and legitimize violence as the primary reason for the suspension.

Facebook's Oversight Board upheld the ban in June 2021, stating that Trump's posts during the Capitol riot "severely violated Facebook's rules and encouraged and legitimized violence." Trump remains banned from Twitter as well.

The former president has reacted with fury to the ongoing ban, labelling it a "total disgrace" and an "embarrassment" to the United States. He has since launched a personal blog to publish statements directly to his supporters, bypassing the traditional social media platforms.

Trump's team has previously hinted at his potential return to social media in a "new form" within the coming months. Advisor Jason Miller described it as a platform that will "completely redefine the game," though details remain scarce.

Despite the significant decrease in online mentions, Trump's influence within the Republican party and his potential impact on the 2024 presidential election remain significant factors to consider. His absence from major social media platforms has undoubtedly altered the political landscape, but his future online presence and its potential impact remain to be seen.

Police Officers Assaulted in US Capitol Riot to Testify Before Congress

In a highly anticipated hearing, a special congressional committee created to investigate the January 6 storming of the US Capitol will hear from police officers assaulted during the incident. The hearing will feature the first public testimony from officers since the event occurred six months ago.

The incident was spurred by former President Donald Trump and claims that the November 2020 election was stolen. Five people died, and dozens of police were wounded during the insurrection.

Maryland Representative Jamie Raskin, a Democrat on the panel, emphasizes the importance of the officers' testimonies. "These officers put their lives on the line to protect our democracy, and it's crucial that we hear their stories and understand the full extent of what happened that day," Raskin said.

The investigation faces GOP opposition, with House Republican leadership pulling appointments to the panel after Democratic objections. Speaker Nancy Pelosi appointed two Republicans critical of Trump to the panel, amid GOP attempts to discredit the probe.

Four police officers are set to testify about their brutal experiences during the riot. Harry Dunn, a Capitol Police Officer, said in a statement, "I want to make sure that the American people know the truth about what happened that day. We were fighting for our lives, and it's important that our stories are heard."

Aquilino Gonell, another Capitol Police Officer, expressed similar sentiments. "We were outnumbered and outmanned, but we fought with everything we had to protect the Capitol and the people inside. It's important that the public knows what we went through."

Michael Fanone, a Metropolitan Police Officer, recalled the violence he faced during the riot. "I was beaten with a flagpole and Tasered. I thought I was going to die. It's important that we hold those responsible accountable for their actions."

Daniel Hodges, also a Metropolitan Police Officer, described the physical and emotional toll of the riot. "I was injured and left with a concussion. The trauma of that day will stay with me forever. It's important that we learn from this and make sure it never happens again."

Republican legislators plan to hold a news conference on the same day as the hearing to highlight the treatment of arrested rioters. Representative Louie Gohmert criticized the investigation, saying, "This is a political witch hunt. We should be focusing on the real issue - the mistreatment of those who were arrested."

However, Raskin countered, "The mistreatment of arrested rioters is a serious issue, but it's not a substitute for a real investigation into the events of January 6. We need to get to the bottom of what happened and hold those responsible accountable."

The hearing is expected to be tense and emotional, as the officers recount the violence and trauma they faced during the riot. It's a critical moment in the ongoing debate over the depth of investigation into the event, with significant Republican opposition.

As the investigation continues, it's clear that the officers' testimonies will play a crucial role in shedding light on the truth behind the US Capitol riot. The public deserves to know what happened that day, and it's up to Congress to ensure that the truth is uncovered.

In a statement, Pelosi emphasized the importance of the investigation. "The American people deserve the truth, and we will not rest until we get to the bottom of this. We owe it to the officers who risked their lives and the families of those who lost loved ones."

The hearing is set to begin at 10 am on Wednesday, and it's expected to be a pivotal moment in the investigation into the US Capitol riot.

In the waning light of a summer’s eve—when the sky blushed as though in timid confession of its follies—and amidst the vast, whispering environs of the Moors, it came to pass that our erstwhile foundling, Jesse Cliffe, now unshackled from the petty concerns of apprenticeship and the trammels of civil society, ventured into a realm of solitude so wide and uncharted that even the most daring souls of the neighbouring hamlets might have deemed it a kind of wild, unbridled liberty. No longer the errant, much-maligned waif whom the rural authorities, with their bureaucratic indifference and abundant superstitions, had seen as naught but a bothersome byword to be lost, recovered, and lost yet again, Jesse had assumed the austere mantle of one who, by his own stray design, had embraced a fate far removed from the lachrymose histories of foundlings and errants. His departure from the employ of that irascible cattle-dealer Samuel Goddard—a man who, in his own fusty manner, had deemed it fit to mould the delicate spirit of youth into the hard-edged apparatus of commerce—was celebrated, if indeed one might speak of such a solitary victory, by the very elements of nature itself. For it was under a vault of deepening purples and dusky blues, with the wind sauntering across the heathered slopes as if in conspiratorial mirth, that Jesse, with a wild gleam kindred to that of the feral creatures which roamed these barren lands, resolved to fashion a life in which survival was a careful art, and convention a despised chain. He set about his new existence with a combination of adroit improvisation and an innate knowledge of the rhythm by which the Moors and their denizens—both beast and bumbling human—must abide; gathering the remnant fruits offered by a barren earth, fashioning shelters from the unyielding bracken, and tracking the denizens of the wilderness with an ease that belied his tender years, he was at once a student of nature’s unspoken laws and a reluctant emissary of its stern populism. Even as the local sportsmen, who once scoffed at the notion of a neglected child becoming more than a mere trifle in the annals of their quotidian amusement, began to whisper his name with a note of grudging admiration—acknowledging, perhaps, that in the art of field-sporting and the quiet lore of the hunt there lay a subtle grace—a certain rough nobility in the boy who neither burgled strictly nor clung wholly to the conventions of society, but instead trod the fine line between necessity and moral rectitude with the balance of a seasoned acrobat, our Jesse pursued his freedom with the unerring determination of one who has long been abandoned to destiny’s whims.

Thus it was that, amid the swirling mists and the echoing calls of the far-off curlews, Jesse Cliffe, now self-proclaimed and unburdened by the petty griefs of neglect and the vexations of unworthy masters, navigated the treacherous interplay between isolation and communion. In his modest lean-to, constructed from the fallen limbs of ancient oaks and the scattered stones of forgotten homesteads, he had, over a scarce period yet measured in the slow rhythm of nature’s pulse, instituted a peculiar order—a veritable code of conduct which shunned both wanton avarice and despair, and rather embraced a conscientious moderation wherein neither plenty nor hunger might reign supreme. His days were marked by the exigencies of the hunt and the careful, almost ritualistic tending to the small plots of wild grains and herbs which he coaxed from the untamed soil; his nights were lit by the flickering dance of a modest fire, whose fleeting light bore witness to whispered soliloquies on duty and desire that he dared not confess to any eavesdropping ear. And though societal reproach and the usual disapproving glances of his erstwhile employers had long receded into the sullen sepia of memory, a community of solitary wanderers—comprising both weathered sportsmen and even the occasional itinerant poet, whose soul found kinship in the lullabies of the heath—would sometimes, in moments of unguarded reverie, acknowledge his modest triumph through nods and murmurs as though he were a figure of myth reawakened. In his careful stewardship of his newfound liberty, there dwelt an ineffable concord between the rugged austerity of the Moors and the tender, unyielding spirit that had once been so neglectfully cast adrift; and thereby, as the wind sighed among the heather and small, cunning animals skittered to and fro in the twilight, the legacy of the forsaken child acquired a gentle, enduring resonance—a testament not only to the sterner elements of nature but also, indeed, to that innate human desire to overmaster even the wildest fortunes in pursuit of a truth that lay hidden, yet persistently beckoning, beyond the confines of polite society.

Mr. Halloway leaned forward and gently took her hand. "Am I not here for that?" he asked. "Here purposely to help you and all who need me in any way? Will it not be my greatest pleasure to do so, as well as my best and truest work? You may be sure, Miss Phebe, I will do all I can for you, with God's help."

"Rather damp for you to be sitting there without a shawl, isn't it, my child?"

It was only Mrs. Anthony's friendly voice, as that lady passed hurriedly by, intent on hospitable duties, but Phebe started guiltily. What right had she to be out here with Mr. Halloway, keeping him from the other girls, when she ought, of course, to be in the parlors seeing that the old ladies got their ice-cream safely? "I'll go right in," she said, rising hastily; but Mr. Halloway drew her hand through his arm to detain her.

"Why? Because it is damp?"

"No; because I ought not to be selfish, ought to go back and help."

"Ah," said he, "I am getting new lights every moment. Then you don't go to parties just to enjoy yourself?"

She opened wide, serious eyes. "Oh, no." He smiled down at her very kindly, "You shall go right away," he said, releasing her. "I will not keep you another instant from dear Mr. Hardcastle and that nice Mrs. Upjohn. But before you go let me tell you, Miss Phebe, that, if only in view of your latest confession, I do not think you commonplace at all!"

GERALD.

It was another article of the Joppian creed, that there was no such thing possible as a purely Platonic friendship between a young man and a young woman; there must always be "something in it": either a mitten for him, or a disappointment for her, or wedding-cake for al–enerally and preferably, of course, the wedding-cake;--and belonging to such friendship as lawfully as a tail belongs to a comet, was a great, wide-spreading area of gossip. It was only in the case of Phebe Lane that this universal and common-sense rule had its one particular and unreasonable exception; and it was acting upon a speedily acquired knowledge of this by-law, that Mr. Halloway boldly pursued his plan for metamorphosing his young friend, right under the open eyes and ears of the Joppites. He lived so near that it was the most natural thing in the world for him to stop for a moment's chat, as every one else did, either inside or outside of the window as he went by; and as he was always sure of meeting others, call when he would, it certainly never could have been asserted of him that he went there only to see Phebe. Indeed, he often scarcely spoke with her at all when he so dropped in, and yet out of these frequent and informal meetings an intimacy had sprung up between them such as Phebe at least had never known before. She submitted herself to him docilely, reading his books patiently even when they bored her unutterably, as not seldom happened, and endeavoring to form her opinion straitly upon his on all intellectual questions, recognizing her own fallibility with a humility that at once touched and charmed him. Real humility is rare enough the world over, but nowhere is it less conspicuously apparent than among the flourishing virtues of Joppa; and it was not long before this fact was discovered by Denham Halloway, who, with all his gayety and light-heartedness, was a keen and discriminating observer of character. He was one of those interesting people whom all other people interest; one of those who derive their peculiar charm more from what they find in you than from what they show you of themselves, though one might be ashamed to confess the truth so baldly. These are the people who, without any especial gift of either mind or person, wheedle your secrets out of you before you know it, possessing all your trust and your liking before they have given any real evidence of deserving your confidence, and yet, somehow or other, though rarely either great or talented, or even heroically good, never for one moment abusing it. Such characters are not at all unusual, yet are generally accounted so; one of their chief qualities, according to their friends, being that they are so unlike everybody else. But Phebe certainly had never met any one at all like Mr. Halloway, and she was soon of the settled conviction that she should never meet any one quite like him again. He was true to his promise to help her; (he never made a promise that he did not honestly try to keep;) and he applied himself to the by no means thankless task with the good-humored directness and energy that characterized all his actions. There was quite a number of young girls in his parish, more proportionately than in the others. Bell Masters and Amy Duckworth had long been hovering on its borders, and the advent of so young and prepossessing a rector had instantly removed their last scruples as to infant baptism, and settled forever their doubts as to the apostolic succession. They had come in at once. It was even whispered that Maria Upjohn had in an incautious moment confessed that she preferred the litany to Mr. Webb's spontaneous effusions, and had been summarily sat upon by her mother, whose Bible contained an eleventh commandment curiously omitted from the twentieth chapter of Exodus in other versions, and reading: "Thou shalt not become an Episcopalian, and if possible, thou shalt not be born one." Then there were Nellie Atterbury, and Janet Mudge, and Polly and Mattie Dexter; there certainly was no lack of active young teachers for the Sunday-school, and Phebe was well content to remain passively aside, as of old. But, as Mrs. Lane remarked, there were no drones allowed in Mr. Halloway's hive, and before long Phebe found herself insensibly drawn in to be one of the workers too, with any amount of business growing upon her hands, and herself, under this new and wise guidance, becoming more and more capable for it every day.

He remembered a letter his mother had written him at college--that mother of half Scotch descent, and touched with Scottish second-sight, who had silently studied his character from infancy, and learned to comprehend it not without fear. He could repeat the letter word for word. It had given him his first hint that he had a character, and a duty to do with respect to it. He had cherished the missive for years, and had read it a thousand times for admonition. Alas! how poor a thing is admonition after all!

"There is one danger point in your character, my son"--he recalled the very look of the cramped words on the page of blue-ruled letter paper--"where I have kept watch since you lay in my arms as a baby, and where you must keep watch hereafter. You have high aims and strong convictions, and you mean to do right. You will never be led astray by others--you are too obstinate for that. If you ever go astray, you must take all the blame on your own head.

"You are generous, and I never knew you to do a meanly selfish thing in your life. And yet your point of danger is selfishness of a kind. I have observed you from infancy, and this is what I have seen. Your desire to accomplish your purposes is too strong. You are not held back by any difficulty. You make any sacrifice in pursuit of your ends. You use any means you can find to carry your plans through, and you are quick at finding means, or making them when you want them.

"I was proud of the pluck you showed in doing almost a slave's work for two years, because you had made up your mind to go through college. But I shuddered at the thought of what such determination might lead to.

"Oh! my son, you will succeed in life. I have no fear of that. But how? Beware the time when your purpose is strong, your desire to succeed great, and the only means at command are dishonest and degrading. That time will come to you, be sure. When it comes you must make a hard choice--harder for you than for another. You will then sacrifice a purpose that it will seem like death to surrender--or you will commit moral suicide! I shall not live to see you so tried; but if I see you practise giving up a little and trying to keep guard at this weak place, I may learn before I die to think of that hour of your trial without the foreboding it gives me now."

That letter was the last his mother ever sent him. It had been a consolation to him that before death summoned her, she had at least read his reply, assuring her of his determination to maintain his integrity in all circumstances.

"You say truly," he wrote, "that I never surrender a purpose or fail to carry it out. Reflect, mother dear, that the strongest purpose I ever had is this--to preserve my character. I will not fail to find means for that when the time comes, as I never fail to accomplish objects of less moment."

"The prophecy of the dear old mother is fulfilled," he muttered, while his nails buried themselves in his unconscious palms. "The time she foresaw has come, and I have committed suicide. Thank God the mother did not live to see! Thank God her vision was no clearer! She had hope for me at least. She did not know."
