An incomplete Supreme Court witnessed Biden’s oath. There’s history there.

Only six of the nine members of the Supreme Court attended President Biden’s swearing-in Wednesday, the first time in more than 20 years that not all of the justices witnessed the ceremony. Justices Clarence Thomas, Stephen G. Breyer and Samuel A. Alito Jr., the court’s three oldest, were the no-shows. “Several of the justices elected not to attend the inauguration ceremony in light of the public health risks posed by the COVID pandemic,” Supreme Court spokeswoman Kathleen Arberg said in a statement.

The justices have not conducted business in person since March — holding private conferences and oral arguments via teleconference — although they gathered at a memorial service for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in September.

Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., for the fourth time, administered the oath of office to the president-elect. But he has yet to see a supporter on the other side of the Bible.

President Barack Obama, whom Roberts swore in twice, voted against his confirmation to the Supreme Court in 2005. So did Biden. And President Donald Trump, to whom Roberts administered the oath in 2017, made clear during the campaign that he considered Roberts a “disaster.”

The relationship during that presidency was a rocky one, and the chief justice had the chore of presiding over Trump’s impeachment trial in the Senate.

But the theme of Biden’s inaugural address was putting differences aside, and the new president may have warmer thoughts these days for Roberts, who turns 66 next week. Roberts was the deciding vote to save Obamacare, the chief domestic accomplishment of the Obama-Biden administration.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, the first Latina on the Supreme Court, swore in Vice President Harris, the first woman to hold the job. Sotomayor did the same for then-Vice President Biden in 2013.

Also in attendance was Justice Elena Kagan, nominated by Obama, and all three of Trump’s selections for the court: Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

That presented more opportunities for awkwardness: They were seated behind Harris, who vigorously opposed all three. In particular, she conducted a heated grilling of Kavanaugh that thrilled liberals and deeply angered conservatives.

As a team, former senators Biden and Harris voted against six of the nine justices on the current court.

That might explain some of the no-shows.

Thomas, 72, and Alito, 70, are a different story.

Biden attempted to filibuster Alito’s nomination and said President George W. Bush’s choice was too conservative to replace Justice Sandra Day O’Connor, who at the time was the Supreme Court’s pivotal justice.

Biden has even more history with Thomas, who was confirmed when Biden was chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee. Thomas’s nomination was disrupted by allegations of sexual harassment leveled by Anita Hill, who previously had worked in government jobs with Thomas.

Thomas made clear in an autobiography, “My Grandfather’s Son,” that he did not consider Biden trustworthy.

And in a documentary released last year, Thomas said that Biden's questioning at the confirmation hearings on the esoteric subject of natural law was just an attempt to force Thomas into taking a position on the issue of abortion.

“I have no idea what he was talking about,” Thomas says in the sympathetic film “Created Equal: Clarence Thomas in His Own Words.”

“I understood what he was trying to do. I didn’t really appreciate it,” he said.

Thomas was confirmed by a vote of 52 to 48 in 1991.

And the confirmation battle was equally bruising for Biden. Conservatives were outraged about the treatment of Thomas, a feeling that has only worsened with time, and liberals thought he did not do enough for Hill.

During the presidential campaign, that became a problem for Biden, and he reached out to Hill to express “his regret for what she endured.”

The campaign apparently decided criticism from Thomas in the film was not a bad thing.

Melania Trump didn't know whether she'd be attending Biden's inauguration until the president tweeted that he'd skip it

First lady Melania Trump found out that she wouldn't be attending President-elect Joe Biden's inauguration when her husband tweeted about it, CNN reported on Thursday.

Before the president's tweet on January 8, the first lady wasn't sure whether he would break from tradition and refuse to attend, symbolically undermining the peaceful transfer of power.

The first lady has largely remained quiet on her husband's campaign to overturn the 2020 election result but appeared to support his efforts by calling for "fair elections" after his loss.

First lady Melania Trump found out that she wouldn't be attending President-elect Joe Biden's inauguration the same way the rest of us did: via her husband's Twitter account.

A senior White House staffer told CNN on Thursday that the first lady hadn't been sure whether the president would break from tradition and refuse to attend the inauguration, symbolically undermining the peaceful transfer of power. She found out she and her husband would not attend when he tweeted about it on January 8.

"It's not the first time she has learned what he was doing because he tweeted it before he told her," the White House staffer told CNN.

The first lady has largely remained quiet about her husband's months-long campaign to overturn the 2020 election result, though she appeared to support his efforts by calling for "fair elections" following his loss.

"The American people deserve fair elections," she tweeted the day after news outlets declared Biden the president-elect. "Every legal - not illegal - vote should be counted. We must protect our democracy with complete transparency."

But even as the president fights to stay in the White House, the first lady has spent the past two months preparing for life after Washington, DC. She has been packing up, putting things in storage, and shipping the family's belongings to the president's Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, as well as arranging for her son, Barron, to attend school in Florida.

After remaining silent for five days following the pro-Trump insurrection at the Capitol on January 6, the first lady released a statement on Monday expressing sympathy for the rioters and police officers who died and accusing critics of spreading "salacious gossip" about her.

"I find it shameful that surrounding these tragic events there has been salacious gossip, unwarranted personal attacks, and false misleading accusations on me — from people who are looking to be relevant and have an agenda," she said.

In Arthur Conan Doyle's narratives, Sherlock Holmes exemplifies a unique blend of moral incentive and intellectual thrill. His motivation to solve mysteries extends beyond mere entertainment; it is intertwined with a strong sense of duty to uncover the truth and seek justice for victims. This moral drive often propels him into the depths of criminal investigation, where he applies his unparalleled deductive reasoning skills. Despite his solitary nature and sometimes asocial behavior, Holmes demonstrates empathy for the victims of the crimes he investigates. He possesses a subtle yet poignant awareness of their suffering, which does not compromise his analytical prowess but serves as an underlying impetus for his actions. For instance, in "The Adventure of the Speckled Band," Holmes is deeply affected by the fate of Helen Stoner, a woman whose life is endangered by her malevolent stepfather. This empathy highlights his ethically plain character, suggesting that while he may function outside societal norms, his underlying motivations are grounded in a desire to protect and serve the afflicted.

Holmes's exceptional skills in observation and deduction often overshadow his moral inclinations, illustrating his independence in investigations. His methods, while driven by a sense of justice, can appear detached or even aloof, thereby reinforcing his position as a revolutionary detective. Holmes navigates complex social dynamics and criminal behavior through the lens of scientific reasoning, often employing techniques that challenge conventional methods of detection. This independence allows him to remain dispassionate, yet effective in his work, as seen in stories like "The Hound of the Baskervilles," where he methodically pieces together clues to reveal the truth behind the supernatural veneer of the case. While his abilities are remarkable, the moral dimension of his character suggests that his ultimate goal is to benefit society, albeit expressed silently amid his eccentricities.

Dr. John Watson serves as a crucial counterbalance to Holmes’s character, facilitating the dynamic that drives the narrative forward. Although often regarded as a secondary character, Watson's role is instrumental in bridging the gap between Holmes's abstract, eccentric thoughts and a more accessible understanding for the reader. His practical nature serves to ground Holmes's more flamboyant eccentricities, allowing audiences to engage with the story while appreciating the detective's genius. Through Watson’s narration, the high-level reasoning of Holmes becomes comprehensible, transforming complex deductions into a shared discovery for the audience. In stories such as "A Scandal in Bohemia," Watson’s perspective enriches the narrative and highlights Holmes's brilliance through relatable observations. By employing a short story structure, Conan Doyle effectively constructs Holmes as a revolutionary detective whose detached character is both a reflection of his intelligence and a narrative device that engages readers, rendering the complexities of deduction into a compelling literary experience.

"Viens donc--je te chanterai des chansons que les esprits des cimetieres m'ont apprises!" MATURIN.

"Baffled!" he exclaimed, with a slight vexed laugh, as the boat vanished from his sight. "By a woman, too! Who would have thought it?"

Who would have thought it, indeed! Sir Philip Bruce-Errington, Baronet, the wealthy and desirable parti for whom many match-making mothers had stood knee-deep in the chilly though sparkling waters of society, ardently plying rod and line with patient persistence, vainly hoping to secure him as a husband for one of their highly proper and passionless daughters,--he, the admired, long-sought-after "eligible," was suddenly rebuffed, flouted--by whom? A stray princess, or a peasant. He vaguely wondered, as he lit a cigar and strolled up and down on the shore, meditating, with a puzzled, almost annoyed expression on his handsome features. He was not accustomed to slights of any kind, however trifling; his position being commanding and enviable enough to attract flattery and friendship from most people. He was the only son of a baronet as renowned for eccentricity as for wealth. He had been the spoilt darling of his mother; and now, both his parents being dead, he was alone in the world, heir to his father's revenues, and entire master of his own actions. And as part of the penalty he had to pay for being rich and good-looking to boot, he was so much run after by women that he found it hard to understand the haughty indifference with which he had just been treated by one of the most fair, if not the fairest of her sex. He was piqued, and his amour propre was wounded.

"I'm sure my question was harmless enough," he mused, half crossly, "She might have answered it."

He glanced out impatiently over the Fjord. There was no sign of his returning yacht as yet.

"What a time those fellows are!" he said to himself. "If the pilot were not on board, I should begin to think they had run the Eulalie aground."

He finished his cigar and threw the end of it into the water; then he stood moodily watching the ripples as they rolled softly up and caressed the shining brown shore at his feet, thinking all the while of that strange girl, so wonderfully lovely in face and form, so graceful and proud of bearing, with her great blue eyes and masses of dusky gold hair.

His meeting with her was a sort of adventure in its way--the first of the kind he had had for some time. He was subject to fits of weariness or caprice, and it was in one of these that he had suddenly left London in the height of the season, and had started for Norway on a yachting cruise with three chosen companions, one of whom, George Lorimer, once an Oxford fellow-student, was now his "chum"--the Pythias to his Damon, the fidus Achates of his closest confidence. Through the unexpected wakening up of energy in the latter young gentleman, who was usually of a most sleepy and indolent disposition, he happened to be quite alone on this particular occasion, though, as a general rule, he was accompanied in his rambles by one if not all three of his friends. Utter solitude was with him a rare occurrence, and his present experience of it had chanced in this wise. Lorimer the languid, Lorimer the lazy, Lorimer who had remained blandly unmoved and drowsy through all the magnificent panorama of the Norwegian coast, including the Sogne Fjord and the toppling peaks of the Justedal glaciers; Lorimer who had slept peacefully in a hammock on deck, even while the yacht was passing under the looming splendors of Melsnipa; Lorimer, now that he had arrived at the Alton Fjord, then at its loveliest in the full glory of the continuous sunshine, developed a new turn of mind, and began to show sudden and abnormal interest in the scenery. In this humor he expressed his desire to "take a sight" of the midnight sun from the island of Seiland, and also declared his resolve to try the nearly impossible ascent of the great Jedkè glacier.

Young Harris, having bidden adieu to Lord Musselburgh’s hansom, and watched it rattle its way toward Victoria Station, turned his steps westward, though with a far less assured and purposeful air than he was wont to display. Indeed, a casual observer might have remarked that the young gentleman seemed scarce aware of his surroundings, his brow knit in a thoughtful, almost troubled frown, his eyes fixed upon some invisible point far beyond the throng of Piccadilly. The raucous cries of the newsboys, the shrill whistles of hansoms vying for trade, the ceaseless rumble of omnibuses – all the usual din of London seemed to pass unnoticed, as if he were traversing some solitary moor rather than one of the city's most bustling thoroughfares. The truth was, Vincent Harris was profoundly, and quite unexpectedly, disquieted. The brief encounter of the afternoon, the glimpse of that fragile, almost ethereal, creature, had stirred within him emotions he had never before experienced, and which he found himself ill-equipped to comprehend. He had witnessed suffering and misery enough in his life, of course – the squalor of the East End was no secret to him, and he was actively engaged in several philanthropic endeavors aimed at ameliorating the lot of the poor and dispossessed. But this was different. This was not a matter of abstract statistics and sociological theories; it was a pang of personal sympathy so acute, so immediate, as to take him quite by surprise. He could still see her face, pale and pinched with cold, her large eyes – eyes that seemed too large for her small, delicate features – filled with a haunting sadness that spoke of hardship and loss. He recalled the threadbare shawl that offered scant protection against the biting wind, the hesitant, almost apologetic manner, and the way she had shrunk back, as if accustomed to rebuffs and unkindness. And he felt, with a force that startled him, an overwhelming desire to help her, to shelter her from the cruel realities of the world, to restore to her the bloom of youth and happiness that had so clearly been stolen away.

It was a curious sensation for a young man of Harris’s background and temperament. He was not, by nature, sentimental; indeed, he prided himself on his clear-headedness, his rational approach to problems, his freedom from the emotional excesses that he saw as a weakness in others. He was well-connected, possessed of a comfortable fortune, and had enjoyed the advantages of a first-rate education. His interests lay primarily in intellectual and political pursuits; he frequented the debates at the Oxford Union, wrote occasionally for the more serious periodicals, and had even entertained, fleetingly, the notion of entering Parliament. Love and marriage were matters that he had, hitherto, regarded with a certain detachment, as topics best left to the novelists and poets. He had observed the matrimonial pursuits of his contemporaries with amusement, if not a little disdain, and had often declared his intention of remaining a bachelor, at least until he had achieved some measure of distinction in the world. He moved in circles where eligible young ladies were plentiful, and he had been exposed to their charms and blandishments from an early age. He found them agreeable enough companions, capable of stimulating conversation and graceful dancing partners, but none had ever succeeded in capturing his imagination or stirring his heart. They were, he supposed, perfectly fine women, but they were, somehow, all of a piece – predictable in their opinions, conventional in their manners, and utterly lacking in that indefinable something that could spark a genuine connection.

And yet, this girl – a complete stranger, encountered only for a fleeting moment – had achieved what all the carefully cultivated graces of London society had failed to do. She had pierced his armor of indifference, touched a chord within him that he had not known existed, and left him utterly bewildered by the strength of his reaction. He found himself dwelling upon her image with a persistence that bordered on obsession. He replayed their brief encounter in his mind, analyzing every word, every gesture, every fleeting expression that crossed her face. He wondered about her circumstances, her history, her hopes and fears. He pictured her alone and vulnerable in the vast, indifferent city, struggling to survive against forces that were far beyond her control. And he felt a surge of protectiveness so powerful that it almost overwhelmed him. He knew, of course, that such feelings were absurd. He was a rational man, a man of the world; he could not allow himself to be governed by sentimentality. He had a duty to himself, to his family, to the causes that he had espoused. He could not allow himself to be distracted by a passing fancy, by a quixotic impulse to rescue a damsel in distress.

Albert read the Consul's letter a second time, holding it at arm's length and tilting his head back, as though he were trying to read a notice in the gallery of a theatre. He had slept late and the morning had advanced to nearly midday while he reread the note, and indulged in the luxury of a lazy smile. He had risen from his cot, and now stood, stretching himself to his full height in the centre of the room. The bamboo walls creaked pleasantly with the movement, and through the open window, he saw the bright blue sky. It was as though the previous months of rain had never been.

He looked around the room, taking in the familiar surroundings: the small writing table with its scattered papers, the hammock swaying gently in the corner, the worn rug on the floor. It was a humble abode, certainly, but it had been his home for the past six months.

It was strange to think that the Consul had left. For all his complaining, Albert had never actually imagined him acting on his threats to depart. He wondered what had finally spurred the man to action. The sudden cessation of the rain, perhaps? Or maybe the prospect of two more months of Stedman's company had finally proven too much.

He chuckled softly to himself. Stedman was still asleep, no doubt, snoring peacefully in the next room. Albert had no intention of waking him just yet. The fellow needed his rest, and besides, Albert was relishing this brief moment of solitude. He walked over to the window, pushing it open wider to allow the fresh air to flow in.

The air was clean and sweet, carrying with it the scent of damp earth and exotic flowers. It was a marked change from the heavy, humid air of the rainy season. In the distance, he could hear the chatter of monkeys and the shrill cries of birds. Everything seemed new and vibrant.

The Consul's words came back to him: "I appoint you my substitute". A wave of amusement, mixed with a touch of apprehension, washed over him. He, Albert Singleton, a writer of romantic adventures, was now the acting Consul of Opeki. It was absurd, preposterous, and yet… strangely exhilarating.

He pulled on his boots and stepped out onto the veranda. The village was slowly coming to life. Women walked to the marketplace, their baskets laden with brightly coloured fruits and vegetables. Children ran laughing through the dusty streets.

From the direction of the beach, he could see the familiar figure of Captain McAndrews striding towards him. The old sea captain had a wide smile on his face, and he waved his hat in greeting.

"Mornin', Mr. Singleton!" he boomed. "Grand day, ain't it? Like the whole world's been washed clean."

Albert grinned back, feeling a surge of optimism. "It certainly is, Captain. It certainly is." He took a deep breath, filling his lungs with the fresh air. Yes, it was a grand day indeed. A new day, full of possibilities. He was no longer simply Albert Singleton, the writer. He was now the acting Consul of Opeki, and he had a feeling that this was only the beginning of a most extraordinary adventure.

Nuclear waste reprocessing seems to be a viable solution for the problems of increasing energy demands and the waste and pollutants created in attempting to meet them. It seems rather wasteful to disregard this massive amount of energy that can be harnessed from the naturally occurring nuclear fuel. It is even more wasteful to only extract such a meager amount of energy as is currently done through light water reactors. The fact that such reprocessing methods as molten salt reactors are capable of generating as much as 75 times more energy than conventional reactors cannot be ignored when considering the benefits of implementing such a technology.

While, there will be an influx of plutonium transportation and storage due to this, there is no evidence that indicates it would increase the risk of malicious theft and weapon production. These risks are already curbed by the Nuclear Repository Committee, which regulates the transportation and storage of radioactive material, and would accommodate a growing number of these new reactors.

Furthermore, the amount of unused nuclear waste and its disposal in the United States is concerning. Not only does it seem archaic to simply bury the radioactive material that is produced from or has come in contact with military or civil nuclear reactions, but it comes with its own risks. Accidents and improper storage could result in such disasters as the one in the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico in 2014. If less actinide waste is made to be disposed of, as is the case after running molten salt reactors, then the risk for such failures would be significantly less.

Overall, the estimates for this new technology appear very promising, but further testing and data is needed to better estimate its effects.

Imagine standing amidst a lush forest, the gentle rustling of leaves, the soft hum of nature. This serene setting mirrors the essence of mindfulness—remaining present, fully engaged with the current moment. In this tranquil state, the shadows of longing and fear begin to dissipate, as you find solace in the simple beauty surrounding you. By consciously choosing to anchor yourself in the 'now', you open a gateway to profound self-awareness.

Embracing the present becomes a potent tool for healing from life's deepest wounds. When faced with the aftermath of great loss, the allure of dwelling on what was can be overwhelming. Yet, by tenderly acknowledging the pain and gently releasing it into the present moment, you allow yourself to process and heal. Like a river carving through a mountain, the relentless flow of now carves away at the barriers erected by past sorrows.

The mental discipline of staying present can serve as a shield against the onslaught of painful memories and fears. Picture these memories as waves in an ocean, cresting and receding with the tides of time. Each wave, though powerful, is temporary, and by observing them from the shore of the present, you gain distance and perspective. This distance allows you to witness your emotions, not as prisoners, but as guests passing through the landscape of your mind.

To cultivate this awareness, consider engaging in a journaling exercise. Each day, jot down your thoughts, feelings, and sensory experiences. This practice acts as a mirror, reflecting your inner world back at you, allowing for deeper introspection and understanding. As you write, you may uncover patterns or triggers that previously eluded your conscious mind, paving the way for new healing strategies.

The sun rose lazily over the small town, casting long shadows across the dirt roads and quaint houses. Grant Thornton, the minister's son, strode purposefully down the street, his mind filled with the weight of his family's financial troubles. As he approached the familiar sight of Deacon Gridley's house, he couldn't help but feel a sense of apprehension.

He rapped on the door, the sound echoing through the quiet morning air. After a moment, the door creaked open, revealing the stern face of Deacon Gridley peering out at him.

“Good morning, Deacon Gridley,” Grant greeted him, trying to keep his voice steady despite the nervous flutter in his stomach.

“Morning, Grant,” the deacon replied, his gaze sharp and calculating. “What brings you here at this early hour?”

Grant took a deep breath, steeling himself for the conversation to come. “I must speak with you about a matter of great importance, Deacon. It concerns my family's financial situation.”

Deacon Gridley raised an eyebrow, his expression unreadable. “I see. Come inside, boy, and tell me what troubles you.”

Grant stepped into the deacon's humble abode, the smell of wood smoke and old books filling his nostrils. He took a seat by the fireplace, the warmth of the flames comforting him as he prepared to lay bare his family's struggles.

“Deacon, as you know, my father's salary as the minister of our church is modest at best,” Grant began, his words measured and careful. “We have always managed to make do, but recently, unexpected expenses have left us in a precarious position.”

Deacon Gridley nodded slowly, his eyes never leaving Grant's face. “I understand the plight of your father, Grant. But all families must learn to live within their means.”

Grant felt a surge of frustration at the deacon's dismissive tone. “With all due respect, Deacon, you do not understand the unique financial burdens that ministers bear. The cost of books, hosting missionaries, and providing for the needs of the church community all add up.”

The deacon's lips twitched in a faint smile. “Perhaps you are right, Grant. But one must always be prudent with money, no matter the circumstances.”

Grant hesitated, unsure of how to broach the subject that weighed heavily on his mind. “Deacon, I have heard that you have some funds that you have collected. I humbly ask if you would consider lending some to my family in our time of need.”

Deacon Gridley leaned back in his chair, steepling his fingers in front of him. “I do have some funds at my disposal, it is true. But I must consider all options before making such a decision. I would need to ensure that any loan I provide would be repaid with interest.”

Grant felt a sinking feeling in his chest, knowing that the deacon's terms would only add to his family's burden. But he also knew that he had no other options. “Deacon, if it is interest you require, then so be it. My family's need is great, and we would be grateful for any assistance you can provide.”

After a moment of contemplation, Deacon Gridley finally spoke. “Very well, Grant. I will lend your father fifty dollars at one percent interest for a month. But mark my words, this is a business transaction, and I expect prompt repayment.”

Grant nodded, his heart heavy with the weight of the deacon's terms. “Thank you, Deacon. We are grateful for your assistance in our time of need.”

As he left the deacon's house, the sun shining down on him once more, Grant knew that the road ahead would be difficult. But he also knew that his family would endure, with the help of kind souls like Deacon Gridley, who despite his stern exterior, had a compassionate heart beneath it all. And so, with a renewed sense of determination, Grant set off to face the challenges that lay ahead, knowing that he had the strength and resilience to overcome them, no matter the cost.

I kind of see where functions and computational complexity intersect in the realm of programming, and it's a fascinating topic. In Python, functions are essentially mini programs or algorithms that perform specific tasks, kind of like pre-made Lego blocks that we can reuse to build more complex structures. There are 'built-in' functions, meaning they come pre-loaded with the language, and 'user-defined' functions that we create ourselves, which is handy for automating repetitive tasks or workflows. For instance, the'sorted' function is a built-in function that arranges elements in a list in ascending order, whereas a user-defined function might be a script that updates a database with new user information.

Now, let's dive into the nitty-gritty of functions. When I create a function, I'm essentially creating an environment where variables and values are bound together. This means that I can reuse those variables and values without having to redeclare them every time I call the function. It's like having a private workspace within the function where all the necessary resources are set up, making it easier to get the job done. But functions aren't just a solo act; they're often grouped together into'modules', which are essentially libraries of related functions that work together to achieve a common goal. Think of modules like a toolbox filled with different tools that I can pick and choose from to build a project. By using modules, I can make my code more modular, easier to manage, and reusable in different contexts. On the other hand, computational 'efficiency' is all about finding the sweet spot between computational and conceptual complexity – essentially, making my code run smoothly without losing sight of the project's goals. Graphs, with their nodes and edges, are a key tool for optimizing tasks, whether it's finding the shortest route between two points or minimizing costs while maximizing profits. Graphs come in different flavors, like directed graphs and trees, but they all help me understand complex data structures and make informed decisions. In the end, it all boils down to finding the 'right' balance and using the 'right' tools to get the job done efficiently.

House Managers Present Case Against Trump, Cite Incitement of Capitol Riot

WASHINGTON – House impeachment managers made a forceful case against former President Donald Trump on the first day of his historic second impeachment trial, asserting that he incited the violent insurrection at the Capitol on January 6 and demonstrated flagrant indifference in its aftermath.

In a meticulously crafted presentation, the impeachment managers showcased audio and video clips that outlined Trump's failure to act as the situation escalated and chaos unfolded in Washington, D.C. Democrats highlighted that the insurrection was a direct consequence of Trump's rhetoric, emphasizing his role in misleading supporters about the election results. "This was a direct attack on democracy itself, and it was carried out at the direction of the man who had sworn to protect it," Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), House impeachment manager, proclaimed during the proceedings.

Impeachment managers pointed out that many rioters believed they were responding to Trump’s instructions, claiming they had come to the Capitol at his invitation. The siege of the Capitol was not just a random occurrence but a planned reaction to Trump's baseless claims of a stolen election. This belief aligned with the incendiary language Trump used in his public statements leading up to and on the day of the riot.

As the violence unfolded, Trump continued to use social media to communicate with his followers. His tweets on January 6 included calls to reject electoral votes and encouraged supporters to "fight." The impeachment managers portrayed these missives as evidence of his complicity in the violent acts that would soon transpire. "The President's words, the words of an American leader, carried weight," Rep. DeGette stated. "He knew exactly what he was doing."

Throughout the chaotic events of the day, Trump remained passive, showing no immediate intention to stop the rioters. This silence was further compounded by his tweet attacking Vice President Mike Pence for not overturning the election results, which was seen by many as a betrayal at a critical moment. Rather than deescalate the situation, Trump's actions appeared to provoke further unrest among his supporters.

Approximately three hours after the storming of the Capitol began, Trump released a video message where he addressed the rioters directly, stating, "We love you, you’re very special. ... But go home and go home in peace." This response drew sharp criticism, as many viewed it as an endorsement of their actions rather than a condemnation.

The impeachment managers also revealed that some of Trump's tweets during the riot were later deleted, highlighting a troubling pattern in his social media behavior. Twitter responded by temporarily banning Trump for 12 hours and ultimately issuing a permanent ban to prevent any further incitement. This action underscored the platform's acknowledgment of the damage wrought by his words.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), who was in communication with Trump during the chaos, confirmed that he had informed the President that Vice President Pence had been evacuated from the Senate chamber due to the rioters' breach. Tuberville recounted the phone call, where Trump allegedly dismissed the urgency by insisting he would “continue objecting” to the electoral results. This interaction raised questions about Trump’s motives at a critical juncture when leadership was required.

Numerous clips presented by the managers painted a timeline of Trump's refusal to intervene while the Capitol was under siege. While the violence escalated outside, he held off on deploying the National Guard and other law enforcement support that might have quelled the chaos. As rioters roamed the halls of Congress, searching for lawmakers, Trump's inaction was likened to condoning the mayhem.

"As you will see, time and again, he directed the mob,” Rep. DeGette reiterated. “He encouraged them. He incited them. And he did it all in plain sight."

Supporters of Trump, in contrast, have claimed that his comments were misinterpreted and that he never directly instructed anyone to resort to violence. Defenders argue that Trump was merely exercising his right to free speech and expressing his dissatisfaction over the electoral outcome. However, the impeachment managers rebutted these claims by arguing that Trump's words had a direct escalation effect.

Cumulative evidence led many to believe that Trump saw the events unfold not as a crisis but as an opportunity to further manipulate and mobilize his base. As lawmakers were evacuated and the siege continued, Trump failed to show the leadership that the situation desperately needed.

The House impeachment managers' arguments were compelling, drawing on the stark contrast between Trump’s incendiary rhetoric and his failure to act decisively amid a national emergency. They framed the insurrection not just as an act of rebellion but as a profound betrayal of the sacred oath Trump took to protect the Constitution.

With the impeachment trial set to continue, many in Congress—both Democrat and Republican—are left grappling with the implications of Trump's actions. The trial will provide a platform for additional testimonies and evidence that could shed light on his responsibility for the events of January 6.

As the nation watches these proceedings unfold, the broader question remains: will accountability follow in the wake of such unprecedented actions by a former president? The stakes could not be higher as lawmakers consider both justice and the future of American democracy in the wake of the Capitol riot.

Angola, located in southern Africa, is a geographically vast country characterized by its rich agricultural land, tropical climate, and significant oil and diamond reserves. Its strategic location along the Atlantic coast and its abundant natural resources have made it a focal point for both internal and external conflicts throughout its history. Angola’s modern history is deeply intertwined with the Cold War, as the global struggle between Western capitalism and Soviet communism extended into the region during its decolonization process. Before gaining independence in 1975, Angola was a Portuguese colony, and the legacy of colonial rule left a complex socio-political landscape that foreign powers sought to exploit.

The Cold War significantly influenced Angola’s decolonization process, as global powers such as the United States, the Soviet Union, and China became deeply involved in the region. These external actors funded and armed various factions, exacerbating the conflict between the three main political groups: the MPLA (Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola), UNITA (National Union for the Total Independence of Angola), and the FNLA (National Front for the Liberation of Angola). Each of these groups was aligned with different ideological and ethnic constituencies, further complicating the conflict. The MPLA, supported by the Soviet Union and Cuba, eventually gained control of the government, while UNITA, backed by the United States and South Africa, continued its insurgency. The FNLA, which received some support from China and Zaire, also played a significant role in the early stages of the conflict.

The involvement of foreign forces, including Cuban, South African, and Zairean troops, further intensified the violence. Cuban soldiers, sent by Fidel Castro in support of the MPLA, played a critical role in several key battles, particularly the Battle of Luanda in 1975. South African forces, on the other hand, intervened in support of UNITA, often crossing into Angola from neighboring Namibia. The conflict became a proxy war, with each side leveraging Angola’s strategic importance and its natural resources, particularly oil and diamonds, to sustain their efforts. Angola’s oil reserves, concentrated in the Cabinda region, were a key factor in attracting foreign interest, as control over these resources could significantly influence the global energy market.

The social and political dynamics of Angola were further complicated by its diverse ethnic composition and the legacy of Portuguese colonial rule. Angola is home to over 30 ethnic groups, with the Ovimbundu, Kimbundu, and Bakongo being the largest. The MPLA, UNITA, and FNLA each drew support from specific ethnic and regional bases, deepening the divide within the country. The Portuguese colonial administration had historically favored certain groups and regions, creating inequalities that persisted after independence. The resulting civil war, which lasted from 1975 to 2002, caused widespread displacement, economic devastation, and a humanitarian crisis. Despite the end of the Cold War and the withdrawal of foreign forces, Angola’s instability persisted, shaped by both internal divisions and external influences.

Today, Angola remains a country marked by its rich natural resources and complex history. Its geographic and economic significance continues to attract global attention, but the scars of decades of conflict remain evident. The interplay of Cold War geopolitics, ethnic divisions, and colonial legacies has left a lasting impact on Angola’s social, political, and economic development, underscoring the intricate ties between global power struggles and local realities.

The anxiety which troubled Lady Lydiard’s mind, as she rose from her chair by the fireside, expressed itself by an act of almost feverish restlessness. Still thinking of Tommie, she moved to the window and looked out.

The prospect, over her ladyship’s pleasure-grounds and park, was blurred by a drizzling rain. The trees drooped mournfully; the last leaves of autumn fell incessantly; the sky and the earth met, and mingled their gloomy grays, on the line of the far horizon. The scene, dreary as it was in itself, harmonised only too well with the doubts and apprehensions that preyed on Lady Lydiard’s mind.

“Isabel!” her ladyship called out, fretfully; “Isabel!” A pause of silence followed. “Where can Isabel be?”

At that moment, the door opened, and a young lady, whose quiet dress and simple grace of movement contrasted strongly with the somewhat over-ornamented appearance of the room, entered, and inquired what her ladyship wished.

“Isabel, my dear, tell me truly, what do you think of Tommie? His looks this morning have made me quite uneasy. Do you think he is really ill?”

“I am afraid, Lady Lydiard, I noticed the same thing this morning at breakfast. He hardly touched his food, and seemed disinclined to move.”

Lady Lydiard sighed. “He is such a dear, affectionate creature! I cannot bear the thought of anything happening to him.”

Her ladyship, rapidly approaching her sixtieth year, possessed still much of the delicacy of complexion, and the youthful blueness of eye, which had first earned for her, among the more poetical of the county beaux, the nickname of “The Summer Sky.” Time, however, which had dealt so mercifully with her complexion, had shown but little indulgence to her figure; and had still less tenderness for the taste in dress which it had pleased her ladyship to adopt. The result of this partial treatment on the part of Father Time, was now visible in a stout lady, arrayed in a costume many years younger than herself; a costume, which, in its rainbow-hued variety of colours, suggested the idea of a garden-border suddenly endowed with life, and indulging in a promenade about the room.

Before Isabel could reply, the sound of footsteps in the corridor outside caught her ladyship’s ear. Her face brightened perceptibly.

“That must be Moody,” she exclaimed. “He will know about those Tollmidge people. And perhaps,” she added, with a sudden change of expression, “he may have heard something about a good veterinary surgeon. Do you think they are all alike, Isabel, or are some of them cleverer than others?”

Before Miss Isabel could deliver an opinion on the relative merits of veterinary practitioners, the door opened, and the person in question entered the room.

The new-comer was a man of perhaps fifty years, dressed entirely in black. His hair was already thickly streaked with gray, and his face bore the unmistakable marks of long and faithful service. His eyes, keen and intelligent, yet softened by an expression of respectful sympathy, rested upon Lady Lydiard, as he stood waiting silently for her to address him.

"It is too late," replied the aunt. "The oil is exhausted, and light is just departing."

Edwin started to his feet, exclaiming passionately--"Let me see her! Let me see her!"

"To see her thus, would be to blow the breath that would extinguish the flickering light," said the aunt. "Go home, young man! It is too late! Do not seek to agitate the waters long troubled by your hand, but now subsiding into calmness. Let her spirit depart in peace."

Florence sunk again into his chair, and, hiding his face with his hands, sat for some moments in a state of a mental paralysis.

In the chamber above lay the pale, almost pulseless form of Edith. A young girl, who had been as her sister for many years, sat holding her thin white hand. The face of the invalid was turned to the wall. Her eyes were closed; and she breathed so quietly that the motions of respiration could hardly be seen. Nearly ten minutes had elapsed from the time a servant whispered to the aunt that there was some one in the parlor, when Edith turned, and said to her companion, in a low, calm voice--

"Mr. Florence has come."

The girl started, and a flush of surprise went over her face.

"He is in the parlor now. Won't you ask him to come up?" added the dying maiden, still speaking with the utmost composure.

Her friend stood surprised and hesitating for some moments, and then turning away, glided from the chamber. She found the aunt and Mr. Florence in the passage below, the latter pleading with the former for the privilege of seeing Edith, which was resolutely denied.

"Edith wants to see Mr. Florence," said the girl, as she joined them.

"Who told her that he was here?" quickly asked the aunt.

"No one. I did not know it myself."

"Her heart told her that I was here," exclaimed Mr. Florence--and, as he spoke, he glided past the aunt, and, with hurried steps, ascended to the chamber where the dying one lay. The eyes of Edith were turned towards the door as he entered; but no sign of emotion passed over her countenance. Overcome by his feelings, at the sight of the shadowy remnant of one so loved and so wronged, the young man sunk into a chair by her side, as nerveless as a child; and, as his lips were pressed upon her lips and cheeks, her face was wet with his tears.

Coming in quickly after, the aunt took firmly hold of his arm and sought to draw him away, but, in a steady voice, the invalid said--

"No--no. I was waiting for him. I have expected him for days. I knew he would come; and he is here now."

All was silence for many minutes; and during this time Edwin Florence sat with his face covered, struggling to command his feelings. At a motion from the dying girl, the aunt and friend retired, and she was alone with the lover who had been false to his vows. As the door closed behind them, Edwin looked up. He had grown calm. With a voice of inexpressible tenderness, he said--

"Live for me, Edith."

"Not here," was answered. "The silver chord will soon be loosened and the golden bowl broken."

"Oh, say not that! Let me call you back to life. Turn to me again as I have turned to you with my whole heart. The world is still beautiful; and in it we will be happy together."

"No, Edwin," replied the dying maiden. "The history of my days here is written, and the angel is about sealing the record. I am going where the heart will never feel the touch of sorrow. I wished to see you once more before I died; and you are here. I have, once more, felt your breath upon my cheek; once more held your hand in mine. For this my heart is grateful. You had become the sun of my life, and when your face was turned away, the flower that spread itself joyfully in the light, drooped and faded. And now, the light has come back again; but it cannot warm into freshness and beauty the withered blossom."

“There now, Samuel,” interrupted Joan. “This is young Mr. Saltren you are speaking to and you are forgetting.”

“I’m not forgetting,” grumbled the old man; “don’t you be always of a flurrying me. Why, if I had had my situation as was promised me, we might have married and reared a family. I reckon one can do that on two shillings a day, and broken victuals from the kitchen. I might take the case into court and sue Captain Saltren for damages.”

“Hush Samuel,” interposed Joan nervously, looking at Giles.

“I aint a-going to be hushed like a baby,” said Samuel Ceely irritably; “I reckon if I don’t get my place, we can’t marry, and have a family, and where will my domestic happiness be? I tell you, them as chucked his lordship down the Cleave, chucked my family as was to be down with him, and if I can’t bring ’em into court for murdering his lordship, I can for murdering my family, of as healthy and red-cheeked children as might have been—all gone,” said the old man grimly. “All, head over heels down the Cleave, along of Lord Lamerton.”

“How can you talk so?” said Joan, reproachfully. “You know you have no children.”

“I might have had—a dozen of ’em—seven girls and five boys, and I’d got the names for them all in my head. I might have had if I’d got the sweeping and the broken victuals as I was promised. What’s the difference in wickedness, I’d like to know?” asked the old man sententiously, and figuring out his proposition on Saltren’s coat with his crooked fingers. “What’s the odds in wickedness, chucking over a horrible precipice a dozen sweet and innocent children as is, or as is to be, my family was as certain as new potatoes in June, and now all gone, chucked down the Cleave. It is wickedness.”

“What is that you hinted about Captain Saltren?” asked Giles gravely.

“Oh, I say nothing,” answered old Samuel sourly. “I don’t talk—I leave that to the woman.”

“It does seem a pity,” said Joan. “Samuel would have been so useful. He might have gone about the park picking up the sandwich-papers and the corks and bottles, after the public.”

“But,” said the young man, “I really wish to know what the talk is about in which my father’s name is introduced.”

“Sir, sir! folk’s tongues go like the clappers in the fields to drive away the blackbirds. A very little wind makes ’em rattle wonderfully.”

“But what have they said?”

“Well”—Joan hesitated. She was a woman of delicate feeling. “Well, sir, you must not think there is anything in it. Tongues cannot rest, and what they say to-day they unsay to-morrow. Some think that as the captain was so bitter against his lordship, and denounced him as ordained to destruction, that he may have had a helping hand in his death. But, sir, the captain did not speak so strong as Mr. Welsh, and nobody says that Mr. Welsh laid a finger on him. Why should they try to fix it on your father and not on your uncle? But, sir, there is no call to fix it on any one. I might walk over the edge of the Cleave. If a man goes over the brink, I reckon he needs no help to make him go to the bottom.”

“The jury couldn’t agree, Joan,” said Samuel. “Two of ’em wanted to bring in wilful murder against the captain.”

“So they did against his lordship in the case of Arkie Tubb. But that was nonsense. His lordship wasn’t there. And this is nonsense, just the same.”

“But the captain was nigh. Mr. Macduff saw him.”

“Well, and he might have seen me, and he did see me a little while afore, as I was coming from Court with some baccy money for you, Samuel. That don’t follow that I killed his lordship. Mr. Macduff see’d also Farmer Yole’s old grey mare. Be you a going accusing of that old mare of having had a hoof in his lordship’s death?”

Two letters; one from Calcutta, one from Oxford.

They came quietly in upon one salver, and were opened and read with pleasurable interest, but without surprise, or misgiving; and without the slightest foretaste of their grave amid singular consequences.

Rivers deep and broad start from such little springs.

David's letter was of unusual length for him. The main topics were, first, the date and manner of his return home. His ship, a very old one, had been condemned in port: and he was to sail a fine new teak-built vessel, the Agra, as far as the Cape; where her captain, just recovered from a severe illness, would come on board, and convey her and him to England. In future, Dodd was to command one of the Company's large steamers to Alexandria and back.

“It is rather a come-down for a sailor, to go straight ahead like a wheelbarrow in all weathers with a steam-pot and a crew of coalheavers. But then I shall not be parted from my sweetheart such long dreary spells as I have been thus twenty years, my dear love: so is it for me to complain?”

The second topic was pecuniary; the transfer of their savings from India, where interest was higher than at home, but the capital not so secure.

And the third was ardent and tender expressions of affection for the wife and children he adored. These effusions of the heart had no separate place, except in my somewhat arbitrary analysis of the honest sailor's letter; they were the under current. Mrs. Dodd read part of it out to Julia; in fact all but the money matter: that concerned the heads of the family more immediately; and Cash was a topic her daughter did not understand, nor care about. And when Mrs. Dodd had read it with glistening eyes, she kissed it tenderly, and read it all over again to herself, and then put it into her bosom as naively as a milkmaid in love.

Edward's letter was short enough, and Mrs. Dodd allowed Julia to read it to her, which she did with panting breath, and glowing cheeks, and a running fire of comments.

“'Dear Mamma, I hope you and Ju are quite well----'”

“Ju,” murmured Mrs. Dodd plaintively.

“'And that there is good news about papa coming home. As for me, I have plenty on my hands just now; all this term I have been ['training' scratched out, and another word put in: C -- R -- oh, I know) 'cramming.'”

“'Cramming,' love?”

“Yes, that is the Oxfordish for studying.”

“'--For smalls.'”

Mrs. Dodd contrived to sigh interrogatively. Julia, who understood her every accent, reminded her that “smalls” was the new word for “little go.”

“'--Cramming for smalls; and now I am in two races at Henley, and that rather puts the snaffie on reading and gooseberry pie' (Goodness me), 'and adds to my chance of being ploughed for smalls.'”

“What does it all mean?” inquired mamma, “'gooseberry pie'? and 'the snaffle'? and 'ploughed'?”

“Well, the gooseberry pie is really too deep for me: but 'ploughed' is the new Oxfordish for 'plucked.' O mamma, have you forgotten that? 'Plucked' was vulgar, so now they are 'ploughed.' 'For smalls; but I hope I shall not be, to vex you and Puss.'”

“Heaven forbid he should be so disgraced! But what has the cat to do with it?”

“Nothing on earth. Puss? that is me. How dare he? Did I not forbid all these nicknames and all this Oxfordish, by proclamation, last Long.”

“Last Long?”

“Hem! last protracted vacation.”

“'--Dear mamma, sometimes I cannot help being down in the mouth,' (why, it is a string of pearls) 'to think you have not got a son like Hardie.'” At this unfortunate reflection it was Julia's turn to suffer. She deposited the letter in her lap, and fired up. “Now, have not I cause to hate, and scorn, and despise le petit Hardie?”

Citigroup's $900 Million Defeat

Citi’s expensive day in court

Citigroup made a huge mistake last summer, when instead of transferring an $8 million interest payment from Revlon to its creditors, it transferred nearly $900 million of the bank’s own funds — the full amount of principal on the loan that wasn’t due for another few years. Some creditors promptly returned $400 million of the mistakenly wired money, but 10 others refused to return $500 million. The dispute ended up in court.

Yesterday, unexpectedly, a New York federal judge said the firms could keep the cash, despite acknowledging that the money had been transferred in error.

Wait, what? The lenders argued that the transfers matched what they were owed, so they could have “reasonably thought the payments were intentional,” assuming that it would be “downright irrational” for Citi to make such a big mistake, the judge, Jesse Furman, concluded. He might have ruled differently if he could “write on a blank slate,” but there were legal precedents supporting the defendants.

“New York law wants to discourage banks from making these kinds of mistakes,” said Adam Abensohn of Quinn Emanuel, who represented the asset managers. “It’s one thing to mistakenly send money to someone with no entitlement to that payment,” he told DealBook. “But there is nothing unfair about keeping that money when it’s owed.”

“At its heart, this case involves a clash between two basic intuitive principles,” the judge said:

“If one party sends money to another by mistake, the latter should generally be required to give it back.”

“On the other hand, if one party owes money to another and pays that money back to the penny, the latter should generally be allowed to keep and use the money as it wishes, without fear that the former will develop a case of borrower’s remorse and claim that the payment was by mistake.”

Where do you stand? The decision — which Citi will probably appeal — raises thorny questions about rules versus principles:

Since it was a mistake by the bank, why not return the money?

What responsibility do creditors have to the bank if it pays them back early?
