"Is it this that has turned your face so grey?" questioned Frank, alluding to the pallor noticed by his uncle; but which the elder and experienced man had refrained from remarking upon.

"I didn't know it was grey," rejoined Bell, his resentful tones cropping up again.

"It's as grey as this powder," persisted Frank, holding forth a delectable compound he was preparing for some unfortunate patient.

"And so, on the strength of this night adventure of yours, Bell, all you men are making holiday to-day!" resumed the doctor.

But Bell, who did not seem to approve of Frank's remarks on his complexion, possibly taking them as ridicule--though he might have known Frank Raynor better--stood in dudgeon, and vouchsafed no reply. Andrew Float took up the retort in his humble, hesitating fashion.

"There ain't one of us, Dr. Raynor, that would venture down to-day after this. When Bell come up to the pit this morning, where us men was collecting to go down, and said the Seven Whistlers had passed over last night at midnight, it took us all aback. Not one of us would hazard it after that. Ross, he stormed and raged, but he couldn't force us down, sir."

"And the Golden Shaft will have the benefit of you instead!" said the doctor.

"Our lives are dear to us all, sir," was the deprecating reply of Float, not attempting to answer the remark. "And I thank ye kindly, sir, for it feels more comfortable like already. They burns be nasty things."

"They are apt to be so when not properly attended to. Your brother should not have allowed it to get into this state."

"Well, you see, Dr. Raynor, some days he's been bad abed, and I didn't trouble him with it then; and young Pellet don't seem to know much about they bad places."

"You should have come to me. Bell, how is your wife to-day?"

"Pretty much as usual," said surly Bell. "If she's worse, it's through the Seven Whistlers. She don't like to hear tell of them."

"Why did you tell her?"

Josiah Bell lifted his cold light eyes in wonder. "Could I keep such a thing as that to myself, Dr. Raynor? It comes as a warning, and must be guarded against. That is, as far as we can guard against it."

"Has the sickness returned?"

"For the matter of that, she always feels sick. I should just give her some good strong doses of mustard-and-water to make her so in earnest, were I you, doctor, and then perhaps the feeling would go off."

"Ah," remarked the doctor, a faint smile parting his lips, "we are all apt to think we know other people's business best, Bell. Float," added he, as the two men were about to leave, "don't you go in for a bout of drinking to-day; it would do your arm no good."

"Thank ye, sir; I'll take care to be mod'rate," replied Float, backing out.

"The Golden Shaft will have a good deal of his company to-day, in spite of your warning, sir; and of Bell's too," observed Frank, as the surgery-door closed on the men. "How grey and queer Bell's face looks! Did you notice it, Uncle Hugh?"

"Yes."

"He looks just like a man who has had a shock. The Seven Whistlers gave it him, I suppose. I could not have believed Bell was so silly."

"I hope it is only the shock that has done it," said the doctor.

"Done what, Uncle Hugh?"

"Turned his face that peculiar colour." And Frank looked up to his uncle as if scarcely understanding him. But Dr. Raynor said no more.

At that moment the door again opened, and a young lady glanced in. Seeing no stranger present, she came forward.

"Papa! do you know how late it is getting? Breakfast has been waiting ever so long."

The voice was very sweet and gentle; a patient voice, that somehow gave one the idea that its owner had known sorrow. She was the doctor's only child: and to call her a young lady may be regarded as a figure of speech, for she was past thirty. A calm, sensible, gentle girl she had ever been, of great practical sense. Her pale face was rather plain than handsome: but it was a face pleasant to look upon, with its expression of sincere earnestness, and its steadfast, truthful dark eyes. Her dark brown hair, smooth and bright, was simply braided in front and plaited behind on the well-shaped head. She was of middle height, light and graceful; and she wore this morning a violet merino dress, with embroidered cuffs and collar of her own work. Such was Edina Raynor.

It is helpful to differentiate the two by meditating on the use of Abraham as an exemplar in both Pauline and Jamesian positions of justification. Paul and James used Abraham to elucidate their doctrine, but they did not choose the same incident of his life. Paul, points to an earlier time in Abraham’s life, before he had Ishmael or Isaac, expounding from Genesis to affirm that this was when Abraham was justified by faith. Abraham believed God, and because of his faith, he was considered righteousness.. James does not quarrel with the truth that Abraham is, in fact, justified by faith. However, James points to an event in Abraham’s life which takes place long after the moment when he offers up Isaac. James is arguing that when Abraham displayed his implicit faith by his works by being tested. God had long before taken inventory of his faith, and yet the world and even Abraham had not received full witnesses of it as it had yet to be tested and give testimony. Another beneficial tool for gaining perspective from both writers is the theme of “works.” Yes, in Romans Paul does instruct that works are unnecessary. Moreover, yes, James teaches that works are essential. Only if the reader assumes that both James and Paul are defining “works” in the same context is there a contradiction. The assumed contradiction resolves when we make the finer distinction that Paul was evaluating the good works that an unsaved person attempts to offer to be justified, gain God’s approval or work his way to heaven. James, on the other hand, was referring to those good works that a saved person performs which is evidential of saving faith. James then is not instructing that good works be necessary to obtain justification and obtain salvation, and Paul never teaches that good works are unnecessary. Faith alone saves, but faith that is unaccompanied is not the genuine article. And not saving faith.

Apparently, Martin Luther came to this settled theological balance at some point in his life concerning saving faith producing justification and good works. We should ponder these words of Luther “Faith is a living, restless thing. It cannot be inoperative. Works do not save us; but if there be no works, there must be something amiss with faith.” At one point Catholics challenged Luther with the argument that if Sola Fide is true, then one could say, "Faith without works justifies, Faith without works is dead. Therefore, dead faith justifies." Luther countered with: “We say that justification is effective without works, not that faith is without works. For that faith which lacks fruit is not an efficacious but a resigned faith. "Without works" is ambiguous, then. For that reason, this argument settles nothing. It is one thing that faith justifies without works; it is another thing that faith exists without works.”

So we can grasp that even though Luther’s opinion concerning the Epistle of James was not regarded as high as the Paulin Epistles, there was still agreement held by Luther with its teaching on works and faith. We must pan out over Luther’s life to include his other statements concerning the Epistle in their time, setting, and context. Luther progressed and made other testimonials defending a balanced position concerning faith and works. Admittedly, when adopting a narrow view concerning the epistle, there are several “thorny” moments concerning its agreement with Pauline theology. We must take a larger view and pan out to consider the full picture that James offers to understand the balance of grace and works. This is perhaps one of the greatest attributes of its canonicity.

The struggle for decolonization in Algeria was led predominantly by the rural masses, a process that resulted in both local and national liberation. This transformation, however, did not come without significant psychological repercussions. The violent conflict waged by France, a country that employed colonial tactics to exploit Algerian resources for its own economic benefit, left an indelible mark on the Algerian psyche (Stora, 2001). The psychological trauma experienced by Algerians during and after the colonial period is best understood through the lens of Sigmund Freud's principles on anxiety. Freud posited that anxiety is an emotional response that connects the recognition of danger with a threat response (Freud, 1926). In the Algerian context, this anxiety was not just a personal response but a national one, stemming from the constant danger and threat posed by French colonial rule.

The violence employed by the Algerian resistance, often in response to the military violence and political oppression perpetrated by France, can be viewed as a forced defense mechanism. In the face of systemic oppression and exploitation, where Algeria's resources were siphoned to benefit the colonial powers, Algerians resorted to violent opposition as a means of protection and survival (Fanon, 1959). This violent struggle was not merely about liberation but also about cultural survival. The French colonial project, with its Manichean worldview that created a divide in socioeconomic status between colonists and natives, led to a cultural identity crisis among Algerians. The discrepancy in population and resources further exacerbated the psychological trauma, as the colonists enjoyed privileged access to resources and power, while the Algerians were subjected to economic exploitation and political disenfranchisement (Sip Migration, 2017).

The long-term mental health implications of this psychological warfare cannot be understated. The Anxiety and Trauma Society of North America (ATSNA, 2018) notes that prolonged periods of anxiety and trauma can lead to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and other mental health issues. For a recovering nation like Algeria, the mental health consequences of decolonization are intertwined with its psychological and cultural recovery. While violent opposition to globalization helped Algerians cultivate a unified national identity, it also came at the cost of deep-seated cultural trauma. The Algerian struggle against French colonialism was thus not just a fight for political independence but also a battle for psychological and cultural liberation from the lasting impacts of colonial trauma. The legacy of this struggle continues to shape contemporary Algerian society and psychology, making it essential to acknowledge and address the psychological and cultural impacts of decolonization.

Press Release: American Medical Association Urges Mandatory COVID-19 Vaccination for Health Care Workers

In a recent statement, Susan R. Bailey, M.D., Immediate Past President of the American Medical Association, emphasized the critical importance of COVID-19 vaccination for health care workers to ensure the safety of both patients and colleagues. Dr. Bailey highlighted that over 300 million doses have been administered in the United States alone, with nearly 4 billion doses administered worldwide, demonstrating the safety and efficacy of the vaccines.

Health care organizations across the country are now advocating for mandatory COVID-19 vaccinations for all health care and long-term care workers. The recent surge in COVID-19 cases, driven by highly contagious variants and pockets of unvaccinated populations, underscores the urgent need for widespread vaccination efforts.

Despite the availability of vaccines, many health care and long-term care workers remain unvaccinated, posing a significant risk to vulnerable populations they serve. In response to this concerning trend, the statement calls for all employers in the health care and long-term care sectors to mandate COVID-19 vaccinations for their employees to ensure the highest standards of safety and care.

Support for universal vaccination of health workers is gaining momentum among experts and institutions, with a growing recognition of the vital role that health care workers play in promoting community health and wellbeing. While some individuals may be exempt from vaccination mandates due to medical reasons, they represent a minority, and efforts should be made to address their concerns and ensure alternative safety measures are in place.

Historically, vaccine mandates have proven to be effective in bolstering overall vaccination rates and reducing the spread of infectious diseases. However, addressing longstanding mistrust in health care institutions and fostering open dialogue with workers are crucial steps in ensuring the success of these mandates.

The leadership shown by the health care community in implementing vaccine mandates sets a positive example for all employers to follow. By prioritizing the health and safety of both employees and those they serve, health care organizations can play a pivotal role in stemming the spread of COVID-19 and protecting vulnerable populations.

Mr. Raby listened with admirable gravity; then fixed his eyes on the pair, in silence; and then said in a tone so solemn it was almost sepulchral, “This very day, nearly a century and a half ago, Sir Richard Raby was beheaded for being true to his rightful king--”

“Eh, dear poor gentleman! so now a walks.” It was Janet who edged in this--

“And,” continued the gentleman, loftily ignoring the comment, “they say that on this night such of the Rabys as died Catholics hold high mass in the church, and the ladies walk three times round the churchyard; twice with their veils down, once with bare faces, and great eyes that glitter like stars.”

“I wouldn't like to see the jades,” quavered Abel: “their ladyships I mean, axing their pardon.”

“Nor I!” said Janet, with a great shudder.

“It would not be good for you,” suggested the Squire; “for the first glance from those dead and glittering eyes strikes any person of the lower orders dumb, the second, blind; the third, dead. So I'm INFORMED. Therefore--LET ME ADVISE YOU NEVER TO GO NEAR CAIRNHOPE OLD CHURCH AT NIGHT.”

“Not I, sir,” said the simple woman.

“Nor your children: unless you are very tired of them.”

“Heaven forbid, sir! But oh, sir, we thought it might be a warning like.”

“To whom?”

“Why, sir, th' old Squire lies there; and heaps more of your folk: and so Abel here was afear'd--but you are the best judge; we be no scholars. Th' old church warn't red-hot from eend to eend for naught: that's certain.”

“Oh it is me you came to warn?” said Raby, and his lip curled.

“Well, sir,” (mellifluously), “we thought you had the best right to know.”

“My good woman,” said the warned, “I shall die when my time comes. But I shall not hurry myself, for all the gentlemen in Paradise, nor all the blackguards upon earth.”

He spake, and sipped his port with one hand, and waved them superbly back to their village with the other.

But, when they were gone, he pondered.

And the more he pondered, the further he got from the prosaic but singular fact.

In the old oak dining-room, where the above colloquy took place, hung a series of family portraits. One was of a lovely girl with oval face, olive complexion, and large dark tender eyes: and this was the gem of the whole collection; but it conferred little pleasure on the spectator, owing to a trivial circumstance--it was turned with its face to the wall; and all that met the inquiring eye was an inscription on the canvas, not intended to be laudatory.

This beauty, with her back to creation, was Edith Raby, Guy's sister.

During their father's lifetime she was petted and allowed her own way. Hillsborough, odious to her brother, was, naturally, very attractive to her, and she often rode into the town to shop and chat with her friends, and often stayed a day or two in it, especially with a Mrs. Manton, wife of a wealthy manufacturer.

Guy merely sneered at her, her friends, and her tastes, till he suddenly discovered that she had formed an attachment to one of the obnoxious class, Mr. James Little, a great contract builder. He was too shocked at first to vent his anger. He turned pale, and could hardly speak; and the poor girl's bosom began to quake.

But Guy's opposition went no further than cold aversion to the intimacy--until his father died. Then, though but a year older than Edith, he assumed authority and, as head of the house, forbade the connection. At the same time he told her he should not object, under the circumstances, to her marrying Dr. Amboyne, a rising physician, and a man of good family, who loved her sincerely, and had shown his love plainly before ever Mr. Little was heard of.

Okay, let's talk about weed. People throw around a lot of scary claims, but frankly, it's time to set the record straight. Some folks worry about marijuana causing mental health issues, but think about this: wouldn't we have noticed by now if it was turning half the population into schizophrenics? The truth is, while marijuana might temporarily worsen symptoms for a tiny minority already struggling, there's zero evidence it actually causes these conditions. In fact, many find it helps them cope with anxiety and depression.

Now, I know what you might be thinking: "But what about the smoke? Doesn't it cause cancer?" Look, I'm not saying you should hotbox your grandma's living room. But guess what? Vaporizers and edibles exist! These methods deliver the good stuff without the carcinogens. And if you're still worried about lung cancer, studies haven't found a link with marijuana use. Let's be real, the government lets us drink alcohol and smoke cigarettes – both significantly more harmful than pot. Shouldn't we be free to choose a comparatively safer option that mostly just affects us, the users? Sure, driving high isn't a great idea, but is it really any riskier than someone driving tired or distracted? And that whole "gateway drug" theory? Just because some people who use marijuana later try other substances doesn't mean marijuana made them do it. By that logic, wouldn't milk be a gateway drug too?

It was with the dawning of the next day, as the softened sun climbed the indigo sky with a languid grace, that Gregory Wilkinson found himself in profound ruminations over the matter of the churn-wash-boiler. His resolution, albeit bootless in the eyes of Susan, still clung to him stubbornly as a shadow to its owner. He believed, perhaps naively, that bestowing this humble artifact upon the orphaned children of the asylum would be an act of magnanimity rather than a source of wretched confusion. Little did he realize, amid all his grand ideals of upliftment and progress, the deeper implications of such a gift remained obscured by an ever-thickening veil of societal expectations.

Not far from where Gregory indulged his thoughts, the sunlit streets of Lewes bustled with a cacophony of merchants and townsfolk, their voices intertwining in a tapestry of rustic life. It was here, near the bustling marketplace, that Reynard Ainsley, a fellow denizen of the town with a penchant for philosophical discourse and an unsettling fascination with the foibles of man, met an alarming sight. Old Jacob, that perennial figure of the tavern, clad in garments as disheveled as his gait, was thundering—if one might call it thus—toward the very heart of public tumult, all the while brandishing that ever-familiar air of obstinacy that invariably accompanied his tipsy revelations.

"Yonder lies our intrepid Gregory, the maker of fine expeditions!" Old Jacob shouted, his voice carrying both the slur of spirits consumed and the audacity of a bard proclaiming tales of yore. Those who had gathered around the cart of Benjamin Stokes, the unflagging fishmonger, turned with mingled expressions of admiration and bewilderment, intrigued by the unfolding spectacle. Reynard, standing by, felt an impulse, bordering on the instinctual, to pry into the great philosopher's confounding ramblings. He approached the old man, keen to administer a modicum of clarity laced with gentle reproach.

"Have you not only recently come down from a revelry, Jacob?" Reynard inquired, casting a cautious glance towards the gathered crowd, who were now leaning in, though strangely fascinated—naught unlike the way one might regard a predilection to misfortune. "It is barely afternoon, yet you exhibit the fervor of one who has voyage upon the sea. Pray, did you indeed embark on an expedition of grotesque proportions with Mr. Wilkinson?"

At these words, Old Jacob’s brow furrowed, furrowing in defined consternation, as shadows danced beneath the creases of his wizened cheeks. "Nay, Reynard, 'tis you who miscomprehend! We beheld the churn, the great vessel of our trials, and it surely sailed upon the currents of the mind as much as the waters," he retorted, his voice climbing in timbre yet laced with the indistinct qualities of disbelief that only Bacchus could inspire. "It bore tales, a great tin hull in which we cast our fates—an odyssey aplenty, made moreover humorous by ol’ Billings the butcher, who dropped his sausages amidst our boisterous laughter!"

Reynard stifled a grin, lest he incite further ire within the tipsy elder, who now perceived the gathering of onlookers as a damning jury. To correct the misconceptions borne from drunken rapture would require not only a shrewd mind but a steady hand, and the novice philosopher sensed the storm brewing within Old Jacob’s splendid confidence. The dusk of sobriety masked by the cascading shadows of day only intensified the theatrics of his accusations. Resolutely, Reynard turned and prepared to effectuate his erstwhile escape, muttering refinements of explanation that would, undoubtedly, settle upon more fruitful occasions. It was clear: in such a moment, clarity was a far friendlier venture than entanglement in this fevered farce of tales and vessels—metaphors now muddled by wine and whimsy.

Referring back to Figure 17, there was a precipitous drop in commuter log submissions in the third month of the project. That was a bit disheartening, and it is hard to say why that might have happened. With the onset of winter at a New England campus, there is clearly a drop in people commuting either by bicycle or by foot, which may account for some portion of the decline. December also marks the end of the fall semester when everyone is very busy finishing schoolwork, processing grades, and so forth. Filling out the commuter log might just have slipped off the radar screen for many folks. In addition, December brings the onset of the busy holiday season and the resulting month-long break for students and faculty, during which time many do not even need to come to campus at all. Classes then resume for the spring semester in late January, perhaps also a clue to the low number of logs for that month. But none of that really explains the low number of submissions for February. One might also conjecture that any project of this type is going to have an initial burst of energy and excitement at the outset, which might then naturally decline. In an effort to combat this trend, we created the Carpool Challenge Week, a special blitz campaign in March to try and reinvigorate the initiative, which did result in an increase in log submissions for that month. Thus, one of the challenges we experienced was how to maintain project momentum in the face of both a natural decrease in engagement, but also specifically the problem of holiday and semester breaks experienced in higher education.

Another challenge for this project (or any alternative commuting project) is the simple fact that people enjoy the freedom, independence, and flexibility of driving their cars. This is deeply embedded in our culture. Therefore, it is essential to provide incentives for engaging in alternative modes of commuting. We gave out a lot prizes in the form of gift certificates to local restaurants, coffee shops, massage therapists, the local independent bookstore, and even some larger national chain stores. It would have been interesting to see, however, how some even larger prizes might have affected participation – such as giving away a nice bicycle, hybrid car, or electric car. This could have also helped to combat that dip in engagement the project experienced. The nature of the prizes didn’t really change during the course of the project. If the prizes, however, were to increase in value over the course of the project, that might have helped. The gift cards seemed to be more than adequate at the outset of the project, but if we had announced in December the addition of a couple of bicycles, and then in January the addition of a hybrid or electric car, one can only think that participating and engagement would have increased instead of decreasing.

Deeper in the city, where the gas lamps cast long shadows across the deserted sidewalks, and the trees in the squares stood like sentinels of a bygone era, the household of Malcolm Evelyn was bathed in a warm, golden light, a beacon of tranquility in the midst of the bustling metropolis. Within the stately mansion, Evelyn herself, a vision of elegance with her raven tresses and porcelain skin, sat poised in the silence, her eyes fixed upon the clock as its delicate hands inched towards the hour of ten, the time when her husband, Reginald, had promised to return from his evening stroll along the river. The soft ticking of the clock was the only sound that broke the stillness, a reminder that time waited for no one, not even the affluent and the esteemed, like the Evelyns. As she sat there, lost in thought, the memories of their whirlwind courtship and the subsequent wedding, which had set tongues wagging among the high society, flooded her mind. It was a union that had raised eyebrows, for Reginald, with his easy charm and roving spirit, had never been one to be tied down, and yet, he had swept Evelyn off her feet with his adventures and tales of the wild west, where he had spent years honing his skills as a marksman and a rider, earning the respect and admiration of his peers.

The door creaked softly as the maid, Emma, entered with a tray bearing a steaming teapot and delicate china cups, the aroma of Earl Grey wafting through the air, a comforting scent that seemed to envelop Evelyn in a sense of peace. As Emma busied herself pouring the tea, Evelyn's thoughts drifted back to Reginald, and the enigma that he was - a man who had effortlessly won the hearts of his comrades, from the rugged cowboys of the open ranges to the refined gentlemen of the university clubs, without ever seeming to try, his natural charisma and sense of fair play earning him a loyalty that bordered on devotion. And yet, despite his many talents and gifts, Reginald had never quite lived up to his potential, his inheritance of a modest fortune sufficient to maintain a comfortable lifestyle, but not enough to indulge his passions and ambitions, leaving him in a state of listless indecision, as if waiting for the winds of fortune to blow in his favor. It was this very lack of direction that had initially drawn Evelyn to him, for in her family, where moral rectitude and a strong sense of purpose were the guiding principles, Reginald's carefree nature had been a breath of fresh air, a reminder that life was to be lived, not just endured. As she raised the cup to her lips, the warmth of the tea spreading through her fingers, Evelyn couldn't help but wonder what the future held for them, whether Reginald would eventually find his calling, or if their marriage would become a testament to the enduring power of love, despite the odds.

The clock struck ten, its chimes echoing through the house, and Evelyn's heart skipped a beat as she rose from her chair, her silk gown rustling softly as she made her way to the window, pulling back the curtain to gaze out into the night. The street was empty, the only sound the distant rumble of a carriage, its wheels echoing off the buildings, a reminder that the city never truly slept. As she stood there, lost in the darkness, Evelyn's thoughts turned to the days ahead, and the challenges that their marriage would inevitably face, for in a world where social standing and family expectations often took precedence over personal desires, their union was not without its risks. And yet, as she thought of Reginald, and the easy smile that could light up a room, Evelyn felt a sense of determination wash over her, a resolve to stand by him, to support him, and to help him find his place in the world, no matter what the future may hold. The door opened, and Reginald walked in, his eyes crinkling at the corners as he smiled, and Evelyn's heart swelled with love, for in that moment, she knew that their bond was strong enough to overcome any obstacle, and that together, they would face whatever lay ahead, side by side. As they sat down to their tea, the warmth and comfort of the evening enveloping them, Evelyn felt a sense of peace settle over her, a sense of belonging, and she knew that she had made the right decision in marrying Reginald, for with him, she had found a love that would last a lifetime.

I concluded I was going to be complimented on the cut of my coat, to be asked the address of my tailor, and to hear the rakish sit of my hat admired. I now began to think I should hear a contention between the lords of the ocean, as to who should have me as a sample middy on their quarter-decks; and I was even framing an excuse to my father's friend for not joining his ship. Judge then of my surprise and mortification, when I was thus accosted in an angry and menacing tone by the oldest of the officers--

"Pray, sir, what ship do you belong to?"

"Sir," said I, proud to be thus interrogated, "I belong to His Majesty's ship, the Le----" (having a French name, I clapped on both the French and English articles, as being more impressive).

"Oh, you do, do you?" said the veteran with an air of conscious superiority; "then you will be so good as to turn round, go down to Mutton Cove, take a boat, and have your person conveyed with all possible speed on board of His Majesty's ship the Lee" (imitating me); "and tell the first lieutenant it is my order that you be not allowed any more leave while the ship is in port; and I shall tell your captain he must teach his officers better manners than to pass the port-admiral without touching their hats."

While this harangue was going on, I stood in a circle, of which I was the centre, and the admiral and the captains formed the circumference; what little air there was their bodies intercepted, so that I was not only in a stew, but stupefied into the bargain.

"There, sir, you hear m–ou may go."

"Yes, I do hear you," thinks I; "but how the devil am I to get away from you?" for the cruel captains, like school-boys round a rat-trap, stood so close that I could not start. Fortunately, this my blockade, which they no doubt intended for their amusement, saved me for that time. I recollected myself, and said, with affected simplicity of manner, that I had that morning put on my uniform for the first time; that I had never seen my captain, and never was on board a ship in all my life. At this explanation, the countenance of the admiral relaxed into something that was meant for a smile, and the captains all burst into a loud laugh.

"Well, young man," said the admira–ho was really a good-tempered fellow, though an odd one--"well, young man, since you have never been at sea, it is some excuse for not knowing good manners; there is no necessity now for delivering my message to the first lieutenant, but you may go on board your ship."

Having seen me well-roasted, the captains opened right and left, and let me pass. As I left them I heard one say, "Just caugh–arks of the dogs' teeth in his heels, I warrant you." I did not stop to make any reply, but sneaked away, mortified and crest-fallen, and certainly obeyed this the first order which I had ever received in the service, with more exactness than I ever did any subsequent one.

During the remainder of my walk, I touched my hat to every one I met. I conferred the honour of a salute on midshipmen, master's mates, sergeants of marines, and two corporals. Nor was I aware of my over complaisance, until a young woman, dressed like a lady, who knew more of the navy than I did, asked me if I had come down to stand for the borough? Without knowing what she meant, I replied, "No."

"I thought you might," said she, "seeing you are so d----d civil to everybody."

Had it not been for this friendly hint, I really believe I should have touched my hat to a drummer.

Having gone through this ordeal, I reached the inn at Plymouth, where I found my captain, and presented my father's letter. He surveyed me from top to toe, and desired the pleasure of my company to dinner at six o'clock. "In the mean time," he said, "as it is now only eleven, you may go aboard, and show yourself to Mr Handstone, the first lieutenant, who will cause your name to be entered on the books, and allow you to come back here to dine." I bowed and retired. And on my way to Mutton Cove was saluted by the females, with the appellation of Royal Reefer (midshipman), and a Biscuit Nibbler; but all this I neither understood nor cared for. I arrived safely at Mutton Cove, where two women, seeing my inquiring eye and span-new dress, asked what ship they should take "my honour" to, I told them the ship I wished to go on board of.

Brady's Impactful Speech, Fournette's Admiration Lead Buccaneers to Super Bowl Victory

As the Tampa Bay Buccaneers emerged victorious in Super Bowl LV, defeating the Kansas City Chiefs 31-9, it was clear that the team's success was not solely due to individual talent. According to Leonard Fournette, the Buccaneers running back, a powerful pregame speech delivered by Tom Brady served as a potent message of motivation, focusing on the importance of playing for honor and the significance of players' last names.

"Tom's speech was incredibly impactful," Fournette said. "He talked about the importance of playing for something bigger than ourselves, and how our last names represent our families and the sacrifices they've made for us. It was a powerful reminder of why we play this game."

Brady, a six-time champion with the New England Patriots, secured his seventh title in his 10th Super Bowl appearance, cementing his legacy as one of the greatest quarterbacks in NFL history. However, it was not just Brady's on-field talent that led to the Buccaneers' victory. Throughout the week leading up to the Super Bowl, Brady sent positive texts to his teammates every morning, boosting their morale and solidifying their focus.

The relationship between the FBI and Martin Luther King Jr. during the 1960s was fraught with tension, particularly as King's activism expanded beyond civil rights to include opposition to the Vietnam War and broader calls for economic justice. This shift in focus, while admirable to many, drew the scrutiny of powerful figures, including President Lyndon B. Johnson and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover, who viewed King's evolving stance as a threat to social stability.

One of the most significant points of contention was King's public opposition to the Vietnam War. Despite his immense contributions to the civil rights movement, Johnson felt personally betrayed by King's stance. In a private conversation, Johnson expressed his frustration, stating, "Here's this fellow King, been helping me all these years with the civil rights thing, and now he goes and does this. I feel like he's just turned his back on everything we've accomplished." Johnson's betrayal stemmed not only from King's criticism of the war but also from the perception that King was overstepping his role as a civil rights leader by addressing foreign policy.

The FBI, under Hoover's leadership, viewed King's activism through a similarly suspicious lens. Hoover's animosity toward King was well-documented, and he saw King's Poor People's Campaign as a subversive attempt to destabilize American society. The campaign, which sought to address systemic poverty and inequality, was particularly concerning to Hoover, who feared it could lead to widespread unrest. In a memo to his agents, Hoover wrote, "King's plans for a mass encampment in Washington, D.C., could result in riots and chaos. We must monitor his activities closely and preempt any potential disruptions."

Hoover's efforts to surveil King included seeking wiretap authorization, though he faced resistance from Attorney General Ramsey Clark, who initially denied the request due to concerns about King's First Amendment rights. Undeterred, Hoover persisted, framing his surveillance as a necessary measure to prevent rioting. However, as historian David Garrow notes, "Hoover's primary interest was not in preventing violence but in discrediting King and his movement." This shift in focus from personal attacks to ideological monitoring reflected Hoover's broader strategy of delegitimizing King's leadership.

King's own pessimism about the success of his campaign was evident in private conversations intercepted by the FBI. In one wiretapped call, King expressed doubt about the effectiveness of nonviolent protest, saying, "I'm beginning to think that maybe we're not making a difference. The system is too entrenched, and the violence in the streets is only going to get worse." These remarks, while reflective of King's growing frustration, were exploited by the FBI to portray him as a radical and unstable figure.

The FBI's concern about the radical nature of King's campaign for economic and social justice was not unfounded in the context of the late 1960s. The nation was grappling with racial tensions, urban unrest, and a divisive war, and King's calls for systemic change resonated with a growing number of Americans. However, from the FBI's perspective, King's vision of a more equitable society posed a direct challenge to the status quo.

Hoover's relentless surveillance of King was not just an attack on an individual but also a reflection of his own conservative values and vision for the FBI. As biographer Tim Weiner writes, "Hoover saw himself as the guardian of American order, and he viewed King's activism as a direct threat to that order." The FBI's actions during this period underscore the tension between dissent and national security, raising questions about the limits of government surveillance and the impact of political ideology on policy decisions.

In summary, the FBI's opposition to Martin Luther King Jr.'s activism was rooted in a complex interplay of political, social, and ideological factors. While King's efforts to address poverty and oppose the Vietnam War were seen by many as a natural extension of his civil rights work, they were perceived by powerful figures like Johnson and Hoover as a threat to stability and order. The resulting surveillance and smear campaigns not only targeted King but also highlighted the broader challenges of balancing dissent with national interests in a turbulent era.

Cuomo Brothers’ Interviews Under Fire Amid Nursing Home Scandal

NEW YORK (AP) – CNN anchor Chris Cuomo's past interviews with his brother, New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, have come under scrutiny following allegations that the governor’s administration underreported COVID-19 deaths in nursing homes. The once-lighthearted segments, which featured playful banter between the siblings, are now characterized by critics as inappropriate given the gravity of the ongoing scandal.

CNN has since reinstated its policy against Chris Cuomo covering or interviewing his brother about these issues after temporarily lifting the restriction during the height of the pandemic in 2020. Critics argue that this relationship created a clear conflict of interest, suggesting that it was unlikely tough questions would be posed regarding Andrew Cuomo's handling of the crisis. Roy Gutterman, a media law professor at Syracuse University, stated, “When you have a family member hosting a public figure, there are real complications. It becomes difficult to maintain journalistic integrity.”

The scrutiny began as reports surfaced indicating that the Cuomo administration had undercounted COVID-19 deaths among nursing home residents. New York's attorney general found evidence that the governor’s office had manipulated data to conceal the true toll, leading to accusations that they were attempting to dodge responsibility for policies that many believe exacerbated the pandemic's impact among vulnerable populations.

While Governor Cuomo has defended his administration, placing the blame for virus spread on nursing home staff, the situation has become increasingly dire for those advocating for transparency. An aide of the governor admitted that they withheld nursing home death tolls out of fear that the information would be weaponized against them by the Trump administration’s Justice Department.

During the peak of the pandemic, Chris Cuomo's interviews were often highlighted, portraying the brothers' camaraderie as a source of comfort for viewers. However, as the nursing home scandal unfolds, critics are calling into question the appropriateness of those past interviews. Jake Tapper, a fellow CNN anchor, openly criticized Governor Cuomo's decision-making during the crisis as “a bad decision that may have cost lives,” asserting that the administration attempted to conceal crucial data.

Despite the backlash, Chris Cuomo has maintained that his interviews with his brother were significant and entertaining for the audience. He has adhered to CNN’s policy of avoiding coverage of related scandals but acknowledged the complexity of the ethical situation in retrospect.

CNN has not shied away from covering the nursing home death scandal across other programming, providing a platform for diverse opinions, including voices that challenge the governor's narrative. Tapper, for example, has been vocal in his assessments, underscoring the pressing need for accountability.

As the controversy continues to unfold, the scrutiny surrounding the Cuomo brothers' interaction on air raises critical questions about journalistic ethics and the implications of familial ties in the public sphere—particularly when the stakes are as high as public health.

The sun hung low in the sky, casting a warm glow over the ancient stone buildings that lined the path to the river. Tom and Markham continued their leisurely stroll, the gentle sound of their footsteps mingling with the distant lapping of the water.

As they walked, a comfortable silence settled between them, broken only by the occasional rustle of leaves in the breeze. Markham glanced at his friend, noting the thoughtful furrow in his brow. Tom's eyes were fixed on the horizon, a distant look of contemplation in their depths.

"I can't shake the feeling that we are merely players in a grand theatrical production," Tom mused, breaking the silence at last. "But the roles we play are not of our choosing, and the script seems to have been written by someone else entirely."

Markham nodded in agreement, understanding the sentiment all too well. "It's as if we are trapped in a narrative that we did not write, forced to act out scenes that we never auditioned for."

They both chuckled at the absurdity of the situation, finding solace in the shared understanding of their predicament. The weight of expectation, both internal and external, hung heavy in the air, like a thick fog obscuring the path ahead.

"I often wonder," Markham began, his voice low and contemplative, "if this is all there is to life. Endless days of study, rigid expectations, and the relentless pursuit of success. Is this truly living, or are we merely existing?"

Tom sighed, a heavy breath that seemed to carry the weight of the world on its wings. "I fear that many of us have lost sight of what it means to truly live. We are so consumed by our ambitions and obligations that we forget to pause and savor the simple joys that make life worth living."

Their conversation continued long into the evening, the setting sun casting long shadows across the cobblestone path. They discussed their hopes and fears, their dreams and disappointments, laying bare their souls in the fading light.

As they reached the riverbank, the last remnants of daylight fading into dusk, Tom turned to Markham with a determined glint in his eye. "We cannot change the roles we have been given, my friend. But we can choose how we play them. Let us not be mere actors on a stage, but authors of our own destinies."

Markham nodded in silent agreement, a newfound resolve shining in his eyes. Together, they stood at the water's edge, the river flowing gently past them, carrying their hopes and dreams on its shimmering surface.

And as the first stars began to twinkle in the evening sky, a sense of peace settled over them, a shared understanding that they were not alone in their journey. For in each other, they had found kindred spirits, fellow travelers on the winding road of life.

FACT SHEET: President Biden's Global COVID-19 Summit: Ending the Pandemic and Building Back Better

A Call to Action for Global Collaboration

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, President Biden convened the Global COVID-19 Summit: Ending the Pandemic and Building Back Better. This virtual summit brought together heads of state, leaders from international organizations, the private sector, philanthropies, NGOs, and other partners to tackle the ongoing pandemic and build a more resilient future.

The Urgency of Ending the Pandemic

President Biden emphasized the need to accelerate global efforts to end the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in light of emerging variants that threaten progress. He called on world leaders to embrace a set of ambitious global targets across four key themes:

  • Vaccinate the World: Ensuring equitable access to vaccines and increasing vaccination rates globally.
  • Save Lives Now: Addressing the oxygen crisis and ensuring widespread availability of tests, therapeutics, and personal protective equipment (PPE).
  • Build Back Better: Preparing all countries for future pandemics by establishing a sustainable health security financing mechanism and demonstrating political leadership.
  • Calling the World to Account: Aligning around common global targets, tracking progress, and holding each other accountable for fulfilling commitments.

Bold U.S. Commitments

President Biden has consistently prioritized ending the pandemic, launching the National Strategy on COVID-19 Response and Pandemic Preparedness and elevating pandemic preparedness as a top national security priority. The United States has already donated more vaccines than any other country and launched a comprehensive U.S. COVID-19 Global Response and Recovery Framework.

During the summit, President Biden announced several new U.S. commitments to accelerate progress towards the global targets:

  • Vaccinating the World:
    • Donating an Additional Half-Billion Pfizer Vaccines: The U.S. will donate an additional 500 million Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccines to low and lower-middle income countries, starting in January 2022. This brings the total U.S. vaccine donations to over 1.1 billion doses, including the 500 million Pfizer doses purchased earlier this year. With this commitment, the U.S. will have donated three doses to the world for every one administered domestically.
    • Shipping Millions More Vaccines: The U.S. has already shipped nearly 160 million doses to 100 countries, donating more than any other nation. Millions more doses are shipped daily, all free of charge and with no strings attached.
  • Saving Lives Now:
    • Addressing the Oxygen Crisis: The U.S. is working with partners to increase oxygen production and distribution in countries facing shortages.
    • Expanding Access to Tests, Therapeutics, and PPE: The U.S. is supporting efforts to make tests, therapeutics, and PPE widely available globally.
  • Building Back Better:
    • Supporting a Sustainable Health Security Financing Mechanism: The U.S. is committed to working with partners to establish a sustainable financing mechanism for global health security.
    • Demonstrating Leadership on Emerging Threats: The U.S. will continue to provide leadership in addressing emerging threats and preparing for future pandemics.

A Collective Effort for a Healthier Future

The Global COVID-19 Summit underscored the need for continued global collaboration to end the pandemic and build a more resilient future. By working together, we can overcome this challenge and ensure a healthier future for all.

Miss Lloyd stood at the lace-draped window of her dimly lit room, gazing out into the yard where the sun, reluctant to show its full face, made shadows dance along the path. It had been two days since she heard the echo of laughter from the Judge’s house, a familiar sound she had come to associate with the arrival of summer. The empty porch, once filled with her friend Rob and the rest of the family, now seemed an island of solitude against the vivid greenery that framed their home. She could scarcely believe that they were all at the seaside, far removed from her, their merriment likely spilling over into the evening air, while she remained behind, her heart heavy with a sense of abandonment.

“Lonely as the last leaf clinging to a tree in autumn,” she muttered under her breath, glancing toward the faded photograph of her mother that hung prominently above the marble mantle. The recent pall over their household weighed heavily upon her heart. It was a bitter truth that Mrs. Lloyd was in no condition to partake in their usual summer rituals, her illness rendering her a mere shadow of her former self. Each day the vibrant energy of their home seemed to dissipate further, until the laughter of the world outside felt like a distant whisper carried away by the wind.

With a sigh, Miss Lloyd turned away from the window, her gaze dropping to the uninviting pile of letters awaiting her attention on the desk. Disappointment washed over her as she noted the absence of any correspondence from friends or acquaintances. Not a single word had made its way to her since the judge’s family left. She could scarcely recall the last time she had felt the rush of excitement upon discovering a letter in the mailbox, its contents promising news, adventures, and sometimes a sliver of affection.

In lieu of letters and laughter, she attempted to find solace in music; yet each note she played on the piano seemed to echo forlornly, colliding with the stark silence that enveloped the home. Her fingers, which once danced upon the keys with joy, now stumbled as they tried to beckon forth melodies that resonated with her heart. Frustrated, she allowed the instrument’s lid to close, its silence matching her own feelings of moral defeat.

Desperate for distraction, Miss Lloyd turned her attention to the well-worn novel lying atop her bedside table. The cover of "Marguerite's Wonder-ball" felt familiar in her hands, its pages imbued with the warmth of her earlier enjoyment. As she settled onto her bed, pulling the quilt around her, the story unfolded, its essence igniting a spark of imagination within her tired mind. Marguerite’s journey to sewing an exquisite gift mirrored her own yearning for connection, a longing for surprises that seemed cruelly distant this summer.

As the tale unfurled, Miss Lloyd's heart felt lighter with each passing chapter. Marguerite, learning to knit under the vigilant eye of her grandmother, brought forth memories of summers spent in joyful productivity with Rob, her confidant and constant companion. They had been inseparable, weaving dreams together just as Marguerite learned to weave her delicate stitches. In her mind’s eye, she could almost hear Rob’s laughter ringing through the air as they concocted plans for elaborate summer escapades. The nostalgia warmed her even as its absence chilled her heart.

The clock on the wall ticked steadily, marking the passage of time with an indifference that only deepened her sense of isolation. Each tick pricked at Miss Lloyd’s conscience, a reminder that her own birthday was upon the horizon, yet it passed without celebration or mention. No jubilant anticipation of gifts or well-wishes awaited her, only the quiet acceptance that her special day would arrive like an uninvited guest, arriving without purpose or fanfare. The prospect weighed upon her like a shroud, suffocating her spirits even as she found herself drawing comfort from Marguerite’s world.

Miss Lloyd found herself wishing, fervently, for her friend to return, for the Judge’s laughter to spill across the lawn once more, transforming the vacant spaces of her life into corners rich with delight and revelry. Until then, she would cling to the tale unfurling beneath her fingers, drifting within its narrative, each stitch knitting together a part of her spirit which felt so irreparably frayed. As the sun crept lower in the sky, shadows cast by the trees began to stretch, and with them a flicker of hope ignited in her heart: perhaps this summer could still hold its wonders, if only she dared to look for them amidst the quiet and change.

COVID-19 Vaccine Safety

Over the past year, results from a series of clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy and safety of COVID-19 vaccines in preventing serious illness, hospitalizations, and deaths.

Yet, with sporadic reports of rare adverse events, one question has remained unanswered: Just how safe are COVID-19 vaccines in the real world, outside of clinical trials?

Get more HMS news here

Now, a study published Aug. 25 in The New England Journal of Medicine by researchers from Clalit Research Institute in Israel, Harvard Medical School, and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health answers that question.

The research, which assessed the safety of the Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine, is based on analysis of data from nearly 2 million individuals in Israel and represents one of the largest real-world assessments of COVID-19 vaccine safety to date.

The findings, the researchers said, affirm the overall safety of the vaccine and underscore that the risk of adverse consequences from actual infection with SARS-CoV-2 far outweighs potential vaccine risks.

The study involved two analyses: A comparison of adverse events between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, and between unvaccinated people infected with SARS-CoV-2 and unvaccinated noninfected people.

The study showed that few adverse events were associated with the vaccine. Myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, the most serious of them, was rare, with a rate of 2.7 excess cases per 100,000 vaccinated people. This means that for every 100,000 individuals, 2.7 more cases of myocarditis occurred than would be expected, the researchers said.

By contrast, the risk of myocarditis was notably higher among infected but unvaccinated individuals, occurring at a rate of 11 excess cases per 100,000 people.

Coronavirus infection—but not vaccination—was also associated with greatly increased risk of pericarditis (an inflammation of the area around the heart), heart arrhythmias, heart attacks, strokes, pulmonary embolism, deep-vein thrombosis, acute kidney damage, among others.

Vaccine hesitancy

“To date, one of the main drivers of vaccine hesitancy has been a lack of information regarding potential side effects of the vaccine,” said study co-author Ben Reis, HMS assistant professor of pediatrics at Boston Children’s Hospital and director of the predictive medicine group in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children’s.

“This careful epidemiological study provides reliable information on vaccine safety, which we hope will be helpful to those who have not yet decided about vaccination,” Reis said.

“Those who have hesitated until now to get vaccinated due to concerns about very rare side effects, such as myocarditis, should be aware that the risks for this very same side effect are actually higher among unvaccinated infected individuals,” Reis said.

The results are based on records from Clalit Health Services in Israel, one of the world’s largest integrated health record databases. The analysis is the largest peer-reviewed evaluation of the safety of a COVID-19 vaccine in a nationwide mass-vaccination setting.

“The extensive nationwide rollout of Israel’s COVID-19 vaccination campaign provided the Clalit Research Institute with a unique opportunity to assess, through its rich and comprehensive digital datasets, the safety of the vaccine in a real-world setting, without needing to rely on individual-driven active reporting of side effects” said study senior author Ran Balicer, director of the Clalit Research Institute and Chief Innovation Officer for Clalit.

“These results show convincingly that this mRNA vaccine is very safe and that the alternative of ‘natural’ morbidity caused by the coronavirus puts a person at significant, higher, and much more common risk of serious adverse events,” Balicer said.

The results of this real-world study confirm, complement, and build on the previously reported findings of the Pfizer/BioNTech phase 3 randomized clinical trial, which involved 21,720 individuals, the researchers noted.

The comprehensive nature of this new analysis and the sheer volume of data involved offer a more detailed assessment of the vaccine’s safety across a wider range of adverse events.

“These data should facilitate informed individual risk-benefit decision-making, and, in our view, make a strong argument in favor of opting in to get vaccinated, especially in countries where the virus is currently widespread,” added Balicer, who also serves as chairman of Israel’s National Expert Advisory Team on COVID-19 response.

Previous efforts to characterize vaccine safety have relied on voluntary active reporting by vaccinated individuals, known to be incomplete. The new study relies on the analysis of millions of anonymized electronic medical records, which are far more comprehensive.

Parallel analyses

In an effort to provide the proper context that is critical for interpreting vaccine safety findings, the researchers also examine a wide range of adverse events both among vaccinated individuals and among unvaccinated individuals who were infected with the coronavirus, conducting two parallel analyses, assessing the occurrence of 25 adverse events in each of these groups.

In the vaccinated subgroup, the researchers compared the outcomes of 884,828 vaccinated individuals 16 years and older with those of 884,828 unvaccinated individuals based on an extensive set of sociodemographic, geographic, and health-related characteristics.

This analysis took place from Dec. 20, 2020, the launch of Israel’s national vaccination campaign, through May 24, 2021.

Some individuals switched groups based on their changing vaccination status, with 235,541 people moving from the unvaccinated group into the vaccinated group during the study.

To provide context for the vaccine safety findings above, a separate analysis was conducted among unvaccinated individuals. This analysis estimated rates of the same 25 potential adverse events among 173,106 unvaccinated individuals who were infected with SARS-CoV-2, compared with 173,106 carefully matched controls not infected with SARS-CoV-2.

This analysis took place from March 1, 2020, the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in Israel, through May 24, 2021.

The vaccine was found to be safe: Out of 25 potential side effects examined. four were found to have a link with the vaccine.

Myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle associated with the vaccine was rare—2.7 excess cases per 100,000 vaccinated individuals. These events were observed mainly among males between the ages of 20 and 34.

In contrast, myocarditis was far more common among unvaccinated individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2. The analysis showed 11 excess cases of myocarditis per 100,000 infected individuals.

Other adverse events moderately associated with vaccination were swelling of the lymph nodes, a mild side effect that is part of a standard immune response to vaccination, with 78 excess cases per 100,000, appendicitis with 5 excess cases per 100,000, likely as a result of swelling of lymph nodes around the appendix.

Reactivation of dormant herpes zoster (chickenpox virus) infection occurred in 16 cases per 100,000.

Unvaccinated risks

These small numbers of adverse events among vaccinated individuals stood in stark contrast with the high rate of multiple and more serious adverse events among unvaccinated individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2.

These included cardiac arrhythmias (a 3.8-fold increase above baseline risk with 166 cases per 100,000 infected patients); kidney damage (14.8-fold increase with 125 excess cases per 100,000); pericarditis (5.4-fold increase with 11 excess cases per 100,000); pulmonary embolism (12.1-fold increase with 62 excess cases per 100,000); deep-vein thrombosis, or a blood clot in the veins (3.8-fold increase with 43 excess cases per 100,000); myocardial infarction, or heart attack (4.5-fold increase with 25 excess cases per 100,000); and stroke (2.1-fold increase with 14 excess cases per 100,000).

Additional investigators on the study included Noam Barda, Noa Dagan, Yair Ben-Shlomo, Eldad Kepten, Jacob Waxman, Reut Ohana, all of the Clalit Research Institute; Doron Netzer of Clalit Health Services; Miguel Hernán and Marc Lipsitch of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; and Isaac Kohane of Harvard Medical School.

The research was funded in part by the newly announced Ivan and Francesca Berkowitz Family Living Laboratory Collaboration at Harvard Medical School and Clalit Research Institute.

The servants of the Hotel Salisbury, which is so called because it is situated on Broadway and conducted on the American plan by a man named Riggs, had agreed upon a date for their annual ball and volunteer concert, and had announced that it would eclipse every other annual ball in the history of the hotel. As the Hotel Salisbury had been only two years in existence, this was not an idle boast, and it had the effect of inducing many people to buy the tickets, which sold at a dollar apiece, and were good for "one gent and a lady," and entitled the bearer to a hat-check without extra charge.

In the flutter of preparation all ranks were temporarily levelled, and social barriers taken down with the mutual consent of those separated by them; the night-clerk so far unbent as to personally request the colored hall-boy Number Eight to play a banjo solo at the concert, which was to fill in the pauses between the dances, and the chambermaids timidly consulted with the lady telegraph operator and the lady in charge of the telephone, as to whether or not they intended to wear hats.

And so every employee on every floor of the hotel was working individually for the success of the ball, from the engineers in charge of the electric light plant in the cellar, to the night-watchman on the ninth story, and the elevator-boys who belonged to no floor in particular.

Miss Celestine Terrell, who was Mrs. Grahame West in private life, and young Grahame West, who played the part opposite to hers in the Gilbert and Sullivan Opera that was then in the third month of its New York run, were among the honored patrons of the Hotel Salisbury. Miss Terrell, in her utter inability to adjust the American coinage to English standards, and also in the kindness of her heart, had given too generous tips to all of the hotel waiters, and some of this money had passed into the gallery window of the Broadway Theatre, where the hotel waiters had heard her sing and seen her dance, and had failed to recognize her young husband in the Lord Chancellor's wig and black silk court dress. So they knew that she was a celebrated personage, and they urged the maître d'hôtel to invite her to the ball, and then persuade her to take a part in their volunteer concert.

Paul, the head-waiter, or "Pierrot," as Grahame West called him, because it was shorter, as he explained, hovered over the two young English people one night at supper, and served them lavishly with his own hands.

"Miss Terrell," said Paul, nervously,--"I beg pardon, Madam, Mrs. Grahame West, I should say,--I would like to make an invitation to you."

Celestine looked at her husband inquiringly, and bowed her head for Paul to continue.

"The employees of the Salisbury give the annual ball and concert on the sixteenth of December, and the committee have inquired and requested of me, on account of your kindness, to ask you would you be so polite as to sing a little song for us at the night of our ball?"

The head-waiter drew a long breath and straightened himself with a sense of relief at having done his part, whether the Grahame Wests did theirs or not.

As a rule, Miss Terrell did not sing in private, and had only broken this rule twice, when the inducements which led her to do so were forty pounds for each performance, and the fact that her beloved Princess of Wales was to be present. So she hesitated for an instant.

"Why, you are very good," she said, doubtfully. "Will there be any other people there,--any one not an employee, I mean?"

Paul misunderstood her and became a servant again.

Hours Before School Shooting, Suspect and Parents Met with School Officials About 'Concerning' Behavior

The suspect in Tuesday's mass shooting at a Michigan high school met with his parents and school officials to discuss his "concerning" behavior hours before the massacre, Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard said at a news conference Wednesday.

Four students were killed and seven people were injured in the shooting at Oxford High School in suburban Detroit. Ethan Crumbley, 15, is charged as an adult with multiple crimes, including terrorism causing death and four counts of first-degree murder. He has pleaded not guilty.

At the news conference, Bouchard said his office had not been made aware of any alarming behavior by the suspect before the shooting. But he said the office had since learned the suspect met with school officials on Monday, and then with his parents and school officials on Tuesday.

"The parents were brought in the morning of the shooting and had a face-to-face meeting with the school," Bouchard said. "The content of that meeting obviously is part of the investigation."

Bouchard said the school district had no record indicating the suspect had been bullied at the school. He added that authorities believe no specific students were targeted in the shooting.

In an interview with CNN, Bouchard said two teachers raised concerns about the suspect's behavior — first on Monday and then on Tuesday. He declined to specify what raised the teachers' concerns, but said that "ultimately it was determined that [the suspect] could go back into class."

Authorities have said the gun used in the attack was purchased by the suspect's father four days prior to the shooting.

Oakland County Prosecutor Karen McDonald said during a Wednesday press conference that her office is considering charging both of the suspect's parents and will make a decision "swiftly."

McDonald did not discuss a motive, but said the facts of the case "suggest this was not just an impulsive act," citing "a mountain of digital evidence, video tape, [and] social media."

CNN reports that the suspect was arraigned Wednesday. PEOPLE has not been able to reach his lawyer. He is being held without bond, The New York Times reports.

At the suspect's arraignment, authorities said they found two videos on his cell phone in which he talked about shooting and killing his schoolmates, CNN reports. According to the outlet, a journal found in the suspect's backpack also detailed plans for a school shooting.

Oakland County Assistant Prosecutor Marc Keast said at the arraignment that video footage shows the suspect emerging from the bathroom with a gun in his hand, Fox2 Detroit reports.

"At that point, he deliberately aimed the gun at students and began firing at students," Keast said. "After students started running he continued down the hallway pointing the gun and firing and firing in classrooms and at students who were unable to escape."

If convicted, the suspect faces life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The four fatal victims of the shooting were Madisyn Baldwin, 17, Tate Myre, 16, Hana St. Juliana, 14, and Justin Shilling, 17.

At her Wednesday press conference, McDonald said the shooting underscored the need for sensible gun-violence prevention laws, saying, "If the incident yesterday, with four children being murdered and multiple kids being injured, isn't enough to revisit our gun laws, I don't know what is," she said.

Michigan Middle School Staffer Arrested for School Threat Notes

ST. CLAIR SHORES, Mich. – A staff member at a Michigan middle school has been apprehended after allegedly leaving threatening notes across the school premises, including one that implied a danger significant enough to close the school. Officials are yet to release the identity of the individual, who was captured on security video as they placed the notes.

Lakeview Public Schools Superintendent Karl Paulson addressed the situation in a communication to district families, assuring them that no lockdowns or additional safety measures were necessary. "It is extremely disappointing that a trusted staff member would engage in such harmful actions during a time when everyone is particularly sensitive to threats," Paulson wrote in his letter.

The school district, located in St. Clair Shores, is now working closely with law enforcement to piece together the case, which has drawn considerable attention in light of Michigan's recent history with school threats. Notably, the threat emerged only two years after the tragic shooting at Oxford High School stirred the community and heightened vigilance in schools across the state.

This incident joins an unsettling pattern of threats disrupting educational operations. Federal agencies were already on higher alert following a wave of anonymous shooting and bomb threats posted on TikTok, prompting school closures nationwide.

Macomb County Prosecutor Peter Lucido emphasized the seriousness of the allegations. "There's enough evidence on the table for us to proceed with several charges," Lucido stated, noting the detrimental impact such actions have on school safety and public trust. He added, "We may never fully understand the staff member's motivation, but these kinds of threats need to be dealt with swiftly and seriously due to the current concerns over school safety."

Superintendent Paulson further stressed the district's commitment to maintaining a safe environment for students and staff. The administration has been proactive in its collaboration with law enforcement, handing over all necessary evidence to facilitate the ongoing investigation.

As students and parents continue to process the arrest in their community, authorities are focused on restoring a sense of security at the middle school. Such an incident underscores the fragile nature of safety in educational settings today and serves as a reminder of the need for vigilance in safeguarding those environments.

Details of the charges against the staff member will be disclosed as the investigation proceeds, with the school district promising transparency about outcomes relevant to the community's safety and peace of mind.

A Royal Paradox: The Lilibet Naming Conundrum

In a world captivated by the complexities of the British royal family, the birth of Meghan Markle and Prince Harry's second child, Lilibet 'Lili' Diana Mountbatten-Windsor, has once again put the Duke and Duchess of Sussex under the spotlight. While most people initially applauded the name choice for its homage to Queen Elizabeth II and the late Princess Diana, it's a decision that deserves closer scrutiny. By selecting "Lilibet," a name intimately connected with the monarchy they previously spoke against, Meghan and Harry find themselves in a paradox of their own making.

It's crucial to recall the explosive interview with Oprah Winfrey, where Meghan and Harry outlined the racial abuse and lack of support they endured from within the royal family. These revelations were significant enough to trigger a global conversation about racism and institutional rigidity within one of the world's most old-fashioned establishments. Their decision to leave royal duties was framed as a protest against these very issues– issues from which they sought refuge and autonomy in the United States.

Given their past criticisms, one has to question why they would choose to bestow upon their daughter a name so steeped in royal tradition. The choice of "Lilibet" as a tribute to Queen Elizabeth II seems counterintuitive for a couple that has publicly accused the royal institution of perpetuating racial prejudice. It's a move that raises eyebrows and leads to questions about their true stance on the royal family they sought to distance themselves from.

The name "Lilibet" could be interpreted as a conciliatory gesture, a olive branch extended towards reconciliation. But can such a gesture coexist with their earlier accusations? Is it possible to seek meaningful change while simultaneously invoking symbols of the institution you have criticized? These are complex questions that require us to ponder the difference between symbolic gestures and real change.

While a name may appear as a sentimental choice to honor family ties, its implications could be interpreted as a signaling of support for the very institution Meghan and Harry criticized. The couple's decisions thus far have had a significant impact on public perceptions of the monarchy, but naming their child after its current head seems more like a step towards personal resolution rather than any meaningful critique or reform.

For true change against racism and systematic issues within the monarchy, more is needed than familial reconciliations and symbolic gestures. A deeper commitment to challenging and reshaping an antiquated institution must continue beyond names and interviews. Conversations and actions on addressing racism are persistent battles that require more than a nod towards family history.

As we continue to dissect the relationship between the Sussexes and the royal family, it's clear that Meghan and Harry should not be viewed as heroes in the fight against racism. Instead, they are family members negotiating their position within an intricate, historically-charged environment. Whether their actions speak to reconciliation or contradiction is a matter open to interpretation, but it serves as a reminder of the complexities inherent in their ongoing narrative.

Majority of Americans Support Trump's Twitter Ban, Survey Reveals

WASHINGTON – A recent survey shows most Americans support the decision by Twitter to permanently suspend former President Donald Trump's account following the Capitol siege, a move seen by many as a necessary step to prevent further violence. However, this view is not widely shared among Republicans, who are split on the issue.

According to the poll, 61% of Americans agree with the ban citing concerns over the risk of additional incitements to violence, while 39% opposed the action. The survey illuminated deep partisan divides in opinions on social media's role in regulating speech and the responsibilities of tech companies in safeguarding democracy.

Facebook has also taken measures against Trump, banning him at least until the inauguration of President-elect Joe Biden, with an indefinite extension of the ban under consideration. John Gerzema, CEO of The Harris Poll, highlighted a significant takeaway from these actions, stating "we see that the American Business Community leadership is being sought out by citizens where they see a void in political action."

Reflecting on party lines, support for the ban varies significantly, with 36% of Republicans backing the decision, sharply contrasted by 80% of Democrats and 59% of independents in favor. This division underscores the broader debate over censorship and the responsibilities of social media platforms.

Among Republicans, concerns over censorship have surged, with 36% of Americans overall worried about the issue, albeit 69% agree that social media companies have the right to remove users who may pose a danger. The retrospective sentiment of 40% of Americans suggests that Trump’s ban was 'too little, too late,' expressing that such action should have been taken earlier.

Approximately 37% of respondents felt embarrassed by the former president's ban from major social media platforms. Meanwhile, 58% of Americans align with the removal of Trump due to his actions, which they consider dangerous, notwithstanding the 42% who fear such moves may set a censorship precedent.

A paralleling Morning Consult poll found that half of Americans believe social media giants should have enacted bans on Trump earlier, albeit with pronounced partisan differences shaping opinions on the bans. This division underscores the evolving debate around freedom of speech, censorship, and the role of social media in public discourse amidst a politically charged climate.
