"And so you sent for hi–nd proposed to him, did you?"

"P'opose to who, Mis' Gladys? I'd see Pete in de sinkin' swamp 'fo' I'd p'opose to him!"

"Then how did you manage it, pray?"

"G'way, Mis' Gladys! Any wide-awake widder 'oman dat kin get a widder man whar he can't he'p but see her move round at her work for two days hand-runnin', an' can't mesmerize him so's he'll ax her to marry hi––m! I'd ondertake ter do dat, even ef I warn't no cook; but wid seasonin's an' flavors to he'p m–aw, chile! dey warn't no yearthly 'scape fur dem chillen!

"I would 'a' waited," she added, presently--"I would 'a' waited a reas'nable time, 'cep'n dat Pete started gwine ter chu'ch, an' you know yo'se'f, missy, when a well-favored widder man go ter seek consolation f'om de pulpit, he's might' ap' ter find it in de congergation."

As I sat listening to her quiet exposition of her scheme, it seemed monstrous.

"And so, Moriah," I spoke now with a ring of real severity in my voice--"and so you are going to marry a man that you confess you don't care for, just for the sake of getting control of his children? I wouldn't have believed it of you."

"Wel–artly, missy." She smiled a little now for the first time. "Partly on dat account, an' partly on his'n. Pete's wife Ca'line, she was a good 'oman, but she was mighty puny an' peevish; an' besides dat, she was one o' deze heah naggers, an' Pete is allus had a purty hard pull, an' I lay out ter give him a better chance. Eve'y bit o' whitewashin' he'd git ter do 'roun' town, Ca'line she'd swaller it in medicine. But she was a good 'oman, Ca'line was. Heap o' deze heah naggers is good 'omans! Co'se I don't say I loves Pete, but I looks ter come roun' ter 'im in time. Ef I didn't, I wouldn't have him."

"And how about his loving you?"

"Oh, Mis' Gladys, you is so searching!" She chuckled. "Co'se he say he loves me already better'n he love Ca'line, but of co'se a widder man he feels obleeged ter talk dat-a-way. An' ef he didn't have the manners ter say it, I wouldn't have him, to save his life; but ef he meant it, I'd despise him. After Ca'line lovin' de groun' he tread fur nine long yeahs, he ain't got no right ter love no 'oman better'n he love her des 'caze he's a-projec'in' ter git married to 'er. But of co'se, Mis' Gladys, I ca'culates ter outstrip Ca'line in co'se o' time. Ef I couldn't do da–n' she in 'er grav–n' me a coo– wouldn't count myse'f much. An' den, time I outstrips her an' git him over, heart an' soul, I'll know it by de signs."

"Why will you know it more than you know it now? He can but swear it to you."

"Oh no, missy. When de rock bottom of a man's heart warms to a 'oman, he eases off f'om swearin' 'bout it. Deze heah men wha' swear so much, dey swear des as much ter convince deyselves as dey does ter ketch a 'oman's ear. No, missy. Time I got him heart an' soul, I looks for him to commence to th'ow up Ca'line's ways ter me. Heap of 'em does dat des ter ease dey own consciences an' pacify a dead 'oman's ghost. Dat's de way a man nachelly do. But he won't faze me, so long as I holds de fort! An' fur de chillen, co'se quick as I gits 'em broke in I'll see dat dey won't miss Ca'line none. Dat little teether, I done tol' Pete ter fetch her over ter me right away. Time I doctors her wid proper teas, an' washes her in good warm pot-liquor, I'll make a fus'-class baby out'n her."

Moriah had always been a good woman, and as she stood before me, laying bare the scheme that, no matter what the conditions, had in it the smallest selfish consideration, I felt my heart warm to her again, and I could not but feel that the little whitewashe– kindly, hard-pressed family man of slight accoun–ould do well to lay his brood upon her ample bosom.

Joyce enters the interview fully prepared, bringing meticulous documentation intended to reinforce her candidacy for the Vice President position. Her comprehensive portfolio clearly demonstrates her superior qualifications and dedicated professional trajectory, carefully curated and substantiated with evidence of tangible successes in prior roles. Her resume details unequivocal achievements that notably exceed the job requirements listed, including leadership in high-profile projects, impactful strategies she developed resulting in measurable growth, and numerous commendations for her innovative problem-solving skills and ethical business practices. Complementing this are various letters of recommendation from respected industry professionals, providing robust validation and credible testimony to her professional abilities, integrity, and outstanding contributions to her former organizations. Given the strength of this documented professional history, Carl, the interviewer, faces significant difficulty in dismissing her candidacy without effectively discrediting the testimonials of highly regarded professionals who explicitly endorse her capabilities. Thus, Joyce ensures that the evaluation of her professional competencies comes from rigorous factual substantiation rather than subjective biases.

However, despite Joyce's evident qualifications, deeper societal issues manifest subtly within the evaluation dynamic. Gender schemas, shaped by cultural norms and expectations established in childhood, often discreetly intervene in workplace interactions, perceptions, and validation processes. Traditional assumptions about gender roles still permeate professional environments, affecting how individuals like Carl subconsciously process evidence of competence and merit. From an early age, societal dynamics frequently instill masculine attributes as inherently synonymous with leadership, decisiveness, and professional assertiveness, while femininity is often associated primarily with nurturing, empathy, and domesticity. Carl's unconscious resistance towards Joyce's candidacy seems to echo these entrenched schemas, revealing an ingrained preference—albeit possibly subconscious—for male leadership behaviors and a parallel unconscious skepticism regarding authoritative and assertive women. His reaction during the interview, characterized by restrained skepticism and cautious questioning, indicates underlying discomfort and resistance to acknowledging Joyce's competency to hold a role traditionally occupied by males. Such subtle resistance illustrates the persistence of outdated perceptions that continue to hinder equitable professional evaluation and advancement opportunities.

Nevertheless, contemporary society increasingly challenges and modifies these traditional gender schemas. Joyce embodies an emerging paradigm—a woman whose professional excellence merges seamlessly with personal commitments, strongly challenging earlier, restrictive frameworks that artificially separate professional and domestic identities. Her clear demonstration of professional prowess confronts and complicates Carl's established internal schemas, compelling acknowledgment of her caliber. This dynamic evidences an evolving societal shift toward recognizing professional women as multifaceted individuals capable of embodying traditionally gendered attributes simultaneously, without diminishing credibility or authority. Shifts in organizational cultures, reinforced continually by visible examples like Joyce, signal incremental yet steady progress toward more inclusive and unbiased evaluations in the workplace. However, as Joyce's experience underscores, such shifts are gradual and continually met with resistance rooted in older, deeply embedded societal attitudes. To fully move forward, organizations must intentionally challenge outdated assumptions through active awareness, open discussion, and consistent adherence to meritocratic evaluation frameworks, thereby fostering an environment centered on genuine professional abilities rather than implicit gender expectations. Joyce's interview predicament, situated within this broader societal and organizational context of evolving but still resistant gender schemas, poignantly illustrates both the progress attained and the remaining hurdles to truly equitable professional assessment and recognition.

I reflect on how the increasing involvement of women in Mexico’s political and social spheres has reshaped our society, opening doors for women in academia, literature, and activism. I see historical developments marked by the emergence of periodicals such as Fem, which have provided a platform for feminist voices over generations. Writers like Aláida Foppa, Elena Urrutia, Margo Glantz, and Marta Lamas have played transformative roles in articulating feminist discourses, offering testimonies and analytical perspectives that challenge the confines of Eurocentric narratives. The academic and literary spaces they helped shape not only capture our nation’s complex history but also validate personal experiences that were once sidelined. Today, contemporary laws offer protections against sexual violence and feminicide, and while abortion remains a battleground yet to be fully legalized, the widespread availability of contraceptives signifies progress. I observe how Mexico functions as a living model for emerging feminist movements, with indigenous initiatives like the Zapatista movement contributing significantly to the national dialogue on gender justice and indigenous rights.

I also acknowledge that many challenges persist despite these advances. Issues such as internal displacement, migration, and drug-related violence continue to undermine the safety and well-being of communities, while neoliberal policies and corruption have affected the competitiveness of workers and the strength of unions in the global economy. Nevertheless, I am inspired by the increasing involvement of women in politics and community engagement, which signals a robust commitment to change. Indigenous feminists, in particular, stand out for raising global awareness on issues such as abortion rights and contraceptive access, calling for an inclusive model that honors diverse cultural identities. This evolution in feminist thought has shifted my perspective from one rooted in skepticism to a more positive view of Mexico, where the struggles and successes of feminist movements have carved out spaces for dialogue, reform, and empowerment. I recognize that while our journey is not without setbacks, the ongoing contributions of these resilient voices promise a future that is more just and truly reflective of the panoramic realities of our society.

In the quietude of a discernibly restless room, where the light of day filtered in through the half-drawn curtains with a slant that played tricks upon the walls, Mr. Neal stood in contemplation, his brow furrowed with the weight of unvoiced emotions. The clattering of wheels and the clamour of voices from the street below rendered the air outside festive, competing markedly with the austere silence that enveloped him. Wildbad, with its lively throngs sauntering unaware of the struggles that burdened him, seemed like a world apart, pulsing with joyous life that he could scarcely touch.

“Mrs. Armadale requires a clearer understanding,” he murmured to himself, his voice scarcely rising beyond the threshold of thought. Yet the thoughts he uttered possessed a gravity that was lost on him alone, for there was no one whispering counsel to ease the tempest within him. His mind raced with considerations, yet each time he drew near to an answer, uncertainty bore him away from it with the swiftness of a crisp autumn wind.

“It is absurd to tarry here during such a moment. I ought to have ventured to her at once,” he said, reflexively brushing back a strand of hair that had wandered loose over his forehead. The words echoed only in the confines of his unease, swallowed by the weighty atmosphere, pregnant with unresolved tension. All the while, he wrestled with the unwelcome knowledge that he required more than mere good intentions to confront Mrs. Armadale about her husband’s condition.

Peering out into the bustling street, a wave of envy washed over him. He saw couples strolling, their hands linked, laughter spilling forth—a stark contrast to the grim narrative he was tethered to. “To be so unencumbered,” he sighed, “is there not something desirable in that?” Yet the question was hollow to him, as he knew well that inside that carefree façade, many held burdens just as heavy, couched in silence as oppressive as his own.

At that moment, a soft knock resounded at his door—tentative, yet somehow instilling a quiver of hope. “Enter,” he called, and the door creaked open to unveil a slight figure swathed in a shawl. It was Ruth, the maid, whose face bore the weariness of one who served beneath the shadow of trouble. Her eyes were bright with something akin to urgency. “Mr. Neal?” she inquired, hesitating on the threshold, her voice a blend of deference and expectation.

“What is it, Ruth?” he answered, tightening the collar of his coat as if it might shield him from the turmoil to come. There was an air of expectation as she shifted her weight from one foot to the other, regarding him with a mixture of sympathy and concern that set his pulse racing in unexpected rhythm.

“It is about Mrs. Armadale, sir. She is in the garden—she’s asking for you,” the maid replied, her voice a tremor in the hushed room. The very mention of her name struck a spark in him, igniting feelings he had sought to suppress. “But she—she may not be in a fit state—”

“Release no words of caution, my dear Ruth,” he interjected sharply, surprising himself with the fervour of his response. “To see Mrs. Armadale is not just necessary, it is essential.” And with that, he felt the gale of resolve sweep through him, chafing against his earlier hesitance.

As he stepped into the garden, its vibrant hues enveloping him like a shawl of vivid warmth, the contrast was stark—the splendor of flowers offering a riot of colour in the very face of his grave pursuit. Yet, amid the blooming flora, there was Mrs. Armadale, seated upon a wooden bench, her countenance the embodiment of sorrowful abstraction as she gazed toward the cerulean sky, unaware of the suffusion of life swirling around her.

“Mrs. Armadale,” he ventured softly, his heart carrying an unfamiliar tenderness as he approached her. But her awareness remained tantalizingly out of reach, as though she dwelled in a realm far removed from their immediate reality, a ghost animated only by the memory of what once was, or might yet be. With an urgency borne from the depths of newfound resolve, he took a breath and resolved to breach the gap that separated them, standing resolute before the embodiment of his own turmoil.

Mr. Beaumont was smoking a cigarette--he was always smoking cigarettes--morn, noon, and night those deadly little rolls of paper were between his thin lips, and though doctors warned him of the danger to his nerves, he laughed at their croakings.

"Nerves, my dear sir," he said lightly; "men in my position can't afford to have nerves; they are a luxury for the rich and foolish. Why should I have nerves? I don't drink; I don't run away with other men's wives; I don't fret over the unavoidable--bah! smoking is my one redeeming vice."

He had a number of other vices, however, as many young men found to their cost. True, he himself did not drink, but he led others to do so, nor did he covet his neighbour's wife, yet he was by no means averse to playing the part of Sir Pandarus of Troy, provided it was to his own interest to do so. Moreover, he gambled.

It was in this terrible passion--rarely, if ever conquered--that he found his greatest delight. The green cloth-covered table, the painted hieroglyphics of the cards, the hopes, the fears, the gains, the losses, were all to him but a representation of his daily life on a small scale. He gambled with men as he gambled with cards, meeting varied fortunes in both, and risking his luck as recklessly in the game of Life as in the game of baccarat. He was a scamp, a scoundrel, a blackleg of the deepest dye, bankrupt in pocket and in illusions; yet he always kept within the limits of the law, and, moreover, sinned in an eminently gentlemanly manner, which robbed the sordid, feverish life he was leading of its most repulsive features.

Why this artificial man, who lived only in the glare of the gas-lamps, and, owl-like, shunned the searching light of the day, had come to such an out-of-the-way village as Garsworth was a puzzle, but nevertheless a puzzle easy of solution. His object was two-fold. In the first place, he had left London to escape the demands of persistent creditors, and in the second, being a native of the dull little hamlet, he had returned to visit the scenes of his youth not seen by him for three-and-twenty years.

It was not a sentimental longing--no, Mr. Beaumont and sentiment had long since parted company; but Garsworth was a dead and alive place where no one would think of looking for him, so he could stay there in safety until he saw a chance of arranging his pecuniary affairs and leaving the Arcadia he detested for the London he loved.

An artist by profession, though he had not touched a brush for years, he found it necessary to resume his old employment as a reason for his sojourn in Garsworth, for the honest rustics were somewhat suspicious of Basil Beaumont, his character having been none of the best when he left his native place to seek his fortune. So he lived quietly at the principal inn of the village, dawdled about the fields, sketched picturesque landscapes in a desultory manner, and in the meantime corresponded with a dear brother hawk in Town as to his chances of return to the metropolis.

His cigarette burnt down rapidly as he leaned over the fence thinking of his future, so throwing away the stump, he took out his tobacco-pouch and a little book of rice paper, in order to manufacture another, talking to himself meanwhile as is the fashion of solitary men.

"Two weeks," he said musingly, while he deftly rolled the tobacco in his slender fingers, "two weeks in this blessed place--well, there's one good thing, the rest will do me good, and I'll go back to Town as steady as a rock; the medicine is disagreeable, but the result will be excellent. What bad luck I've had lately--everything seems against me. I'll have to make a big effort to get some cash, or I'll end my days in a workhouse--ugh!" shivering again, "not that--God, how I dread poverty! Never mind," he went on gaily, shrugging his shoulders, "there are plenty of fools in this world, and as everything was created for a special purpose, I presume le bon Dieu made fools to feather clever men's nests."

It was a morning of unlooked-for felicity. The warm sun, shining brightly in a sky of the purest azure, cast its golden rays upon the happy faces of the inmates of Cleeve. The anxiety which had, of late, beset the countenance of Mrs. Cusworth, had, to Salome's delighted observation, materially lessened; her eyes, those bright and expressive orbs, sparkled with a renewed luster, and her step, though still slightly languid, betokened a growing strength. It was a day that well nigh seemed to justify the oft-repeated augury of a kindly fate.

As Salome descended to the morning room, her eyes met those of her mother, and a tender smile rewarded her. "Mama, you are looking better, I do declare!" she exclaimed, her voice, like the gentle music of a silver brook, flowing with joy and relief. Mrs. Cusworth's countenance flushed with pleased gratification, and she extended her hand, which Salome, with expressions of affection, took and pressed against her cheek. It was a tender moment, a moment pregnant with sweet and tender feeling, and Salome felt her heart overflowing with love and tenderness for this dear, delicate, and suffering mother of hers.

In this happy frame of mind, Salome refrained from communicating the singular circumstance which had occurred during the previous night. She knew that an unnecessary alarm might prove hurtful to her mother, and so, she wisely suppressed the knowledge of the mysterious nocturnal visitor, to whose footsteps she had been witness. A fleeting thought, however, crossed her mind, a thought which she was at no loss to interpret. She suspected that the careless neglect of one of the domestics had led to the open door, and that the midnight prowler, with feet so silent as a ghost, had availed himself of the opportunity thus offered.

Her suspicions, however, were not directed towards any one in particular, and she could not bring herself to accuse any of the household servants. She had indeed some reason to believe that the maid, Emily, who was responsible for locking the doors and windows, might have overlooked her duty in some measure, though she flatly denied any such negligence, with a vehemence that seemed almost ill-concealed. Salome, however, was not convinced by the maid's assertion, and her thoughts were busy with a plan of investigation which, she hoped, would elicit the truth, and bring the careless culprit to a sense of shame.

She therefore decided upon a course of action, one which would render it impossible for the miscreant to escape detection. The walls surrounding the garden were high and substantial, and the short side of the enclosure was divided into separate sections by a low palisade, with a convenient gate in the centre. Salome thought of placing one of her brother's traps near this gate, which, when sprung, would leave no doubt as to the escape route taken by the midnight visitor. But, alas! in her haste to effect this end, she overlooked the importance of securing the other side, the long side, where a bough of the ancient casement tree, a tree of gnarled and twisted limbs, stretched far and near, forming a useful ladder to the top of the wall, and thus a secret passage for escape. This grave oversight did not escape her thoughts, though, for a short time, she was not aware of the extent of the consequences that might ensue.

Her mother's improvement served as a timely distraction, a gentle breeze that swept away the clouds of anxiety, and, as they sat together in the morning room, Mrs. Cusworth, with an air of quiet satisfaction, announced that a change, a pleasing and unexpected change, had occurred in their fortunes. A legacy, received from a distant relative, which had been assumed to be of a trifling nature, turned out to be of considerable value, a sum sufficient to render any financial uncertainty quite impossible. "We shall not, dear Salome," she said with a gentle smile, "be compelled to leave Cleeve after all. The idea of moving to Redstone is, therefore, quite abandoned. We shall remain here, and I have determined to devote myself to the pleasures of our quiet country life."

Salome's countenance remained unaltered, though her inward amazement at her mother's decision was not to be gainsaid. She had taken measures for securing lodgings at Redstone, and was already satisfied that the prospect of that quiet, rural life, far removed from the bustling world, would be a charm to them both. "But, dear mother," she said, after a moment's consideration, "what is the reason for this change of purpose? I had, as you know, already secured lodgings at Redstone, and I was beginning to feel that the transition would be a welcome one."

In the entrance hall of the Cass household, the absence of family photos serves as a poignant symbol of emotional emptiness. The bare walls reflect a profound lack of familial bonds and shared memories, suggesting that meaningful connections are as absent as the images that should have adorned them. Instead of photographs that capture moments of joy and unity, the space feels cold and void, much like the interactions within the family itself. This emptiness echoes the household's inability to foster warmth and affection, setting a somber tone that resonates throughout the home.

The fire that crackles in the hearth holds a dual significance. While it should provide warmth and comfort, it instead symbolizes Godfrey Cass's lack of passion in his marriage to his wife, Molly. The fire's play of light and shadow mirrors Godfrey's flickering emotions and hidden frustrations. He stands with his back to the fire, unconsciously distancing himself from its warmth, much like he distances himself from confronting his own simmering unhappiness and concealed anger toward his brother, Dunstan. The flames express his internal conflict, flickering with an intensity that parallels the burning resentment he holds but chooses to ignore.

As the unmistakable smell of flat ale permeates the room, coupled with the presence of hunting gear left carelessly about, they represent a sense of stagnation within the Cass household. The ale, stale and unappealing, invokes a life that lacks freshness and vigor, suggesting a home where time stands still and genuine engagement is lacking. Similarly, the hunting gear, symbols of past excitement and escapades, now lie dormant, reflecting the household's static nature and the characters' inability to move forward or find purpose.

The colors within this setting further illustrate Godfrey’s somber and angry mood. Muted and dark hues cloak the space, reflecting his inner turmoil and pervasive gloom. The absence of bright, lively colors mirrors the absence of love and vitality in both his marriage and familial relationships. His mood casts shadows on anyone who enters the room, reinforcing the parallel between his internal state and the physical environment.

In stark contrast to Godfrey's subdued manner, Dunstan's entrance is marked by a heavy step and a cheerful whistle. These contrasting actions highlight Dunstan's reluctance cloaked beneath an air of arrogance. While his heavy step conveys a sense of guilt and an unspoken burden, his whistle feigns nonchalance and defiance. This duality illustrates the tension between the brothers, a sentiment also reflected in the spaniel's anxious behavior, sensing the charged atmosphere. The animal's nervousness is indicative of the underlying hostility simmering between Godfrey and Dunstan, further compounded by the physical space devoid of any inviting warmth or color.

The Cass household, through its symbolic imagery, paints a portrait of a family in disarray. From the emotional emptiness signified by the lack of family photos to the stagnant air of flat ale and abandoned hunting gear, the setting serves as an extension of the characters' internal struggles. The interplay of sensory details and contrasting actions further reveals the deep-seated emotions that bind and divide Godfrey and Dunstan Cass, ultimately underscoring the absence of love that pervades their home.

He was relieved to find the landlord was not present in person, and so confided his business to the bar-keeper. At first it appeared that that functionary declined interference, and with many head-shakings and audible misgivings was inclined to await the coming of his principal, but a nearer view of Jeff's perplexed face, and an examination of Jeff's gun, and the few coins spread before him, finally induced him to produce certain articles, which he packed in a basket and handed to Jeff, taking the gun and coins in exchange. Thus relieved, Jeff set his face homewards, and ran a race with the morning into the valley, reaching the “Half-way House” as the sun laid waste its bare, bleak outlines, and relentlessly pointed out its defects one by one. It was cruel to Jeff at that moment, but he hugged his basket close and slipped to the back door and the kitchen, where his aunt was already at work.

“I didn't know ye were up yet, aunty,” said Jeff submissively. “It isn't more than six o'clock.”

“Thar's four more to feed at breakfast,” said his aunt severely, “and yer's the top blown off the kitchen chimbly, and the fire only just got to go.”

Jeff saw that he was in time. The ordinary breakfast of the “Half-way House,” not yet prepared, consisted of codfish, ham, yellow-ochre biscuit, made after a peculiar receipt of his aunt's, and potatoes.

“I got a few fancy fixin's up at the Summit this morning, aunty,” he began apologetically, “seein' we had sick folks, you know--you and the young lady--and thinkin' it might save you trouble. I've got 'em here,” and he shyly produced the basket.

“If ye kin afford it, Jeff,” responded his aunt resignedly, “I'm thankful.”

The reply was so unexpectedly mild for Aunt Sally, that Jeff put his arms around her and kissed her hard cheek. “And I've got some quail, aunty, knowin' you liked em.”

“I reckoned you was up to some such foolishness,” said Aunt Sally, wiping her cheek with her apron, “when I missed yer gun from the hall.” But the allusion was a dangerous one, and Jeff slipped away.

He breakfasted early with Yuba Bill that morning; the latter gentleman's taciturnity being intensified at such moments through a long habit of confining himself strictly to eating in the limited time allowed his daily repasts, and it was not until they had taken the horses from the stable and were harnessing them to the coach that Jeff extracted from his companion some facts about his guests. They were Mr. and Mrs. Mayfield, Eastern tourists, who had been to the Sandwich Islands for the benefit of their daughter's health, and before returning to New York, intended, under the advice of their physician, to further try the effects of mountain air at the “Summit Hotel,” on the invalid. They were apparently rich people, the coach had been engaged for them solely--even the mail and express had been sent on by a separate conveyance, so that they might be more independent. It is hardly necessary to say that this fact was by no means palatable to Bill--debarring him not only the social contact and attentions of the “Express Agent,” but the selection of a box-seated passenger who always “acted like a man.”

“Ye kin kalkilate what kind of a pardner that 'ar yaller-livered Mayfield would make up on that box, partik'ly ez I heard before we started that he'd requested the kimpany's agent in Sacramento to select a driver ez didn't cuss, smoke, or drink. He did, sir, by gum!”

“I reckon you were very careful, then, Bill,” said Jeff.

“In course,” returned Bill, with a perfectly diabolical wink. “In course! You know that 'Blue Grass,'” pointing out a spirited leader; “she's a fair horse ez horses go, but she's apt to feel her oats on a down grade, and takes a pow'ful deal o' soothin' and explanation afore she buckles down to her reg'lar work. Well, sir, I exhorted and labored in a Christian-like way with that mare to that extent that I'm cussed if that chap didn't want to get down afore we got to the level!”

On the Night of the Strange Bird, many people at Sidderton (and some nearer) saw a Glare on the Sidderford moor. But no one in Sidderford saw it, for most of Sidderford was abed.

All day the wind had been rising, so that the larks on the moor chirruped fitfully near the ground, or rose only to be driven like leaves before the wind. The sun set in a bloody welter of clouds, and the moon was hidden. The glare, they say, was golden like a beam shining out of the sky, not a uniform blaze, but broken all over by curving flashes like the waving of swords. It lasted but a moment and left the night dark and obscure. There were letters about it in Nature, and a rough drawing that no one thought very like. (You may see it for yourself--the drawing that was unlike the glare--on page 42 of Vol. cclx. of that publication.)

None in Sidderford saw the light, but Annie, Hooker Durgan's wife, was lying awake, and she saw the reflection of it--a flickering tongue of gold--dancing on the wall.

She, too, was one of those who heard the sound. The others who heard the sound were Lumpy Durgan, the half-wit, and Amory's mother. They said it was a sound like children singing and a throbbing of harp strings, carried on a rush of notes like that which sometimes comes from an organ. It began and ended like the opening and shutting of a door, and before and after they heard nothing but the night wind howling over the moor and the noise of the caves under Sidderford cliff. Amory's mother said she wanted to cry when she heard it, but Lumpy was only sorry he could hear no more.

That is as much as anyone can tell you of the glare upon Sidderford Moor and the alleged music therewith. And whether these had any real connexion with the Strange Bird whose history follows, is more than I can say. But I set it down here for reasons that will be more apparent as the story proceeds.

Sandy Bright was coming down the road from Spinner's carrying a side of bacon he had taken in exchange for a clock. He saw nothing of the light but he heard and saw the Strange Bird. He suddenly heard a flapping and a voice like a woman wailing, and being a nervous man and all alone, he was alarmed forthwith, and turning (all a-tremble) saw something large and black against the dim darkness of the cedars up the hill. It seemed to be coming right down upon him, and incontinently he dropped his bacon and set off running, only to fall headlong.

He tried in vain--such was his state of mind--to remember the beginning of the Lord's Prayer. The strange bird flapped over him, something larger than himself, with a vast spread of wings, and, as he thought, black. He screamed and gave himself up for lost. Then it went past him, sailing down the hill, and, soaring over the vicarage, vanished into the hazy valley towards Sidderford.

And Sandy Bright lay upon his stomach there, for ever so long, staring into the darkness after the strange bird. At last he got upon his knees and began to thank Heaven for his merciful deliverance, with his eyes downhill. He went on down into the village, talking aloud and confessing his sins as he went, lest the strange bird should come back. All who heard him thought him drunk. But from that night he was a changed man, and had done with drunkenness and defrauding the revenue by selling silver ornaments without a licence. And the side of bacon lay upon the hillside until the tallyman from Portburdock found it in the morning.

The next who saw the Strange Bird was a solicitor's clerk at Iping Hanger, who was climbing the hill before breakfast, to see the sunrise. Save for a few dissolving wisps of cloud the sky had been blown clear in the night. At first he thought it was an eagle he saw. It was near the zenith, and incredibly remote, a mere bright speck above the pink cirri, and it seemed as if it fluttered and beat itself against the sky, as an imprisoned swallow might do against a window pane. Then down it came into the shadow of the earth, sweeping in a great curve towards Portburdock and round over the Hanger, and so vanishing behind the woods of Siddermorton Park. It seemed larger than a man. Just before it was hidden, the light of the rising sun smote over the edge of the downs and touched its wings, and they flashed with the brightness of flames and the colour of precious stones, and so passed, leaving the witness agape.

The clock on the mantel struck nine as the Baroness sat serenely in her parlor, the golden glow of the candles casting long shadows on the plush surroundings. Her hands, encircled by delicate lace cuffs, busied themselves with the embroidery hoop—an emblem of calm diligence amidst the tumult of her private life. Her grace and poise remained undisturbed by the tumultuous revelations of the evening prior, yet behind the veil of composure, a quiet resilience thrummed, like a tightly-wound harp string on the verge of release.

Seated opposite her, Crevel continued, his chest puffed with the swagger of a man who relishes his own indispensability. Despite the affection he held for his words, there was a curiosity in his gaze, an eagerness to see the ripples they might cause in the Baroness’s calm sea. "Madame, one cannot help but admire your remarkable fortitude. Many would have stormed an affront, but you, like a seasoned mariner, steer through tempests unperturbed."

Her needle danced through the fabric with elegant precision, and only a subtle lifting of her brow acknowledged his remark. "Monsieur Crevel, one must choose which storms are worth braving," she replied, her voice like the whisper of silk.

"And yet," Crevel persisted, crossing his legs with an air of nonchalance, "does it not fatigue you to maintain such vigilance over his lordship's wanderings? His indiscretions are numerous as the stars—each twinkling with its own tale of fancy and folly." There was an unexpected softness in his tone, as if the follies and failures of others had become a source of personal amusement.

The Baroness paused her work, diverting her gaze to the moonlit gardens beyond the window. "My husband," she mused, "is like the roses outside—each bloom a marvel in its own right, but shielded by thorns. One must appreciate the flowers without resentment for their nature."

Crevel marveled at her philosophical demeanor, leaning conspiratorially closer. "You have the wisdom of Catherine the Great, yet your charms lie in simplicity rather than imperial grandeur. There is something more profound than beauty at your command."

Still focused on her embroidery, the Baroness allowed a hint of a smile. "And yet wisdom and charm, dear Monsieur Crevel, are but scant currency in the dealings of the heart." Her calm observations masked an inner strength, felt but unseen, like the hidden currents of a placid lake.

More than captivated, Crevel edged further into indulgence, swaying between admiration and calculated intent. "It would seem, madame, that one cannot earn your admiration by modest conquests of talent. Although," he added, leaning near, "a man might be as courageous as a lion and still lose favor with the court of your heart."

"Indeed," she replied, "for are we not all poor relations in the court of our own hearts, my dear Crevel? Ever in search of something beyond the gilded cage to which we are accustomed."

A curious silence ensued, interrupted only by the measured rustle of leaves in the evening breeze. An understanding, unspoken yet profound, passed between them. The Baroness did not merely seek emotional security; her desires reached realms unarticulated by men consumed by superficial pursuits.

"May I," ventured Crevel at last, "offer an advocate's confession? I once harbored the belief that I might, through enterprise and wit, win a place at your side. But it seems I have permanently assumed the role of a jester—entertaining, yet ineffectual."

She looked at him with an enigmatic expression, eyes gleaming like stars through the night's obscurity. "Monsieur Crevel," she began, "your affections honor me, yet a wife must strategize wars unwaged, battles unsung. And such paths, alas, are solitary ones."

Crevel, touched by her candor, felt the weight of a truth universally acknowledged: in rooms adorned with artifice and masquerade, genuineness stood as the loftiest embellishment. As he rose to depart, he placed a hand upon his heart—a silent salute to a sovereign of unyielding dignity.

Late November evenings often carried with them a distinct chill, the kind that crept into the bones and wrapped itself around the heart. It was 1986, and I had just turned thirteen—a threshold into tumultuous years marked by newfound rebellion and the faint afterglow of childhood. Having just recovered from chicken pox, I felt the first stirrings of independence, a sense that I could step into the world without the confines of my childhood maladies. On this particular night, I was with Erica, my adventurous friend who had taught me the art of smoking—a kind of rite of passage for kids too young to grasp the weight of their actions. The taste of nicotine was foreign but exciting, a blend of rebellion and maturity that made my heart race with both guilt and thrill. We fabricated a story about going for a stroll, swift glances between us affirming our shared secret, as we sat on the cold grass at the base of the driveway, debating our next steps.

The night wrapped around us like a thick blanket, heavy with anticipation. We chose to stay put, told ourselves that walking could wait. As we took our first puffs, the smoke curling into the frozen air, we shared nervous giggles that pierced the stillness. The world stretched out before us in exaggerated silence, the distant rustling of leaves blending with our whispered conversation. That’s when I noticed it—a faint sound, reverberating in the distance like the promise of an approaching storm. A motorcycle, its headlight shining bright like a beacon, emerged from the inky blackness, its engine growling in a manner which both excited and unnerved us. It took too long to close the distance, and in that moment of drawn-out anticipation, I felt something shift in the atmosphere around us, a calm that was both mesmerizing and heavy with meaning.

As the motorcycle drew closer, the blinding headlight cast eerie shadows across the terrain, illuminating the trees with ghostly outlines. I squinted into the light, heart pounding loud enough that I thought it might betray me, and then I saw him—the rider. He wore silver aviator sunglasses, an odd choice for nighttime, and I felt an inexplicable mix of confusion and clarity wash over me. It wasn’t just any rider; it was Uncle Mark. Four months had passed since that tragic accident stole him from our lives, yet there he was, as vibrant and alive as I remembered. His stature, his familiar smile, the way he tilted his head ever so slightly—it was an image etched into my memory. Dressed in the leather jacket that still hung in my Aunt’s closet, he glided past us without sound, a ghost of all that had been, all that we had lost.

I couldn’t speak, my voice swallowed by the weight of my disbelief. The quiet night buzzed around us, time suspended in that singular moment; a dagger of sorrow and reassurance pierces my very core. There was no stopping, no words exchanged—only a lingering gaze, an unbreakable connection even in the realm of the supernatural. As swiftly as he had appeared, Uncle Mark faded into the enveloping darkness, his taillight a lone ember flickering out of sight. Erica, beside me, was as speechless as I was, the truth of that encounter settling heavily in the air, heavy yet oddly comforting. We sat in silence, two children woven together by threads of loss and unexplainable mystery, each puff of smoke now tasting of something more profound than rebellion—a reminder that love transcends even the barriers of life and death.

Forensic experts question Tiger Woods crash probe after new finding

The LA County Sheriff’s Department made several critical decisions in the investigation of Tiger Woods’ devastating crash that were favorable to the golfing legend — who was given the benefit of the doubt despite indications he was inattentive or had dozed off, according to a report.

Sheriff Alex Villanueva announced on Feb. 23 — when Woods crashed a loaned Genesis GV80, breaking several bones in his leg — that his deputies “did not see any evidence of impairment.”

A day later, he announced that the crash was “purely an accident” and said there had been no need to bring in a drug recognition expert to evaluate the 45-year-old Woods for impairment.

But several forensic experts told USA Today Sports that the available evidence in the case indicates Woods was inattentive or asleep when the SUV went right into a median instead of staying in the lane as it curved right.

They cited clues, including the lack of skid marks indicating braking, for questioning the sheriff’s department’s decision to quickly label the crash an “accident” and to not bring in an expert to have Woods’ blood examined.

“LASD is not releasing any further information at this time,” the sheriff’s department told USA Today Sports in a statement. “The traffic collision investigation is ongoing and traffic investigators continue to work to determine the cause of the collision.”

Woods’ agent, Mark Steinberg, didn’t return a message from the news outlet seeking comment.

Accident reconstruction experts said the links legend’s inability to remember driving at all was reason enough to bring in a drug recognition expert, or DRE.

“I would have thought that you would have him evaluated by a DRE to see whether or not there are some physical clues beyond the operation that would point to impairment,” said Charles Schack, a former New Hampshire state trooper who is now president of Crash Experts, which analyzes accidents.

“To an untrained person, sometimes the effects are a bit more subtle, and require a bit more in-depth examination to bring out the evidence of impairment,” he told USA Today Sports.

DREs make a determination of whether blood should be tested by questioning the driver about medications and examining the person’s eyes and vital signs, according to the report.

If a DRE had evaluated Woods at the hospital, a blood test could have shown whether there were any medications or other drugs in his system — for which he could have been charged with misdemeanor driving under the influence.

Instead, a day after the accident, Villanueva said the deputy at the scene concluded that “there was no evidence of any impairment whatsoever.”

“He was lucid, no odor of alcohol, no evidence of any medication, narcotics or anything like that would bring that into question. So that was not a concern at the time. So therefore, obviously no field sobriety test and no DRE,” the sheriff added.

But former detective Jonathan Cherney, who walked the scene after the crash, also said the evidence suggests it was “like a classic case of falling asleep behind the wheel” because “the road curves and his vehicle goes straight.”

If Woods had been looking at his phone momentarily, investigators would expect to see evidence that he braked or tried to steer out of the median long before the wreck.

“Impaired people have a tendency of crashing, so if you have a situation like this one, where you have a single-vehicle crash, with out-of-the-ordinary-type circumstances, that should trigger the first responder to inquire further and to explore impairment as a possible cause of the collision,” Cherney told the outlet.

The accident reconstructionist agreed that the fact that Woods twice told deputies he couldn’t remember driving at all “absolutely” is a clue suggesting impairment.

“I do know significant head injuries can cause people to not know what happened or forget what happened,” Cherney said. “The fact that he doesn’t remember driving at all is also indicative and consistent with the objective symptom of impaired driving.”

However, it is now too late to get access to Woods’ blood and medical reports at the hospital without his cooperation or a search warrant, according to the report.

To get a warrant, police would need to convince a judge it is necessary and show probable cause that a crime had been committed — which would be “difficult,” Chris Taylor, managing attorney at Taylor & Taylor, a DUI defense specialist in Southern California, told USA Today Sport.

The sheriff’s department eventually executed a search warrant to obtain the “black box” data from the SUV that could show how fast Woods was traveling, plus any braking or steering activity prior to impact.

The department has not released any of the findings.

During emergency surgery at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center, Woods had a rod inserted into his tibia and pins and screws in his foot and ankle. Three days later, he was transferred to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center and underwent follow-up procedures.

“Correct!” cried Stanhope. “I knew you would grasp the idea, Frank.”

“We will at once start for the North Pacific. Have your effects ready.”

“They are all ready!” declared Stanhope. “I have explored every country upon the face of the earth. Now it is my happy privilege to explore the bed of the sea. Am I not a lucky man?”

“Begorra, Misther Frank,” cried a rollicking voice from the yard. “We have ivery bit of provisions aboord, an’ shure it’s all ready to start we are!”

“Good!” cried Frank. “There shall be no delay on my part. We will be off at the quickest possible moment.”

Stanhope at once went out and telegraphed Mrs. Tucker in San Francisco.

DEAR MADAM,—We start very soon in the submarine boat Dolphin for the North Pacific in quest of the white whale. Let us hope we shall find the evidence to clear your husband. Be of cheerful mind.

GEORGE STANHOPE.

The remainder of the day was spent in completing the preparations for the start.

The next morning all was announced in readiness.

The Dolphin floated in the tank all ready for the start.

The voyagers went aboard, and Frank gave orders for the big gates to be opened. This was done, and the boat floated into the canal.

Here it was in plain view of the great crowd which was waiting outside to greet it with cheers. The Dolphin floated down the canal toward the river.

Soon it was in the current of the larger stream, and then Frank started the electric engines to greater speed.

This sent the Dolphin ahead at a lively rate and Readestown began to fade from view.

All of the voyagers were upon the main deck by the open door of the pilot-house. Frank was at the wheel.

“Take a good look at Readestown,” said the young inventor. “It may be your last one!”

Instinctively Barney and Pomp turned.

“Begorra, it’s the foinest spot on earth!” cried the Celt. “May we live to return to dear old Radestown!”

“Golly! I done fink dat we mus’ do dat,” averred Pomp. “Dis chile neber gwine to leabe his bones in no oder place!”

“Don’t yez be too shure, naygur,” declared Barney, shaking his head. “Shure, it’s many a close call we’ll be afther havin’ yit, me lad. There’s no spendin’ a year or more at the bottom av the say widout some bit av a risk.”

“You are right, Barney,” said the explorer, Stanhope; “but we are going to look upon the bright side of this thing. We shall sail the North Pacific, capture the silver whale, return and see old America again in safety. Mark my prophecy.”

“I hope you have hit it right, George,” laughed Frank; “at least you are right in looking on the bright side.”

So the submarine voyagers left home in quite a cheerful frame of mind.

But they little dreamed of the thrilling experiences which the near future held.

They had no means of guessing the terrible perils through which they were to pass.

A voyage under the sea can scarcely be attended by aught but danger and risk.

Readestown was soon left out of sight.

The Dolphin sped on down the river current to the sea. Thus far Frank had kept the boat on the surface.

When the open sea was reached he said:

“I think that for the first thousand miles of our course we will travel faster under water. I have studied the ocean bed, and there are no obstructions to encounter at the proper mean elevation.”

“Then we are to start out at once with a thousand mile voyage under water?” asked the explorer Stanhope.

“Yes.”

“Good! I am very glad of that. There is much in the Atlantic worthy of study. You will make the Pacific by way of Cape Horn?”

To Stanhope’s surprise Frank shook his head.

“No,” he said. “That is the longest route.”

An Incomplete Supreme Court Witnessed Biden's Oath: A Glimpse into History

Only six of the nine Supreme Court justices attended President Biden's inauguration, marking the first time in over two decades that the entire court wasn't present. Justices Clarence Thomas, Stephen G. Breyer, and Samuel A. Alito Jr., the court's three eldest members, were absent. Citing "public health risks posed by the COVID pandemic," Supreme Court spokeswoman Kathleen Arberg explained their absence.

The pandemic has significantly impacted the court's operations, forcing them to conduct business remotely since March. While they gathered for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's memorial service in September, their usual in-person conferences and oral arguments have been held via teleconference.

This inauguration marked the fourth time Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. administered the presidential oath. However, his relationship with presidents has been complex. President Barack Obama, whom Roberts swore in twice, voted against his 2005 Supreme Court confirmation. Biden, too, opposed his appointment. President Donald Trump, sworn in by Roberts in 2017, openly criticized the Chief Justice, calling him a "disaster" during his campaign. Their relationship remained strained throughout Trump's presidency, with Roberts presiding over his impeachment trial in the Senate.

Despite past differences, President Biden's inaugural address emphasized unity. He may now hold a more favorable view of Roberts, who turns 66 next week and was the deciding vote in preserving Obamacare, a key achievement of the Obama-Biden administration.

Vice President Kamala Harris was sworn in by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, the first Latina Supreme Court Justice. Sotomayor had also sworn in then-Vice President Biden in 2013.

Other attendees included Justice Elena Kagan, nominated by Obama, and all three of Trump's appointees: Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. Their presence created a potentially awkward situation, as they were seated behind Harris, who had vehemently opposed their confirmations. Notably, she engaged in a heated exchange with Kavanaugh during his confirmation hearings, which pleased liberals and angered conservatives.

As former senators, both Biden and Harris voted against six of the nine current Supreme Court justices. This history might explain the absence of some justices, particularly Thomas and Alito.

Biden attempted to filibuster Alito's nomination, arguing that President George W. Bush's choice was too conservative to replace Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, then the Supreme Court's swing vote.

Biden's history with Thomas is even more significant. Thomas's confirmation occurred while Biden chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee. The process was marred by allegations of sexual harassment against Thomas by Anita Hill, a former colleague.

The incomplete Supreme Court at Biden's inauguration serves as a reminder of the court's evolving composition and the complex relationships between its members and the executive branch. It also highlights the ongoing impact of the pandemic on the court's operations and the potential for future challenges as the nation grapples with a divided government and a changing Supreme Court landscape.

Golf icon Tiger Woods sustained serious injuries in suburban Los Angeles on Tuesday when his SUV rolled over and ended up on its side, as stated by authorities. Following the accident, Woods was extricated from the vehicle and was reported to be undergoing surgery for leg injuries by his agent.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reported that Woods, who was driving the SUV solo, encountered the accident just before 7:15 a.m., with no involvement of other vehicles.

The circumstances leading to the crash remain unclear. The road where the accident occurred features a steep descent for northbound drivers — like Woods was — and is outfitted with signage cautioning truck drivers to downshift. The speed limit in the area is 45 mph.

Aerial footage from KABC-TV captured the vehicle on its side, the front end severely damaged and airbags deployed, off the roadside near a hillside. The 45-year-old was transported to the hospital by ambulance.

Mark Steinberg, Woods' manager, in a statement said, "Tiger Woods was in a single-car accident this morning in California where he suffered multiple leg injuries. He is currently in surgery and we thank you for your privacy and support."

The incident occurred near the border of Rolling Hills Estates and Rancho Palos Verdes, affluent communities around 20 miles south of downtown Los Angeles.

In an additional but minor incident, a vehicle that had stopped to assist Woods was struck, but no injuries were reported, according to Christopher Thomas, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Fire Department.

Over the past weekend, Woods was in Los Angeles hosting the Genesis Invitational at Riviera Country Club, even presenting the trophy on Sunday. His itinerary included filming with GOLFTV, whom he endorses, on Monday and Tuesday. Woods was seen in high spirits in a tweeted photo with comedian David Spade during a TV shoot for celebrity on-course lessons at Rolling Hills Country Club.

Woods, who ties with Sam Snead for the most PGA Tour wins at 82 and is a 15-time major champion, has been on the mend from a back surgery on December 23. This marked his fifth back operation, following a significant spinal fusion surgery in April 2017 which enabled a remarkable comeback, highlighted by his fifth Masters win in 2019.

Woods, even at 45, continues to be a massive draw for the sport, having dramatically influenced TV ratings and prize money growth through his career. He was last seen playing at the PNC Championship in Orlando, Florida, on December 20, alongside his son, Charlie. Woods is also a father to a 13-year-old daughter.

The evening light filtered through the high, intricately carved windows, casting a warm glow upon the room, wherein shadows danced playfully upon the walls, as if joining in the wonderment that lay in every corner. Each glance exchanged among them bore the weight of unspoken gratitude, for they had found themselves embraced by a hospitality that seemed a peculiar blend of fortune and kindness.

Jane, with her delicate fingers brushing the smooth wood of a finely crafted tablet, marveled aloud, “I fear I shall never grow accustomed to this strangeness. How wonderful it is, and how very strange!” Her voice trailed off, wrapped in the softest echoes of awe, her eyes glancing upward to the soaring ceilings adorned with splendid carvings of ships battling titanic waves. Draxy, seated nearby, could not help but feel a wave of warmth surge through her as she recalled Aunt Emma’s words — spoken so earnestly just days before — concerning the many challenges that yet lay before Captain Melville and his dear wife.

“Do you think,” Draxy mused, her voice a gentle thread woven in with Jane’s own reverie, “that they need our assistance? Before they could indulge in any further contemplation, Mrs. Carr, an ever-dutiful soul, entered the room, her arms cradling a tray that bore a steaming teapot alongside dainty cups that shone with the brilliance of porcelain. “Ah, my dears,” she proclaimed in a voice that resonated with a gentle authority, “it is time for our evening respite. “Thank you, dear Mrs. Carr,” Jane replied, her countenance transforming into one of heartfelt appreciation. “We scarcely know how to express our gratitude for your generosity.” She took a cup, warmth enveloping her fingers as the tender steam kissed her face.

Just as they began to sip their tea, an enthusiastic voice burst through the doorway. “What ho! His eyes alighted upon Draxy, catching her by surprise. Michigan Schools Grapple with Fear, Anxiety, and Disruption in Aftermath of Oxford High School Shooting

By
Canton, Michigan - In the wake of the tragic shooting at Oxford High School on November 30, 2021, schools across Michigan are grappling with a surge of fear, anxiety, and disruption. The incident, which claimed the lives of four students and injured several others, has left students and teachers shaken and questioning their safety within educational institutions.

Widespread Threats and Closures

In the days following the Oxford shooting, dozens of schools across Michigan received threats of violence, leading to widespread disruption and closures. Plymouth-Canton Community Schools, for instance, dismissed high schools early on December 2 due to significant disruption caused by threats, although no direct threat was identified at any of the schools.

Heightened Concerns Among Students

Teachers across Michigan are reporting that their students are more concerned about their safety than ever before. Many students are asking questions about school safety procedures, such as locking doors and ALICE training protocols.

"My students are asking me, 'What are we going to do if this happens here?'" said Richard Mui, an Advanced Placement U.S. History and Civics teacher at Canton High School. "They're scared, and I don't blame them."

ALICE Training and Preparedness

ALICE (Alert, Lockdown, Inform, Counter, Evacuate) training has been widely implemented in schools across the country since the Columbine High School shooting in 1999. The program teaches proactive response strategies to active shooters, including how to lock doors, barricade windows, and evacuate if necessary.

However, some educators feel that ALICE training alone is not enough to fully prepare students and staff for the possibility of a school shooting.

"ALICE training is helpful, but it's not a silver bullet," said Stacey Olsen, a social studies teacher at Seaholm High School. "We need to do more to address the root causes of gun violence."

Educators' Frustration and Anger

Many teachers in Michigan are expressing tiredness, frustration, and anger over the continued occurrence of gun violence in schools. They feel that not enough is being done to prevent these tragedies from happening.

"I'm tired of being afraid for my students' lives," said Ryan Werenka, an Advanced Placement Government and Political Science teacher at Troy High School. "I'm tired of having to worry about whether or not I'm going to make it home safely at the end of the day."

Balancing Safety and Normalcy

In addition to their concerns about student safety, teachers are also grappling with how to maintain a sense of normalcy for their students amidst the heightened fear and anxiety.

"We want our students to feel safe, but we also don't want them to live in fear," said Jason Towler, a teacher consultant with the Washtenaw Intermediate School District's Young Adult Project. "It's a delicate balance."

School Security Measures

In response to the recent threats, school districts across Michigan have implemented various security measures to enhance student safety. These measures include installing new surveillance systems, upgrading emergency communication systems, and increasing the number of school resource officers.

Parents' Concerns

As parents themselves, teachers are also wrestling with how to address their own children's fears and concerns about school safety.

"I have two young children, and I worry about them every day," said Mui. "I want them to be safe, but I also don't want them to be afraid to go to school."

Need for Comprehensive Solutions

The recent events in Michigan have highlighted the urgent need for comprehensive solutions to address school safety and gun violence. Educators, parents, and policymakers must work together to create safer learning environments for students and ensure that tragedies like the Oxford High School shooting never happen again.

Calls for Confrontation: Waters' Remarks Stir Political Tensions over Chauvin Trial

Washington CNN –

As the nation anxiously awaits the verdict in the high-profile trial of Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer charged with murdering George Floyd, political tensions reached a boiling point this weekend. Democratic Representative Maxine Waters made headlines when she called for protesters to be "more confrontational" if Chauvin is acquitted, comments that have sparked heated debate and criticism from Republican counterparts.

While speaking to a crowd in Brooklyn Center, Minnesota—where protests have erupted over the recent police killing of Daunte Wright—Waters communicated her steadfast support for the movement against systemic racism and police brutality. "We’ve got to stay on the street," Waters said, encouraging demonstrators to continue their advocacy. "We’ve got to get more confrontational. We’ve got to make sure that they know that we mean business."

Waters' comments quickly drew backlash from Republican leaders who accused her of inciting violence. "This weekend in Minnesota, Maxine Waters broke the law by inciting violence and should be held accountable with censure by Congress," asserted House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy, who announced plans to introduce a resolution to that effect.

Judge Peter Cahill, overseeing the Chauvin trial, remarked that Waters' statements could serve as grounds for an appeal should Chauvin be convicted. "I’ll give you that Congresswoman Waters may have given you something on appeal that may result in this whole trial being overturned," Cahill said, drawing attention to the potential impact of her words on the judicial process.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell also criticized Waters, describing her comments as "beyond the pale" and urged that action be taken to ensure such rhetoric is not normalized in political discourse. "It is harder to imagine anything more inappropriate than a member of Congress flying in from California to inform local leaders and law enforcement on how they should react," McConnell said.

Despite the uproar, Waters has stood firm, clarifying that her use of "confrontational" was in reference to nonviolent actions and efforts to hold the justice system accountable. "I am nonviolent," she insisted. "Confrontational does not mean violence. My record speaks for itself. My message is about speaking up and standing against injustices without resorting to violence."

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi came to Waters' defense, dismissing the accusation that her colleague incited violence and denying any need for an apology. "Maxine talked about confrontation in the manner of the civil rights movement," Pelosi explained. "I'm confident that she's doing that in a non-violent way."

House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer supported Waters but voiced concern regarding the potential implications of her comments on the trial. "While it is clear that she was advocating for peaceful protest, there is some worry about her comments being used to sway legal outcomes," Hoyer noted, emphasizing the importance of a fair trial.

The tension surrounding Waters' remarks underscores a broader, ongoing conflict over how America's leaders respond to protest and calls for reform. This conflict is particularly stark considering the GOP's varied responses to other recent provocative political rhetoric, including the January 6 Capitol insurrection and past controversial comments by individuals such as Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene.

In defense, Waters pointed to a double standard within political narratives. "For someone to call out and criticize my words while ignoring the fight for truth and justice we’re involved in is astonishing," she iterated. Critics argue that swift condemnations of Waters starkly contrast with the GOP's handling of statements advocating violence by members like Greene.

Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, no stranger to controversy herself, took to social media to suggest that Waters' remarks represented a dangerous precedent. "Once again, Maxine Waters shows herself to be a threat to our country," Greene tweeted, using the situation to highlight what she considers inconsistencies in accountability.

As calls for justice continue across Minnesota and the nation at large, the political ramifications of Waters' comments remain a focal point in the national dialogue. The debate over her words signifies a deeper schism between parties over how elected officials should interact with protest movements, particularly those addressing systemic race issues within law enforcement.

With the Chauvin verdict looming, tensions are high, and eyes remain on Minneapolis as the nation grapples with questions about police reform, systemic inequity, and the bounds of free speech in the context of political leadership.

As these questions reverberate across a divided Congress and public, one thing is certain: the conversations sparked by Waters' statements are far from over, promising to shape policy discussions and political strategies in the months to come.

Felix Canaris sank back upon the rickety chair, his heavy eyes growing dim, as though the very weight of his thoughts were lulling him toward a dark oblivion. The flames crackled before him, embers dancing in a pitiful send-off of unsung melodies, and he mourned, not merely for the parchment that crumbled into ashes, but for the vivacity of hope that had once coursed through his veins.

Silence enveloped the chamber, broken only by the occasional howl of the wind as it swirled around the desolate building, an insistent whisper from the ether that mourned the unfulfilled promises of life and art. Each gust seemed to echo his own demons, igniting a faint flicker of life in his chest—a defiance against the cold that sought to extinguish him, even as he considered yielding to it entirely. Tall and cloaked, the man bore an air of otherworldliness, his features obscured beneath the hood of his travel-worn garment. Felix squinted, the insipid glow of the flames framing the intruder in an ethereal glow as he took his first tentative step into the room.
