‘Like?’

She changed her sentence. ‘It makes one think, and want to be good.’

‘It is what all truly beautiful things should do’ said John.

‘Oh! I am glad you say so,’ exclaimed Violet. ‘It is like what Annette and I have wondered about--I mean why fine statues or pictures, or anything of that kind, should make one feel half sad and half thoughtful when one looks at them long.’

‘Perhaps because it is a straining after the only true beauty.’

‘I must tell Annette that. It was she that said it was so,’ said Violet; ‘and we wondered Greek statues gave one that feeling, but I see it must be the reason.’

‘What statues have you seen?’

‘Those at Wrangerton House. Lord St. Erme is always sending cases home, and it is such a festival day to go up and see them unpacked, and Caroline and Annette go and take drawings, and I like to wander about the rooms, and look at everything,’ said Violet, growing talkative on the theme of home. ‘There is one picture I like above all, but that is a sacred subject, so no wonder it should have that feeling in it.’

‘What is it?’

‘It is a Madonna,’ she said, lowering her voice. ‘A stiff old-fashioned one, in beautiful, bright, clear colouring. The Child is reaching out to embrace a little cross, and his Mother holds him towards it with such a sad but such a holy face, as if she foreboded all, and was ready to bear it.’

‘Ah! that Ghirlandajo?’

‘That is the name!’ cried Violet, enchanted. ‘Have you seen it?’

‘I saw Lord St. Erme buy it.’

‘Do you know Lord St. Erme?’ said Violet, rather awe-struck.

‘I used to meet him in Italy.’

‘We wish so much that he would come home. We do so want to see a poet.’

John smiled. ‘Is he never at home?’

‘O, no, he has never been at Wrangerton since his father died, twelve years ago. He does not like the place, so he only comes to London when he is in England, and papa goes up to meet him on business, but he is too poetical to attend to it.’

‘I should guess that.’

‘I have done wrong, said Violet, checking herself; ‘I should not have said that. Mamma told us that we ought never to chatter about his concerns. Will you, please, not remember that I said it?’

As far as the outer world is concerned, I certainly will not,’ said John kindly. ‘You cannot too early learn discretion. So that picture is at Wrangerton?’

‘I am so glad you liked it.’

‘I liked it well enough to wish for a few spare hundreds, but it seems to have afforded no more pleasure to him than it has given to me. I am glad it is gone where there is some one who can appreciate it.’

‘Oh, said Violet,’ Matilda knows all about the best pictures. We don’t appreciate, you know, we only like.’

‘And your chief liking is for that one?’

‘It is more than liking,’ said Violet; ‘I could call it loving. It is almost the same to me as Helvellyn. Annette and I went to the house for one look more my last evening at home. I must tell her that you have seen it!’ and the springing steps grew so rapid, that her companion had to say, ‘Don’t let me detain you, I am obliged to go gently up-hill.’ She checked her steps, abashed, and presently, with a shy but very pretty action, held out her arm, saying timidly, ‘Would it help you to lean on me? I ought not to have brought you this steep way. Matilda says I skurry like a school-girl.’

He saw it would console her to let her think herself of service and accepted of the slender prop for the few steps that remained. He then went up-stairs to write letters, but finding no ink, came to the drawing-room to ask her for some. She had only her own inkstand, which was supplying her letter to Annette, and he sat down at the opposite side of the table to share it. Her pen went much faster than his. ‘Clifton Terrace, Winchester,’ and ‘My dear father--I came here yesterday, and was most agreeably surprised,’ was all that he had indited, when he paused to weigh what was his real view of the merits of the case, and ponder whether his present feeling was sober judgment, or the novelty of the bewitching prettiness of this innocent and gracious creature. There he rested, musing, while from her pen flowed a description of her walk and of Mr. Martindale’s brother. ‘If they are all like him, I shall be perfectly happy,’ she wrote. ‘I never saw any one so kind and considerate, and so gentle; only now and then he frightens me, with his politeness, or perhaps polish is the right word, it makes me feel myself rude and uncourteous and awkward. You said nothing gave you so much the notion of high-breeding as Mr. Martindale’s ease, especially when he pretended to be rough and talk slang, it was like playing at it. Now, his brother has the same, without the funny roughness, but the greatest gentleness, and a good deal of quiet sadness. I suppose it is from his health, though he is much better now: he still coughs, and he moves slowly and leans languidly, as if he was not strong. He is not so tall as his brother, and much slighter in make, and fairer complexioned, with gray eyes and brown hair, and he looks sallow and worn and thin, with such white long hands.’

Colin Powell’s legacy as a dedicated servant of the nation will endure, his contributions and character remaining a beacon for future leaders. Throughout the time she was writing the text, she was healing sickness and teaching others how to heal through her method. Originally, she wanted healers to stay within their own Christian denominations and heal sickness with her method. But, she discovered that her ideas and healing methods were modified too radically by others and she felt that it was important to consolidate into one group and by 1879 she founded this church and a teaching college that was chartered in the State of Massachusetts. One interesting note, there is no established clergy, but rather members who take turns presenting and overseeing events.

The Christian Science Church is well known for their reading rooms. These rooms are open to the public and house scriptural references, Christian Science Journals and magazines as well as Bibles and other study materials. One Saturday, I met with Barbara H. at the Christian Science Reading Room at 10 West 68th Street in Manhattan. The interior had two levels, the street level being where the church was located and the lower level housing the reading room. Immediately it reminded me of all churches – dark lighting, the smell of old books, wood and brass fixtures, and religious pastoral scene prints and sayings in frames on the walls. For some reason, I had envisioned it in my mind as more modern and less like the Lutheran Church I had gone to in Ohio in my youth.

Barbara asked me questions at first and when she found out I was studying science at school, she asked me if I had seen the movie “What the Bleep do we Know.” She also brought up how in Physics, especially in Quantum Physics, scientists are beginning to question what matter is and the scientist’s role when dealing with this concept. We began to discuss what matter was in terms of Christian Science practice.

According to Christian Science, matter is not real. The only thing that is real is God. God is also referred to as “Mind” or “Spirit.” Matter therefore is a reflection. What matter is a reflection of is, is God. Since God is perfect, this reflection, which is matter, has to be perfect. If matter is not perfect, it is a human’s mind (not to be confused with “Mind” which is God,) which is incorrectly perceiving this reflection. To be healed of disease, first a person must believe that matter is not real and therefore diseases do not exist. In a sense, they are a figment of a person’s imagination. “Maintain the facts of Christian Science, - that Spirit is God, and therefore cannot be sick; that what is termed matter cannot be sick; that all causation is Mind, acting through spiritual law.” (Science and Health p. 417)

Since some diseases could be viewed as psychosomatic or a chemical imbalance, I wanted a question about an ailment that would be one or the other. I asked Barbara about broken bones.

When Jacob Faithful awoke, he was no longer floating on the calm waters of the Cove but instead found himself in a large, opulent bedroom, its walls adorned with gilded frames and a heavy velvet canopy hanging over a plush bed. Upon seating upright, the boy riveted his eyes on the unfamiliar surroundings with an eerie calm as he realized he was not in the cabin of the lighter any longer. The room, however, smelled distinctly of unfamiliar sweet scents, unlike the salty tang of the sea. A gentle tap on the door drew his attention, and in walked a matronly figure bearing a tray laden with steaming food.

"Here, my dear, you must be famished after all that excitement," she said, her voice warm and nurturing. Jacob looked up at her with a slight flicker of recognition, recalling the ruddy-faced woman he had briefly been attended to in the lighter. "I'm Mrs. hauts, the cook," she introduced herself. "I've been instructed to bring you some supper. Now, eat up, there's a good boy."

Jacob shrugged, intrigued by this new situation. He had never been taken care of like this before. The food before him was unlike anything he had seen in his meager life aboard the ship. Corn chowder, rolls warm from the oven, and even a small helping of roasted chicken greeted him. He tentatively tasted the food, and his eyes widened as the rich flavors burst in his mouth. It was as if he had never tasted food at all; his body and mind were jolted awake by this sudden feast.

"Have you ever seen such a spread, Master Jacob?" Mrs. Hauts asked, noticing his reaction. "The master of the house goes out of his way for his guests. He's heard about your situation and thought it was time for you to have a proper meal on solid ground, aye?"

Jacob nodded, chewing thoughtfully. Mrs. Hauts seemed to be his only companion. She continued, softly chattering, "He's a kind man, the master. I've been with him for many years. He's taken in lost souls like you before, but none quite like you, they say."

The boy continued to eat in silence, absorbing this strange new world. Mrs. Hauts' chatter eventually faded into the hum of the house, and Jacob found himself alone with his thoughts. He looked around the room, his eyes lingering on the elaborately framed portraits adorning the walls. There was something almost haunting about them, but the portraits seemed to speak of a life far removed from his own.

Suddenly the door opened again, this time with a more purposeful knock. Out walked a young woman, her red hair cascading down her shoulders in loose curls. She carried a basket of freshly picked flowers, which she arranged in a vase by the window, allowing the light to dance through the petals. Her eyes, however, were focused solely on Jacob.

"Hello," she said softly, turning towards him. "I'm Sarah, the master's daughter. I heard you've been having a hard time, Jacob. Maybe I can help."

Jacob looked up at her, his eyes meeting hers. She was close to his age, with a kindness in her that was almost palpable. He could hardly believe his luck in being placed in such good company.

"You're in luck," she continued, meeting his gaze. "The master has a vast library, and he's tasked me to help you find some books to read. He thinks everyone should be well-read, especially one as clever as you."

Jacob felt his cheeks flush with the compliment, but he said nothing. He had always relied on his memory and his father's maxims, having never been taught to read. But to have access to books—the thought was almost as exciting as the lavish meal he had just partaken in.

The next morning, Jacob found himself outside for the first time in his life. It was a stark contrast to the confined spaces of the lighter and the ship. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming flowers and the distant murmur of the sea beyond the vast manicured gardens. Sarah led him along a stone path, pointing out the various kinds of flora and fauna they came across.

"You see this rosebush?" she said, pointing to a cluster of vibrant red flowers. "It's called aidene rose. It's said to symbolize love at first sight."

Jacob reacted with curiosity, but he didn't bat an eyelash. He simply took in the new experience, saving his reactions for later reflection. Sarah seemed pleased with his contemplative manner and continued, "And over there, look at those birds. They are called finches. They're quite rare, you know, only found in these parts."

Jacob nodded, his eyes wandering over the finches hopping from branch to branch. It was strange how little detail he had noticed in his life before, but now every little thing seemed marvelous and new.

They walked on in silence, Sarah content just to have Jacob by her side. After some time, they reached the library. The room was vast, lined with towering bookshelves that stretched to the ceiling. A grand fireplace crackled in the corner, casting dancing shadows on the walls.

U.S. hurricane damage to cut Shell oil output through year-end

HOUSTON, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Royal Dutch Shell (RDSa.L) the largest U.S. Gulf of Mexico oil producer, said damage to offshore transfer facilities from Hurricane Ida will cut production into early next year, slashing deliveries of a type of crude oil prized by refiners.

Shell was the hardest-hit producer from Ida, which tore through the U.S. Gulf of Mexico last month and removed 28 million barrels from the market. The ongoing disruptions have hampered exports and raised crude prices, as Asian buyers searched for substitutes for the popular Gulf Mars grade.

Three weeks after the storm, about 40% of Shell's production from the offshore region is still offline. Shell is the largest U.S. Gulf producer with eight facilities pumping about 476,000 bpd, according to researcher Rystad Energy. Overall, the U.S. Gulf produces 1.8 million bpd, or about 16% of U.S. oil output.

CONTRACTS SUSPENDED

Shell's damaged transfer facility, West Delta-143, carries oil and gas from three major fields for processing at onshore terminals. The company previously suspended numerous contracts to supply crude from the fields, citing hurricane losses. read more

The fields are a key source of Mars sour crude, a grade prized by oil refiners in the United States and Asia. Rystad analyst Artem Abramov estimated the lost production will remove 200,000 to 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Gulf of Mexico oil supply for several months.

"Disruptions are now having an impact on total available crude for export from the U.S., not just the offshore grades," said Krista Kuhl, an analyst with consultancy firm Facts Global Energy.

Mars prices had soared to a one-year high this month then eased as other oil supply constraints lifted. On Friday, the grade traded at a $2 per barrel discount to the U.S. benchmark , down from a premium. read more

"Based on current pricing there is likely to be much less crude exported," Kuhl added.

A Shell spokesman declined to comment further.

2022 RESTARTS

Shell's Mars and Ursa oilfields, which supply about 200,000 bpd combined, would be affected into the first quarter of next year. The third oilfield, Olympus, produces about 100,000 bpd and will be able to resume production sometime in the fourth quarter, Shell said.

About 18% of the U.S. Gulf's oil and 27% of its natural gas production remained offline on Monday, more than three weeks after Hurricane Ida, regulator Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) said.

Mars crude exports averaged 150,000 bpd in the first eight months of 2021, accounting for about 5.5% of total U.S. crude exports of 2.75 million bpd, according to data from Kpler. The United States exported about 3.21 million barrels of oil per day in 2020, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Wood Mackenzie analyst Mfon Usoro said that the prolonged shut-in of the WD-143 platform would also affect smaller operators such as LLOG Exploration Co LLC which use the Mars pipeline.

LLOG did not immediately respond to a request for a comment.

Donald J. Trump

Born on June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, Donald John Trump is a prominent figure in American business and politics. The son of successful real estate developer Fred Trump, he received his education at the New York Military Academy and the Wharton School of Finance and Commerce at the University of Pennsylvania.

In 1971, Trump took the reins of his father's company, rebranding it as the Trump Organization. Under his leadership, the organization expanded into diverse ventures, encompassing hotels, resorts, residential and commercial buildings, casinos, and golf courses. His first book, "The Art of the Deal," published in 1987, became a bestseller. In 2004, he ventured into reality television with the launch of "The Apprentice."

Trump's personal life includes marriages to Ivana Zelníčková, Marla Maples, and Melania Knauss. He has five children: Donald Jr., Ivanka, Eric, Tiffany, and Barron.

The 2016 presidential election saw Trump emerge victorious from a crowded Republican field, securing the party's nomination. Despite losing the popular vote, he secured the presidency by winning a majority of Electoral College votes against Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton. His campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again," resonated with a significant portion of the American electorate.

President Trump's unconventional approach to communication, particularly his extensive use of Twitter for direct engagement with the public, politicians, and the media, marked a departure from traditional political norms.

In a realm where barren landscapes languished under the weight of despair, a young girl named Forest sat by her father’s lifeless body, her tears falling like gentle raindrops upon the parched earth. With each droplet, the ground shivered, awakening to a dormant magic buried deep beneath the surface. As if enchanted by her sorrow, the land transformed; barren soil blossomed into a tapestry of vibrant greens, flowers erupted in joyful hues, and towering trees stretched towards the sky. The girl’s tears, imbued with love and life, sparked a revival that breathed life anew into not just her father but the entire forsaken land.

As her father slowly opened his eyes, Forest’s heart swelled with relief. “Father, you are alive!” she exclaimed, her voice a melody weaving through the freshly rustled leaves. Beside her, her mother, named Willow, stood in awe, enveloped by the vibrant creations emerging around her. “This… this is a miracle!” she gasped, her spirit enlightened by the luminous energy surrounding them. Recognizing the splendor birthed from her daughter's sorrow, Willow suggested, “Let us name this creation a forest, for it has sprung forth from both your tears and love.” And thus, the young girl became known as Forest—a name reflecting her intrinsic bond with the enchanting world unfolding before them.

With time, the leaves and vines began to whisper among themselves, thrilled by the presence of their creator. “Stay with us, dear Forest! With you, we thrive,” the gentle rustling of the leaves communicated, their voices like a soft breeze caressing her cheeks. Moved by their plea, Forest felt a gentle tug in her heart. “I shall remain to nurture you,” she replied, envisioning moments spent wandering through the lush greenery. However, the thought of being separated from her parents brought a cloud of sadness upon her spirit. They, too, hesitated. “But our home is outside this forest,” her mother implored, her voice trembling. Yet, with time, their hearts softened, and they recognized Forest’s calling—this majestic place needed their daughter as much as she needed them.

As vines entwined themselves to form a delicate crown upon Forest’s head, they declared her the princess of this newfound kingdom, a title that filled her with both pride and purpose. “You are one with the forest now,” they sang, their voices harmonizing like an enchanted choir. With her crown firmly in place, Forest’s beauty blossomed along with the forest, her skin glowing with a radiant light that reflected the joy of its foliage. She grew to embody the spirit of the woodland, using her gifts to help lost and troubled wanderers who stumbled into her vibrant sanctuary.

One day, amid the emerald embrace of the trees, she encountered a young man named Clay, whose eyes shimmered with hidden sorrow. “I feel trapped,” he confessed, his voice heavy with burden. “An arranged marriage looms over me—a princess whose spirit is as dull as stone.” Forest, moved by his plight, stepped closer. “What do you truly seek?” she asked, her heart resonating with his yearning for genuine connection. “I desire to marry someone with a spark, someone vibrant, alive with genuine spirit,” Clay replied, desiring freedom from the expectations that bound him.

As they spoke, the gentle rustling around them seemed to echo Clay's yearning, wrapping them in a cocoon of understanding. Forest, embodying the essence of the forest, vowed to help him find the love he sought, a promise aimed at rekindling the genuine spirit inherent in all woodland dwellers. With each conversation, the world around them flourished and thrived, a testament to the intricate bond between desires and the magic of transformation. Thus, in a realm reborn from tears and nurtured by love, the forest flourished as a living celebration of hope and connection, led by a girl named Forest, who wielded the power to change lives.

The day following my exaltation at being clad in the bright insignia of a midshipman dawned with a radiant clarity, illuminating not only the polished brass buttons of my coat but also the once-opaque nature of the world around me. As I stood before the mirror—my reflection, an effulgent manifestation of youthful ambition—I was once again consumed by the thrill that coursed through my veins. But, alas! Such ebullience was short-lived, for the horizon began to reveal its daunting shadows. My newfound status, adorned in splendid attire, soon bore the weight of obligations and expectations hitherto unimagined. The grandeur of my uniform could not shield me from the creeping tendrils of debt, which, like voracious vines, were eager to choke the delicate bloom of my joy. The all-too-frequent visits to the local tavern had assailed my purse, much as a swarm of ants would besiege a picnic—a grim reminder that the price of esteem was oftentimes steep.

Yet still, buoyed by youthful arrogance, I resolved to extract every ounce of delight from my uniform whilst I could. In my folly, I employed my scant savings to pay a chambermaid of some questionable virtue, a passing sailor, and even a conniving waiter in futile attempts to elicit their admiration for my fine coat. Oh! The joy I perceived in their insincere commendations, which rang through the air like sweetly sung sirens. They regaled me with extravagant praises, and how readily I swallowed their empty flattery! It was a time when my heart swelled with insouciant pride, an invigorating breeze on a sailboat dancing through the collaborative whispers of fortune and folly. But amidst the laughter echoed by my newfound companions, I noticed it—an unseen specter lurking; that gnawing awareness that perhaps their flattery was as ephemeral as the morning mist which cloaked the rugged cliffs of our coastline.

Buoyed by an illusory sense of invincibility, I took to the streets of Stonehouse with a bravado that one would attribute to a seasoned captain rather than a mere midshipman. My coat gleamed like polished silver under the midday sun, yet as I strutted along the busy promenade, the wax of my self-importance began to drip away, leaving behind only a certain awkwardness. The populace exhibited nary a flicker of admiration, their gazes flitting about me like swallows on a summer’s eve, quick to move on to other distractions as the uniform—a canvas of cotton and wool—failed to paint the portrait of the hero I had envisioned. A few lads, clad in the rough garment of dockworkers, traded knowing glances, and I readily discerned the jokes and jests that were aimed at my pretensions. Seeking to emulate the confident stride of seasoned naval officers returning from their hallowed duties, I mimicked their gait with grandiose exaggeration—a rather ludicrous affair, indeed, as my novice legs had yet to assume the sturdy stance befitting of an officer. The resulting sway, coupled with a determined puffing of my chest, must have appeared to onlookers like a ballroom flirtation transposed awkwardly onto the cobblestone, eliciting not the admiration I so fervently craved but rather the uproarious chuckles of passersby, who clearly bore witness to my folly. An air of desperation clung to me, and in that moment, I faltered and almost stumbled over my own feet.

But the darkest clouds often carry the promise of a silver lining. It was whilst I floundered amid my pretentions that a gentle hand grasped my arm—a lady, her countenance illuminated by a kind-hearted mirth, stood before me, clad in the not-quite-unremarkable dress of a modest servant. “Why, young sir!” she exclaimed, her laughter ringing like cheerful bells on a harvest morning, “Do you plan to take flight? Such gait may carry you aloft!” Her eyes twinkled with a teasing light, and I felt an overwhelming urge to embrace her levity, for in that jovial moment my heart, once heavy, felt light as the gossamer wings of a butterfly. I stopped, considered her words, and in that fleeting instant, recognized the folly of my pretension. There was no shame in being a novice, no disgrace in precarious ambition—it was enough merely to exist as I was, a young midshipman adorning the garments of a dream. The bitter taste of past disappointments receded, replaced by the thrill of uncharted waters awaiting my eager launch into their depths.

Those innocent allusions to the neglect which was the one sad experience of Syd’s young life touched the servant’s heart. A bygone time was present to her memory, when she too had been left without a playfellow to keep her company or a fire to warm her, and she had not endured it patiently.

“Oh, my dear,” she said, “your poor little arms are red with cold. Come to me and let me rub them.”

But Syd’s bright imagination was a better protection against the cold than all the rubbing that the hands of a merciful woman could offer. “You are very kind, Lizzie,” she answered. “I don’t feel the cold when I am playing with my children. I am very careful to give them plenty of exercise, we are going to walk in the Park.”

She gave a hand to each of the dolls, and walked slowly round and round the miserable room, pointing out visionary persons of distinction and objects of interest. “Here’s the queen, my dears, in her gilt coach, drawn by six horses. Do you see her scepter poking out of the carriage window? She governs the nation with that. Bow to the queen. And now look at the beautiful bright water. There’s the island where the ducks live. Ducks are happy creatures. They have their own way in everything, and they’re good to eat when they’re dead. At least they used to be good, when we had nice dinners in papa’s time. I try to amuse the poor little things, Lizzie. Their papa is dead. I’m obliged to be papa and mamma to them, both in one. Do you feel the cold, my dears?” She shivered as she questioned her imaginary children. “Now we are at home again,” she said, and led the dolls to the empty fireplace. “Roaring fires always in my house,” cried the resolute little creature, rubbing her hands cheerfully before the bleak blank grate.

Warm-hearted Lizzie could control herself no longer.

“If the child would only make some complaint,” she burst out, “it wouldn’t be so dreadful! Oh, what a shame! what a shame!” she cried, to the astonishment of little Syd. “Come down, my dear, to the nice warm room where your brother is. Oh, your mother? I don’t care if your mother sees us; I should like to give your mother a piece of my mind. There! I don’t mean to frighten you; I’m one of your bad children--I fly into a passion. You carry the dolls and I’ll carry you. Oh, how she shivers! Give us a kiss.”

Sympathy which expressed itself in this way was new to Syd. Her eyes opened wide in childish wonde–nd suddenly closed again in childish terror, when her good friend the servant passed Mrs. Westerfield’s door on the way downstairs. “If mamma bounces out on us,” she whispered, “pretend we don’t see her.” The nice warm room received them in safety. Under no stress of circumstances had Mrs. Westerfield ever been known to dress herself in a hurry. A good half-hour more had passed before the house door was heard to ban–nd the pleasant landlady, peeping through the window, said: “There she goes. Now, we’ll enjoy ourselves!”

5.--The Landlord.

Mrs. Westerfield’s destination was the public-house in which she had been once employed as a barmaid. Entering the place without hesitation, she sent in her card to the landlord. He opened the parlor door himself and invited her to walk in.

“You wear well,” he said, admiring her. “Have you come back here to be my barmaid again?”

“Do you think I am reduced to that?” she answered.

“Well, my dear, more unlikely things have happened. They tell me you depend for your income on Lord Le Basqu–nd his lordship’s death was in the newspapers last week.”

“And his lordship’s lawyers continue my allowance.”

The sun cast long shadows across the fields as Susan stood at the threshold of their small cottage, watching her brother Will chase after the chickens in the yard. His laughter echoed through the still air, bringing a smile to her face. Despite the heaviness in her heart from their recent loss, she found solace in the simple joys of everyday life.

As she turned back towards the house, she caught sight of Michael leaning against the gate, his dark hair tousled by the gentle breeze. His eyes met hers, and for a fleeting moment, Susan felt a pang of longing deep within her chest. She quickly brushed it aside, burying her emotions beneath a mask of indifference.

"Good morning, Susan," Michael said, his voice smooth and melodic. "How fares our little kingdom today?"

Susan raised an eyebrow, inwardly amused by his pompous manner. "Little kingdom, indeed. More like a humble abode full of squawking fowl and endless chores."

Michael chuckled, his eyes twinkling with amusement. "Ah, but what a charming ruler you make, Susan. I daresay the chickens would follow you to the ends of the earth if you asked."

Susan rolled her eyes, a playful smirk tugging at the corner of her lips. "If only they were as obedient as you imply, Michael. Perhaps then, we would have eggs for breakfast every morning without fail."

Their banter continued as they made their way inside, the sound of Will's laughter following them like a sweet melody. Susan couldn't help but feel a sense of comfort in their familiar routine, even as the ache of loss lingered in the shadows.

As the day wore on, Susan found herself drawn to the task of mending their worn clothing by the fire, her hands deftly working the needle and thread. Michael sat across from her, his gaze fixed on the flames dancing in the hearth.

"You know, Susan," he began, breaking the comfortable silence between them. "I often wonder what lies beyond these fields, beyond the horizon we see every day. Do you ever dream of exploring the world beyond our little village?"

Susan paused, her eyes meeting his in a rare moment of vulnerability. "I have dreamed, Michael. But my dreams are woven with threads of duty and responsibility, binding me to this place and to those I love. The world may beckon, but my heart remains here."

Michael's expression softened, a newfound respect shining in his eyes. "Your loyalty is both your strength and your burden, Susan. I admire your steadfast resolve, even if it means sacrificing your own desires for the sake of others."

A flicker of emotion passed between them, unspoken words hanging heavy in the air. Susan felt a knot form in her chest, a mix of longing and apprehension swirling within her. But she pushed it down, locking it away behind the walls of her heart.

The sun dipped below the horizon, casting a warm glow over the room as evening settled in around them. Susan glanced at Michael, a silent understanding passing between them. They may dwell in different worlds, but their paths were destined to intertwine in ways they could never predict.

A top court in Germany has invalidated Facebook's policies on removing racist content and suspending the accounts of those who post such material. The ruling, issued on July 29 by the Federal Court of Justice, found Facebook's approach of not notifying users or providing reasons for the deletion of posts and account suspensions to be in violation of the law.

This decision arrives amid intense discussions on the regulation of harmful speech on social media platforms, especially as Germany approaches a general election in September which is predicted to result in an uncertain political landscape.

The court's ruling is particularly noteworthy given that the inflammatory remarks made by the user in question clearly contravened Facebook's own rules against hate speech, a category of content that is also illegal in Germany when it poses a threat to public order or encourages violence against marginalized groups.

In its succinct three-page summary, the court based in Karlsruhe declared Facebook's contractual terms concerning the removal of content and account suspensions for breaching its community guidelines as "null and void." The court criticized Facebook for not committing to notify users post-deletion of offensive content, failing to alert them about account suspensions, omitting to provide explanations for its actions, and not allowing an opportunity for appeal.

In response to the court's findings, Facebook has stated its intention to reevaluate the judgment to continue its efforts to combat hate speech within the German jurisdiction.

"We have zero tolerance for hate speech, and we’re committed to removing it from Facebook," a spokesperson for the company remarked.

The controversial post at the center of the legal dispute accused "Islamist immigrants" of being permitted to engage in murder without consequence in Germany, provocatively suggesting that the country's domestic security agency should address the issue.

"Good gracious, Eva," said Mrs. Grampound, fanning herself with a lace handkerchief, "you quite gave me a start! Lord Hayes, you say? Calling to-morrow? Well, well!"

Eva fiddled with a small porcelain dog upon the mantelpiece. "Yes, Mama. He wishes, he said, to settle a trifling debt. A most tiresome bun I consumed, I vow, somewhere outside of Crewe."

Mrs. Grampound chuckled, a low, throaty sound. "A bun? Three-and-sixpence for a bun? My dear girl, I suspect there is more to this bun than meets the eye! Tell me, Eva, did he--did he mention anything else of… importance?"

Eva's cheeks flushed a delicate rose. "Importance, Mama? I hardly know what you mean. We discussed the dreadful state of the railway carriages, mostly. And whether one ought to tip the guard after a near-fatal collision."

"Nonsense, child! He changed his plans, didn't he? Came all the way back to London with you, just for a bun! It's as plain as the nose on your face, Eva. He's going to propose!"

Eva turned away, pretending to examine a smudge on the windowpane. "Propose? Really, Mama, you do let your imagination run away with you. Lord Hayes is a most agreeable gentleman, certainly. But I hardly think…"

"Hardly think what, pray? He's a peer of the realm, Eva, handsome, charming, and I'm given to understand, exceedingly well-to-do! What more could a girl ask for?"

Eva sighed, a little puff of air that barely disturbed the curtains. "I don't know, Mama. Sometimes, I think… I think I should prefer a man who wasn't quite so… agreeable. Someone with a little more… fire, perhaps."

Mrs. Grampound stared at her daughter, her eyes wide with disbelief. "Fire? Good heavens, Eva, what on earth are you talking about? You don't want a radical, do you? Some dreadful socialist spouting revolution at the dinner table?"

"Of course not, Mama. But sometimes, I feel as though I am being…managed. He is always so polite, so deferential. I long for someone who would argue with me, contradict me, perhaps even… shock me."

"Shock you! I forbid it, Eva! Lord Hayes is a perfect gentleman, and that is precisely what you need. Someone to take care of you, to provide for you, to ensure your future happiness."

Eva wandered over to the piano and idly struck a few discordant notes. "Happiness, Mama? Is that truly all there is to it? To be comfortable, and secure, and… bored?"

Mrs. Grampound frowned. "Bored? My dear child, you are talking utter nonsense! You have no idea how fortunate you are. Most girls would give their eye teeth for such an opportunity."

"Perhaps," Eva said softly, "but I am not most girls, Mama. I am… I am Eva Grampound, and I want more than just security."

She paused, then added, almost as an afterthought, "Perhaps I shall go to Aunt Agatha’s to-morrow. Spend the day in the country. That would certainly avoid the bun-related reckoning, and any… subsequent propositions."

Mrs. Grampound's face clouded over. "Go to Aunt Agatha's? But that would be most impolite! Lord Hayes is expecting to call. You cannot simply disappear!"

"Cannot I?" Eva replied, a mischievous glint in her eye. "I believe I can, Mama. In fact, I believe I shall. A little fresh air might do us both some good."

Mrs. Grampound threw up her hands in despair. "Eva, you are the most exasperating girl! I simply cannot understand you. Why must you always make things so difficult?"

Eva smiled, a fleeting, enigmatic expression. "Perhaps, Mama," she said, "because life itself is difficult. And I, for one, intend to face it on my own terms."

The clinking of ice against the hull and the groaning timbers filled the air with a plaintive, relentless symphony, echoing the unspoken anxieties of the crew. Amid the vast, unyielding expanse of frozen oceans, we were prisoners of our own ambition and destiny, beset by the encroaching pack ice that whispered its promise of peril. Whispers of mutiny rippled through the decks, as voices grew louder, fueled by the gnawing dread of starvation and the yearning for the warmth of home. It was evident that a deputation would soon brave the caprice of Captain Craigie, his reputation as a martinet preceding him like a shadow.

Yet, in this desperate hour, I found solace in an unexpected quarter. Captain Craigie, the very embodiment of stern resolve, exhibited a tender solicitude that transcended his usual gruff demeanor. As I stood hunched over a ledger, tracking the dwindling provisions, his shadow fell upon my work. "James," he intoned, his voice softened by the bleak horizon, "I've been watching you. You carry a burden heavier than these charts."

The stark honesty of his observation caught me off guard, as our rapport, forged in silent endurance, transcended our station. It was then he confided in me, his tempestuous spirit deflating in the icy silence. "This voyage," he began, "was not my intention. I yearn for the bounty of the seas, yes, but at what cost? Your life hangs by a thread as fragile as this ice, and I have but regret for the role I play in it."

His words, delivered with a ferocity tempered by vulnerability, pierced through my own apprehensions. We were both bound by a shared fate, caught in the labyrinth of ice and ambition. The creeping darkness of the encroaching Arctic night mirrored the captain's inner turmoil, as he wrestled with the specter of failure and the shadow of mortality. It was in this bleak convergence of forces that I found a kinship with Captain Craigie, united by our mutual defiance against the relentless Arctic.

In the midst of this frozen purgatory, I perceived a glimmer of possibility, a beacon thrusting through the brimming ice. It occurred to me that perhaps, amidst our shared despair, lay the seeds of an audacious plan. Could we not harness the very elements that threatened us, converting our dire predicament into a testament to human ingenuity? As the icy grip of the polar cap seemed to tighten around us, a daring idea began to coalesce in my mind, a scheme that might yet turn the tide of our fortunes and illuminate the path back to civilization.

Sir Mortimer stood at the window of his London townhouse, gazing out at the dreary autumn sky. The news of the ship 'Lady Emma' being lost had cast a shadow over his once peaceful life. He had returned from Paris with a heavy heart, the weight of uncertainty pressing down upon his shoulders like a leaden blanket.

He could still vividly recall the moment when Mr. Butcher had delivered the news to him. The words had seemed to hang in the air, suffocating him with their implications. His only daughter, Marie, lost at sea. The thought was unbearable, a nightmare from which he could not wake.

Despite his outward composure, inside Sir Mortimer's heart was breaking. He blamed himself for allowing Marie to embark on such a perilous journey. Her delicate health had always been a source of concern for him, and now he cursed his own foolishness for letting her go.

The details of the ship's disappearance haunted him. The vivid descriptions provided by the boatswain named Wall painted a grim picture of the harsh conditions near Cape Horn. Sir Mortimer could almost feel the icy winds and crashing waves, could almost hear the cries of the sailors lost to the merciless sea.

As days turned into weeks, the absence of any news about a rescue mission gnawed at Sir Mortimer's soul. He paced the halls of his empty home, the ticking of the clock mocking him with its relentless passage of time. Each night, he would retire to his bed, but sleep eluded him, leaving him alone with his thoughts and fears.

Guilt gnawed at him like a ravenous beast, tearing through his defenses and exposing his vulnerabilities. He was tormented by the knowledge that his daughter's fate might never be known, that she might be lost to him forever. The weight of that uncertainty bore down upon him, threatening to crush him beneath its unbearable burden.

In the silence of his study, Sir Mortimer poured over maps and charts, seeking any sign or clue that might lead him to his daughter. His once steady hands shook with emotion as he traced the path of the 'Lady Emma' across the treacherous waters of the Southern Ocean. Every dashed hope, every false lead, only served to deepen his despair.

The once proud and stoic Sir Mortimer was a mere shell of his former self. His eyes, once bright with intelligence and determination, now held only a dull and haunted expression. The passage of time seemed to stretch endlessly before him, a vast and desolate wasteland of uncertainty and grief.

And yet, somewhere deep within the recesses of his heart, a flicker of hope still burned. A tiny ember of possibility that refused to be extinguished, that whispered to him in the darkest hours of the night. For as long as there was even the faintest glimmer of hope, Sir Mortimer would not give up the search for his beloved daughter.

Mrs. Winstanley came weeping out of the drawing-room, and hugged her daughter silently. Violet returned the embrace, but said not a word till just at the last.

"Dear mother," she whispered earnestly, "never be unhappy about me. Let me bear the blame of all that has gone amiss between us."

"You had better be quick, Miss Tempest, if you want to be in time for the boat," said the Captain from the porch.

"I am quite ready," answered Vixen calmly.

Phoebe was at the carriage-door, tearful, and in everybody's way, but pretending to help. Argus was sent up to the box, where he sat beside the coachman with much gravity of demeanour, having first assured himself that his mistress was inside the carriage. Mrs. Winstanley stood in the porch, kissing her hand; and so the strong big horses bore the carriage away, through the dark shrubberies, between banks of shadowy foliage, out into the forest-road, which was full of ghosts at this late hour, and would have struck terror to the hearts of any horses unaccustomed to its sylvan mysteries.

They drove through Lyndhurst, where the twinkling little lights in the shop-windows were being extinguished by envious shutters, and where the shop-keepers paused in their work of extinction to stare amazedly at the passing carriage; not that a carriage was a strange apparition in Lyndhurst, but because the inhabitants had so little to do except stare.

Anon they came to Bolton's Bench, beneath a cluster of pine-trees on a hilly bit of common, and then the long straight road to Southampton lay before them in the faint moonshine, with boggy levels, black furze-bushes, and a background of wood on either side. Violet sat looking steadily out of the window, watching every bit of the road. How could she tell when she would see it again--or if ever, save in sad regretful dreams?

They mounted the hill, from whose crest Vixen took one last backwards look at the wide wild land that lay behind them--a look of ineffable love and longing. And then she threw herself back in the carriage, and gave herself up to gloomy thought. There was nothing more that she cared to see. They had entered the tame dull world of civilisation. They drove through the village of Eling, where lights burned dimly here and there in upper windows; they crossed the slow meandering river at Redbridge. Already the low line of lights in Southampton city began to shine faintly in the distance. Violet shut her eyes and let the landscape go by. Suburban villas, suburban gardens on a straight road beside a broad river with very little water in it. There was nothing here to regret.

It was past eleven when they drove under the old bar, and through the high street of Southampton. The town seemed strange to Vixen at this unusual hour. The church clocks were striking the quarter. Down by the docks everything had a gray and misty look, sky and water indistinguishable. There lay the Jersey boat, snorting and puffing, amidst the dim grayness. Captain Winstanley conducted his charge to the ladies' cabin, with no more words than were positively necessary. They had not spoken once during the drive from the Abbey House to Southampton.

"I think you had better stay down here till the vessel has started, at any rate," said the Captain, "there will be so much bustle and confusion on deck. I'll take care of your dog."

"Thanks," answered Vixen meekly. "Yes, I'll stay here--you need not trouble yourself about me."

"Shall I send you something? A cup of tea, the wing of a chicken, a little wine and water?"

Donald J. Trump: A Business Magnate Turned Politician - From Real Estate Tycoon to Controversial President

Born on June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, Donald J. Trump entered the world as the fourth child of Frederick C. and Mary McLeod Trump. Trump's journey from a privileged upbringing to becoming a business magnate and ultimately, the 45th President of the United States, is a testament to his relentless ambition and controversial style.

In 1971, at the age of 25, Trump took over his father's real estate company, Elizabeth Trump & Son, and transformed it into a global business empire. His ventures expanded beyond real estate into sectors such as construction, hospitality, and entertainment.

Trump's literary accomplishments include the best-selling business book, "The Art of the Deal," published in 1987, and his reality TV show, "The Apprentice," which aired from 2004 to 2015. The show, known for Trump's signature catchphrase, "You're fired," brought him further into the public eye.

The 2016 Presidential Election marked a significant turning point in Trump's career. Defying the odds, he defeated Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton with a majority of Electoral College votes, securing his place in history.

Trump's presidency brought about significant policy changes, including the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, trade tariffs to protect American industries, and the appointment of conservative judges to the federal bench. One of his most notable actions was moving the U.S. Embassy in Israel to Jerusalem in May 2018.

In late 2018, a partial government shutdown occurred due to disagreements between Trump and Congress over funding for a border wall. The standoff lasted for 35 days, the longest government shutdown in U.S. history.

In December 2019, Trump was impeached by the House of Representatives over allegations of obstruction of Congress and abuse of power. The first impeachment trial ended with his acquittal by the Senate in February 2020.

Trump's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic was widely criticized, with over 400,000 American lives lost by the end of his term in January 2021. His response to the crisis was marked by a lack of a coordinated federal response and conflicting messages about the severity of the virus.

On January 6, 2021, a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol in an attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 Presidential Election. In response, Trump was impeached for a second time, this time on charges of incitement of insurrection.

Trump left office on January 20, 2021, with his presidency marked by both significant achievements and controversial decisions. His legacy will continue to be debated, and his impact on American politics is undeniable.

Insurer of ship that blocked Suez Canal says reduced claim still high

CAIRO, May 10 (Reuters) - UK Club, an insurer of the container ship that blocked the Suez Canal in March, said on Monday a reduced compensation claim made by the Egyptian authorities for almost $600 million to free the vessel and cover related losses was still "exceptionally large".

The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) adjusted its claim from an initial $916 million in an effort to settle out of court, SCA head Osama Rabie told private TV network MBC Masr on Saturday.

The Ever Given, one of the world's largest container ships, was jammed across the canal for six days from March 23, stopping traffic in both directions.

The vessel, still loaded with thousands of containers, is being held in a lake between two stretches of the canal amid the dispute about the level of compensation SCA has claimed from the Japanese owner Shoei Kisen.

Rabie said on Saturday there was no immediate prospect of a settlement. "We haven't seen any response from their side so far, so we are moving forward with the issue, as we were, in the court," he said.

UK Club said the reduced amount proposed had not been reflected in SCA's claim filed at court.

"The Ever Given's owners still have not been provided with evidence that would support a claim of this size, which remains exceptionally large. The Ever Given's interests continue to negotiate in good faith with the SCA," it added.

An Egyptian economic court is due to hold a hearing on May 22 to consider the SCA claim for what it describes as losses due to the blockage and costs for dislodging the ship, SCA sources said.

An Egyptian investigation into the incident found no wrongdoing by the SCA or its pilots, the sources said, without elaborating.

One source said the court could authorise the SCA to auction off the ship if the owner rejected any ruling to compensate the canal authority. Rabie has also mentioned such an outcome.
