Sir John and Lady Wetheral were blessed with four fine little girls, who promised to be all the fond heart of a parent could wish; for, as her ladyship observed with pride, "their forms were perfect, and their features were faultless." There was no exuberance of shape to rectify, there was no limb distorted, and, above all, there were no thick ankles, or dumpy-looking hands to shock a refined taste. The four girls were sprightly, lovely little beings, who would in due time create an immense sensation, and ultimately form connexions with noblemen, or with "county kings," which was even more desirable. Sir Watkin Williams Wynn was considered "Prince of Wales," and there were one or two gentlemen who might claim the title of King of Shropshire, if immense property conferred that title. The Miss Wetherals were born distinguished looking, and their career would be triumphant. Lady Wetheral loved also an even number; four daughters were not too alarming: five or three would have been an indefinite half-vulgar fraction. Her ladyship hated any thing vulgar.

But events are not in our own hands; and the systems we prepare and digest with patient calculation are overturned in one luckless moment by unforeseen circumstances. Lady Wetheral had scarcely decided in her own mind, that five daughters were an indefinite vulgarity, when another helpless innocent appeared to crush her hopes, and disturb her tranquillity. This was, indeed, a blow. All fear of increasing her family had passed from Lady Wetheral's mind so completely, that it was an overpowering disappointment. Five years had stolen away since the birth of Clara, and now to recommence the troubles and miseries of nursing, with an uncertain vista before her! Suppose she had twelve? suppose she had fifteen? suppose she had five-and-twenty? where might all this end? How very provoking and vexatious!

Lady Wetheral felt it was vain to utter lamentations: she must lie up, and take care of herself, and avoid the children's noise, and do exactly as she had done before under the same affliction. It might prove an heir. If so, her ladyship would not complain: a son would secure the entailed property, and keep up the family name and honours. The name of Wetheral would be extinguished, unless a son resumed the honourable title after poor Sir John was gone, and a fine aristocratic-looking boy ranging through the castle would be a proud sight, certainly. He might marry a duke's heiress. Yes, a magnificent boy would be welcomed.

Nothing could exceed Lady Wetheral's chagrin at giving birth in due time to a daughter. Her anger was scarcely repressed by her command of temper, or by the lectures of her unworldly husband. Lady Wetheral loved her husband with the utmost propriety, too, and never acted in decided opposition to his expressed wishes, but she turned in disgust from his arguments, and generally contrived to manœuvre his good nature into an unwilling approval of her plans, by unceasing fluency, and a code of principles, which bewildered and silenced him. Sir John Wetheral only endured the fate of many husbands, who are linked with "remarkably chatty clever women:" he objected, demurred, and gradually yielded to views which he disapproved, but could never successfully combat. His first visit to his lady's chamber, after the unwelcome little stranger's appearance upon the stage of life, was characteristic, and displayed the principles which influenced the heart and conduct of each parent.

"Well, Sir John, shake hands, love; but we need not congratulate each other. I did hope a son might have repaid me for all this annoyance, but here is another wretched girl, and the little animal looks determined to live."

"What I almost wish I had not done now," replied he, mournfully; "but it is done, and--"

"And what, father?"

"I am a murderer, I suppose," replied Rushbrook. "He would have peached, Joey--have had me transported, to work in chains for the rest of my days, merely for taking a few pheasants. Let us go home;" but Rushbrook did not move, although he proposed so doing.

He leant upon his gun, with his eyes fixed in the direction where Byres had fallen.

Joey stood by him--for nearly ten minutes not a word was spoken. At last Rushbrook said--

"Joey, my boy, I've killed many a man in my time, and I have thought nothing of it; I slept as sound as ever the next night. But then, you see, I was a soldier, and it was my trade, and I could look on the man I had killed without feeling sorrow or shame; but I can't look upon this man, Joey. He was my enemy; but--I've murdered him--I feel it now. Go up to him, boy--you are not afraid to meet him--and see if he be dead."

Joey, although generally speaking fear was a stranger to him, did, however, feel afraid; his hands had often been dyed with the blood of a hare or of a bird, but he had not yet seen death in his fellow-creatures. He advanced slowly and tremulously through the dark towards the furze-bush in which the body laid; Mum followed, raising first one paw and pausing, then the other, and as they came to the body, the dog raised his head and gave such a mournful howl, that it induced our hero to start back again. After a time Joey recovered himself; and again advanced to the body. He leant over it, he could distinguish but the form; he listened, and not the slightest breathing was to be heard; he whispered the pedlar's name, but there was no reply; he put his hand upon his breast, and removed it reeking with warm blood.

"Father, he must be dead, quite dead," whispered Joey, who returned trembling. "What shall we do?"

"We must go home," replied Rushbrook; "this is a bad night's work;" and, without exchanging another word until their arrival, Rushbrook and Joey proceeded back to the cottage, followed by Mum.

THE SINS OF THE FATHER ARE VISITED UPON THE CHILD.

Jane had remained in a state of great anxiety during her husband's absence, watching and listening to every sound; every five minutes raising the latch of the door, and looking out, hoping to see him return. As the time went on, her alarm increased; she laid her head down on the table and wept; she could find no consolation, no alleviation of her anxiety; she dropped down on her knees and prayed.

She was still appealing to the Most High, when a blow on the door announced her husband's return. There was a sulken gloom over his countenance as he entered: he threw his gun carelessly on one side, so that it fell, and rattled against the paved floor; and this one act was to her ominous of evil. He sat down without speaking; falling back in the chair, and lifting his eyes up to the rafters above, he appeared to be in deep thought, and unconscious of her presence.

"What has happened?" inquired his wife, trembling as she laid her hand on his shoulder.

"Don't speak to me now," was the reply.

"Joey," said the frightened woman in a whisper, "what has he done?"

Joey answered not, but raised his hand, red with the blood which was now dried upon it.

Jane uttered a faint cry, dropped on her knees, and covered her face, while Joey walked into the back kitchen, and busied himself in removing the traces of the dark deed.

A quarter of an hour had elapsed--Joey had returned, and taken his seat upon his low stool, and not a word had been exchanged.

CNN's 'Cuomo Prime Time' Plummets to Record Lows Amid Host's Scandals

CNN's flagship primetime show, 'Cuomo Prime Time,' has experienced a precipitous decline in viewership, reaching its lowest point since the onset of the coronavirus pandemic. The show's host, Chris Cuomo, has been embroiled in a series of scandals involving his brother, New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, who faces accusations of sexual harassment, verbal threats, and covering up nursing home COVID-19 deaths.

According to Nielsen data, 'Cuomo Prime Time' averaged 1.31 million viewers the week of March 15, down from its 2020 average of 1.8 million. The show also performed poorly in the key demographic of adults aged 25-to-54, averaging only 439,000 viewers compared to its 2020 average of 629,000.

The viewership decline comes as CNN falls behind Fox News in ratings. In February, Fox News averaged 2.3 million primetime viewers, while CNN averaged 1.3 million.

CNN has been criticized for allowing Chris Cuomo to conduct interviews with his brother during the pandemic, which some have seen as a conflict of interest. In March, CNN announced that Chris Cuomo would no longer cover his brother's scandals, citing a long-standing rule with a previous exception.

The scandals surrounding Governor Andrew Cuomo have also cast a shadow over CNN. CNN executive vice president Allison Gollust has prior connections to the governor, having worked as his communications director from 2012 to 2018.

Despite the scandals and bipartisan calls for his resignation, Governor Andrew Cuomo has refused to step down. He has denied the sexual harassment allegations and has said that he will not resign over the nursing home deaths, which he has blamed on federal guidance.

The scandals have taken a toll on Chris Cuomo's reputation and have damaged CNN's credibility. It remains to be seen whether the network can recover from the fallout and regain its position as a leading news source.

Nuclear energy is often promoted as a cleaner alternative to carbon-emitting sources such as coal and oil, making it an appealing option to address the growing global energy demand while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, with its benefits come significant risks, notably the potential for catastrophic disasters like those seen at Three-Mile Island, Fukushima, and Chernobyl. These incidents serve as stark reminders of the dangers associated with nuclear energy production, highlighting the importance of robust safety measures and waste management strategies.

One of the main challenges in the nuclear energy sector is the management of radioactive waste, which poses long-term environmental and health risks if not handled properly. New technologies for recycling nuclear waste have emerged as potential solutions to mitigate pollution and energy problems. Countries like France have successfully implemented waste reprocessing technologies, demonstrating the feasibility of recycling nuclear materials to generate energy efficiently while minimizing environmental impact.

Despite the potential benefits of nuclear waste recycling, political and social controversies continue to hinder its widespread adoption. In the United States, legislation enacted since 1977 has imposed limitations on nuclear energy use until more effective waste management solutions are developed. This cautious approach reflects the recognition of the potential risks associated with nuclear energy production, as well as the need to address public concerns regarding safety and environmental impact.

The growing energy demands and environmental concerns worldwide have propelled the shift towards clean energy sources like nuclear and renewable energy. While nuclear energy extraction carries inherent risks due to the possibility of uncontrolled reactions leading to disasters, reprocessing nuclear waste offers a promising solution to address waste management challenges. However, opposition based on safety and practicality concerns continues to impede the widespread implementation of nuclear waste recycling technologies.

In conclusion, the discussion around nuclear energy and waste management underscores the complex interplay between benefits and risks associated with this energy source. By considering examples from past nuclear disasters, technical advancements in waste reprocessing, legislative frameworks, and international experiences like France's successful waste recycling practices, a more nuanced understanding of the global context surrounding nuclear energy emerges. Despite uncertainties and opposing viewpoints, the pursuit of innovative solutions to handle nuclear waste is essential in ensuring a sustainable and safe energy future for generations to come.

I have no doubt that Miss Forsythe's household, quiet as it was, possessed a gravity and a richness of its own, like the soft and mellowed tones of a well-loved and well-played violin. The trees that stood sentinel in the garden, their branches swaying in the gentle breeze, seemed to vibrate with an almost palpable sense of serenity, as if the very air was laced with the sweetness of unspoken understanding.

As I sat in the parlor, surrounded by the worn and well-thumbed volumes of her bookshelves, I felt myself becoming increasingly drawn into the orbit of this dignified and reserved woman, who seemed to embody the very essence of unassuming kindness. Her niece, on the other hand, was a constant source of vibrant and mercurial energy, flitting about the room with an air of restless curiosity, like a hummingbird sipping nectar from a flower.

Miss Forsythe herself remained seated, her slender fingers moving deftly as she worked the needles of her knitting, the soft clicking of the wood closing and opening a gentle accompaniment to the low murmur of her niece's conversation. I found myself becoming increasingly absorbed in the tranquil scene, my mind working to unravel the subtle threads of character and temperament that seemed to define this enigmatic woman, whose surface, as smooth as the churned soil after a spring rain, seemed to conceal depths and complexities that might take lifetimes to fully comprehend.

As the afternoon wore on, the conversation turned to the subject of the Niger Expedition, and Miss Forsythe's eyes, bright with interest, sparkled with a light that cast a warm and engaging beam across the room. Her niece, on the other hand, seemed to be listening with a mixture of skepticism and impatience, her brow furrowed in a manner that suggested she saw little use in romanticizing the actions of men such as General Gordon, with all their grandiose ideas and ill-fated endeavors.

"It's all so...quixotic," she said, her voice dripping with a faint air of condescension, "this notion of furthering the Empire, of spearheading the charge of civilization into the heart of Africa. What need have we of such grandiose projects, when so much remains to be done at home?" Miss Forsythe's eyes dropped for a moment, and I detected a flicker of a smile, like the soft play of sunlight on a still pond, before she spoke, her voice warm and unruffled.

"Ah, but my dear, you would see things from a different perspective," she said, her words dropping like the measured beat of a drum, "if you were to see the injustice and suffering that exists beyond our shores. We may have our share of problems here at home, but is it not our duty to do what good we can, in the name of Christian charity and compassion?" Her niece raised an eyebrow, her lips curling in a wry and skeptical smile, before replying, in a voice whose tone was equal parts mocking and obsessive.

"Christian charity, indeed. And what of those who see the Empire as a vehicle for selfish ambitions, rather than a divine calling? Does the Bible not teach us to love our neighbors, not simply those of our own nation?" Miss Forsythe regarded her with a calm and unyielding gaze, like a stone standing firm against the river's flow.

"I would not say it is a contradiction, my dear," she said, her voice unwavering, "to serve our own community, while also acknowledging the needs of the wider world. We must be mindful of our own doorstep, to be sure, but that does not mean we should neglect the broader reach of our responsibility." Her niece nodded, her face a mask of understanding, but her eyes betrayed a glint of skepticism, a spark that danced like fireflies on a summer's eve.

As the conversation continued, I found myself drawn into the complex web of Miss Forsythe's thinking, finding myself entangled in the skein of her ideas, like a fly in the silken threads of a spider's web. Her words danced on the air, like the leaves of a tree rustling in the autumn breeze, and I felt myself becoming increasingly lost, yet delightfully so, in the quiet richness of her mind, a treasure trove of insights and experiences that seemed to hold secrets and surprises at every turn.

The comparative analysis of William Shakespeare's Othello, Nella Larsen's Passing, and F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby reveals striking parallels and contrasts in their exploration of themes, character motivations, and narrative structures. Each work delves into the complexities of identity, ambition, and societal expectations, yet they do so through distinct lenses shaped by their historical and cultural contexts.

In Othello, the tragedy unfolds as Iago's manipulation triggers Othello's fatal flaw, or hamartia, which is his intense passion and jealousy. While Iago sets the plot in motion, it is Othello's susceptibility to doubt and insecurity that accelerates his downfall. This aligns with the Aristotelian model of tragedy, where the protagonist's internal flaw leads to anagnorisis, or recognition of his mistake. The handkerchief incident serves as a pivotal moment, symbolizing Othello's loss of control and his descent into madness. His belief in the handkerchief as a tangible proof of Desdemona's infidelity underscores his tragic inability to distinguish appearance from reality.

Similarly, in The Great Gatsby and Passing, themes of appearance versus reality and class differences dominate. In Gatsby, the opulent yet hollow world of the Jazz Age contrasts sharply with the moral decay beneath its surface. Gatsby's obsession with Daisy represents his idealized vision of love, which ultimately leads to his destruction. The climactic scene in Gatsby's mansion, where Tom confronts Gatsby about Daisy, mirrors the tension in Othello's handkerchief incident, as both moments expose the fragility of illusion. In Passing, the theme of appearance versus reality is explored through the characters' racial identities and their attempts to pass as white. Irene and Clare's lives are built on a foundation of deception, which ultimately leads to their tragic ends.

Unique thematic elements further distinguish these works. The Great Gatsby delves into the concept of the "east versus west," symbolizing the clash between old money and new wealth, while also exploring the motif of sight and blindness, as seen in Gatsby's "green light" and the billboard of the oculist. In contrast, Passing focuses on the racial tensions of the 1920s, examining how characters navigate the fluid boundaries of racial identity. While both works critique societal ambition, Gatsby warns against the dangers of materialism and idealism, whereas Passing cautions against the erasure of racial and cultural heritage.

Character parallels and contrasts also enrich this comparative analysis. Gatsby and Clare both die as a result of their respective pursuits, yet their circumstances differ significantly. Gatsby's death stems from his unwavering belief in his romantic ideal, while Clare's death reflects the psychological toll of living a double life. Additionally, Nick Carraway and Irene Redfield share subtle homosexual undertones in their relationships, though Nick's internal conflict is more explicitly explored than Irene's. Gatsby's meticulous planning contrasts with Clare's spontaneity, highlighting their divergent approaches to love and ambition.

In conclusion, while Othello, Passing, and The Great Gatsby differ in their specific themes and characterizations, they all grapple with the destructive power of illusion, ambition, and societal pressures. Through their exploration of appearance versus reality, class distinctions, and racial identity, these works offer timeless critiques of human nature and the complexities of existence. Each protagonist's downfall, whether driven by jealousy, materialism, or the weight of deception, underscores the universal truth that the pursuit of unattainable ideals often leads to tragedy.

The sun hung low in the afternoon sky, casting a warm golden hue over the landscape as Justina and James continued their leisurely stroll along the serene banks of the river. The gentle lapping of the water against the edge of the towpath provided a soothing accompaniment to their conversation, while the faint rustle of leaves overhead hinted at the whispering presence of the late summer breeze.

"I must confess," Justina began, a look of earnestness coloring her features, "that my recent performances reached the ears of a rather critical audience—none other than my father. His sentiments were rather less than encouraging when it came to my last portrayal. 'Acting is an art, Justina,' he insisted, 'not a mere pastime to be indulged in like a fleeting fancy.' It stung my very heart, I assure you."

James turned, his keen gaze resting on her countenance, eager to capture the depth of emotion that flickered like a candle's flame in the twilight. "Your father is, I dare say, a man of firm opinion. Yet, is it not the fate of all artists to endure the barbs of those who do not comprehend the delicate craft?"

Justina's brow furrowed slightly, a perplexity washing over her. "But is it not more disheartening still to realize one possesses the art and yet, in the eyes of one’s kin, appears a mere impostor?"

James could not help but smile. There was a charm in her earnestness, a refreshing innocence that cast a veil of intrigue over her woes. "Ah, but let not his words deter your spirit," he replied, a hint of encouragement pinnacling his tone. "Attend instead to the hearts that respond to the truth you convey—myself included."

In that moment, a soft warmth unfurled within Justina, igniting a spark of newfound confidence. Yet, her reverie was swiftly disrupted as Maurice Clissold drew nearer, raising his voice above the gentle sounds of the river.

"Come, friends! The city beckons, and I possess a route far more enchanting, one that will lead us swiftly through a goodly patch of green yet rich in character." His tall frame drew attention, his stride eager and inviting as he gestured toward a narrow path beside the water.

“I trust you, Maurice,” James offered with a light-hearted chuckle, while Justina remained momentarily preoccupied by the thought of her father’s stern words. They fell into step behind their companion, the symphony of voices and excitement steadily growing closer as they approached the city.

As they ambled along, the towpath soon blossomed with life. A brimming crowd gathered in the distance, laughter spilling like cascades of melody while the heady scent of baked goods and spirited conversation mingled in the soft air. James admired the diversity of characters before them: fine-livered gentlemen in crisp waistcoats exchanged verbal parries, while clusters of ladies, adorned in delicate muslin dresses, fluttered by like vibrant butterflies.

Justina, her thoughts drawn momentarily from her troubles, marveled at a merchant peddling charming trinkets, each one more delightful than the last. Her heart fluttered at the careless abandon with which the city ebbed and flowed, life erupting in vibrant display in every corner.

Yet, as the three came closer, an elderly gipsy woman, her heavily adorned attire caught by the wind, intercepted their path, her discerning gaze locking upon James. Her hands, weathered as the very pathways they walked, rose dramatically in a bid for attention.

"Hoy, young sir! Spare a moment for a glimpse into your destiny, and you shall find—" she paused, eyes glinting with the spark of prophecy. "A love as rare as the twilight star that shines brightest o’er the sea."

James chuckled lightly, his amusement combined with a touch of skepticism. "I’m afraid my future calls for more concrete forecasts than shadows and stars, dear lady."

The gipsy’s eyes narrowed, a playful annoyance flaring within her expression. "The stars, fine youth, do no lie; your heart is as labyrinthine as the rivers we traverse. Be wary, for love will find you when you least expect it."

Justina, caught in the charm of the encounter, leaned closer to James, curiosity twinkling in her gaze. "Perhaps we should listen, if only to entertain the vein of folly within us."

Maurice, ever the pragmatist, bestowed a quirk of his lips. "Shall we leave to the fates, or seek our excitement in better pursuits?"

"Adventure lies in all corners, dear fellows," James replied, a light twinkle dancing in his eye. "Let us proceed with an open heart to whatever fate the tides may deliver."

The gipsy cackled softly, her laughter a melody intermingling with the ambient hum of the gathering. And with that, they set forth, eager to unravel the threads of a day ripe with possibility, unaware of how love’s enigmatic course might weave itself into their very lives.

As no one was injured, and Barney needed a good rest, he finally turned in and fell asleep.

Frank then relieved his sable friend of the wheel.

“We will assume the first watch,” he suggested.

“To be sho’,” assented Pomp. “Am yo’ satisfied wif her, Massa Frank?”

“Yes; the machine is certainly the greatest invention I have ever turned out. And she’s the simplest kind of an air-ship to work. It is only necessary to elevate the angle of the propeller plane, drive her faster, and ascend to any height. To go down, the impinging edge of the forward plane is simply depressed, and she descends. To remain at a fixed altitude we have only to keep the rudder perfectly horizontal.”

“No gas bags to bust wif dis high flyer.”

“And as long as our mechanism operates she’ll go ahead.”

“But s’posin’ de propellers done stop?”

“She would fall gently, as her planes would act on the wind like parachutes,” replied Frank, promptly.

“Dat make her safer yet, don’ it, chile?”

“Of course,” Frank assented, with a nod.

“Yo’ gwine straight to de Gulf of Mexico?”

“I am. In two or three days we’ll reach it, too.”

“Dat am if nuffin’ happen, sah.”

Frank nodded and smiled, and examined the electric motors to see that the current did not vary.

The dynamo was working under full load of five hundred volts, with an output of thirty kilowatts at the terminals, and as the gloom of night had fallen, Frank turned one of the switches.

It sent the electric current into the searchlight, and a brilliant flood of fifty thousand candle power light gushed out.

A funnel-shaped streak of white light was projected a mile ahead by the powerful lens, and the barometer showed the inventor that they had gone up to a height of nine hundred and sixty rods, or three miles.

People on the earth imagined the searchlight was a comet with an extremely long tail, when the clouds did not conceal its flight across the firmament.

Although the wind was dead ahead, and the strata they were in blew at the velocity of fifty miles an hour, the Jove was forging into it at the rate of forty miles an hour.

Frank depressed the rudder, and the machine slowly drifted downward, as she was then in an extremely cold region.

At two o’clock Zamora and Barney relieved the inventor and the coon, who thereupon turned in.

The airship traveled stiffly, steadily and well for two days, traversing the continent in a southerly direction and passing the most diversified scenery.

When night fell upon the scene again the sky had a dark, ominous appearance.

Indeed, Frank realized that as they were in the tropical cyclone region he had cause to fear a heavy storm, and for that reason he refused to retire.

Barney remained up with him that night.

Toward midnight the airship stood at an altitude of 5,280 feet in the air, when a jet-black cloud was encountered.

She was rushing toward it, and the cloud ran at her.

In a moment she was shot into the middle of it.

Her entrance into the cloud seemed to agitate it.

At first the motion was easy, but gradually it intensified, and began to shake and toss the Jove.

Then it began to whirl.

Soon this motion grew furious.

The airship was checked in its flight, and spun around with the gyrating cloud at an appalling speed.

“A cyclone!” gasped Frank, in alarm.

“Look out!” yelled Barney. “We’re upsettin’!”

The Jove was suddenly hurled high up into the air like a mere wisp of straw in the terrible blast.

It was then dashed downward by a reacting gust, and as it fell, it swung over upon its side and suddenly capsized.

A scene of terrible confusion followed.

It would appear that the design choices these artists are making now will illustrate what we can expect for the future, both in what trends will continue for the future and what will be replaced or altered.

Because the sheer number of websites on the Internet today is so large, one could argue that the process of categorizing them into specific groups to analyze design trends might be a daunting if not impossible task. If one breaks their elements down into the basics, however, concrete modern styles emerge.

Perhaps the most important element of any website is its text: without the written word to deliver information to the user, most websites are rendered without function and nothing more than works of art. The text found on most websites today tends to share certain characteristics. According to the article “Future Web Design Trends” by Computer Arts, “we’re noticing a lot of sites designed with bigger typefaces, and many that utilize unusual fonts” (Web). Building on this idea, the idea of matching a typeface’s perceived identity with an idea is also becoming more apparent, as Usability for the Web: Designing Websites That Work states: “if your client is looking for a highly professional but somewhat modern look, you’ll want to use a typeface that supports that feel. Thus, you wouldn’t use an old gothic type, but rather something elegant and formal, such as [a serif font]” (Brinck 310-11). As previously mentioned, because the written information on the Internet is so important, sites today are trying to make it stand out from the competition through use of larger, bolder, unique faces. Unfortunately, even the best designed type cannot mask imperfections with writing: Dr. Jacob Nielson laments in an interview with Digital Web Magazine, “[It is] very rare to see writing that's to the point and focuses on answering customers' questions without smothering the info in marketese” (Web). Jonathan Price, author of Hot Text: Web Writing That Works, claims that appearance is just as important as the tone and message word choice can relay.

For the most part, this trend seems to suggest that it is most important to speak to your audience in a very human, compassionate way, or one risks losing users by being too robotic, too general, too routine. As Price warns, “you must give some real value when you customize and personalize your content, or they will rebel, clicking away from the page, or deleting your e-mail in disgust” (16). Some studies suggest that word choice and descriptive language may be extremely persuasive on a person’s interpretation of an idea: in a study on color theory and high-intensity language versus low-intensity language, participants seemed to respond so acutely to the differences in word choice – adjectives like “drastic, severe, and excruciating” for one group and no strong descriptors in the other – that elements like varying colors played virtually no role (Bankhead).

As I sit here, sipping my coffee and scrolling through my fantasy baseball league, I’m struck by how deeply competitive people can be—even over something as trivial as a made-up team. It’s like a microcosm of our society’s obsession with winning and losing. Just last week, my league-mate texted me in all caps after I drafted a pitcher he wanted, declaring, “YOU’VE RUINED EVERYTHING!” And honestly, I kind of love it. There’s something almost Shakespearean about the drama of it all—triumph, defeat, betrayal, and the occasional trade deadline heartbreak. It’s all so absurd, yet we’re all in on it, hook, line, and sinker.

Speaking of absurdity, I can’t help but think about how companies like Downy have mastered the art of turning everyday products into cultural spectacles. Remember that Mike Birbiglia commercial where he hilariously “discovers” the effectiveness of Downy by pretending to be a clueless guest at a party? It’s genius because it’s so over-the-top, yet it somehow works. I mean, who hasn’t had that moment where they’re like, “Wait, does my laundry smell like pine? Oh, it’s because I used Downy!” It’s the kind of marketing that makes you roll your eyes but also kind of makes you want to buy the product just to feel included in the joke.

Then there’s Rebecca Black’s “Friday,” a song that’s been endlessly mocked for its cringeworthy lyrics and questionable music video. But here’s the thing: isn’t that just a more exaggerated version of what pop music does every day? I mean, have you listened to the latest TikTok hit? It’s like a game of Telephone where the message gets more nonsensical with each iteration. But why do we pick on Rebecca Black so much? Maybe it’s because her song feels too self-aware, too meta for its own good. It’s the kind of thing that could only exist in the postmodern era, where irony and sincerity collide in a way that’s both hilarious and heartbreaking.

And let’s not forget the never-ending cycle of remakes and retellings. From “Clueless” being a modern retelling of “Emma” to the endless stream of superhero movies rebooting the same stories, pop culture is basically Groundhog Day. But here’s the thing: sometimes these retellings are brilliant, like how “Clueless” satirizes Austen’s novel while still paying homage to it. Other times, they’re just lazy cash grabs. Either way, it’s a reflection of our collective inability to let go of the past—or maybe just our love for a good story, no matter how many times we’ve seen it before. And speaking of satire, have you checked out McSweeney’s lately? It’s like a modern-day Punch and Judy show, poking fun at everything from corporate greed to the absurdity of modern parenting. It’s a reminder that even in our most chaotic, over-the-top moments, there’s always room for a good laugh—or at least a knowing smirk.

Pfizer and BioNTech Announce Positive Phase 2/3 Trial Results for COVID-19 Vaccine in Children Aged 5 to 11

NEW YORK AND MAINZ, Germany – Pfizer Inc. and BioNTech SE have just released highly promising results from their Phase 2/3 trial of the COVID-19 vaccine in children aged 5 to 11. The trial demonstrated a favorable safety profile and robust antibody responses with a 10 µg dose regimen, marking a significant step in expanding vaccine protection to this younger age group.

Albert Bourla, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Pfizer, emphasized the urgency of extending vaccine coverage to children amidst the surge in pediatric cases, particularly driven by the highly transmissible Delta variant. Bourla stated, "Protecting children against COVID-19 is crucial in controlling the spread of the virus and safeguarding public health."

Dr. Ugur Sahin, CEO and co-founder of BioNTech, expressed satisfaction with the trial data, noting its alignment with results seen in older populations. Dr. Sahin remarked, "The robust immune responses observed in children aged 5 to 11 are a testament to the effectiveness of our vaccine platform across age groups."

The trial enrolled 2,268 participants in the 5 to 11 age group who received two doses of the 10 µg vaccine. Results illustrated strong immune responses in children, comparable to those seen in the 16 to 25 age group following the 30 µg dose, indicating the vaccine's efficacy in younger individuals.

Pfizer and BioNTech are now poised to submit the trial data for Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) in the United States, as well as update the existing EU Conditional Marketing Authorization. This milestone highlights the companies' steadfast commitment to advancing vaccine access for all age groups and bolstering global vaccination efforts.

The trial conducted is part of a larger study encompassing children aged 6 months to 11 years, aimed at evaluating the vaccine's safety and efficacy across various pediatric cohorts. This comprehensive approach underscores Pfizer and BioNTech's dedication to ensuring the vaccine's suitability for younger populations.

COMIRNATY (COVID-19 Vaccine, mRNA) by Pfizer and BioNTech is currently FDA-approved for individuals 16 and older, with EUA covering administration for individuals 12 and older, including a third dose for certain immunocompromised individuals. As further phase 3 trial data is shared, the companies aspire to obtain regulatory approvals for younger pediatric populations, reinforcing their mission to safeguard public health.

For more information and updates regarding the COVID-19 vaccine's efficacy and availability for children, Pfizer and BioNTech encourage the public to stay informed and continue following health authorities' guidance.

When, however, half a century had fairly glided down the stream of time, Miss Ferret transferred with honest zeal all those exertions to the circle which surrounded her, which had hitherto proved inefficacious while applied to her own use; and as the materials upon which she worked were often widely different from those on which her skill had been originally employed, the success was proportionate; and Jemima Ferret rose to the highest pinnacle of consideration, as the most adroit and judicious negociator who ever made a match, and brought together two individuals in the holy bands of wedlock. Such was the profound sagacity, such the acknowledged ability and discretion of this hymeneal plenipotentiary, that she was always given carte blanche to proceed according to her own views, and there was a general understanding that whatever she "brought about," was effected in the very best manner.

In fact, such was the confidence which she inspired, that her neighbours frequently avoided betraying their wishes in any direct commission, relying upon her tact and penetration for discovering the secret purpose of their hearts, and forwarding their wishes if no pre-arrangement of her own militated against them; in which case it was well known that her manoeuvring so far surpassed any tactics which could be brought in opposition, as to secure the crown of victory, and render vain every effort at competition.

Not to lead our readers into any false conclusions, which a little trouble in the way of explanation might prevent, it may be well to state the motives which induced an activity of zeal so very striking and conspicuous. Be it known, then, that Miss Ferret's income was a very small one, and though since she had given up all hope of bettering her fortune by a lucrative barter of such qualifications as she had to exchange for their money price, she had improved her means, by sinking her little capital for an annuity, it was not so liberal a stipend as to render her by any means indifferent to increase of comfort; and she prudently considered that the next best thing to forming a good establishment for herself, which we have hinted had hitherto proved impracticable, would be to secure as many settlements as she could for her friends, amongst whom she might pass from house to house much to the solace of her spirits and the relief of her purse.

In this office of match-making, then, which she raised to the dignity of a regular trade, or profession, she put forth all the strength of her talents, and prospered exceedingly. She had all sorts, sizes, and descriptions under her patronage; and her powers were so generally known, that though people did not like to own their obligation to a third person in matters of so delicate a nature, they were nevertheless secretly felt to be of such importance, that to conciliate Miss Ferret's regards became a point of rivalry in and about the town in which she resided.

Mr. Hartland, without being aware of the honour, was placed at the head of her list for matrimonial preferment as soon as he had come into possession of Henbury; but for once, Jemima was puzzled about a help-mate for him, some objection having occurred to three several young ladies, whom she kept constantly in mind, and who were still on the unattached service. When things are least expected, however, they often come to pass, and it so chanced, that while Hymen's chargé d'affaires was at fault for her game, Miss Robinson came to pay a visit at Colbrook, the seat of Sir Roger Goodman, an opulent and corpulent Baronet, who lived within the district which Miss Ferret resolved should limit the circuit of her exertions; because to have engaged in distant experiment would have increased difficulties, and diminished the probability of successful result.

The implementation of a genetic algorithm (GA) in a virtual organism simulation involved the design of the Anim class. This class served as a blueprint for the virtual organisms, governing their behaviors and interactions within the simulated environment. Each Anim object, representing an individual organism, possessed a set of characteristics and abilities defined by the class structure.

Public functions within the Anim class, namely Move(), Hunt(), Eat(), and Think(), represented the organism's observable actions in the virtual environment. These functions translated the organism's internal state and decisions into movements and interactions displayed on the screen. The character representing the organism in the virtual world was defined by the static constant character ANIM_CHAR. Internally, the organisms utilized private functions such as Move_GA(), Hunt_GA(), Think_GA(), move_results(), hunt_results(), and decision() to process genetic instructions and environmental feedback. These private functions remained hidden from the external environment, emphasizing the encapsulation of the GA's inner workings. The organisms' current state was tracked using integer variables, 'energy' and 'fitness,' initialized to 400 and 0, respectively, upon the creation of each new Anim object via the class constructor.

The genetic algorithm, embedded within the Anim class, employed binary strings to represent instructions for the organism's actions. These strings encoded behavioral patterns that influenced the organisms' movements, hunting strategies, and overall decision-making processes. The algorithm utilized a crossover rate of 0.07 and a mutation rate of 0.025 to introduce genetic diversity within the simulated population. This genetic variation, a cornerstone of evolutionary processes, ensured a range of behaviors within the virtual environment. The fitness function, a critical component of the GA, evaluated the effectiveness of each organism's genetic code in navigating the simulated world. By favoring organisms with higher fitness scores, the algorithm facilitated the survival and reproduction of the fittest individuals, driving the evolutionary process. The implementation allowed for customized fitness functions and variables tailored to specific activities within the virtual environment.

Inline functions streamlined the execution of dynamic calls, enhancing the simulation's efficiency. The Move() function translated the binary instructions encoded in the organism's genetic code into directional movements within the virtual world. These movements consumed energy, reflecting the biological cost of movement in real organisms. The Hunt() function utilized sensor-like mechanisms to detect prey within the environment, guiding the organism to approach and attack, a process that also consumed energy. Successful hunts triggered the Eat() function, which calculated the energy obtained from consuming prey and replenished the organism's energy reserves. Debugging and optimization efforts focused on ensuring the effectiveness of random number generation, fine-tuning mutation and crossover rates, and refining the code for maximum efficiency.

The rector and the warden continued their conversation as they strolled through the quaint village streets on a sunny afternoon. The topic of discussion had shifted from Sara Carroll to the state of affairs in their small community. It seemed that change was in the air, and the rector couldn't help but feel a sense of unease at the shift in atmosphere.

"I do not think there is now as much of--of the unity we once had," the rector remarked pensively, glancing around at the bustling streets. "It seems that the bonds that once held us together are fraying, and I fear what that may mean for the future of our parish."

The warden nodded in agreement, his brow furrowed in contemplation. "Indeed, the times are changing, and with them, so too must we adapt. But it is not just the unity that concerns me; it is also the sense of purpose that seems to have waned in recent years."

As they continued their leisurely stroll, the warden raised a point that had been weighing on his mind. "I must say, I have observed that young Sara Carroll's absence from our church activities has not gone unnoticed by the other parishioners. Her reserved nature may be mistaken for aloofness, and I fear that she may be inadvertently causing rifts within our community."

The rector sighed, knowing all too well the challenges of balancing personal obligations with one's responsibilities to the church. "Indeed, it is a delicate balance to strike, especially for a young woman like Sara who has shouldered so much burden at such a tender age. But we must remember that each member of our parish brings their own unique gifts and struggles, and it is our duty to support them in whatever way we can."

The warden nodded thoughtfully, his gaze fixed on the distant horizon. "You speak true, my friend. It is easy to forget that we are all imperfect beings, each grappling with our own demons. As they reached the end of their walk, the rector and the warden exchanged a knowing look. They both understood that the future of their parish depended on their ability to bridge the gaps that had formed between them. And as they prepared to face the challenges ahead, they knew that with patience, understanding, and a generous spirit, they could build a stronger, more united community for all.

The little kitchen was an exceedingly alluring place, gay in the bravery of fresh paint and spotless, shining utensils. There were even crisp curtains--at eight cents a yard--tied back at the high, wide-silled, triple window with its diminutive panes. It needed only a pot or two of growing plants in the window, and a neat-handed Phyllis in a figured gown, to be the old-time kitchen of one's dreams.

But it was upon the rooms on the upper floor that Juliet had exhausted her imagination and effort. Nothing could have been conceived of more dainty than they. Here her denims and muslins had run riot. Low dressing-tables clad in ruffled hangings, their padded tops delicate with the breath of orris; beds valanced with similar stuffs; high-backed chairs, their seats cushioned into comfort--everything was done in the cleverest imitation of the ancient styles in keeping with the old-fashioned house. It all made one think of the patter of high-heeled, buckled slippers, and stiff, rustling, brocaded gowns, and powdered hair, and the odours of long ago. Anthony would never know what his friendly home-maker had put into these rooms of sentiment and charm.

At the door of the blue-and-white room, the one upon which the girl had lavished her most tender fancies, she stood at length, looking in. And as she looked something swam before her eyes. A sob rose in her throat. She choked it back; she brushed her hand across her face. Then she tried to laugh. "Oh, what a goose I am!" she said sternly to herself. And then she ran across the room, sank upon her knees before the window-seat with its blue and white cushions, and burying her face in one of them cried her wretched, jealous, longing heart out.

Anthony, coming in hastily but softly through the small kitchen, heard the rush of footsteps overhead, and stopped. He waited a moment, listening eagerly; then he came noiselessly into the living-room and stood still. His face, always strong and somewhat stern in its repose, had in it to-night a certain unusual intensity. He looked at his watch and saw that there was an hour before train time. Then he sat down where he could see the top of the staircase and waited.

By and by light footsteps crossed the floor above and came through the little hall. From where he sat Anthony caught the gleam of Juliet's crisp linen skirt. Presently she came slowly down. As she turned upon the landing she met Anthony's eyes looking up. In a fashion quite unusual to the straightforward gaze of his friend her eyes fell. He saw that her cheeks were pale. He rose to meet her.

"Come and rest," he said. "You are tired. You have worked too hard. Such a helper a man never had before. And you have made a wonderful success. Juliet, I can't thank you. It's beyond that."

But she would not be led to the cosy corner by the window. She found something needing her attention in the curtain of the bookcase in the dimmest corner of the room, and began solicitously to pull it in various ways, as if there were something wrong with it. He watched her, standing with his arm on the high chimney-piece.

"I think you enjoyed it just a little bit yourself, though," he observed. "Didn't you, chum?"

"Yes, indeed," said Juliet.

Her back was toward him, her head bent down, but his quick ear detected a peculiar quality in her voice. He questioned her again hurriedly.

"You're not sorry you did it?"

"Oh, no," said Juliet.

Calculus and mathematics, often perceived as daunting subjects, are in reality indispensable tools for problem-solving and critical thinking, essential components of a well-rounded education. The foundational understanding of functions developed in algebra serves as the bedrock for comprehending the intricate systems encountered in calculus. A student grappling with algebraic equations that model projectile motion is, in essence, preparing for the more complex differential equations that describe fluid dynamics in calculus. This progression isn't merely about learning formulas; it's about cultivating a structured approach to dissecting and resolving intricate problems. The challenges inherent in mathematical problem-solving are strikingly analogous to those faced by modern programmers. Just as a calculus student must deconstruct a complex integral into manageable components, a programmer must break down a sophisticated software application into smaller, testable modules. The logical rigor demanded by both disciplines fosters a systematic and analytical mindset, equipping individuals with the ability to approach novel problems with confidence and precision. By learning to think algorithmically through mathematical problem-solving, students build a foundation for success in fields far beyond the traditional STEM disciplines.

Despite its profound importance, the current US education system often falls short in effectively integrating relevant mathematical concepts into its curriculum. The abstract nature of the subject can be perceived as disconnected from real-world applications, leading to disengagement and a lack of appreciation for its inherent beauty and power. This sentiment is powerfully countered by figures like UC Berkeley Professor Edward Frenkel, who, in his book "Love and Math," passionately advocates for the subject’s intrinsic aesthetic appeal and its profound impact on logical thought. Frenkel’s work illustrates that a strong mathematical foundation transcends mere computational ability; it cultivates a more nuanced and logical way of thinking, enhancing one’s capacity for critical analysis and innovative problem-solving in all areas of life.

The versatility of calculus is undeniable, making it beneficial for students across diverse fields. At UC Berkeley, professors leverage calculus in groundbreaking research that spans an array of disciplines. For instance, Brian Barsky, a professor of Computer Science, employs calculus in his research on visual aberration correction, developing algorithms that improve the clarity and quality of images and displays. Similarly, Professor David Culler of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, utilizes calculus to develop optimized algorithms for wireless networks, enhancing communication efficiency and reliability. These examples underscore the pervasive influence of calculus in shaping technological advancements. The ability to master such a complex subject not only fosters logical thinking but also instills a sense of accomplishment and self-pride. Learning calculus, therefore, is not merely an academic exercise; it is an investment in a student's cognitive abilities and confidence, making it a crucial element of a comprehensive education.

Betty laughed at them sometimes, but she touched the little books with reverent fingers, when she remembered how old they were, and how long ago their first childish readers laid them aside. The hands that had held them first had years before grown tired and wrinkled and old, and had been lying for a generation under the myrtle and lilies of the churchyard outside.

Many an afternoon she had spent, perched in the high window, with her feet drawn up under her on the sill, reading aloud to Davy, who lay outside on the grass, staring up at the sky. Davy's short fat legs could not climb from the board to the window-sill, and since this little Mahomet could not come to the mountain, Betty had to carry the mountain to him.

The reading was slow work sometimes. Davy's mind, like his legs, could not climb as far as Betty's, and she usually had to stop at the bottom of every page to explain something. Often he fell asleep in the middle of the most interesting part, and then Betty read on to herself, with nothing to break the stillness around her but the buzzing of the wasps, as they darted angrily in and out of the open window above her head.

To-day Betty had read nearly an hour, and Davy's eyelids were beginning to flutter drowsily, when they heard the slow thud of a horse's hoofs in the thick dust of the road. Betty stopped reading to listen, and Davy sat up to look.

"It's Jake," he announced, recognising the boy who had helped his father with the ploughing.

"Hope he won't see us," said Betty, in a low tone, drawing in her head. "We are not hurting anything, but maybe some of the church people wouldn't like it, if they knew I climbed in at the window. They might think it wasn't respectful."

"He's looking this way," said Davy, who had stood up for a better view, but squatted down again at Betty's command.

It was too late. Jake had recognised Davy's shock of yellow hair, and called out, good-naturedly, "Hello, stickin'-plaster, where's Betty? Somewhere around here, I'll bet anything, or you wouldn't be here. I've got a letter for her."

At that, Betty leaned so far out of the window that she nearly lost her balance and toppled over. "Oh, run and get it, quick, Davy," she cried. The little bare feet twinkled through the grass to meet the old sorrel horse, and two brown hands were held up to receive the letter; but Jake preferred to deliver the important document himself.

"Here you are," he said, riding alongside the window and dropping the letter into her eager hands.

"Oh, thank you, Jake," she cried. "It makes me feel as if Christmas was coming. I never got a letter in my life except in my Christmas boxes. My godmother always writes to me then, and this must be from her, too. Yes, it is, I know her handwriting."

If Jake expected her to tear it open instantly and share the news with him before she had examined every inch of the big square envelope, he was disappointed. The old blaze-faced sorrel had carried him out of sight before she had finished cutting it open with a pin. Then she spread the letter out on her knees, drawing a long breath of pleasure as the faintest odour of violets floated up from the paper with its dainty monogram at the top.

Davy waited in silence, watching a flush spread over Betty's face as she read. Her breath came short and her heart beat fast.

"Oh, Davy," she exclaimed, in a low, wondering tone. "What do you think? It is an invitation to a house party at Locust; Lloyd Sherman's house party. Oh, it's like a lovely, lovely fairy tale with me for the princess. I've never travelled on the cars since I was old enough to remember it, and they've sent passes for me to go. I've never had any girls to play with in all my life, and now there will be two besides Lloyd; and, oh, Davy, best of all, I'll see my beautiful, beautiful godmother! I shall be there a whole month, and she knew my mamma and was her dearest friend. I haven't seen her since I was a baby, when she came to my christening, and of course I can't remember anything about that."

In the heart-wrenching landscape of war-torn Afghanistan, loyalty and discrimination intersect in the lives of individuals, leaving a profound impact on personal relationships. As Mariam endures the cruel punishment of eating rocks by her father, leading to broken teeth, the brutality and malevolence of his actions are laid bare. Through this harrowing act, the essence of cruelty in personal relationships is starkly illuminated, leaving a lasting mark on Mariam's psyche and physical well-being.

Meanwhile, in the midst of war, Laila's home and family are destroyed, underscoring the senseless and evil nature of the conflict that ravages their land. The devastation wrought upon her life serves as a poignant reminder of the indiscriminate harm caused by war, tearing apart families and communities with callous abandon.

In the face of despair and upheaval, Mariam displays unwavering loyalty and strength by waiting outside Jalil's house all night, a testament to her resilience and devotion. Her steadfastness stands as a beacon of hope amidst the chaos, symbolizing the power of loyalty to sustain individuals in times of adversity.

Mullah Faizullah emerges as a loyal and constant presence in Mariam's life, offering unwavering support and devotion that serves as a source of solace and comfort. His steadfastness underscores the profound impact of loyalty in sustaining individuals through hardship and turmoil.

Despite the raging war and intense fighting, Mariam's mother demonstrates loyalty by choosing to remain in Afghanistan, a decision that speaks volumes about her commitment to her homeland and family. Her unwavering dedication in the face of danger highlights the depth of loyalty that can thrive even in the midst of conflict and strife.

Similarly, Laila exhibits loyalty by staying with her father, a selfless act that underscores her profound sense of duty and sacrifice, despite her own desires and wishes. Her steadfastness in the face of adversity reflects the enduring power of loyalty to bind individuals to their loved ones, even in the darkest of times.

However, amidst displays of loyalty, discrimination rears its ugly head, as Mariam faces societal scorn and contempt as a 'harami,' condemned for her father's actions. The stigma and discrimination she endures serve as a stark reminder of the cruelty and injustice that pervade societal attitudes towards marginalized individuals.

Furthermore, Jalil's actions highlight the discrimination faced by women, exposing the lack of agency and autonomy young women have in marriage decisions, underscoring the oppressive gender dynamics that compound the challenges they face. The lack of control and vulnerability experienced by Mariam in response to an unwanted advance underscores the threatening nature of her circumstances, prompting reflection on the moral and ethical implications of such power imbalances.

In conclusion, the intertwining themes of loyalty, cruelty, discrimination, and the impact of war on personal relationships underscore the profound challenges faced by individuals in times of conflict. Through the lens of diverse characters, the grave consequences of war on families and communities are laid bare, inviting readers to contemplate the enduring power of loyalty in the face of adversity, as well as the insidious nature of discrimination that plagues societal norms.

I find on referring to my note-book that for weeks we travelled over the prairies without any incident of unusual interest. To me the scenery was interest enough; and I do not remember a more striking picture than to see the long caravan of waggons, "the prairie ships," deployed over the plain, or crawling slowly up some gentle slope, their white tilts contrasting beautifully with the deep green of the earth. At night, too, the camp, with its corralled waggons, and horses picketed around, was equally a picture. The scenery was altogether new to me, and imbued me with impressions of a peculiar character. The streams were fringed with tall groves of cottonwood trees, whose column-like stems supported a thick frondage of silvery leaves. These groves meeting at different points, walled in the view, so dividing the prairies from one another, that we seemed to travel through vast fields fenced by colossal hedges.

We crossed many rivers, fording some, and floating our waggons over others that were deeper and wider. Occasionally we saw deer and antelope, and our hunters shot a few of these; but we had not yet reached the range of the buffalo. Once we stopped a day to recruit in a wooded bottom, where the grass was plentiful and the water pure. Now and then, too, we were halted to mend a broken tongue or an axle, or help a "stalled" waggon from its miry bed.

I had very little trouble with my particular division of the caravan. My Missourians turned out to be a pair of staunch hands, who could assist one another without making a desperate affair of every slight accident.

The grass had sprung up, and our mules and oxen, instead of thinning down, every day grew fatter upon it. Moro, therefore, came in for a better share of the maize that I had brought in my waggons, and which kept my favourite in fine travelling condition.

As we approached the Arkansas, we saw mounted Indians disappearing over the swells. They were Pawnees; and for several days clouds of these dusky warriors hung upon the skirts of the caravan. But they knew our strength, and kept at a wary distance from our long rifles.

To me every day brought something new, either in the incidents of the "voyage" or the features of the landscape.

Gode, who has been by turns a voyageur, a hunter, a trapper, and a coureur du bois, in our private dialogues had given me an insight into many an item of prairie-craft, thus enabling me to cut quite a respectable figure among my new comrades. Saint Vrain, too, whose frank, generous manner had already won my confidence, spared no pains to make the trip agreeable to me. What with gallops by day and the wilder tales by the night watch-fires, I became intoxicated with the romance of my new life. I had caught the "prairie-fever!"

So my companions told me, laughing. I did not understand them then. I knew what they meant afterwards. The prairie fever! Yes. I was just then in process of being inoculated by that strange disease. It grew upon me apace. The dreams of home began to die within me; and with these the illusory ideas of many a young and foolish ambition.

My strength increased, both physically and intellectually. I experienced a buoyancy of spirits and a vigour of body I had never known before. I felt a pleasure in action. My blood seemed to rush warmer and swifter through my veins, and I fancied that my eyes reached to a more distant vision. I could look boldly upon the sun without quivering in my glance.

Had I imbibed a portion of the divine essence that lives, and moves, and has its being in those vast solitudes? Who can answer this?

Growing up in the heart of the Midwest, I've always found it surprisingly easier to connect with individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds than to navigate the nuances of my own cultural heritage. This disconnect, as odd as it may sound, has been a defining aspect of my life. When it comes to engaging with folks from different corners of the world, I seem to effortlessly blend in, picking up on cultural cues and adopting a chameleon-like adaptability. However, when I find myself amidst traditional mid-western individuals, I often feel a strange unease, as if I'm slightly off-kilter, unable to fully align with the unsaid expectations of my surroundings.

As a 'bicultural chameleon,' my identity has always been in flux, constantly rearranging itself as it adapts to different environments. My personal cultural identity isn't static; rather, it's a dynamic canvas upon which various cultural influences paint their hues. The metaphor of the chameleon is particularly fitting here, as it beautifully encapsulates my ability to blend into various cultural landscapes while retaining the core essence of who I am. It's fascinating how personal transformation mirrors this idea of cultural rearrangement, much like a quote from a cultural studies textbook suggests: "Our identities are like a kaleidoscope, always shifting, yet always holding a unique pattern."

At the core of my ever-shifting cultural identity lies my faith, a steadfast beacon amidst the fluidity of external influences. It's the one aspect of my identity that I allow to stand out proudly, a constant reminder of who I fundamentally am. Embracing the chameleon metaphor, I've come to appreciate how my adaptability is not merely a surface-level change but a profound acceptance of the ongoing creative process that is cultural interaction. Each encounter, each conversation, becomes a brush stroke in the ever-evolving portrait of my identity. In this dance of cultural exchange, I've realized that culture isn't a fixed entity but rather something malleable and ever-changing, shaped by our travels, experiences, and the myriad cultures we encounter.

She was haunted by an uneasy sense of doubtfulness as to her social position. Mr. Lord followed the calling of a dealer in pianos; a respectable business, to be sure, but, it appeared, not lucrative enough to put her above caring how his money was made. She knew that one’s father may be anything whatever, yet suffer no social disability, provided he reap profit enough from the pursuit. But Stephen Lord, whilst resorting daily to his warehouse in Camberwell Road--not a locality that one would care to talk about in ‘cultured’ circles--continued, after twenty years, to occupy this small and ugly dwelling in Grove Lane. Possibly, owing to an imperfect education, he failed to appreciate his daughter’s needs, and saw no reason why she should not be happy in the old surroundings.

On the other hand, perhaps he cared very little about her. Undoubtedly his favourite was Horace, and in Horace he had suffered a disappointment. The boy, in spite of good schooling, had proved unequal to his father’s hope that he would choose some professional career, by preference the law; he idled away his schooldays, failed at examinations, and ultimately had to be sent into ‘business.’ Mr Lord obtained a place for him in a large shipping agency; but it still seemed doubtful whether he would make any progress there, notwithstanding the advantage of his start; at two-and-twenty he was remunerated with a mere thirty shillings a week, a nominal salary,’ his employers called it. Nancy often felt angry with her brother for his lack of energy and ambition; he might so easily, she thought, have helped to establish, by his professional dignity, her own social status at the level she desired.

There came into view a familiar figure, crossing from the other side of the way. Nancy started, waved her hand, and went to open the door. Her look had wholly altered; she was bright, mirthful, overflowing with affectionate welcome.

This friend of hers, Jessica Morgan by name, had few personal attractions. She looked overwrought and low-spirited; a very plain and slightly-made summer gown exhibited her meagre frame with undue frankness; her face might have been pretty if health had filled and coloured the flesh, but as it was she looked a ghost of girlhood, a dolorous image of frustrate sex. In her cotton-gloved hand she carried several volumes and notebooks.

‘I’m so glad you’re in,’ was her first utterance, between pants after hasty walking and the jerks of a nervous little laugh. ‘I want to ask you something about Geometrical Progression. You remember that formula--’

‘How can I remember what I never knew?’ exclaimed Nancy. ‘I always hated those formulas; I couldn’t learn them to save my life.’

‘Oh, that’s nonsense! You were much better at mathematics than I was. Do just look at what I mean.’

She threw her books down upon a chair, and opened some pages of scrawled manuscript, talking hurriedly in a thin falsetto.

Her family, a large one, had fallen of late years from a position of moderate comfort into sheer struggle for subsistence. Jessica, armed with certificates of examinational prowess, got work as a visiting governess. At the same time, she nourished ambitions, discernible perhaps in the singular light of her deep-set eyes and a something of hysteric determination about her lips. Her aim, at present, was to become a graduate of London University; she was toiling in her leisure hours--the hours of exhaustion, that is to say--to prepare herself for matriculation, which she hoped to achieve in the coming winter. Of her intimate acquaintances only one could lay claim to intellectual superiority, and even she, Nancy Lord to wit, shrank from the ordeals of Burlington House. To become B.A., to have her name in the newspapers, to be regarded as one of the clever, the uncommon women--for this Jessica was willing to labour early and late, regardless of failing health, regardless even of ruined complexion and hair that grew thin beneath the comb.

Norsk Hydro's Defiant Stand Against Ransomware: A Case Study in Cyber Resilience

Oslo, Norway – In a bold display of resilience against cyber threats, Norsk Hydro, a prominent Norwegian renewable energy and aluminum manufacturing company, refused to bow to the demands of hackers who launched a crippling ransomware attack on the company in 2019. The incident, which occurred on the same day Hilde Merete Aasheim assumed the role of CEO, serves as a compelling case study in the importance of robust cybersecurity measures and unwavering leadership in the face of adversity.

A Crippling Blow to Norsk Hydro's Digital Infrastructure

The ransomware attack, launched on March 19, 2019, unleashed a wave of disruption across Norsk Hydro's digital infrastructure. Over 3,000 servers and thousands of PCs were locked out, with key areas of the IT network encrypted, effectively paralyzing the company's operations.

"It was a very sophisticated attack," Hilde Merete Aasheim, CEO of Norsk Hydro, recalled in an interview with TIME. "We were completely taken by surprise."

The attack's impact was immediate and severe. Production facilities ground to a halt, communication systems were disrupted, and employees were left scrambling to maintain operations amidst the chaos.

Refusing to Pay the Ransom: A Principled Stand

Despite the severity of the attack and the pressure to restore operations swiftly, Norsk Hydro made a resolute decision: they would not pay the ransom demanded by the hackers.

"We had a very clear policy against paying ransoms," Jo De Vliegher, CIO of Norsk Hydro, explained. "We didn't want to encourage this type of criminal behavior."

This principled stance, while admirable, came with significant challenges. Without a quick fix, Norsk Hydro faced the daunting task of manually restoring its operations, a process that would require weeks of painstaking effort.

A Herculean Effort: Manual Operations and Cybersecurity Collaboration

Undeterred by the magnitude of the task, Norsk Hydro embarked on a herculean effort to manually handle operations. Production lines were kept running through pen-and-paper processes, while IT teams worked tirelessly to decrypt the affected systems.

"It was like going back in time," Aasheim remarked. "But we were determined to keep our operations going, no matter what."

To bolster their efforts, Norsk Hydro enlisted the expertise of cybersecurity experts and forged collaborations with Microsoft and the Norwegian National Cyber Security Centre. This collective effort proved instrumental in accelerating the recovery process.

Counting the Costs: Financial Losses and Lessons Learned

The ransomware attack exacted a heavy toll on Norsk Hydro's operations. The company incurred significant financial losses, estimated to be around $70 million. Production disruptions, reputational damage, and the costs associated with recovery efforts all contributed to this substantial setback.

However, the incident also served as a catalyst for change. Norsk Hydro underwent a comprehensive reevaluation of its cybersecurity measures, prioritizing investments in preventive technologies and employee training.

"We learned a lot from this attack," Aasheim reflected. "We've made significant improvements to our cybersecurity posture, and we're now better prepared to face future threats."

A Cautionary Tale: The Perils of Ransom Payments

Norsk Hydro's experience aligns with the advice of cybersecurity experts who strongly discourage organizations from paying ransoms to hackers.

"Paying ransoms only fuels the criminal economy and encourages further attacks," warned Eric Goldstein, an official at the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). "Organizations should focus on prevention and response strategies to mitigate the impact of ransomware attacks."

A Legacy of Resilience: Norsk Hydro's Triumph Over Adversity

Norsk Hydro's unwavering stance against paying ransoms and its successful recovery from the ransomware attack stand as a testament to the company's resilience and commitment to cybersecurity. Under the leadership of Hilde Merete Aasheim and Jo De Vliegher, Norsk Hydro emerged from this crisis stronger and more determined to safeguard its operations against future cyber threats.

Their story serves as an inspiration to organizations worldwide, demonstrating the importance of robust cybersecurity measures, unwavering leadership, and a collective commitment to combating cybercrime.

To avoid such discrimination claims, mentoring should be a standard practice for all applicants, ensuring equal opportunities for career development.

Considering Carl's biases, he could recuse himself and let another manager interview Joyce.
