My home isn't just a house; it's a precarious perch on the steepest slope in a neighborhood that seems perpetually on the verge of sliding into the sea. Sidewalks? A luxury unheard of here. We're all forced to be intimately acquainted with the asphalt, dodging the occasional car as we walk to catch a glimpse of the water. Not that seeing the water is always easy, thanks to the arboreal behemoths we call evergreen trees.

They stand like stoic sentinels, these pines and firs, but to many residents, they're more like overgrown nuisances, stubbornly guarding the coveted ocean views. I understand the frustration. Everyone on this hill has stretched their wallet to include these massive glass walls facing the ocean. But I find a strange comfort in their shadows, a buffer against the often-unyielding wind. I find it difficult to dislike the trees because they’re part of the charm of this place.

Weather here is a personality, a moody, tempestuous one. We're more acquainted with rain and stormy weather than sunshine. The power lines, strung precariously along the winding roads, are constant victims, succumbing to the wind's will more often than we'd like. Candlelight dinners become less romantic and more a recurring necessity. The upside is the dramatic display of nature's fury, the waves crashing against the shore, the wind howling through the trees.

The climate's dampness paints the world in shades of green, a deep, verdant green that clings to everything. Moss is the neighborhood artist, adorning rooftops, fences, and even the rough bark of those dreaded evergreens. It’s a lush, damp embrace that you either surrender to or constantly battle. I've mostly surrendered.

Children's laughter is a rare sound in this neighborhood. It's a community of seasoned souls, folks who've gathered stories and wrinkles along the way. Dogs, however, are plentiful. Every other resident seems to have a canine companion, padding along the roadside, noses twitching with the scent of the sea. They provide a symphony of barks and tail wags, replacing the shrieks and cries of children.

And then there's the wildlife. Rabbits, bless their cotton tails, are a constant battle for any gardener brave enough to plant something other than moss. They’re cute, admittedly, until they're decimating your prize-winning petunias. Birds flit about – sparrows chirping in the bushes, hummingbirds buzzing around the few flowering plants that survive the rabbit onslaught, hawks circling overhead, and the ever-present crows, their caws echoing through the misty air.

While we may lack a local grocery store or even a simple corner shop, we are not entirely deprived of civilization. A string of waterfront restaurants beckons from the lower stretches of the coast, offering fresh seafood and breathtaking views, a siren song that pulls us down the hill, despite the uphill trek that awaits us later. They are the culinary heartbeat of our little enclave, a reward for braving the hills, the weather, and the occasional power outage.

Despite the challenges, I find a strange, comforting beauty in this hillside haven. It's a place where the elements are raw, the views are stunning, and the community, though quiet, is resilient. It's a place where the moss grows thick, the evergreens stand tall, and the ocean whispers its endless stories. It's home.

The meeting was opened with prayer. Deacon Bates remarked prefatorily that such would be the proper thing in a class composed of adults, and then he looked around hesitatingly for the proper man to make the first formal committal of the class into the hands of the Lord; but Squire Woodhouse saved him the trouble by springing to his feet and volunteering to Heaven an address so concise that there remained nothing unsaid. Then Bibles were distributed, and opened at the fifth chapter of Matthew's Gospel, and every one looked unspeakably profound, though Mr. Hopper had the presence of mind to place his hand beneath his coat-tails and take hold of the review containing the paper on "The True Location of the Holy Sepulchre," so as to be ready in case occasion offered.

"Let us begin with the beatitudes," said the leader. "'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' By the way, I would suggest that each member speaks in the order of his sitting. Mr. Lottson," continued Deacon Bates, addressing the insurance president, "whom do you suppose Jesus referred to as 'the poor in spirit'?"

"Before answering that question," said Mr. Lottson, "I think attention should be called to a passage in the opening of the chapter. It is said that 'When he was set, his disciples came unto him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying,' etc. Now, before we try to understand this beautiful succession of blessings, we should realize whom they were spoken to--to the disciples, who had left all and followed him, and therefore to a set of men to whom he could say things which it would be nonsensical for him to say to the common people and business men around him. The disciples were out of business, and lived on their friends--it was right enough for them to do so under the circumstances, but for this very reason Jesus told them the things which nobody else could understand. This sermon was preached to self-forgetting preachers, not to men who had to make their living and take the world as they found it; and I suppose the first beatitude meant to them just what it said. They were poor in spirit--any man has to be, if he be willing to go around without a cent in his pocket--but to pay them for it he gave them the kingdom of heaven, that is, the church of which Christ is prophet, priest, and king. It's the greatest charge in the world; all business enterprises are nothing in comparison with it; but Jesus showed his divine nature by giving them this, for while they managed it splendidly, it's the only great affair in the world that a lot of poor-spirited men could manage without running it into the ground."

"That depends upon what 'poor in spirit' means," remarked Squire Woodhouse. "President Lottson seems to think it's the same thing as mean-spirited, but if it is, I can tell him that there's more money for that kind of chaps in other businesses. Now I'm a farmer--my principal crop is hay, and when my barn burned down last winter with eleven tons loose and forty odd tons pressed, and I went to the insur----"

"The members will please speak as called upon," said the leader, whose watchful ear imagined it detected a personality in the immediate future of the Squire's address. Squire Woodhouse subsided after a soft whisper to his right-hand neighbor, which caused that gentleman to notice that President Lottson's face was flushing a little, and his lips touching each other more firmly than usual.

"It seems to me," said Mr. Radley, who was next called upon, "that the passage means just what it says. The kingdom of heaven means the place we all hope to get to some day, and the poor in spirit are the people who aren't touchy and don't put on airs Christ was a man of this kind himself, and he knew by experience what he was talking about."

On the evening of October 1, 2017, Las Vegas, Nevada, became the site of the deadliest mass shooting committed by an individual in United States history. Stephen Paddock, positioned in a suite on the 32nd floor of the Mandalay Bay Hotel, unleashed a barrage of gunfire upon the unsuspecting crowd attending the Route 91 Harvest music festival. The outdoor venue, packed with concertgoers enjoying the final night of the festival, was filled with anticipation for the headlining performance. Country music star Jason Aldean had just taken the stage, entertaining thousands, when the horrific event unfolded.

The initial bursts of gunfire were largely dismissed as fireworks by many in the audience. However, the rapidly escalating and sustained nature of the noise quickly dispelled that notion, giving way to widespread panic. Paddock, armed with multiple rifles, including those modified with bump stocks, fired over 1,100 rounds into the crowd below. These bump stocks enabled his semi-automatic rifles to function with a rate of fire similar to that of fully automatic weapons. The festival grounds were transformed into a scene of utter chaos, as concert attendees desperately sought cover, trampling each other in their frantic attempts to escape the relentless gunfire. Wounded individuals lay scattered across the venue, while the sound of screams mingled with the incessant rattle of gunfire.

Law enforcement responded swiftly, converging on the Mandalay Bay Hotel in an effort to locate the source of the attack. An hour passed before police officers were able to breach Paddock's hotel room. Inside, they discovered that Paddock had already taken his own life. The immediate aftermath of the shooting was marked by disbelief and grief. Fifty-eight people were killed, and another 851 sustained injuries, a staggering toll that underscored the magnitude of the tragedy. The event dominated national and international news cycles, drawing significant attention to the issue of gun control and, in particular, the legality and accessibility of bump stocks. Investigative reports were launched to dissect the events leading up to the shooting and to examine Paddock's motives, which remained largely unknown.

In the wake of the massacre, the Las Vegas community rallied to support the victims and their families. Long lines formed at blood donation centers, as residents sought to contribute in any way they could. Nevada Governor Brian Sandoval issued a statement condemning the shooting as a "heinous, unspeakable act of violence." The Route 91 Harvest festival shooting left an indelible mark on the city of Las Vegas and the nation as a whole, serving as a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of mass violence and prompting ongoing debates about gun control measures.

Louise placed the dishes upon the table mechanically. The tenor sat himself at the board, and tucked a napkin in his neck.

“Ze Bénédiction? Ah! One encore. One on–lee. Zese pigs of Américains. I t’row my pairls biffo’ swine. Chops once more! You vant to mordair me? Vat do zis mean, madame? You ar–r–r–re in lig wiz my enemies. All ze vorlt is against ze ar–r–r–teest!”

The storm that followed made the first seem a zephyr. The tenor exhausted his execratory vocabulary in French and English. At last, by way of a dramatic finale, he seized the plate of chops and flung it from him. He aimed at the wall; but Frenchmen do not pitch well. With a ring and a crash, plate and chops went through the broad window–pane. In the moment of stricken speechlessness that followed, the sound of the final smash came softly up from the sidewalk.

“Ah–a–a–a–a–a–a–a–a–a–ah!”

The tenor rose to his feet with the howl of an anguished hyena.

“Oh, good gracious!” cried his wife; “he’s going to have one of his creezes—his creezes de nare!”

He did have a crise de nerfs. “Ten dollair!” he yelled, “for ten dollair of glass!” He tore his pomaded hair; he tore off his bib and his neck–tie, and for three minutes without cessation he shrieked wildly and unintelligibly. It was possible to make out, however, that “arteest” and “ten dollair” were the themes of his improvisation. Finally he sank exhausted into the chair, and his white–faced wife rushed to his side.

“Louise!” she cried, “get the foot–tub out of the closet while I spray his throat, or he can’t sing a note. Fill it up with warm water—102 degrees—there’s the thermometer—and bathe his feet.”

Trembling from head to foot, Louise obeyed her orders, and brought the foot–tub, full of steaming water. Then she knelt down and began to serve the maestro for the first time. She took off his shoes. Then she looked at his socks. Could she do it?

“Eediot!” gasped the sufferer, “make haste! I die!”

“Hold your mouth open, dear,” said Madame, “I haven’t half sprayed you.”

“Ah! you!” cried the tenor. “Cat! Devil! It ees you zat have killed me!” And moved by an access of blind rage, he extended his arm, and thrust his wife violently from him.

Louise rose to her feet, with a hard, set, good old New England look on her face. She lifted the tub of water to the level of her breast, and then she inverted it on the tenor’s head. For one instant she gazed at the deluge, and at the bath–tub balanced on the maestro’s skull like a helmet several sizes too large—then she fled like the wind.

Once in the servants’ quarters, she snatched her hat and jacket. From below came mad yells of rage.

“I kill hare! give me my knife—give me my rivvolvare! Au secours! Assassin!”

Miss Slattery appeared in the doorway, still polishing her nails.

“What have you done to His Tonsils?” she inquired. “He’s pretty hot, this trip.”

“How can I get away from here?” cried Louise.

Miss Slattery pointed to a small door. Louise rushed down a long stairway—another—and yet others—through a great room where there was a smell of cooking and a noise of fires—past white–capped cooks and scullions—through a long stone corridor, and out into the street. She cried aloud as she saw Esther’s face at the window of the coupé.

She drove home—cured.

"I never met your friend–olonel and Mrs. King. We are not military in Oxford. But they see–o judge from their letter–o be very nice people," said the Professor, his tone, quite unconsciously, suggesting the slightest shade of patronage.

"Oh, they're dears," said the girl warmly. "They were awfully good to me."

"Cannes was very gay, I suppose?"

"We saw a great many people in the afternoons. The Kings knew everybody. But I didn't go out in the evenings."

"You weren't strong enough?"

"I was in mourning," said the girl, looking at him with her large and brilliant eyes.

"Yes, yes, of course!" murmured the Reader, not quite understanding why he felt himself a trifle snubbed. He asked a few more questions, and his niece, who seemed to have no shyness, gave a rapid description, as she sipped her tea, of the villa at Cannes in which she had passed the winter months, and of the half dozen families, with whom she and her friends had been mostly thrown. Alice Hooper was secretly thrilled by some of the names which dropped out casually. She always read the accounts in the Queen, or the Sketch, of "smart society" on the Riviera, and it was plain to her that Constance had been dreadfully "in it." It would not apparently have been possible to be more "in it." She was again conscious of a hot envy of her cousin which made her unhappy. Also Connie's good looks were becoming more evident. She had taken off her hat, and all the distinction of her small head, her slender neck and sloping shoulders, was more visible; her self-possession, too, the ease and vivacity of her gestures. Her manner was that of one accustomed to a large and varied world, who took all things without surprise, as they came. Dr. Hooper had felt some emotion, and betrayed some, in this meeting with his sister's motherless child; but the girl's only betrayal of feeling had lain in the sharpness with which she had turned away from her uncle's threatened effusion. "And how she looks at us!" thought Alice. "She looks at us through and through. Yet she doesn't stare."

But at that moment Alice heard the word "prince," and her attention was instantly arrested.

"We had some Russian neighbours," the newcomer was saying; "Prince and Princess Jaroslav; and they had an English party at Christmas. It was great fun. They used to take us out riding into the mountains, or into Italy." She paused a moment, and then said carelessl–s though to keep up the conversation--"There was a Mr. Falloden with the–n undergraduate at Marmion College, I think. Do you know him, Aunt Ellen?" She turned towards her aunt.

But Mrs. Hooper only looked blank. She was just thinking anxiously that she had forgotten to take her tabloids after lunch, because Ewen had hustled her off so much too soon to the station.

"I don't think we know him," she said vaguely, turning towards Alice.

"We know all about him. He was introduced to me once."

The tone of the eldest Miss Hooper could scarcely have been colder. The eyes of the girl opposite suddenly sparkled into laughter.

"You didn't like him?"

"Nobody does. He gives himself such ridiculous airs."

"Does he?" said Constance. The information seemed to be of no interest to her. She asked for another cup of tea.

"Oh, Falloden of Marmion?" said Dr. Hooper. "I know him quite well. One of the best pupils I have. But I understand he's the heir to his old uncle, Lord Dagnall, and is going to be enormously rich. His father's a millionaire already. So of course he'll soon forget his Greek. A horrid waste!"

"He's detested in college!" Alice's small face lit up vindictively. "There's a whole set of them. Other people call them 'the bloods.' The dons would like to send them all down."

Mr. Blossom would have recalled this speech as soon as it escaped him, lest it should lead to a revelation from the truthful Mistress Thankful of her relations with the Continental captain. But to his astonishment, and, I may add, to my own, she showed nothing of that disposition she had exhibited a few moments before. On the contrary, she blushed slightly, and said nothing.

And then the conversation changed,--upon the weather, the hard winter, the prospects of the Cause, a criticism upon the commander-in-chief's management of affairs, the attitude of Congress, etc., between Mr. Blossom and the count; characterized, I hardly need say, by that positiveness of opinion that distinguishes the unprofessional. In another part of the room, it so chanced that Mistress Thankful and the baron were talking about themselves; the assembly balls; who was the prettiest woman in Morristown; and whether Gen. Washington's attentions to Mistress Pyne were only perfunctory gallantry, or what; and if Lady Washington's hair was really gray; and if that young aide-de-camp, Major Van Zandt were really in love with Lady or whether his attentions were only the zeal of a subaltern,--in the midst of which a sudden gust of wind shook the house; and Mr. Blossom, going to the front door, came back with the announcement that it was snowing heavily.

And indeed, within that past hour, to their astonished eyes the whole face of nature had changed. The moon was gone, the sky hidden in a blinding, whirling swarm of stinging flakes. The wind, bitter and strong, had already fashioned white feathery drifts upon the threshold, over the painted benches on the porch, and against the door-posts.

Mistress Thankful and the baron had walked to the rear door--the baron with a slight tropical shudder--to view this meteorological change. As Mistress Thankful looked over the snowy landscape, it seemed to her that all record of her past experience had been effaced: her very footprints of an hour before were lost; the gray wall on which she leaned was white and spotless now; even the familiar farm-shed looked dim and strange and ghostly. Had she been there? had she seen the captain? was it all a fancy? She scarcely knew.

A sudden gust of wind closed the door behind them with a crash, and sent Mistress Thankful, with a slight feminine scream, forward into the outer darkness. But the baron caught her by the waist, and saved her from Heaven knows what imaginable disaster; and the scene ended in a half-hysterical laugh. But the wind then set upon them both with a malevolent fury; and the baron was, I presume, obliged to draw her closer to his side.

They were alone, save for the presence of those mischievous confederates, Nature and Opportunity. In the half-obscurity of the storm she could not help turning her mischievous eyes on his. But she was perhaps surprised to find them luminous, soft, and, as it seemed to her at that moment, grave beyond the occasion. An embarrassment utterly new and singular seized upon her; and when, as she half feared yet half expected, he bent down and pressed his lips to hers, she was for a moment powerless. But in the next instant she boxed his ears sharply, and vanished in the darkness. When Mr. Blossom opened the door to the baron he was surprised to find that gentleman alone, and still more surprised to find, when they re-entered the house, to see Mistress Thankful enter at the same moment, demurely, from the front door.

When Mr. Blossom knocked at his daughter's door the next morning it opened upon her completely dressed, but withal somewhat pale, and, if the truth must be told, a little surly.

Federal Disaster Assistance in Louisiana Exceeds $2 Billion Two Months after Hurricane Ida

BATON ROUGE, La. – Since Hurricane Ida barreled across Southeast Louisiana two months ago, leaving dozens of parishes with severe damage and losses, disaster survivors have received more than $889 million in federal grants and been approved for more than $816 million in low-interest loans to enhance their recovery. Another $297 million has been paid to survivors in National Flood Insurance Program claims.

Survivors – and their communities – continue to clean up, begin to repair or rebuild their homes with future disasters in mind, and support their neighbors. The response by the state of Louisiana, FEMA and local and nonprofit partners has helped to put Louisiana on the road to recovery, and survivors can be sure FEMA and its partners will continue to work together to help those affected by Ida rebuild their lives and communities. The deadline to apply with FEMA for assistance has been extended to Nov. 29, 2021.

As of Oct. 28, total federal disaster assistance includes:

More than $889 million in total financial help and direct services to those who have necessary eligible expenses following the disaster and are unable to meet those needs through insurance or other means.

$492 million of that amount includes housing assistance to help homeowners repair or replace residential property damage from the disaster and/or for a safe place to stay while they recover.

$396 million is for Other Needs Assistance to cover necessary, disaster-related expenses such as medical bills, cleaning, repair or replacement of essential household items or vehicles and other non-housing needs.

More than $816 million approved in U.S. Small Business Administration loans, with more than $782 million for homeowners and renters and more than $34 million for businesses to repair, rebuild and replace damaged property and contents and for economic injury.

More than $297 million in claims paid to more than 4,500 National Flood Insurance policyholders.

Federal housing assistance is providing:

Rental assistance for more than 179,000 homeowners and renters.

Direct Temporary Housing assistance for 10 of the most impacted parishes, making available several housing solutions for Louisiana survivors.

As FEMA’s direct temporary housing gains momentum, the state is assisting survivors in the most heavily impacted parishes who have immediate sheltering needs. Survivors interested in the state-run Hurricane Ida Sheltering Program can visit idashelteringla.com or call 844-268-0301 to register.

In another milestone, contractors for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers have installed 33,200 "blue roofs" in the storm-affected area, enabling survivors to live in their own homes while they make repairs.

FEMA Disaster Recovery Centers have received nearly 33,269 visitors seeking disaster assistance or information, while Disaster Survivor Assistance outreach teams have visited 143,544 homes, made 27,812 referrals to various community resources and helped 15,254 individuals apply with FEMA.

The fastest ways to apply for FEMA assistance remain applying online at DisasterAssistance.gov or by phone at 800-621-3362 or (TTY) 800-462-7585. Phone lines operate from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. seven days a week.

Imagine walking into a crowded room where conversations float around you, each one shaping the atmosphere in its own way. This, my friends, is our society – a tapestry woven by countless individual threads, each influenced by their unique cultural backgrounds. As Christians, we are part of a vibrant subculture, the evangelical community, which also plays a role in this grand narrative. Our challenge? To ensure we don't get lost in the crowd.

Enter Mark A. Noll with his profound discussion on the evangelical mind, where he introduces the term'scandal.' At first, his ideas seemed dense to me, hanging on by a thread as I tried to grasp the depth of their richness. Noll's work isn't for the faint of heart; it demands deep contemplation and intellectual rigor. Yet, once the pieces started falling into place, I realized the urgency behind his call for adaptability and engagement with the wider culture.

There's a silence in our evangelical circles that worries me – a dearth of critical thinking on government, economy, and the arts. We live inside a bubble, sometimes so engrossed in our own worldviews that we forget to look beyond our walls. It's as if we're blindfolded, missing out on the larger societal picture.

I resonate deeply with Noll's emphasis on 'circumstances attending our perception of the world outside ourselves.' He's urging us to peel back the layers of our comfort zone and see the broader landscape. In doing so, we might prevent the decline of our societal influence. But it requires more than just faith; it demands an openness to the world around us.

As Noll suggests, understanding and adapting to cultural shifts is crucial. If we hang on to outdated perspectives, we risk being left behind in the relentless march of society. Let's step out of our bubble, engage with diverse ideas, and challenge ourselves to think critically about the world beyond our immediate horizons. After all, isn't that what being an evangelical mind is all about – not just standing firm, but growing, adapting, and influencing the world with grace and wisdom?

As the ladies retired, a faint air of tranquility settled over the dining-room, like the stillness that precedes the gentle lapping of the waves on a summer's shore. Lord Denyer's studiously pleasant countenance, however, refused to be easily lulled into complacency. His eyes, which had been following his hostess with a most becoming interest throughout the dinner, now wandered carelessly about the room, as if involuntarily drawn to the tedium which awaited him.

The dinner, it must be confessed, had not been lacking in effects of a rather too-vivid nature. Lady Maulevrier's sparkling eyes appeared to sparkle with an undue brilliancy; the daintiness of her features seemed exquisitely set off by an almost too-bright complexion; and her laughter sounded with a tinkling clarity which, in spite of its sweet musicality, grated terribly on Lord Denyer's rather sensitive ears.

As he pushed back his chair and relieved the tension of his waistcoat by a gentle expansion of his chest, Lady Maulevrier lingered by his side, her eyes fixed upon his with an unwonted animation. 'And now, Lord Denyer,' she said, 'I have you to myself; shall we walk through the gardens?' Her manner, as she spoke, seemed as delicate as a flower in bloom, yet conveyed an unmistakable hint of a resolve, as if she were merely taking a forward step toward some goal whose nature she reserved for herself.

Her host, that gentleman of out-of-doors inclinations, declined the invitation with a veritable flourish, doing full justice to his aristocratic birth by a generous surveillance of the clock. 'Alas! Madam, I fear I am already unpardonably behindhand; the bathtime, as you know, awaits me with smiling face.' Lady Maulevrier, her features now somewhat clouded by a brief flutter of disappointment, replied with a toss of her head, yet, in spite of this demurring, did not relinquish her hold on Lord Denyer's arm, which she still retained in her grasp, as the ladies continued to congregate about the fire with nervous, eager conversation.

His lordship's countenance, as the group of ladies emerged from the dining-room, disclosed all the tranquility of a tempestuous sea. His eyes strayed furtively over the assembly, noting with whom she was conversing. He seemed about to approach her; perhaps, indeed, to ask for a dance, but a sudden inhospitable glance from the diameter of his hostess, which regarded him with a richness of meaning that he well understood, drew him back to his chair, as one who apprehends a hostile storm gathering in the distance.

During dinner, Lady Denyer had mainly devoted herself to Lady Maulevrier, making her courtesy and enthusiasm undergo a magisterial review by reason of her approving gaze. Now, grasping the faint indications of deference in the Count's manner, she took possession of the entire room with her magnetic presence, challenging Lord Denyer's bashful smile and, regarding every murmur and whisper that broke the air as a subtle anticipation of her own grand rôle.

In the corner by the window, three of the ladies assembled to enquire on whose behalf Lord Maulevrier had resigned his Indian post. These whispers were forced to pause for the entrance of the two menservants who solemnly bore in a majestic silver tray to display the customary after-dinner wine decanters. While a trio of near-discouraged gentleman sequestered themselves in some detached comfort, watching with notions of tedium how the women would overthrow such a fascinating line of talk as had their hostess precipitated about the dinner-table.

As they passed the conversation back and forth, it accumulated into the neat point of women's employment - then festive nuptials. Lord Denyer maneuvered well-accredited amusement when calling Lady Maulevrier 'dainty nymphs of companied order of wifehood to compare, whose submissive understanding who well can delight him sufficiently on whimsical excess; was she Ulysses back in the Odyssey who longed compared to smother frustration - expressed in greyer town profounders stepwise suited, Lord Maulevrier returning year after year before..."

Lord Spoonbill was not less disappointed than the Countess of Smatterton, to hear that Penelope was in daily expectation of seeing her father. Hereditary legislators are sometimes perplexed, and in the present case the son of the Earl of Smatterton was in a state of grievous doubt and agitation.

His object in the first instance had been to take Penelope under his protection, and he supposed that if the correspondence between her and Robert Darnley could be broken off, there would be very little difficulty in inducing her to comply with his proposals. For it was his intention to make a most liberal settlement and to place her in a very handsome establishment. Living as he had always in splendour, and enjoying the luxuries and ostentation of wealth, though accustomed to them from his birth, he thought, that to one educated in such humble obscurity as Penelope had been, these fascinations would be irresistible. During the short time that he had been under the same roof with her, he had seen and observed more of the character of her mind, and he felt that it was not personal beauty alone that she possessed, but that her disposition was kind and her temper beautiful; and therefore he loved her with a much purer regard than ever he had before entertained for any one of the sex. He loved her so much, in fact, that he absolutely regretted that her rank in life was not nearer to his own.

It now also occurred to him, from what he had heard in the autumn, that it was very probable that Robert Darnley might be in England, and that through the intervention of Mr Primrose some explanation might bring the parties together again, and thus his lordship's hopes would be disappointed and his schemes frustrated. Then there came into his lordship's mind the thought of the intercepted letters, and with that thought the fear that a discovery might be made as to the manner in which, and the person by whom, they had been intercepted. But that fear was transient, for his lordship confidently said to himself, "It is absolutely impossible that Nick Muggins should betray me." What could his lordship be thinking about when he uttered this soliloquy? Did the Right Honorable Lord Spoonbill think that the principle of honor was stronger in the mind of Nick Muggins, the Smatterton post-boy, than it was in his own Right Honorable self? Wherein, did his lordship imagine, consisted the essential superiority of the high born above the sons of the peasantry? Did his lordship imagine that the only difference was in titles and soft white hands? It is not for us to know what lords may think, it is enough for us to gaze with wonderment on what they do.

Present circumstances and present feelings compelled Lord Spoonbill to enter into serious deliberation with himself as to what step he should pursue. He could not for a moment admit the possibility of making an honorable offer of his hand to the young lady; such a proposal would have been the death of the Earl of Smatterton. That offer, which his lordship gravely called the other proposal, required a little more circumlocution and management; for his lordship was not quite so simple as not to be aware that, if making the first proposal was condescension on his part, accepting the latter would be condescension on the part of the lady. There was required for this purpose a tolerably strong attachment to his lordship, which might not yet exist in the lady's mind. And though Lord Spoonbill was not by any means a man of great understanding or extraordinary penetration, yet in those matters in which he was most conversant he was not altogether unskilful. In pursuits of a similar nature to the present, his lordship was by no means inexpert; but, in the present instance, he knew that the person in question was gifted with mental powers superior to those which had belonged to his previous victims, and his own regard for her was somewhat more tender and respectful.

At the instigation of Mr. Jones, a proposition was made to modify the present arrangement by dividing the property into three parts, it being understood amongst them that they would still continue to conduct the business of Brown, Jones, and Robinson as a trio. Mr. Brown, however, exhibited considerable reluctance at this proposal. His countenance darkened with a frown as he perused the rough draft of the division proposed by Mr. Jones.

'This will never do,' exclaimed Mr. Brown, his eyes flashing with a fierce disdain. 'I will not hear of it, I assure you.' Mr. Jones looked at him in stolid inquiry, his brow furrowed in surprise at his partner's sudden vehemence. 'What is the matter with it?' he inquired, his deep, measured voice calm and unruffled, though tinged with a slight note of vexation.

Mr. Robinson, who had been quietly watching this colloquy, intervened at this juncture. His deep, sonorous voice imparted gravitas to his words, and his tone was courteous and measured as ever. 'My dear Jones,' he said, 'do not press the matter. Mr. Brown's scruples are not to be gainsaid. He is, as you are well aware, a man whose esteem for the pecuniary difficulties attendant upon the profession, is second to none.'

Mr. Brown looked at him, his countenance softening somewhat at Mr. Robinson's words, and his eyes, though still perturbed, betraying a certain instinctive regard for the intelligent and level-headed advice offered to him by his friend. 'Yes,' he murmured, as he roughly adjusted his gloves, 'I should be the first to acknowledge the weight of these scruples, but at the same time, I declare to you, Mr. Jones, that we must continue to carry on our business together. I will not part with you, under present circumstances.' Mr. Jones nodded, a trifle reluctantly, in assent to this proposition.

As the proceedings continued, Mr. Robinson gradually drew himself into the conversation. He had in his mind a notion, which, though not strictly pertinent to the problem at hand, had been forming in his brain for some time past. The seed of an idea had been sown there during his leisurely strolls in Regent's Park, where, one day, he had chanced to meet a charming young lady, a certain Miss Brown, who had captivated him with her beauty and lively conversation. 'It strikes me,' he quoth, 'that rather than fritter away our resources on this wretched business, we might turn to a different pursuit altogether. The advertisement possibilities in the trade of haberdashery are considerable, I am assured by those who have given the subject some little consideration.'

'Oh, come!' exclaimed Mr. Brown, whose face had darkened once more at the suggestion. 'That is an outlandish proposition. A butter-maker is a butter-maker, and will continue to be, I suppose, for the rest of his days.' Mr. Robinson smiled good-humouredly at this sally, which, however, was not meant to be taken in the spirit in which it was delivered. His countenance continued serene and benevolent, as he remarked, 'Though the product of our present endeavour may be sought after in butter, our fortunes might increase tenfold if we we were to turn to a pursuit which commands a greater degree of attention and allure.' Mr. Jones coughed, a gesture which indicated a curiosity at the suggestion.

The girl had never in her life been for a walk by herself. Jane had been her companion for the last fifteen years, and Jane's legs preferred an equable and leisurely method of progression along a good road, with, if possible, some such goal as Mrs. Battishill's farm, and a prospect of new milk, or perhaps junket. Consequently, country-bred though she was, Elaine was almost a stranger to rambles and scrambles up the cliff, to running races, scaling precipices, bird's-nesting, or any of those pursuits which usually come as naturally to the girl as to the boy who is reared "far from the maddening crowd."

Had she had a companion to suggest such sports, they would have been delightful to her; but hers was eminently an imitative and not an original mind, so she walked along passively at Jane's side, letting the parasol, which had been given her to protect her complexion, drag behind her, its point making a continuous trail in the white dust.

She was walking through a scene of beauty such as might have moved a far less emotional temperament than Allonby's. Behind her back were the waters of the bay, one sheet of flame in the vivid light, while here and there gleamed the sails of some proud ship steaming slowly down the Channel. The road she was treading ran along the western side of the valley; to her right all was deep, mysterious shadow, and beyond it the lofty swell of the more easterly of the two hills which bounded Edge Combe. High on the side of the Copping, as this eastern hill was called, was the long white front of Edge Willoughby, and a full view of the terrace glowing with its crimson and scarlet glory of climbing geraniums.

Every gateway that they passed disclosed a wealth of luxuriant grass, almost as tall as Elaine herself, ready and waiting for the mower's hand. The white butterflies flew here and there, dancing with glee. The sunshine, striking through the larch plantation on the left, flung bars of light and shadow across the road; and under the trees the fern-fronds were rearing their lovely heads, uncurling in crown-like grace and beauty.

All so still; nothing but the sleepy, hushed murmur which comes from nowhere and yet fills the air of a summer's day. In the silence the call of the chough on the terrace could be distinctly heard right across the combe.

"Hark at Jacky!" said Elaine, with a little laugh. She rested her arms on the stile, and gazed away over the laughing meadow at the terrace. "I can see Aunt Ellen's head at the window," said she, "and here comes Aunt Char with a watering-pot. I hope she won't forget to water my nasturtiums just around the corner. Do you know I've got one of those new coral-colored ones, Jane?"

"If we don't push on, miss, we'll not get to Poole and back before tea," was Jane's remark.

"I do think it's a shame to send me all the way to Poole such a day as this," sighed the girl, as she reluctantly rose and continued her way.

She did not care in the least for the beautiful landscape. Its monotony was thoroughly distasteful to her. What mattered it whether beautiful or not, so long as it never changed? Variety was the need of her young life: something fresh--something different. Had she come upon a cargo of bricks and mortar, and workmen hacking down the finest trees in order to erect a villa, the sight would have afforded her the liveliest relief.

Presently they left the high-road, and crossed a bit of furzy common--just a small piece of waste ground, with the water lying in picturesque pools and clumps of starry yellow blossoms brightening the sandy soil.

The days at Newport had been blissful, filled with sunshine, sea breeze, and the company of a companion who had quickly become dear to the protagonist's heart. Each passing day only served to deepen the fondness that had blossomed between them, his consideration and devotion never failing to touch her soul. Promises made to meet each afternoon were always eagerly kept, forming a routine that brought comfort and joy to both parties.

But all good things must come to an end, as the inevitable departure from Newport loomed on the horizon. The protagonist's Aunt Eliza, always a part of their lives in one way or another, decided to leave as well, casting a slight shadow over the otherwise idyllic days spent at the seaside town. Despite the sense of impending change, the protagonist felt a sense of contentment in the knowledge that she would soon be reunited with her family.

As November approached, discussions of marriage began to take precedence in the household. Consultations with the protagonist's mother resulted in an arranged marriage with Samuel Uxbridge, a man of good standing and reputation. While the decision was made with careful consideration, the protagonist couldn't help but notice the unusual restlessness that seemed to have taken hold of Aunt Eliza, her normally composed demeanor showing cracks of unease.

The day of the marriage arrived quietly, with Aunt Eliza noticeably absent from the proceedings. Despite her absence, the protagonist found herself happily following her new husband's plans, content in the belief that she was fulfilling her duty as a wife. The days passed in a blur of domesticity and routine, with her husband's desires taking precedence over her own wishes.

But in March, a sudden communication from Aunt Eliza shattered the tranquil facade that the protagonist had built around her new life. The news of Lemorne's defeat came as a shock, sending ripples of doubt and suspicion through her mind. As she drifted into an uneasy sleep that night, a feverish dream clouded her thoughts, revealing a disturbing truth about her husband that she had never dared to acknowledge before.

She kissed him, and went to meet Elsie.

"And you are the dear girl who has been playing and singing for my boy, a wounded stranger here alone among his foes?"

"Yes, and for all the others, too."

Mrs. Cameron seized both of her hands and looked at her tenderly.

"You will let me kiss you? I shall always love you."

She pressed Elsie to her heart. In spite of the girl's reserve, a sob caught her breath at the touch of the warm lips. Her own mother had died when she was a baby, and a shy, hungry heart, long hidden from the world, leaped in tenderness and pain to meet that embrace.

Elsie walked with her to the door, wondering how the terrible truth of her boy's doom could be told.

She tried to speak, looked into Mrs. Cameron's face, radiant with grateful joy, and the words froze on her lips. She decided to walk a little way with her. But the task became all the harder.

At the corner she stopped abruptly and bade her good-bye:

"I must leave you now, Mrs. Cameron. I will call for you in the morning and help you secure the passes to enter the hospital."

The mother stroked the girl's hand and held it lingeringly.

"How good you are," she said softly. "And you have not told me your name?"

Elsie hesitated and said:

"That's a little secret. They call me Sister Elsie, the Banjo Maid, in the hospitals. My father is a man of distinction. I should be annoyed if my full name were known. I'm Elsie Stoneman. My father is the leader of the House. I live with my aunt."

"Thank you," she whispered, pressing her hand.

Elsie watched the dark figure disappear in the crowd with a strange tumult of feeling.

The mention of her father had revived the suspicion that he was the mysterious power threatening the policy of the President and planning a reign of terror for the South. Next to the President, he was the most powerful man in Washington, and the unrelenting foe of Mr. Lincoln, although the leader of his party in Congress, which he ruled with a rod of iron. He was a man of fierce and terrible resentments. And yet, in his personal life, to those he knew, he was generous and considerate. "Old Austin Stoneman, the Great Commoner," he was called, and his name was one to conjure with in the world of deeds. To this fair girl he was the noblest Roman of them all, her ideal of greatness. He was an indulgent father, and while not demonstrative, loved his children with passionate devotion.

She paused and looked up at the huge marble columns that seemed each a sentinel beckoning her to return within to the cot that held a wounded foe. The twilight had deepened, and the soft light of the rising moon had clothed the solemn majesty of the building with shimmering tenderness and beauty.

"Why should I be distressed for one, an enemy, among these thousands who have fallen?" she asked herself. Every detail of the scene she had passed through with him and his mother stood out in her soul with startling distinctness--and the horror of his doom cut with the deep sense of personal anguish.

"He shall not die," she said, with sudden resolution. "I'll take his mother to the President. He can't resist her. I'll send for Phil to help me."

She hurried to the telegraph office and summoned her brother.

THE GREAT HEART

The next morning, when Elsie reached the obscure boarding-house at which Mrs. Cameron stopped, the mother had gone to the market to buy a bunch of roses to place beside her boy's cot.

As Elsie awaited her return, the practical little Yankee maid thought with a pang of the tenderness and folly of such people. She knew this mother had scarcely enough to eat, but to her bread was of small importance, flowers necessary to life. After all, it was very sweet, this foolishness of these Southern people, and it somehow made her homesick.

In a world often preoccupied with standardized testing and quantifiable outcomes, the Waldorf educational system stands apart as a beacon of holistic development. Unlike traditional models that prioritize rote learning and academic achievement above all else, the Waldorf method, developed by the Austrian philosopher Rudolf Steiner nearly a century ago, aims to cultivate well-rounded individuals capable of independent thought and creative expression. Rooted in the philosophy of anthroposophy, which posits a spiritual dimension to human experience, Waldorf education emphasizes imagination and critical thinking as the cornerstones of learning.

One of the most striking departures from conventional schooling lies in the Waldorf approach to curriculum and instruction. Teachers, often seen as facilitators rather than instructors, are encouraged to adapt their lessons to the evolving interests of their students. This dynamic approach, free from the constraints of standardized exams and grades, allows for a highly individualized and engaging learning experience. Instead of relying on textbooks, particularly in the early years, Waldorf students engage in experiential learning, documenting their observations and insights in meticulously kept journals.

Art, music, and foreign languages, often relegated to the periphery in other systems, are central to the Waldorf curriculum. These disciplines are not seen as mere electives but as fundamental to nurturing creativity and fostering a deeper understanding of diverse cultures. Even the teaching of reading and writing takes a unique approach. Waldorf schools emphasize oral storytelling and language mastery before introducing formal literacy skills, recognizing the importance of cultivating a love of language before focusing on its technical aspects.

Central to the Waldorf philosophy is the creation of a nurturing and supportive learning environment. Classrooms are typically designed with natural materials and soft colors, fostering a sense of warmth and tranquility conducive to learning. Decision-making within the school is often democratic, with teachers playing an active role in shaping the educational direction. This collaborative approach extends beyond the classroom walls, with parents often actively involved in school life, creating a strong sense of community.

While Waldorf education might appear unconventional to some, its impact is undeniable. Graduates of Waldorf schools are often described as independent thinkers, creative problem solvers, and compassionate individuals. They are encouraged to question, explore, and forge their own paths, equipped with the skills and confidence to navigate an increasingly complex world.

In recent years, the principles of Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) have found a natural synergy with the Waldorf method. SEL programs, which focus on developing self-awareness, empathy, and relationship skills, complement the holistic approach of Waldorf education, further enhancing students' emotional intelligence and capacity for meaningful social interaction. As educators and parents increasingly recognize the importance of nurturing the whole child, the Waldorf method, with its emphasis on creativity, independent thinking, and emotional intelligence, offers a compelling alternative to traditional educational paradigms.

Following the end of former President Donald Trump's second impeachment trial, analysis revealed that the proceedings extended beyond 27 hours, encompassing more than 140,000 words spoken throughout the duration. This is according to a study conducted by the Washington Post, which dissected the trial transcripts. The analysis showed that the nine House impeachment managers contributed over 91,000 words, while Trump's defense team accounted for nearly 33,000 words.

Unlike the first impeachment trial where Rep. Adam B. Schiff (D-Calif.), as the lead impeachment manager, dominated the conversation, this trial saw a more equitable distribution of speaking time among the participants. Rep. Jamie B. Raskin (D-Md.), serving as the lead impeachment manager for this trial, led with a contribution of just over 26,000 words. Following closely were Rep. David N. Cicilline (D-R.I.), Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Colo.), and Del. Stacey Plaskett (D-Virgin Islands), along with Trump's attorneys David Schoen and Bruce L. Castor Jr., each delivering more than 10,000 words. Michael T. van der Veen, another attorney for Trump, played a significant role towards the trial's conclusion, speaking 9,600 words.

During the trial, Schoen launched a vigorous challenge against the trial's constitutionality, whereas Castor and van der Veen were more prominent towards the end. The defense team utilized only a fraction of the time allotted to them, in contrast to the House managers who employed videos, testimonials, and audio clips from the January 6 events, with Trump's defense presenting video compilations of Democrats and media commentary.

Both sides made extensive use of video presentations during their opening arguments. According to the trial protocol, senators were instructed to maintain silence, under the threat of imprisonment, which restricted most to minimal verbal contributions, mainly consisting of "yes" or "no" responses to procedural motions and constitutional considerations. On the fourth day, however, some senators actively posed questions to both sides.

A few participants spoke more frequently. Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer (D-N.Y.) voiced 1,256 words, primarily through procedural motions and daily recess calls. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) articulated 342 words, notably making an objection during the proceedings. Sen. Patrick J. Leahy (D-Vt.), presiding over the trial as the Senate president pro tempore, contributed more than 12,800 words. Other contributors included the acting Senate sergeant at arms, the chaplain, and the clerk, who read the article of impeachment.

The glow of the late October sun, streaming through the breakfast-parlour window, found Miss Charlecote still lingering over her letters. Humfrey, having exhausted the sporting news in the 'Times,' had wandered out to consult with Brooks about the planting of some new shrubs, a project upon which Miss Charlecote's heart was set.

Humfrey's uncharacteristic silence during old Giles' reminiscences the previous morning had not escaped Honora's notice. The mere mention of the last festive gathering at Charlecote, a celebration marking the squire's marriage, had sent a blush into the young man's cheeks and a stammer into his usually confident voice. Honora, with a knowing smile playing about her lips, could only conclude that her usually forthright cousin was harbouring some secret sentimentality. Was it possible, she dared to wonder, that Humfrey, at the ripe old age of twenty-five, was entertaining thoughts of matrimony himself?

Her musings were interrupted by the entrance of Sarah, her placid face creased with a slight frown.

'Honora, dear,' she began, her voice tinged with concern, 'have you finished with the 'Illustrated London News'? I promised Mrs. Ashton I would return it this morning.'

'Of course, Sarah,' replied Honora, her fingers deftly refolding the newspaper. 'I trust you assured her that the account of the Grand Bazaar for the Distressed Needlewomen was most moving? Such worthy causes always tug at one's heartstrings.'

'Indeed, indeed,' murmured Sarah vaguely, her gaze falling upon a small vase of autumn leaves, artfully arranged by Honora on the writing desk. 'Those leaves are rather striking, aren't they? Though perhaps a trifle...abundant?'

Honora, ever sensitive to any perceived criticism of her handiwork, arched a delicate eyebrow. 'Abundant, Sarah? I should say they possess a certain artistic profusion. Don't you agree, Humfrey?' she added, as her cousin strolled back into the room.

Humfrey, his hands clasped behind his back and a thoughtful expression on his face, paused before the arrangement. 'I find them rather charming, Honora,' he declared, a twinkle in his eye. 'They possess a certain...untamed beauty, wouldn't you say?'

Sarah, never one to argue matters of taste, merely smiled benignly and retreated with the 'Illustrated London News' tucked safely under her arm. Honora, however, was not quite finished with the subject.

'Untamed, Humfrey?' she echoed, her tone laced with amusement. 'Is that how you see me? A wild, unkempt creature in need of taming?'

Humfrey, his cheeks colouring slightly, stammered, 'I...that is to say...'

Honora, her eyes sparkling with mischief, laughed lightly. 'Fear not, dear cousin,' she said, rising from her seat. 'I have no intention of running wild in the woods just yet. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have a basket of apples that requires my attention. Mrs. Morris is expecting them for her pies.'

And with a swish of her skirts and a mischievous smile over her shoulder, Miss Charlecote took her leave, leaving Humfrey to ponder the true nature of her untamed spirit.

In the gentle warmth of a languid afternoon, the narrator found himself once more ensconced within the embrace of the ancient demolished abbey. The rays of the setting sun cast a golden hue upon the weathered stones, as if to remind him of the grandeur of yore. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming flowers that had taken root amidst the decaying remnants of the once mighty edifice. Mr. Malone, ever the stalwart companion, was by his side, his keen eyes scanning the debris-laden landscape with a gardener's interest.

"Pray, Mr. D.," he inquired, his voice barely above a whisper, "Do you recall the tale of our dear old lady, Queen Anne's Lace? I've always believed she is the spirit of the abbey, reigning over these ruins with her delicate charm." The narrator nodded, his gaze following the playful dance of the wind through the tufts of grass that waved among the crumbling columns.

As they traversed the path, their conversation turned towards the delicate threads of time and memory. "No doubt," Mr. Malone observed, "the search for Phoebus has taken ahold of your fancy, dear fellow, but remember, time tends to smooth the rough edges of our obsessions. It will not be long before the quest for this lost dahlia is but a faded memory, like the sweet Petrovaria that bloomed in the shade of the abbey's overgrown walls last season."

The narrator smiled at his friend's wisdom, allowing his thoughts to drift away from the all-consuming quest. Yet, as they paused to observe the vibrant flora that thrived in the decay, a sudden shift in the breeze brought a whiff of something unusual. Mr. Malone caught it too, his expression turning sharp. "What's this?" he murmured, bending down to sniff the fetid earth.

To the narrator's disbelief, his fingers brushed against something smooth and silken, hidden beneath the mounds of manure. There, in all its radiant splendor, was Phoebus, the most vibrant dahlia he had ever laid eyes upon. It seemed to bloom with a life of its own, defying the unspectacular surroundings that had harbored its secret growth. Surrounded by the ruins of time, the future's forgotten trend was revealed, and with it, the abbey's whispers echoed anew.

Citigroup Loses Battle to Recover $500 Million in Mistaken Transfer to Revlon Creditors

In a stunning blow to Citigroup, a New York federal judge has ruled that a group of 10 creditors can keep nearly $500 million that the bank mistakenly transferred to them, instead of the intended $8 million interest payment from cosmetics giant Revlon. The error, which saw nearly $900 million of Citigroup's own funds transferred in August 2020, has sparked a heated debate over the responsibilities of creditors in such cases.

Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, cited legal precedents and the creditors' reasonable belief that the massive payment was intentional due to its precision. "The fact that Citibank made the transfers with such precision — down to the penny — is powerful evidence that it intended to make the transfers," he said.

Adam Abensohn, representing the asset managers at Quinn Emanuel, argued forcefully in defense of the creditors. "There is nothing unfair about keeping money that is owed," Abensohn stated, emphasizing the creditors' right to retain funds that were accurately repaid according to their contracts with Revlon.

The case has posed a moral and legal dilemma, pitting the principle of returning mistakenly sent money against the right to use funds that have been precisely repaid. New York law, which aims to discourage such errors by banks, played a crucial role in the judge's decision. This ruling could have far-reaching implications for financial transactions and the expectations placed on banks and creditors alike.

"Citigroup's mistake was a whopper, but the law is the law," said a legal expert familiar with the case, speaking on condition of anonymity. "This decision underscores the importance of diligence and accuracy in financial transactions, particularly for institutions of Citigroup's size and stature."

Some of the creditors who received the overpayment, including investment firms Brigade Capital Management, HPS Investment Partners, and Symphony Asset Management, initially returned $400 million. However, the remaining 10 creditors refused to return their share, leading Citigroup to pursue legal action.

Citigroup, in a statement, expressed disappointment with the ruling and hinted at the possibility of an appeal. "We respectfully disagree with the court's decision and are evaluating our options," a spokesperson for the bank said.

The case has sparked a broader conversation about the balance between rules and principles in finance. DealBook, the New York Times' financial newsletter, is inviting readers to share their opinions on the matter, which could be featured in a future edition.

There, in the deepening dusk of the garden, stood Captain Carroll, his gaze fixed upon the threshold of the summer-house, a figure of suspense and expectancy. The faded hues of the day lingered, dappling the air with their last reluctant caress. The pear-tree, a relic of forgotten summers, stood with bent boughs as if whispering to the wind of bygone days. Its gnarled form, draped in moss and ivy, bore testament to a lifetime’s story, and its branches, heavy with the weight of leaves that had turned amber before the season's end, seemed to rustle with secrets known only to it.

At his feet, the rose-leaves lay strewn, a tapestry of crimson and gold that mocked the fading light with their fervent display. They lay scattered as if the very fingers of the night had plucked them, and yet, they spoke of a grave—a grave of lost love or departed dreams, whose scent lingered despite the encroaching chill.

Carroll, still as a sentinel, awaited the arrival of the woman who had claimed his thoughts. The murmur of the evening breeze through the foliage was his only company, and yet, it seemed to him a chorus of whispers, urging him to hasten, to anticipate the arrival of the enigmatic figure whose passage through the garden would forever alter the course of his life.

In her presence, he felt a strange mixture of trepidation and elation. She had the power to captivate, to draw forth the innermost yearnings of any man fortunate enough to find her glance, and yet, she was elusive, as fleeting as the petals that adorned her hair. Each movement suggested a dance, a performance that held him entranced, uncertain if it were real or but a figment of his longing.

Through the myriad of leaves, a soft voice called out, "Captain Carroll?" Startled, he turned to see Brianna, her form illuminated by the last rays of the setting sun. She held out a hand, adorned with a single rose, its petals reflecting the twilight sky.

"I see you have not abandoned your vigil," she said, her voice a melody that matched the cadence of the wind. "The night grows colder, and yet, you remain."

His heart quickened at the sight of her, the simple gesture of offering a rose a bold declaration of intent. He took her hand and drew her closer, under the canopy of ancient branches that seemed to approve their union.

"Brianna," he began, his words spilling forth like a dam breaking, "I have been waiting for you, not just here, but in my dreams each night. You are the reason the stars shine, the perfume that lingers long after the rose has faded."

She smiled, a tender, knowing smile that spoke volumes of their shared understanding. "And what would Captain Carroll have me do with my stars and my rose, if I were to grace him with my presence?"

The question hung between them, a delicate proclamation of their mutual attraction. He leaned in, his breath mingling with hers, the anticipation building as they stood there, suspended in the twilight.

"Captain Carroll," she whispered, her eyes shimmering with unspoken promises, "perhaps it is time to write another chapter, one where we are not merely actors in someone else's tale, but creators of our own destiny."

It was a morning of singular beauty that dawned upon Murkley, with a sky so bright and unclouded, that it seemed almost an insult to the solemn and sorrowful business that had brought him hither. He had slept little, his mind being in a state of wakeful perturbation, but the freshness of the air and the dewy charm of the morning, soon dispelled the dark clouds that had gathered there, and he felt his spirits lift and rise, like the morning itself, as the sun burst over the hills. He rose from his chamber in the old castle, and descended to the hall, where he found a fire already burning, and a servant in wig and livery, with a breakfast tray, bearing all the finery of the castle's culinary art.

His guest, for he was a guest, in a manner of speaking, had been so well-fed, that he ate his repast with something like relish, and even found himself in a not untoward mood, considering the sombre and serious business that lay before him. The morning sun streamed in through the large windows, and his eyes wandered to the windows, where he had spent many an hour, in idle contemplation, while he was a boy, and Sir Patrick, alive and in the prime of life, would often sit with him, and talk of the future. He had come to Murkley, with a purpose, but as he sat there, the morning sun shining on his face, he could not help but feel a tinge of doubt and uncertainty. Had he done right, in coming here? Or was he betraying the trust of a man, whom he had loved and reverenced, by following out his expressed wish, when it suited his own purposes?

The servant, a neat and tidy man, who had been in the castle service, for many a year, came in, with a whisper of the post from Edinburgh. He handed a letter, which his guest took, and broke the seal, and read the contents. It was from the old rector of the parish, a man of some twenty years his senior, who had been a friend of Sir Patrick's, and a guide and mentor to all his life. The letter was brief, and to the point, and told him, that the old man had not been well, and was growing feeble, and that he wished to see him, before he died. This intelligence, threw a flood of light on the darkness of his heart, and he felt a pang of sorrow and regret, at the thought of the old man's approaching end, and the sorrow that it would cause to all who knew and loved him.

He walked out, into the garden, with the letter in his hand, where the morning dew still sparkled, and the trees and flowers seemed to stir, and swell, and lift their leaves, in the morning breeze. The world was full of beauty and life, and yet, he felt a sense of desolation, and disquietude, as if some part of his own heart, was gone, and he was left to carry on, in a world, that was not the same, without him. He walked on, slowly, lost in thought, the trees, and flowers, and the grass, seemed to fade, into the background, as he thought of the old man, and the trust, that he had placed in him. He walked, till he came to the very spot, where he had spoken to Sir Patrick, the last time he had seen him, and where he had pledged his word, and his heart, to follow out his wishes, and keep his secrets. He stopped, and looked around, and a sense of peace, and quietude, came over him, as if the burden of his doubts, and fears, had been lifted, and he was free to go on, with his heart, unencumbered, and his spirit, untroubled.

He drew a deep breath, and felt a sense of determination, and purpose, come over him, as he thought of what he had to do, and the ends, he had to serve. He looked at the letter, in his hand, and knew, that he had to see the old man, before it was too late, and that he had to follow out, the wishes, that Sir Patrick, had expressed, to the letter. He folded the letter, and put it in his pocket, and turned, to go back, to the castle, where his breakfast, still waited, but he was no longer hungry, for his heart, was full, and his mind, was at peace. He walked, with long strides, through the garden, and out, into the bright sunlight, where the world, and all its wonders, were waiting, to be explored, and enjoyed.

He reached the courtyard, where a small pony, and a gig, were waiting, with a servant, who had been ordered, to take him, to the old rector's house, as soon as he was ready. He took his seat, and the pony, started, and they moved off, through the quiet streets, of the little town, and out, into the open country, where the hills, and the moors, stretched, and the wind, and the sun, blew, and sparkled, in the morning dew.

Murdock quailed before his victim’s reproachful burning glance for Joe had correctly surmised the dark plot he had in view.

His nervousness only lasted a moment for he quickly recovered.

“Fool!” he hissed, getting enraged at the thought that his wicked scheme was suspected. “How dare you hint that I’d do such a thing?”

“Because I know you are a villain.”

“What!” roared Murdock, furiously. “You insult me. I’ll pound the life out of you, you infernal young scoundrel!”

And he sprang at the boy and dealt him a savage blow that knocked him over upon the floor, rushed up to him and began to kick him about the head.

Weak from past privations, and unable to defend himself, poor Joe groaned in a heart-rending manner, and cried, piteously, as the hot tears ran down his pale, thin cheeks:

“Oh, don’t—don’t, Mr. Murdock!”

“I’ll kill you!” yelled the brute.

“For pity’s sake! Oh, the pain! Stop—I can’t stand it!”

Just then the servant rushed in.

“Shame!” she cried, indignantly.

“Get out of here!” roared Murdock. “I’ll discharge you!”

“If you beat poor Joe any more I’ll have you arrested!” This threat caused the broker to say, hastily:

“He provoked me to it. I don’t intend to hit him again.”

Satisfied with this assurance, the girl went out.

Poor Joe, cut, bleeding and black-and-blue, crept toward the door.

The man glared at him a moment and then hissed:

“Get up, there! Get up, I say! I’ll have a final settlement with you! Put on your hat. It is eight o’clock now. The lawyer who has charge of your money has gone home. He lives out of town. You come with me to his house. You’ll get your money. Then you can clear out of here and never trouble me again.”

“Gladly!” exclaimed Joe, in eager tones.

He knew that with plenty of money he could easily get along in the world and be under no obligations to this fiend.

Murdock scowled at him and prepared to go out.

Hearing them coming the detective left the stoop and got behind an adjacent tree where he was unseen.

He had scarcely concealed himself when he saw Martin Murdock come out with Joe, hail a passing cab, get in and ride away.

The detective had overheard all they said in the parlor, and with his suspicions of the broker aroused, he pursued the cab, resolved to see the termination of the affair.

Murdock did not utter a word to the boy, but kept watching him and deeply thinking over a dark scheme he had in view.

The boy feared this man, but he was so eager to have a final settlement with him that he did not hesitate to go with him.

Reaching the railroad depot they embarked on a train.

“I’ll take him to an unfrequented place and put an end to him!” thought Murdock, grimly. “He stands in my way to nearly a million. The stakes are enormous. It is worth the risk. I’m bound to have the money.”

Unluckily for him, the detective was on the same train.

They were whirled away.

Several hours passed by, when the end of the road was reached.

“Readestown! All out! Last stop!” called the conductor.

Murdock and the boy were the only ones in that car, and they arose, alighted and strode away.

Tom Reynard pursued them.

The place was a noted little city in which dwelt a celebrated young inventor named Frank Reade, Jr.

Skirting the suburbs of the city, Murdock led his victim toward a magnificent big mansion in which dwelt the inventor alluded to.

In the extensive grounds surrounding the house were a number of immense workshops, in which the inventor constructed his marvelous contrivances.

“There’s where the lawyer lives,” Murdock said to the boy, as he pointed at the mansion, although he had never been in Readestown before.

Tiger Woods Involved in Serious Car Accident, Sheriff's Department Seeks Black Box Data

Golf legend Tiger Woods was involved in a serious car accident on Tuesday, with a local resident finding him unconscious in his SUV. The Los Angeles Sheriff's Department is now seeking to review the vehicle's black box data to understand the pre-collision speed and brake usage.

According to Sheriff Alex Villanueva, "We are trying to determine if there was any distracted driving, or if he had fallen asleep at the wheel." Villanueva added that there were no signs of impairment by substances, and hence no tests were administered nor charges filed against Woods.

The first responder, a mystery man living near the crash site, attempted to communicate with Woods but received no response. Woods was described as 'calm and lucid' when fire officials extricated him from the wreckage.

Woods suffered a shattered ankle, two leg fractures, and has had multiple surgeries. He testified to deputies that he had no recollection of driving or how the accident happened.

The golfing community has rallied around Woods, with Rory McIlroy and other golfers wearing red and black in solidarity, expressing their well-wishes for Woods' recovery. Woods himself thanked fellow golfers and fans for their support in his first public comment since the accident.

The accident occurred on Tuesday morning, when Woods' SUV crashed into a tree in the Rolling Hills Estates area of Los Angeles. The Sheriff's Department received a call at 7:12 AM, and deputies arrived to find Woods trapped in the vehicle.

The investigation into the accident is ongoing, with the Sheriff's Department seeking to retrieve data from the vehicle's black box. The black box, also known as an Event Data Recorder, captures information about the vehicle's speed, braking, and other relevant data in the moments leading up to a crash.

Sheriff Villanueva stated that the black box data would be crucial in determining the cause of the accident. "We want to know what was happening in the moments leading up to the crash," he said. "The black box will give us a better understanding of what occurred."

Woods' agent, Mark Steinberg, released a statement expressing gratitude for the support Woods has received. "Tiger and his family are grateful for the outpouring of support and encouragement they have received from the golf community and fans around the world."

Steinberg also provided an update on Woods' condition, stating that he was "resting comfortably" and "receiving excellent care" at the hospital.

The accident has sparked a renewed debate about the dangers of distracted driving. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving was responsible for 3,166 deaths in the United States in 2017.

The Sheriff's Department has urged drivers to remain vigilant and avoid distractions while behind the wheel. "Distracted driving is a serious issue that can have devastating consequences," said Villanueva. "We urge all drivers to stay focused on the road and avoid distractions."

As the investigation into the accident continues, the golfing world remains optimistic about Woods' recovery. McIlroy, who wore red and black in solidarity with Woods, expressed his support for the golfing legend. "We're all thinking of Tiger and wishing him a speedy recovery," he said.

Woods' accident serves as a reminder of the dangers of distracted driving and the importance of staying focused on the road. As the Sheriff's Department continues its investigation, the golfing community remains united in their support for Woods' recovery.

"Now's the time," thought I.

"Samuel, my dear nephew," said she, "your first name you received from your sainted uncle, my blessed husband; and of all my nephews and nieces, you are the one whose conduct in life has most pleased me."

When you consider that my aunt herself was one of seven married sisters, that all the Hoggarties were married in Ireland and mothers of numerous children, I must say that the compliment my aunt paid me was a very handsome one.

"Dear aunt," says I, in a slow agitated voice, "I have often heard you say there were seventy-three of us in all, and believe me I do think your high opinion of me very complimentary indeed: I'm unworthy of i–ndeed I am."

"As for those odious Irish people," says my aunt, rather sharply, "don't speak of them, I hate them, and every one of their mothers" (the fact is, there had been a lawsuit about Hoggarty's property); "but of all my other kindred, you, Samuel, have been the most dutiful and affectionate to me. Your employers in London give the best accounts of your regularity and good conduct. Though you have had eighty pounds a year (a liberal salary), you have not spent a shilling more than your income, as other young men would; and you have devoted your month's holidays to your old aunt, who, I assure you, is grateful."

"Oh, ma'am!" said I. It was all that I could utter.

"Samuel," continued she, "I promised you a present, and here it is. I first thought of giving you money; but you are a regular lad; and don't want it. You are above money, dear Samuel. I give you what I value most in lif–he p,--the po, the po-ortrait of my sainted Hoggarty" (tears), "set in the locket which contains the valuable diamond that you have often heard me speak of. Wear it, dear Sam, for my sake; and think of that angel in heaven, and of your dear Aunt Susy."

She put the machine into my hands: it was about the size of the lid of a shaving-box: and I should as soon have thought of wearing it as of wearing a cocked-hat and pigtail. I was so disgusted and disappointed that I really could not get out a single word.

When I recovered my presence of mind a little, I took the locket out of the bit of paper (the locket indeed! it was as big as a barndoor padlock), and slowly put it into my shirt. "Thank you, Aunt," said I, with admirable raillery. "I shall always value this present for the sake of you, who gave it me; and it will recall to me my uncle, and my thirteen aunts in Ireland."

"I don't want you to wear it in that way!" shrieked Mrs. Hoggarty, "with the hair of those odious carroty women. You must have their hair removed."

"Then the locket will be spoiled, Aunt."

"Well, sir, never mind the locket; have it set afresh."

"Or suppose," said I, "I put aside the setting altogether: it is a little too large for the present fashion; and have the portrait of my uncle framed and placed over my chimney-piece, next to yours. It's a sweet miniature."

"That miniature," said Mrs. Hoggarty, solemnly, "was the great Mulcahy's chef-d'oeuvre" (pronounced shy dewver, a favourite word of my aunt's; being, with the words bongtong and ally mode de Parry, the extent of her French vocabulary). "You know the dreadful story of that poor poor artist. When he had finished that wonderful likeness for the late Mrs. Hoggarty of Castle Hoggarty, county Mayo, she wore it in her bosom at the Lord Lieutenant's ball, where she played a game of piquet with the Commander-in-Chief. What could have made her put the hair of her vulgar daughters round Mick's portrait, I can't think; but so it was, as you see it this day. 'Madam,' says the Commander-in-Chief, 'if that is not my friend Mick Hoggarty, I'm a Dutchman!' Those were his Lordship's very words. Mrs. Hoggarty of Castle Hoggarty took off the brooch and showed it to him.

Dick Marden had an uncle living at Timberville, Michigan, who was old and feeble, and who was having a great deal of trouble about some timber lands which he claimed, but which an Englishman and a French Canadian were trying to get away from him.
