As the warm sunlight streamed through the windows of General Trednoke's library, casting a golden glow over the rows of leather-bound volumes, the professor settled into his favorite armchair, a look of rapt attention on his face. The general, pacing slowly back and forth across the room, continued to speak of Grace Parsloe, his voice filled with a deep affection for the young woman. "And so, Meschines, I insisted that she take a leave of absence from the store, and come to me in the country, where the fresh air and quiet would do her a world of good."

The professor nodded thoughtfully, his eyes narrowing as he considered the general's words. "I must admit, Trednoke, that I am surprised by your interest in this young woman," he said, his voice tinged with a hint of curiosity. "You have always been a staunch advocate for the aristocracy, and yet you seem to be taking a keen interest in the welfare of a shop-girl." The general smiled, his eyes twinkling with amusement, as he paused in his pacing to regard the professor.

"Ah, but that is where you are mistaken, my dear Meschines," he replied, his voice filled with a deep conviction. "I am not merely taking an interest in Grace Parsloe's welfare, I am invested in her future. You see, I believe that this young woman has the potential to rise above her humble beginnings, to make a name for herself in society, and I am determined to help her do just that." The professor raised an eyebrow, clearly skeptical, as the general resumed his pacing.

"As you know, Meschines, I have always been a firm believer in the power of social mobility," the general continued, his voice filled with passion. "I believe that anyone, regardless of their background or circumstances, can rise to greatness with the right combination of hard work, determination, and opportunity. And I believe that Grace Parsloe has all of these qualities in abundance." The professor snorted, a look of disdain on his face, as he shook his head.

"Social mobility, Trednoke, is all well and good, but let us not forget that there are limits to how far one can rise," he said, his voice dripping with skepticism. "A shop-girl, no matter how clever or energetic, can never truly be a part of our social circle. She will always be an outsider, looking in." The general stopped pacing, his eyes flashing with anger, as he turned to face the professor.

"I disagree, Meschines," he said, his voice firm. "I believe that with the right guidance and support, anyone can overcome their humble beginnings and take their rightful place in society. And I intend to provide that guidance and support to Grace Parsloe, no matter what the cost." The professor raised an eyebrow, clearly taken aback by the general's vehemence, as he leaned forward in his chair.

As the two men sat in silence for a moment, the only sound the ticking of the clock on the mantle, the general's thoughts turned to Grace Parsloe, and the circumstances that had brought her to his attention. He had met her, quite by chance, on a visit to the dry-goods store where she worked, and had been immediately struck by her intelligence and charm. Despite her humble surroundings, she had carried herself with a quiet confidence and dignity that had impressed him deeply.

And so, when he had learned of her illness, he had not hesitated to offer her a place to stay, in the hopes that a change of climate and scenery would help her to recover. The professor, however, seemed less than convinced of the wisdom of this decision, and the general could not help but wonder what lay behind his friend's skepticism. Was it merely a desire to protect him from the perceived dangers of associating with someone from a lower social class, or was there something more at play?

As the silence between them grew, the general decided to press on, to see if he could uncover the root of the professor's concerns. "Tell me, Meschines," he said, his voice gentle, but probing. "What is it that you fear? Is it that I will be taken advantage of, or that Grace Parsloe will somehow embarrass me in public?" The professor shifted uncomfortably in his chair, his eyes avoiding the general's, as he cleared his throat.

"I fear, Trednoke, that you are being naive," he said finally, his voice low. "You are a wealthy and influential man, and there are those who would seek to take advantage of your good nature. I fear that Grace Parsloe may be one of them, that she may be using her charms to manipulate you into doing her bidding." The general's face darkened, his eyes flashing with anger, as he listened to the professor's words.

The general's mind was racing with thoughts of Grace Parsloe, and the possibilities that lay ahead. He knew that the professor's words were not entirely without merit, that there were indeed those who would seek to take advantage of his good nature. But he also knew that he was not a foolish man, that he was capable of discerning the true intentions of those around him. And he was determined to prove the professor wrong, to show him that Grace Parsloe was not the manipulative social climber that he believed her to be.

It is not long ago that the last conservative resident of Bond Street, proud of his ancient possessorship and no doubt loving the big brick structure with arched doorway and dormer windows in which he first saw the light, felt himself relentlessly swept from that interesting quarter by the stout besom of commerce. Interesting the street really is for all to whom old things appeal with any charm. It is characteristic of our brilliant New York, however, that few antiquarian feet tread her pavements, and that she is too busy with her bustling and thrifty present to reflect that she has ever reached it through a noteworthy past. Some day it will perhaps be recorded of her that among all cities she has been the least preservative of tradition and memorial. The hoary antiquity of her transatlantic sisters would seem to have made her unduly conscious of her own youth. She has so long looked over seas for all her history and romance, that now, when she can safely boast two solid centuries of age, the habit yet firmly clings, and she cares as little for the annals of her fine and stately growth as though, like Troy, she had risen, roof and spire, to the strains of magic melody.

It might be of profit, and surely it would be of pleasure, were she to care more for the echoes of those harsh and sometimes tragic sounds that have actually blent their serious music with her rise. As it is, she is rich in neglected memories; she has tombs that dumbly reproach her ignoring eye; she has nooks and purlieus that teem with reminiscence and are silent testimonials of her indifference. Her Battery and her Bowling Green, each bathed in the tender glamour of Colonial association, lie frowned upon by the grim scorn of recent warehouses and jeered at by the sarcastic shriek of the neighboring steam-tug. She can easily guide you to the modern clamors of her Stock-Exchange; but if you asked her to show you the graves of Stuyvesant and Montgomery she might find the task a hard one, though thousands of her citizens daily pass and re-pass these hallowed spots. Boston, with its gentle ancestral pride, might well teach her a lesson in retrospective self-esteem. Her own harbor, like that of Boston, has had its "tea-party," and yet one whose anniversary now remains a shadow. On Golden Hill, in her own streets, the first battle of our Revolution was fought, the first blood in the cause of our freedom was spilled; yet while Boston stanchly commemorates its later "massacre," what tribute of oratory, essay or song has that other momentous contest received? This metropolitan disdain of local souvenir can ill excuse itself on the plea of intolerance toward provincialism; for if the great cities of Europe are not ashamed to admit themselves once barbaric, Hudson in fray or traffic with the swarthy Manhattans, or old Van Twiller scowling at the anathemas of Bogardus, holds at least a pictorial value and significance.

Bond Street has always been but a brief strip of thoroughfare, running at right angles between the Bowery and Broadway. Scarcely more than thirty years ago it possessed the quietude and dignity of a patrician domain; it was beloved of our Knickerbocker social element; it was the tranquil stronghold of caste and exclusiveness. Its births, marriages and deaths were all touched with a modest distinction. Extravagance was its horror and ostentation its antipathy. The cheer of its entertainments would often descend to lemonade and sponge-cake, and rarely rise above the luxury of claret-punch and ice-cream. Its belles were of demurer type than the brisk-paced ladies of this period, and its beaux paid as close heed to the straight line in morals as many of their successors now bestow upon it in the matter of hair-parting. Bond Street was by no means the sole haunt of the aristocracy, but it was very representative, very important, very select. There was even a time when to live there at all conferred a certain patent of respectability. It was forgiven you that your daughter had married an obscure Smith, or that your son had linked his lot with an undesirable Jones, if you had once come permanently to dwell there. The whole short, broad street was superlatively genteel. Nothing quite describes it like that pregnant little word. It dined at two o'clock; it had "tea" at six; its parties were held as dissipated if they broke up after midnight; its young men "called" on its young women of an evening with ceremonious regularity, never at such times donning the evening-coat and the white neck-tie which now so widely obtain, but infallibly wearing these on all occasions of afternoon festivity with an unconcern of English usage that would keenly shock many of their descendants.

The miami where these last were was at some little distance from the other two, and I thought I saw a fourth figure; but when I came up I found only the old man and the lads. I asked where the other man was, but they denied that any other man had been there. I could see, however, they were lying, and believed that, from the glimpse I had got, it was Bobby Peel, although he was without his European clothing, and had on a 'possum-skin cloak. I had distinctly seen his face by the light of the fire, as I quietly approached from the huts across the grass of the paddock; and, although I had not met him since the day of our first interview, his features were too strongly impressed upon my memory for me to forget them. I found shortly afterwards that he had excellent reasons for keeping out of the way.

After staying some time, and having my pockets emptied of the tobacco which was in them, I left and strolled on to the river. As I drew near its margin I heard a slight splash, as of a turtle startled by my step, and throwing itself into the water; but all was quiet when I reached it; no cry of duck or other waterfowl broke the stillness of the night; and the stream itself, fifty or sixty feet in depth, flowed on silently. The banks were very steep, and the surface of the water was some four yards beneath the level where I stood. There were no trees growing anywhere near; but the dead trunks of several left by former floods projected above the water, or rested against the banks, where, in the dim light, they resembled so many huge antediluvian reptiles. The opposite side of the river, which was 100 yards wide, was an island formed by an ana[1] branch, which left the main stream four miles above the paddock, and joined it again just below it. As I stood looking down on the dark waters, and up and down the reach, and observed that the blacks' fires were less than fifty yards off, I could not help thinking how easily their enemies, if still in the neighbourhood, could, under cover of the river banks, steal unawares upon them. I little thought that in the deep shade beneath the very spot I was then standing on, in the water at my feet, and with their heads concealed behind one of the tree trunks on the margin, already lay hidden the murderous band who, twice baffled, had stolen back for their revenge.

As I walked past them on my way back to the hut, the blacks began one of their monotonous chants, to which the two women beat time with sticks, which they struck together, their eyes sparkling and white teeth glistening in the firelight, as they shouted a merry 'Good-night, doc, doc,' to me.

At the door of our hut I found the superintendent, who had just dismounted. Harris had gone to bed. 'I have some news for you,' Stevenson said to me when we had entered.

He hung his saddle up on a peg projecting from the partition which divided it into two parts, one being used as a storeroom, the other as a bed and sitting, as well as a dining-room. The beds being boards or sheets of bark, with sheepskins laid on them, on which were stretched mattresses stuffed with the 'wongul,' or down of the reeds which abounded everywhere near the river banks. Feds Investigate Companies' Roles in SolarWinds Hack

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is reportedly probing whether companies failed to disclose their involvement in the SolarWinds cyber-breach, marking the first regulatory inquiry related to December's unprecedented hack.

The SEC has sent investigative letters to public issuers and investment firms, asking for voluntary information regarding the effects of the SolarWinds hack and any disclosure failures, according to Reuters.

The SEC's investigation focuses on whether affected companies had lapses in internal controls and issues related to insider trading, in addition to assessing company policies on protecting customer information.

"Our priority at SolarWinds is to work closely with our customers to understand and remedy any issues arising from the attack," a spokesperson for SolarWinds told Al Jazeera English.

The SEC's press office declined to comment on the investigation.

The SolarWinds breach, attributed to Russia's SVR by the U.S. and U.K., allowed hackers to access data from thousands of companies and government offices, affecting SolarWinds' share price.

U.S. securities law mandates that companies must disclose material information, including cyber-breaches, that may affect share prices.

The SEC investigation could lead to enforcement actions for historical disclosure and control failures, but companies responding to the SEC's letters with breach details may be able to avoid such actions.

Kiersten Todt, managing director at the cybersecurity consulting group Liberty Group Ventures LLC, told Reuters that companies may only disclose a breach as material when it immediately affects operations or finances.

The SEC inquiry comes as companies scramble to assess the scope of the breach and determine the severity of its impact on their operations, finances, and customer information.

The SEC's letters were reportedly sent to companies with significant operations in the U.S. and included questions about the companies' awareness of SolarWinds' security vulnerabilities and any related insider trading issues.

In the wake of the SolarWinds hack, cybersecurity experts and government officials have urged companies to shore up their defenses and strengthen their internal controls to prevent and detect future breaches.

The SolarWinds breach has also heightened concerns about the potential for state-sponsored cyberattacks against critical infrastructure and private sector companies.

As the SEC investigates companies' roles in the SolarWinds hack, it remains to be seen whether the probe will lead to stricter disclosure requirements and greater accountability for companies that fail to protect their customers' data.

In the meantime, companies that have been affected by the breach are working to address the vulnerabilities that allowed hackers to gain access to their systems and data.

SolarWinds, for its part, has said that its priority is to work closely with customers to understand and remedy any issues arising from the attack.

As the investigation continues, it is likely that more details about the extent and impact of the SolarWinds breach will come to light, shedding further light on the scope and scale of this unprecedented cyber-breach.

The sun, now dipping low behind the cypress trees, cast long, skeletal shadows across the veranda as the two figures, Courtland and Miss Sally, lingered over their now-abandoned task. The hammer lay silent on the porch, a small, silver glint in the fading light, while the laths leaned precariously against the railing, forgotten monuments to their industrious afternoon.

A moment of companionable silence fell between them, broken only by the chirping of crickets in the rose bushes. Courtland, emboldened by the ease of their conversation, and perhaps by the faint flush he had observed upon Miss Sally's cheek as she recounted her triumphs over adversity, found himself reluctant to part company.

“Yo' seem mighty interested in all this, co'nnle,” Miss Sally finally remarked, her eyes twinkling with a mixture of amusement and something that might have been, dare he hope, admiration. “A city gent like yo', wi' yo' fine clothes and fancy ide's.”

Courtland straightened, a slight defensiveness coloring his tone. “But I assure yo', Miss Sally, my interest is not merely academic. I have long held that the future of this nation lies in the land, in its proper management, in the resilience and ingenuity of those who till it.”

Miss Sally inclined her head, a graceful gesture that belied the calloused hands she now discreetly concealed beneath the folds of her skirt. “Resilience and ingenuity is all we got, suh. After the… trouble. Ain’t much else left.”

He winced, the careless euphemism grating on his ear. The “trouble,” as it was so delicately termed, had left scars far deeper than any plow could turn. Yet, here she stood, a delicate flower blooming amidst the ruins, a testament to the indomitable spirit of Southern womanhood.

“Yo' speak of the future, co'nnle,” she continued, her gaze drifting towards the darkening fields. “But the future requires capital. An' that’s somethin’ mighty scarce ’round heah these days.”

Courtland’s mind raced. He had come to the South as an observer, a student of its economic woes. But now, confronted with the tangible reality of Miss Sally’s struggles, he felt a sudden, almost overwhelming desire to participate. To lend his aid, his expertise, his… well, his resources.

“Perhaps,” he began, choosing his words carefully, “perhaps I might be of some assistance. I have certain… connections. Certain avenues for investment that might prove beneficial.”

Miss Sally turned back to him, her expression unreadable. “Investment? Yo’ talkin’ about lendin’ money, co’nnle? Cause we ain’t askin’ for charity.”

“Certainly not charity!” Courtland exclaimed, his voice perhaps a tad too emphatic. “I envision a partnership, Miss Sally. A mutually beneficial arrangement. Yo' have the land, the knowledge, the… the grit. I possess the means to help yo’ expand, to modernize, to realize the full potential of this estate.”

He paused, catching his breath, suddenly aware of the audacity of his proposition. He, a mere acquaintance, offering to meddle in the affairs of a woman he had barely known for a few hours.

But Miss Sally did not dismiss him out of hand. Instead, she studied him with a shrewdness that belied her youthful appearance. “And what,” she asked, her voice low and thoughtful, “would yo’ get out of this ‘mutually beneficial arrangement,’ co’nnle? Business ain’t never purely charitable, I reckon. Not even from a city gent like you."

Courtland hesitated. He could cite profit margins, return on investment, the satisfaction of contributing to the region’s economic recovery. But those felt hollow, inadequate. The truth was, he felt something stirring within him, something far more complex than mere financial calculation.

“I confess, Miss Sally,” he said finally, meeting her gaze directly, “I am drawn to yo’ vision. Yo’ energy. Yo’… determination. I believe that yo’ are doing something truly remarkable heah. And I want to be a part of it.”

A long silence followed, broken only by the rustling of leaves in the evening breeze. Then, a slow, deliberate smile spread across Miss Sally’s face.

It is with the study, or Miss Thornycroft's parlour, that we have to do today. Its window is thrown open to the hot July sun--to the green lawn and the shrubs underneath--to the bare plateau beyond, on whose edge a coastguardsman was pacing on duty--to the sparkling sea in the distance. The paper of the room was of white and gold, pretty drawings and landscapes in water-colours adorning it. Some of them had been done by Miss Thornycroft, some by her late mother. The carpet and chairs were green; the piano, cabinets, and other furniture were handsome; the white curtains waved in the gentle breeze--altogether it was a room pleasant to look upon.

Seated on the music-stool, her face to the door, was a little middle-aged, brown woman, unmistakably French, without her tongue, which was going fluently, a look of reproach on her naturally placid face. It was Mademoiselle Derode, the governess, resident now some five years at the Red Court. A simple-minded woman, accomplished though she was--good as gold, and timid as her own nature. Richard Thornycroft had related to her some of the ghostly tales connected with the Red Court--or rather with its immediate environs--and she would not have stirred out at night alone for the world. Her chamber window when she first came faced the plateau; after hearing the stories she begged and prayed to be removed into another. Mrs. Thornycroft, alive then, complied with a sad smile, and reproved Richard in her gentle manner for saying anything. If whispers were to be believed, these same ghostly rumours were even then helping to kill Mrs. Thornycroft.

Mademoiselle Derode was en colère this morning with her pupil. French, German, English; good music, harp, and piano; drawing and painting; she was thoroughly versed in all, and had as thoroughly taught. For her age, Miss Thornycroft was an exceedingly well-educated girl, but apt at times to be a rebellious one. In fact she was growing quite beyond the control of the little governess.

The young lady stood by the table facing the window--a tall, very handsome girl of nearly sixteen, with her brother Isaac's fair skin and bright features, and a suspicious look of Richard's resolute lip. She wore a blue muslin dress, blue ribbons in her fair hair; her pretty hands were tossing, not in play but petulance, a large white rose, broken short off from its stalk; her well-shaped head was thrown back; her light clear blue eyes looked out defiantly.

"As if there could be reason in it!" spoke mademoiselle in her quaint but well-pronounced English. "You did but the little half of your lessons yesterday; the other day before it you went out without saying to me the one word; and now this morning you want to go out again. You will not do any one little thing! I say, Miss Mary Anne, that it has not reason in it."

"I promised Captain Copp I would go, mademoiselle. Mrs. Copp will be waiting for me."

"And I promise you that you cannot go," returned the governess, decisively. "My faith! you go, you go, you go; yesterday, today, tomorrow; and where are your studies? I might as well take my departure; I am of no longer use."

"I wish I was that douanier," spoke the young lady with an angry stamp, looking out at the preventive man pacing the edge of the plateau.

"I wish you were--for one day; you would soon wish yourself back again into yourself, Miss Thornycroft. Will you sit down and begin your studies?"

"No; it is too hot to work. German would give me the headache today, mademoiselle."

"I wish your papa, Monsieur the Justice, was at home. I would appeal to him."

These days the name of Lavinia Edwards is but a whisper among the few who still remember her as a prominent figure in the literary circles of rural Vermont. Yet, when one speaks of "Elmwood Manor," a sense of recognition stirs, evoking memories of her most celebrated work, which first saw the light of day in 1895. Though it slipped quietly from the public eye, "A Gentle Summer Breeze" remains a testament to her unique ability to weave the fabric of life in rural America into the intricate tapestry of her novels.

Lavinia Edwards, however, was more than just an author; she was an ardent supporter of the fledgling settlement movement, which aimed to bring people together in harmony with nature. She played a pivotal role in the establishment of the Green Mountain Colony, a utopian community nestled deep within the heart of the Vermont woods. It was here that she not only brought her own writing to life, but also found a sense of purpose in the rustic rhythms and struggles of the settlers.

It was during one of these tumultuous winters, when snowdrifts reached the eaves of the community's communal barn, that Lavinia found inspiration for her most personal work to date. A poignant story of love and loss, "The Fireside Hearth" captures the essence of a young couple's struggle to build a life together amidst the unforgiving beauty of the Vermont wilderness. As the flames danced within the hearth, casting shadows upon the rough-hewn walls, Lavinia's pen moved with a fervor that seemed to channel the very spirits of the forest.

These days, however, few are familiar with Lavinia's oeuvre, and the once-celebrated stories that poured forth from her heart are all but forgotten. The fleeting nature of fame and the relentless march of time have conspired to reduce her to a mere footnote in the annals of literary history. Yet, in the dusty recesses of old bookstores and antiquarian shops, one may still discover a tattered copy of "The Maple Leaf's Lullaby," a poignant ballad that showcases Lavinia's earliest attempts at poetry.

As the seasons passed, and the Green Mountain Colony grew and prospered, Lavinia's own heart began to wander. She found herself drawn to the storied cities of the East, where the thrum of urban life beckoned like a siren's call. It was here, amidst the shifting tides of society and the endless stream of new ideas, that Lavinia would stumble upon a new passion – one that would forever alter the course of her life and guide her toward the creation of her greatest masterpiece, a sweeping epic that would captivate the hearts of readers everywhere and make her name synonymous with the golden light of the American countryside.

Fritz was put out. He had not at all intended to be ferocious to Lotta, and to be made ferocious in the very beginning of the ball was more than he could bear with equanimity. Of all things, this was the very thing which he had most taught himself to dread. He had seen something of the world, though his world had been comprised within narrow limits, and had taught himself to believe that from such a girl as Lotta Schmidt no treatment but tyranny was to be expected. A man must assert himself at once, or she would walk over him as she did over those unfortunate women, her aunts.

Now, he had asserted himself, as he told himself, from the very first. When he found her standing up to dance with Herr Planken, he had at once cut out that old sinner, and had carried off Lotta as his own lawful prize. At that moment he had felt himself to be master of the situation. But how was it with him now? He had asked her to dance again, simply meaning to be kind, and she had snubbed him before the whole room. And how well he had seen that she enjoyed the triumph! He liked her courage, her beauty, her power; but he would let her know that she was not, therefore, to be empress of him.

So he danced with Adela Bruhl, and talked with a gayety that was quite foreign to his habits. Adela Bruhl had fifteen hundred florins! What was fifteen hundred florins to him? She was but a little chit of a thing, who was not for a moment to be compared to Lotta. He waltzed, however, with the one; and when, as he stood fanning himself after his exertions, he saw the other standing opposite to him, he could not resist the temptation of asking her to sup with him.

“Supper!” said Lotta, affecting surprise. “What, already? Is it not too early, Herr Richter?”

Now, Fritz, though he was aware that it wanted an hour to the recognized time, though he would have preferred to postpone the important act for another half-hour at the least, was not the man to be laughed out of his proposition by his own lady-love, in the face of a whole ball-room. It was the very thing to make him carry it out instantly, though it would be sure to be uncomfortable to Lotta, and though he himself would be only too conscious how much more pleasantly the time might be spent.

“Not at all too early for me,” said he. “I suppose I may have supper when I please.”

“Oh, certainly,” said Lotta.

“Will you do me the honour?”

“The honour!” said Lotta.

“If you will condescend so far,” said Fritz, making a bold attempt to regain his good humour.

“I am very hungry, I own,” said Lotta; “and it is better to eat while one has an appetite. Will you take my hand to the supper-room, Herr Richter?”

There was nothing more to be said, and Fritz led her away to the supper-room. It may be doubted whether either of them much enjoyed that slow progression. But this, at any rate, was the fact, that everybody saw that they went together; and everybody knew that Lotta Schmidt had refused to dance with the man who was now taking her down to supper. This is one of those triumphant moments in the career of a young lady which go far to make up for any previous little reverses. There is, of course, something of the bitterness of purchased triumph in it. Such a moment is no doubt somewhat dangerous, as it must be built more or less on deceit. But how many moments come in the lives of young ladies when some amount of such danger must be incurred; and then, how sweet is the triumph!

When at last they were alone, or as nearly alone as they could be in a supper-room, which, to give the manager of the Red Lion his due, was by no means badly crowded, Fritz thought that it became him to begin and make himself agreeable.

“Don't let us stay here all night,” he said, “it’s so terribly hot.”

“Go as soon as you like, then,” said Lotta. “But I am hungry; and as it was your own proposition, you have no right to hurry me.”

This was not fair, and Fritz felt that it was not fair. He had proposed to stay there all night, nor even to hurry Lotta. It had been her special request to him. But he was a man, and it behoved him to bear this.

“But I am hungry too,” he said, “and I want to have some supper.”

The second gong sounded. In the back-verandah, the long table--too long, as though always expecting guests--was laid for three persons. The native butler and half-a-dozen boys stood waiting by the servers' tables and the two sideboards. The butler at once began to fill the soup-plates; and two of the boys placed the three plates of soup on the table, on top of the folded napkins which lay on the dinner-plates. Then they waited again, while the soup steamed gently. Another boy filled the three tumblers with large lumps of ice.

The girl came in, humming a tune. She was perhaps seventeen, and resembled her divorced mother, the resident's first wife, a good-looking half-caste, who was now living in Batavia, where she was said to keep a discreet gaming house. The young girl had a pale olive complexion, sometimes just touched with a peach-like blush; she had beautiful black hair, curling naturally at the temples and wound round her head in a heavy coil; her black pupils and sparkling irises swam in humid bluish-whites, over which her thick lashes flickered up and down, and up again. Her mouth was small and a little full; and her upper lip was just shadowed by a dark, downy line. She was not tall and was already too fully formed, like a hasty rose that has bloomed too soon. She wore a white piqué skirt and a white linen blouse with lace insertions; and round her throat was a bright yellow ribbon that accorded well with her olive pallor, which sometimes flushed up, suddenly, as with a rush of warm blood.

The young man came sauntering in from the front verandah. He was like his father, tall, broad and fair-haired, with a thick, fair moustache. He was barely twenty-three, but looked quite five years older. He wore a suit of white Russian linen, but with a shirt-collar and tie.

Van Oudijck also came at last: his firm step approached as though he were always busy, as though he were now coming just to have some dinner in the midst of his work.

"When does mamma arrive to-morrow?" asked Theo.

"At half-past eleven," replied Van Oudijck; and, turning to his body-servant behind him, "Kario, remember that the mem-sahib is to be fetched from the station at half-past eleven to-morrow."

"Yes, excellency," murmured Kario.

The fish was served.

"Doddie," asked Van Oudijck, "who was with you at the gate just now?"

"At ... the gate?" she asked slowly, in a very soft accent.

"Yes."

"At ... the gate?... Nobody.... Theo perhaps."

"Were you at the gate with your sister?" asked Van Oudijck.

The boy knitted his thick, fair eyebrows:

"Possibly.... Don't know.... Don't remember...."

They were all three silent. They hurried through dinner: sitting at table bored them. The five or six servants, in white cotton jackets with red linen facings, moved softly on their flat toes, waiting quickly and noiselessly. Steak and salad was served, and a pudding, followed by dessert.

"Everlasting rumpsteak!" Theo muttered.

"Yes, that cook!" laughed Doddie, with her little throaty laugh, clipping her sentences in the half-caste fashion. "She always gives steak, when mamma not here; doesn't matter to her, when mamma not here. She has no imagination. Too bad though!"

They had been twenty minutes over their dinner when Van Oudijck went back to his office. Doddie and Theo sauntered towards the front of the house.

"Tedious," Doddie yawned. "Come, we play billiards?"

In the first inner gallery, behind the satin portière, was a small billiard-table.

"Come along," said Theo.

They played.

"Why am I supposed to have been with you at the gate?"

Upon my word, Mercy, your sarcasm is as sharp as ever, I perceive. Yet, Ferdinand, you seem to take these jests lightly; they are not without sting. "I am but a man of decorum, Mercy, not a creature of whimsy," I remonstrated, my voice tinged with mock indignation.

"Oh, but you are, dear Cello," she retorted with a gleam in her eye that bespoke of mischief brewing. "You are a veritable statue, standing rigid against the gale of life's frivolities."

I could not help but join in their jest, laughter punctuating my reply, "A statue, indeed! Pray, do not mistake my upright nature for stiffness. I am merely steadfast in my convictions."

Mercy, ever the rebel, rolled her eyes. "Your convictions are as unyielding as the marble you resemble. Pray, tell us, how do you foresee navigating the tempestuous seas of diplomacy?"

Her jest struck a note of truth that I could not ignore. "I have faith in my abilities, Mercy," I replied, striving for sincerity. "I believe that my adherence to principle will stand me in good stead."

"Faith, indeed!" she scoffed. "You are like a ship anchored in calm waters, convinced that the storm will pass you by. Do not delude yourself, brother. The tides of politics are not predictable, nor is the mercurial nature of alliances."

I bristled at her words, yet knew she spoke with the wisdom of one who had observed more than her fair share of human folly. "Your pessimism is unwarranted, Mercy," I insisted, though doubt began to creep into my heart.

She sighed, a rare display of vulnerability. "It is not pessimism; it is realism. You are spirited, brother, and your spirit will serve you well... provided you temper it with wisdom."

Just then, our father, Father Tiberius, appeared at the threshold, his countenance grave. "Mercy, Ferdinand, step this way," he commanded, his voice a solemn echo in the room.

We approached, curiosity piqued, as he regarded us with an expression that was equal parts fatherly concern and stern authority. "Diplomacy, my son, is as much an art as it is a science. It requires finesse, discretion, and above all, a cool head."

He paused, gathering his thoughts as if bracing himself for a difficult revelation. "Know this, my boy: in our family's history, there have been those who faltered in this art. Relatives in Madrid... let us say, their legacies were not untarnished by the excess of emotion."

His words hung heavy in the air, a reminder of the burdens that weighed upon our lineage. "Control your emotions, Ferdinand, as you would a skittish steed," he continued, "and you shall find your path in diplomacy smoother than you might imagine."

Mercy's expression softened as she regarded me. "Father Tiberius is right, Ferdinand. Be not ashamed to show compassion, but remember, the mask of diplomacy is thin. Wear it well."

As our father's words reverberated in my mind, I felt a resolve stir within me. Mercy's concern was heartfelt, and Father's advice profound. With a newfound determination, I vowed to navigate the tempest of diplomacy with the steadiness of a vessel cut from a marble of resolve, yet flexible enough to ride the waves of change.

"I shall endeavor to meet this challenge with the grace and fortitude you both suggest," I declared, my voice firm. "Our family legacy shall not be one marked by excess, but by balance."

Mercy smiled, a rare expression of approval gracing her lips. "That, dear brother, is the mark of a true diplomat."

But as we turned to leave, the warmth of our exchange was tempered by the stark reminder of the distance that lay between us; the distance forged by differing perspectives and the unspoken scars of our past. Yet, in the quiet understanding passed between siblings, I found solace, a silent promise that, despite our disparate views, our bond remained unbroken.

And so, as night descended upon us, I contemplated the path ahead, a path paved with the lessons of family, the weight of history, and the enduring truths of human nature. It was a path I knew would test my mettle, but with Mercy's support and Father Tiberius' wisdom, I felt ready to embrace the challenges that lay before me.

"He--he dared to think," Harriet gasped, her voice shaking with the echo of suppressed fury, "that I, Harriet Ellison, could ever stoop to such a fate! To be spirited away like some silly, lovestruck child, stripped of my name, my standing, my very dignity!" Her hands, clenched tightly in her lap, trembled with the effort of restraint.

Mattie watched her, her own brow furrowed with concern. "He believed you loved him, then?"

"Loved him!" The very notion was met with a burst of bitter laughter. "He, with his honeyed words and duplicitous smiles! Oh, he played the ardent suitor well enough, I'll grant him that. He mistook my kindness, my willingness to believe in the good in others, for some foolish infatuation." She rose and paced the room, her agitation lending a swift, agitated grace to her movements.

"How could you bear it, Harriet? To know his intentions, to see through his facade..." Mattie's voice trailed off, the sheer audacity of such deception leaving her momentarily speechless.

"It was a game, my dear," Harriet replied, her voice regaining its usual strength, though laced now with a steely undertone. "He laid his trap, and I, unwittingly, stepped into its perimeter. But I am not so easily ensnared, Mattie. I saw the threads of his deceit long before he thought to tighten them."

A wry smile touched her lips as she recalled the moment clarity pierced through Darcy's web of lies. It had begun innocently enough, a seemingly impromptu invitation to accompany him on a trip to Dover. He spoke of urgent business, of needing a trusted companion, his words dripping with concern and veiled urgency. A lesser woman, Harriet mused, might have been swayed by his earnestness, blinded by his carefully constructed facade.

But Harriet was made of sterner stuff. His very eagerness, the way his eyes darted nervously as he spoke, betrayed the falsity of his words. And then, there was the matter of the carriage he had so thoughtfully arranged - one that bore the distinct markings of a route extending far beyond the shores of England. Dover, she realised with a chilling certainty, was but a stepping stone in his scheme, a mere prelude to whisking her away to some remote corner where her name, her reputation, would count for nothing.

She had allowed him to spin his tale, playing the part of the unsuspecting fool, all the while her mind raced, plotting her escape from this charade. She would not afford him the satisfaction of seeing her fear, her vulnerability. No, she would meet his deception with a cunning of her own.

As they journeyed towards Dover, Harriet feigned ignorance, her demeanour a careful blend of naive trust and quiet anticipation. She listened patiently to his meandering tales of urgent business affairs, her responses measured, her thoughts a whirlwind of anger and quiet calculation.

The anger, she realized, was not for herself alone. It was for the audacity of his presumption, for the belief that he could so easily manipulate and control a woman of her standing. It was for the insult to her intelligence, her ability to discern truth from the elaborate fabrication he had woven around them.

Yet, even in her fury, a sense of grim satisfaction settled upon her. She had seen through his deceit, she had played his game and emerged victorious. And now, she would turn the tables entirely.

With each passing mile, a plan began to form in her mind, a plan that would see her safely away from Darcy's clutches, her dignity intact. It would unfold subtly, she decided, like the slow unfurling of a rose, revealing its thorns only at the final, decisive moment.

They would stop at Ashford, she announced, feigning a sudden bout of fatigue. The change in plans, though unexpected, did not seem to raise Darcy's suspicions. He readily agreed, his eagerness to appease her momentarily eclipsing any lingering doubts.

It was at Ashford, Harriet knew, that their paths would diverge, hers leading towards safety and freedom, his towards the bitter sting of failure. And as the carriage rumbled closer to their destination, a flicker of something akin to triumph danced in her eyes, a testament to the resilience of a woman scorned.

The town of Micklethwayte was rising and thriving. There were salubrious springs which an enterprising doctor had lately brought into notice. The firm of Greenleaf and Dutton manufactured umbrellas in large quantities, from the stout weather-proof family roof down to the daintiest fringed toy of a parasol. There were a Guild Hall and a handsome Corn Market. There was a Modern School for the boys, and a High School for the girls, and a School of Art, and a School of Cookery, and National Schools, and a British School, and a Board School, also churches of every height, chapels of every denomination, and iron mission rooms budding out in hopes to be replaced by churches.

Like one of the animals which zoologists call radiated, the town was constantly stretching out fresh arms along country roads, all living and working, and gradually absorbing the open spaces between. One of these arms was known as St. Ambrose's Road, in right of the church, an incomplete structure in yellow brick, consisting of a handsome chancel, the stump of a tower, and one aisle just weather-tight and usable, but, by its very aspect, begging for the completion of the beautiful design that was suspended above the alms-box.

It was the evening of a summer day which had been very hot. The choir practice was just over, and the boys came out trooping and chattering; very small ones they were; for as soon as they began to sing tolerably they were sure to try to get into the choir of the old church, which had a foundation that fed, clothed, taught, and finally apprenticed them. So, though the little fellows were clad in surplices and cassocks, and sat in the chancel for correctness sake, there was a space round the harmonium reserved for the more trustworthy band of girls and young women who came forth next, followed by four or five mechanics.

Behind came the nucleus of the choir--a slim, fair-haired youth of twenty; a neat, precise, well-trimmed man, closely shaven, with stooping shoulders, at least fifteen years older, with a black poodle at his heels, as well shorn as his master, newly risen from lying outside the church door; a gentle, somewhat drooping lady in black, not yet middle-aged and very pretty; a small eager, unformed, black-eyed girl, who could hardly keep back her words for the outside of the church door; a tall self-possessed handsome woman, with a fine classical cast of features; and lastly, a brown-faced, wiry hardworking clergyman, without an atom of superfluous flesh, but with an air of great energy.

'Oh! vicar, where are we to go?' was the question so eager to break forth.

'Not to the Crystal Palace, Nuttie. The funds won't bear it. Mr. Dutton says we must spend as little as possible on locomotion.'

'I'm sure I don't care for the Crystal Palace. A trumpery tinsel place, all shams.'

'Hush, hush, my dear, not so loud,' said the quiet lady; but Nuttie only wriggled her shoulders, though her voice was a trifle lowered. 'If it were the British Museum now, or Westminster Abbey.'

'Or the Alps,' chimed in a quieter voice, 'or the Ufizzi.'

'Now, Mr. Dutton, that's not what I want. Our people aren't ready for that, but what they have let it be real. Miss Mary, don't you see what I mean?'

'Rather better than Miss Egremont herself,' said Mr. Dutton.

'Well,' said the vicar, interposing in the wordy war, 'Mrs. Greenleaf's children have scarlatina, so we can't go to Horton Bishop. The choice seems to be between South Beach and Monks Horton.'

Colonial Pipeline Ransomware Attack Highlights Urgent Need for Cybersecurity Overhaul

In a brazen cyberattack, Colonial Pipeline, operator of the largest fuel pipeline in the United States, has fallen victim to a ransomware attack by the notorious DarkSide group. The attackers managed to steal over 100GB of sensitive data, prompting Colonial Pipeline to pay a hefty ransom of nearly $5 million for a decryption key.

DarkSide, known for its double-extortion tactic, has yet to post Colonial Pipeline's data on its leak site, sparking speculation that the group may be reconsidering its strategy due to potential "social" problems. Despite this, the attack has already raised concerns about the vulnerability of critical US infrastructure to cyber threats.

As of May 11, Colonial Pipeline's data had not appeared on DarkSide's leak site, leading some to speculate that the group may be reconsidering its strategy. However, the damage has already been done, with the attack highlighting systemic vulnerabilities in the country's critical infrastructure.

The Colonial Pipeline attack is just the latest in a series of high-profile cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure. In April, a ransomware attack forced a city in Florida to shut down its drinking water system, while a power outage in Ukraine was caused by a cyberattack in 2015. These incidents underscore the urgent need for a review and improvement of cybersecurity practices in the US.

In response to the growing threat of ransomware attacks, Bitdefender has noted the increasing appeal of critical infrastructure to ransomware operators, citing remote maintenance vulnerabilities as a key concern. To address this issue, a new order has been issued emphasizing cybersecurity measures such as multi-factor authentication, data encryption, and a zero-trust security model.

To enforce and monitor these new security protocols, a Cybersecurity Safety Review Board will be established. The board will be responsible for ensuring that critical infrastructure operators are taking the necessary steps to protect their systems from cyber threats.

The Colonial Pipeline attack serves as a stark reminder of the importance of cybersecurity in today's digital age. As more and more critical infrastructure is connected to the internet, the risk of cyberattacks will only continue to grow. It is imperative that steps are taken to protect these systems and ensure the safety and security of the public.

In conclusion, the ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline highlights the urgent need for a review and improvement of cybersecurity practices in the US. The establishment of a Cybersecurity Safety Review Board and the emphasis on cybersecurity measures such as multi-factor authentication, data encryption, and a zero-trust security model are positive steps towards addressing this issue. It is crucial that critical infrastructure operators take the necessary steps to protect their systems from cyber threats and ensure the safety and security of the public.

Cuomo's Shadow Lingers in New York Politics Amid Ongoing Speculation

CNN – More than three months after his resignation in the wake of multiple sexual harassment allegations, former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo remains a notable figure in the state's political landscape. While his departure marked a significant moment in New York's political history, the controversy surrounding him does not seem to have subsided, with discussions and speculations about his future continuing to swirl.

A recent report from the New York state assembly concluded that there was "overwhelming evidence" to support accusations against Cuomo of sexual harassment and a lack of transparency regarding COVID-19-related deaths in nursing homes during his tenure. Despite this, Cuomo continues to assert his innocence, maintaining that he did not engage in any misconduct and characterizing his profits from a pandemic-themed memoir as fully compliant with ethical standards.

"We’re challenging the credibility of the report and have a strong basis for our defense," said Rita Glavin, Cuomo's lawyer. Her comments reflect a consistent narrative from Cuomo and his team, who have strenuously denied the allegations and remain engaged in legal battles related to the findings of the New York Attorney General’s investigation.

As the newly appointed Governor Kathy Hochul steps into her leadership role, she is seen as ushering in a more collaborative and inclusive political era. Hochul's rise comes at a time when Cuomo's lingering influence continues to hover over New York politics. Local politicians express mixed feelings about the ramifications of Cuomo's possible return to political life.

"Cuomo's legacy is undeniably complex," remarked State Senator Andrew Gounardes. "While he has made substantial contributions to New York's infrastructure and policy, the allegations against him cast a long shadow over any potential resurgence." The juxtaposition of Cuomo's achievements against the controversies he faced has created a nuanced dialogue among the state's political class.

Within Cuomo's inner circle, speculation has emerged about potential paths he might pursue, including a bid for the office of state attorney general, a position he previously occupied from 2007 to 2010. "You never want to count anyone out in politics," noted Chris Coffey, a New York political strategist. "Cuomo has a history of resilience, and if the narrative shifts in his favor, he could try to make a comeback."

However, skepticism remains about Cuomo's ability to rally the financial resources necessary for a new campaign. Legal expenses stemming from the harassment allegations are reported to have taken a toll on his finances. "At this stage, it’s uncertain just how deep his pockets are," said Jay Jacobs, New York's state Democratic Party chairman. "The political landscape may not be kind to someone with a checkered past."

Cuomo's communication with the public is largely filtered through his spokesman, Rich Azzopardi, who vehemently denies any wrongdoing. Azzopardi stated, "The narrative against the Governor is not backed by facts, and we will continue to fight against these unfounded allegations." This defense underscores Cuomo’s strategy of remaining in the public eye—even if indirectly—while still contesting the findings of the investigation.

In the past few months, speculation about Cuomo’s future plans has elicited mixed reactions among progressive circles. Political consultant Monica Klein pointed out, "His presence has become a cautionary tale for those in office. It raises the question of how to move forward without fully reckoning with the past." This creates tension for Democrats, who must navigate the delicate intersection of Cuomo's past governance and their need for progressive reform.

Despite being sidelined, Cuomo’s future in politics remains a topic ripe for media speculation, fueled by whispers of possible comebacks. As the narrative surrounding his resignation continues to evolve, it remains to be seen whether he can truly step back into the arena he once dominated, or if his legacy will forever be marred by the shadows of controversy.

On market-days alone, its Great Place suddenly leaped out of bed. On market-days, some friendly enchanter struck his staff upon the stones of the Great Place, and instantly arose the liveliest booths and stalls, and sittings and standings, and a pleasant hum of chaffering and huckstering from many hundreds of tongues, and a pleasant, though peculiar, blending of colours,--white caps, blue blouses, and green vegetables,--and at last the Knight destined for the adventure seemed to have come in earnest, and all the Vaubanois sprang up awake. And now, by long, low-lying avenues of trees, jolting in white-hooded donkey-cart, and on donkey-back, and in tumbril and wagon, and cart and cabriolet, and afoot with barrow and burden,--and along the dikes and ditches and canals, in little peak-prowed country boats,--came peasant-men and women in flocks and crowds, bringing articles for sale. And here you had boots and shoes, and sweetmeats and stuffs to wear, and here (in the cool shade of the Town-hall) you had milk and cream and butter and cheese, and here you had fruits and onions and carrots, and all things needful for your soup, and here you had poultry and flowers and protesting pigs, and here new shovels, axes, spades, and bill-hooks for your farming work, and here huge mounds of bread, and here your unground grain in sacks, and here your children's dolls, and here the cake-seller, announcing his wares by beat and roll of drum. And hark! fanfaronade of trumpets, and here into the Great Place, resplendent in an open carriage, with four gorgeously- attired servitors up behind, playing horns, drums, and cymbals, rolled "the Daughter of a Physician" in massive golden chains and ear-rings, and blue-feathered hat, shaded from the admiring sun by two immense umbrellas of artificial roses, to dispense (from motives of philanthropy) that small and pleasant dose which had cured so many thousands! Toothache, earache, headache, heartache, stomach-ache, debility, nervousness, fits, fainting, fever, ague, all equally cured by the small and pleasant dose of the great Physician's great daughter! The process was this,--she, the Daughter of a Physician, proprietress of the superb equipage you now admired with its confirmatory blasts of trumpet, drum, and cymbal, told you so: On the first day after taking the small and pleasant dose, you would feel no particular influence beyond a most harmonious sensation of indescribable and irresistible joy; on the second day you would be so astonishingly better that you would think yourself changed into somebody else; on the third day you would be entirely free from disorder, whatever its nature and however long you had had it, and would seek out the Physician's Daughter to throw yourself at her feet, kiss the hem of her garment, and buy as many more of the small and pleasant doses as by the sale of all your few effects you could obtain; but she would be inaccessible,--gone for herbs to the Pyramids of Egypt,--and you would be (though cured) reduced to despair! Thus would the Physician's Daughter drive her trade (and briskly too), and thus would the buying and selling and mingling of tongues and colours continue, until the changing sunlight, leaving the Physician's Daughter in the shadow of high roofs, admonished her to jolt out westward, with a departing effect of gleam and glitter on the splendid equipage and brazen blast. And now the enchanter struck his staff upon the stones of the Great Place once more, and down went the booths, the sittings and standings, and vanished the merchandise, and with it the barrows, donkeys, donkey-carts, and tumbrils, and all other things on wheels and feet, except the slow scavengers with unwieldy carts and meagre horses clearing up the rubbish, assisted by the sleek town pigeons, better plumped out than on non-market days. While there was yet an hour or two to wane before the autumn sunset, the loiterer outside town-gate and drawbridge, and postern and double-ditch, would see the last white-hooded cart lessening in the avenue of lengthening shadows of trees, or the last country boat, paddled by the last market-woman on her way home, showing black upon the reddening, long, low, narrow dike between him and the mill; and as the paddle-parted scum and weed closed over the boat's track, he might be comfortably sure that its sluggish rest would be troubled no more until next market-day.

Buddhism's establishment in Thailand, a process spanning over two millennia, was facilitated significantly by the patronage of Emperor Asoka of the Mauryan Empire. While Asoka’s personal interpretation of Buddhist tenets bore traces of his Hindu background, its direct impact on doctrinal Buddhism remained relatively limited. His enduring contribution lay in his active propagation of the faith across his vast empire, which indirectly facilitated the transmission of Buddhism to regions including what is now Thailand. This initial introduction, however, provided only the seed; it would be centuries before uniquely Thai expressions of Buddhism emerged, particularly with the rise of the Thudong tradition.

The late 19th century in Thailand witnessed the burgeoning of the Thudong tradition, a movement marked by the emergence of forest-dwelling monks who deliberately distanced themselves from the scholarly pursuits and institutionalized routines of established monasteries. These monks embraced a lifestyle of deliberate austerity and wandering. They forsook the relative comfort and security of temple life to inhabit the forests, subsisting solely on alms obtained through daily begging rounds. Their existence was a constant negotiation with the challenges presented by the natural world. They faced the ever-present threat of encounters with wild animals, risked contracting illnesses without access to conventional medical care, and, as their spiritual practices emphasized introspection, sometimes grappled with perceived encounters with malevolent spirits in the solitude of the forest.

The asceticism practiced by Thudong monks involved a complex relationship with accepted Buddhist texts and practices. While the Pali Canon remained the foundation of their belief system, the Visuddhimagga (The Path of Purification), a later commentary not officially part of the Canon, held particular significance. This text, detailing a systematic approach to meditation and spiritual progress, served as a practical guide for their intensive efforts to attain enlightenment. In embracing the Visuddhimagga with such fervor, the Thudong monks arguably prioritized a text of later origin over the established canon, a deviation from more conventional Theravada Buddhist practice. Further defining their distinct practices was the adoption, to varying degrees, of the Dhutangas, a set of thirteen ascetic observances designed to strip away attachments and cultivate detachment. These observances included dwelling only in forests, living under trees, wearing robes made from discarded cloth, and eating only one meal a day taken directly from alms bowls.

The Thudong tradition, with its emphasis on forest dwelling, reliance on begging, and embrace of ascetic practices, engendered a unique religious culture within Thai Buddhism. By actively choosing a lifestyle characterized by minimal possessions, physical hardship, and intensive meditation, the Thudong monks distinguished themselves from more conventional monastic orders. Their choices, influenced by a desire for accelerated spiritual growth and a return to what they perceived as the original spirit of Buddhist practice, created a distinct form of Buddhism characterized by its rigorous asceticism and deep connection with the natural world, one that continues to influence religious practice in Thailand today.

Facebook warns of slower revenue growth amid fight against fake news

Facebook continues to attract users even as lawmakers and regulators increase pressure on the world's largest social network to crack down on misinformation, but it warned that it expects revenue growth to slow down in the third and fourth quarters.

Facebook said Wednesday that 2.9 billion people visit the social network every month, a rise of 7% from the second quarter last year. The steady stream of users pushed the company's revenue and earnings for the April-June quarter above Wall Street's expectations.

Facebook raked in $29.07 billion in revenue, a 56% rise from the same quarter a year earlier. The company chalked up $3.61 in earnings per share, beating the $3.03 forecast by analysts surveyed by Thomson Reuters.

The strong results come as Facebook continues to face criticism it isn't doing enough to fight false claims about coronavirus vaccines. US President Joe Biden has urged platforms like Facebook to tackle the problem.

The social network says it directs people to authoritative sources of information, labels posts and works with fact-checkers. The spread of misinformation has been an ongoing problem for the social network, including during the US presidential election. On Wednesday a group of Facebook critics placed body bags in front of the social network's offices in DC as part of a protest against disinformation.

Despite the company beating Wall Street's expectations, Facebook stock was down more than 4% in after-hours trading, to $356.46 per share. Though the company grew its monthly active users globally, Facebook's European users dropped by 2 million, to 420 million monthly active users, from the first to the second quarter. The number of US Facebook users remained flat at 259 million.

Facebook CFO Dave Wehner said in a call with analysts that the drop in European users was due to "seasonal slowness" and the impact of countries reopening after more than a year of lockdowns because of the coronavirus pandemic.

A new Apple feature that restricts Facebook's ability to gather data from its users has also prompted questions about how successfully it'll be able to target ads.

"We continue to expect increased ad targeting headwinds in 2021 from regulatory and platform changes, notably the recent iOS updates, which we expect to have a greater impact in the third quarter compared to the second quarter. This is factored into our outlook," Facebook said in a statement.

Investing in creators, new features

Facebook, like its rivals Twitter and TikTok, has been ramping up efforts to attract more creators to the social network. The company said it plans to invest more than $1 billion in creators who make content for Facebook and its photo and video app Instagram.

The company also rolled out a live audio product, a website to create and share newsletters, and other tools to help creators earn more money. Increasing the quality of content on the social network could help Facebook entice users to spend more time on the site and compete against video apps such as TikTok.

Facebook has also been testing out different types of ads, including in virtual reality.

Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg told analysts the company's investment in creators and e-commerce is going to be an important part of the "metaverse" the social network is building. Zuckerberg described the metaverse as "a virtual environment where you can be present with people in digital spaces."

"Digital goods and creators are just going to be huge, right, in terms of people expressing themselves through their avatars," Zuckerberg said.

Facebook said this week it formed a group that focuses on the metaverse and is ramping up hiring. On Wednesday, the company like Google said it will require that workers who return to the office in the US be vaccinated.
