There was something in Robert’s tone that struck Frederic as disingenuous, though he could not pinpoint exactly what it was. Perhaps it was the faint flicker of triumph in the younger man’s eyes, or the subtle air of self-assurance that seemed to have taken root in him since his rise.

“Your gratitude is well-placed,” Frederic said curtly, unable to disguise the bitterness in his voice. “I trust you will serve my aunt with the same dedication you have displayed thus far.”

Robert’s smile widened, and for a moment, Frederic fancied he saw a glint of steel beneath the younger man’s quiet demeanor. “I shall do my utmost, sir,” he said, bowing slightly before turning to leave.

As the door closed behind Robert, Frederic sank back into his chair, his mind a whirlwind of conflicting emotions. He could not deny that the younger man had a certain tenacity about him, a quality that Frederic had always lacked. Yet the thought of Robert occupying the position that had once been his was galling, and he could not shake the feeling that he had been supplanted not merely by merit, but by fate itself.

The days that followed were a flurry of activity as Frederic sought to secure new lodgings and make the necessary arrangements for his transition. Mrs. Vernon had been true to her word, providing him with a sum sufficient to cover his immediate needs, though she had made it clear that further support would depend on his ability to stand on his own.

In the evenings, as he sat alone in his new quarters, Frederic often found himself reflecting on his recent circumstances. The loss of his position had been a blow to his pride, yet he could not deny that the freedom from mundane tasks was something of a relief. Still, the thought of Robert Frost taking his place gnawed at him, a constant reminder of his own failings.

One evening, as he walked through the park, he encountered Robert, who was deep in conversation with a gentleman whose air of importance suggested he was a man of consequence. Frederic paused, his curiosity piqued, as he listened to snippets of their dialogue.

“I am most grateful for the opportunity, sir,” Robert was saying, his tone deferential yet firm. “I assure you, Mr. Thompson, that your confidence in me will not be misplaced.”

The gentleman nodded, his expression one of approval. “I have heard much about your diligence, Frost. I am confident that you will serve me well.”

Frederic felt a strange mix of admiration and discomfort as he watched Robert walk away with a spring in his step. The younger man’s confidence was almost palpable, and it was clear that his prospects were rising swiftly.

As he turned to leave, Frederic could not help but wonder if there was a lesson to be learned from Robert’s success. Perhaps, just perhaps, there was still time for him to emulate the determination that had carried Robert so far. Though the path ahead was uncertain, he could not shake the feeling that his own future might yet hold possibilities he had never dared to imagine.

Citi's $900 Million Blunder: A Wake-Up Call for User Experience in Financial Software

In an astonishing mishap that seems more like a cautionary tale than reality, Citibank accidentally transferred $900 million to its client’s creditors, a staggering 100 times more than the intended $7.8 million payment. The root cause of this blunder? A poorly designed user interface within the bank’s software. This error brought to fore the perils of design debt in corporate software, casting a shadow over traditional banking operations and raising serious questions about the future of user experience (UX) design in the financial industry.

A subsequent court ruling turned heads when it was decided in favor of the creditors. The verdict shed light on the human aspect of the error, pointing to the software's complicated instruction manual and Citi's internal 'six eyes process' – a review protocol requiring three people to approve a transaction. Despite these measures, the failure happened, underscoring the critical role that software design plays in operational efficiency and risk management.

The banking software at the center of this controversy, known as Flexcube, was flagged for having a design defect that significantly contributed to the $900 million mistake. This mishap is a glaring example of design debt, where compromises in UX design accumulate over time, eventually leading to catastrophic errors.

Experts argue that improving employee UX design offers a substantial opportunity to minimize errors and boost productivity across various industries. However, despite the critical nature of such interfaces, only about half of design teams are currently focused on employee-facing software — a proportion that is expected to increase in light of recent events.

Citi, while having shown a commitment to consumer-facing UX with substantial investments, appears to have overlooked the importance of employee-facing software, like Flexcube. This incident serves as a harsh reminder of the need for a balanced focus on both external and internal software environments.

The Flexcube debacle may now force software vendors to reconsider their priorities, with an increased emphasis on UX improvements to preclude similar financial fiascos. Historical instances of bad UX have led to significant mistakes, including the USS John McCain naval accident, the false Hawaii missile test warning, and the Three Mile Island meltdown, all underscoring the profound impact of UX design on safety and operational integrity.

In conclusion, Citi's $900 million error underlines a critical juncture for businesses everywhere. Emphasizing better UX in software design is not just about enhancing aesthetics or functionality; it’s about securing the foundation of our financial and operational systems against the risks of human error. For businesses, the path forward is clear: invest in UX to foster higher employee satisfaction, accelerate training processes, capture greater market share, and, most importantly, avoid costly mistakes that can have far-reaching consequences.

It wouldn’t do, I told myself, to appear too eager. Their very celebrity, now faded but once so potent, seemed to hang about them like the scent of lavender, pleasant enough but suggestive of a certain mustiness, of things past their prime. I toyed with my pen, tapping it lightly against the polished mahogany of my desk, a habit Mrs. Monarch seemed to find endearing. Her lips, once famed for their cupid’s bow, twitched upwards in what I supposed was meant to be a playful moue. The Major, however, remained stoic, his military bearing as impeccable as ever, though his uniform, I noted with a touch of pity, was beginning to show its age.

“We understand, of course,” he boomed, his voice still retaining its parade-ground resonance, “that you may have reservations. Amateurs, after all…”

“Oh, but Major,” Mrs. Monarch interjected, her voice a delicate flutter compared to her husband’s pronouncements, “we are hardly amateurs, not in the strictest sense. Why, our likenesses have graced countless publications!”

“Indeed,” the Major chimed in, “cartes de visite, cabinet cards, even those new-fangled photographic postcards. Our faces, my dear sir, are familiar to thousands.”

I allowed myself a small, carefully neutral smile. Familiarity, in my line of work, was a double-edged sword. While it was true that the public might find a certain comfort in recognizing the Monarchs, there was also the risk of their features seeming, dare I say it, somewhat shopworn. The very ubiquity of their images, once a testament to their desirability, now threatened to undermine the very quality they sought to peddle: their ability to embody, to represent, rather than simply be.

And yet, I had to admit, there was an undeniable allure to their proposition. The opportunity to capture such renowned visages, to immortalize them (for what else was illustration but a form of immortality?) in the pages of an édition de luxe, was tempting, to say the least. My mind raced with possibilities, envisioning their faces etched into copperplate, their forms lending themselves to the delicate strokes of steel engraving.

“Have you, by any chance,” I ventured, “retained copies of these… publications?”

“Oh, mountains of them, dear boy, mountains!” boomed the Major, a touch too eagerly, I thought. Mrs. Monarch, however, seemed to sense my hesitation.

“Perhaps,” she suggested, her voice soft as velvet, “a more… intimate setting would be conducive to your deliberations. We are, as it happens, quite at home in front of the camera. A private viewing, so to speak, at your convenience?”

There it was, the subtle reminder of their past glory, the unspoken implication that I would be privy to a glimpse of something rare and precious. I confess, my curiosity was piqued. Could these faded celebrities, these relics of a bygone era, still possess the power to captivate, to inspire? The thought, I realized, both intrigued and terrified me.

“That,” I replied, allowing a sliver of interest to creep into my voice, “could be arranged.”

The Paradise of Unregarded Desolate Longings

As I stood beside the Sierra Nevada's rugged shore, the moonlight casting an argent glow upon the tranquil lake that lay before me, I could not shake off the feeling of wistfulness that had settled within my breast. The recollection of the events of the day still lingered vividly, and my imagination, now freed from the delirious haze of Philip Traum's sorcery, struggled to reconcile the hideous tragedies of the past with the indelible imprint of bliss that seemed, against all reason, to cling to the memory of that ill-fated hour.

The storm that had ravaged the castle, the fire that had devoured its ancient stones, and the earthquake that had rent asunder its very foundations – all these seemed to have transpired in a far-off realm, and not in this so peaceful landscape, where the only sounds to be heard were the gentle lapping of the waves against the shore and the soft rustle of the reeds that swayed in the breeze. Yet, the visions of the day still danced before my eyes, like specters of a ghastly dance.

And now, as I stood there, lost in the profundity of my own thoughts, the heavens above me began to darken, as if in sympathy with the turmoil that raged within my soul. The moon, a silver crescent now, seemed to be shrouded in a veil of gloom, and the stars twinkled with a distant, mournful light. The air grew thick with an oppressive silence, as if the very earth itself held its breath in anticipation of some impending calamity.

As the shadows deepened and the night grew more somber, I felt a presence beside me, and, turning to my right, I beheld Philip Traum standing by the lake's edge, his eyes gleaming with an otherworldly light, and his smile, a thin-lipped, diabolical thing, which seemed to rake the darkness for its own hidden secrets. His voice, low and husky, spoke words that were an eerie echo of my own thoughts: "In this realm of shadows and silences, where the winds howl like a chorus of the damned, is it not fitting that we should meet once more?"

In the pause that followed, I felt the weight of his gaze upon me, a piercing scrutiny that seemed to probe the very recesses of my being. His eyes, bright with an infernal light, seemed to hold a secret, a gleam of knowledge that I could not quite fathom. I felt a creeping sense of unease, a feeling that I was being drawn, inexorably, into some infernal scheme, some web of sorcery from which there was no escape.

As we stood there, the only sound being the soft lapping of the water against the shore, the darkness around us began to take on a life of its own, as if the very shadows themselves were alive and coalescing into some ghastly form. The moon, now hidden behind a veil of cloud, cast an eerie, sickly light upon the landscape, a light that seemed to sear the very soul.

And then, with a suddenness that was almost palpable, the air around us seemed to thicken, and I felt a weight, a presence that pressed upon me like a physical force. It was as if some unseen hand had jerked the very fabric of reality, and we were left floating, suspended, in a world that was both familiar and strange.

Philip Traum's laughter, a low, mirthless sound, broke the spell, and I felt myself drawn back to the world of men, though a world that seemed to be shrouded in a grotesque, impossible light. His eyes, still fixed upon me, seemed to laugh at some private joke, a jest that I could not comprehend. And as I gazed into their depths, I felt my own sanity begin to slip, as if I were being pulled down some dark and winding stair, into a realm where the very laws of reality no longer held sway.

In that moment of disorientation, the world around me seemed to dissolve, leaving only the presence of Philip Traum, an unseen force that drew me, inexorably, into some abyss of the unknown. His smile, that thin, inhuman thing, seemed to mock me, to mock the very fabric of reality itself. And I knew, in that instant, that I was lost, forever lost, in a world of horrors, a world of unregarded desolate longings.

The darkness closed in around me, a living, breathing thing, and I felt myself succumb to its tender ministrations. The world, now a twisted, grotesque thing, seemed to writhe and twist beneath me, as if in agony. And in the midst of this chaos, Philip Traum stood, a calm, untroubled figure, his eyes aglow with an otherworldly light, a light that seemed to draw me, inexorably, into the very depths of hell itself.

Sen. Graham Vows Action Against Twitter, Challenges Big Tech Legal Protections

WASHINGTON (WCSC) – In response to Twitter's controversial decision to permanently ban President Donald Trump from the platform, U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham has vowed to take legislative action to remove protections that shield tech companies like Twitter from lawsuits. The move comes as part of a broader critique of "Big Tech" and its influence on public discourse.

The contentious ban was enacted after Twitter assessed that two tweets from Trump contravened its policies against promoting violence. One of the tweets declared Trump would not attend President-elect Joe Biden's inauguration, a statement Twitter argued could potentially be interpreted as encouragement for violent acts similar to those seen at the U.S. Capitol.

"This decision by Twitter not only silences the sitting President of the United States but also highlights a double standard," Graham remarked. He compared Trump's ban to the active presence of foreign leaders, such as Iran’s Ayatollah, who are permitted to tweet freely. The senator expressed concern over the influence and power these platforms wield.

Graham claims that social media giants enjoy "absolute immunity from being sued," a state he asserts is granted by Congress through Section 230. This section provides a legal shield for tech companies against liability for content posted by users on their platforms. Graham is advocating for its repeal, aiming to place these tech entities on the same legal footing as other American companies.

The outcry from Graham and other conservatives comes amidst heightened scrutiny of social media's role in the events leading to the Capitol riot. Following the unrest, which followed a rally where Trump reiterated unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud, Twitter locked his account citing rhetoric that some say incited violence.

Twitter defended its decision, expressing its reasoning in more detail. The platform stated that Trump's language, specifically the use of "American Patriots" in his tweets, could be interpreted as support for the rioters. Twitter further justified the ban by pointing to discussions of future violence, including possible armed protests and further attacks on government buildings.

Graham’s push to remove these protections underscores a growing battle between lawmakers and influential tech companies. As political figures grapple with the implications of digital platforms in shaping national discourse, calls to regulate or reform the tech industry have gained momentum.

The discourse surrounding Section 230 and the role of Big Tech is poised to become a focal point of legislative efforts as policymakers like Graham seek to rebalance the legal and ethical landscape of social media. With the future of online speech and tech accountability at stake, the conversation promises to remain highly charged in the coming months.

The man in the doorway smiled as over the misdemeanour of somebody very dear and lovable, and rising from his chair felt his way to a corner shelf, took down a box, and drew from it a violin swathed in a silk bag. He removed the covering with reverential hands. The tenderness of his face was like that of a young mother dressing or undressing her child. As he fingered the instrument his hands seemed to have become all eyes. They wandered caressingly over the polished surface as if enamoured of the perfect thing that they had created, lingering here and there with rapturous tenderness on some special beauty—the graceful arch of the neck, the melting curves of the cheeks, the delicious swell of the breasts.

When he had satisfied himself for the moment, he took the bow, and lifting the violin under his chin, inclined his head fondly toward it and began to play.

The tone at first seemed muffled, but had a curious bite, that began in distant echoes, but after a few minutes’ playing grew firmer and clearer, ringing out at last with velvety richness and strength until the atmosphere was satiated with harmony. No more ethereal note ever flew out of a bird’s throat than Anthony Croft set free from this violin, his liebling, his “swan song,” made in the year he had lost his eyesight.

Anthony Croft had been the only son of his mother, and she a widow. His boyhood had been exactly like that of all the other boys in Edgewood, save that he hated school a trifle more, if possible, than any of the others; though there was a unanimity of aversion in this matter that surprised and wounded teachers and parents.

The school was the ordinary district school of that time; there were not enough scholars for what Cyse Higgins called a “degraded” school. The difference between Anthony and the other boys lay in the reason for as well as the degree of his abhorrence.

He had come into the world a naked, starving human soul; he longed to clothe himself, and he was hungry and ever hungrier for knowledge; but never within the four walls of the village schoolhouse could he seize hold of one fact that would yield him its secret sense, one glimpse of clear light that would shine in upon the darkness of his mind, one thought or word that would feed his soul.

The only place where his longings were ever stilled, where he seemed at peace with himself, where he understood what he was made for, was out of doors in the woods. When he should have been poring over the sweet, palpitating mysteries of the multiplication table, his vagrant gaze was always on the open window near which he sat. He could never study when a fly buzzed on the window-pane; he was always standing on the toes of his bare feet, trying to locate and understand the buzz that puzzled him. The book was a mute, soulless thing that had no relation to his inner world of thought and feeling. He turned ever from the dead seven-times-six to the mystery of life about him.

He was never a special favourite with his teachers; that was scarcely to be expected. In his very early years, his pockets were gone through with every morning when he entered the school door, and the contents, when confiscated, would comprise a jew’s-harp, a bit of catgut, screws whittled out of wood, tacks, spools, pins, and the like. But when robbed of all these he could generally secrete a fragment of india-rubber drawn from an old pair of suspenders, and this, when put between his teeth and stretched to its utmost capacity, would yield a delightful twang when played upon with the forefinger. He could also fashion an interesting musical instrument in his desk by means of spools and catgut and bits of broken glass. The chief joy of his life was an old tuning-fork that the teacher of the singing-school had given him, but, owing to the degrading and arbitrary censorship of pockets that prevailed, he never dared bring it into the schoolroom. There were ways, however, of evading inexorable law and circumventing base injustice. He hid the precious thing under a thistle just outside the window. The teacher had sometimes a brief season of apathy on hot afternoons, when she was hearing the primer class read, “I see a pig. The pig is big. The big pig can dig”; which stirring phrases were always punctuated by the snores of the Hanks baby, who kept sinking down on his fat little legs in the line and giving way to slumber during the lesson. At such a moment Anthony slipped out of the window and snapped the tuning-fork several times—just enough to save his soul from death—and then slipped in again. He was caught occasionally, but not often; and even when he was, there were mitigating circumstances, for he was generally put under the teacher’s desk for punishment. It was a dark close, sultry spot, but when he was well seated, and had grown tired of looking at the triangle of black elastic in the teacher’s “congress” shoe, and tired of wishing it was his instead of hers, he would tie one end of a bit of thread to the button of his gingham shirt, and, carrying it round his left ear several times, make believe he was Paganini languishing in prison and playing on a violin with a single string.

Winter Storm Uri Raises Questions About Climate Change and Extreme Cold Events

Winter Storm Uri brought unprecedented cold and extreme weather across the United States, especially affecting states like Texas that are unaccustomed to such severe conditions. The cold snap led to massive spikes in energy demand, overwhelming the power grid and leaving millions of people without electricity during a critical time. As the nation grapples with the aftermath of the storm, the debate among scientists over the role of climate change in such extreme cold events has been reignited.

According to Walt Meier, a Senior Research Scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, the issue of whether climate change influences extreme cold events is a point of contention among scientists. Some researchers argue that global warming could potentially decrease the likelihood of such events, while others suggest that the warming in the Arctic may lead to more frequent cold spells moving further south.

Karin Gleason, a Climate Scientist at the National Centers for Environmental Information at NOAA, points out that complex factors such as sudden stratospheric warming and variations in the Arctic Oscillation played significant roles in shaping the recent cold weather patterns. The Arctic, in particular, is warming at a rate almost twice as fast as the rest of the planet, raising concerns about its impact on extreme weather patterns in the future.

Jennifer Francis, a Senior Scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, highlights that the current cold event aligns with predictions that extreme weather events, both hot and cold, may become more common in a warming climate. She emphasizes that the meandering jet stream can create conditions where extreme heat and cold coexist, leading to unpredictable and severe weather patterns.

Francis underscores the importance of considering the broader context of climate change when assessing individual weather events. "We need to look at the bigger picture and how these extreme events fit into the overall trend of a changing climate," she says. The warming Arctic, she adds, can disrupt the jet stream, potentially leading to more persistent weather patterns that result in prolonged cold spells.

On the other hand, James Screen, an Associate Professor of Climate Science at the University of Exeter, expresses skepticism about directly linking climate change to an increase in extreme cold events. Screen highlights the complexities of atmospheric dynamics and the need for further research to establish a clearer understanding of the relationship between climate change and extreme weather occurrences.

As communities affected by Winter Storm Uri work to recover and rebuild, the conversation about the intersection of climate change and extreme weather events continues to evolve. While the exact influence of climate change on extreme cold events remains a subject of debate, one thing is clear: the need for comprehensive research and preparedness to address the challenges of a changing climate is more urgent than ever.

Third Stimulus Check: Do Non-U.S. Citizens Qualify?

President Joe Biden has signed the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 into law, granting another round of stimulus checks to those in need. But does that mean non-citizens who reside in the United States will receive the check?

In some cases, yes. Anyone who pays taxes in the United States as a resident is eligible for a stimulus payment. The American Rescue Plan has specific eligibility requirements for who can receive a stimulus check. Lawful permanent residents and some qualifying resident aliens with Social Security Numbers will receive a payment.

Third Stimulus Check Calculator: Estimate How Much You’ll Receive

Which Non-U.S. Citizens Are Eligible for Stimulus Checks?

First and foremost: Only people with valid Social Security numbers will be eligible to receive a stimulus payment. That means undocumented immigrants and immigrants who file their taxes with an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) are not eligible for a payment.

There is one specific difference with this stimulus package compared to the CARES Act, however. Last spring, families with mixed immigration status, where one family member filed tax returns with an ITIN, disqualified the entire family from receiving stimulus funds. Nearly 5.1 million U.S. citizens or permanent resident immigrants in the spring were affected by the provision, according to The Guardian. The most recent stimulus package now includes those families.

Here are the non-U.S. citizens also eligible for stimulus checks (if they have a valid Social Security number):

Lawful permanent residents

Lawful permanent residents are individuals who are legally residing permanently in the U.S. as an immigrant, according to the IRS. Generally, these individuals are granted an alien registration card, also known as a green card.

Qualifying resident aliens

It’s possible to be a qualifying resident alien without having a green card. Under IRS guidelines, this includes people who are physically present in the U.S. on at least 31 days during the current year, 183 days in the past three years (including the current year) and have a valid Social Security number for employment. These individuals cannot be claimed as a dependent of another taxpayer in order to be eligible for a stimulus check.

That means participants in the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program (commonly referred to as DREAMers), Temporary Protected Status (TPS) individuals and H1-B visa holders with Social Security numbers are eligible for stimulus checks.

There are certain people who might pass the substantial presence test mentioned above, but are exempt individuals—meaning they are nonresident aliens and don’t qualify for stimulus checks. That includes:

Foreign government-related individuals. That includes people those under an “A” or “G” visa (except for “A-3” or “G-5” visa holders).

Teachers or trainees. They typically hold “J” or “Q” visas.

Foreign students. This includes those who hold a “F”, “J”, “M” or “Q” visa.

Professional athletes. This includes those temporarily in the U.S. to compete in a charitable sports event.

Don’t Forget: U.S. Citizens Living Abroad are Also Eligible for a Stimulus Check

U.S. citizens who live abroad are still eligible for a stimulus check as long as they meet the income thresholds and other qualifying criteria.

Those individuals will receive their payment the same way they received their previous stimulus checks; it will either be a direct deposit into the bank account on file with the IRS, or sent as a paper check to the address listed on your 2019 tax return, if you haven’t yet filed for 2020.

If you didn’t receive your first two stimulus checks, you may be able to claim them when you file your 2020 taxes this spring by claiming the Recovery Rebate Credit with Form 1040 or 1040-SR.

Tiger Woods Undergoes Additional Surgeries Following Los Angeles Car Accident

FBI's Counterterrorism Approach to Capitol Attack: Arrests, Tips, and Corruption Probes

CNN – As the FBI continues its investigation into the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, new evidence suggests the assault was not only planned but involved weapons and tactics. According to law enforcement officials, some participants in the pro-Trump rally may have left the area early to retrieve weapons for the assault on the Capitol.

The FBI is employing counterterrorism strategies to examine travel and communications records, focusing on potential suspects who may have traveled from out of state to participate in the riot. Corruption prosecutors have also been brought in due to their expertise in financial investigations, following the money trail linked to the Capitol attack.

The FBI has received over 126,000 digital tips regarding the Capitol attack. Among these tips, there are claims that show members of Congress were present with riot participants, and these allegations are under investigation for their veracity. The FBI and prosecutors are urging participants to turn themselves in for potential leniency in their sentences.

Two arrests have been made using counterterrorism strategies: Henry "Enrique" Tarrio, the leader of the far-right Proud Boys group, and Eduard Florea, who is accused of assaulting a Capitol Police officer with a flagpole. Tarrio was arrested on charges unrelated to the Capitol riot but is still under investigation for his involvement.

The comprehensive approach to the Capitol attack investigation was compared to counterterrorism operations by DC US Attorney Michael Sherwin. He stated, "We're treating it like a terrorism investigation because we believe based on the evidence we have that there were a number of people who came in to D.C. intentionally to commit violence."

As the investigation unfolds, arrests continue to be made with minimal charges to remove potential threats. The FBI emphasizes that these initial charges do not reflect the full extent of the investigation. The agency is working diligently to identify and apprehend all those involved in the Capitol attack.

The FBI and U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia are urging the public to provide any information related to the Capitol attack, emphasizing that every tip helps in the investigation. The FBI's tip line number is 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324), and tips can also be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov.

Intermountain Healthcare Mandates COVID-19 Vaccination for Caregivers in Response to Federal Rules

Intermountain Healthcare, one of Utah's largest healthcare systems, has taken the significant step of requiring all caregivers to be fully vaccinated against COVID-19. This decision comes in response to pending federal regulations that dictate Medicare and Medicaid will only cover services from health care providers with fully vaccinated employees.

Dr. Mark Briesacher, the Chief Physician Executive at Intermountain Healthcare, emphasized the necessity of this measure, stating, "This step is essential for us to continue caring for patients who have federal health insurance." He added that approximately 80% of Intermountain's care providers have already completed their vaccination regimens.

Employees who have not yet received the vaccine have the option to seek exemptions for medical reasons or based on religious beliefs. This process mirrors typical vaccination requirements in healthcare settings.

Effective January 5, unvaccinated employees without approved exemptions will be placed on administrative leave. By February 9, those who remain unvaccinated may face separation from the organization. The implications of this mandate remain uncertain, as it is yet to be seen how many employees may choose to leave or be let go due to non-compliance with the vaccine mandate.

Queen Victoria, bless her heart, reportedly couldn't bear the thought of anyone uttering "leg" in her presence. One can only imagine her reaction to more, shall we say, earthy expressions. But beneath her aversion to anything remotely suggestive of human anatomy or, heaven forbid, pleasure, lies a cunning strategy for societal control. For what better way to keep the populace in check than by making them too ashamed to acknowledge their own bodies, let alone question the injustices inflicted upon them? And so, the Victorian era, with its corseted waists and stifled whispers, became a masterclass in the art of repression. Kurt Vonnegut, that sly observer of human folly, undoubtedly appreciated the sheer genius of it all. Oh, those Victorian mothers! Masters of mental gymnastics, they trained their families to navigate the world with blinders on, carefully averting their eyes (and minds!) from anything that might stir those pesky natural impulses. Sex? Never heard of it. Poverty? Look away, darling, it's terribly impolite to stare. And on and on, the charade went, each societal ill conveniently swept under the rug of propriety.

Vonnegut, never one to shy away from a bit of literary firebombing, throws a Molotov cocktail of satire with his short story "The Big Space Fuck." The title alone, a gloriously subversive use of language, sets the stage for a story that tackles societal decline with a grin and a wink. Welcome to the dystopian hellscape of 1989, where Earth, choking on its own pollution, staggers towards oblivion. Our only hope? A ragtag crew on a desperate mission to blast human genetic material into the cosmos, ensuring the survival of the species. Because, you know, when all else fails, there's always the primal urge to fall back on. The absurdity of it all, the sheer audacity of launching sperm into the void as a last-ditch effort to save humanity, is precisely the point. Through this outrageous scenario, set against a backdrop of rapidly evolving (or devolving?) legal definitions of parental responsibility, Vonnegut skewers our obsession with progress, our blind faith in technology, and our remarkable ability to ignore the writing on the wall, even as the planet crumbles around us.

Growing up, my childhood was blessed with the unwavering love and support of my family, particularly the strong personalities of my parents, who instilled in me a deep sense of values and morals. My father, an adventurous soul with an insatiable spirit, played a significant role in shaping my childhood. I cherish the memories of our motorcycle trips, speeding down winding roads with the wind in my hair and sun on my face. It was during these thrilling escapades that I learned to take risks and push beyond my limits, skills that would later serve me well in my own pursuits. My father's leniency also extended to my fascination with the rollerblades that I would tirelessly glide across the showroom floor, much to his amusement and occasional chagrin. His loving patience and encouragement fostered an environment that allowed me to experiment and explore the world around me.

My mother, on the other hand, was the pillar of our family business, with her keen eye for detail and dedication to our family's shop. Her organizational skills and business acumen were an invaluable asset to our company, but it was her compassion and nurturing spirit that touched the lives of everyone around her. As part of the Missionettes program, she had a profound impact on our community, spreading love and kindness to those in need. Her commitment to serving others ignited a fire within me, driving me to explore the world beyond our small town. One trip that stands out in my mind was the family vacation to Japan when I was twelve years old. Watching my mother interact with people from a different culture sparked my curiosity about the diversity of the world and left an indelible mark on my heart. She always made everyone feel welcome, showing me that our faith was not confined to our community but could transcend borders and cultures. This trip laid the foundation for my passion for serving others, but it was a missions trip to the Philippines at fourteen that solidified my calling as a missionary. Witnessing the resilience of the Filipino people, their unwavering faith, and their deep love for one another, I was forever changed.

High school was a pivotal time in my life, a crucible where my spiritual and personal growth flourished under the guidance of our church leaders. The emphasis on ministry and service in our community became a beacon that directed my path. I made the conscious decision to prioritize my faith and church involvement over the typical high school social scenes, which often seemed hollow in comparison to the richness of our church family. As I entered adulthood, I found myself drawn to the Philippines once more, this time with a deep longing to return as a missionary. My desire to serve others was now tempered with a growing awareness of the importance of relationships. The cultural emphasis on waiting for the perfect partner in Christian communities influenced my views on love and marriage. I began to envision a future spouse who would stand by my side as we served the Lord together, a partner who would walk alongside me in my journey to make a difference. Looking back, I see the fingerprints of my father's adventurous heart, my mother's compassion, and the lessons from our various travels as the foundational blocks of my identity – an intricate tapestry rich with the love and values instilled in me by my family and faith.

The square was now moving slowly on a line parallel with the rocks, stopping every few minutes to pick up wounded, and to allow the screw-guns and Gardner to make themselves felt. The men looked serious, for that spring on to the rocks of the Arab army had given them a vague glimpse of the number and ferocity of their foes; but their faces were set like stone, for they knew to a man that they must win or they must di–nd die, too, in a particularly unlovely fashion. But most serious of all was the general, for he had seen that which brought a flush to his cheeks and a frown to his brow.

"I say, Stephen," said he to his galloper, "those Mallows seem a trifle jumpy. The right flank company bulged a bit when the niggers showed on the hill."

"Youngest troops in the square, sir," murmured the aide, looking at them critically through his eye-glass.

"Tell Colonel Flanagan to see to it, Stephen," said the general; and the galloper sped upon his way. The colonel, a fine old Celtic warrior, was over at C Company in an instant.

"How are the men, Captain Foley?"

"Never better, sir," answered the senior captain, in the spirit that makes a Madras officer look murder if you suggest recruiting his regiment from the Punjab.

"Stiffen them up!" cried the colonel. As he rode away a colour-sergeant seemed to trip, and fell forward into a mimosa bush. He made no effort to rise, but lay in a heap among the thorns.

"Sergeant O'Rooke's gone, sorr," cried a voice. "Never mind, lads," said Captain Foley. "He's died like a soldier, fighting for his Queen."

"Down with the Queen!" shouted a hoarse voice from the ranks.

But the roar of the Gardner and the typewriter-like clicking of the hopper burst in at the tail of the words. Captain Foley heard them, and Subalterns Grice and Murphy heard them; but there are times when a deaf ear is a gift from the gods.

"Steady, Mallows!" cried the captain, in a pause of the grunting machine-gun. "We have the honour of Ireland to guard this day."

"And well we know how to guard it, captin!" cried the same ominous voice; and there was a buzz from the length of the company.

The captain and the two subs. came together behind the marching line.

"They seem a bit out of hand," murmured the captain.

"Bedad," said the Galway boy, "they mean to scoot like redshanks."

"They nearly broke when the blacks showed on the hill," said Grice.

"The first man that turns, my sword is through him," cried Foley, loud enough to be heard by five files on either side of him. Then, in a lower voice, "It's a bitter drop to swallow, but it's my duty to report what you think to the chief, and have a company of Jollies put behind us." He turned away with the safety of the square upon his mind, and before he had reached his goal the square had ceased to exist.

In their march in front of what looked like a face of cliff, they had come opposite to the mouth of the gully, in which, screened by scrub and boulders, 3,000 chosen dervishes, under Hamid Wad Hussein, of the Baggaras, were crouching. Tat, tat, tat, went the rifles of three mounted infantrymen in front of the left shoulder of the square, and an instant later they wore spurring it for their lives, crouching over the manes of their horses, and pelting over the sandhills with thirty or forty galloping chieftains at their heels. Rocks and scrub and mimosa swarmed suddenly into life. Rushing black figures came and went in the gaps of the bushes. A howl that drowned the shouts of the officers, a long quavering yell, burst from the ambuscade. Two rolling volleys from the Royal Wessex, one crash from the screw-gun firing shrapnel, and then before a second cartridge could be rammed in, a living, glistening black wave, tipped with steel, had rolled over the gun, the Royal Wessex had been dashed back among the camels, and 1,000 fanatics were hewing and hacking in the heart of what had been the square.

The air, thick with the scent of lilies and the low hum of polite discourse, seemed suddenly to press upon young Mr. Ainsworth with a weight quite disproportionate to its inherent mass. He found himself, in the wake of that tremulous query – that plea, indeed – regarding kindness, holding his breath, suspended as if from a silken thread over a chasm of unforeseen consequence. Her face, tilted ever so slightly upward, caught the light from the chandelier in a manner that transformed its familiar contours into something altogether new, something… arresting. He had known Miss Everly for a season now, danced with her at balls, exchanged pleasantries over teacups, yet never, not once, had he perceived this potent undercurrent of… what? It was beyond mere sympathy, beyond even affection.

She considered him for a moment, her gaze unwavering, and then, with a voice so low it was almost lost amidst the murmur of the gathering, she replied, “Kindness, Mr. Ainsworth, is a commodity too readily dispensed, too often mistaken for true understanding. I should aspire, surely, to offer you something…more.” The word hung in the air, pregnant with unspoken implication. Ainsworth, a man more comfortable amidst the intricacies of legal contracts than the labyrinthine pathways of feminine sentiment, felt a tremor of disquiet, yet also, undeniably, a thrill of anticipation. What manner of “more” did she contemplate? And, perhaps more importantly, was he prepared to receive it?

He noticed, with a start, the subtle tightening around the eyes of the formidable Lady Beaumont, who, moments before, had been holding Miss Everly captive within a lengthy dissertation on the merits of pre-Raphaelite art. Lady Beaumont, a woman not easily trifled with, clearly did not approve of this sudden secession, this flagrant abandonment of her artistic pronouncements. Miss Everly, however, appeared wholly unconcerned, her attention riveted upon Ainsworth with an intensity that bordered, he thought, upon the theatrical. It was a bold move, a defiance of the social proprieties that governed their world, and it served only to deepen Ainsworth’s fascination.

“The evening grows late,” she murmured, her hand resting lightly upon his sleeve. He felt the touch, a fleeting pressure, like an electric shock. “And I find myself weary of pronouncements upon art, however learned. Pray, Mr. Ainsworth,” she continued, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, “are you perchance driving tonight? I find my own conveyance has…suffered a temporary indisposition.” The implication, of course, was as transparent as the finest Venetian glass. She was offering him an escape, a tête-à-tête far removed from the stifling constraints of polite society.

His mind, normally a well-ordered repository of legal precedent and financial strategy, felt suddenly and delightfully scrambled. Here was this woman, this Miss Everly, brazenly flouting convention, risking the disapproval of the assembled gentry, all, it seemed, for the sake of… what? A shared carriage ride? A whispered conversation under the cloak of night? Or something altogether more profound? He considered the implications, the potential for scandal, the inevitable gossip.

He looked at Miss Everly again, her eyes alight with a mischievous gleam, and found that all such considerations, all such societal constraints, seemed to pale into utter insignificance. He was, quite simply, captivated. “I should be utterly delighted,” he heard himself say, the words tumbling forth with an alacrity that surprised even himself. He paused, and then, emboldened by her unwavering gaze, added, "Utterly, utterly delighted."

The autumn had its customary turn toward winter, cloaked the landscape in a shroud of frost and barren branches, yet within the sanctuary of the house, the days were as still as the evergreens that bordered its windows. In the library, where the fireplace glowed like a witness to many unspoken reckonings of the past, Miss Blake found herself once again drawn to the subject that had so subtly woven itself into the fabric of her thoughts.

She had vowed to herself, in the wake of Mrs. Elmsdale's stern admonitions, to refrain from any jesting at the expense of the departed Mr. Elmsdale. Yet, even as she upheld her promise, it was not the caricature of his peculiar diction or his marital mispronunciations that commanded her attention, but rather the specter of his fate—a fate that, like the autumn leaves drifting through the window, seemed inextricably bound to the heart of her dear sister.

Her reverie was abruptly interrupted by the brisk entrance of Miss Helena Elmsdale, whose eyes, usually the color of a clear, quiet lake, were now veiled with a storm of unexpected resolve. She intimated, with a voice tinged with the remnants of her earlier reprimand, that it was time to set aside the past and face forward. The mention of their brother-in-law's memory was to be done sparingly, with an air of resignation that belied the fervent wish to erase the very notion from existence.

"We must," Miss Helena began, her voice carrying the weight of a sorrow that sought solace in the mere act of speech, "remember him not as the man whose tongue faltered, but as the architect of his own demise. His downfall was not but the culmination of choices, ones that we must learn from, yet not dwell upon."

Miss Blake acquiesced, though not without a pang of guilt for the relief she felt at the chance to mend her father-in-law's tarnished reputation. She pondered over the mansion's library collection, seeking a volume that might counsel her in the art of forgiveness, perhaps even expiation. Her fingers traced the spines of leather-bound tomes, pausing at a treatise on finance which chronicled the rise and fall of numerous men ensnared by the very same allure that had ensnared Mr. Elmsdale—greed.

As the afternoon deepened into evening, the sisters convened once more, their conversation edging close to the delicate subject of their brother-in-law's finances. It was Miss Blake who ventured, her voice soft as the whisper of the wind through the night, "I have observed, dear sister, that while we lament his misfortunes, we must also acknowledge the role his ventures played in shaping the very reality we find ourselves in."

Miss Helena, her expression contemplative, replied, "Indeed, it would seem that even in his shadow, we continue to grapple with the echoes of his choices. Yet, let us not forget the tradition of our family, which, like sturdy oaks, endures through seasons and winds alike."

The spectral presence of Mr. Elmsdale, with his quirks and contradictions, lingered on, a reminder that in the heart of every household, there are secrets—some whispered, some shouted, and others, carried silently on the breath of time. And as the sisters sat in the twilight, the sanctuary of the library enfolding them, they found solace not in forgetting, but in the quiet understanding that the past is a labyrinth of lessons, each step leading them ever closer to the truth—the elusive balance between forgiveness and remembrance.

Derek Chauvin, a former police officer who was convicted of killing George Floyd in Minneapolis, has been sentenced to 22 and a half years in prison. Dressed in a light gray suit, Chauvin offered his condolences to Floyd's family before receiving his sentence. Under Minnesota guidelines, he is required to serve two-thirds of this term, which amounts to 15 years, before being eligible for supervised release for the remaining time.

The sentence handed down surpasses the state's recommended range of nearly 11 to 15 years for the crime, reflecting the national outcry and protests over police brutality following Floyd's death. Judge Peter Cahill emphasized that the sentencing was guided not by public sentiment or emotion but by a duty to recognize the profound pain endured by all families involved, particularly Floyd's.

Judge Cahill's exhaustive 22-page memorandum outlined significant aggravating factors that contributed to the decision for a more severe sentence: Chauvin's abuse of his position and his particularly cruel treatment of Floyd. Cahill critical of Chauvin's indifference to Floyd's pleas for his life, detailed that the restraint on Floyd was notably prolonged and painful compared to usual cases within the specified murder and manslaughter charges.

For the time being, Chauvin is being held in a restricted section at the Minnesota Correctional Facility- Oak Park Heights, away from the general population for his safety. His final placement will remain undetermined for now, with priority given to his security.

Chauvin, 45, faced conviction for second-degree unintentional murder, third-degree murder, and second-degree manslaughter in Floyd's death. His sentencing marks a significant occasion, underscoring the systemic racial injustices highlighted by Floyd's death and the resultant global protests.

In Minneapolis, at the corner where Floyd died, individuals gathered to watch the sentencing on their phones. The verdict has evoked mixed feelings among Floyd's supporters, with calls for continued efforts towards police reform and equality.

Bridgett Floyd, George Floyd’s sister and founder of the George Floyd Memorial Foundation, acknowledged the sentencing as a critical step towards addressing police brutality, yet highlighted the ongoing need for systemic change. Ben Crump, the attorney for Floyd's family, viewed the sentencing as a historic moment that advances the nation towards healing by ensuring accountability and closure.

This landmark sentencing is seen as a pivotal moment in the fight for racial justice and police reform, symbolizing a shift towards greater accountability and recognition of the deep-seated issues within law enforcement and the broader criminal justice system.

This was one night when Van Twiller had wandered into the club, turned over the magazines absently in the reading-room, and wandered out again without speaking ten words. The most careless eye would have remarked the great change that had come over Van Twiller. Now and then he would play a game of billiards with De Peyster or Haseltine, or stop to chat a moment in the vestibule with old Duane; but he was an altered man. When at the club, he was usually to be found in the small smoking-room up-stairs, seated on a fauteuil fast asleep, with the last number of The Nation in his hand. Once, if you went to two or three places of an evening, you were certain to meet Van Twiller at them all. You seldom met him in society now.

By and by came whisper number two--a whisper more emphatic than number one, but still untraceable to any tangible mouthpiece. This time the whisper said that Van Twiller was in love. But with whom? The list of possible Mrs. Van Twillers was carefully examined by experienced hands, and a check placed against a fine old Knickerbocker name here and there, but nothing satisfactory arrived at. Then that same still small voice of rumor, but now with an easily detected staccato sharpness to it, said that Van Twiller was in love--with an actress! Van Twiller, whom it had taken all these years and all this waste of raw material in the way of ancestors to bring to perfection--Ralph Van Twiller, the net result and flower of his race, the descendant of Wouter, the son of Mrs. Van-rensselaer Vanzandt Van Twiller--in love with an actress! That was too ridiculous to be believed--and so everybody believed it. Six or seven members of the club abruptly discovered in themselves an unsuspected latent passion for the histrionic art. In squads of two or three they stormed successively all the theatres in town--Booth’s, Wallack’s, Daly’s Fifth Avenue (not burnt down then), and the Grand Opera House. Even the shabby homes of the drama over in the Bowery, where the Germanic Thespis has not taken out his naturalization papers, underwent rigid exploration. But no clue was found to Van Twiller’s mysterious attachment. The opéra bouffe, which promised the widest field for investigation, produced absolutely nothing, not even a crop of suspicions. One night, after several weeks of this, Delaney and I fancied that we caught sight of Van Twiller in the private box of an up-town theatre, where some thrilling trapeze performance was going on, which we did not care to sit through; but we concluded afterwards that it was only somebody who looked like him. Delaney, by the way, was unusually active in this search. I dare say he never quite forgave Van Twiller for calling him Muslin Delaney. Ned is fond of ladies’ society, and that’s a fact.

The Cimmerian darkness which surrounded Van Twiller’s inamorata left us free to indulge in the wildest conjectures. Whether she was black-tressed Melpomene, with bowl and dagger, or Thalia, with the fair hair and the laughing face, was only to be guessed at. It was popularly conceded, however, that Van Twiller was on the point of forming a dreadful mésalliance.

Up to this period he had visited the club regularly. Suddenly he ceased to appear. He was not to be seen on Fifth Avenue, or in the Central Park, or at the houses he generally frequented. His chambers--and mighty comfortable chambers they were--on Thirty-fourth Street were deserted. He had dropped out of the world, shot like a bright particular star from his orbit in the heaven of the best society.

Having received a classical education in England, he returned home and entered the University of Virginia, where, after an extravagant course, followed by reformation at the last extremity, he was graduated with the highest honors of his class. Then came a boyish attempt to join the fortunes of the insurgent Greeks, which ended at St. Petersburg, where he got into difficulties through want of a passport, from which he was rescued by the American consul and sent home. He now entered the military academy at West Point, from which he obtained a dismissal on hearing of the birth of a son to his adopted father, by a second marriage, an event which cut off his expectations as an heir. The death of Mr. Allan, in whose will his name was not mentioned, soon after relieved him of all doubt in this regard, and he committed himself at once to authorship for a support. Previously to this, however, he had published (in 1827) a small volume of poems, which soon ran through three editions, and excited high expectations of its author’s future distinction in the minds of many competent judges.

That no certain augury can be drawn from a poet’s earliest lispings there are instances enough to prove. Shakespeare’s first poems, though brimful of vigor and youth and picturesqueness, give but a very faint promise of the directness, condensation and overflowing moral of his maturer works. Perhaps, however, Shakespeare is hardly a case in point, his “Venus and Adonis” having been published, we believe, in his twenty-sixth year. Milton’s Latin verses show tenderness, a fine eye for nature, and a delicate appreciation of classic models, but give no hint of the author of a new style in poetry. Pope’s youthful pieces have all the sing-song, wholly unrelieved by the glittering malignity and eloquent irreligion of his later productions. Collins’ callow namby-pamby died and gave no sign of the vigorous and original genius which he afterward displayed. We have never thought that the world lost more in the “marvellous boy,” Chatterton, than a very ingenious imitator of obscure and antiquated dulness. Where he becomes original (as it is called), the interest of ingenuity ceases and he becomes stupid. Kirke White’s promises were indorsed by the respectable name of Mr. Southey, but surely with no authority from Apollo. They have the merit of a traditional piety, which to our mind, if uttered at all, had been less objectionable in the retired closet of a diary, and in the sober raiment of prose. They do not clutch hold of the memory with the drowning pertinacity of Watts; neither have they the interest of his occasional simple, lucky beauty. Burns having fortunately been rescued by his humble station from the contaminating society of the “Best models,” wrote well and naturally from the first. Had he been unfortunate enough to have had an educated taste, we should have had a series of poems from which, as from his letters, we could sift here and there a kernel from the mass of chaff. Coleridge’s youthful efforts give no promise whatever of that poetical genius which produced at once the wildest, tenderest, most original and most purely imaginative poems of modern times. Byron’s “Hours of Idleness” would never find a reader except from an intrepid and indefatigable curiosity. In Wordsworth’s first preludings there is but a dim foreboding of the creator of an era. From Southey’s early poems, a safer augury might have been drawn. They show the patient investigator, the close student of history, and the unwearied explorer of the beauties of predecessors, but they give no assurances of a man who should add aught to stock of household words, or to the rarer and more sacred delights of the fireside or the arbor. The earliest specimens of Shelley’s poetic mind already, also, give tokens of that ethereal sublimation in which the spirit seems to soar above the regions of words, but leaves its body, the verse, to be entombed, without hope of resurrection, in a mass of them. Cowley is generally instanced as a wonder of precocity. But his early insipidities show only a capacity for rhyming and for the metrical arrangement of certain conventional combinations of words, a capacity wholly dependent on a delicate physical organization, and an unhappy memory. An early poem is only remarkable when it displays an effort of reason, and the rudest verses in which we can trace some conception of the ends of poetry, are worth all the miracles of smooth juvenile versification. A school-boy, one would say, might acquire the regular see-saw of Pope merely by an association with the motion of the play-ground tilt.

Heroic Teen Tate Myre Remembered as a Selfless Protector in Oxford School Shooting

Oxford, Michigan - In the aftermath of the tragic school shooting at Oxford High School, the community mourns the loss of four innocent lives, including that of Tate Myre, a 16-year-old student and athlete who displayed remarkable bravery during the horrific event.

Tate, a sophomore at Oxford High School, was one of the four students who tragically lost their lives due to gunshot wounds sustained during the attack. His untimely passing has left a profound void in the hearts of his family, friends, and the entire community.

The young hero's funeral is scheduled for 10 a.m. Tuesday at Kensington Church in Lake Orion, where loved ones and community members will gather to pay their respects and celebrate his life.

While initial reports suggested that a civilian or student may have attempted to disarm the shooter, Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard clarified that there is no video evidence to support this claim.

"We have no video evidence of a civilian or student attempting to disarm the shooter," Sheriff Bouchard stated during a press conference. "We're still reviewing all the evidence, but at this time, there's no indication that anyone other than the shooter fired a weapon."

Tate Myre was known throughout the community for his exceptional athleticism and unwavering commitment to his team. He excelled in both wrestling and football, earning the admiration of his coaches and teammates.

"Tate was a special young man," said JR Laefner, the public address announcer at Oxford football games and a close friend of the Myre family. "He was always willing to sacrifice for others. He was a star athlete, but he was also a great student and a kind friend."

Ross Wingert, Tate's football and wrestling coach, echoed these sentiments, describing Tate as a selfless individual who always put the team's success above his own.

"Tate was the kind of kid who would do anything for his team," Coach Wingert said. "He was a natural leader, and he always had a positive attitude. He was a joy to coach."

Tate's willingness to sacrifice for others was evident in his decision to shift positions on the football team for the betterment of the team.

"Tate was a running back, but we needed him to play linebacker," said Zach Line, Oxford's football coach. "He didn't hesitate to make the switch. He knew it was what was best for the team, and he was willing to do whatever it took to help us win."

Tate's heroic actions during the school shooting have inspired an outpouring of support from the community. An online petition has garnered over 75,000 signatures, calling for the renaming of the Wildcat Stadium as Tate Myre Stadium in honor of his bravery.

"Tate is a hero," said Kurt Richardson, the Clarkston coach. "He sacrificed his own life to try to save others. He is an inspiration to us all."

Tony Patritto, the Rochester Adams coach, agreed, saying, "Tate's actions were nothing short of heroic. He is a true hero, and he will never be forgotten."

Scott Merchant, the Clinton Township Chippewa Valley coach, added, "Tate is a symbol of hope for our community. He showed us that even in the darkest of times, there is still good in the world."

As the community continues to grieve the loss of Tate Myre and the other victims of the Oxford school shooting, they find solace in the young hero's bravery and selflessness. Tate's legacy will forever be remembered as a shining example of courage and compassion.

"I sometimes think even He forgets me," moaned the poor girl, "when I see rich folks having all things they desire, and such as me almost starving, working night and day for a mere crust."

"I once said so to mother," remarked the child, "but she opened our Bible, and bade me read a verse she pointed out. Shall I tell you what it was?"

"Yes," was the reply.

Pollie folded her hands, and repeated--

"Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me, lest I be full and deny Thee, and say, Who is the Lord? or lest I be poor and steal, and take the name of my God in vain."

And then she turned to another to comfort me, and this is it--

"Be careful for nothing; but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."

When the child ceased speaking, she looked up into the face of her listener, whose head was bent in reverence to God.

"O Pollie!" she said at last, as again taking up her heavy load she proceeded slowly onwards, "I wish I had a good mother."

"Come over to us sometimes," said the child, eagerly.

"Will your mother let me?" was the question.

"Yes, I am sure she will; she is so good," was the reply.

And then the two friends went on up Drury Lane, not speaking much; but as they were parting Lizzie stooped down, and kissing the child lovingly, said softly--

"Good-bye, and thank you, little Pollie."

"Would you like a bunch of violets?" she asked. "I can divide the other between mother and Mrs Flanagan."

The poor seamstress was unable to speak from emotion, but held out her hand with trembling eagerness for the flowers.

How glad was the child in being able to give a pleasure to her lonely neighbour. She felt more joy in seeing Lizzie Stevens' glad smile than even in the magnificent sum of money wrapped in her handkerchief; for she experienced "it is more blessed to give than to receive;" and after seeing her friend disappear through the dingy doorway which led to the garret called her "home," she turned with a light heart into the entry which led to her own place, eager to see mother and tell her all; but in doing so almost fell over a little cripple boy who sat crouched on the door-steps.

"O Jimmy! did I hurt you?" she asked in alarm.

"No. Everybody knocks me about; I'se used to it," was his answer.

"Poor Jimmy!" said the little girl. "Where's your mother?"

"Down there, drunk again," he replied, pointing his thin finger in the direction of what in other houses would be the kitchen, but which was his "home," if it could be dignified by so sacred a name.

Pollie looked sorrowfully on the poor boy, whose thin, wizened face, with large, hungry eyes, was placed on a shrunk and distorted body. His mother was the pest of the court, always drunk, and in her drunken fury beating her wretched offspring. Half-starved and half-clothed, he passed his time on the door-step, gazing vacantly at the passers-by, uncared for, unloved amidst the many.

"Poor Jimmy!" repeated the little girl. "Would you like some of my sweet violets?"

The boy, unused to even a breath of kindness, gazed some few seconds at her with his eager eyes.

"You be Pollie Turner, bain't yer, what lives upstairs with yer mother?" he asked at last.

"Yes," she replied, and repeated her question, as she took some of the flowers from her last bunch. "Would you like these?"
