"There you are at last, Basil, my dear boy!" she exclaimed as the two siblings entered. Her gaze then fell upon Ermengarde, and the hint of a frown flickered across her face. "And Ermengarde, late as usual. I trust there is a perfectly good reason for this tardiness?"

Basil, ever the dutiful protector of his beloved sister, stepped forward. "The fault lies entirely with me, Miss Nelson," he declared, his voice ringing with sincerity. "I fear I detained Ermengarde with my own dawdling."

Miss Nelson regarded him with a knowing look. She saw through his little charade, of course, but chose to indulge him. Basil, with his kind heart and gentlemanly manners, was undeniably her favorite amongst the Wilton brood.

"Very well, Basil. See that it doesn't happen again." Her tone, though firm, held a distinct lack of its usual reprimand.

Relieved, Basil steered Ermengarde towards the tea table, already laden with an assortment of tempting treats. As they took their places amongst their siblings, Miss Nelson allowed herself a small sigh. While she shared in the general merriment of the occasion, a shadow of unease lingered at the back of her mind.

The summer stretched before them, long and, she feared, potentially fraught with the usual childish squabbles and misadventures. Eric, with his boundless energy and penchant for mischief, was sure to be at the heart of most of them. The thought of navigating the next few months, attempting to maintain some semblance of order amidst the chaos, filled her with a distinct sense of foreboding. With a deep breath and a silent prayer for patience, she turned her attention back to her charges, determined to enjoy the festivities, however fleeting they might be.

Facebook and Multiple Apps Experience Worldwide Outages; Internal Systems Fail, Affecting Thousands of Employees

On Monday, Facebook employees faced significant disruptions as they were unable to access buildings due to a badge system failure. Conference rooms and other internal systems also became inaccessible, forcing employees to resort to using text messaging and Outlook email for internal communication during the outage.

Simultaneously, users worldwide began reporting issues on DownDetector, which tracks real-time outages of various online platforms. The Facebook outage also extended to Facebook Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp, affecting millions of users globally.

Facebook acknowledged the outages via Twitter, stating, "We're aware that some people are having trouble accessing our apps and products. We're working to get things back to normal as quickly as possible, and we apologize for any inconvenience." At the time of publishing, the outages had not been resolved.

The outages led to a significant impact on Facebook's bottom line. CEO Mark Zuckerberg's net worth dropped by nearly $7 billion in just 5 hours, while Facebook's stock fell by about 5% during the outage period.

Before that pleasant day was over we had compared notes on almost every department of girl-life. I had confided to her my newly awakened feelings of dissatisfaction as to my want of feminine tastes and tendency to "tomboyishness," and she on her side had told me that she was often afraid of growing too prim or narrow-minded in the well-arranged regularity of her own home-life.

"That was why," she said, "I was so glad to travel a little. I feel as if I needed to rough it in some ways. Father is too careful of me, too unselfish. I am afraid I have always been a spoilt child, and having no brothers, you see, may make me selfish without knowing it!"

She looked up at me anxiously with her sweet brown eyes. What was it they reminded me of? I had already noticed that her people called her by some peculiar pet name; I had not caught it exactly.

"What is it that your sister and father call you sometimes?" I said. "Is it `Ella'?"

Isabel blushed a little.

"No," she said, "it is Zella. Rather a silly name, I am afraid. It came from a fancy of father's that my eyes were like a gazelle's."

"And so they are!" I exclaimed; "that is the look I have seen in them-- some dogs have it too! I don't think it is at all a silly name. Will you let me call you by it sometimes?" for of course under the circumstances there had been no question of anything but "Isabel" and "Regina" between us from the first.

"Of course you may, if you like," she said. "But--" and she hesitated.

"But what?" I asked.

Isabel smiled.

"You mustn't be vexed with me," she replied, "if I can't promise to call you `Reggie,' as your brother does. I don't like it--and Regina is such a pretty name and uncommon too."

"Mother never calls me anything else," I said, "but I am afraid I am half a boy. You must civilise me--mother will be eternally grateful to you if you do."

"I don't think you need civilising," said Isabel; "but perhaps in our different ways we may do each other good. I do hope your people will let you come to stay with us when we go home."

"I should love it of all things," I said. "I have scarcely ever paid any visits, and I have seen very little of England except quite near our own home. Is it very pretty where you live?"

"Not so much pretty as picturesque," Isabel replied. "To begin with, it is very, very out of the way; we are six miles from a railway station of any kind, and sixteen from an important one. But papa's people have lived there for so long, that it doesn't seem out of the way to us. It is a place that changes very little."

"Then it is to be hoped that you have some nice and interesting neighbours," I said. "Near us there are so few young people."

"And there are not many near Millflowers either," said Isabel; "at least not within a good long drive. I hope you would not find it dull. There are interesting walks, if you care for wild, rugged scenery. The village itself is quite tiny. There is only one house of any importance besides the vicarage and ours, and that is--no good," she added, rather abruptly.

"Why not?" I inquired. "Is it uninhabited?"

Isabel hesitated.

"No," she replied. "The same people have lived in it for a great many years. They were there before father came into possession, on my uncle's death. But--" and again she paused.

My curiosity was aroused.

"Do tell me about them," I said.

"Well, yes, I don't see why I shouldn't," answered Isabel. "Father always tells us not to gossip about the Grim House, but you are sure to notice it when you come, so I may as well prepare you beforehand."

“And yet,” added Fanny in a mingled feeling of jest and earnest, “there seems to be small chance of the prophecy coming true.” Before Colin could reply, a noise without was heard of the tread of numerous feet, mingled with the sound of carriage wheels as they slowly advanced down the road, cracking and crushing the dry gravel. Relates the triumph of the Doctor, and the manner in which he achieved it.--Lawyer Skinwell's death-bed, and what happened there.

The evening was warm and fine; and the gentle slope, on the top of which Dr. Rowel's establishment stood, was coloured with the setting light of the sun; as, with the glass-doors, which opened from his drawing-room upon the lawn, thrown wide back to admit the scarcely stirring air,--the doctor himself sat near it and alone, in an attitude of thought, meditating mischief. A dash of vermilion-coloured light shot athwart the lower part of his person, while the upper portion was covered with that kind of illuminated shadow, that clear obscure, which, to the delicate perception of a painter, constitutes one of Nature's greatest beauties. But the thoughts and reflections in which the doctor indulged were deeply at variance with those which the scene before him, and the character of the hour, were calculated to suggest. It was not with him--“how much do I now enjoy?” but the morose reflection--“how long shall I enjoy it?” His present happiness was swallowed up in the anticipation of possible coming evil.

“What matters it,” thought he, “when tomorrow, perhaps, that treacherous villain may make everything known? Nay, how do I know he has not done so already? True, I have had him watched. I know everything he has done, and something that he has said; and this very day again he is gone to York. To-morrow I may wake to be arrested,--to have my house searched, and Woodruff set at liberty.”

As the doctor then mused, the door opened, and a stranger was ushered in.

“Doctor,” said he in a hurried tone, “lawyer Skinwell has just got thrown out of his gig, and is almost killed. He has been insensible ever since.”

“Ah! Impossible!” exclaimed Rowel starting to his feet with surprise. “Are you sure, man?”

“It is quite true, sir,” replied he, as though scarcely knowing what to make of the doctor's strange manner, the latter gentleman regarding him for a moment with an eye of unaccountable incredulity; for the idea had instantaneously flashed across his mind that he might be deceived by his own imagination, and that it was only the devil that was tempting him. A minute or two elapsed; when, recovering himself, he replied in a more subdued and professional tone, “I will be there immediately,” on which the man disappeared.

Such indeed was the happy fortune of the quaint and secluded village of Mapledell, nestled amidst rolling hills and verdant valleys a mere stone’s throw from the bustling metropolis. Here, life unfolded at its own leisurely pace, unburdened by the relentless march of progress that so often threatened to extinguish the flickering flame of individuality. The inhabitants of Mapledell, much like the wildflowers that carpeted the surrounding meadows, grew in wild and wondrous profusion, their personalities as varied and vibrant as the hues of a summer sunset. It was a place where eccentricities were not merely tolerated but celebrated, where the ordinary had a peculiar habit of transforming into the extraordinary, and where the tapestry of life was woven with threads of both the sublime and the ridiculous.

And what, pray tell, could be more conducive to the pursuit of amusement than the contemplation of these human oddities, these delightful aberrations from the mundane norm? For it is in the very act of laughter, that uniquely human expression of mirth and merriment, that we find solace from the weight of our mortal coil. Like a refreshing spring bubbling forth from the parched earth, laughter has the power to quench our thirst for the unexpected, to cleanse our palates from the bitter aftertaste of life's inevitable sorrows. Is it not, therefore, a gift of divine providence, this ability to find humor even in the darkest of corners, to illuminate the shadows with the radiant glow of good cheer?

It was on a crisp autumn afternoon, as the leaves on the maple trees that gave the village its name blazed with fiery brilliance, that a most peculiar event transpired in Mapledell. The annual Harvest Festival was in full swing, and the village green buzzed with activity. Farmers proudly displayed their prize-winning pumpkins and plump turkeys, while children shrieked with delight as they bobbed for apples in overflowing barrels. The air was thick with the aroma of freshly baked pies and the sound of fiddle music, and even the most stoic of souls could not help but be swept up in the festive atmosphere.

Amidst this scene of rustic revelry, a stranger arrived in Mapledell. His name was Professor Algernon P. Whipplethorpe, and he cut a rather dashing figure with his neatly trimmed beard, pince-nez spectacles perched precariously on the bridge of his nose, and a carpetbag that seemed to bulge with mysterious instruments and contraptions. As I prepare to conduct the final two research sessions of my ethnography in Bensonhurst, I am aware that my identity as a Chinese individual may significantly influence the interviews that I conduct. My purpose is to shed light on the growing Chinese population in Bensonhurst and to explore how this increasing diversity affects residents' perceptions of other races.

I plan to conduct these interviews in a park in Bensonhurst, a location that I hope will provide a relaxed and natural setting for participants to share their thoughts and opinions. I have chosen a park setting not only for its practicality but also because it reflects the community's character. "O," he answered apologetically, "only seeing you here, that's all. It's so unusual."

He passed on, looking once or twice behind him. Unusual? Of course it was unusual. Everything was unusual, everything in the world, which seemed to be turned topsy-turvy. If the people in the street had walked on their heads instead of their feet it would not have surprised me very much. I should have regarded it as quite in keeping with the fact that I was standing at my own street-door in idleness at half-past eight o'clock on a Saturday morning; I could not remember the time when such a thing had occurred to me.

Standing thus in a state of semi-stupefaction, the postman came up and gave me a letter. This recalled me to myself.

"Now," thought I, as I turned the envelope over in my hand, "whom is it from, and what does it contain?"

At first I had an unreasonable hope that it was from my employers, imploring me to come back, but a glance at the address convinced me that it was a foolish hope. The writing was strange to me, and the envelope was a common one, and was fastened with sealing-wax bearing the impression of a thimble. I opened and read the letter, and although it did not contain the offer of a situation, or hold out the prospect of one, the contents interested me. I shall have occasion presently to refer to this letter more particularly, and shall at present content myself with saying that had it not arrived this story would never have been written. While my wife and I were at breakfast we spoke of it, and I said it was my intention to comply with the request it contained.

Over breakfast, also, we reviewed our position. During my years of employment I had managed to save very little money, and upon reckoning up what I had in my purse and what I owed, I arrived at a balance in my favour of a little less than four pounds, which represented the whole of my worldly wealth. A poor look-out, and I was reflecting upon it gloomily, when my good little wife, with a tender deprecatory smile, laid before me on the table a Post Office savings-book.

"What is this?" I asked.

"Look," she replied.

The book was made out in her name, and the small deposits, extending over a number of years, made therein showed a credit of more than twenty pounds.

"Yours?" I said, in wonder. "Really yours?"

"No," said my wife. "Yours."

My heart beat with joy; these twenty pounds were like a reprieve. I should have time to look about, without being tortured by fears of immediate want. I drew my wife to my side, and embraced her. Twenty pounds, with which to commence over again the battle of life! Why it was a fortune! How the little woman had contrived to save so much out of her scanty housekeeping money was a mystery to me, but she had done it by hook or by crook, as the saying is, and she now experienced a true and sweet delight in handing it over to me.

"Well," said I, rubbing my hands cheerfully, "things might look worse than they do--a great deal worse. We have a little store to help us over compulsorily idle days, and, thank God, all the children are well."

It was much to be grateful for, and we kissed each other in token of our gratitude, and also as a pledge that we would not lose heart, but would battle bravely on.

His limbs were trembling so that he could not stand, and my wife, much alarmed, started up and helped him into a chair.

Southeast U.S. Gas Shortage Spirals Out of Control as Drivers Ignore Government Pleas

ATLANTA, May 12 (Reuters) – Panic buying and hoarding of gasoline in the Southeast United States has reached crisis levels, with drivers ignoring government pleas not to stockpile fuel amid a major pipeline shutdown.

Lines formed at gas stations across the region, with many running out of fuel due to increased demand. Fistfights and altercations over gasoline were reported in several locations, highlighting the desperation of motorists.

According to data from GasBuddy, a fuel price tracking app, nearly 60% of gas stations in metro Atlanta, and over 70% in Charlotte, Raleigh, and Pensacola, were without gas on Wednesday. The average national gasoline price rose to above $3.00 a gallon, the highest since October 2014.

The Colonial Pipeline shutdown, caused by a ransomware hack, heavily affects the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic. The Biden administration warned against hoarding and filling plastic bags with fuel, urging drivers to stay calm and avoid exacerbating the situation.

Georgia Governor Brian Kemp temporarily suspended gas taxes to ease price hikes, but it remains to be seen if this measure will have a significant impact on the shortage.

Some individuals, disregarding official advice, are going to great lengths to stockpile fuel. DoorDash driver Ronald Ross, who has been unable to work due to the shortage, said, "I've been filling up my tank every chance I get. I don't want to be stranded on the side of the road."

James Jones, a contractor in Atlanta, added, "I've never seen anything like this. People are getting desperate, and it's scary."

Cherie Thomas, manager of an Exxon Mobil station in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, expressed frustration with the situation, saying, "We're doing our best to keep up with demand, but it's just not possible. People need to stop hoarding and let us get back to normal."

Rob Underwood, president of the Energy Marketers of America, urged drivers to stay calm and not panic buy. "We understand the concern, but hoarding is not the solution. Let's work together to get through this."

As the shortage continues to grip the region, motorists are bracing for a long and difficult recovery. "It's going to be a while before things get back to normal," said Ross. "But we'll get through it together."

Russia Sees Increased Social Media Activity Amid Facebook Outage

MOSCOW, Oct 5 – Russian social networks reported a significant surge in activity during Facebook's global outage on Monday, with officials suggesting that the incident supports the country's push to develop sovereign internet platforms.

The outage, which affected Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, left billions of users worldwide without access to the popular social media services for several hours. In Russia, the disruption prompted a notable shift in online activity, with users turning to domestic platforms.

"The situation with Facebook has shown that Russia needs its own social networks," said Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's Foreign Ministry. "We cannot depend on foreign companies that can be used as a tool of political pressure."

Vkontakte, Russia's largest social network, reported an 18% increase in video views and a 21% increase in messages during the Facebook outage. The platform's audience also grew by 19% compared to the day before the outage.

"We saw a significant increase in activity on our platform during the Facebook outage," said Marina Krasnova, Head of Vkontakte. "This shows that Russian users are looking for alternative social media platforms that are reliable and independent."

Odnoklassniki, another popular Russian social network, also reported increased activity during the outage. The platform saw a 15% increase in traffic and a 20% increase in messages.

Russia's increased focus on developing sovereign internet platforms is part of a broader effort to protect the country from potential disruptions to foreign internet infrastructure. Earlier this year, Russia conducted tests to disconnect from the global internet, demonstrating its ability to operate independently if necessary.

The push for internet sovereignty aligns with Russia's broader geopolitical strategy of reducing its reliance on Western technology and services. By developing domestic alternatives to foreign platforms, Russia aims to ensure its continued access to critical online services and protect its national security interests.

The Facebook outage has highlighted the vulnerability of relying on centralized social media platforms and the importance of having diverse and resilient internet infrastructure. Russia's experience during the outage underscores the need for countries to develop their own sovereign internet capabilities to mitigate the risks associated with disruptions to foreign services.

Mr. Hoopdriver, once again upon his mount, felt the peculiar thrill of triumph mingled with chagrin as he stood defiantly atop his bicycle. The heathkeeper, a fixture of rough-hewn character, loomed nearby, observing with a gaze that seemed carved from a stone of irrelevance and mischief. The sun bore down, indifferent to human struggle, casting elongated shadows that danced mockingly at Mr. Hoopdriver’s feet. He could see the figure of the man glowering through the dust, a visage filled with bushy eyebrows and a furrowed brow, the self-appointed critic of his every manoeuvre.

"Mind yer hands, mate," said the heathkeeper suddenly, breaking the silence that hung thick and heavy, as if conjured from the very air surrounding them. "Fiddlin' with that contraption an' gettin' all hot 'n bothered over naught. Not very wise, is it—eh?"

Mr. Hoopdriver looked up, caught in the act of tightening a particularly obstinate screw. The heathkeeper’s presence gnawed at him as if a persistent gnat on sultry summer days. “I am perfectly aware of what I am doing,” he shot back, his tone edged with irritation more than intended. “Such as it is, the mechanics of this machine are hardly conducive to tampering under the sun’s unforgiving eye.”

"Course they ain't," retorted the heathkeeper nonchalantly, his arms crossed over his ample chest. "But you could use a friendly hand or two—or at least a bit of good counsel.” He raised a finger, pointing at the now-repaired pedal, a crooked smile wrestling with his beard. “That bit there? You want it tighter, not looser. I don’t fancy a gent of your ilk takin’ liberties with gravity.”

Mr. Hoopdriver, oscillating between irritation and incredulity, gripped the handlebar tighter still. “As a matter of fact,” he declared, striving for a tone that resonated with dignity, “I’m quite well versed in the nuances of my bicycle, not that it delights you to understand this.” He squared off against the scornful glance of the heathkeeper; it felt as though he were attempting to match wills with a stone wall.

“Fancy that!” the heathkeeper shot back, nearly laughing now, a melodic sound in the oppressive silence of the heath. “A man behind a wheel thinkin’ he rules the world. But I wager you’d be lost without a map, eh?” The words stung sharper than they ought to have, piercing Mr. Hoopdriver's already ruffled feathers.

With renewed fervor, Mr. Hoopdriver adjusted his spectacles and resolved to ignore the specter beside him. “I assure you,” he replied with a haughty tilt of his chin, “that I am capable of navigating any road.” His fingers danced with a fervent intention, driven by the edges of both mischief and outright arrogance.

“By the looks of your rear, I’d say fast isn’t in your repertoire,” the heathkeeper retorted sharply, stepping forward, impudently judging Mr. Hoopdriver’s physique as if it were a curious specimen on display.

“Oh, do go chase the lowly hare,” Mr. Hoopdriver returned, his voice a mix of indignation and amusement. “Your presence, while cacophonous, inspires no feelings of inadequacy—merely curiosity. I shall show you that a man, regardless of his station, is capable of more than mere laughter.”

With that, Mr. Hoopdriver mounted his trusty steed, taking a deep breath that spurred the exhilarating rush of defiance within. The tension hung momentarily, taut as the string of a bow, before he pushed off, the bicycle smoothly gliding beneath him—an antidote to the grating voice of the heathkeeper. The wheels spun with an unexpected zest, harmonizing with the rhythm of determination and abandon.

And as he began to ride, the wilderness flashed by—not a mere landscape but a canvas painted vividly by the brush of movement. The agitation bred from annoyance now simmered down into a fierce propulsion, a whisper in his ear that urged him onward, the ride becoming a fleeting escape from the mockery tethered to that very moment. Mr. Hoopdriver felt not only confidence blooming where there had been self-doubt, but a sort of ironic laughter rising within, as if the universe itself had conspired to embrace his racing heart.

Marguerite Verne sat by the window, her thoughts as restless as the leaves that danced upon the autumn breeze outside. The conversation with Phillip Lawson still lingered in her mind, a subtle disturbance beneath the surface of her usual composure. His earnest manner had been both disarming and perplexing, as though he possessed an uncommon depth of understanding, rare among the young men of her acquaintance. She had always been struck by his quiet demeanor, the way his eyes seemed to steady when he spoke of his thoughts, as though he weighed each word before letting it fall. Yet, now, as she considered their exchange, a strange unease stirred within her. Was it friendship that compelled her to linger on his words, or something more intangible, more troubling?

The prospect ofPhillip's visit had brought a peculiar flush to her cheeks, a phenomenon she attributed to the warmth of the fire—or perhaps the exertion of walking to the village earlier that day. She had dismissed it readily, chiding herself for such fanciful notions. And yet, the memory of his gaze, the earnestness of his tone, lingered, refusing to be banished. Marguerite was a creature of reason, or so she believed herself to be, and she resolved to dismiss such trifling emotions as the idle musings of a mind weary of the monotonous routine of country life.

The approach of footsteps interrupted her musings, and a knock upon the door announced the arrival of her brother, Robert. His entrance was accompanied by the usual flurry of youthful energy, though his expression was marked with a seriousness she had come to associate with his recent preoccupations. "Marguerite," he began, his tone grave, "the Listers are expected this eve. Mother has taken it upon herself to prepare a supper befitting a grand occasion, though I can scarce see the necessity of such exertion."

Marguerite raised an eyebrow, her lips twitching into a faint smile. "And what objection have you to Mother's efforts, Robert? Surely, you do not begrudge the prospect of a hearty meal and a few moments away from your studies."

Her brother flushed, a sheepish grin spreading across his face. "Not at all, dearest sister. 'Tis merely that I have scarce a moment to prepare myself for their arrival."

Marguerite's smile widened, a sound chuckle escaping her lips. "Nonsense, Robert. You will do quite well, as you always do. Besides, the Listers are no strangers to our household, and I doubt they will hold you to any higher standard than you are wont to meet."

As Robert departed with a nod and a grin, Marguerite's thoughts returned to Phillip, his presence lingering in her mind like the scent of autumn leaves. She could not deny the turmoil his visits occasioned, though she steadfastly refused to entertain the notion that it was anything beyond a deepening friendship. To acknowledge otherwise would be to admit a vulnerability she had long since buried beneath layers of self-reliance and reserve.

The arrival of the Lister family brought with it a flurry of activity, the house coming alive with the hum of voices and the clatter of feet. Marguerite greeted them with the warmth expected of her, though her heart was not entirely in the welcome. The eldest Miss Lister, with her effusive manner and tendency to overwhelm with her demonstrations of affection, was particularly testing. Her younger sisters, though less theatrical in their expressions of regard, were no less taxing in their relentless chatter and ceaseless demands for attention.

Among the group, Mrs. Lister moved with the air of one who had been appointed the role of matchmaker to the Familie Verne. Her eyes darted between Marguerite and Robert with a calculating intensity, as though she were arranging a chessboard to suit her design. Her six daughters, each named for a muse, were but pawns in her grand scheme, their existence seemingly dedicated to the task of securing a suitable match for their parents' approval. Marguerite could not help but feel a twinge of pity for the young women, their lives so neatly arranged by the hand of their mother, as though they were but pieces in a game devoid of choice.

As the evening progressed, Marguerite found herself drawn into conversation with Miss Lister, whose effusiveness grew tiresome with each passing moment. "Oh, dear Marguerite," the girl exclaimed, her voice tinged with what Marguerite could only describe as excessive enthusiasm, "your presence here is truly a delight! I do hope you will grace us with your company often, for I find your wit and charm most refreshing."

Marguerite smiled, a polite but forced expression that did little to warm her heart. "I am flattered, Miss Lister. I assure you, it is always a pleasure to entertain such delightful visitors."

The evening wore on, each moment a testament to the toll of polite society, until finally, the Lister family took their leave, their departure met with a collective sigh of relief from the Verne household. Marguerite retired to her chamber, her thoughts once more consumed by the enigmatic figure of Phillip Lawson. His visit had stirred within her a depth of emotion she was ill-prepared to confront, and though she endeavored to dismiss it as mere friendship, the truth of her feelings lingered, a shadowy presence that refused to be ignored.

The basket remained on the doorstep, an enigma wrapped in wicker.

Jack stood transfixed, his errand quite forgotten. What could it contain? Who could have left it there? He glanced back at the window, half expecting to see Aunt Rachel’s gaunt face peering out, her brow furrowed with suspicion. But the window was dark, save for the faint glow of the fire within.

He approached the basket cautiously, as if it might bite him. It was not a large basket, but of a sturdy make, woven of thick reeds. A coarse linen cloth covered its contents, tied at the corners with twine.

“Well, I never did see the likes of this,” he muttered to himself, his young brow creasing with perplexity.

He hesitated. Should he bring it inside immediately, or should he first venture to the grocer’s, as Aunt Rachel had instructed? The thought of facing her displeasure if he delayed his errand warred with his consuming curiosity.

Curiosity, as it invariably does with youth, won the day.

Untying the twine with trembling fingers, he slowly lifted the linen cloth. The first thing he saw was a small, earthenware jar, its surface glazed a rich, honeyed brown. Beside it lay a loaf of bread, still warm to the touch, wrapped in a clean, white napkin.

Jack’s eyes widened. He reached into the basket, carefully lifting the jar. It felt heavy in his hands. He sniffed at it cautiously. The aroma that wafted up was rich and savory – a scent that spoke of roasted meats and fragrant herbs.

“Soup!” he exclaimed softly. “It must be soup!”

He replaced the jar and examined the loaf of bread. It was a crusty, country loaf, the kind that Jack had only ever seen in the windows of the finer bakeries, the kind that was far beyond Aunt Rachel’s meagre budget.

Beneath the bread, he discovered other treasures. A small pat of butter, wrapped in waxed paper. A handful of apples, their skins gleaming red and gold. And, nestled amongst the apples, a small, folded note.

Jack eagerly unfolded the note. It was written in a neat, delicate hand.

“For the New Year,” it read. “With best wishes.”

No signature. No clue as to the sender.

Jack’s mind raced. Who could have sent this unexpected bounty? Was it a prank? A mistake? Or was it a genuine act of kindness, bestowed upon them by some unknown benefactor?

He remembered Mary’s words, spoken just that morning – her unwavering faith in Providence. Could this be an answer to their prayers? A sign that even in their darkest hour, they were not forgotten?

He clutched the basket tightly to his chest. He knew, with a certainty that warmed him from the inside out, that this was no ordinary gift. This was a symbol of hope, a beacon of light in the midst of their financial gloom.

He could almost hear Aunt Rachel’s voice, sharp and skeptical, questioning the motives of the unknown giver. But Jack refused to allow her cynicism to dampen his spirits. He would carry this basket inside, and he would share its contents with her and Mary, and perhaps, just perhaps, it would thaw the ice that had settled around her heart.

He turned and hurried into the tenement, his heart lighter than it had been in many a day. He would face Aunt Rachel’s questions with courage and conviction. For he knew, deep down, that this unexpected gift was a blessing, a small miracle in their lives. And he would cherish it, not only for its material value, but for the hope and promise that it represented.

Colonial Pipeline Cyberattack Halts Operations, Efforts Underway for Restoration

Colonial Pipeline, a critical fuel delivery system spanning 5,500 miles from the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast, has been halted due to a cyberattack that struck on May 7. As of May 10, the main lines remain non-operational, exacerbating concerns over fuel transportation in the southeastern United States amidst rising demand. While the company has made progress with smaller lines that are currently functioning, the impact of this major disruption has already begun to ripple through the economy, highlighting the essential role of the pipeline in transporting key fuels such as gasoline, diesel, heating oil, and jet fuel.

In an effort to mitigate the effects of the outage, Colonial Pipeline has announced plans to restore service by the end of the week. However, officials caution that even once service resumes, pipeline flow may be slow, leading some areas to rely on existing inventories for days as they await the return to normalcy. This situation is particularly critical for the Southeast, where fuel supplies are already strained.

To ensure that consumers have access to fuel during this challenging time, the Southeast will depend on inventory levels and alternative sources such as the 720,000 barrels per day Products (SE) Pipeline. Additionally, markets along the Atlantic Coast will have the option to import fuel and utilize marine shipments to supplement supplies, while the Central Atlantic and Northeast regions are looking towards importing fuel from Europe and Canada or tapping into in-region refineries. These strategies may help alleviate some pressure on regional fuel supplies as Colonial Pipeline works diligently to restore its main operations.

In response to the crisis, regulatory waivers have been issued to ease trucking restrictions for petroleum product deliveries across 17 states and the District of Columbia. This regulatory relief is expected to expedite fuel distribution and help stabilize supplies throughout the affected regions. As the situation unfolds, authorities are closely monitoring developments while reinforcing the need for robust cybersecurity measures in critical infrastructure sectors.

Testimony in Chauvin Trial Focuses on Knee on Floyd's Neck

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) – The trial of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin continued on Thursday, featuring gripping testimony from Jody Stiger, a use-of-force expert from the Los Angeles Police Department, who stated that Chauvin had his knee on George Floyd's neck area for the entire encounter. Stiger's testimony emphasized the prolonged pressure applied by Chauvin on Floyd's neck during the restraint.

Stiger told the court that based on his analysis of the video evidence, Chauvin consistently applied pressure on Floyd's neck or neck area throughout the period of restraint. This assertion contradicted the defense's argument, as attorney Eric Nelson suggested that Chauvin's knee was at times positioned on Floyd's shoulder blade or the base of his neck, not solely on his neck.

In a significant moment during the trial, Minnesota state investigator James Reyerson admitted to misinterpreting a statement made by George Floyd regarding drug use. Reyerson initially misheard Floyd's words but clarified his understanding after a longer video clip was played in court, underscoring the meticulous examination of evidence being conducted during the proceedings.

Chauvin is facing charges of murder and manslaughter in the death of George Floyd, who died during an arrest for allegedly using a counterfeit $20 bill. The defense has highlighted the presence of fentanyl and methamphetamine in Floyd's system, insinuating that drug use and underlying health conditions may have contributed to his death, a point contested by the prosecution.

During his testimony, Stiger acknowledged that while police actions can be deemed 'lawful but awful', he also discussed the impact of an onlooking crowd perceived as hostile by the police. Stiger's analysis shed light on the challenging dynamics present during Floyd's arrest and the role of external factors in influencing police behavior.

Chauvin's defense attorney, Eric Nelson, argued that Chauvin's actions should be evaluated from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, rather than in hindsight. Nelson emphasized the split-second decisions that officers are often required to make in volatile situations, urging the jury to consider the circumstances faced by Chauvin during the arrest.

Stiger further testified that Chauvin utilized pain compliance techniques on Floyd and failed to ease up on the pressure despite Floyd's visible distress. Stiger's assessment delved into the specific actions taken by Chauvin during the encounter and their impact on Floyd's well-being, providing critical insights for the prosecution's case.

James Reyerson, the lead Minnesota state investigator, provided testimony regarding the timeline of Chauvin's knee placement after Floyd ceased talking and moving. Reyerson's account focused on the crucial moments leading up to Floyd's loss of consciousness, painting a detailed picture of the events that transpired during the fateful arrest.

As the trial progresses, the courtroom remains attentive to the testimonies and evidence presented, seeking to unravel the circumstances surrounding George Floyd's tragic death. The proceedings have brought into sharp focus the complex issues of police conduct, use of force, and accountability, igniting a national debate on racial justice and law enforcement practices.

The trial of Derek Chauvin continues to captivate the nation, as each witness testimonial and piece of evidence adds another layer to the intricate narrative surrounding George Floyd's untimely death. The pursuit of justice in this landmark case remains paramount, with the eyes of the public fixed on the outcome of the trial and its implications for policing and civil rights in America.

It was curious to watch the hawks, which to my surprise had followed us all day, ever since we left the home station. They had found out by experience that when the dogs accompanied the horsemen a dinner was always left for them on the plains. High above us they followed the course of the chase, and when kangaroo and dogs were lost in the timber, we could always tell, by watching the hawks, the direction they were taking. At the cattle-station where we passed the night, the old stockman, Steve, assured me that these birds had learned to distinguish between his cattle dogs and the kangaroo hounds, as they never offered to accompany him in his daily rides unless he had the latter with him.

The consequences of all this rough bush-riding were, however, rather unpleasant to me, who had not mounted a horse except at rare intervals for years; and when we started next morning to resume our journey I had some difficulty in reaching my saddle, and hoped that our ride home would be a more quiet one. In this, however, I was disappointed, for we had scarcely left the cattle-station a mile before the dogs sighted an emu; and, after killing that, some wild cattle from the mallee were seen, and a long gallop after them ensued, in which my horse, a wilful, hard-mouthed brute, would take part, despite my protests to the contrary; so that by noon I was completely done up, and heartily wished the day's ride were ended.

As we came up to an out-station hut close to the border of the cattle-run, the hut-keeper stood at the door to receive us.

'I expected you yesterday, sir,' he said; 'or else old Steve.'

'Why?'

'Didn't you get my message?' the man asked.

'No; I got no message. What about?'

'There's been some games going on among the cattle,' replied the hut-keeper. 'The shepherd thought he heard a shot early in the morning, and saw them scampering out of the timber on to the plain where his sheep were. Here is the shepherd coming now,' he added; 'he must have seen you riding across the plain.'

The man presently reached the hut, and corroborated the hut-keeper's statement, adding that he thought he saw a spear sticking in the side of a beast which passed nearer him than the rest of the herd.

'I knew there were blacks about the day before, for I see their tracks; and I bet any money,' he added, 'it's that vagabond Bobby Peel and his mob have been killing a beast.'

'He had better not go too far,' said Stevenson, with an ominous look. 'Which part of the timber was it, Dick, and when did it happen?'

'Day before yesterday; there was a traveller passed here that morning on his way down to the river, and he said he intended staying that night at the head station, and would tell you.'

'He never called. What kind of a traveller--a horseman?'

'No, sir; a shepherd looking for a job, with his swag on his back. He must have passed the station and gone on to the public-house; yet he promised faithfully to tell you.'

'OLD MAN TOBY.'

'Well, Dick,' said Stevenson, after a thoughtful pause, 'you had better go back to your flock. Show us the place you saw the cattle come out of.'

The man pointed out a spot on the line of timber, about two miles off, and left us, while we rode off to the place indicated. For some time the superintendent remained in deep thought; then, addressing the young man, he said,--

'You heard what the shepherd said about sending me a message by a traveller?'

'Yes.'

'Well, three weeks or a month ago, when I was over on the Wakool, Mr. James asked me if I had engaged the two men he had sent me, as I had told him one day when he was passing our way that I was short-handed, and asked him to direct any men who might be looking for work over to me. Neither of those men ever came. One started two days before the other, and there is no station between James's place and our own. Still, I did not think it strange, as these men might have been mere skulkers, walking from out-station to out-station, and only pretending to look for a job. There are hundreds of such fellows tramping about the colony. But now--I don't half like the look of it!'

THE VOYAGE.

Ships, ships, I will descrie you Amidst the main, I will come and try you, What you are protecting, And projecting, What’s your end and aim. One goes abroad for merchandise and trading, Another stays to keep his country from invading, A third is coming home with rich and wealthy lading. Hallo! my fancie, whither wilt thou go? OLD POEM.

To an American visiting Europe, the long voyage he has to make is an excellent preparative. The temporary absence of worldly scenes and employments produces a state of mind peculiarly fitted to receive new and vivid impressions. The vast space of waters that separate the hemispheres is like a blank page in existence. There is no gradual transition by which, as in Europe, the features and population of one country blend almost imperceptibly with those of another. From the moment you lose sight of the land you have left, all is vacancy, until you step on the opposite shore, and are launched at once into the bustle and novelties of another world.

In travelling by land there is a continuity of scene, and a connected succession of persons and incidents, that carry on the story of life, and lessen the effect of absence and separation. We drag, it is true, “a lengthening chain” at each remove of our pilgrimage; but the chain is unbroken; we can trace it back link by link; and we feel that the last still grapples us to home. But a wide sea voyage severs us at once. It makes us conscious of being cast loose from the secure anchorage of settled life, and sent adrift upon a doubtful world. It interposes a gulf, not merely imaginary, but real, between us and our home– gulf, subject to tempest, and fear, and uncertainty, rendering distance palpable, and return precarious.

Such, at least, was the case with myself. As I saw the last blue lines of my native land fade away like a cloud in the horizon, it seemed as if I had closed one volume of the world and its concerns, and had time for meditation, before I opened another. That land, too, now vanishing from my view, which contained all most dear to me in life; what vicissitudes might occur in i–hat changes might take place in me, before I should visit it again! Who can tell, when he sets forth to wander, whither he may be driven by the uncertain currents of existence; or when he may return; or whether it may be ever his lot to revisit the scenes of his childhood?

I said, that at sea all is vacancy; I should correct the impression. To one given to day-dreaming, and fond of losing himself in reveries, a sea voyage is full of subjects for meditation; but then they are the wonders of the deep and of the air, and rather tend to abstract the mind from worldly themes. I delighted to loll over the quarter-railing or climb to the main-top, of a calm day, and muse for hours together on the tranquil bosom of a summer’s sea; to gaze upon the piles of golden clouds just peering above the horizon, fancy them some fairy realms, and people them with a creation of my own;--to watch the gently undulating billows rolling their silver volumes, as if to die away on those happy shores.

There was a delicious sensation of mingled security and awe with which I looked down, from my giddy height, on the monsters of the deep at their uncouth gambols: shoals of porpoises tumbling about the bow of the ship; the grampus, slowly heaving his huge form above the surface; or the ravenous shark, darting, like a spectre, through the blue waters. My imagination would conjure up all that I had heard or read of the watery world beneath me; of the finny herds that roam its fathomless valleys; of the shapeless monsters that lurk among the very foundations of the earth; and of those wild phantasms that swell the tales of fishermen and sailors.

As I walk through the exhibition, I am struck by how consistently art reflects, and perhaps even shapes, our deepest human desires. It’s not merely about capturing a moment in time, but about eternal longings for beauty, power, understanding, and connection. My gaze is immediately drawn to a magnificent gilt bronze clock, a testament to this very principle. It’s more than just a timepiece; it’s a synthesis of luxury, art, and technology. The intricate details speak of a desire for opulent beauty, the mechanics a thirst for knowledge and control over time itself. The sheer extravagance suggests a life free from temporal constraints. This piece, I believe, embodies the ongoing thread of human desire that stretches across centuries.

Its French influence is undeniable; a hallmark of artistic sophistication and refinement. The very use of gilt bronze elevates the piece beyond mere functionality, imbuing it with an inherent value. The beauty of the clock, and I suspect the subtle religious symbolism often woven into such pieces, undoubtedly adds to its appeal. It's easy to imagine this clock as a centerpiece in a grand hall, a conversation starter, a symbol of status and discerning taste. It possesses a relatability, albeit one specific to wealthy collectors, tapping into their desire for prestige and aesthetic fulfillment.

Reflecting on this, I am reminded of other pieces within the exhibition. Saint Peter Repentant, for instance, embodies a desire for forgiveness and redemption. Conversely, the microscope, a seemingly disparate object, showcases our insatiable curiosity and desire to unravel the secrets of the universe. Both religious and practical themes are intertwined in our artistic and scientific pursuits, fueled by these fundamental drives.

Of course, no exploration of human desire in art would be complete without acknowledging the profound influence of Gian Lorenzo Bernini. Bernini, for me, represents the epitome of artistic mastery. His versatility is astounding, encompassing sculpture, architecture, and even stage design. He demonstrates a deep understanding of human emotion and a technical skill that allowed him to translate those emotions into tangible forms.

Looking at his diverse works, from religious iconography to secular portraiture, it becomes clear that Bernini was driven by a desire to capture the essence of his subjects. His ability to work with different materials, breathing life into marble and bronze, is truly remarkable.

But it is perhaps his piece, Pluto and Proserpina, that most powerfully illustrates his genius, especially his grasp of the human form. The sheer detail of the figures, the palpable tension in Pluto's grip, the desperate resistance etched on Proserpina's face – these are not merely representations of a mythological story, but embodiments of power, lust, and the pain of abduction. The sculpture captures the very core of these dark desires. I marvel at the way Bernini transforms cold marble into something so intensely emotional and alive. The artworks within this exhibition showcase a poignant dance of desire and human familiarity. They prompt me to consider how art, at its heart, is a mirror reflecting our deepest selves.

"Now, children," resumed Sam, steadily applying himself to the task of straightening a tough handful of flax, as if industrious conduct were the main virtue, "ye've heard o' the grand livin' o' that General Sullivan o' Roxbury, an' the folly and vanity o' puttin' trust in earthly possessions an' sichlike; but let me set yer minds at ease with yet another true tale, for it shows well enough what rewards await the simple, honest folk what spends their days mindin' their duty, an' not goin' gaudy after fallals an' fancies."

"Ay, tell it, Uncle Sam," said Harry eagerly, stealing a look aside at the narrator, who nodded encouragement. So the old man drew a solemn breath, eased his broad shoulders back against the rough barn-wall, and cast one eye carefully askance toward Aunt Lois, who sat stitching diligently at her patchwork beside the open barn-door, evidently keeping a watchful ear upon the conversation unfolding.

Sam coughed once, then began, in his thoughtful, measured way: "Ye see, folks, in them days, when there were grand goings-on with General Sullivan's finery an' grandeur, there lived also, hard by the river-bank at our own Oldtown shore, a simple an' poor fisherman named Ephraim Carter—though I s'pose none o' ye recall him now. Ephraim never troubled himself with climbin' higher than his callin', nor with envy o' how others fatted themselves upon this world's leisures. Nay, he took his share o' trout an' bass from the river, pulled in his nets, an' lived humble an' pious-like with his daughter Charity."

The barn-chamber was hushed now, save only for the monotonous sound of flax being hatchelled, the steady ticking of Aunt Lois's needle, and a distant music of birdsong from the fields beyond the barn. Sam paused, weighing the wisdom of his next sentence, before proceeding onward. "'Tis often the simple souls o' humble means that Providence keep most keenly under its wing, an' so it proved with Ephraim an' Charity. One summer's night, when wild thunder an' lightnin' tore the sky, an' the river rose fierce in a rage o' wrath an' foam, Ephraim heard apiteous cries comin' from downstream. He took no second thought o' risk, but put himself straightway into his leaky boat, an' went bravely out upon the water in obedience to duty an' mercy."

"What became of him?" asked Harry breathlessly, his fingers momentarily idle upon the flax fibres. Sam shook a thoughtful finger at him, continuing gently, "Ephraim found driftin' mid-river, tossed about upon a bit o' planking, no less a person than Mister Jonathan Hartwell, rich merchant of Boston town, come visitin' General Sullivan but lately, an' carried down-river by storm an' mischance. There upon the tossin' waves, Ephraim saved him, an' carried him safe ashore to his humble hearth an' home, where charity an' kindness, my lads, took the place o' grand furniture an' foreign dainties."

Sam paused, reflectively twisting a flaxen strand 'tween his fingers, his eyes fixed on distant memory. "The merchant Hartwell, he saw clearer worth in them simple offerings o' Charity an' her pa, than in General Sullivan's velvet couches, golden plate, an' costly lace. An' Ephraim's reward, though little looked for by such humble souls, weren't small neither—for Mister Hartwell took the old fisherman into kindly favor, an' helped young Charity an' her humble father find ease an' comfort through good honest work an' quiet industry."

At this Aunt Lois looked up briefly, and added with firm approval, "'Twas the blessin' o' Providence, sure enough, an' truthful proof how our simple duty done without murmurin' an' strivin' after vain earthly follies brings peaceful contentment at last." Silence settled again for a tranquil moment, as each listener seemed lost in contemplation of the lesson offered by stern Providence. Soon the sound of Sam's steady voice rose once more, carrying gently through the sunny barn-chamber: "Many's the time I've thought, lads, though this world's wealth an' grandeur may dazzle an' deceive for an hour, yet peace an' humble contentment do lighten the heart forever, with a treasure more precious than all the riches o' kings an' conquerors."

In appearance, so far as generalities were concerned, the contrast between the two girls was less marked. Both were of the dark type, but Laura's complexion was paler than Adele's and her hair was blacker, as well as thicker and more glossy. Laura's eyes were large, very deep set, and dark. There was something strange in their look, something quite unusual, and which might almost be called holy, if that were not too strong a word to use in connexion with a woman of the world. Spicca, the melancholy duellist, who was still alive at that time, used to say that no one could possibly be as good as Laura Carlyon looked; a remark which showed that he was acquainted with the sayings of a great English wit, and was not above making use of them. Probably some part of the effect produced by Laura's eyes was due to the evenly perfect whiteness of her skin and the straight black brows which divided them from the broad low forehead. For her hair grew low, and she wore it in a simple fashion without that abundance of little curls which even then were considered almost essential to woman's beauty. Her pallor, too, was quite natural, for she had a good constitution and had rarely even had a headache. In figure she was well proportioned, of average height and rather strongly made, with large, firm, well-shaped hands. On the whole, a graceful girl, but not in that way remarkable among others of her own age. In her face, and altogether in her presence, the chief attraction lay in the look of her eyes, which made one forget to notice the well-chiselled nose,--a little short perhaps,--the really beautiful mouth, and the perfect teeth. The chin, too, was broad and firm--too firm, some might have said, for one so young. Considering all these facts together, most people agreed that Laura was not far from being a great beauty.

Adele was somewhat shorter than her step-sister, and more inclined to be stout. Her black eyes were set nearer together, and her eyebrows almost met, while her lustreless hair curled naturally in a profusion of tiny ringlets upon her forehead. The small fine nose reminded one of a ferret, and the white teeth looked sharp and pointed when the somewhat thin lips parted and showed them; but she was undoubtedly pretty, and something more than pretty. Her face had colour and animation, she carried her small head well, and her gestures were graceful and easy. She was fluent, too, in conversation and ready at all times with a quick answer. Any one could see, in spite of her plump figure, that she was of a very nervous constitution, restless, unsettled, and easily moved, capable of considerable determination when really affected. She never understood Laura, nor did Laura really understand her.

In the natural course of events, social and domestic, it became necessary to choose a husband for Adele so soon as she made her first appearance in society. At that time Laura was not yet seventeen. Gerano had already looked about him and had made up his mind. He was a little dark-eyed man, grey, thin and nervous, but gifted with an unusually agreeable manner, a pleasant tone of voice, a frank glance, and an extremely upright character--a man much liked in the world and a good deal respected.

He had determined that if possible his daughter should marry Don Francesco Savelli, a worthy young person, his father's eldest son, heir to a good estate and a still better name, and altogether a most desirable husband from all points of view. Gerano met with no serious difficulty in bringing about what he wished, and in due time Don Francesco was affianced to Donna Adele, and was privileged to visit at the Palazzo Braccio almost as often as he pleased. He thus saw Laura Carlyon often, and he very naturally fell in love with her. He had no particular inclination to marry Donna Adele, but obeyed his father blindly, as a matter of course, just as Adele obeyed Gerano. That was a part of the old Roman system. Laura, however, did not fall in love with Francesco. She was perhaps too young yet, or it is quite possible that Francesco was too dull and uninteresting a personage in her eyes. But Adele saw these things, and was very angry when she was quite sure that her future husband would have greatly preferred to marry her step-sister. She may be pardoned for having been jealous, for the situation was hardly bearable.

Cassidy Defends Impeachment Vote Amid Criticism, Finds Support

BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) – U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) has expressed a sense of peace with his decision to convict former President Donald Trump in the impeachment trial, despite facing criticism and censure from the Louisiana Republican Party. Cassidy, one of seven Senate Republicans who voted to convict Trump for inciting the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol, diverged from his colleague, Sen. John Kennedy, who voted against conviction.

In an interview, Cassidy acknowledged the backlash he has received from some party members but believes it does not represent the broader Republican opinion. He emphasized his commitment to upholding his oath to support and defend the Constitution, stating, "I took an oath to the Constitution, not to a political party."

Cassidy's vote drew criticism from the Louisiana Republican Party, which censured him for his decision. However, he has also received support and respect from some Republicans who appreciate his willingness to put the country's interests above partisan politics.

Despite the controversy surrounding his vote, Cassidy has sought to focus on other pressing issues, including the confirmation of President Joe Biden's cabinet nominees and recovery efforts in the wake of severe weather in Louisiana. He believes that these matters are of greater importance to his constituents and the state as a whole.

However, Cassidy continues to face criticism from Trump supporters, who have called for his exclusion from Republican events. Several local GOP groups have also condemned his vote, further deepening the divide within the Louisiana Republican Party.

The Senate's 57-43 vote to convict Trump fell short of the two-thirds majority required for conviction. Some Republicans who acquitted Trump disputed the evidence presented during the trial or argued that Congress lacked jurisdiction over a former president.

Cassidy's decision to convict Trump has placed him in a unique position within the Republican Party. While he has faced criticism from some party members, he has also gained respect and support from others who value his commitment to the Constitution and his willingness to make difficult decisions based on principle.
