Can't give a nigger religion without his gettin' a big devil in him at the same time."

Manfredo passes the wine to her guests, in sullen silence, and they drink to the prosperity of the house.

And now it is past midnight; the music in the next parlor has ceased, St. Michael's clock has struck the hour of one, and business is at an end in the house of the old hostess. A few languid-looking guests still remain, the old hostess is weary with the fatigues of the night, and even the gas seems to burn dimmer. The judge and Mr. Snivel are the last to take their departure, and bid the hostess good-night. "I could not call the fellow out," says the judge, as they wend their way into King street. "I can only effect my purpose by getting him into my power. To do that you must give me your assistance."

"Remain silent on that point," returns the other. "You have only to leave its management to me. Nothing is easier than to get such a fellow into the power of the law."

On turning into King street they encounter a small, youthful looking man, hatless and coatless, his figure clearly defined in the shadows of the gas-light, engaged in a desperate combat with the lamp-post. "Now, Sir, defend yourself, and do it like a man, for you have the reputation of being a craven coward," says the man, cutting and thrusting furiously at the lamp-post; Snivel and Sleepyhorn pause, and look on astonished. "Truly the poor man's mad," says Sleepyhorn, touching his companion on the arm--"uncommonly mad for the season."

Mr. Snivel whispers, "Not so mad. Only courageously tight." "Gentlemen!" says the man, reproachfully, "I am neither mad nor drunk." Here he strikes an attitude of defence, cutting one, two, and three with his small sword. "I am Mister Midshipman Butto–o madman, not a bit of it. As brave a man as South Carolina ever sent into the world. A man of pluck, Sir, and genuine, at that." Again he turns and makes several thrusts at the lamp-post, demanding that it surrender and get down on its knees, in abject obedience to superior prowess.

"Button, Button, my dear fellow, is it you? What strange freak is this?" inquires Mr. Snivel, extending his hand, which the little energetic man refuses to take.

"Mister Midshipman Button, if you please, gentlemen," replies the man, with an air of offended dignity. "I'm a gentleman, a man of honor, and what's more, a Carolinian bred and born, or born and bre–ut it as you like it." He makes several powerful blows at the lamp-post, and succeeds only in breaking his sword.

"Poor man," says the judge, kindly, "he is in need of friends to take care of him, and advise him properly. He has not far to travel before he gets into the mad-house."

The man overhears his remarks, and with a vehement gesture and flourish of his broken sword, says, "Do you not see, gentlemen, what work I have made of this Northern aggressor, this huge enemy bringing oppression to our very doors?" He turns and addresses the lamp-post in a tone of superiority. "Surrender like a man, and confess yourself vanquished, Northern aggressor that you are! You see, gentlemen, I have gained a victor–et all his bowels out. Honor all belongs to my native stat– shall resign it all to her." Here the man begins to talk in so wild a strain, and to make so many demands of his imaginary enemy, that they called a passing guardsman, who, seeing his strange condition, replaced his hat, and assisted them in getting him to a place of safety for the night, when sleep and time would restore him to a sound state of mind.

Como Agua Para Chocolate is the original Spanish title for the 1989 book (and subsequent 1992 film) “Like Water for Chocolate” by Mexican author Laura Esquivel. I chose this book to reexamine because it (and the film) was used in my third-year Spanish class in high school. It was the first time I really remember feeling confident that I could read in Spanish, and the first time I was able to watch a film in Spanish without panicking about needing to read subtitles.

The book begins each chapter with a receta, a recipe. They seem like serious recipes at first, but they segue into stories in the life of Josefita (Tita) de la Garza. Tita is the youngest of three daughters of Mama Elena on a ranch near the U.S. / Mexico border during the Mexican Revolution. Tita’s fate as the youngest daughter, according to family tradition, is to never marry and take care of her mother until the mother dies (Tita’s father dies when she is a child, and bears almost nothing on the plot).

Tita is raised in the kitchen as an apprentice to the cook, Nacha, where she becomes a phenomenal cook with a very deep, personal connection to food, to the point where her emotions become imbued in every dish she makes (the novel falls into the Magic Realism genre, where the supernatural is treated as commonplace). Tita is in love with ranch hand Pedro, who returns her affections. When Mama Elena refuses to consent to their marriage because of the aforementioned tradition, Pedro marries Tita’s eldest sister, Rosaura, to be closer to Tita. The recipes explore what happens with the ups and downs of that relationship and the food Tita produces because of it: tears in the batter of the wedding cake cause everyone at Rosaura and Pedro’s wedding to become very ill, and the sadness kills Nacha; a lusty dish of quail in a sauce of petals from roses given to Tita by Pedro cause middle sister Gertrudis to literally start a fire with lust and run off into the arms of a passing revolutionary soldier, etc. Pedro and Tita become even closer, arranging secret meetings under the context of him seeking to feed Roberto, his son with Rosaura, because Rosaura cannot breastfeed. Mama Elena suspects the relationship between Tita and Pedro, and insists that Rosaura take her husband and son and move to San Antonio. Roberto dies very shortly thereafter, but Rosaura manages to have another child before being rendered sterile: a daughter named Esperanza. Tita takes Roberto’s death very hard, and, following an argument with Mama Elena, she secludes herself in the chicken coop (or, more properly translated, a dovecote). Doctor John Brown is called to institutionalize Tita, but decides to take her to his home and care for her there with his son, Alex. They become very close, almost as family, but Tita forever loves Pedro. Dr. Brown understands this, and lets Tita go.

I lay long awake, my thoughts in a sad turmoil. The visitant of the night, whether real or the figment of a fevered brain, haunted me with a persistence that bordered on torment. Who could it have been? And what motive could prompt such a strange and unsettling apparition? Was it a playful jest, cruelly executed? Or something far more sinister?

The monotonous tramping from the room above had ceased some hours since, yet the echo of it seemed to reverberate still within the confines of my skull. It was a sound that chilled me to the very marrow, devoid of any discernible rhythm or purpose, yet filled with an indefinable menace. I dared not conjecture what manner of creature, human or otherwise, could be responsible for such a dispiriting din.

At length, weary with speculation and worn down by the lack of sleep, I drifted into a troubled slumber, punctuated by fitful dreams wherein the kiss, both tender and unsettling, was re-enacted with an alarming regularity. Phantoms danced attendance in the shadows, their faces obscured, their intentions inscrutable. I awoke with a start as dawn threatened to break, my heart pounding, my brow slick with perspiration.

The first rays of the sun, pale and hesitant, filtered through the gaps in the heavy curtains, casting long, distorted shadows upon the walls. I rose from my bed, feeling strangely weak and disoriented, and proceeded to dress myself with a listlessness that belied my youth. The world beyond my window seemed cloaked in a somber gray, reflecting the mood that gripped my soul.

Having made such toilette as I could muster, I ventured forth from my chamber, intent upon seeking out Mrs. Dance and, if possible, extracting from her some morsel of information that might shed light upon the mysteries that enshrouded Dupley Walls. I descended the staircase with trepidation, each creak of the aged timbers seeming to amplify the silence that pervaded the house.

I found Mrs. Dance in the stillroom, busying herself amongst a profusion of herbs and spices, her face illuminated by the morning sun. She greeted me with a kindly smile, though I thought I detected a certain wariness in her gaze.

"Good morning, Miss Holme," she said. "Did you rest well?"

I hesitated, unsure of how to broach the subject that weighed so heavily upon my mind. "Not entirely," I replied, choosing my words with care. "I found the night somewhat… unsettling."

Mrs. Dance’s eyes narrowed slightly. "Unsettling, you say? In what way, pray?"

"There was a… noise," I began, "from the room above. A constant tramping that prevented me from sleeping."

"Ah, yes," she said, with a dismissive wave of her hand. "That would be Mr. Grimes. He is of a restless disposition, and often paces his chamber at odd hours."

"Mr. Grimes?" I echoed, my curiosity piqued. "And who, may I ask, is Mr. Grimes?"

A shadow seemed to cross Mrs. Dance’s face. "Mr. Grimes is… a guest of Lady Pollexfen," she said, her voice carefully neutral. "He has been residing here for some time."

"And what manner of man is he?" I pressed, unable to resist the urge to delve deeper into the mysteries of Dupley Walls.

Mrs. Dance sighed, a hint of exasperation in her eyes. "Miss Holme," she said, "I must implore you to curb your curiosity. Lady Pollexfen does not take kindly to being questioned, and it would be best for you to avoid arousing her displeasure."

"But surely," I protested, "I am entitled to know something of the circumstances that surround me. I have been brought here under the pretext of companionship, yet I am treated with suspicion and kept in the dark about everything."

"I understand your frustration," Mrs. Dance said, softening her tone. "But I am not at liberty to divulge any information that Lady Pollexfen deems confidential. Suffice it to say that there are forces at work here that are beyond your comprehension."

She paused, and regarded me with an expression of mingled pity and concern. "Believe me, Miss Holme," she added, "it is for your own good that you remain ignorant of these matters. The less you know, the safer you will be."

"But I cannot help but feel that I am in danger," I said, my voice trembling slightly. "The kiss, Mrs. Dance, during the night...!"

Mrs. Dance gasped and she placed a comforting hand upon my arm. "You cannot trust such fancies, Miss Holme, sometimes at night the mind may play tricks."

Google's work environment consistently earns high praise, receiving a formidable 4.4 out of 5 rating on Glassdoor, thereby solidifying its status as one of the premier companies to work for globally. This accolade can be attributed in part to the company's unique office culture, which emphasizes creativity, inclusivity, and employee well-being. Google's ability to foster an engaging and innovative environment sets it apart from other tech giants, such as Microsoft and Yahoo!, which suffer from more negative perceptions regarding management and overall employee satisfaction. Internally, Google emphasizes a work culture that encourages collaboration and innovation, with one employee noting, "The company empowers us to bring our whole selves to work and to think outside the box."

However, securing a position at Google is known to be a formidable challenge, with the company's interviews often being perceived as some of the most difficult in the industry. With a selective hiring process that sees only approximately 0.2% of applicants being employed each year, Google's recruitment strategy is rigorous, incorporating multiple interviews and requiring active participation from current employees. Candidates are evaluated on leadership abilities, role-related knowledge, problem-solving skills, and the elusive quality of 'Googleness,' which refers to cultural fit and alignment with the company's values. Google's emphasis on cultural fit is significant, as the company seeks long-term employees who can contribute positively and adapt seamlessly to its innovative climate.

Over the years, Google has successfully diversified its business portfolio by acquiring more than 170 companies, with notable acquisitions including YouTube and Motorola. The purchase of Motorola, in particular, has been strategic, enabling Google to produce its own line of smartphones under the Nexus brand. This move into hardware reflects Google's broader vision of creating a more interconnected ecosystem of devices and services. On the advertising front, however, Google faces criticism from some quarters for its inability to customize ads as effectively as Facebook, which benefits from a more granular understanding of social data to target audience preferences. Despite this weakness, Google's advertising platform remains one of the most powerful globally, leveraging robust data analytics and a vast user base.

While Google remains a respected industry leader with a keen focus on innovation, its hiring practices and internal culture distinguish it from other technology companies. Compared to its peers, Google maintains a streamlined and meritocratic approach to recruiting talent, prioritizing individuals who can thrive in a dynamic environment. This emphasis on cultural fit and long-term contribution contrasts with common criticisms of Microsoft's and Yahoo!'s management and organizational challenges, which have sometimes stymied their ability to attract and retain top talent. With a commitment to maintaining a high bar in its hiring practices, and refining its strategies to address areas like ad customization, Google reinforces its reputation as a formidable and forward-thinking market leader.

HE thought he had already, poor John Berridge, tasted in their fulness the sweets of success; but nothing yet had been more charming to him than when the young Lord, as he irresistibly and, for greater certitude, quite correctly figured him, fairly sought out, in Paris, the new literary star that had begun to hang, with a fresh red light, over the vast, even though rather confused, Anglo-Saxon horizon; positively approaching that celebrity with a shy and artless appeal. The young Lord invoked on this occasion the celebrity’s prized judgment of a special literary case; and Berridge could take the whole manner of it for one of the “quaintest” little acts displayed to his amused eyes, up to now, on the stage of European society--albeit these eyes were quite aware, in general, of missing everywhere no more of the human scene than possible, and of having of late been particularly awake to the large extensions of it spread before him (since so he could but fondly read his fate) under the omen of his prodigious “hit.” It was because of his hit that he was having rare opportunities--of which he was so honestly and humbly proposing, as he would have said, to make the most: it was because every one in the world (so far had the thing gone) was reading “The Heart of Gold” as just a slightly too fat volume, or sitting out the same as just a fifth-act too long play, that he found himself floated on a tide he would scarce have dared to show his favourite hero sustained by, found a hundred agreeable and interesting things happen to him which were all, one way or another, affluents of the golden stream.

The great renewed resonance--renewed by the incredible luck of the play--was always in his ears without so much as a conscious turn of his head to listen; so that the queer world of his fame was not the mere usual field of the Anglo-Saxon boom, but positively the bottom of the whole theatric sea, unplumbed source of the wave that had borne him in the course of a year or two over German, French, Italian, Russian, Scandinavian foot-lights. Paris itself really appeared for the hour the centre of his cyclone, with reports and “returns,” to say nothing of agents and emissaries, converging from the minor capitals; though his impatience was scarce the less keen to get back to London, where his work had had no such critical excoriation to survive, no such lesson of anguish to learn, as it had received at the hand of supreme authority, of that French authority which was in such a matter the only one to be artistically reckoned with. If his spirit indeed had had to reckon with it his fourth act practically hadn’t: it continued to make him blush every night for the public more even than the inimitable feuilleton had made him blush for himself.

This had figured, however, after all, the one bad drop in his cup; so that, for the rest, his high-water mark might well have been, that evening at Gloriani’s studio, the approach of his odd and charming applicant, vaguely introduced at the latter’s very own request by their hostess, who, with an honest, helpless, genial gesture, washed her fat begemmed hands of the name and identity of either, but left the fresh, fair, ever so habitually assured, yet ever so easily awkward Englishman with his plea to put forth. There was that in this pleasant personage which could still make Berridge wonder what conception of profit from him might have, all incalculably, taken form in such a head--these being truly the last intrenchments of our hero’s modesty. He wondered, the splendid young man, he wondered awfully, he wondered (it was unmistakable) quite nervously, he wondered, to John’s ardent and acute imagination, quite beautifully, if the author of “The Heart of Gold” would mind just looking at a book by a friend of his, a great friend, which he himself believed rather clever, and had in fact found very charming, but as to which--if it really wouldn’t bore Mr. Berridge--he should so like the verdict of some one who knew. His friend was awfully ambitious, and he thought there was something in it--with all of which might he send the book to any address?

Strange to say, the appellation of this waste piece of land, with its wild bushes, was the "Dark Plain." Why? The plain was not dark: it was not shaded: it stood out, broad and open, in the full glare of sunlight. That certain dark tales had been handed down with the appellation, is true: and these may have given rise to the name. Immediately before the archway, for some considerable, space, the ground was entirely bare. Not a blade of grass, not a shrub grew on it. Or, as the story went, would grow. It was on this spot that the appearance, the Shadow, as mentioned by Charlotte Pain, would be sometimes seen. Whence the Shadow came, whether it was ghostly or earthly, whether those learned in science and philosophy could account for it by Nature's laws, whether it was cast by any gaseous vapour arising in the moonbeams, I am unable to say. If you ask me to explain it, I cannot. If you ask, why then do I write about it, I can only answer, because I have seen it. I have seen it with my own unprejudiced eyes; I have sat and watched it, in its strange stillness; I have looked about and around it, low down, high up, for some substance, ever so infinitesimal, that might cast its shade and enable me to account for it: and I have looked in vain. Had the moon been behind the archway, instead of behind me, that might have furnished a loophole of explanation: a very poor and inefficient loophole; a curious one also: for how can an archway in the substance be a bier and two mourners in its shadow? but, still, better than none.

No; there was nothing whatever, so far as human eyes--and I can tell you that keen ones and sceptical ones have looked at it--to cast the shade, or to account for it. There, as you sat and watched, stretched out the plain in the moonlight, with its low, tomb-like bushes, its clear space of bare land, the archway rising behind it. But, on the spot of bare land, before the archway, would rise the Shadow; not looking as if it were a shadow cast on the ground, but a palpable fact: as if a bier, with its two bending mourners, actually stood there in the substance. I say that I cannot explain it, or attempt to explain it; but I do say that there it was to be seen. Not often: sometimes not for years together. It was called the Shadow of Ashlydyat: and superstition told that its appearance foreshadowed the approach of calamity, whether of death or other evil, to the Godolphins. The greater the evil that was coming upon them, the plainer and more distinct would be the appearance of the Shadow--the longer the space of time that it would be observed. Rumour went, that once, on the approach of some terrible misfortune, it had been seen for months and months before, whenever the moon was sufficiently bright. The Godolphins did not care to have the subject mentioned to them: in their scepticism, they (some of them, at least) treated it with ridicule, or else with silence. But, like disbelievers of a different sort, the scepticism was more in profession than in heart. The Godolphins, in their inmost soul, would cower at the appearance of that shadowed bier; as those others have been known to cower, in their anguish, at the approach of the shadow of death.

This was not all the superstition attaching to Ashlydyat: but you will probably deem this quite enough for the present. And we have to return to Mrs. Godolphin.

Five years before the present time, when pretty Cecilia was in her fifteenth year, and most needed the guidance of a mother, Mrs. Godolphin died. Her illness had been of a lingering nature; little hope in it, from the first. It was towards the latter period of her illness that what had been regarded by four-fifths of Prior's Ash as an absurd child's tale, a superstition unworthy the notice of the present-day men and women, grew to be talked of in whispers, as something "strange." For three months antecedent to the death of Mrs. Godolphin, the Shadow of Ashlydyat was to be seen every light night, and all Prior's Ash flocked up to look at it. That they went, is of no consequence: they had their walk and their gaze for their pains: but that Mrs. Godolphin should have been told of it, was. She was in the grounds alone one balmy moonlight night, later than she ought to have been, and she discerned people walking in them, making for the ash-trees.

The gaslights of the boulevard flickered against the deepening dusk, casting a golden haze over the bustling street. Paris had become a mosaic of light and shadow, a vivid painting brought to life by the city’s own breath. Lucien, infused with a sense of both wonder and apprehension, ambled his way through the bustling throng. The swirls of evening mist only heightened his impression that he was wading through a reverie. Paris—capricious mistress, beguiling and cruel in turns—had him entranced. It was here, in her embrace, that he intended to forge his destiny.

Before him lay a glittering new world, and with it, he harbored aspirations as endless as the September sky. His new attire—exquisite and tailored with precision—cocooned him in the guise of a true Parisian dandy. The silk of his waistcoat shimmered beneath the evening sky, each thread singing silent promises of possibility and acclaim. He cast a sidelong glance towards the reflecting glass of a shop window, marveling at his transformation from provincial poet to urban sophisticate. Yet, despite this exterior metamorphosis, an undercurrent of unease wove through his thoughts as insidious as smoke slipping beneath a closed door.

Paused at the entrance to Tortoni’s, he was greeted by the glow of elegance within. Drawing a deep breath, he ventured inside, conscious that the clientele bore that ineffable air of worldly nonchalance. He nodded with forced bravado to the doorman and settled at a small, marble-topped table near a bay window, considering his next move within this labyrinthine society. As the waiter approached, he ordered rather too elaborately for his means, betraying his own insecure desire for acceptance among such illustrious company.

Lucien’s gaze flitted from face to face in the café, each more intriguing than the last, like characters torn from novels he had read in his youth. They each seemed to shine with an inner light, born of experience and cunning sophistication. Nearby, a gentleman with a regal bearing gestured passionately as he recounted tales of the latest political intrigue. It seemed to Lucien that here was the very pulse of Paris' heart, throbbing with its own indomitable spirit.

But beneath this spirited façade, questions lingered—how much of this life would cost him more dearly than coin? He rested his arms on the table, contemplation etched upon his visage. The weight of an uncertain future pressed heavily upon his shoulders even as he embarked on this glittering adventure. Would this city, so filled with allure, grant him his dreams or devour them whole?

Here and there, laughter rose like champagne bubbles around him as conversations touched on art, love, and scandals. The resonance was intoxicating, and Lucien longed to be one of them—to bask in the luminescence of their collective joie de vivre. Yet, for all his desire, it became increasingly clear to him that he was but an outsider; there were secrets yet to decipher, an intricate dance of nuance and subtlety that he must learn to navigate. Simply put, he was adrift on a sea and the stars by which to guide him had yet to reveal themselves.

Even as he indulged in a cup of delicate porcelain, the world seemed to spin around him with dizzying speed. Lost in thought, he scarcely noticed the approach of a figure until a soft voice interrupted his abstraction. "Monsieur de Rubempré, I believe?" inquired an elegant lady, her eyes alight with calculated interest. She wore her charm like an adornment, as natural as the silken folds of her green gown. Lucien nodded, lips curving into a polite smile, his interest piqued.

Her presence was like a doorway into realms unexplored, and for a moment, it seemed as if Providence itself had cast its luminous gaze upon him. She spoke in shaded tones, her words both inquiry and invitation. Her laughter was a melody played upon the strings of intrigue, and Lucien, a willing accompanist, found himself drawn into her orbit. It was a curious dance—they wove the fabric of new acquaintance with neither overstated gesture nor unnecessary pause.

In this unexpected encounter lay the potential for encounter after encounter, introducing openings to that rarefied world he yearned to inhabit. Like a moth to moth-light, he felt the pull of ambition yet undaunted by its possible perils. As their conversation unfurled, an awareness of his growing complicity settled upon him as if forewarned he might become not just an observer but a player upon Paris's grand stage.

Yet within this carefully architected world, one truth shone with the clarity of a revelation: he must rise or fall by his own reckoning. A final flourish punctuated their parting pleasantries, and she disappeared into the milieu as effortlessly as she had arrived. With newfound resolve, Lucien stood and exited the café, stepping into the evening's embrace, certain of one thing—he was at the very beginning of something momentous. The labyrinth awaited, and with it, the promise that discovery lay at every turn.

While the general historical narrative of Asian immigration from the late 19th to mid 20th century is one of poor immigrants, the narrative of Asian immigration in the late 20th through the 21st century is quite different. Due to the combination of a quota and preference system in the 1964 Immigration Act, more affluent immigrants are now favored. Clutter’s family’s story is a common one in the restricted sphere of Asian immigration after 1964. In contrast, the story Yung tells of a well-off student, Jane Kwong Lee, who travels by ship from China to San Francisco, succeeds in getting an education, and becomes fairly successful afterwards is relatively rare for Asian immigration of that time. It is important to note that aspects of Clutter’s story may be as rare for Asian immigration today as Lee’s story is for Asian immigration in the past. This is the danger of creating an analysis from one person’s story. It would also be simplistic to equate Clutter’s story entirely with Lee’s; economic affluence is clearly a huge advantage in any situation, but many other factors are involved. Racial paradigms, for example, changed greatly over the 20th century, and this is especially true in the case of Chinese immigration. Yung ends her story with the 1940s so we cannot follow Lee’s experience of the Red Scare in the 1950s, but Ngai writes that Chinese immigrants suddenly came under suspicion due to fear of communism, and their legality was questioned. Even affluent immigrants were at risk of deportation if they were proven to be “paper sons” and had ties to communists or labor organizations. Since Clutter’s family immigrated in 2005, quite a bit later than the end of the Cold War, and after American society had changed so that it was socially unacceptable to assert that people were untrustworthy entirely due to their race, their experience as affluent Asian immigrants is distinct from affluent Asian immigrants of the past. To be sure, racism still exists, but it manifests itself in much different ways.

In fact, Mike Clutter does not believe racism has played a significant role in his life as an American immigrant. His family chose to move to Potomac, MD, because it was near his father’s new job in Northern Virginia and because his mother had a cousin who had already moved to Potomac. Potomac has a large Asian population, with a significant percentage of that being Taiwanese, and Clutter says that this “helped with home-sickness”. As Clutter finished up high school, he started out spending most of his time with Asian immigrants and Asian Americans.

Although Clutter first became friends with other Asians - shorthand for East Asians in Potomac - he soon made friends from other ethnic groups common in Potomac, including South Asians, Iranians, Jews, and even some white Christians. He considered Potomac to be ethnically integrated, but pointed out that his family would sometimes get together with other Taiwanese families to stay connected. He says he felt “comfortable” and “welcomed” in Potomac and continued to feel the same way after he left to go to college at the University of Pennsylvania. Of course, it is possible that Clutter experienced racism and chose not to talk about it. It is also possible that he is lying about feeling comfortable and getting along well with his white friends, and the danger of an oral history is that he could conceivably be lying about everything the interviewer does not have personal knowledge of. However, that is unlikely. A more plausible explanation in which Clutter did in fact experience racism would be that the racism was too subtle for him to be sure of its motives, too rare for him to deem worth mentioning, or too uncomfortable a subject for him to be willing to talk about. It is only possible to interpret whether one of these is the case by considering the information Clutter does give. He was successful in his education and social life, he felt that he was able to keep in touch with Taiwanese culture adequately (more on that later), and he described the environment of Potomac as a comfortable one. From this evidence, I can only assume that any racism Clutter experienced was something he considered insignificant and did not have a substantial detrimental effect on his life.

Hospitals in Hurricane-Ravaged Houma Strained by 'Perfect Twin-Demic'

HOUMA, La. (AP) – Amidst the devastation brought by Hurricane Ida, the medical community in Houma faces a different type of peril – an overwhelming surge of COVID-19 patients colliding with the storm's catastrophic aftermath. Leonard J. Chabert Medical Center and Terrebonne General Health System, two hospitals in the heart of the impact zone, confront challenges unlike ever before.

Richard Zuschlag, owner of Acadian Ambulance Service, described the intensity: "This 'perfect twin-demic' has a horrendous impact. It is something I pray we never witness again."

Hurricane Ida wreaked havoc on Chabert Medical Center. Water poured in from the ceiling, and structural damage threatened the facility's integrity. Meanwhile, the hospital was brimming with COVID patients, leaving scant resources for hurricane relief. The severity of patients' conditions and neighboring hospitals filled with COVID patients made evacuation unfeasible.

"Ida was a hell of a storm," said Dr. Chuck Burnell, chief medical officer of Acadian Ambulance. "The real concern is the evacuation of 100 patients, 60 of whom have tested positive for COVID-19. It's a scenario that presents immense difficulty."

Hospitals' staff endured unprecedented mental stress as they pleaded for divine protection during the hurricane while fearing their building could crumble around them. Terrebonne General Health System didn't fare better; its roof buckled, and windows shattered under Ida's wrath.

"Protecting our patients and staff was the upmost priority," Burnell added. "But I cannot deny the added pressure of the storm and the pandemic combined."

The coordinated evacuation mission unfolded post-hurricane. Terrebonne General's ambulances secured travel to Baton Rouge for a portion of their patients, managing the colossal task in phases to safeguard everyone's well-being.

Zuschlag weighed in on the relief efforts: "The medical community's unified response to this predicament underscores their commitment to the community."

As the dust from Ida settles and recovery begins, the unparalleled impact of two concurrent disasters leaves an imprint on a battered yet resilient Houma.

Readily and cheerfully have I acceded to this request; and with the more relish, as I shall thus be furnished with an authentic occasion to present to the world the many valuable thoughts and eloquent utterings of my late distinguished pupil, and now beneficent patron, the Hon. Middleton Flam, long a representative of this Borough and the adjacent district in the Congress of the United States.

I pretend to no greater merit in this execution of my task than what an impartial spirit of investigation, a long acquaintance with persons of every degree connected with this history, an apt judgment in discriminating between opinions, a most faithful and abundant memory, a careful store of documentary evidence, an unalterable devotion to the great principles of Quodlibetarian Democracy, and, for the expounding of all, a lucid and felicitous style, may allow me to claim as the chronicler of this Borough.

The better to assure you, my friendly reader, that, in temper and condition, I may demand somewhat of the confidence due to the character of a dispassionate commentator on the times, I would have you understand that I am now on the shady side of sixty, unmarried, and in possession of an easy revenue of four hundred dollars per annum, which is voted to me by our commissioners, for instructing in their rudiments thirty-seven children of both sexes; that I have a plate at the table of my patron, the Hon. Middleton Flam, my former pupil, every Sunday at dinner; and that he, being aware for some time past of my purpose to treasure up his remarkable sayings, has, with a generous freedom, often repeated to me many opinions which otherwise would have been irretrievably lost. Moreover, since I am now brought before the public under circumstances in which reserve on my part would be no better than affectation, I would also advertise my indulgent reader of the fact that I belong to the Quodlibetarian New-Light Club, whereof I some time officiated as Secretary, and which club generally meets on Saturday night at Ferret's; that the members of the same, noting my staidness of deportment and the careful deliberation with which I guard myself in the utterance of any discourse, do frequent honor to the temperance of my judgment by making me the arbiter of such casual controversies as arise therein, touching the true import and application of the principles of our New-Light Democracy; and--if I run no risk of being charged with offering a trivial evidence of the reputation I have earned in the club--I would also mention, that some of our light wags have gone so far--facetiously and with a commendable good nature, knowing that I would not take it ill, as more peevish men might, in their jocular pleasantry--as to call me, in allusion to my natural sedateness, SOBER SECONDTHOUGHTS:--the rogues!

And now, amiable and considerate reader, you have "ab imo pectore" my honest avouch for what I propose to lay before you, and a plain confession of my weaknesses. I come with a clean breast to the confessional. We shall have a frugal banquet of it, but the fruits, I make bold to promise, shall be wholesome and of the best. Now turn we to it in good earnest. If this little chronicle--for my book shall not be overgrown and apoplectic, but rather, as you shall find it, "garrulous and thin"--do not bring you to a profound sense of the value of this Amaranth of Republicanism, the New-Light Quodlibetarian Democracy, then say it to my teeth, there is no virtue in SOBER SECONDTHOUGHTS. Go thy ways--"The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walketh in darkness."

The Impact of Negative Emotions on Learning

Negative emotions have a pervasive and debilitating impact on student motivation and focus in learning environments. Research has consistently shown that evaluative appraisals of performance and surrounding emotional states influence learning and achievement. For instance, a study by Borke (2005) found that students' emotional experiences and their evaluations of their abilities were significant predictors of their motivation and performance. These findings suggest that a supportive and inclusive learning environment is crucial in mitigating the negative effects of negative emotions on student learning.

Recent studies in neuroscience have shed light on the neural mechanisms underlying the impact of negative emotions on learning. Research indicates that during negative emotional states, the right hemisphere of the brain becomes more active (Damasio, 2004). Interestingly, the concept of 'activity inhibition' (AI), which involves the frequent use of the word 'not' and relates to brain hemisphere function, is associated with increased activity in the right hemisphere (Bogen, 1993). Experiments have shown that participants with higher AI levels tend to respond quicker to visual stimuli presented in the left visual field, engaging the right hemisphere (Kolb & Whishaw, 1998). Moreover, negative emotions such as frustration have been found to increase engagement of the right hemisphere and AI levels, further exacerbating the negative impact on learning (Taylor et al., 2003). These findings suggest that the way students process and respond to information is influenced by their emotional states and the lateralization of brain function.

The concept of cerebral lateralization plays a significant role in student learning and emotional states (LeDoux, 2000). Research has shown that students exhibit different learning styles, influenced by their hemispheric preferences (visual/analytical) (Sperry, 1974). However, traditional educational approaches often favor left-hemisphere preferred education methods, focusing on facts and verbal instruction, which can result in neglecting students with right-hemisphere preferences (Gardner, 1985). To address this issue, researchers recommend the adoption of affective education, which aims to balance right- and left-hemisphere learning styles (Kimura, 1999). By incorporating more holistic and creative approaches to learning, educators can foster a more inclusive and supportive learning environment, one that acknowledges the diverse cognitive and emotional needs of students and promotes optimal learning outcomes.

"Hast thou seen him?" quoth I, with a gaze as piercing as the northern star.

"Nay, but I've had him itemized to me by the wife o' Samson Slumber, a teller of tales as fervent as a hermit's prayer. A chin as sharp as a blade, a brow as creased as the earth after a tempest, he hath the visage of one who hath known both triumph and tribulation."

"Methinks," spake I, my voice a melody somber and deep, "that man's visage doth bear the stamp of his own mettle; a chin carved by determination, a brow furrowed by the weight of mankind's follies."

"Indeed, Master Sharrow," retorted she, her voice brimming with the fervor of a bard recounting an age-old saga, "this Lord Silex stands as a relic of a time forgotten, a demon from the tales 'neath the moonlight."

"Yet," mused I, a twinkle in my eye as subtle as the flicker of a candle's flame, "there is within me a something that doth stir on his behalf, as if the mere mention of his name weaves a tale of redemption amidst the shroud of scandal."

"By my troth!" exclaimed my spouse, her countenance one of disbelief, "I do believe, Master Sharrow, that thou'dst offer solace to a ghost in the gloaming."

Just then, there came a knock at our chamber door, and forth stepped Lady Adella Trenyon, her gaze as keen as a falcon's and her silhouette as regal as a queen's. She had overheard our discourse and was plied by the tales of Lord Silex.

"Do tell me more, dear Marian," beseeched Lady Trenyon, her countenance alight with curiosity, "for I have long held disdain for tales of gossip, yet this Lord Silex intrigues me as does a riddle wrapped in enigma."

Marian, with a nod, continued her narration, her voice a tapestry of vivid descriptions and hushed whispers. She painted Lord Silex as a phantom of vengeance, his wrath eternal, his spirit as restless as a ghost in the night, driven by a betrayal so profound it had turned his very soul to stone.

"Yet," mused Lady Trenyon, her wisdom as timeless as the echoes of ancient ballads, "we often judge men by the stories spun around them, much like we perceive a forest by the single tree we gaze upon. One act can cast a long shadow, but let us not forget that a man's life is a book, not a mere chapter."

As if summoned by the very mention of his name, Sir John Trenyon, Lady Trenyon's venerable uncle, entered the room, a figure straight out of history's pages. His presence was commanding, his stories as rich as the tales told by the ancient bards.

"Ah, Lady Trenyon," greeted Sir John, his voice a deep baritone as resonant as a cathedral's bell, "I've heard whispers of Lord Silex, a man shaped by the very currents of fate. Let me share with you a slice from the tapestry of his story, for in the annals of our family, his name is woven like a thread of gold."

And so, as the twilight bled into night, Lady Trenyon listened, her heart a vessel of both skepticism and longing for tales of yore, tales intertwined with the threads of loyalty and betrayal. The room filled with the murmurs of the past, a past where Lord Silex, the demon of Denbeigh, loomed large, yet within the shadows, a flicker of compassion dared to dance.

"So, dear Marian, tell me," implored Lady Trenyon, her voice a melody as delicate as a dancer’s step, "was Lord Silex, in his bleakest hour, a man deserving of mercy, or merely a specter of his own making?"

And thus, the tale unfolded, a narrative as intricate as the web spun by a spider, as enigmatic as the whisper of the wind. Each syllable, a step further into the labyrinth of Lord Silex's life, where the lines between villain and victim blurred amidst the tapestry of human frailty and ambition.

Lord Silex, the epitome of a man whose past was as dark as the deepest abyss, whose future as uncertain as a vagabond's journey, stood at the crossroads of redemption, a figure as captivating as the moon beholds the stars.

"And so," mused Lady Trenyon, her eyes reflective pools of contemplation, "might not the very essence of Lord Silex's being be the embodiment of hope, concealed within the guise of villainy, waiting for the moment when truth shall unveil his hidden visage?"

As the embers of the fire danced in the hearth, Lady Trenyon’s mind was a canvas upon which the story of Lord Silex was painted anew, each stroke of her imagination bringing the figure of the infamous lord closer to a semblance of humanity, a being entwined with the very fabric of existence.

The first baritone sits on the corner, his frame unlike those of the other men, it is as if his strength has been lent to him from above, and the bars of his bass clef seem to swirl with the bold strokes of a landscape painter. He is not one for airs or flair but a genuine soul with a voice born of the iron heart of the mountains. Don't think for a moment he is that massive frame you hear come marching down the street, all flex and show, although he has his turns on the operatic stage, no, it's this quiet one who has the raw force that comes through in song.

They say he plays the bass in the town band, not that elaborate theorbo they've got at the opera but a simple but firm thump on the side of the tuba that'll make your heart move. You should hear him on Sunday afternoons, his full chest swelling with the hymns, a sort of personal conductor securing the lifeline that binds us all to ourselves. He thinks a lot on these matters, the first baritone; considers if the wooden beam across the piazza does not roar with the undertones of what it is to be a part of a great storm, a unity of song and wind.

You may doubt him at first, with his rugged build and dull visage, that the high tenor here and there so lightly means a man of disfigurations lower than he, but his countenance, while non-descript, allows the kind of quiet that you need. Listen to him and he'll pass you on by with eyes bright but not perturbated. The ground beneath you shudders beneath the vivacity of his violin-ready 'conversations', never anything else but weaving into the precincts like a light spilled in tunnels bringing the hand and the heart at one. Listen closely to his fiddle song, you see that by his warble he will tell the dreams worn off one anonymous sheet of yellowed, petrified fibres entwined.

During Donald Trump's Presidency, America Underwent Significant Changes

Donald Trump reshaped the landscape of American politics when he won the presidency in 2016, marking the first time an individual without prior governmental or military service ascended to the nation's highest office. His tenure was marked by deep societal divisions and confirmed his unique position in U.S. history.

As a businessman from New York and a former reality TV star, Trump captured the presidency after a campaign that broke conventional norms and kept the public riveted. His governing style was no less unconventional, diverging from the tradition of seeking national unity post-election. Throughout his term, Trump indulged in political combat, often using his position to target a wide array of perceived opponents, including members of the media, his administration, bipartisan politicians, and international leaders. His prolific use of Twitter to share his thoughts on various matters led to his permanent suspension from the platform due to the controversial nature of his posts. Notably, Trump was the first president to be impeached twice, with the second impeachment related to inciting an insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, and he was the first in over 150 years to skip the inauguration of his successor.

Trump's presidency brought significant policy shifts both domestically and internationally. Domestically, he achieved notable conservative wins, such as unprecedented corporate tax cuts, the rollback of numerous environmental protections, and a transformation of the federal judiciary. Internationally, he implemented stringent immigration restrictions, exited several multilateral treaties, strengthened ties with Israel, and engaged in an economic confrontation with China to address perceived economic disparities.

The full impact of Trump's legacy and his potential future political role remains to be fully understood. However, it's evident from recent years' studies, including those from the Pew Research Center, that his presidency coincided with or catalyzed several major societal shifts.

This analysis of the changes in the U.S. during Trump's presidency draws from Pew Research Center surveys, governmental data, news reports, and other sources, aiming to provide a comprehensive overview.

Divisions Deepened on Partisan and Personal Lines

Trump's presidency intensified partisan and personal divides within the American populace. His unorthodox approach and directness contributed to him being a continuous center of attention, deepening the rift between Republicans and Democrats.

Before even assuming office, Trump polarized the two major political parties more than any president in recent decades. This division only widened during his presidency, with Republican approval consistently high and Democratic approval strikingly low, showcasing an unprecedented partisan gap. His approval ratings remained below 50%, dipping to 29% following the Capitol riots.

The perception of Trump's character and persona sharply differed between Republicans and Democrats. A 2019 survey revealed that while a significant portion of Republicans felt hopeful, entertained, informed, happy, and proud by Trump's words, a larger percentage of Democrats reported feeling concerned, exhausted, angry, insulted, and confused by his rhetoric.

The Unanswered Question: What If Tom Brady Joined the Saints in 2020?

Drew Brees' decision to return for the 2020 season with the New Orleans Saints was met with both excitement and concern. On one hand, fans eagerly awaited another shot at a second Super Bowl victory. On the other hand, Brees' age and a season marred by injuries left many wondering if it was the right call. As it turns out, Brees' choice not only impacted his own journey but also potentially altered the course of NFL history.

According to ESPN reporter Jeff Darlington, speaking on 'Get Up', Tom Brady was "very, very close" to signing with the Saints before ultimately choosing the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Brady's interest in the Saints was genuine, but Brees' decision to continue playing played a crucial role in the six-time Super Bowl champion's ultimate decision.

"Brady was seriously considering the Saints," Darlington said. "I think it's fair to say that if Drew Brees had retired, Tom Brady would have been a New Orleans Saint."

This hypothetical scenario raises intriguing questions about the Saints' potential success in 2020. With Brady under center, key players like Rob Gronkowski, Antonio Brown, and Leonard Fournette might have been tempted to join forces, creating a powerhouse team that could have dominated the league.

Throughout the 2020 season, Brady's health and performance metrics were significantly better than Brees'. He threw for 4,633 yards, 40 touchdowns, and only 12 interceptions, leading the Buccaneers to a Super Bowl victory. In contrast, Brees dealt with multiple injuries, including a punctured lung and multiple rib fractures, affecting his performance on the field.

While the "what-if" game can be endless, it's impossible to ignore the potential impact Brady could have had on the Saints' season. Could they have made a deeper playoff run? Would they have hoisted the Lombardi Trophy once again? These are questions that will forever remain unanswered.

Now, with Brees retired, the Saints have turned to former Buccaneers quarterback Jameis Winston as their new signal-caller. Winston, known for his big-play potential, brings a different dynamic to the Saints' offense. As the team embarks on a new era, fans and analysts alike will be watching closely to see if he can fill the void left by Brees.

For more Saints news, updates, and analysis, be sure to follow Canal Street Chronicles. The future may be uncertain, but one thing is clear: the story of the New Orleans Saints continues to unfold in fascinating ways.

Legislation surrounding surrogacy demonstrates considerable variation across states, with jurisdictions such as Illinois and Texas establishing comprehensive statutes that delineate the rights and responsibilities of both surrogates and intended parents. In these jurisdictions, statutes are enforced through carefully drafted contracts that often hinge on the state's definition of “family.” This definitional framework is central to judicial reasoning, as courts review whether surrogacy contracts align with statutory mandates that protect the welfare of all parties involved. The judicial system, when interpreting these contracts, examines evidentiary support, the explicit nature of the intent, and the comprehensive disclosure of obligations to ensure that legally binding agreements reflect mutual consent. In Illinois, the legal framework often emphasizes both the surrogate’s autonomy and the intended parents’ interests, while Texas highlights contractual obligations that must be adhered to throughout the surrogacy process. This dichotomy underscores the importance of consistent legislative language that aligns contractual obligations with overarching definitions of family within specific state contexts.

Legal inconsistencies become pronounced when comparing the surrogacy frameworks of states such as Nevada and Washington. Nevada permits surrogacy agreements for married heterosexual couples, thereby institutionalizing a framework that privileges conventional family structures while discriminating against homosexual and unmarried couples. Conversely, in Washington, compensation for surrogacy is limited, with statutes permitting payment only if it does not exceed reimbursement for reasonable expenses. This restriction reinforces the notion of “altruistic surrogacy,” a term used to denote arrangements in which a surrogate acts without monetary gain beyond necessary budgetary expenditures. Judicial opinions in Washington often reference the sanctity of the human body, arguing that additional payments risk commodifying the surrogate’s reproductive capabilities. These contrasting legal models—where one state endorses surrogacy under rigid family and marital conditions and another imposes strict compensatory limits—highlight the prevailing societal debates on whether surrogacy constitutes a socially beneficial act or an ethically fraught transaction.

In stark contrast, several jurisdictions such as Arizona, Michigan, and the District of Columbia prohibit surrogacy altogether, a stance that exemplifies deep ideological and ethical concerns within conservative circles. In these regions, surrogacy practices are not only legally forbidden but are often characterized by legislators as forms of “reproductive prostitution,” reflecting a societal apprehension toward the commercialization of childbirth. Courts in such areas are wary of legal agreements that might commodify the womb and undermine moral and ethical standards. Additionally, certain statutes fail to address the marital status of the surrogate, creating a potential double standard by applying distinct regulatory frameworks to the surrogate and the intended parents. This lapse in statutory detail further complicates legal disputes, as judicial reasoning must reconcile ambiguities in legislative intent with underlying social values. Overall, the landscape of surrogacy law reflects profound differences in legal interpretation and sociopolitical priorities, making it a vivid example of how legislative frameworks are deeply interwoven with societal conceptions of family, morality, and human dignity.

It was a morning of peculiar tranquility at Barton Cottage, where a gentle breeze, barely lifting the lace curtains, ushered in a day that seemed pregnant with possibilities. Mrs. Dashwood, having set aside her mourning garb for less austere attire, sat by the window with an air of contemplative contentment. Her thoughts, accustomed to flit like a ruffled bird from one concern to another, now hovered over the subject of Elinor's future—most particularly in the form of a certain Mr. Edward Ferrars, whose visits had become notably frequent of late.

Elinor, ever engaged with her embroidery, seemed the picture of serene industriousness, though her needle threaded lighter and less purposeful than usual. So incipient was the tenderness she had developed for Edward, it appeared with the translucence of new bloom, yet shimmered with the promise of an enduring attachment. And although no formal proposal had yet been made, Mrs. Dashwood sensed a mutual understanding blooming between them, one that revealed itself in shared glances and shades of unspoken affection, perceptible only to those observers with the most discerning eyes.

Marianne, meanwhile, reclined in the sunlight near her sister, an anthology of poetry languidly held in her lap but largely unread. Her mind wandered through the verdant lanes of her youthful imagination, dreaming up a vision of love much more fiery and tempestuous than the gentle affection unfolding before her. That she held a genuine fondness for Edward, Marianne would not dispute; yet his presence stirred neither intense admiration nor serious critique in her heart. For Marianne, love had always been an affair tempestuous and grand, sung with fervent abandon across the windswept cliffs and groves that she often wandered.

Yet Marianne's effervescence had a quiet acceptance for Edward's growing place in their lives, astutely recognizing that his qualities spoke deeply to her sister's own tastes and temperament. She observed Edward's willingness to listen, truly listen, when Elinor spoke of art or philosophy, even if his responses were measured in comparison to her own enthusiasms. Understandably, his lack of profound intimacy with the arts left Marianne somewhat cold, but she could not deny the sincerity of his character and the gentle steadiness of his affection for Elinor.

Edward, for his part, seemed to find an uncommon solace within the walls of Barton Cottage. He deftly tailored his sensibilities to fit the patterns of its domesticity, far removed from the oppressive expectations imposed upon him by his family. Here, in the company of those unswayed by vanity and moneyed ambition, Edward felt more himself, his spirit unburdened by the fear of disappointing others. His shyness, which elsewhere might have confined his thoughts and feelings to the inner recesses of his heart, gradually dissolved in Elinor's presence, revealing a man of depth and empathy beneath his unremarkable exterior.

Mrs. Dashwood spoke little of her observations, yet her maternal instincts compelled her to pave an unobtrusive way towards Elinor's happiness. She took pleasure in arranging opportunities for the young couple to indulge in private discourse, advocating subtly through the practicalities of everyday life. Whether suggesting Edward join them for their outdoor walks or encouraging him to linger over dinner, her actions were rife with an almost unnoticeable intention.

Any reservations present in Elinor's heart, however slight, could be traced back to a cautiousness engrained by experience. Her profound sense of duty, shaped by the spectres of past disappointments, gently tempered the ebullience of her affection. She weighed the consequences and the responsibilities that might accompany such an attachment, mindful of her family's financial constraints and Edward's own familial obligations.

Thus, in fits and starts, Elinor plucked the petals of her burgeoning love, counting each as either a blessing or a burden until she reached a decision known only to herself. To an outside observer, she appeared self-possessed and tranquil, her outward calm belying the inner confusions of her heart. The cares of prudence whispered in her ear even as her heart beat a fervent melody of its own.

Within this interplay of emotions, there emerged in Elinor's heart a conviction that Edward's earnest affection, albeit quiet, was strong enough to bridge the gulf between their hopes and constraints. Yet, as in all matters of great consequence, the path ahead remained fraught with the inherent uncertainties of life, each step requiring a deliberation and courage uniquely her own.

Meanwhile, the sun, now climbing higher in the azure sky, marked the arrival of a new visitor—an arrival that would punctuate the Dashwood household with yet another shift in their evolving narrative. The gentleman entered the drawing-room with a briskness that suggested both purpose and amiability. He was Charles Brandon, an acquaintance from the neighborhood, possessing manners that were courteous, if not slightly officious, but entirely congenial.

Charles's presence served to break the introspective quietude of the morning, his conversation reaching out with polite inquiries and genial observations upon the weather and local happenings. Although his visits were infrequent, they were no less welcomed, as Charles had—through good humour and impeccable decorum—endeared himself to the family's sensibilities. His admiration for Elinor was evident in his regard, though tempered by an awareness of a certain disparity in their affections.

In undertaking the complexities of their delicate quadrille, the Dashwoods and their visitors found themselves navigating the shifting currents of propriety, affection, and irretrievable circumstance, all the while maintaining a fragile dance between personal obligation and the heart's ineffable inclinations. Thus, the morning drew itself into afternoon, drawing gently—as if on invisible threads—the lives of our characters ever further into the richly interwoven tapestry of love and life at Barton Cottage.

Mrs. Jake and Mrs. Martin were quite familiar with the story of the night when there were no candles and Mr. Thacher had broken his leg, having been present themselves early in the morning afterward, but they had listened with none the less interest. These country neighbors knew their friends' affairs as well as they did their own, but such an audience is never impatient. The repetitions of the best stories are signal events, for ordinary circumstances do not inspire them. Affairs must rise to a certain level before a narration of some great crisis is suggested, and exactly as a city audience is well contented with hearing the plays of Shakespeare over and over again, so each man and woman of experience is permitted to deploy their well-known but always interesting stories upon the rustic stage.

"I must say I can't a-bear to hear anything about ghosts after sundown," observed Mrs. Jake, who was at times somewhat troubled by what she and her friends designated as "narves." "Day-times I don't believe in 'em 'less it's something creepy more'n common, but after dark it scares me to pieces. I do' know but I shall be afeared to go home," and she laughed uneasily. "There! when I get through with this needle I believe I won't knit no more. The back o' my neck is all numb."

"Don't talk o' goin' home yet awhile," said the hostess, looking up quickly as if she hated the thought of being left alone again. "'T is just on the edge of the evenin'; the nights is so long now we think it's bedtime half an hour after we've got lit up. 'T was a good lift havin' you step over to-night. I was really a-dreadin' to set here by myself," and for some minutes nobody spoke and the needles clicked faster than ever. Suddenly there was a strange sound outside the door, and they stared at each other in terror and held their breath, but nobody stirred. This was no familiar footstep; presently they heard a strange little cry, and still they feared to look, or to know what was waiting outside. Then Mrs. Thacher took a candle in her hand, and, still hesitating, asked once, "Who is there?" and, hearing no answer, slowly opened the door.

In the mean time, the evening had been much enjoyed by the brothers who were spending it together in Martin Dyer's kitchen. The houses stood side by side, but Mr. Jacob Dyer's youngest daughter, the only one now left at home, was receiving a visit from her lover, or, as the family expressed it, the young man who was keeping company with her, and her father, mindful of his own youth, had kindly withdrawn. Martin's children were already established in homes of their own, with the exception of one daughter who was at work in one of the cotton factories at Lowell in company with several of her acquaintances. It has already been said that Jake and Martin liked nobody's company so well as their own. Their wives had a time-honored joke about being comparatively unnecessary to their respective partners, and indeed the two men had a curiously dependent feeling toward each other. It was the close sympathy which twins sometimes have each to each, and had become a byword among all their acquaintances. They were seldom individualized in any way, and neither was able to distinguish himself, apparently, for one always heard of the family as Jake and Martin's folks, and of their possessions, from least to greatest, as belonging to both brothers. The only time they had ever been separated was once in their early youth, when Jake had been fired with a desire to go to sea; but he deserted the coastwise schooner in the first port and came home, because he could not bear it any longer without his brother. Martin had no turn for seafaring, so Jake remained ashore and patiently made a farmer of himself for love's sake, and in spite of a great thirst for adventure that had never ceased to fever his blood. It was astonishing how much they found to say to each other when one considers that their experiences were almost constantly the same; but nothing contented them better than an uninterrupted evening spent in each other's society, and as they hoed corn or dug potatoes, or mowed, or as they drove to the Corners, sitting stiffly upright in the old-fashioned thorough-braced wagon, they were always to be seen talking as if it were the first meeting after a long separation. But, having taken these quiet times for the discussion of all possible and impossible problems, they were men of fixed opinions, and were ready at a moment's warning to render exact decisions. They were not fond of society as a rule; they found little occasion for much talk with their neighbors, but used as few words as possible. Nobody was more respected than the brothers. It was often said of them that their word was their bond, and as they passed from youth to middle age, and in these days were growing to look like elderly men, they were free from shame or reproach, though not from much good-natured joking and friendly fun. Their farm had been owned in the family since the settlement of the country, and the house which Martin occupied was very old. Jake's had been built for him when he was married, from timber cut in their own woodlands, and after thirty years of wear it looked scarcely newer than its companion. And when it is explained that they had married sisters, because, as people said, they even went courting together, it will be easy to see that they had found life more harmonious than most people do. Sometimes the wife of one brother would complain that her sister enjoyed undue advantages and profits from the estate, but there was rarely any disagreement, and Mrs. Jake was mistress of the turkeys and Mrs. Martin held sway over the hens, while they divided the spoils amiably at Thanksgiving time when the geese were sold. If it were a bad year for turkeys, and the tender young were chilled in the wet grass, while the hens flourished steadily the season through, Mrs. Jake's spirits drooped and she became envious of the good fortune which flaunted itself before her eyes, but on the whole, they suffered and enjoyed together, and found no fault with their destinies. The two wives, though the affection between them was of an ordinary sort, were apt to form a league against the brothers, and this prevented a more troublesome rivalry which might have existed between the households.

In the somber ambiance of the dawn's first light, Sergeant O'Reilly traversed the cobblestone alleys of Bath, the remnants of the city's elegance dulled by the pallor of his mind. The weight of his recent tribulations bore heavily upon him; the suicide of Colonel Hargrove had cast a shadow over his own soul, a shadow deepened by the silence he had kept regarding the stolen diamond. The evidence was as elusive as the morning mist, and he chose discretion above all else, lest he be implicated in the colonel's deceit or, worse, involve himself in a scandal that would tarnish the reputation of his erstwhile superior.

Illness, like a relentless shadow, had shadowed his days, a condign companion to his grief. His body had been wracked, his spirit battered, by the dual blows of despair and ailment. Yet, even as his heart lamented the passing of his beloved Eleanor, whose demise struck him like a bolt from the azure, he found within himself an unexpected resilience. The circumstances of his life, once precarious, now seemed a path paved with purpose. With a determination forged by the fires of sorrow and the crimson stains of his thoughts, he donned the uniform anew, bound for the distant shores of China, where the regiment awaited.

The years that followed were a tapestry woven in hues of duty and distant horizons, far removed from the familiarity of England's verdant landscapes. The sergeant became a solitary figure amidst the cacophony of foreign tongues and alien customs, his solitude both a sanctuary and a crucible, testing the mettle of his resolve. Yet, amid the trials, he found solace in the simple routines of soldiering, a rhythm that offered a balm to the wounds of his past.

Upon his return, the sergeant found the world unchanged, yet irrevocably different. England, with her customary charm, welcomed him back with open arms, yet the heart he had carried across the seas remained weighted with the unresolved matters of his previous life. With a sense of duty that now bordered upon a pilgrimage, he sought out Lady Pollexfen, the citadel of the Pollexfen lineage, to deliver the message that had been entrusted to him by Colonel Hargrove.

As he stood before her, the sergeant's hands trembled not from fear but from the gravity of his errand. "Your ladyship," he began, his voice gravelly from years spent overseas, "I bear a message from one no longer with us, a message of respect and gratitude—and, I fear, of sorrow." Lady Pollexfen's gaze, initially filled with curiosity, softened at his words, her eyes belying a well of unseen emotion.

"He could not write," the sergeant explained, his voice carrying the weight of unuttered truths, "for the Colonel Hargrove was as illiterate as myself. But it was his wish that I convey to you his humble regard and deep appreciation for the hospitality once extended to him." Lady Pollexfen, her composure momentarily faltering, retrieved an aged letter from a forgotten drawer, its edges frayed and its seal, broken—a relic of a bygone era, its significance now laid bare.

The sergeant watched as she unfolded the parchment, her hands trembling as though they too bore the weight of the secrets it held. "This," she said softly, her voice a whisper against the silence, "this was written by the Colonel himself. A testament to a friendship forged under the most trying of circumstances, a bond unbroken by time or distance." The sergeant nodded, understanding the silent dialogue that passed between them, a testament to the enduring legacy of a man whose life, though cut short, had left an indelible mark upon those he touched.

As the dawn light spilled through the windows, casting a golden glow upon the room, a sense of closure, fragile yet profound, settled between the sergeant and Lady Pollexfen. The message delivered, their fates intertwined no longer by the specter of Colonel Hargrove's demise but by the shared memory of a life lived and the hope for a new beginning. The sergeant, as he departed from the sanctuary of Lady Pollexfen's abode, carried with him not only the promise of the past but the seeds of a future yet to unfold—a future where the shadows of old regrets might finally be left behind, and the morning sun could shine upon new horizons.

Part of this reason is the fact that Germany was not united until the 1870's, and thus the border cultures tended to take in similarities to their neighbors, and their neighbors took in parts of German. Next we have Mitteldeutsch (Middle German) through the middle of the country, with the Fränkisch dialect within its borders, that follows the Main river. Alemannisch in Switzerland and the Bavarian-Austrian dialect.
