Through this evidence-based approach, the true potential of mentoring relationships can be realized, offering proteges comprehensive guidance and a diverse array of opportunities for growth.

Sir John was silent for some moments, as if his thoughts and feelings were too powerful to produce utterance. Clara did not, or would not, perceive his emotion; she continued eating her biscuit and strawberries with calm unconcern, not at all disconcerted by the deep silence which followed her mother's speech. Sir John at length rose, and, with great solemnity of tone and manner, addressed his youngest daughter, who was seated a silent spectator of the whole scene.

"Chrystal, it is time for me to take some steps towards removing you from such examples. I shall accompany you to Brierly to-morrow, and place you, for the present, under Boscawen's care. He will take charge of you till I can claim you in peace. When I have deposited you in safety, I shall remove from Wetheral for ever. Your mother and sister will accompany me into Scotland, as I shall reside in future at Fairlee."

Nothing could exceed Lady Wetheral's terror at these words, spoken so calmly and so decidedly. She rushed towards her husband, and seized his arm with nervous trepidation.

"Don't go into Scotland, John! oh, don't go there, to horrid Fairlee! I shall die there--no, no; say you will not take me from Wetheral, and I will promise any thing, John!" Her ladyship's alarm became very powerful, and she sank to the ground. Christobelle would have flown to the bell to summon Thompson, but her father forbade the action; he begged that such scenes might never be disclosed to the eyes of the household. He raised her, and laid her on a sofa, but it was some time ere her senses returned. She wandered evidently for some hours in her conversation, and was at length placed in bed, under the influence of a powerful narcotic. Christobelle watched by her as she slept.

Sir John Wetheral felt all this most painfully; but he was now awake to the weakness of his conduct in placing such implicit confidence in his lady's system of education; he felt too late how indolently he had succumbed to her tears and reproaches against his own better judgment, even to the sacrifice of Julia; and now he was resolved to save Clara, at the risk of sacrificing for ever all future hopes of domestic felicity. Her ladyship's fearful apprehensions of Fairlee threatened an illness: but Sir John was firmly resolved to quit Shropshire; to leave at once the scene of deception which irritated his mind; to save, if possible, the fate which awaited Clara, should her evil genius give her into the power of Sir Foster Kerrison.

Christobelle was still watching in her mother's room, when she opened her eyes, and faintly called for Thompson. Christobelle did not reply, but walked softly to the side of her bed, to inquire how she felt after her long sleep. Her eyes were heavy, for she closed them as she spoke.

"Is that you, Thompson? I have had such horrible dreams: your master is going into Scotland, and poor Miss Clara will be taken away from Sir Foster, after all my trouble."

"It is me, mamma," whispered Christobelle.

"Well, well," replied her mother, petulantly, "never mind who it is, you are equally included in this dreadful Fairlee business. I shall never live to reach Scotland: the dullness of the place--no neighbourhood--all old married men--not a match there fit for Clara--altogether it will kill me."

A silence of some moments ensued, and she spoke again in low complaining tones.

"Your poor father's violence has made me seriously ill, Bell, and he must lay my death at his own door. Sir Foster has been extremely ill used, and all the neighbourhood will think so, after his proposal being accepted, and his attachment made so public! My poor child Clara! it is very cruel by her, and the affair has broken my heart."

The emergence of Buddhism in Thailand is intricately linked to the political and cultural influence of the Mauryan Emperor Asoka, who reigned from the mid-3rd century BCE. While Asoka's interpretation of Buddhism was influenced by his Hindu background, his impact on doctrinal Buddhism was relatively minor. His efforts, however, played a significant role in establishing Buddhism in the region, including Thailand, over two thousand years ago. The Emperor commissioned the building of monasteries, the propagation of the Dharma, and the conversion of subjects, thereby laying the groundwork for Buddhist teachings to take root in the country.

In the late 19th century, a unique Buddhist tradition emerged in Thailand known as Thudong, characterized by forest-dwelling monks who renounced scholarly life in favor of asceticism. These monks, adhering to the tradition known as森林 Bhikkhu, thrust themselves into forest environments, shunning the comforts of city monasteries and academic pursuits. Their lives were marked by simplicity, relying solely on alms given by laypeople for sustenance and making use of minimal possessions. Despite the rudimentary nature of their living conditions, Thudong monks upheld a rigorous training regime, often undertaking arduous ascetic practices such as the sixteen dhutanga practices, a set of austerities designed to refine the mind and accelerate spiritual growth.

Thudong monks sustained their lives in the wild, facing myriad challenges along the way. They were not immune to the harsh realities of their surroundings; wild animals, illnesses, and supernatural entities posed constant threats. Yet, their determination to live according to the teachings of the Buddha and the Visuddhimagga, a key text on the perfection of practice despite not being a canonical text, remained unwavering. The Visuddhimagga, which outlines the path to liberation, served as a guide and inspiration, although it deviated from the traditional Pali Canon, setting the Thudong tradition apart from more conventional forms of Buddhism.

The unique lifestyle of the Thudong monks who chose to dwell in forests and engage in minimalistic, ascetic practices led to the establishment of a distinctive form of Thai Buddhism.Their commitment to the dhutanga practices, including eating only one meal a day, sleeping on the ground, and wearing coarse robes, differentiated them from the more mainstream Theravada monastic practices. This spiritual path, rooted in the simplicity and asceticism of the Buddha himself, created a stark contrast with the more structured and urban approach of mainstream monastic life in Thailand. Thus, the Thudong tradition, born out of a strong sense of conviction and a desire to emulate the teachings of the Buddha in their purest form, has carved out a unique niche within Thai Buddhism, leaving an indelible mark on the religious landscape.

Beneath an ashen sky and amid the forlorn horn-blasts of a tempest now dissipated, the remnants of the once-proud transport lay scattered upon the rugged shore of Spain. The sea, whose savage moods had laid claim to many a stout-hearted crew, whispered its lament over broken timbers and shattered masts. In that ominous twilight, the survivors huddled together, their souls as battered as the vessel that had borne them through a night of ghastly fury. The scene spoke of both nature’s unbridled might and the resilient human spirit that, though bruised, still dared to hope beneath the gathering gloom.

In the heart of this despair strode Captain Milburn, a man whose commendable proficiency in the languages of commerce and diplomacy had earlier secured the salvation of nearly all souls aboard. With a sagacity borne of hardened experience, he had negotiated passage on the lips of acquainted locals, promising assistance in exchange for the safe conveyance of his charges. Yet, that same art of persuasion, which had once kindled the fires of charity and succour, now found him burdened by an overwhelming responsibility. His heart, heavy with the memory of fallen officers and lost comrades, beat in discord with the unyielding mandates of duty and honor in a land foreign to both kin and comfort.

In the days that followed, as the once-furious winds laid themselves to rest and the brooding heavens yielded to reluctant light, the survivors were ushered into the modest shelter of a coastal hamlet. Here, the officer assumed the gravest of responsibilities: to defray the costs incurred in rescuing and sustaining those who had escaped the clutches of a merciless sea. Yet, when back in England his entreaties for recompense reached the stony ears of home authority, he found himself ensnared in a thicket of bureaucratic contempt. The very state that had, in better times, applauded his selfless actions now dismissed his petitions as fanciful expense, leaving him burdened with debts that none but his own conscience could bear.

Frustration, like a malignant fever, began to smolder in the breast of this indefatigable officer. The harsh rebuff from his sovereign realm ignited in him a wrath that none might deem befitting a man of his station and cultivated discourse. In a moment of dire disillusionment, he resorted to a violent measure against a man of influence—an act that sealed his fate and cost him the coveted Indian appointment, his prior honor now sullied by reckless impetuosity. This act, though born of desperation and wounded pride, served as a damning indictment of the state of affairs in England—a nation, perhaps, too engrossed in its own self-interest to genuinely hold its valiant servants in esteem.

Meanwhile, in the quiet solitude of his family’s modest estate, the officer’s uncle, an elderly and contemplative man of a peculiar disposition, found himself gripped by a vision both strange and portentous. In the twilight hours, as he wandered a shadowed orchard, a spectral figure appeared—a prophet clad in enigmatic raiment, bearing a message of doom for the Western powers. The vision spoke of a reckoning by a force ancient and inexorable: a cleansing wrought by Islam, whose ascendant tide would, in its inexorable advance, sweep away the vestiges of a crumbling empire. This revelation, as profound as it was alarming, lingered in his mind like the echo of a distant alarm, portending a future in which old certainties would be razed to leave fertile ground for radical change.

As word of these dire misfortunes spread from the disconsolate harbor to the troubled hearts of inland communities, an air of disillusionment and quiet rebellion began to gather. The rescued passengers, though grateful for their deliverance from the caprices of nature, found themselves marooned not only by geography but also by the cold neglect of a state impervious to human suffering. Their voices, once raised in hopeful exultation, now murmured a grateful resignation tinged with bitter cynicism—a sentiment that would soon echo in the halls of power and the narrow lanes of their newfound refuge alike.

Thus, beneath a sky still heavy with the lingering sorrows of last night’s tempest and the more inexplicable turmoil of human allegiances, the threads of fate were drawn taut. In the interplay of personal misfortune and the inexorable march of prophecy, the stage was set for further trials and tribulations. The calm before a tempestuous moral reckoning had settled over these forlorn souls—a reckoning that would see the valiant, the disillusioned, and even the visionary united in a struggle against forces both external and within. In that uncertain realm of light and shadow, where honor battled despair and the promise of a new epoch trembled on the brink of realization, each man and every whispered prophecy contributed to the unfolding drama of an age imperiled by its own hubris.

Tiger Woods Crash Investigation Concludes, Cause Undisclosed

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department has concluded its investigation into Tiger Woods' car crash on February 23, but the cause of the accident remains undisclosed due to privacy concerns.

"We have reached out to Tiger Woods and his personnel," said Sheriff Alex Villanueva. "If they waive the privacy, then we will be able to release the information."

The crash occurred when Woods' SUV struck a sign, sheared through a tree, and landed in the brush with significant damage. Woods was unconscious at some point after the crash but conscious when deputies arrived.

"A witness reported that Mr. Woods was unconscious at the scene," said Deputy Johann Schloegl, the traffic collision investigator.

Woods underwent emergency surgery for significant injuries to his right lower extremity and returned home in mid-March to continue his recovery.

"Tiger is focused on his recovery," said a source close to the golfer. "He feels lucky to be alive and appreciates the access to great medical care."

Woods confirmed on social media that he is back home continuing his recovery and has reunited with his children.

"I'm so grateful for the support and love I've received during this difficult time," Woods wrote. "I'm making progress and feeling better every day."

The investigation into the crash has been thorough, according to Villanueva.

"We have interviewed all the witnesses, collected all the evidence, and analyzed all the data," Villanueva said. "We have determined the cause of the crash, but we cannot release that information at this time."

Villanueva said the decision to withhold the information was made after consulting with the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.

"We have a responsibility to protect the privacy of all individuals involved in this case," Villanueva said. "We believe that releasing the cause of the crash at this time would violate that privacy."

Woods' team has not yet responded to the Sheriff's Department's request to waive the privacy.

"We are hopeful that they will cooperate with us," Villanueva said. "We believe that the public has a right to know the cause of this crash."

The crash has been a major setback for Woods, who was just starting to return to competitive golf after a long layoff due to back injuries.

"Tiger is a fighter," the source said. "He's going to come back from this and be even stronger than before."

Meanwhile, Sir Jasper had resumed his old career in London as though there had never been a break in it. The young ladies saw little more of their father after the second Lady Pengarvon's death than they had before. He went down to Broome occasionally for a few days at a time, but that was all. He lived five years longer; then one morning he was found dead in his Mayfair lodging with a bullet through his heart. Once more he had come to the end of his resources. It was hopeless to think of marrying a third fortune. There stared him in the face an old age of obscure penury away from the haunts he loved so well, and the prospect daunted him. He died as he had lived, an utter pagan.

A few years later, the aunt with whom Isabel had gone to live died, and Miss Pengarvon found herself under the necessity of sending Barney Dale for the child, there being no other home for her than Broome. Isabel at this time was a blue-eyed, yellow-haired little lady of seven, the very presentment in features and expression of a certain youthful Miss Pengarvon whose portrait by Sir Joshua graced the gallery at Broome. In truth, the drysalter's little grand-daughter had all the traditional beauty of the women of her father's race--a beauty which had so unaccountably lapsed in the case of her elder half-sisters, niece though their mother had been to an earl.

It was in the dusk of an autumn afternoon that Barney Dale and his charge reached Broome. The Misses Pengarvon were awaiting the child in the old oak parlor, which even on the brightest day in summer was gloomy and full of strange shadows. The elder sister came forward a step or two, and taking Isabel by the hand, gazed down in frowning silence on the fair young face, which returned her look with wondering, frightened eyes. A faint momentary color flushed her sallow cheeks. Then she stooped and pressed her thin, cold lips to Isabel's forehead.

"So you are come back to Broome, child. They had better have found you another home," she said in her dry, hard voice, in which not the slightest chord of sympathy ever seemed to vibrate. Miss Letitia, who copied her sister in everything, went through a similar formula.

Isabel gazed from one stern, sad-faced woman to the other, and her lips quivered. She turned and clung to Barney's arm.

"Oh, take me away! take me away! I want to go back!" she cried.

Miss Pengarvon turned away in high displeasure, and Barney led the tearful child from the room.

That first night, and many nights afterwards, Isabel cried herself to sleep in the huge four-poster, with its funereal draperies, in which they put her to bed. All her life she had been used to being petted and made much of, and had hardly known what it was to be alone. But now she was left by herself in a great ghostly room from six o'clock at night till seven next morning. She felt herself to be quite an unconsidered trifle in that huge ocean of bed. She was morally sure that those grim portraits on the walls--dark, frowning gentlemen in perukes and embroidered clothes, and stately ladies in hoops and high-heeled shoes--whispered to each other about her, Isabel Pengarvon; and that after the candle was taken away they stepped down out of their frames, and hastened to join the other ghosts in the long gallery, where they danced and flirted and took snuff with each other, till some watchful cock on a faraway farm sounded the warning note which sent them back to their faded frames, there to attitudinize in silent mockery till another midnight should come round.

Newsom Proposes Largest State Tax Rebate in U.S. History with $11.9B Golden State Stimulus Expansion

California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Thursday, May 13, announced a proposed expansion of the Golden State Stimulus, which includes $600 checks for Californians earning up to $75,000, rent relief, and utility bill assistance as part of a $100 billion California Comeback Plan.

Newsom stated, "We're on the road to recovery, and it's time to put cash back in the pockets of Californians." The proposal, which leverages $26 billion in federal relief funds, aims to address the economic disparity caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially among low-wage workers and people of color.

Senator Nancy Skinner (D-Oakland), lead of the Senate budget committee, shared her support for the plan: "These payments will be a game-changer for millions of struggling Californians. Senate Democrats have been advocating for direct relief to help families stay afloat during these challenging times."

Phil Ting (D-San Francisco), Assemblymember and counterpart to Skinner, added, "Californians have faced unprecedented hardships during this pandemic, and they need real help now. The Governor's proposal will provide relief to millions and help lift our economy."

Republican gubernatorial candidates, including John Cox and Kevin Faulconer, criticized the plan as politically motivated due to the impending recall election. Cox stated, "Californians don't need more handouts. They need jobs, they need affordability, and they need a governor who will put their interests first."

Anna Hasselblad, Public Policy Director for United Ways of California, emphasized the need for greater relief for undocumented immigrants: "We're pleased to see Californians receiving much-needed support, but we cannot forget the undocumented community, who has been largely excluded from federal relief."

Newsom's proposal includes $11.9 billion for $600 payments, $5.2 billion for rent relief, $2 billion for utility bills, and $1 billion in college grants. The state reports a $75.7 billion surplus, allowing Newsom to propose the largest state tax rebate in U.S. history.

California's eviction moratorium is set to expire on June 30, making the rent relief proposal urgent. Gov. Newsom acknowledged the urgency, stating, "We know that the moratorium will soon expire, and we cannot let our most vulnerable residents face eviction."

John Chiang, a former California state controller and candidate for controller in the upcoming recall election, voiced his support for the Golden State Stimulus, stating, "This is exactly the kind of bold action our state needs to get back on track."

The expanded Golden State Stimulus would provide relief to 78% of California tax filers. Gov. Newsom concluded, "This is just the beginning. We will continue working to build a stronger, more equitable California for all."

"The days is gittin' cooler, 'spesh'ly ez night comes on. Draw up to the fire, suh--an', heah, tek this cheer; it's comf'tabler then that'n'," she said hospitably, ejecting a big tortoise-shell cat from the depths of a cushioned rocker which she pulled forward.

"My name is Dudley, madam; Abner Dudley," said the guest as he exchanged the straight, split-bottom chair for the rocker. "I learned from Squire Osborne, of Bourbonton, that a teacher was wanted in this neighborhood. I had intended going to Major Gilcrest's to-night, but made the wrong turning, and then met your old servant, who directed me here."

"You're welcome, I'm shore, 'spesh'ly ef you're a schoolmastah. We'd begun to think we warn't to hev no school a'tall this wintah. Folks 'roun' heah air beginnin' to tek big stock in schoolin'," she went on as she resumed her seat and began to sew.

"So Squire Osborne told me," answered Dudley. "I'm glad the people are interested in educational matters."

"Yes; Mr. Rogers, Hirum Gilcrest an' John Trabue air plum daft about it. Preachah Stone said last time he preached fur us thet we sartainly air progressin', an' I'm glad on it, too, though I never hed edvantiges myse'f. When I wuz a little gal down in Car'liny, I went to school long 'nough to l'arn my a-b-c's. Then the redskins broke up the school, an' we didn't hev no more tell I wuz a big gal an' 'shamed to go an' l'arn my a-b abs 'long with the little shavers. When I wuz 'bout sixteen, 'long comes Mr. Rogers, an' I didn't keer nothin' more 'bout school. You know, when a gal gits marryin' in her haid, thar ain't no room left in it fur book-l'arnin'. Mason he wuz a sprightly, well-sot-up young fellah, an' soon's I laid eyes on him (it wuz at a house-raisin' party), I wuz ready to say 'snip' ez soon ez he'd say 'snap.' Folks them days didn't fool 'way much time a-courtin'. A man'd see a likely gal, an' soon's he'd got a piece o' ground cl'ared an' a cabin raised, they'd be ready to splice. So Mason an' me wuz married, an' moved up to Kaintuck. Thet fust wintah, while we wuz a-livin' in the fort, Mason he broke his laig out huntin', an' while he wuz laid up a spaill, he l'arned me to read an' write an' ciphah some. I reckon ef it hadn't 'a' been fur thet crippled laig o' his'n, I'd nevah l'arned even thet much." She dropped her work for a moment as she reviewed this incident of her early married life.

"Doubtless, madam, you underrate your stock of learning. I dare say you made rapid progress," said Dudley, politely.

"Oh, I l'arned the readin' an' writin' all right, but, la! I nevah hed no haid fur figgahs. I jogged 'long purty brisk with the addin' an' subtractin', but them multiplyin' tables floored me. To this day I allus staggers at the nines, an' ef you wuz to ax me how much wuz seven times nine, I'd haf to count on my fingahs before I could tell whuthah it made forty-eight or fifty-seven--though I know it's one or tuthah. But times is changed, an' I want my childurn edicated in all the accompaniments."

"How many children have you?"

"Six livin'. We lost our fust two. Henry is goin' on seventeen, an' he jes' natch'ally teks to books--knows more'n his pap now, I reckon. Why, he kin figgah ez fast ez I kin ravel out a piece o' knittin', an' I nevah in my borned days heard nobody, 'cept mayby Preachah Stone, whut could read lak him. He kin run 'long ovah them big names in the papah an' them generalgies in the Bible lak a racin' pony. Susan, our eldest gal, is a little the rise o' fourteen, an' wuz counted the best spellah in the school last wintah. The twins, Lucindy an' Lucy, air real peart, too, fur ther age, jes' turned intah ther ninth year. Tommy, he's only five, but his pap'll sign him, too; fur we want him brung 'long fast in his books befoh he's big 'nough to holp with the wuck."

US military’s hacking unit publicly acknowledges taking offensive action to disrupt ransomware operations

CNN — Cyber Command, the US military’s hacking unit, has taken offensive action to disrupt cybercriminal groups that have launched ransomware attacks on US companies, a spokesperson for the command confirmed to CNN Sunday.

The spokesperson declined to specify what actions the command had taken. But it’s one of the first, unequivocal acknowledgements from Cyber Command since the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in May that the command has targeted criminal gangs that hold the computer systems of US businesses hostage.

New comments by Gen. Paul Nakasone, head of Cyber Command and director of the National Security Agency, which the New York Times reported earlier Sunday, signal that the US military’s computer operatives have been increasingly willing to hack criminals, and not just state actors, who pose a threat to US critical infrastructure.

Security agencies across the US government have ramped up their pursuit of ransomware groups after hacks brought Colonial Pipeline, a major transporter of US fuel, and a major meat processor to a standstill earlier this year. CNN reported in June that the US government had taken offensive steps in response to ransomware, including compromising and surveilling cybercriminal networks, according to sources familiar with the situation.

Nakasone said last month that the US government had “conducted a surge” against ransomware operators, including by trying to cut off the hackers’ sources of funding.

Nakasone reiterated that message in an interview with the New York Times this weekend.

“Before, during and since, with a number of elements of our government, we have taken actions and we have imposed costs,” Nakasone told the newspaper. “That’s an important piece that we should always be mindful of.”

The US government counteroffensive against ransomware groups, many of which are based in Eastern Europe and Russia, has also included indicting alleged extortionists and sanctioning a cryptocurrency exchange accused of laundering money for the hackers.

The White House has tried to pressure the Russian government into cracking down on cybercriminals operating from Russian soil. It remains to be seen whether that will happen – Moscow has often turned a blind eye to hackers who do not target Russian organizations, analysts say.

President Joe Biden will hold a video call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday. The two men will discuss cybersecurity, according to the White House, six months after Biden exhorted Putin to take action against hackers during a meeting in Geneva.

A chill morn lightens the dim corridors of the gaol, where shadows of sorrow and desolation cling to every stone and beam. The heavy air, redolent of damp decay and lingering despair, seems to mourn the fallen fortunes of men who once walked in brighter realms. In the small cell where Tom Swiggs rests in a forlorn slumber, Spunyarn, the sailor of steadfast kindness, stands watchful, his eyes reflecting the silent promises of friendship and care, as if to challenge the cruel inevitability of fate.

Within these cold confines, the aged jailer paces with a sorrowful resignation, recalling long-ago acts of redemption that have long since faded into the mists of memory. His heart, tender in its empathy for the wretched souls entrusted to his charge, brims with a melancholy understanding that some afflictions lie beyond the reach of earthly remedy. He speaks in quiet tones to the vigilant Spunyarn, whose gentle countenance belies an inner fortitude and a readiness to face the encroaching bleakness with humble courage.

A sudden clamor at the iron-bound door disrupts the morning’s stillness; a silken voice, steeped in both disdain and pity, announces the approach of Mr. Mingle—clad in his striking red shirt, which, though vivid, appears as an exclamation of tragedy in the dreary refuges of the prison. His words, sharp and barbed by the bitterness of past transgressions, echo through the narrow hall as he laments that whisky has transformed even the noblest among men into pitiable shadows dancing at the edge of ruin. Yet beneath his cynical utterances lies a recognition of the fickleness of society’s patronage, a truth as piercing as it is undeniable.

As Mr. Mingle strides down the corridor, his gait bearing the marks of countless misadventures and political missteps, a fresh face appears: a young attendant with eyes full of blurred hope and timid deference. Charged with the responsibility of conveying the guard of the newly arrived magistrate, this youth hesitates at the intersection of duty and the unspoken, sorrowful narrative that has long plagued the walls of this institution. The attendant’s trembling manner speaks volumes of the unsayable truths that reside behind every barred window and rusted bolt.

Within the depths of the prison’s inner sanctum, Spunyarn’s countenance softens as he surveys the still form of Tom Swiggs, whose rapturous sleep in the midst of despair hints at the transitory reprieve of a smothered spirit. The sailor murmurs silently to the comatose friend, vowing to protect him from further misfortune and to kindle, however faintly, the dying embers of the man that once harboured ambition and honor. His voice, low and earnest as the roll of distant thunder, dares to defy the prevailing gloom, casting gentle light upon Tom’s darkened soul.

In a quiet alcove adjacent to the cell, the elderly jailer reclines upon a splintered bench, his thoughts consumed by the inexorable passage of time and the irrevocable waste of human potential. With every measured step, he is reminded of his own share of misfortune—a life spent in service of an institution that offers neither solace nor redemption. Yet, in his quiet resignation, there exists a glimmer of nobility, for he perceives in each condemned soul the tragic echo of a once-beating heart, now resigned to the cold machinations of fate.

Beyond the prison walls, the city awakens to a solemn cadence of protest and disquiet. Citizens, embittered by political intrigues and social decay, gather to debate the legitimacy of the regime that imprisons not merely bodies but also the spirit of a nation. Their voices, mingling with the distant toll of church bells, rise in a lamentable chorus that speaks of broken dreams and the promise of new beginnings—a promise as ephemeral as the morning mist that now recedes before the advancing light.

In the quiet corridors of the gaol, Mr. Mingle pauses by a small window, his eyes drawn to the hush of dawn. Amid the interplay of light and shadow, he reflects on the perennial irony that has come to define his existence. For a man who has been both the architect of his own despair and a reluctant witness to the fall of once-stately virtues, the arrival of the day serves as a stark reminder that redemption, however elusive, remains an ever-distant possibility in a world ruled by the caprices of ill fortune.

As the magistrate’s carriage creaks into the yard with an air of imperious dignity, a palpable tension settles upon the assembled souls of the institution. The magistrate, a dignified figure whose eyes betray a lifetime of service to justice, inspects the proceedings with a measured detachment. His presence instills in the prison a mixture of hope and dread; hope that perhaps, in some act of measured mercy, the eternity of suffering might be alleviated, and dread that the unyielding hand of law shall further entrench the tragic patterns of moral decline.

Deep in the recess of the prison, where cold stone meets the human heart’s relentless yearning for salvation, Spunyarn gently lifts Tom Swiggs from his uneasy repose. With deliberate care, he guides him along the somber passage towards a modest chamber where warmth and quiet solace await. Thus unfolds an unspoken pact between the friend and the fallen, an enduring testament to the transformative power of loyal human affection amidst a world bereft of grace, where even the misbegotten find, if only for a fleeting instant, the sanctuary of compassion.

East Coast Transit Systems Face Unyielding Challenges from Climate Change

NEW YORK (AP) – With Hurricane Ida and a slew of other aggressive summer storms battering the East Coast, the resilience of transit systems in cities like New York, Boston, and Philadelphia is under sharp scrutiny. Despite significant investments in coastal flooding defenses since the devastation of Superstorm Sandy in 2012, recent weather events underscore a pressing need for ramped-up efforts to guard against an increasingly volatile climate.

"We've made strides, but the recent storms are a wake-up call," said Janno Lieber, Acting CEO of the Metropolitan Transit Authority. “We need to be more aggressive with our planning and execution.”

In New York City, proposals are being put forward to combat future flood risks, including constructing canals and installing curbs at subway entrances to restrain water ingress. This comes as an acknowledgment that billions spent post-Sandy were not entirely sufficient to weather the storms of the future.

Over in Boston, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority is prioritizing resilience efforts on the Blue Line, which is particularly vulnerable to coastal flooding. Joe Pesaturo, the agency’s spokesperson, confirmed plans to "implement a significant seawall and upgrade current pumps," endeavoring to mitigate water encroachments.

Philadelphia's experience during recent storms revealed mixed outcomes from their post-Sandy initiatives. Bob Lund, Deputy General Manager of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, maintained a positive outlook, stating, "Continued reinforcement of our shoreline infrastructure with concrete blocks is essential to protect the system."

Washington's WMATA is similarly taking action by developing a comprehensive climate resiliency plan, with improved drainage systems and the installation of more pumping stations already in motion. "We are committed to making our infrastructure more resilient," declared Sherrie Ly, spokesperson for WMATA, noting future plans will continue to prioritize these improvements.

Despite these efforts, skepticism remains regarding the adequacy of current plans to address the magnitude of climate change challenges. Jesse Keenan, an associate professor at Tulane University, critiqued, “There's a real concern that transit systems aren't planning ambitiously enough. What's required is nothing short of a transformation in how we prepare for climate impacts.”

International cities like London and Zhengzhou are grappling with similar flood management problems, suggesting the complexity of urban transit sustainability is a global challenge. Researcher Michael Martello from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology pointed out, “These issues are not just local; they're reflective of a global need for upgraded urban infrastructure.”

Even as collaborations and technological innovations promise improvements, funding remains a sizeable barrier for many cities trying to adopt these ambitious projects. It’s an obstacle that must be overcome to adequately prepare transit systems for the challenges ahead.

As the East Coast braces for further unforgiving storms, these transit authorities understand more than ever the need to act swiftly to bolster infrastructure—ensuring that the public transit systems millions rely upon can withstand whatever Mother Nature throws their way.

He criticizes government-controlled economies as harmful to citizens, asserting that "the interference of government in the management of the internal concerns of the nation, is a violation of the principles of liberty," which can lead to a situation akin to feudalism, where the ruling class exploits the working class for its own benefit, as aptly described by the phrase "the lords of the loom and the lords of the forge have taken the place of the lords of the manor." Taylor believes that protective tariffs harm commerce, especially agriculture, as "the agriculturists, who are the most numerous class, and the main support of the nation, are the ones who suffer most from the evils of the system," because they are forced to pay higher prices for manufactured goods while their own products are subject to tariffs and trade restrictions.

Taylor criticizes exporting as the key to economic success post-war due to falling prices, arguing that "the extraordinary exportation of produce, during the late war, was the consequence of high prices, and not the cause of low ones," and that "when the prices fall, the exportation must cease, and the produce remain on hand, to the great injury of the agriculturists." He claims that government oversteps its constitutional power by regulating individual commerce, stating that "the power to regulate commerce, is a power to destroy it, and the power to impose taxes, is a power to oppress," which is a notion that echoes the sentiments of the founding fathers, who warned against the dangers of government overreach, as exemplified by the statement "that government is best which governs least." Taylor admits a preference for agriculturalists and a disdain for mechanicks, comparing the tariff system to feudalism, arguing that it benefits capitalists over agriculturalists, and asserting that "the system of protection, is a system of exclusive privileges, bestowed upon the mechanicks, at the expense of the agriculturists," which is detrimental to the overall economy, as "the prosperity of a nation, depends on the prosperity of its agriculturists." As Taylor aptly puts it, "the agriculturists are the bones and sinews of the nation, and the mechanicks are only the fingers and toes," highlighting the crucial role that agriculturalists play in the economy.

While proponents of protective tariffs argue that they are necessary to protect domestic industries, Taylor proposes removing protective duties to save the agricultural system, arguing that "the removal of the protective duties, would be a measure of relief to the agriculturists, and would enable them to compete with the foreign producer," which would ultimately lead to a more prosperous and equitable economy. He views liberty as needing protection from government tyranny, which can arise without opposition, as "the liberty of a nation, is never in greater danger, than when it is entrusted to the discretion of a single man, or a single body of men," and that "the only security against tyranny, is the diffusion of power, and the imparting of it to the people." Taylor's critique of protective tariffs serves as a warning against the dangers of government overreach and the importance of protecting individual liberty, as he so eloquently states, "the people must be vigilant, and jealous of their rights, or they will be trampled upon, and their liberty destroyed." By examining the historical context and the impact of protective tariffs on different sectors of the economy, it becomes clear that Taylor's argument is not only relevant but also crucial in understanding the complexities of economic systems and the importance of limited government intervention.

"There was no rest for Elijah Martin," he muttered, pacing the crude bark hut that had become his domain, "now that the eyes of the tribe had turned towards him like the sun." The moon hung low and full in the sky outside, its silver glow casting a long shadow over his anxious face, yet it did nothing to quell the turmoil within him.

"He's somethin' remarkable," mused Jim, the braves' eldest and most respected. His voice carried the weight of years lived, and held the sort of graveness usually reserved for the recounting of legends. Jim nodded towards the center where Elijah stood tall, fists clenched, as he relayed his latest strategy to the council. "Few could've stood before them that way, and kept his dignity."

The council buzzed with activity, braves murmuring in agreement, a mixture of respect and awe in their tones. Elijah's leadership had transformed from a sudden revelation to a settled truth; the outcast was now the vanguard, his decisions shaping the course of their collective future.

"He's the man now," whispered Tom, a young brave whose loyalty to Elijah was unwavering. "He's got a way about him, like a river finds its path through mountains. They listen, Jim, they really do."

As the tribe gathered to celebrate the successes brought about by Elijah's foresight, whispers circulated like wildfire amongst them. The captives set free had returned with tales of the tribe's valor and strength, and Elijah's name rang through the encampment. He had not only freed them but had done so with a boldness that echoed through the canyons, a testament to his newfound stature.

The council chamber, once a place of dispute, now became a beacon of unity under Elijah's guidance. The agent, a stern-faced man with cold eyes, had been outwitted in the negotiations, leaving the tribe with bountiful resources and the promise of fair trade. It was Elijah who had ensured this, employing a wit sharp as a warrior's blade, yet subtle as the whisper of the wind.

"You’re one of 'em," Tom said, a smile tugging at his lips. "Born to lead and a right fist to punch with."

The tribe flourished under Elijah's stewardship, a prosperity born not from greed but from wisdom. As settlements took root, the people found balance—a harmony between old customs and the new ways of strength. They lived without the fear that had once chained their spirits, a freedom Elijah had wrought with his courage and foresight.

It was during one of these moments, as the sun dipped low and cast long shadows over the feasting grounds, that Elijah paused to reflect on the path he had forged. He knew that the road ahead would be fraught with challenges, but he stood ready to face them with the steadfast resolve that had earned him his place among them.

"He's not just a leader," Jim concluded, his voice deep and sure. "He's the pulse of this tribe, the very life that flows through our veins."

As the fires burned bright against the encroaching night, Elijah Martin, once the despised outcast, now stood as a pillar of strength, his spirit as indomitable as the mountains that towered above them. And with him at their helm, the tribe of Redwood Camp found not just survival, but a legacy born of wisdom and courage, reaching toward the horizon like the branches of a mighty oak.

Senate Democrats Push for $2,000 Stimulus Checks, GOP Opposes

Senate Democrats, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have been pushing for an increase in stimulus checks from the existing $600 to $2,000. However, their efforts have been met with resistance from Senate Republicans, who argue that the higher amount is too costly and inefficiently targeted.

Schumer took to the Senate floor to advocate for the increased amount, emphasizing the need to support struggling families. "The American people are hurting, and they need our help," he said. "A $2,000 check would go a long way in helping them pay their bills, put food on the table, and get back on their feet."

Senator Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, also pushed for a vote on the $2,000 checks. He proposed a compromise involving Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's alternative bill, but it was blocked by Senate Republicans.

McConnell expressed his opposition to the $2,000 checks, citing fiscal concerns. "We cannot afford to spend money we don't have," he said. "We need to be responsible stewards of the American people's tax dollars."

Senator John Thune, the Senate Majority Whip, echoed McConnell's sentiments. "We need to be mindful of the long-term effects of our spending decisions," he said. "The $600 checks are a more targeted and fiscally responsible approach."

Despite the opposition, Sanders remained determined to push for a vote on the $2,000 checks. "The American people are crying out for help, and we must listen to their voices," he said.

Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, expressed his frustration over the Senate's inability to vote on the $2,000 checks. "We need to do better than this," he said. "The American people deserve better than this."

Hawley shared stories of Americans in need, highlighting the urgency of passing the $2,000 stimulus checks. "I've heard from people in my state who are struggling to make ends meet," he said. "They need our help, and they need it now."

Sanders also used personal stories to emphasize the importance of passing the $2,000 checks. "I've met people who are working two or three jobs just to get by," he said. "They're not asking for a handout; they're asking for a hand up. And that's exactly what the $2,000 checks would provide."

The House of Representatives has already passed a measure to increase stimulus checks to $2,000, following President Trump's urging for the higher amount. However, the Senate's inability to vote on the measure has stalled its progress.

President Trump criticized the originally negotiated $600 direct payments as too low after signing the coronavirus relief bill. "The $600 checks are not enough," he said. "We need to do more to support the American people."

Senator John Cornyn, a Republican from Texas, objected to Sanders' motion on behalf of Senator Pat Toomey, further stalling the bill's progress. Cornyn argued that the $2,000 checks would be too costly and inefficiently targeted.

Despite the opposition, Senate Democrats remain committed to pushing for a vote on the $2,000 stimulus checks. "We will not give up on this fight," Schumer said. "We will continue to push for what the American people need and deserve."

By chance I found myself with both hands on his arms, and I knew that no man could break that hold when once set, for vast strength of forearm and wrist was one of the inheritances of all men of the Cowles family. I drew him steadily to me, pulled his head against my chest, and upended him fair, throwing him this time at length across my shoulder. I was sure I had him then, for he fell on his side. But even as he fell he rose, and I felt a grip like steel on each ankle. Then there was a snake-like bend on his part, and before I had time to think I was on my face. His knees were astride my body, and gradually I felt them pushing my arms up toward my neck. I felt a slight blow on the back of my head, as though by the edge of the han–ight, delicate, gentle, but dreamy in its results. Then I was half conscious of a hand pushing down my head, of another hand reaching for my right wrist. It occurred to me in a distant way that I was about to be beaten, subdue–, John Cowles!

This had been done, as he had said of my own work with Singleton, as much by the momentum of my own fall as by any great effort on his part. As he had said regarding my own simple trick, the time of this was perfect, though how far more difficult than mine, only those who have wrestled with able men can understand.

For the first time in my life I found myself about to be mastered by another man. Had he been more careful he certainly would have had the victory over me. But the morning was warm, and we had worked for some moments. My man stopped for a moment in his calm pinioning of my arms, and perhaps raised his hand to brush his face or push back his hair. At that moment luck came to my aid. He did not repeat the strange gentle blow at the back of my hea–ne which I think would have left unconscious a man with a neck less stif–nd as his pressure on my twisted arm relaxed, I suddenly got back my faculties. At once I used my whole body as a spring, and so straightened enough to turn and put my arm power against his own, which was all I wanted.

He laughed when I turned, and with perfect good nature freed my arm and sprang to his feet, bowing with hand upreached to me. His eye had lost its peculiar stare, and shone now with what seemed genuine interest and admiration. He seemed ready to call me a sportsman, and a good rival, and much as I disliked to do so, I was obliged to say as much for him in my own heart.

"By the Lord! sir," he sai–ith a certain looseness of speech, as it seemed to me, for a minister of the gospel to employ, "you're the first I ever knew to break it."

"'Twas no credit to me," I owned. "You let go your hand. The horse is yours."

"Not in the least," he responded, "not in the least. If I felt I had won him I'd take him, and not leave you feeling as though you had been given a present. But if you like I'll draw my own little wager as well. You're the best man I ever met in any country. By the Lord! man, you broke the hold that I once saw an ex-guardsman killed at Singapore for resistin–roke his arm short off, and he died on the table. I've seen it at Tokio and Nagasak–hy, man, it's the yellow policeman's hold, the secret trick of the Orient. Done in proper time, and the little gentleman is the match of any size, yellow or white."

I did not understand him then, but later I knew that I had for my first time seen the Oriental art of wrestling put in practice. I do not want to meet a master in it again. I shook Orme by the hand.

"If you like to call it a draw," said I, "it would suit me mighty well. You're the best man I ever took off coat to in my life. And I'll never wrestle you again unless"--I fear I blushed a little--"well, unless you want it."

The sun, though bright, seemed to cast a dim and heavy light over theExecutive Mansion, as if the very heavens themselves were draped in mourning. The air was thick with the scent of lilacs and roses, yet Mrs. Cameron’s heart felt as if it were encased in lead. She walked beside her daughter, Elsie, her steps measured and deliberate, though her mind whirled with a thousand fears and forebodings. The bouquets of roses she held were a stark contrast to the gloom that weighed upon her spirit, their vibrant colors a shallow attempt to mask the despair that threatened to overwhelm her.

"Shall we wait until the afternoon?" Elsie asked, her voice steady though her hands trembled slightly. "The crowds are thinner then, and we might have better luck."

Mrs. Cameron shook her head, her lips pressed into a thin line. "No, Elsie. We must see him now. Every moment we delay is a moment our boy suffers. We cannot afford to wait."

Elsie nodded, her dark eyes reflecting the same determination that had brought them this far. She tightened her grip on her mother’s arm, her touch both reassuring and commanding. "Very well. But remember, Mother, the President is a just man. He may not see us this morning, but he will listen. I am certain of it."

The gates of the White House loomed before them, guarded by men in uniform who regarded them with a mix of curiosity and suspicion. Elsie’s heart raced as she scanned the faces of the crowd gathered outside. Men, women, and children milled about, their voices a low murmur of whispered prayers and desperate hopes. Some clutched letters in trembling hands, others held babes swaddled in faded shawls. All of them shared the same unspoken plea: mercy.

"Stay close," Mrs. Cameron murmured, her voice barely audible over the din. "We must not lose each other in this throng."

Elsie nodded, her eyes darting to the flags that flapped listlessly in the breeze. The sight of the Stars and Stripes, once a symbol of unity and pride, now seemed to mock her. How could such a banner,once a source of hope, now weigh so heavily upon her soul?

As they pushed through the crowd, Elsie’s mind raced. She had heard tales of mothers who had waited days, even weeks, to speak with the President. Some had been granted audiences, their pleas met withkindness and understanding. Others had been turned away, their tears and sorrow ignored. Elsie could not allow her mother to face such rejection. Not now, not after everything they had endured.

"Mother," she said, her voice firm despite the trembling in her hands, "I will speak to the guard. I have a letter from Father, from before the war. It might help."

Mrs. Cameron’s eyes widened in surprise, then filled with a flicker of hope. "A letter? From your father?"

Elsie nodded, her fingers brushing against the pocket of her dress where the folded paper lay hidden. "A letter of introduction, Mother. It will give us the edge we need."

The guard at the gate spared them a cursory glance, his expression unreadable behind his bushy mustache. He muttered something under his breath before stepping aside, his movements slow and deliberate. Elsie’s heart leapt with relief as she guided her mother through the gates, the weight of the world seeming to lift from her shoulders.

Inside, the Executive Mansion was no less imposing. The walls seemed to breathe with the weight of history, each step echoing too loudly in the silence. Elsie’s eyes darted to the grand staircase, her imagination running wild with the possibilities of what lay ahead. Would they be granted an audience? Would Lincoln even deign to see them?

Mrs. Cameron’s hand tightened on her arm, grounding her in the moment. "Elsie, what if he refuses us? What if he turns us away?"

Elsie squeezed her mother’s hand in return, her voice steady despite the turmoil within. "Then we will find another way, Mother. We always do."

The words were little comfort, but they were all she could offer. Together, they made their way to the vestibule, where a sea of hopeful faces waited. Some sat on wooden benches, their expressions etched with exhaustion and despair. Others stood in small groups, their whispered conversations filled with fragments of prayers and pleas.

Elsie’s eyes locked with those of a woman sitting nearby, her face gaunt and drawn. The woman’s eyes were red-rimmed, her hands clutching a baby wrapped in a shawl. In that moment, Elsie felt a connection, a shared desperation that transcended words. They were sisters in sorrow, bound by the grief that had brought them here.

"Elsie," Mrs. Cameron whispered, her voice trembling, "I cannot bear to see Margaret like this. She is so young, so innocent. I cannot let her endure such pain."

Elsie’s heart ached at the mention of her younger sister. Margaret, with her golden curls and innocent smile, was the light of their household. To see her shattered by grief was a fate worse than death. "We will protect her, Mother," Elsie said firmly. "We will find a way to shield her, no matter the cost."

The words were hollow, even to her own ears. How could they protect Margaret when they themselves were so deeply wounded? The weight of their secret—their son’s fate—pressed down upon them, a burden they could scarcely bear.

As they waited, the minutes dragged by like hours. The air grew heavier, the silence oppressive. Elsie’s mind wandered to the letter in her pocket, the ink still fresh from her father’s pen. It was a letter of recommendation, a plea for mercy written in the hand of a man who had long since passed into memory. Would it be enough?

Then, as if in answer to her doubts, a young man in a tailored suit emerged from the shadows, his eyes sharp and calculating. He took one look at them, then another, his expression unreadable. "Mrs. Cameron?" he said at last, his voice smooth but tinged with suspicion.

Elsie’s heart leapt. This was their chance. She thrust the letter into his hands, her fingers trembling as they released it. "Yes," she said, her voice steady despite the turmoil within. "And this is from my father, Colonel Cameron."

The man scanned the letter, his brow furrowing as he read. Then, as if struck by a revelation, his expression softened, his eyes narrowing in recognition. "I remember now," he said, his voice tinged with a mixture of respect and pity. "Colonel Cameron. A fine man. A hopeless romantic, but a man of principle."

Elsie’s heart soared, her spirits lifting for the first time in what felt like an eternity. "Thank you," she said, her gratitude evident in her tone. "We only ask for a moment of his time. For my brother."

The man nodded, though his expression remained guarded. "The President will see you," he said at last, his voice heavy with significance. "But be warned, Mrs. Cameron. The President does not take kindly to those who waste his time."

Elsie’s breath hitched in her throat, her heart pounding in her chest. This was it. The moment they had waited for, the chance to plead their case before the most powerful man in the land. She turned to her mother, her eyes reflecting the mixture of hope and fear that gripped her soul.

"Mother," she said, her voice barely audible, "we are about to meet the President."

Mrs. Cameron’s face paled, her lips parting in a silent prayer. "God grant us strength," she whispered, her voice trembling. "For we shall need it."

As they followed the man into the heart of the Executive Mansion, Elsie felt the weight of the world upon her shoulders. The journey was far from over, but for the first time since their ordeal began, she allowed herself a flicker of hope. They had come too far to fail now.

U.S. clinical trial results show Novavax vaccine is safe and prevents COVID-19

Results from a Phase 3 clinical trial enrolling 29,960 adult volunteers in the United States and Mexico show that the investigational vaccine known as NVX-CoV2373 demonstrated 90.4% efficacy in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 disease. The candidate showed 100% protection against moderate and severe disease. In people at high risk of developing complications from COVID-19 (people 65 years or older and people under age 65 with certain comorbidities or with likely regular exposure to COVID-19), the vaccine showed 91.0% efficacy in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 disease.

Safety data indicate the investigational vaccine was generally well-tolerated. Mild-to-moderate injection site pain and tenderness were the most common local symptoms among participants, and fatigue, headache and muscle pain lasting less than two days were the most common systemic symptoms.

Novavax, Inc., of Gaithersburg, Maryland, developed the investigational vaccine and led the clinical trial known as PREVENT-19. The Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA), a component of the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response, and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the National Institutes of Health, provided funding support for the trial as part of the federal COVID-19 response.

The PREVENT-19 trial began in late December 2020 and enrolled adult volunteers at 119 study sites, including those in the NIAID-supported COVID-19 Prevention Network (CoVPN). Participants were randomly assigned to receive two shots, 21 days apart, of either the investigational vaccine or a saline placebo. Randomization occurred in a 2:1 ratio with two volunteers receiving NVX-CoV2373 for each one who received placebo. Because the trial was blinded, neither investigators nor participants knew who received the candidate vaccine.

PREVENT-19 was designed to evaluate whether NVX-CoV2373 can prevent symptomatic COVID-19 disease seven or more days after the second injection relative to placebo. The results shared today are based on 77 cases of symptomatic COVID-19 that investigators observed among trial participants from January 25 through April 30, 2021. Investigators recorded 63 cases among the approximately 10,000 participants who received placebo and 14 cases among the approximately 20,000 participants who received the investigational vaccine. Of the 63 COVID-19 cases in the placebo group, investigators classified 10 as moderate and four as severe. There were no cases of moderate or severe disease in the investigational vaccine group.

NVX-CoV2373 is a subunit vaccine made from a stabilized form of the coronavirus spike protein using the company’s recombinant protein nanoparticle technology. The purified protein antigens in the vaccine cannot replicate or cause COVID-19. The vaccine also contains a proprietary adjuvant, MatrixM™. Adjuvants are additives that enhance desired immune system responses to vaccine. NVX-CoV2373 is administered by injection in liquid form and can be stored, handled and distributed at above-freezing temperatures (35° to 46°F.) A single vaccine dose contains 5 micrograms (mcg) of protein and 50 mcg of adjuvant. The vaccine is administered as two intramuscular injections 21 days apart. The technology used for this vaccine was developed under a long-standing contract with the Department of Defense.

Results from a Phase 3 clinical trial enrolling 15,000 adults in the United Kingdom showed a two-dose regimen of NVX-CoV2373 was highly effective in preventing symptomatic COVID-19 overall and also demonstrated high efficacy against the Alpha variant strain of SARS-CoV-2.

An independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) is overseeing PREVENT-19 to ensure the safe and ethical conduct of the study. All Phase 3 clinical trials of candidate vaccines supported through the federal COVID-19 response are overseen by a common DSMB convened by NIAID.

In May 2021, PREVENT-19 was expanded to evaluate the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of NVX-CoV2373 in adolescents aged 12-17. Adolescent enrollment recently completed with 2,248 participants. For more information about PREVENT-19, see preventcovid.org, view the trial protocol, or visit ClinicalTrials.gov and search identifier NCT04611802.

About the COVID-19 Prevention Network: The COVID-19 Prevention Network (CoVPN) was formed by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) at the U.S. National Institutes of Health to respond to the global pandemic. Through the CoVPN, NIAID is leveraging the infectious disease expertise of its existing research networks and global partners to address the pressing need for vaccines and antibodies against SARS-CoV-2. CoVPN will work to develop and conduct studies to ensure rapid and thorough evaluation of vaccines and antibodies for the prevention of COVID-19. The CoVPN is headquartered at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center. For more information about the CoVPN, visit: coronaviruspreventionnetwork.org.

The hazy afternoon sun cast a golden hue over the peaceful Mission of San Pablo, where Father Jose Antonio Haro stood pensively in the shadow of the adobe walls. His keen eyes swept across the bustling courtyard, where indigenous converts mingled with Spanish settlers in a harmonious blend of cultures. The scents of burning incense and fresh bread wafted through the air, mingling with the strains of sacred hymns sung by the choir in the mission church.

As Father Haro wandered through the mission grounds, his thoughts turned to the conversion efforts that had brought such profound change to the indigenous communities of Upper California. The relentless zeal of Father Junipero Serro had paved the way for the rapid establishment of missions, each one a beacon of Spanish civilization in the untamed wilderness. The once-wandering tribes now lived in neat rows of adobe huts, their lives filled with the daily rituals of baptism, communion, and confession.

Despite the tranquility that enveloped the mission, Father Haro felt a restless longing in his soul. The unspoiled landscapes of California beckoned to him, their hidden wonders calling out to be discovered. He yearned to venture beyond the familiar boundaries of the mission, to explore the rugged coastline and towering redwood forests that lay beyond. And in the depths of his heart, there stirred a longing for something more elusive than the uncharted wilderness—a yearning for a love that had eluded him in his vows to the church.

The days following our encounter on the frozen pond had passed with a strange tranquility. I found myself consumed by thoughts of Florence, her voice echoing in my mind with every turn of the page. I wrestled with conflicting emotions, torn between the rational understanding that I could never claim her affections and the inexplicable yearning that burned within.

"Henry," I confided one evening, seeking solace in the familiar presence of my friend. "I find myself in a quandary that none can comprehend but that which troubles my heart."

He regarded me with a mixture of curiosity and concern. "What troubles thee, old friend?"

"Florence...she has revealed to me a secret that has shaken the very foundations of my resolve."

Henry listened with an attentiveness that I had grown to appreciate over the months we'd spent together. When I finished, he sighed deeply, his eyes reflecting a contemplative gaze.

"Now I see," he said softly. "Yet, my dear Damon, know that Florence speaks highly of thee to me. Despite her own affections, she knows the depth of thy character."

Encouraged by his words, I pressed on, eager to unburden my troubled soul further. "And what of Ralph Buckstone, Henry? What have you seen in him that Florence, in her honest heart, has overlooked?"

Henry's expression darkened ever so slightly. "Ralph Buckstone is a man of ambition, no doubt, but his pursuit of success is marred by a reckless disregard for those around him. He dismisses the efforts of others with a cavalier indifference that Florence, with her keen heart, ought not to ignore."

His words, though delivered with restraint, struck a chord within me. It was as if a veil had been lifted, revealing the shadow that Ralph cast over their relationship.

Days turned to weeks, and the crisp air of winter gave way to the gentle embrace of spring. The town buzzed with life, as our scholarly pursuits resumed with fervor. Yet, amidst the bustling classrooms and lively discussions, my heart remained entwined in the delicate dance of unrequited love.

One afternoon, as I sat poring over tomes of literature, a knock came at my door. Florence stood before me, her cheeks flushed with the exertion of walking through the brisk breeze.

"Damon," she began hesitantly, "I hope you will not hold my previous words against me. I have been wrestling with my own conscience, and I must admit that your character has left an indelible impression upon me. Ralph and I...we are not suited, as I once believed."

Her confession took me by surprise, yet a sense of relief washed over me, delicate and serene.

"Florence," I replied, my voice steady despite the tumult of emotion, "I would not wish to burden you with my own longings. You have my word—our confidences shall remain as they were."

She smiled, a genuine warmth that seemed to brighten the very walls of my study. "Thank you, Damon. Your kindness is a beacon in these tumultuous times."

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the campus, I realized that my journey was far from over. The road ahead was uncertain, fraught with challenges and adversity. Yet, with Florence's newfound clarity and my steadfast resolve, I found a renewed sense of purpose.

The tale of "The Turning of Griggsby" was but a prelude to the adventures that lay ahead. Together with Florence, Henry, and our mutual friend Ralph Buckstone, we would navigate the complexities of love, ambition, and the fleeting nature of youth. And as I embarked on this grand voyage, unwavering in my determination, I carried with me the knowledge that true growth often lies within the labyrinth of the heart.

Elinor Dashwood, though but nineteen years of age, possessed a composure of spirit and a sense of resolved duty which belied her youthful countenance. Having witnessed the sorrowful spectacle of her father’s last hours, she had found herself duly occupied in providing reassurance to her mother and younger sister, Marianne, whose disposition was still too tender to bear the sudden and grievous loss. The air within the parlor of Norland Park hung heavy, seemingly laden with unspoken sentiments; and it was amid this atmosphere of subdued anguish that a new moment of strife was destined to emerge.

Mr. John Dashwood had, upon the solemn promise he made to his father, now set about contemplating the measures which might be taken to fulfil his obligations towards his stepmother and half-sisters. Yet, the intersection of good intentions and practical limitations has oft inspired the most curious of dilemmas. Soon after he had parted from the funeral rites, and with the enterprise of his own mortal responsibilities now diminished, he allowed himself the luxury of deliberating upon just how much prosperity he might extend towards them, his mind racing through the decimal points of his financial prospects and weighing these against the unwieldy contours of family claim.

It was on the morning following their father’s funeral that Mrs. John Dashwood made her entrance, as if conjured by his very thoughts—an arrival most untimely. Her cavalcade of carriages rustled through the drive with a bluster that startled the somber echo of grief still throbbing within the walls of Norland. Mrs. Dashwood, adorned in the finery bestowed by an amiable fortune, swept into the room with a demeanor that seemed altogether divorced from the delicate sensibilities that enveloped the bereaved. Her inquiries into the estate’s well-being were thus articulated with a cheerfulness that could not avoid the accusation of insensitivity, as her calculated remarks on beneficence and connivance were flung like gilded pearls into waiters' hands rather than bestowed upon the hearts of her relatives.

In the presence of such dissonance, Mrs. Dashwood felt her composure begin to unravel. This conduct from one who was to occupy her household—a progeny of her late husband's fortunes—stirred the embers of pain. She had in her breast a lingering doubt, an unsettling frustration that threatened to rise to the surface and shatter her delicate display of decorum. Yet, before she could yield herself to despair and consider departing from a home so wrested from her, the steadying hand of her daughter Elinor interceded, as if wreathed in an aura of sagacity that belied her years.

“Dearest mama,” Elinor spoke, her voice low but firm against the encroaching disquiet, “Let us not suspect ill by way of careless manners nor regard the grief we bear as a burden unshared. Perhaps Mrs. John Dashwood seeks not to examine her expressions in the reflective pool of our sorrow, but rather understands her wealth as a means of engaging in her own grief.” The wisdom behind such reflection was not lost upon Mrs. Dashwood, who gazed upon her daughter with renewed respect; the lucid thought of a girl with the temperament of a woman wrapped her mother in a soothing embrace.

Inspired by the eloquence of her daughter, Mrs. Dashwood settled into her chair, taking a deep and steadying breath. The two women’s solace drew them closer, forming a mutual resolve to withstand whatever trials the day’s tumultuous events might unveil. With Marianne quietly tucked beside them, her own spirit buoyed by the counsel of her sister, the three ladies resolved to navigate the treacherous waters ahead, even if they felt unnerved by the uncertainties of the future. In the silence that ensued, they found not escape, but rather the subtle promise that endurance would grant them strength to embrace together the unpredictable mantle of their new reality.

I had succeeded in killing a hawk and two crows when I came within sight of the mansion; and then, relinquishing further depredations, I sauntered on, to have a look at the old place, and see what changes had been wrought in it by its new inhabitant. I did not like to go quite to the front and stare in at the gate; but I paused beside the garden wall, and looked, and saw no change—except in one wing, where the broken windows and dilapidated roof had evidently been repaired, and where a thin wreath of smoke was curling up from the stack of chimneys.

While I thus stood, leaning on my gun, and looking up at the dark gables, sunk in an idle reverie, weaving a tissue of wayward fancies, in which old associations and the fair young hermit, now within those walls, bore a nearly equal part, I heard a slight rustling and scrambling just within the garden; and, glancing in the direction whence the sound proceeded, I beheld a tiny hand elevated above the wall: it clung to the topmost stone, and then another little hand was raised to take a firmer hold, and then appeared a small white forehead, surmounted with wreaths of light brown hair, with a pair of deep blue eyes beneath, and the upper portion of a diminutive ivory nose.

The eyes did not notice me, but sparkled with glee on beholding Sancho, my beautiful black and white setter, that was coursing about the field with its muzzle to the ground. The little creature raised its face and called aloud to the dog. The good-natured animal paused, looked up, and wagged his tail, but made no further advances. The child (a little boy, apparently about five years old) scrambled up to the top of the wall, and called again and again; but finding this of no avail, apparently made up his mind, like Mahomet, to go to the mountain, since the mountain would not come to him, and attempted to get over; but a crabbed old cherry-tree, that grew hard by, caught him by the frock in one of its crooked scraggy arms that stretched over the wall. In attempting to disengage himself his foot slipped, and down he tumbled—but not to the earth;—the tree still kept him suspended. There was a silent struggle, and then a piercing shriek;—but, in an instant, I had dropped my gun on the grass, and caught the little fellow in my arms.

I wiped his eyes with his frock, told him he was all right and called Sancho to pacify him. He was just putting little hand on the dog’s neck and beginning to smile through his tears, when I heard behind me a click of the iron gate, and a rustle of female garments, and lo! Mrs. Graham darted upon me—her neck uncovered, her black locks streaming in the wind.

‘Give me the child!’ she said, in a voice scarce louder than a whisper, but with a tone of startling vehemence, and, seizing the boy, she snatched him from me, as if some dire contamination were in my touch, and then stood with one hand firmly clasping his, the other on his shoulder, fixing upon me her large, luminous dark eyes—pale, breathless, quivering with agitation.

‘I was not harming the child, madam,’ said I, scarce knowing whether to be most astonished or displeased; ‘he was tumbling off the wall there; and I was so fortunate as to catch him, while he hung suspended headlong from that tree, and prevent I know not what catastrophe.’

‘I beg your pardon, sir,’ stammered she;—suddenly calming down,—the light of reason seeming to break upon her beclouded spirit, and a faint blush mantling on her cheek—‘I did not know you;—and I thought—’

She stooped to kiss the child, and fondly clasped her arm round his neck.

Retail sales explode in March as consumers use stimulus checks to spend heavily

A fresh batch of stimulus checks sent consumer purchases surging in March as the U.S. economy continued to get juice from aggressive congressional spending. Advance retail sales rose 9.8% for the month, the Commerce Department reported Thursday. That compared to the Dow Jones estimate of a 6.1% gain and a decline of 2.7% in February.

Sporting goods, clothing and food and beverage led the gains in spending and contributed to the best month for retail since the May 2020 gain of 18.3%, which came after the first round of stimulus checks. A separate report showed first-time filings for unemployment insurance plunged, with the Labor Department reporting 576,000 new jobless claims for the week ended April 10. That was easily the lowest total since the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic and represented a sharp decline from the previous week's total of 769,000. The Dow Jones claims estimate was 710,000.

As the jobs picture brightened, consumers took their $1,400 stimulus checks and spent aggressively. The money came courtesy of the nearly $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan Act that Congress passed in March. The legislation took total stimulus and rescue payments approved in the year since the pandemic began to about $5 trillion, fueled by red ink that fiscal authorities say is necessary to keep the economy running. Spending for the month was broad-based, boosting sales by nearly 28% from March 2020 as pandemic-related business closings began. The critical bar and restaurant industry saw a 13.4% surge, thanks to the increasing relaxing of restrictions as Covid vaccines accelerate to a pace of more than 3 million a day. Sporting goods spending was the highest percentage gainer at 23.5%, followed by clothing and accessories at 18.3% and motor vehicle parts and dealers at 15.1%. March's retail sales report was another sign that consumers overall are willing to spend, even though increasing amounts of stimulus checks are going towards savings rather than spending. "Spending will almost certainly drop back in April as some of the stimulus boost wears off, but with the vaccination rollout proceeding at a rapid pace and households finances in strong shape, we expect overall consumption growth to continue rebounding rapidly in the second quarter too," wrote Michael Pearce, senior U.S. economist at Capital Economics. A recent report from the New York Federal Reserve indicated that stimulus recipients expect to save 41.6% of their checks and spend 24.7%. Following the first round of checks in the spring of 2020, consumers saved 34.5% and spent 29.2%. As the recovery has gained speed, consumers have had to deal with the strongest signs yet of inflationary pressures building. The consumer price index rose 2.6% in March from a year ago, thanks in part to a surge in gasoline prices. The year-over-year gain was the largest since August 2018.

Jobless claims brighten employment picture

Thursday's economic data also showed more signs of a thawing in the labor market. The plunge in jobless claims generated the lowest weekly number since March 14, 2020, just after the official pandemic declaration. Nearly two weeks later, weekly claims filings would top out at a staggering 6.15 million, easily the worst week in U.S. history. Since then, the jobs market has improved dramatically, with the unemployment rate falling from a pandemic peak of 14.7% to its current 6%. The nonfarm payroll addition of 916,000 in March brought more hope that the healing is accelerating. Despite the big decline in weekly claims, continuing claims were little changed at 3.73 million.
