'Rust' Armorer's 'Mentor' Supplied Gun That Alec Baldwin Used in Death of Cinematographer: Report

Rust armorer Hannah Gutierrez-Reed was reportedly mentored by a gun expert listed as part of the crew of the fatal movie.

Producers for the film hired Seth Kenney, who owns a licensed weapon and prop rental company in Lake Havasu City, Arizona, as an "armorer mentor" for Gutierrez-Reed, according to a new report by the Los Angeles Times.

Jason Bowles, an attorney for Guttierez-Reed, told PEOPLE Kenney was hired as an armorer mentor and that Kenney supplied the firearms and "most of the ammunition" for the set.

Kenney did not immediately respond to PEOPLE's request for comment. A spokesperson for the production did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to the Times, Kenney recommended Gutierrez-Reed, 24, for the job of armorer on the set of the Alec Baldwin film, according to one source the newspaper did not identify. He also reportedly supplied the guns used in the movie, including a Colt .45 that Baldwin used on Oct. 21 when he accidentally shot and killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. The Times report says that information came from "six people familiar with the matter," whom the newspaper did not identify.

Kenney has advised about weapons use before: he is listed as a "weapons consultant" on the 2015 Shia LaBeouf film Man Down on IMDb.

Sante Fe County Sheriff's spokesperson Juan Ríos said he could not confirm the Times's reporting.

Last week, Gutierrez-Reed said through Bowles in a statement shared with PEOPLE that she did not think live bullets would end up on the Rust set "in a million years," and she did not know how they got there.

"Hannah Gutierrez-Reed would like to add a few points to the continuing narrative on the tragic events surrounding the shooting on the Rust set," Bowles stated. "First, Hannah was incredibly safety conscious and took her job very seriously from the moment she started on Oct. 4."

He added, "She did firearms training for the actors as well as Mr. Baldwin, she fought for more training days and she regularly emphasized to never point a firearm at a person. Never in a million years did Hannah think that live rounds could have been in the 'dummy' Round box. Who put those in there and why is the central question."

In the statement shared with PEOPLE, Bowles said Gutierrez-Reed "kept guns locked up, including throughout lunch" on the day Hutchins was shot and killed. "She instructed her department to watch the cart containing the guns when she was pulled away for her other duties or on a lunch break," Bowles added.

"Hannah did everything in her power to ensure a safe set. She inspected the rounds that she loaded into the firearms that day. She always inspected the rounds. She did again right before handing the firearm to Mr. Halls, by spinning the cylinder and showing him all of the rounds and then handing him the firearm," Bowles stated. "No one could have anticipated or thought that someone would introduce live rounds into this set."

Gutierrez-Reed previously broke her silence about the shooting on set, saying in a statement via her lawyers that "untruths that have been told to the media," and that she was "devastated and completely beside herself over the events that have transpired."

Her attorneys claimed Gutierrez-Reed had "no idea where the live rounds came from" and said she was under pressure on the set from working two jobs as both armorer and props assistant.

Gutierrez-Reed told deputies that she had checked the rounds inside the firearm Baldwin used the day of the shooting to make sure the gun was loaded with "dummies," not real bullets, and that she locked up the guns in a safe on the prop truck, according to the search warrant affidavit. She also said no live ammunition was ever kept on the Rust set.

The Santa Fe County Sheriff refuted Gutierrez-Reed's claims about live bullets, telling Today on Oct. 28 that the armorer's statement was "obviously" not correct after Hutchins was killed on set by a live round.

"No, obviously it isn't," Sheriff Adan Mendoza said. "That was a live round that struck and killed Ms. Hutchins so that's not an accurate statement as far as I'm concerned."

On Oct. 27, Mendoza said during a press conference that investigators had discovered "500 rounds of ammunition" on the film set, which included "a mix of blanks, dummy rounds and what we are suspecting are live rounds."

Filming on Rust has been halted and an investigation into the Oct. 21 incident is ongoing. No charges have been filed at this time.

QAnon Shaman Jacob Chansley Sentenced to 41 Months in Prison for Capitol Riot

Jacob Chansley, the man known as the "QAnon shaman" for his distinctive headdress and role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot, was sentenced to 41 months in prison on Friday. Judge Royce Lamberth found Chansley's remorse genuine but emphasized the seriousness of his actions, which he described as an "assault on the democratic process."

Prosecutor Kimberly Paschall sought a 51-month sentence, highlighting Chansley's early and prominent participation in the riot. During the hearing, a video was presented showing Chansley howling inside Congress, which the prosecution described as "chilling."

Defense attorney Albert Watkins argued for a lighter sentence, citing Chansley's remorse and mental health issues. In his address to the court, Chansley cited various figures and works as lessons for his repentance but stressed he is not a violent man or a domestic terrorist.

Chansley, who pleaded guilty to a single count of obstructing a proceeding of Congress, will receive credit for time served since his arrest in January. His conduct was criticized for undermining the peaceful transfer of presidential power.

Judge Lamberth: "Your actions that day were completely unacceptable. They were an assault on the democratic process."

Prosecutor Paschall: "He was one of the first rioters to enter the Capitol. He was one of the most prominent rioters inside the Capitol."

The epic traffic jam of 400 ships caused by the Ever Given blockage of the Suez Canal is cleared, Egyptian authorities say

A shipping backlog of more than 400 ships was caused by the Ever Given blocking the Suez Canal.

The 61 ships that remain stranded are expected to pass through the waterway on Saturday.

Problems caused by the blockage could take months to resolve, the world's biggest shipping company warned.

The shipping backlog that built up after the Ever Given container ship became lodged in the Suez Canal should come to an end on Saturday, authorities told Reuters.

The 61 remaining ships of the 422 that were left stranded after the major blockage are expected to pass through the waterway imminently, the Suez Canal Authority's chairman, Osama Rabie, said.

Around 85 ships in total are set to pass through the canal on Saturday, he added.

Last Monday, the Egyptian president's advisor for the canal authority told Bloomberg that it could take "around a week" to get all of the ships out of the canal's corridor.

If the remaining ships successfully pass through the waterway on Saturday, the backlog's end will have beaten expectations by a couple of days.

The reopening of the canal, however, will likely not mark the end of the disruption.

The world's biggest shipping company, Maersk, warned on Monday that the shipping problems caused by the Ever Given could take months to resolve, Insider's Sinéad Baker reported.

"Even when the canal gets reopened, the ripple effects on global capacity and equipment are significant and the blockage has already triggered a series of further disruptions and backlogs in global shipping that could take weeks, possibly months, to unravel," Maersk said.

The 1,300-foot Ever Given container ship was stuck for about 152 hours, with the blockage's total costs reaching an estimated $60 billion.

Rabie told local television stations that an investigation into what caused the costly jam is ongoing and will reach its conclusion next week, Reuters reported.

"The investigation is going well and will take two more days. Then we will announce the results," Rabie said.

Herman Melville's enigmatic sailor, Tommo, sought solace and reinvention on the shores of the Marquesas Islands. In the heart of the Pacific, he apprenticed under a skilled artisan, his calloused hands learning the rhythms of a foreign craft. As I delved into Tommo's story, I felt a kinship with his yearning for transformation, for the shedding of old selves in the embrace of the unfamiliar. He traded his sailor's garb for the simple loincloth, his palate adjusting to the flavors of breadfruit and roasted pig. The weight of his former life, the unspoken sorrows, seemed to lift as he participated in the vibrant tapestry of island existence.

His depression, a specter that had clung to him since his arrival, gradually dissipated amidst the laughter and rituals of the Taipi people. Theirs was a world of communal harmony, of kinship ties that ran deeper than blood. It was in this world that he encountered Fayaway, a woman whose beauty was as radiant as the tropical sun. Their love affair, chronicled by Melville with a blend of tenderness and exoticism, spoke of a profound human connection that transcended cultural boundaries. It was a testament to the power of shared experience, of finding solace and kinship in the most unexpected of places.

Yet, paradise, even one found in the embrace of a foreign culture, can be a fickle mistress. Tommo's initial enchantment began to wane, replaced by a creeping sense of unease. The customs that had once intrigued him now felt alien, the language a barrier to true understanding. His anxieties festered, echoing the very paranoia he had sought to escape. It was a stark reminder that cultural adaptation is not a linear journey but a complex dance between acceptance and resistance.

The arrival of a traveler, a harbinger of the outside world, served as a catalyst, reawakening Tommo's dormant longings for escape. He found himself torn between the allure of the familiar and the intoxicating, albeit unsettling, embrace of the Marquesan life. His internal struggle mirrored the broader human experience of displacement, of grappling with the allure and disorientation of cultural immersion.

Cabeza de Vaca, a Spanish explorer shipwrecked on the shores of the New World, faced a more brutal and prolonged encounter with the unknown. Stripped of his former identity, he and his companions were thrust into a desperate struggle for survival. They adapted, learning the languages and customs of the indigenous tribes they encountered. Over time, they transitioned from captive outsiders to respected healers, their skills a testament to their forced acculturation. Cabeza de Vaca's journey, fraught with hardship and unexpected transformation, highlights the extraordinary resilience of the human spirit and its capacity for adaptation in the face of adversity.

His story, like that of Tommo, underscores the profound and often unpredictable ways in which cultural encounters can reshape individual destinies. Both Melville, through his fictional avatar, and Cabeza de Vaca, through his harrowing first-hand account, emerged from their experiences irrevocably altered. Their narratives serve as powerful reminders of the transformative nature of travel, of the ways in which immersion in foreign cultures can shatter preconceptions, forge unexpected connections, and ultimately redefine our understanding of ourselves and the world around us.

The colonial interactions and uprisings in Samoa and Namibia during the late 19th and early 20th centuries presented distinct characteristics, shaped by the unique historical contexts and European perceptions of the indigenous populations. In Samoa, European colonizers held relatively positive views of the native Samoans, which was reflected in the limited white settlement in the region due to its tropical climate. This climate not only deterred large-scale European migration but also influenced the nature of colonial rule, with a greater emphasis on indirect governance and less on the displacement of native populations. Additionally, Samoa had developed advanced native education systems, which included secular schools that provided a foundation for future generations. This educational infrastructure was a result of early missionary activities and the Samoan desire for modernization, which distinguished Samoa from other colonized regions.

In stark contrast, the situation in Namibia was marked by a starkly different dynamic. European settlers, predominantly German, held disdainful views of the native Nama people, which was exacerbated by the competition for land and resources. Unlike in Samoa, where education was somewhat prioritized, in Namibia, settlers actively worked to block educational improvements for the native population, seeking to maintain their superiority and control. The tensions between the Germans and the Ovaherero and Nama populations eventually culminated in the Ovaherero uprising, which began in January 1904. The uprising was a response to unfair legal and business practices imposed by the German colonizers, including the expropriation of land and cattle, which were central to the Ovaherero economy and culture. Initially, the Germans struggled to quell the uprising, indicative of the military prowess and determination of the Ovaherero.

The tide of the conflict turned with the appointment of General Lothar von Trotha, who replaced Governor Leutwein and led a brutal military campaign against the Ovaherero and subsequently the Nama. Von Trotha's campaign was marked by extreme violence, including the use of concentration camps and the forced labor of prisoners, which resulted in the genocide of tens of thousands of Ovaherero and Nama. By the end of the war in 1907, it is estimated that the Ovaherero population had been reduced from approximately 80,000 to just 20,000, while the Nama suffered equally devastating losses. The aftermath of the war marked the end of African political significance in South West Africa, as the German colonial administration tightened its grip on the territory, imposing harsh rules and erasing indigenous autonomy. This period of colonial rule in Namibia stands in stark contrast to the experiences of Samoa, where colonial rule, though certainly oppressive, did not reach the same levels of brutality and genocide.

The comparative analysis of colonial interactions in Samoa and Namibia highlights the variability in European colonial policies and their impacts on indigenous populations. While Samoa experienced a form of colonial rule that was less confrontational, albeit still exploitative, Namibia was the site of one of the most egregious examples of colonial violence and genocide. The statistical data on population decline among the Ovaherero and Nama serves as a stark reminder of the human cost of colonial ambitions. The historical accounts of these periods also underscore the importance of education and the role it played in the different trajectories of these colonized regions. In Samoa, education contributed to a level of autonomy and modernization, whereas in Namibia, its denial was a tool of oppression, reinforcing the subjugation of the native populations. These narratives serve as critical lessons in understanding the complexities and brutality of colonial rule and its lasting impacts on the political, social, and economic landscapes of these regions.

The rain pattered dismally against the windowpanes, weaving a melancholic symphony that seemed to echo in the very marrow of the old house. Kitty sat by the hearth, her thoughts churning like autumn leaves caught in a bluster. The task of unraveling the knot that Jabez had unwittingly tied was daunting, yet she felt a flicker of resolution in her heart. It was clear to Kitty that a word with Father was indispensable, a word that might steer their home away from the restructuring hands of Aunt Pike.

Betty, meanwhile, lingered by the door, enviously eyeing the carriage preparations. "Oh, Kitty," she sighed, "I do envy you the drive to town. Especially in such weather—what adventure!"

Kitty managed a faint smile, though her mind wandered elsewhere. "I hardly call it an adventure, Betty. The rain makes everything seem so—" She paused, searching for the word, "—cluttered, somehow."

Betty brightened, shrugging off Kitty's misgivings. "Oh, but that's the charm—the thrill of it all. Are you taking Phipps with you?"

Kitty nodded absently, leaning closer to the window to glimpse Prue being readied, Jabez fumbling with the harness as raindrops streaked his broad back. The poor man seemed thoroughly sodden, both in garments and spirit. It tugged at Kitty's heart to see him so. Might it be that Jabez, so gruff and doubtful in his affections, was just as disheartened by Aunt Pike’s impending domination as they themselves were?

"'Tis not his fault," Kitty murmured softly, as much to herself as to her sister. "He didn't mean for things to spiral so."

Betty crossed to her sister, laying a tentative hand on her shoulder. "Then let us hope he finds the courage to face her. I daresay she’ll have her thumb upon all our heads if Father doesn't act."

The sound of footsteps thick against the wooden floor heralded Father's approach. Kitty seized the moment, straightening with an urgency borne of necessity. "Come, Betty, there waits Jabez with Prue."

They navigated the dim corridor, where faded portraits watched with silent symmetry. Meeting Father in the hall, Kitty took his hand, the warmth of it reassuring amid her gathering trepidation.

"Father," she began, drawing him aside with an earnestness that brooked no delay, "you know that Aunt Pike means to place us all in neat order as though we were no more than pins in her sewing box."

He sighed, his eyes kind but tired. "My dear, there are times when changes in the household are—well, necessary."

"But Father, she seeks to order the very life from us!" Her words tumbled faster now, the dam of reticence broken. "Can you not speak with her? Make her see that we can manage well enough on our own."

Father rubbed his brow, musing over the weight of family duty that rested upon him. "Kitty, understand that Aunt Pike means well. Her methods may seem...stringent, but they stem from genuine care."

Yet Kitty was determined not to relent. "But Father," she insisted, lowering her voice to a conspiratorial whisper, "consider Jabez—it is torment to him already. And think of our home life, how dear it is, unspooled by someone else's hand."

He hesitated, just long enough for Kitty to catch the flicker of uncertainty in his gaze. "Very well, Kit. I shall speak with her—but don't expect too much. Her mind can be as unmovable as a moorrock."

A breath of relief escaped her, gratitude weaving through her tension like a balm. "Thank you, Father." She squeezed his hand with renewed faith and a bolstered spirit.

With a nod to her sister, Kitty made haste to the phaeton where Jabez awaited, his face a peculiar blend of relief and worry. The clouds had opened their grey mouths wide, torrents now drenching rather than merely drizzling. Kitty climbed aboard, pulling her cloak tight around her.

Jabez handed her the reins. "Take care, Miss Kitty. The roads'll be slicker than a greased pig," he warned, trying to mask his concern with humor.

Kitty laughed lightly, feeling the wind stinging her cheeks as she took her place. "I'll mind it, Jabez. Thank you."

With Prue snorting impatiently and the wheels crunching over the gravel drive, Kitty set off. The tempest around her mimicked the storm within, but Kitty was resolute. She would see this journey through, the same faith she placed in Prue's sure hoofbeat holding her heart steady as they ventured into the rainwashed world beyond.

Think of it this way, unemployment is a huge problem in California, this idea would create new jobs. Surely there is an abundance of bilingual people living in California; I know at least five personally. Really, something like this would benefit the whole community too.

Then there is the idea of mainstream immersion, that is, English being the dominant language in the classroom, and that the Spanish speaking children will pick it up. Such programs are a perfectly horrible idea by themselves, as they pave the way for many children to fall through the cracks. “ELLs in English-only programs often fall behind academically. Many ELLs who are assessed using traditional methods are referred for special education. Such children often become school drop-outs.” But combining the idea, with the dual language system, I think is a pretty decent way to go. “Studies have shown that children who receive several years of instruction in their native language learn English faster and have higher overall academic achievement levels that those who do not.” You may be asking yourselves, how could we possibly facilitate both, aren't they opposites? More or less, yes they are opposites, but both can be implemented, if we consider age appropriateness. What I am suggesting, is the dual language approach all of the time for younger students, and the majority of the time for older students in which schedules lessons to be taught only in English. This will allow first language Spanish students access to clarification when they don't understand, the majority of the time, with lessons meant to challenge them, and keep them from using the duel language program as a crutch. Sort of how we go about teaching second languages in the college setting. At first, a lot of the dialog and instruction is in English, but as the students improve, more and more of the second language is used for dialog and instruction. As the children get older and older, and progress through the grades, we can cut down on the duel language approach. For most students, by high school, ideally they would be learning in an English dominant environment.

Another necessity, I believe, is the existence of ESL classes available to students. If the foundation for correct English learning isn't there, neither immersion nor a dual language system will do much good. I can say this because I have studied both French and Spanish. I can tell you, that when I am in an environment where a language is completely foreign to me, I don't pick up on anything. I simply stew in confusions. For example, foreign films. Any film I try to watch, without subtitles that is not in French or Spanish, I don't pick up any of the language, none. But films that are in French or Spanish, not only do I pick up some of the language (and sometimes I can follow what is going on without subtitals), I find myself eager to try and decode what is being said, and what is happening.

The idea of a paperless office is like the holy grail of modern workplaces—everyone talks about it, and many even dream about achieving it, but few really know how to get there. On one hand, who wouldn’t want to save money on endless reams of paper and expensive ink cartridges? I mean, have you seen what they charge for toner these days? It feels like I’m buying a gold brick every time I replenish my printer! Plus, using digital communication and storage methods not only enhances efficiency but also improves the company’s image—nothing says “we’re modern and eco-conscious” like ditching the paper clutter. And let’s be real: going green is not just good for the planet; it makes my company look like the superhero of sustainability. It’s quite the shiny badge of honor. Yet, despite these perks, I know there are challenges. Some of my colleagues act like their laptops are cursed relics from an ancient civilization. Seriously, you’d think they are trying to summon demons when they click on a PDF! Not to mention the cost of system upgrades, which can feel like a financial black hole, or the fact that our IT department turns into a 24/7 helpline as soon as we try to go digital. Balancing this tech revolution while keeping everyone sane feels like walking a tightrope.

When I think of higher education, I can’t help but roll my eyes at the sheer amount of paper used for assignments and reports. Sure, tablets can replace textbooks—and believe me, my back is singing praises for that! But often, both students and faculty seem baffled by these digital wonders. I’ve watched students fumble around apps like they’re trying to decode ancient hieroglyphs! So, how do we fix this? Training sessions! Imagine a world where everyone actually knows how to use their gadgets! It could be a game-changer. We could ditch the paper mountain in the faculty’s office and simply swipe through reports on our screens. The beauty of digital reading is how quick I can search for specific details—a feat that could take me a toddler’s attention span to accomplish with physical pages. While I see the hesitance—a mix of nostalgia and technophobia—embracing a paperless office isn’t just about trading paper cuts for digital headaches. It's about efficiency, sustainability, and making work-life a bit easier. With humor, patience, and the right training, we can turn this dream into reality, one digital document at a time!

"A singular fancy, Saltire, a passing drollery, no more," observed Densil, his voice a low rumble against the stone walls. He watched the Earl pace the room, a splash of velvet and Parisian tailoring against the gloom.

"Drollery, say you?" Saltire retorted, pausing by the barred window. "Perhaps. Yet, a fellow of such resolute cheer in this den of melancholia is a treasure, Densil, a veritable diamond in the dust-heap. I collect such curiosities, you know. Diversions against the ennui. Tell me, what would you ask for this…" he paused, snapping his fingers, "...this 'Curly'?"

Densil did not reply, lost in his own dark thoughts. He was a man haunted by a past he could neither escape nor reconcile. Saltire had found him thus, mired in regret, his spirit as gray as the walls that confined him.

"Come now, Densil," Saltire continued, his tone softening slightly. "Don't tell me you have grown sentimental over a mere servant. Sentiment is a luxury we can ill afford in this world. And, from what I gather, you have been wallowing in that luxury for far too long."

He turned from the window, his face etched with a faint weariness beneath the carefully cultivated air of nonchalance. He was, in truth, a man well-acquainted with the darker corners of the human heart, despite his outward display of levity. He was here for a reason, driven by a quiet conviction that Densil, for all his apparent despair, was not beyond redemption.

"You see, Densil," Saltire began again, "you are letting yourself become undone by this…this…situation. A man of your standing, your breeding, reduced to this. It is quite lamentable, I assure you."

Densil stirred, a spark of defiance flickering in his eyes. "Lamentable, is it? And what, pray tell, would you have me do? Rejoin the festivities? Pretend that the past is but a dream? The chasm is too wide, Saltire, too deep."

Saltire waved a dismissive hand. "Chasms can be bridged, my dear fellow. Gaps can be filled. It requires merely a little ingenuity, a little…effort. Tell me, Densil, what truly lies at the heart of this…estrangement?"

Densil hesitated, the words catching in his throat. "My…my brother," he finally managed, the name a bitter taste on his tongue. "He has all that was meant to be mine."

"Ah, the old story," Saltire sighed, though his eyes glinted with a sharper interest. "Primogeniture, sibling rivalry, the age-old tale of Cain and Abel. A tiresome drama, but not, I trust, beyond resolution. Family, after all, is family. Blood is thicker than water, as they say, even when the water is muddied with old grievances."

He paused, taking a step closer to Densil. "Have you considered, my friend, that your brother might also be suffering? That he might yearn for reconciliation as much as you do? Pride, Densil, is a dangerous foe. It blinds us to the truth, hardens our hearts, and leaves us isolated in our own self-inflicted misery."

Saltire clapped Densil on the shoulder, his touch surprisingly firm. "Come now, old boy. Let us consider a truce. Let us bury the hatchet, smoke the peace pipe, and all that sort of thing. What say you? A tentative olive branch, a gesture of good faith? It cannot hurt to try, can it?"

Densil looked at Saltire, a flicker of hope igniting in his gaze. "And what, pray tell, is the first step in this grand reconciliation?"

Saltire grinned, a flash of genuine warmth in his eyes. "Why, to seek out this 'Curly', of course. A clean face, a cheerful disposition, the very embodiment of optimism. He might just be the catalyst we need. Besides," he added with a wink, "I still intend to buy him from you. A drollery, perhaps, but a drollery with a purpose."

You know, folks, it's a weird feeling to look back and see yourself as the villain of the story. Yep, I've got victims out there who bear the brunt of my past shenanigans. Back in the day, I was the guy who saw the glamour in a quick hustle and sold fantasy over reality. That fantasy eventually landed me convicted on federal felony charges. Yessiree, I went to prison. You’d think that’s the point where they make an epic Netflix documentary about me, but real life isn’t quite as dramatic.

Once the cell door clanged shut, and I had plenty of time (like way too much time) to think, I swore to turn over a new leaf. Post-prison life might not be the red carpet, but it's a clean slate. I paid back the money I swiped because, hey, righting a wrong starts somewhere, right? But boy, was I in for a surprise; those I wronged weren’t ready to let bygones be bygones. What I stole wasn’t their bread and butter—it was Prada, baby! But, to them, a delayed vacation meant world war three. It's ironic, isn't it? The hatred can still light up a room like Times Square on New Year's Eve, all because I set back their Italian getaway plans.

Finding out they'd formed entire online clubs just to chat about yours truly? Yeah, that was a trip. I even snuck into those groups just to read about their fantasies of me getting my comeuppance behind bars. It's kind of hilarious how creative people can get when imagining prison life. Sorry to disappoint, but my stint wasn't the action-packed, prison-break drama they hoped for. I spent more time watching Seinfeld reruns than dodging shiv fights.

Coming across these extreme fantasies, I had to chuckle: did they think I was running Shawshank Penitentiary? The boredom was the real killer, folks, not the fellow inmates. Yet, despite the fact I've cleaned up my act and laid bare my regrets, I'm still the bad guy in a story with an overinflated soundtrack. Don’t you think it’s time to cue the country song about redemption and moving forward? Call me naive, but I imagined my apologies and monetary repayments would do more to mend those fences. Instead, it seems like some folks have got their pitchforks and torches ready for life.

Look, I’m all about accepting my past and making amends—heck, I've even swapped those scams for honest work. So, here's to hoping we can all someday gather round, toast with discarded grudges, and if not, well, can't say I didn't try. When you take a stroll down "Coulda, Woulda, Shoulda" lane, you realize we all trip over our own shoelaces occasionally. Just trying to make sure that my future doesn’t fall flat on its face the way my past often did. To everyone reading this, thanks for tuning into my candid tale of comeuppance and attempted reconciliation. Life’s a winding journey, ain't it?

The other main challenge to information service for Indigenous communities is the location of the space. Many communities have established libraries or cultural centers within their immediate location but such projects require funding. Public libraries may be in proximity to the community but may not provide adequate services in respect to the Indigenous culture. Such public libraries also allow access to all patrons to view material—but perhaps a particular community wants only their own members as patrons. Additionally, as Burns, Doyle, Joseph, & Krebs argue, “even for Indigenous people who do ‘technically’ live inside a library services catchment area, there continue to be many visible and invisible barriers presented through library practices, collections, and services”. The issue of location could partially be solved by the number of grants that are available for establishing tribal libraries and centers, though that is but one aspect for solving such a challenge. 

My views on librarianship have changed. For the most part, I have believed that librarianship is mostly a means for providing a cultural education of sorts to its patrons. Whether a patron is reading a fiction book, referencing a fact in a nonfiction book, or utilizing library computers, those patrons are becoming immersed in a greater culture—of which, the library holds the key. Now I can see that it is not just the responsibility of librarians to present a culture and to educate their patrons on it, it is also their responsibility to assist in the preservation of culture in its original forms and intentions—and as in accordance with those within the culture.

In the kitchen the cook, with a face like a pleasant copper saucepan, rosy and shining and round, was moving about leisurely, giving this and that a final unhurried wipe. "You going, too, I suppose?" said the sullen parlor-maid.

"Why, yes. 'Ain't I done everything? There's no need of my staying, is there?" The kitchen-maid went home for the night, too.

"No, I don't suppose there is. I just thought you might happen to be, that's all."

The kitchen-maid sat down a minute, in a tired, ungirt position, and looked over at the parlor-maid with good-natured young eyes grown a trifle speculative. The latter let her glance wander over the day's newspaper, brought down-stairs until inquired for.

"Tell you what I'd like to do!" exclaimed the kitchen-maid.

"What'd you like to do, Sally?"

"That's to come back again after I've been home for just a minute."

The parlor-maid looked up, unable altogether to conceal her interest. The house was very quiet. Through the clock-ticks, at perfectly regular intervals, came the muffled sound of Jetty's disconsolate yaps. Neither of the girls appeared to hear them.

"You don't mean just to oblige, do you, Sally?"

"Well, I'd do it in a minute for nothing else beside, but that ain't quite all I was thinking of just this once. Miss Catherine"--she hesitated, then, enthusiastically--"have you seen 'em up-stairs? the whole hundred of 'em laid out off Mrs. Darling's bedroom? I saw 'em when Mrs. Bonnet she sent me up for the lamps to clean. Law! Wouldn't any child like to see a sight like that! There's a little girl in my tenement, she'd just go crazy. Do you think there'd be any harm in it if I was to bring her over and let her get one peep? She's as clean a child as ever you saw. She comes of dreadful poor folks, but just as respectable! She never seen anything like it in her life. Law, what would I have done when I was a young one if I'd seen that? I'd thought I was dead and gone to heaven. I say, Miss Catherine, d' you think any one would mind?"

"How'll they know?" said Miss Catherine, callously. "Look here, Sally; you go along just as fast as you can and fetch your young one. And when you've got back, perhaps I'll step out a minute, two or three doors up street, and you can answer the bell while I'm gone. Now hurry into your things. I'll give you your car fare."

"Miss Catherine, you're just as good as you can be, and I'll do something to oblige you, too, some time," said Sally, her face aglow with delight; and having hurried into her jacket and tied up her head in a worsted muffler, was off.

She almost ran over the packed snow down the street. She had soon left the quiet rows of private dwelling-houses and come where hundreds of lights glittered across the rose-tinged snow. At every few rods a street band tootled and blared, covering the scraping of snow-shovels and jingle of bells. "How gay it is!" she thought; "won't it be a treat!"

Massive Texas Crash Claims Five Lives Amid Icy Storm

A devastating multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 35 near Fort Worth, Texas, has left at least five people dead and an unknown number injured. The tragic incident occurred during a winter storm that brought freezing rain, sleet, and snow across a large swathe of the United States.

The pileup, involving 75 to 100 vehicles, unfolded on Thursday morning, creating a chaotic scene on the busy interstate. Emergency responders are still working to clear the wreckage and assess the full extent of the damage. A reunification center has been established at a local community center to assist families affected by the tragedy.

The icy conditions caused by the storm also led to numerous other crashes throughout the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, including two fatal accidents in Dallas and one in Arlington. In Austin, a 24-vehicle pileup on an icy road left one person injured.

Power outages have been reported across the region, with over 125,000 homes and businesses without electricity in Kentucky and West Virginia alone.
