“The days of national conquest are over, I guess,” said Frank. “At least I hope so. That is a custom relegated to the dark ages.”

“Hard luck fer ould Oireland,” declared the Celt; “shure av it was to-day she was free, England wud niver conquer her thin.”

“Golly! yo’ might borrow dis air-ship from Marse Frank an’ set yo’ island free if yo’ wanted to,” declared Pomp; “shuah, yo’ cud blow up de hull lot ob dem Britishers.”

Barney’s eyes blazed.

“Bejabers, it’s no more thin they desarve, bad cess to thim,” he declared. “Shure, they’ve had their feet on sufferin’ Oireland’s neck long enuff.”

And so Barney continued to dilate upon the wrongs, real and fancied, of his native isle. He kept on until Pomp began to guy him.

Then he got angry.

“Huh!” cried the darky, “if yo’ people was set free dey nebber cud govern demselves! Shuah dey wud be eatin’ each other up fo’ a fac’!”

“Phwat’s that yez say?” blustered Barney, angrily; “don’t yez cast no aspersions on the ould sod, yez black pickaninny! Shure yez own people wud niver have got free av it hadn’t been fer Gineral Lincoln!”

“Dat shows all yo’ know ’bout fings,” sniffed Pomp; “dar warn’t no sich man as Gineral Linkum.”

“Hey! phwat’s that, naygur? Don’t yez give me de lie!”

“Huh! Linkum warn’t no gineral, sah! He was de President, I’d hab yo’ know, sah!”

Barney elevated his nose contemptuously.

“Be me sowl it’s mighty little yez know onyway. An’ ain’t the President commander-in-chief av the army an’ navy? An’ don’t that make him the bigges’ gineral in the land?”

Pomp saw the point and wilted. He slunk into the galley, muttering:

“I jes’ fix dat I’ishman fo’ pretendin’ to know so much. I jes’ hab a dose ready fo’ him yet!”

What this was we must wait for a later hour to decide. For the present we will consider nearer incidents.

In due course New Orleans was sighted. The air-ship hung over the southern city.

Frank looked for a certain signal, which he saw finally upon the roof of one of the houses.

It was a yellow flag.

At once the air-ship bore down upon it and soon descended within fifty feet of the roof. Up through a skylight popped Captain Nicodemus.

“Ahoy the ship!” he cried.

“Ahoy!” replied Frank.

“I am ready to come aboard. Throw out your gangway!”

“Is that roof strong enough to bear the weight of the air-ship?” asked Frank.

“Surely, mate! Come down.”

“All right!”

Frank let the air-ship descend and rest upon the roof of the building. Then he sprang down and shook hands with the captain.

Nicodemus was delighted.

He was all equipped for the trip.

But his personal appearance was startling as well as amusing in the extreme.

The old captain had got himself up in the style of the privateer captain of forty or fifty years previous. He wore fancy high boots, clinging cutlass, pistols in belt, a velvet blouse and pea-jacket.

He looked as if equipped for a privateering or piratical cruise, and Frank could not help a smile.

“You look as if you expected trouble,” he exclaimed. “Why have you armed yourself?”

“Hang me high!” cried the captain, fiercely; “are we not going into a land full of sharks and cuttlefish? Keep your eye on your outfit, lad. We will need a little powder and ball and cold steel before we get home.”

“Well,” said Frank, “you may be right; but I never employ arms until the necessary time comes. You are taking time by the forelock.”

“Which is correct, skipper. I once knew a fair ship to become overrun with pirates out in the Maldives, just because the skipper would not carry powder for fear of blowing up the ship. He had an aversion to the smell.”

The next afternoon, the butler announced Miss Irene Forsyte, and old Jolyon rose with a faint stir of anticipation. He had not seen her since their encounter at the opera, and the memory of her smile, both kind and reserved, lingered in his mind. She entered the drawing-room, her figure slightly inclined, as though her height made her movements deliberate. Her gown was of a muted green, not overly elaborate, yet it suited her complexion, and her hair, arranged simply, framed her face with a soft, golden hue.

The dog, Balthasar, who had been dozing by the hearth, lifted his head at the sound of her footsteps. Irene knelt down, her skirts pooling around her, and extended a hand to stroke him. The animal nuzzled her with a gratitude that seemed almost human, as though he had missed her presence.

“Your dog seems to remember me,” she remarked, her voice soft but clear.

Old Jolyon smiled, a touch of amusement in his eyes. “He has a keen sense for kindness, I think. He does not tolerate everyone.”

Irene laughed gently, the sound like a ripple of water. “I am glad to know I am tolerated, then.”

The conversation flowed easily, as though the pause at the opera had never happened. They spoke of the Ravogli’s performance, of the opera, and of the curious habits of the city’s inhabitants. Irene’s observations were sharp, her opinions well-considered, and yet there was a hesitancy in her manner, as though she were weighing her words before committing them to air.

“Do you often come to the opera alone?” Jolyon asked, curious.

Irene’s gaze dropped for a moment, her fingers absently tracing a pattern on the edge of her gloves. “Not often, but it is a refuge of sorts. I find it difficult to be at home when the house is quiet.”

Jolyon nodded, his mind racing. He had not expected such candor from her, and yet it seemed natural. “A refuge, you say? I can understand that. The city has a way of enforcing solitude, does it not?”

Irene looked up, her eyes meeting his with a clarity that was both unsettling and oddly comforting. “It does, but I find solace in music. It is a language that transcends words.”

The room seemed to hum with an unspoken understanding, as though the very air between them vibrated with the possibility of deeper connection. Jolyon found himself drawn to her, not merely by her beauty, but by the quiet strength that underlay her manner. She was not the typical society woman he was accustomed to; there was a depth to her that intrigued him.

As the afternoon wore on, their conversation turned to her work. Irene spoke of her students with a warmth that lit her face, her hands gesturing as though she were conducting an orchestra. “I teach music to children, but it is not just about the notes,” she said. “It is about giving them a way to express themselves, to find hope.”

Jolyon listened, his interest piqued. “That sounds like a noble endeavor.”

“It is, but it is not without its challenges. Many of the children come from difficult circumstances, and their families… well, they do not always understand.”

There was a pause, as though she were considering whether to speak further. Jolyon waited, sensing that there was more to her story. “You have a gift for it, I think,” he said finally.

Irene’s smile was both gracious and bittersweet. “Thank you. It is… rewarding, in its own way. But it is not easy.”

Jolyon’s mind raced, piecing together the fragments of her life. The quiet strength, the dedication to others, the subtle air of melancholy that clung to her like a fragrance. She was not the sort of woman who would be content with the trivialities of society, he realized. She was driven by something deeper, something that gave her purpose.

As the afternoon progressed, the topic of his family arose, though Irene handled it with the deft skill of one who knows when to steer a conversation. She asked about his children, his grandchildren, and listened with genuine interest, her questions revealing a sharp understanding of family dynamics. Jolyon found himself opening up in ways he had not expected, sharing stories of his past with a ease that surprised him.

When the butler announced tea, Irene’s eyes sparkled with atouch of mischief. “I do hope you are not expecting me to decline this time,” she said, her tone light but with an undercurrent of humor.

Jolyon chuckled, the sound rich and warm. “I would not dare to presume, but I must say, it is a rare pleasure to converse with someone who does not treat me as a relic of the past.”

Irene’s laughter was a melodic sound, one that seemed to fill the room with a warmth that countered the chill of the afternoon. “You flatter me, sir. I assure you, you are far from being a relic.”

The tea was served, and as they sipped, their conversation took on a more personal tone. Irene spoke of her mother, who had passed away some years ago, her voice tinged with a mixture of sorrow and gratitude. “She taught me the value of kindness,” Irene said, her eyes distant for a moment. “And she taught me to never underestimate the resilience of the human spirit.”

Jolyon listened, his heart stirred by her words. There was a vulnerability in her that was both endearing and enigmatic, as though she carried the weight of the world on her shoulders but bore it with an uncommon grace.

As the afternoon drew to a close, Jolyon found himself making an impulsive decision. “I should like to see your work,” he said, his voice firm but hesitant. “If you would allow it, I would like to visit the school where you teach.”

Irene’s eyes widened, her expression a mix of surprise and cautious hope. “That would be… very kind of you, Mr. Forsyte. I… I would be honored.”

Jolyon nodded, the corners of his mouth lifting into a satisfied smile. “Then it is settled. Next week, perhaps? I think Monday afternoon would suit me.”

Irene inclined her head, her smile radiant. “Monday would be perfect, sir. I shall look forward to it.”

As she prepared to leave, Balthasar, ever the sentinel, rose from his nap and padded over to her, his tail wagging with a enthusiasm that belied his age. Irene knelt once more, her hands finding his ears, and he nuzzled her with a gentle affection that seemed almost proprietorial.

Jolyon watched the exchange with a faint smile. The dog had always been a creature of strong opinions, and to see him so clearly at ease with Irene was, in its own way, a confirmation of her character.

When Irene had departed, Jolyon found himself walking through the rooms, his thoughts returning to their conversation. She was a woman of depth and compassion, and yet there was an air of mystery about her that intrigued him. The nominal visit to her school was, in truth, an excuse to learn more about her, to uncover the layers of her character.

As he sat down by the fire, the warmth of the flames a comforting contrast to the chill of the day, Jolyon found himself wondering what other facets of Irene’s life might be uncovered in the days to come. The promise of their meeting next week hung in the air, a silent expectation that both intrigued and excited him.

The city outside was alive with the sounds of evening, the distant rattle of horse-drawn carriages and the murmur of voices carried on the breeze. But inside, the room was quiet, save for the crackle of the fire and the occasional creak of the wooden floors. Old Jolyon leaned back in his chair, his mind awhirl with thoughts of Irene, her presence lingering in the room like the faint echo of a melody.

Behold, fair reader, the sun dips low, its golden rays painting the heavens with hues of amber and rose. The gentle breeze whispers through the ancient oaks, their gnarled branches stretching like supplicating hands toward the celestial tapestry above. In this sacred glade, where the wild roses bloom in untamed beauty, the spirit of the Earth herself seems to sigh. Here, amidst the verdant chaos, young Clorin, with eyes wide as the morning dew, kneels before the revered effigy of Diana, the huntress. Her heart, though mortal, beats in rhythm with the pulse of the forest, her soul stirring with a divine longing. Yet, within her breast, a tempest of doubt brews, for she is but a daughter of the soil, a mere shepherdess, and yet the satyr's fervent adoration perplexes and terrifies her.

"Fair Clorin," the satyr intones, his voice a blend of reverence and rustic charm, "thy grace doth outshine the stars in their celestial array. In thee, I see the hand of the gods, a fleeting glimpse of their immutable perfection." Clorin, flushing under his gaze, turns her eyes to the ground, where the wild violets nestle among the moss. "Nay, kind sir," she demurs, her voice soft as the first buds of spring, "I am but a child of the earth, my spirit no more divine than the brook that sings its way down yon hillside."

Her hands, though, tremble as she offers him a crown of woven ivy, a token of humility. The satyr takes it with a reverence that chills her to the core, for in his eyes, she sees not the reflection of a mortal, but the awe reserved for the gods themselves. Yet, as night descends, her resolve falters. The moon, full and luminous, casts its argent glow upon her face, revealing the faint scar on her cheek, a reminder of her mortality—a wound from a thorn, a mark of her fleshly frailty.

In the quiet of her chambers, Clorin ponders her mother's words, spoken on a summer night beneath the stars. "Child," her mother had said, her voice a gentle lullaby, "thy purity is thy shield, a barrier against the darker shadows of the world. The gods themselves may watch over thee, for in thy heart beats the innocence of the dawn." Clorin turns to the spring by her window, her reflection gazing back, unremarkable save for the radiance of her spirit. Yet, even as she looks, she feels the weight of her mortality, a shadow that clings despite her mother's assurances.

As the night wears on, thoughts of Phoebe drift into her mind, a spirit as wild and free as the wind. In the dell below, Phoebe tends her garden, a sanctuary where every bloom whispers secrets of the wild. Jesse, with a heart as pure as the morning dew, gathers the forest's bounty—fragrant herbs, plump berries, and the delicate wings of butterflies—laying them at Phoebe's feet. The two share a bond deeper than words, a communion with nature that transcends the mortal coil, a dance of souls in harmony with the earth.

In these moments, Clorin finds solace, a reminder that even in the shadow of doubt and fear, beauty and love endure. For though she may not be a goddess, her spirit, like the wild flowers, shines with an untamed glory, a beacon in the twilight of mortality.

The contemporary analysis of Algerian decolonization frequently invokes perspectives from scholars like Jeffrey C. Alexander, who explores the intricate dimensions of cultural and psychological trauma that emerge from historical ruptures. Alexander argues that the Algerian experience is emblematic of a trauma that is not confined merely to psychological afflictions but is deeply embedded in cultural and socioeconomic transformations. In Alexander's framework, trauma manifests both psychologically and culturally, integrating layers of individual suffering with broader societal wounds that defy simple depictions, such as those presented in works like The Wretched of the Earth.

At the core of this complex trauma is the concept of social systems, defined as organized networks of interpersonal relations and institutional structures that include economic, legal, and familial roles. These systems offer the context within which various forms of violence—be they physical, psychological, or socio-economic—are perpetuated and normalized over time. Examination of Algerian history under French colonial rule reveals that imported capitalist and Western industrial values not only disrupted indigenous social orders but also imposed novel hierarchies that continue to influence collective memory and identity. The imposition of such systems underscores the lasting impact of colonial policies that subverted and reoriented indigenous cultural norms.

Cultural trauma, a term referring to the deliberate and often orchestrated efforts by cultural carriers—politicians, intellectuals, and other authority figures—to redefine collective narratives—further complicates the legacy of decolonization. This process involves the production and perpetuation of symbols and myths that reshape public understanding, frequently glossing over the brutal realities of oppression and exploitation. In Algeria, the deliberate cultural narratives constructed during and after colonial rule serve to mediate the harsh legacy of French colonialism. The privileging of certain groups, notably a small elite of colonized intellectuals who benefit economically from the colonial order, contrasts starkly with the experiences of the rural masses, who bear the brunt of systemic neglect and exploitation.

An enduring division emerges between nationalist political leaders—who, in their quest for economic legitimacy, often prioritize the gains accruing from postcolonial power over substantive support for rural communities—and the isolated rural masses, whose participation in the struggle for decolonization is driven by desperation and hope. This disparity intensifies both cultural and psychological trauma. The rural populace, engaged actively as the primary forces of decolonization, experiences a profound sense of abandonment; their socio-political agency is undermined by leadership that appears disconnected from their hardships. Consequently, the resulting trauma is both internalized at the psychological level and expressed through disrupted cultural identities.

The case of Algeria thus exemplifies how the intermeshing of imposed social systems and deliberate cultural narratives yields a multifaceted trauma that endures through successive generations. The decolonization process, rather than fully alleviating colonial residues, multiplies social fractures by privileging sectors over others, leaving the rural masses to navigate a legacy of profound cultural and psychological dislocation. This layered trauma necessitates a nuanced understanding of its origins and illustrates the importance of addressing both the immediate and systemic causes embedded within the larger social and historical framework.

Derek Chauvin's History of Excessive Force Revealed in Preceding Arrests

As the trial of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin continues, new details have emerged regarding his history of using strong-arm tactics against suspects, including six instances since 2015. According to a report by The Marshall Project, Chauvin's use of neck restraints on people of color has been well-documented, with one alleged victim, Zoya Code, sharing her harrowing experience of being restrained by Chauvin in 2017.

Code, who is African American, told The Marshall Project that Chauvin pressed harder on her neck when she challenged him, causing her to lose consciousness. Prosecutors in Chauvin's case are seeking to use details of Code's arrest to support their second-degree murder charge against him. A judge approved the use of Code's case but excluded five other instances of Chauvin's alleged use of excessive force from the trial.

The Marshall Project interviewed other alleged victims and witnesses, all people of color, who had violent encounters with Chauvin. These incidents include Chauvin putting a man in a chokehold as an off-duty security guard and another where he allegedly maced and restrained a man asking for a ride. Victims of these encounters expressed fear for their lives, drawing parallels to George Floyd's death.

Chauvin's lawyer, Eric Nelson, argued that these prior incidents were not unreasonable or unauthorized, and Chauvin committed no crimes. Nelson did not respond to requests for comment from The Marshall Project, but in court papers, he stated that there was no improper action by Chauvin.

Zoya Code, the alleged victim who was restrained by Chauvin in 2017, spoke to The Marshall Project about her experience. "I thought I was going to die," she said. "I thought he was going to kill me."

Julian Hernandez, another alleged victim of Chauvin's excessive force, shared his story with The Marshall Project. "I was scared, I was terrified," he said. "I thought he was going to kill me."

Jimmy Bostic, a witness to one of Chauvin's incidents, told The Marshall Project that he saw Chauvin macing and restraining a man who was asking for a ride. "I was scared for his life," Bostic said. "I thought he was going to die."

Sir Rilee Peet, another witness to one of Chauvin's incidents, also spoke to The Marshall Project. "I was scared for his life," Peet said. "I thought he was going to die."

Monroe Skinaway, an eyewitness to one of Chauvin's incidents, told The Marshall Project that he saw Chauvin using excessive force on a suspect. "I was scared for his life," Skinaway said. "I thought he was going to die."

As the trial of Derek Chauvin continues, these incidents serve as a reminder of the systemic issues within the Minneapolis Police Department and the need for greater accountability and transparency. The use of excessive force by police officers can have devastating consequences, as seen in the death of George Floyd and the countless other victims of police brutality. It is crucial that we continue to shine a light on these issues and work towards a safer and more just society for all.

WhatsApp Outage Exposes Its Pivotal Role in the Global South

The widespread outage of Facebook on Monday sent shockwaves around the globe, but the impact was particularly severe in countries like Brazil due to the unavailability of WhatsApp. For millions in the Global South, where high SMS and cellular data costs are bypassed through the app, WhatsApp isn't merely a convenience—it's a lifeline.

In regions such as Brazil, India, Kenya, South Africa, Nigeria, Argentina, Malaysia, and Colombia, WhatsApp has become so ingrained in daily life that its role transcends that of a mere messaging platform. It is considered akin to a public utility, its sudden absence disrupting everything from small local economies to governmental operations. "WhatsApp has embedded itself into every aspect of our lives," explains David Nemer, a Professor at the University of Virginia. "Its outage revealed just how significant it is, not just for individual communication, but for our broader societal functioning."

Since Facebook's acquisition of WhatsApp for $21.8 billion, the service has seen its user base more than quadruple. This growth has only heightened the world's dependency on Facebook's suite of products, raising concerns about the concentration of digital power. Similarly controversial has been Facebook's Free Basics program, which, though designed to expand internet access, faced backlash for fostering a monopolized market, especially within these vulnerable regions.

Critics have leveled accusations of 'digital colonialism' against Facebook, asserting that through practices like zero-rating, the company encourages a more closed web from which it can extract valuable data. Gabriel Pereira, a Doctoral Fellow at Aarhus University, pointed out, "This forms a new type of digital ecosystem that erodes the open internet and consolidates Facebook's, especially WhatsApp's, position of power."

WhatsApp's importance in the digital and economic life in the Global South was further magnified during Monday's platform downtime. In Brazil and India, WhatsApp has expanded its services to include in-app financial transactions, integrating even deeper into the fabric of daily life. For many businesses and individuals, the disruption was not just inconvenient but financially damaging.

Business owner Daniella Goulart shared her struggle, saying, "Without WhatsApp, our operations grind to a halt. It is not just about messaging; it's about business transactions, customer service, and communication. This outage was a stark reminder of how dependent we have become."

Other messaging platforms available in Brazil and similar countries simply cannot compete with the cultural and economic power of WhatsApp. The outage underscored the platform's unparalleled role and the lack of viable alternatives.

This extraordinary dependency on WhatsApp, and by extension Facebook, has attracted the attention of lawmakers and regulators around the globe. Discussions regarding antitrust actions and the potential regulation of WhatsApp as a public utility are gaining momentum. As societies worldwide consider the implications of this digital concentration, Monday's outage serves as a critical reminder of the power wielded by WhatsApp and the need for a diversified and open digital marketplace.

The little red-roofed town of Hayes lies in a furrow of the broad-backed Wiltshire Downs; it was once an important posting station, and you may still see there an eighteenth century inn, much too large for the present requirements of the place, and telling of the days when, three times a week, the coach from London used to pull up at its hospitable door, and wait there half-an-hour while its passengers dined. The inn is called the Grampound Arms, and you will find that inside the church many marble Grampounds recline on their tombs, or raise hands of prayer, while outside in the churchyard, weeping cherubs, with reversed torches, record other pious and later memories of the same family.

But almost opposite the Grampound Arms you will notice a much newer inn, where commercial gentlemen make merry, called the Aston Arms, and on reference to monumental evidence, you would also find that cherubs are shedding similar pious tears for a Sir James Aston, Bart., and his wife, and, thirty years later, for James Aston, first Lord Hayes, and his wife. But for the Astons, no marble knights keep watch on Gothic tombs.

The river Kennet, in its green wanderings, has already passed, before it reaches Hayes, two houses, one close down by the river, the other rather higher up and on the opposite bank. The smaller and older of the two is the residence of Mr. Grampound, the larger and newer of Lord Hayes. These trifling facts, which almost all the inhabitants of Hayes could tell you, will sufficiently indicate the mutual position of the two families in the latter half of the nineteenth century.

Grampound House was a pretty, ivy-grown old place, with a lawn stretching southwards almost to the bank of the river, and shaded by a great cedar tree, redolent of ancestors and as monumental in its way as the marble, sleeping figures in the church. It was useful, however, as well as being ancestral, and at this moment Mrs. Grampound and her brother were having tea under it.

It was a still, hot day at the beginning of August, and through the broad, fan-like branches, stray sunbeams danced and twinkled, making little cores of light on the silver. Down one side of the lawn ran a terrace of grey stone, bordered by a broad gravel walk, and over the terrace pale monthly roses climbed and blossomed. Most of the windows in the house were darkened and eclipsed by Venetian blinds, to keep out the sun which still lingered on the face of it; and Mr. Martin, also--Mrs. Grampound's brother--was in a state of eclipse for the time being, for he wore a broad-brimmed Panama hat, which concealed the upper part of his face, while a large harlequin tea-cup prevented any detailed examination of his mouth. Mrs. Grampound sat opposite him in a low, basket chair, and appeared to be thinking. It is a privilege peculiar to owners of very fine, dark grey eyes, to appear to be thinking whenever they are not talking.

Mr. Martin finished his tea, and lit a cigarette.

"They've begun cutting the corn," he said; "it's very early."

Mrs. Grampound did not answer, and her brother, considering that he had made his sacrifice on the altar of conversation, relapsed into silence again.

Perhaps the obvious inference that the summer had been hot reminded her that the day was also hot, for in a minute or two she said,--

"Dear Eva! what a stifling journey she will have. She comes back to-night; she ought to be here by now."

"Where has she been staying?"

"At the Brabizons. Lord Hayes was there. He comes home at the end of the week; his mother arrived yesterday."

In the realm of poetic expression, Walt Whitman unfolds a canvas where his experiences shimmer like stars, illuminating his role as a teacher. With the weight of countless experiences orbiting his being, he secures his position as an erudite guide, embodying the wisdom acquired through life's eclectic pathways. In passage 16, he transcends the ordinary, presenting himself as an omniscient, god-like figure, a beacon of insight whose vision embraces the vast expanse of human experience. Through the resounding refrain of "I am," he conjures a universal tapestry woven with the threads of shared existence, asserting not only authority but an intrinsic connectedness to the collective narrative of humanity.

Whitman’s active perception manifests in his poetic attention to the world around him. He embodies the role of the attentive listener and keen observer, transforming simple encounters into profound revelations. Each moment resonates with potential, every whisper from the wind or glimmer of sunlight treated as sacred texts laden with significance. In flaunting his myriad experiences, he demands acknowledgment, not for vanity's sake, but to nurture a deeper understanding of self and society in his audience. He yearns for his students to transcend his insights, encouraging them to forge paths rich with their unique experiences, fostering a lineage of growth and wisdom.

As a tireless advocate of equality, Whitman expertly interweaves this theme through the fabric of his poetic discourse. In passage 15, he illuminates an array of occupations—be it a humble laborer or a great thinker—to underline a profound assertion: every role holds intrinsic value, each a vital cog in the machinery of a thriving nation. His inclusive imagery invites every soul to recognize their significance, conjuring a vision of societal harmony grounded in mutual respect and shared endeavor.

Through this lens of equality, Whitman imagines a collective consciousness, a society blossoming into a cohesive nation, where every individual finds belonging in the symphony of existence. In casting himself as both a witness and a participant, he invites all to embrace their experiences and foster connections that elevate the human spirit, crafting a future woven with the threads of unity and recognition. In Whitman's world, the individual experiences transform into collective strength, forming a majestic tapestry of life, where the essence of equality permeates every stitch.

Why Twitter finally banned Trump

Twitter permanently suspended President Donald Trump’s social media account on Friday afternoon, citing the risk of further incitement of violence.

The decision comes in the wake of Trump’s encouragement of a rally in Washington, DC, that resulted in a mob storming the Capitol building and at least five deaths. For years, the president has used his Twitter account to reach his nearly 90 million now-former followers on the platform as a means to bypass traditional media. Many critics have long argued that Twitter should take a firmer stance against Trump due to his dangerous use of the platform to spread lies and violent rhetoric.

While some may see the move as too little, too late, and Trump’s supporters are questioning it entirely, it nevertheless marks a historic exertion of Twitter’s ability to influence politics during a time when the strength of democracy in the US is being seriously tested.

“In the context of horrific events this week, we made it clear on Wednesday that additional violations of the Twitter Rules would potentially result in this very course of action,” read a company blog post on Friday explaining the decision. Despite the fact that Twitter has generally allowed world leaders like Trump to post more controversial content than the average user since their tweets are deemed newsworthy, the company said that these accounts are still “not above our rules entirely and cannot use Twitter to incite violence, among other things.”

Ahead of the permanent ban, Twitter had previously temporarily suspended Trump’s tweets on Wednesday for violating its policies on civic integrity and violence, and warned that it may permanently suspend him if he continued to violate its policies. Now, users can no longer see Trump’s tweets, and the president is unable to post on his account.

The move comes as hundreds of Twitter’s own employees urged CEO Jack Dorsey to suspend Trump permanently, according to a report by the Washington Post.

The day before Twitter’s permanent suspension, Facebook blocked Trump’s account on its platform, which has tens of millions of followers, from posting and emphasized that the ban would be in place for at least two weeks until President-elect Joe Biden’s inauguration.

Recent events leading to the decision

Twitter’s official explanation for why it permanently blocked Trump’s account was that his last two tweets violated the company’s Glorification of Violence policy and were part of a broader pattern of encouraging violence during the transition of presidential powers. Twitter specifically cited a concern that Trump’s followers seemed to interpret his announcement about not attending Biden’s inauguration as a signal that it would be a “safe” target for violent acts.

The first tweet that pushed Trump past Twitter’s tipping point stated that he would not attend Joe Biden’s inauguration. The second declared that the “75,000,000 great American Patriots” who voted for Trump would not be “disrespected or treated unfairly in any way, shape or form!!!”

Twitter said that, when read in the broader context of the recent violence in DC and how Trump’s tweets can be mobilized by his followers to incite further violence, those two tweets impelled the platform to suspend his account.

In the past week, a growing chorus of leaders in the political and tech communities have been placing more pressure than ever on social media companies to permanently ban Trump. Their concerns correspond with fears that Trump is encouraging his followers to stage some sort of coup by forcefully rejecting the certified results of the presidential election declaring Biden the next president.

“Now is the time for Silicon Valley companies to stop enabling this monstrous behavior — and go even further than they have already by permanently banning this man from their platforms,” former first lady Michelle Obama said in a statement Thursday afternoon.

In the technology industry, early Twitter investor Chris Sacca and former Facebook chief security officer Alex Stamos similarly called for Twitter to cut off the president’s access to social media.

And hundreds of Twitter’s employees — who have rarely publicly protested the company’s decisions — said that they felt the company had a moral obligation to shut down Trump’s account.

“We play an unprecedented role in civil society and the world’s eyes are upon us,” the employees wrote in a letter to Jack Dorsey and Twitter executives. “Our decisions this week will cement our place in history, for better or worse.”

People in Trump’s inner circle such as Donald Trump Jr. quickly derided Twitter’s decision, arguing that the company is holding his father to a double standard by not taking down the accounts of Iran’s Ayatollah Khamenei and “numerous other dictatorial regimes.”

A history of controversial tweets

Trump launched his political career on Twitter spreading racist “birtherism” conspiracy theories about former President Obama. And as he continued to gain political power, he has been a prolific user of the platform, regularly spreading false statements, conspiracy theories, and, at times, what many see as dangerous rhetoric veering on inciting violence.

Over the years, the former reality TV star has repeatedly used the platform to retweet conspiracy theorists such as QAnon supporters, spread medical misinformation about Covid-19, suggest potentially shooting into crowds of Black Lives Matter protesters, and at multiple points inched toward potentially provoking a nuclear war via the platform.

And for four years, Trump’s incendiary social media posts have largely gone unchecked by Twitter and other major tech companies. That’s because Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and other companies have repeatedly said they don’t want to interfere in politics but rather act as neutral platforms committed to free speech values.

Those limits have been tested by Trump’s repeated attempts to interfere with the integrity of the US elections process via social media. In the months leading up to and following the 2020 presidential election, Trump has endlessly spread baseless conspiracy theories about the election being purportedly “stolen” from him, despite having no substantial proof of any such allegations. His repeated assertion that the election was rigged has also inspired some of his fervent followers to doubt the legitimacy of the US Electoral College, fueling the “Stop the Steal” protests which led to Wednesday’s violence.

For some critics of Trump’s Twitter behavior, the company’s actions to limit the president’s tweets are several years overdue. Trump has already built an infrastructure of highly networked social media followers who continue to organize in private groups, alternate social media platforms like Gab and Parler, as well as through the Twitter accounts of other prominent Trump supporters.

What’s next

If Trump tries to start another Twitter account, per Twitter’s ban evasion policy, he’s liable to get kicked off the platform again.

However, his administration still has access to two official US government accounts: @POTUS and @WhiteHouse. Those accounts will be handed over to the Biden administration soon, according to Twitter. The company has said it will not suspend those accounts unless it deems that course of action absolutely necessary to alleviate real-world harm.

On Friday evening, Trump posted several tweets to the @POTUS criticizing Twitter for suspending his account and alleging without evidence that “Twitter employees have coordinated with the Democrats and the Radical Left in removing my account from their platform.” Twitter quickly deleted the tweets.

It’s unclear where Trump will go from here. The natural social media platform for Trump to migrate to, Parler, has fewer rules around content moderation, but those policies are suddenly proving problematic. Around the same time that Twitter permanently suspended Trump, Google banned Parler from its app store, and Apple has warned it may do the same if the platform doesn’t start moderating content more aggressively.

Twitter’s action in banning Trump was an unprecedented move by a major tech company to limit the platform of a major political figure in the interest of preserving democratic stability. And there’s a good chance we’ll be seeing more of that from other companies in the future, too.

In today's society, there is a prevailing tendency to dismiss the validity of mental illness, as if the American population lacks any genuine insight into its actual complexities. Many cling to the cliché that mental illness is merely an "invisible wound" beyond help, a phrase that, when closely examined, reveals a shallow misinterpretation of nature's more mysterious domains. Misconceptions proliferate as societal narratives insist that only those with so-called "real causes" qualify as legitimately ill. Aren’t such definitions inherently flawed? This reductionist view ignores the rich, multifaceted experiences of individuals who struggle without obvious traumatic histories. Instead of cultivating understanding, society indulges in stereotypes that invalidate these experiences. It is not uncommon to hear remarks like "If you haven't been through something terrible, you can't really understand mental illness." Such statements betray a tacit belief that personal suffering must be extreme to count, and in doing so, they contribute to an environment where blame is unjustly assigned—either to the sufferers themselves or to their families. Consequently, guilt and shame become the unwelcome byproducts of misguided judgment, serving as a barrier to the empathy and support that are so desperately needed.

Societal culture perpetuates a notion that individuals are solely responsible for their mental state, a line of thought that both simplifies and distorts the reality of mental health conditions. Why should mental illness become a personal failing rather than a complex interplay of genetics, experience, and circumstance? With a slash of sarcasm, one might ask, “Is it any wonder then that those suffering are shunned, as if their struggles are a matter of choice?” This cultural tendency to justify avoidance by exonerating oneself from perceived responsibility further isolates those who most need assistance. The tendency to reduce mental disorders to moral lapses is not only intellectually lazy but also socially damaging, as it reinforces an environment where open discussion and support remain stifled. The blame game not only ignores the scientific and medical realities of mental health but also ignores the human element of care and concern. One must question: Does society benefit by denying the full scope of mental illness, or does it merely fortify the walls of isolation and misunderstanding that plague those already on the margins?

“Ah! here they come!” exclaimed Jekyl, not sorry for the event which so opportunely interrupted Dalton's unpromising history. And now a heavy travelling-carriage, loaded with imperials and beset with boxes, was dragged up to the door by six smoking horses. The courier and the landlord were immediately in attendance, and after a brief delay the steps were lowered, and a short, stout man, with a very red face and a very yellow wig, descended, and assisted a lady to alight. She was a tall woman, whose figure and carriage were characterized by an air of fashion. After her came a younger lady; and lastly, moving with great difficulty, and showing by his worn looks and enfeebled frame the suffering he had endured, came a very thin, mild-looking man of about sixty. Leaning upon the arm of the courier at one side, and of his stout companion, whom he called Doctor, at the other, he slowly followed the ladies into the house. They had scarcely disappeared when a caleche, drawn by three horses at a sharp gallop, drew up, and a young fellow sprang out, whose easy gestures and active movements showed that all the enjoyments of wealth and all the blandishments of fashion had not undermined the elastic vigor of body which young Englishmen owe to the practice of field sports.

“This place quite deserted, I suppose,” cried he, addressing the landlord. “No one here?”

“No one, sir. All gone,” was the reply.

Haggerstone's head shook with a movement of impatience as he heard this remark, disparaging as it was, to his own importance; but he said nothing, and resumed his walk as before.

“Our Irish friend is gone away, I perceive,” said Jekyl, as he looked around in vain for Dalton. “Do you believe all that story of the estate he told us?”

“Not a syllable of it, sir. I never yet met an Irishman and it has been my lot to know some scores of them who had not been cheated out of a magnificent property, and was not related to half the peerage to boot. Now, I take it that our highly connected friend is rather out at elbows!” And he laughed his own peculiar hard laugh, as though the mere fancy of another man's poverty was something inconceivably pleasant and amusing.

“Dinner, sir,” said the waiter, entering and addressing the Colonel.

“Glad of it,” cried he; “it's the only way to kill time in this cursed place;” and so saying, and without the ceremony of a good-bye to his companion, the Colonel bustled out of the room with a step intended to represent extreme youth and activity. “That gentleman dines at two?” asked he of the waiter, as he followed him up the stairs.

“He has not dined at all, sir, for some days back,” said the waiter. “A cup of coffee in the morning, and a biscuit, are all that he takes.”

The Colonel made an expressive gesture by turning out the lining of his pocket.

“Yes, sir,” replied the other, significantly; “very much that way, I believe.” And with that he uncovered the soup, and the Colonel arranged his napkin and prepared to dine.

WHEN Dalton parted from his companions at the “Russie,” it was to proceed by many an intricate and narrow passage to a remote part of the upper town, where close to the garden wall of the Ducal Palace stood, and still stands, a little solitary two-storied house, framed in wood, and the partitions displaying some very faded traces of fresco painting. Here was the well-known shop of a toy-maker; and although now closely barred and shuttered, in summer many a gay and merry troop of children devoured with eager eyes the treasures of Hans Roeckle.

The trees stood like sentinels, their branches etched in sharp relief against the bleak evening sky, as the last wisps of daylight struggled to penetrate the encroaching gloom. The air was heavy with the scent of damp earth and decaying leaves, a morbid perfume that clung to the nostrils like a damp shroud. Mr. Harland, a man of unflappable temperament, yet increasingly beset by the whispers of doubt, wandered listlessly through the orchard, his shoes crunching upon the brittle grass.

The trees, soon to be stripped of their verdant garb, now stood as skeletal sentinels, their branches creaking ominously in the faint breeze. A shower of dry leaves rustled through the air, their fragile forms like fluttering specters, as if fleeing some unspoken terror. The grass, too, seemed to have withered, its vibrant hue reduced to a dull, forlorn grey, like the sombre mood that had taken hold of Mr. Harland's heart.

The wind, a gentle zephyr that mere moments before had been a soothing balm, now picked up, its whispers growing into a mournful sigh that seemed to echo the turmoil brewing within Mr. Harland's mind. He felt lost, adrift in a sea of uncertainty, his thoughts as treacherous as the tide. The moon, a ghostly galleon, hung low in the sky, casting an eerie glow over the orchard, as if trying to illuminate the path ahead.

His footsteps, slow and measured, wove a winding course through the rows of trees, his eyes roving over the landscape with a sense of disquiet. The trees, their limbs stark and unforgiving, seemed to loom over him, their branches like skeletal fingers reaching out to snatch at his very soul. Mr. Harland's heart ached with a sense of foreboding, as if the very fabric of his reality was unraveling before his eyes.

In the distance, the drive-house loomed, a sombre presence that seemed to draw Mr. Harland inexorably towards it. Its walls, a dull, weathered grey, seemed to absorb the faint light, leaving it to pool in the dusty air like a stagnant puddle. The wind whipped through the estate, sending the leaves dancing in its path, as if trying to convey some hidden message that only the trees might decipher.

The air grew colder, the shadows lengthening and deepening as the moon climbed higher in the sky. Mr. Harland quickened his pace, his feet carrying him towards the drive-house with an almost mechanical precision, as if driven by some unseen force. The trees, their limbs creaking in the wind, seemed to watch him with a mournful air, their branches like Nature's own twisted fingers reaching out to snatch at his very heart.

As he approached the drive-house, the sound of footsteps echoed through the stillness, and Mr. Harland's eyes narrowed, his mind racing with a mixture of curiosity and trepidation. He had not expected to encounter anyone, yet here was proof that he was not alone in this forsaken place. The footsteps drew closer, heavy and deliberate, as if the person had a purpose, a destination to reach.

His eyes scanned the darkness, trying to discern the figure that emerged from the shadows. The moon, now high in the sky, cast an eerie glow over the drive-house, illuminating the man's features as he stepped into the light. Mr. Thaddeus, a man with a reputation for cunning, stood before him, a sly glint in his eye that sent a shiver down Mr. Harland's spine.

The air seemed to vibrate with tension as the two men faced one another, the silence between them stretching out like a fragile thread that might snap at any moment. Mr. Harland's heart pounded in his chest, his mind racing with a mixture of emotions, as he struggled to comprehend the significance of this unexpected encounter. The drive-house loomed behind Mr. Thaddeus, its walls a dull, oppressive presence that seemed to weigh upon them both like a physical force.

The wind, now a mournful sigh, seemed to carry Mr. Harland's thoughts back to the conversation they had been about to have. The task, once thought trivial, now loomed large, its outcome hanging in the balance like a fragile thread. And Mr. Thaddeus, with his sly smile, seemed to know it, to be using this encounter to his advantage, to ensure that the outcome would be in his favor.

In Perrier Jouet's advertising strategy, a comparison of their ads over time highlights a shift in branding approach. One notable example is the 1980 bottle ad, which exemplifies the brand's marketing strategy during a specific historical context. Following World War II, the U.S. experienced significant economic growth and demographic changes, leading to an expanded market for luxury goods including fine wines like Perrier Jouet.

The 1980 Perrier Jouet ad features a photograph of a bottle of Champagne on a table with glasses and confetti scattered around it. The ad is conveyed using figurative text that juxtaposes the bottle and the luxurious elements in a static and formal setting. The ad's design reflects the technological advancements in color photography at the time, with vibrant yet muted colors used to present the scene. The overall tone of the ad, however, is unexciting and lacks a sense of dynamism. Historians note the influence of traditional Dutch painting, particularly the "Still Life" genre, on the ad's composition and use of light.

In the early 1980s, wine consumption was not as widespread as it is today, and mixed drinks dominated the American market. As a result, Perrier Jouet's advertising strategy targeted affluent buyers, emphasizing the luxurious aspects of the brand and the sophistication it conveyed. The ad appears factual and realistic, aiming to reassure potential customers of the quality and class associated with Perrier Jouet. While the ad does not evoke an emotional response, it effectively communicates the brand's value proposition to its target audience.

In contrast to more recent ads, such as the 2002 "Nude Ad," the 1980 Perrier Jouet ad lacks the shock and emotional impact that became a hallmark of later marketing campaigns. The "Nude Ad," with its striking image of a model removing her dress, marked a significant departure from traditional advertising techniques. It was more sensational and attention-grabbing, aiming to create an emotional connection with the viewer. In comparison, the 1980 ad adheres to a more conservative approach, reflecting the conservative market and cultural attitudes at the time.

Perrier Jouet's advertising strategy changed over the years to stay relevant in the ever-evolving market. The 1980 ad reflects the company's initial approach to the U.S. market post-World War II. Following significant expansions in wine consumption, later ads shifted towards a more emotive and provocative tone. The 2002 ad, with its bold imagery and message, exemplifies this shift towards a more attention-grabbing and emotional advertising approach.

Historical influences, such as the Dutch "Still Life" genre, are evident in Perrier Jouet's advertising design. The use of formal and static compositions, accompanied by vibrant yet muted colors, pays homage to the art movement's focus on everyday objects and textures. This continuation of historical influences reflects the brand's ongoing commitment to maintaining an air of sophistication and tradition.

Once more, the procedures used were almost identical to those in the previously mentioned experiments, but this time around after the completion of the first trial, the experimenter asked the 6- and 9-year-old participants whether they believed the postage stamp's alteration had been achieved via magical means (i.e. the experimenter's manipulation of an object). This follow-up experiment revealed that child participants were more likely to attribute the event to a magical rather than ordinary physical cause when explicitly asked about the possibility of a magical influence being in effect. Furthermore, Subbotsky contends that “this confirms the 'open nature' of the original phenomenalistic judgments that can later be developed either into a magical or a natural-physical explanation, depending on the circumstances”. In essence, Subbotsky believes that phenomenalism is an open system that admits variation—e.g. toward magical or scientific reasoning—when specific conditions are met.

In light of this evidence, it is illuminating to note the Woolley et al. study, in which both magical and scientifically-based causal reasoning in children are shown to be limited by at least two of the same basic principles. Although children are aware that the world is governed by laws that prevent them from affecting their physical environments through sheer mental force, younger children still engage in the practice of wish-making with substantial belief in its efficacy.

When most people conceive of cause and effect in ordinary events, three principles are considered inviolable: priority, in which the cause of an event occurs prior to the effect; consistency, in which the cause of an event is consistent with its outcome; and exclusivity, in which an effect can have only one cause. The aim of the experiment was to determine if these inviolable properties of ordinary causality were also in force within the domain of wish-making. Participants watched as an experimenter wished for specific items to appear within a box that had been contrived to dispense the wished-for items when manipulated by another experimenter. Woolley et al. found in a sample of participants of ages 3-6 that during trials when children observed an experimenter violating either the principle of priority or exclusivity, they were significantly more likely to claim that the experimenter had not produced the object by wishing. Further experiments that tested the responses of 3-6-year-old participants to violations of ordinary causality (e.g. a toy-chute contraption familiar to many of the participants that was rigged to dispense marbles into a cup) yielded similar results, showing that children did not believe the experimenter's actions to be the cause of a familiar, ordinary event when there was a clear disruption in priority, exclusivity, or consistency. The overlap between two of the three constraints is apparent and suggestive of a common source from which ordinary and magical causality arise. In fact, Woolley et al. connect the results of their experiments to Subbotsky's verbal and behavioral hypothesis, speculating that the fact that older children wished for desirable objects with nearly the same frequency as younger children, despite attesting to a disbelief or lesser belief in wish-making, may “reflect verbal-behavioral dissociations in which children's beliefs in magic disappear first in verbal responses and later in their behavior”. To name another example, Subbotsky's study of 17 college students once again reveals that behavior often belies verbal expression: when the participants were presented with the choice of allowing a “witch” to hex their lives, not one of them gave their consent in spite of the fact that they all professed to disbelieve in magic.

In the delicate twilight of a Parisian evening, when the glow of gaslight mingled with the receding vestiges of day and the murmurs of high society commingled with the innocent laughter of the theater’s audience, Van Twiller found himself entranced once more by the ineffable charm of Mademoiselle Olympe. Her stage presence, both poised and incautiously natural, recalled to him the serene dignity of an artisan unaware of the manifold passions she so effortlessly incited. In the rare intervals of lapsed attention, the observer in him wavered between the delight of secret admiration and the quiet torpor of familial duty, each sentiment weighing upon his heart with a subtle, almost imperceptible balance.

It was by the darkened corridors of his own conscience and the gentle prodding of rumor that the truth of his nightly vigils was unburied. Though he endeavored to attend her performances with the stealth of a shadow, a whisper had reached his family—a murmur that grew with each retelling—that the admired youth wandered too oft to the noble theater in the hours of the night. His mother, Mrs. Vanrensselaer Vanzandt Van Twiller, possessed both the sharp eye of a matron and the tender intuition of one who cherished propriety. With a determined air befitting one accustomed to the unyielding demands of society, she resolved to ascertain the veracity of these murmurs, thereby setting in motion a chain of events that both vexed and ennobled her son.

The inevitable confrontation, resplendent with the candor known only to the most intimate of familial bonds, unfolded in the somber study of the ancestral home. Van Twiller, unable to veil his fascination any longer, confessed—though with a tremulous breath and a genteel humility—that the heart would stray from its prescribed vector when met with the radiant allure of Mademoiselle Olympe. His words, tender and unadorned by artifice, met the measured gaze of his mother, whose concern was tempered by the dignified pride of a lineage steeped in both honor and restraint. In that poignant moment, it was agreed that the pursuit of such a delicate sentiment must be navigated with the precision of an experienced mariner charting treacherous waters.

As the evening's discourse waned, a thoughtful resolve settled upon the venerable matron, who insisted upon an immediate return to the sanctity of home—a move designed not solely to corral his wandering affections but to remind him of the sacrosanct obligations imposed by name and station. Van Twiller, though disconcerted by the unaccustomed directness of his mother's interrogations, submitted with a mixture of relief and apprehension, his spirit buoyed by the unexpected warmth of maternal solicitude. It was in this measure of intergenerational understanding that his pathway to discreet courtship would first be sanctioned, though hinting at future trials where both heart and honor might be weighed anew.

In the days that followed, as spring unfurled its gentle blossoms along the Boulevard St. Germain, Van Twiller took upon himself the task of preparing an offering worthy of the ineffable enchantment of Olympe. With resolute determination and the imperious refinement expected of his family name, he procured a bracelet of exquisite diamonds—a brilliant constellation of imperishable fire set in a circlet of purest silver. This token, an emblem of his newfound admiration, was to be presented with the slightest whisper of confession, thereby preserving the delicate equilibrium between his secret passion and his publicly esteemed pedigree.

Upon that fateful soirée, in the gilded recesses of a modest salon attended by glittering society, fate conspired to orchestrate a meeting marked by both euphoric uncertainty and the austere decorum of polite convention. Mademoiselle Olympe, arrayed in the resplendent simplicity of a dress that spoke of an understated opulence, listened with attentive grace as Van Twiller—his voice tempered by the soft cadence of his heartfelt declarations—unveiled the modest yet significant gift. It was a moment ensconced in a quiet resplendence, wherein the ardor of his concealed passion met the indifference of a stage-bound vocation.

Thus, amidst the lingering echoes of music and laughter and the transient magic of an evening suspended between the realm of dreams and the rigors of duty, Van Twiller’s delicate enterprise found its fortuitous beginning. In that ephemeral juncture, both the earnest vulnerability of his affections and the immutable demands of a storied heritage were harmonized, as though by some invisible arbiter of destiny, to set forth on a journey steeped equally in the sublime beauty of the heart and in the immutable solemnity of societal convention.

We're science fiction and fantasy fans, and our media nowadays tends to be made by geeky guys who grew up watching Star Trek and Doctor Who, and all of whom secretly want their own lightsabers. Some of them are really, really good at creating, writing, and developing female characters. Some aren't. In general, when they write female characters as actual people, given actual development and interests and goals and opinions and lives, we say, "Frak, yeah, she's awesome!" And still, the writers are mostly guys, and while the guys are peripherally aware of rape and battery and pay disparity and the Mommy Wars and all the other things that inform the day-to-day lives of women, they don't have to live them and they don't have to think about them unless they want to. While they may even have been personally touched by sexual violence, they haven't, for example, spent years talking with friends about what happened when they were drunk or drugged or otherwise coerced into sex, and they can, but usually don't, bring that background onto the page and into the characters. Traumatic, life-changing experiences become jokes, and the ages-old "Well, she deserved it for wearing that outfit / being out alone at night / believing him" is at best addressed in a metaphor with vampires but more typically doesn't even make the cut in character motivatons except in shoehorned revelatory backstories about childhood abuse. There isn't the understanding that fear of rape is present, in whatever small doses and buried under however much denial, in every woman's daily life from the day she's old enough to know what it is. It informs clothing choices and activities and dating partners, and while those writers capture the form of it, very few grok that the fear extends towards the male heroes too. So we see a fantasy world that resembles ours, but with off-kilter differences, and sometimes that's a good thing – Dr. Merlin watches cartoons preferentially because sometimes a Y-7 safety zone is the best thing to maintaining one's sanity – and sometimes it's a reminder that, to half the population, we are often as exotic and incomprehensible as Moon maidens.

That doesn't mean men can't write female characters. That doesn't mean men shouldn't write female characters. It means that any given male writer is, from time to time, going to screw up writing about women, that he's going to get called on it, especially from female fans who have seen these same damned problems before, and that he's going to have to decide whether to get defensive or fix the problem for next time. It means he's going to have to stand back and see the world from the point of view of someone raised female in a culture that celebrates masculinity and denigrates things associated with femininity (while fetishizing particular body parts, as if those are not part of the whole).

CNN has announced the indefinite suspension of prime-time anchor Chris Cuomo, pending further review, following revelations about his inappropriate cooperation with aides to his brother, former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo.

In light of these developments, "Anderson Cooper 360" extended to fill Cuomo's time slot on Tuesday evening, with a Covid-19 town hall scheduled for Wednesday.

The suspension, a significant event in cable news, comes amid heightened scrutiny of Cuomo's actions. Despite his high-profile status at CNN and his determination to remain on air amidst his brother's sexual misconduct scandal—which ultimately led to the governor's resignation—new evidence suggested Chris Cuomo played a more significant role in crafting his brother's defense than previously admitted.

CNN issued a statement highlighting that the newly publicized documents from the New York Attorney General's office revealed Chris Cuomo's deeper involvement, noting that although he previously acknowledged providing advice, the extent of his engagement was not fully known to the network until now.

Chris Cuomo responded to his suspension on his SiriusXM show, expressing his embarrassment and commitment to respecting the review process of his conduct while emphasizing his intention to never compromise his colleagues.

The decision has stirred reactions, with some CNN staffers dismayed by Cuomo's actions and critics like Charlotte Bennett, a former aide to Andrew Cuomo and accuser of sexual harassment, calling for his firing for failing to uphold journalistic standards.

The sudden suspension caught both Cuomo's and Cooper's teams off guard, with emotional discussions occurring among Cuomo's staff post-announcement. Viewer responses have been mixed, with some disappointed by his absence.

As CNN contemplates the future of Cuomo's time slot, the controversy underscores the broader implications of the released documents by Attorney General Letitia James, including text messages and interview transcripts that probe deeper into the allegations against Andrew Cuomo.

"Then, in your opinion, Killian," the young man Fritz interjected, his youthful face alight with fervor, "it is just this quality—this industrious spirit of the Grünewalders—that has made them so revered outside their borders?"

"Indeed, young sir," replied Killian, with the hint of a smile which might have suggested pride in his own kind. "The folk of Grünewald possess a vigor that is much to be admired; every tree felled in the mighty pine forests, every parcel of land tilled with care, speaks to their unyielding commitment to toil. Contrast that with the languid pace of Gerolstein, and one cannot help but envy the relentless spirit of the principality."

"Is it envy, or perhaps more a begrudging respect?" asked Otto, concealing a smile behind his raised glass. He had taken note of the glint of admiration flickering in Fritz’s eyes as he glanced toward the rocky spires that crowned the distant horizons. "For if admiration be the guise of envy, then you may brother with the very trees you flatter."

Fritz looked quizzically at Otto, who took care to conceal a sympathetic chuckle. It was the way of princes to employ wit as an obfuscation, a truth that Otto knew all too well. "Nay," added Fritz, recovering himself, "I confess I am but a simple observer of the fruits borne of good labor, and as such, holds no ill towards those who spend their days in ease. Yet, is it not a weakness of princes to disassociate themselves from such noble endeavors?"

Killian nodded gravely, the shadows of the tavern lending him a somber air. "You may speak truthfully, young man. It is common opinion—the princely life is perceived as one devoted to idle pursuits, while their subjects labor in the fields. But allow me to declare, it is a grievous misjudgment when one considers the weight of a crown upon a brow, how heavy that is to bear."

Otto, for his part, leaned forward ever so slightly, coaxed by curiosity as much as by the keen words of the men with whom he presently mingled. "Indeed, Killian, however burdensome that crown might rest, it is oft times those who see it shining gold upon the head of a prince who know not of the trials hidden from the light of day."

"In truth," said Killian, eyeing him closely, "do you not feel that princes might benefit from casting off their adornments upon occasion? Might they not tread among their people, incognito, and partake in simple joys—the laughter of children or the vitality of unchained women working the harvest?"

Otto allowed himself a moment of pensive silence; it was an alluring notion, one of which he had often dreamed amidst the confines of courtly obligation. "Yet consider this, my friends: if a life so simple could promise pleasure untainted by ambition, would not a prince’s absence from the court sow seeds of discontent? For what becomes of a principality when its leader is lost among shadows?"

"I maintain," Fritz insisted, furrowing his brow, "that the pulse of a principality cannot merely dwell in the hearts of its royal figures but must echo within the souls of its common folk. The leader must rise amongst them, not soar above them."

This sentiment was met with a flicker of tension, for the words held weight, like a stone cast into still waters. Killian, a man steeped in the pragmatic principles of life outside the privilege of titles, regarded his young companion thoughtfully. "It is true, Prince Otto, you may find solace in innocent amusements amidst the company of men such as us. But what if I told you that your very essence could light the darkened corners of Grünewald? That an understanding borne of shared responsibility would make for a happier crown?"

"You speak ill," Otto replied firmly, masking his intrigue beneath a veil of jest. "I ask you how far, dear Killian, before the very ground beneath us turns into marsh and mire if a crown takes to wandering without weighty purpose?"

Fritz glanced from one to the other, perceiving the delicate balance they navigated—a dissection of authority and existence, of command and empathy. “What say you to this,” he ventured, “perhaps experience educates both prince and peasant alike? In truth, they exist in a shared tapestry, and their separation only serves to fray the edges.”

As the light flickered from an overhead lamp, casting dancing shadows upon the rough wooden walls, Otto slowly sipped from his glass, the weight of their discourse heavy in the air. "Let us hope, dear friends, that we might weave these threads into something that binds us all, lest they lie frayed and broken in the dust.”

Forty men, their faces etched with the endurance of yesterday's labors, were summoned before dawn to transform the nascent road into a thoroughfare worthy of the advancing army's demands. The morning sun cast a golden hue upon the hillside, illuminating the dedicated craft of their endeavor. The sergeant, a seasoned veteran with eyes that held the tales of countless marches, paced amongst them, his boots clicking against the uneven earth.

A volunteer officer, a figure more accustomed to the pens of strategy than the grime of construction, shadowed the sergeant's steps. His queries, though often irrelevant, served to lighten the mood, and laughter occasionally broke the silence as tools clashed against the rocky soil. Colonel Osborne's age exceeded her father's by about a month, and as he was now past fifty, he might be considered perhaps, in that respect, to be a safe friend for a young married woman. But he was in every respect a man very different from Sir Marmaduke. Sir Marmaduke, blessed and at the same time burdened as he was with a wife and eight daughters, and condemned as he had been to pass a large portion of his life within the tropics, had become at fifty what many people call quite a middle-aged man. That is to say, he was one from whom the effervescence and elasticity and salt of youth had altogether passed away. He was fat and slow, thinking much of his wife and eight daughters, thinking much also of his dinner. Now Colonel Osborne was a bachelor, with no burdens but those imposed upon him by his position as a member of Parliament,--a man of fortune to whom the world had been very easy. It was not therefore said so decidedly of him as of Sir Marmaduke, that he was a middle-aged man, although he had probably already lived more than two-thirds of his life. And he was a good-looking man of his age, bald indeed at the top of his head, and with a considerable sprinkling of grey hair through his bushy beard; but upright in his carriage, active, and quick in his step, who dressed well, and was clearly determined to make the most he could of what remained to him of the advantages of youth. He always rode a pretty horse, and mounted his groom on one at any rate as pretty. He was known to have an excellent stud down in the shires, and had the reputation of going well with hounds. Poor Sir Marmaduke could not have ridden a hunt to save either his government or his credit. When, therefore, Mrs. Trevelyan declared to her sister that Colonel Osborne was a man whom she was entitled to regard with semi-parental feelings of veneration because he was older than her father, she made a comparison which was more true in the letter than in the spirit. Colonel Osborne had indeed known her when she was a baby, and had in old days been the very intimate friend of her father; but of herself he had seen little or nothing since those baby days, till he had met her just as she was about to become Mrs. Trevelyan; and though it was natural that so old a friend should come to her and congratulate her and renew his friendship, nevertheless it was not true that he made his appearance in her husband's house in the guise of the useful old family friend, who gives silver cups to the children and kisses the little girls for the sake of the old affection which he has borne for the parents. We all know the appearance of that old gentleman, how pleasant and dear a fellow he is, how welcome is his face within the gate, how free he makes with our wine, generally abusing it, how he tells our eldest daughter to light his candle for him, how he gave silver cups when the girls were born, and now bestows tea-services as they get married,--a most useful, safe, and charming fellow, not a year younger-looking or more nimble than ourselves, without whom life would be very blank. We all know that man; but such a man was not Colonel Osborne in the house of Mr. Trevelyan's young bride.

The winter is a hard season for the poor. It multiplies their necessities, while, in general, it limits their means and opportunities of earning. The winter of 1836-37 was far from being an exception to this rule. It was worse than usual, on account of the general stagnation of business.

There was another member of the household who would be highly offended if she were not introduced, in due form, to the reader. This was Miss Rachel Crump, maiden sister of Uncle Tim, as he was usually designated.

Miss Rachel was not much like her brother, for while the latter was a good-hearted, cheerful easy man, who was inclined to view the world in its sunniest aspect, Rachel was cynical, and given to misanthropy. Yes; it must be said--Rachel Crump was an old maid; not from choice, but hard necessity. Being unblessed with earthly means, she had accepted the hearty invitation of her brother, and become an inmate of his family, where she paid her board by little services about the house, and obtained sufficient needle-work to replenish her wardrobe as often as there was occasion.
