Armorer's Negligence, Cost-Cutting Measures Led to Fatal Shooting on 'Rust' Set

On the set of Alec Baldwin's film "Rust," 24-year-old armorer Hannah Gutierrez-Reed's carelessness with guns had been a concern prior to the fatal shooting that killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins and injured director Joel Souza. Gutierrez-Reed served as the head armorer on the set where Baldwin discharged a prop gun, resulting in the tragic accident.

Hannah Gutierrez-Reed, in a podcast interview earlier this year, admitted to feeling overwhelmed with her responsibilities on the set of "The Old Way," her first film as head armorer. "I was really nervous about it at first, and I almost didn't take the job because I wasn't sure if I was ready," Gutierrez-Reed said in the "Voices of the West" podcast.

Production sources on the set of "Rust" have cited the accident as a result of overall failings, including budget and safety measures. At least two prior incidents of accidental gun discharges occurred on the "Rust" set before the fatal shooting. Assistant director Dave Halls, who declared the gun "cold" before handing it to Baldwin, is now deemed partially responsible for not adequately checking the weapon. Halls previously had a gun mishandling incident on the set of "Fargo" in 2019.

Mamie Mitchell, the script supervisor on the "Rust" set, described the shooting as "negligent homicide." She revealed that there were complaints about safety practices and previous gun misfires made to the production team. "There were no safety meetings. There was no assurance that it wouldn't happen again. All they wanted to do was rush, rush, rush," Mitchell said.

Richard Howell, a film armorer with Foxtrot Productions, emphasized the armorer's responsibility for weapons safety on set. "The armorer is the last line of defense. They're the one that's responsible for making sure that the weapon is safe, that it's not loaded with live rounds," Howell explained.

The production company behind "Rust" is being criticized for cost-cutting measures that compromised safety on set. Gutierrez-Reed is described as inexperienced, with "Rust" being one of her first jobs as head armorer. Reportedly, she only had half a day of safety training prior to the start of filming.

Safety protocols dictate that the armorer should be present when a firearm is loaded or discharged, yet Gutierrez-Reed was not on set when the fatal shooting occurred. The prop gun that killed Hutchins and injured Souza was left unattended and unsecured on a cart.

A search warrant executed by the Santa Fe County Sheriff's Office revealed that Gutierrez-Reed had laid out three prop guns on a cart outside the set location. Halls grabbed the gun from the cart and brought it inside to Baldwin, bypassing Gutierrez-Reed.

As the investigation into the fatal shooting on the "Rust" set continues, concerns about safety protocols and the responsibility of the armorer and assistant director have come to light. The tragic incident underscores the importance of adhering to strict safety guidelines when working with firearms on film sets.

In a recent column, I explored the idea of renaming the Super Bowl MVP Trophy after Tom Brady, given his unparalleled success in the NFL, including winning the accolade five times. The question was paired with an informal survey to gather opinions.

Currently, the trophy bears the name of the late NFL commissioner Pete Rozelle, a figure instrumental in shaping the NFL and the Super Bowl as we know them. However, the thought of renaming the trophy after a player, particularly one of Brady's caliber, piqued my curiosity. After all, the Super Bowl Trophy itself is named in honor of Vince Lombardi, a coach. Expanding this tradition to players, especially for the Super Bowl MVP Trophy, seemed a fitting gesture to some.

Responses to this idea varied, with some backing the proposal enthusiastically. For example, Tom from Ohio humorously pointed out the mismatch in honoring a commissioner rather than a player with a Most Valuable Player award. Similarly, Derrick from Virginia suggested repurposing the Rozelle Trophy to honor the year's top coach, general manager, or franchise, preserving Rozelle's legacy in a different form.

Yet, there were staunch defenders of Rozelle's name remaining on the MVP trophy, citing various reasons. Among them, Jim from Massachusetts argued that renaming the trophy would be disrespectful to Rozelle. He also brought up past controversies surrounding Brady, including the infamous Deflategate scandal, arguing that such blemishes should disqualify Brady from this honor. While the debate around Deflategate continues, it was a common theme among opponents of the name change.

Supporters of renaming the trophy to honor Brady often simply referred to him as the "GOAT" (Greatest of All Time), a testament to his unparalleled achievements on the field. Yet, some, like Rich from Venice, Florida, suggested waiting until Brady retires and a grace period passes before making such a change, to ensure a respectful distance from his active career.

Others, like Chris from North Carolina, believed any consideration of renaming the trophy should wait until Brady is inducted into the Hall of Fame, emphasizing the importance of honoring the game's history before making such significant changes.

Among the dissenting voices, Matt from Indiana highlighted that football is a team sport and that Brady, despite being one of the greatest quarterbacks ever, didn't win Super Bowls alone. This sentiment reflects the complexity of individual awards in a team-centric sport.

In sum, the proposal to rename the Super Bowl MVP Trophy after Tom Brady sparked a diverse range of opinions, underscoring the deep respect for NFL history and the challenges of balancing individual achievement with legacy and tradition.

Just at this moment, when my bewilderment was fast verging on exasperation, relief came. The circle opened, and a little elderly man, who had evidently come in haste, confronted me, and, bowing very politely, addressed me in English. His voice was the most pitiable abortion of a voice I had ever heard. While having all the defects in articulation of a child's who is just beginning to talk, it was not even a child's in strength of tone, being in fact a mere alternation of squeaks and whispers inaudible a rod away. With some difficulty I was, however, able to follow him pretty nearly.

"As the official interpreter," he said, "I extend you a cordial welcome to these islands. I was sent for as soon as you were discovered, but being at some distance, I was unable to arrive until this moment. I regret this, as my presence would have saved you embarrassment. My countrymen desire me to intercede with you to pardon the wholly involuntary and uncontrollable mirth provoked by your attempts to communicate with them. You see, they understood you perfectly well, but could not answer you."

"Merciful heavens!" I exclaimed, horrified to find my surmise correct; "can it be that they are all thus afflicted? Is it possible that you are the only man among them who has the power of speech?"

Again it appeared that, quite unintentionally, I had said something excruciatingly funny; for at my speech there arose a sound of gentle laughter from the group, now augmented to quite an assemblage, which drowned the plashing of the waves on the beach at our feet. Even the interpreter smiled.

"Do they think it so amusing to be dumb?" I asked.

"They find it very amusing," replied the interpreter, "that their inability to speak should be regarded by any one as an affliction; for it is by the voluntary disuse of the organs of articulation that they have lost the power of speech, and, as a consequence, the ability even to understand speech."

"But," said I, somewhat puzzled by this statement, "did n't you just tell me that they understood me, though they could not reply, and are they not laughing now at what I just said?"

"It is you they understood, not your words," answered the interpreter. "Our speech now is gibberish to them, as unintelligible in itself as the growling of animals; but they know what we are saying, because they know our thoughts. You must know that these are the islands of the mind-readers."

Such were the circumstances of my introduction to this extraordinary people. The official interpreter being charged by virtue of his office with the first entertainment of shipwrecked members of the talking nations, I became his guest, and passed a number of days under his roof before going out to any considerable extent among the people. My first impression had been the somewhat oppressive one that the power to read the thoughts of others could be possessed only by beings of a superior order to man. It was the first effort of the interpreter to disabuse me of this notion. It appeared from his account that the experience of the mind-readers was a case simply of a slight acceleration, from special causes, of the course of universal human evolution, which in time was destined to lead to the disuse of speech and the substitution of direct mental vision on the part of all races. This rapid evolution of these islanders was accounted for by their peculiar origin and circumstances.

Some three centuries before Christ, one of the Parthian kings of Persia, of the dynasty of the Arsacid, undertook a persecution of the soothsayers and magicians in his realms. These people were credited with supernatural powers by popular prejudice, but in fact were merely persons of special gifts in the way of hypnotizing, mind-reading, thought transference, and such arts, which they exercised for their own gain.

As Densil descended the highlands into the verdant vale where Ravenshoe lay, his heart swelled with a mix of nostalgia and trepidation. The scant fortnight in the Eternal City had imprinted itself upon his spirit, much like the intricate patterns of a Roman mosaic entailing fragments of faith and doubt. The sun painted the countryside in hues of amber and gold, casting long shadows that danced with the promise of days forgone.

The villagers, unaware of Densil's metamorphosis, thronged the village square, their laughter and chatter echoing through the chattering breeze. Amongst them, Father Clifford stood, his visage a tableau of surprise and guarded expectation. The sight of his old friend was not devoid of warmth, yet there lingered an unspoken query, like the shadow of a cloud obscuring the morning sun.

Densil's companion, a young woman whose ethereal beauty captivated even the indifferent, looped her arm through his. Her presence was a testament to the whirlwind journey that had carried them from the heart of Rome, a testament that would spark curiosity and whispers within the close-knit community. As they approached, the villagers parted like the Red Sea before Moses, onlookers eager to decipher the enigma that Densil had become.

The dogs, once loyal guardians of Ravenshoe, now barked with a mixture of bewilderment and joy, their tales of Densil's return already woven into the tapestry of village lore. His falcon, too, perched upon the falconer's wrist, her eyes inquisitive, recalling the days when she was Densil's confidante and companion through the vast skies.

Amidst this tableau, the old priest greeted Densil with an outstretched arm, his smile genuine and tinged with the wisdom of centuries passed. The warmth of his welcome, however, carried with it a subtle undertone of intrigue, as the village fathers' eyes flickered between the unconventional couple.

"Welcome home, Densil," Father Clifford began, his voice rich with the vibrations of time and the assurance of faith. "We have heard tales of Rome's grandeur, yet none could have prepared us for this sight." His gaze, both admiring and filled with unspoken questions, seemed to seek clarity in the unexpected chapter that had unfolded before him. "May God bless this union and guide you both on the path ahead."

Densil, with a nod of gratitude, addressed the crowd, his voice steady and resonant. "This is Isabella, my dear Isabella. She is not of our faith, yet she has embraced the spirit of Ravenshoe with open arms. Together, we return, not as conquerors, but as seekers of a common ground between our beliefs."

As the village folk absorbed this revelation, the air hummed with a mixture of awe and apprehension. For in the quiet town of Ravenshoe, where traditions ran deep and where the echo of history lingered in every cobblestone, a new chapter was about to unfold—one that would intertwine the threads of devotion, doubt, and destiny.

Fortunately for the tranquillity of Mrs. Peters, the landlady of the lodgings, on being questioned, gave it as her opinion that the chapel at the Hot Wells, which was within a very pleasant walk, would be more likely to offer accommodation to strangers than the parish church, that being always crowded by the resident families; so to the chapel at the Hot Wells Mrs. Barnaby resolved to go, and the tea-urn was ordered half an hour earlier than usual, that time enough might be allowed to "get ready."

"Now do make the best of yourself, Agnes, to-day, will you? I am sure those men are not Bristol people.... So different they looked--didn't they?--from all the rest. Of course, you will put on your best crape bonnet, and one of my nicest broad-hemmed white crape collars ... there is one I have quite clean ... I have no doubt in the world we shall see them."

Having finished her breakfast, and reiterated these orders, Mrs. Barnaby turned her attention to her own toilet, and a most elaborate one it was, taking so long a time as to leave scarcely sufficient for the walk; but proving at length so perfectly satisfactory as to make her indifferent to that, or almost any other contretems.

On this occasion she came forth in a new dress of light grey gros-de-Naples, with a gay bonnet of paille de riz, decorated with poppy blossoms both within and without, a "lady-like" profusion of her own embroidery on cuffs, collar, and pocket-handkerchief, her well-oiled ringlets half hiding her large, coarse, handsome face, her eyes set off by a suffusion of carmine, and her whole person redolent of musk.

This was the figure beside which Agnes was doomed to make her first appearance at the crowded chapel of the Hot Wells. Had she thought about herself, the contrast its expansive splendour offered to her own slight figure, her delicate fair face seen but by stealth through her thick veil, and the sad decorum of her sable robe, might have struck her as being favourable; instead of that, however, it was another contrast that occurred to her; for, as she looked at Mrs. Barnaby, she suddenly recollected the general look and air of her aunt Compton, just at the moment when the widow attacked her so violently on the meanness of her apparel during their terrible encounter at the village school, and she could not quite restrain a sigh as she thought how greatly she should have preferred entering a crowded and fashionable chapel with her.

But no sighing could effect the change, and they set forth together, as strangely a matched pair in appearance as can well be imagined. They entered the crowded building just as the Psalms concluded, and were stared at and scrutinised with quite as much attention as was consistent with the solemnity of the place: moreover, seats were after some time offered to them, and there was no reason in the world to believe that they were in any way overlooked. Nevertheless Mrs. Barnaby was disappointed. Neither the tall gentleman nor his companion were there; nor did Major Allen, or any one like him, appear to reward her labour and her skill.

Long and wearisome did the steep up-hill walk back to her lodgings appear after this unpropitious act of devotion, and sadly passed the remainder of the day, for it rained hard ... no strollers, not even an idle endimanché, came to awaken the musical echo she loved to listen to from the pavement under the windows. In short, it was a day of existence lost, save that she found out one or two new defects in Agnes, and ended at last by very nearly convincing herself that it was in some way or other her fault that it rained.

The study was dimly lit, the heavy drapes drawn against the fading afternoon light. Soames Forsyte sat at his desk, the scent of cigar smoke lingering in the air. His eyes, sharp and piercing, rested on a letter lying before him, its contents weighing heavily on his mind. The parchment was creased, the ink smudged, as though the very paper bore the marks of the turmoil within him. His fingers drummed absently on the desk, a restless rhythm that seemed to echo the turmoil of his thoughts.

The letter was from his brother, Jolyon, a missive that had arrived earlier that day. Soames had read it twice, each time his face darkening as though the words themselves carried a tangible weight. The news within had shaken him, a revelation that chipped away at the carefully constructed edifice of his pride. Jolyon had written of his latest acquisition, a property in Montpellier Square, a neighborhood that was rapidly becoming a hub of the city’s elite. The timing, Soames thought acidly, could scarcely have been more inconvenient.

He had always prided himself on his acumen in matters of real estate, a skill honed from years of dealing in property and investments. The Forsyte name was synonymous with land and wealth, a legacy that had been Built, stone by stone, by their father, Superior Dosset Forsyte, a man who had risen from humble beginnings as a stonemason to become a master builder, leaving behind a fortune that had only grown with each generation. Soames had inherited a mind as sharp as his father’s, and a nose for profit that was equally keen. But now, as he read Jolyon’s missive, he couldn’t shake the feeling that the ground beneath him was shifting, that the very foundations of their family’s success were being called into question.

The sound of footsteps echoed outside the door, a reminder that he was not alone. Soames pushed the letter aside, his face hardening into the mask of calm that he had long since mastered. The door creaked open, and his wife, Irene, entered, her presence a storm in itself. Her eyes, sharp and gimlet-like, immediately locked onto the letter, her curiosity piqued.

“Who is it from?” she demanded, her voice laced with an impatient edge that Soames had long since learned to ignore.

“Jolyon,” he replied, his tone measured, “he’s made another purchase.”

Irene’s eyes narrowed, her mind already racing. “Another one?” she scoffed, her lips curling into a disdainful smile. “Does the man never learn? First it was that ridiculous estate in Dorsetshire, now this. What on earth does he think he’s doing?”

Soames said nothing, his silence a deliberate rebuke. He knew well enough that Irene’s opinions on Jolyon’s investments were coloured by her own pride, a pride that mirrored his own. The Forsyte name, she believed, was above such ventures, above the sort of risks that Jolyon seemed so eager to take. But Soames, though he would never admit it to her, knew that the world was changing, and with it, the rules of the game.

The conversation turned, as such things inevitably did, to the family’s ancestral home in Dorsetshire, a place that Irene had always regarded with a mixture of disdain and envy. The house, she claimed, was a relic of a bygone age, a reminder of their grandfather’s modest beginnings. But to Soames, it was a symbol of their strength, a testament to the hard work and determination that had elevated the Forsythe name to its current prominence.

The discussion was interrupted by the arrival of their brother, James, his face flushed from the exertions of a long walk. His entrance was abrupt, as it always was, the door banging open with a force that made Irene glance up in annoyance. James, ever the outsider in their family, seemed to carry an air of discomfort with him, as though the very walls of the house were too tight, too constricting for his restless spirit.

“Well?” Irene demanded, her tone sharp. “What brings you here so unexpectedly?”

James hesitated, his eyes darting between his brother and sister-in-law. “I wanted to speak with Soames,” he said finally, his voice betraying a nervousness that was unusual for him. “About the land in Montpellier Square.”

Soames inclined his head, his curiosity piqued. “And what of it?”

James ran a hand through his thick, dark hair, his eyes flickering with a mix of unease and determination. “I’ve been thinking,” he began, his voice low, “that perhaps we should consider investing in that area. The potential, Soames, it’s there. I can see it.”

Soames’s lips tightened into a thin line, his mind racing. James’s suggestion was unexpected, and not entirely unwelcome. The land in Montpellier Square was indeed prime, a location that would doubtless bring in a hefty profit. But to invest in it now, to align themselves with Jolyon’s decision, was risky, a move that could set a dangerous precedent. The Forsyte name, he reminded himself sternly, was built on stability, on a reputation for caution and prudence. To throw caution to the wind now, to follow in Jolyon’s footsteps, was to risk all that they had worked so hard to build.

Irene, however, was less inclined to hesitation. “It’s madness,” she declared, her voice sharp. “A fool’s errand. The man has no sense, no understanding of what it means to preserve the family’s good name.”

Soames said nothing, his mind a whirlwind of conflicting thoughts. On one hand, he recognised the potential of Jolyon’s investment, the lucrative opportunities that such a location offered. On the other, he was acutely aware of the risks, the danger of aligning themselves too closely with a venture that, if it failed, could tarnish their name beyond repair. The tension in the room was palpable, the air thick with unspoken words and latent conflict.

James, sensing the storm that was brewing, shifted uncomfortably in his seat. “I only meant to suggest,” he said, his voice faltering, “that we consider the possibilities. It’s not every day that such an opportunity comes along.”

Soames’s gaze locked onto his brother, his eyes narrowing as he assessed the younger man’s motives. There was a fire in James’s eyes, a determination that was both admirable and unsettling. It reminded Soames of the younger, more impulsive version of himself, the version that had long since been tamed by the responsibilities of wealth and status.

The discussion continued, each brother and sister weighing in with their opinions, their voices rising and falling in a cacophony of conflicting perspectives. Through it all, Soames remained silent, his mind a whirlwind of thoughts, his pride warring with his pragmatism. The weight of the family’s legacy pressed down on him, a burden that he had long since accepted, but one that now felt heavier than ever.

As the evening drew to a close, and the discussion finally began to wind down, Soames found himself alone once more, the silence of the study wrapping around him like a shroud. The letter from Jolyon lay before him, its contents a constant reminder of the choices that lay ahead. The decision he was faced with was not merely a financial one, he realised; it was a decision that would shape the future of the Forsyte name, a name that had been built on a foundation of strength and resilience.

But as he sat there, the weight of his thoughts pressing heavily on his mind, Soames could not shake the feeling that the world was changing, that the rules that had governed their success were no longer sufficient. The Forsyte name, he mused, had always been a symbol of stability, of enduring power. But in a world that was rapidly evolving, stability could be a double-edged sword, a shield that could as easily become a prison.

And so, as the night wore on, Soames Forsyte sat in his study, the letter from his brother a visible reminder of the choices that lay ahead, and the weight of his family’s legacy pressing down on him with a force that was both familiar and terrifying. The future, he knew, was uncertain, but he was determined to face it with the same resilience and determination that had defined his forebears. For the Forsyte name, he thought sternly, was built to last, and he would see to it that it did.

Yet he knew at the bottom of his heart that he had already decided. It seemed to him as if he had been saved from a fatal exposure by the drift of circumstances. But for Sophy's violent temper she would either have been with him when his cousin met him at Innsbruck, or George would have pursued his journey to the Ampezzo valley, and found them there. Then it would have been impossible to conceal the truth--the hateful truth--any longer. That would have been utter ruin for them both. He could do nothing to maintain a wife or, indeed, himself, if his uncle disinherited him. So far he had never earned a six-pence in his life. If he acknowledged Sophy just now, it would only be to bring her to destitution; or to make himself dependent upon her exertions.

He went back to his hotel, and wrote a long letter to his young wife, carefully worded, lest it should fall into wrong hands. He told her to make her way as directly as possible to England to her father's house; and to let him know immediately of her return there. She could reach it by tolerably easy railway journeys in about a week; and he carefully traced out her route, entering the moment of departure for each train she must take, and telling her at what hotels she must stay. It was now a week since he had left her, and he had no doubt she was on her way after him. It seemed to him as though he was taking an almost tender care for her safety and comfort, more than she deserved; and thought she ought to be very grateful to him for it. He urged the utmost prudence upon her in regard to their secret.

He left this letter with the landlord of the Goldne Sonne, doing so with considerable caution, very well concealed. It was addressed to S. Martin only, and might have been either for a man or a woman. If no person claimed it, it was to be forwarded to him intact at the end of three months, when he would send a handsome acknowledgment for it. But it would probably be asked for in the course of a few days; for Sidney reminded himself, with self-gratulation, that at both of the hotels he had quitted lately he had left instructions for Sophy; with a careful description of her appearance, that no wrong person should receive them.

These steps set his conscience at rest; and he returned to England with no heavier burden on his spirits than the dread of discovery, which must be borne as long as he was absolutely dependent upon his uncle's favor.

A FORSAKEN CHILD.

Sophy finished her letter, the letter which was to be posted the next day. But before the morning came her child was born, and the young mother lay speechless and motionless, unconsciously floating down the silent sea of death. There was no one with her but Chiara, the working housekeeper of the inn; but there was no sign that the girl felt troubled or lonely. Chiara laid the baby across her chilling, heaving breast, and for a moment there flickered a smile about her pale lips, as she made a feeble effort to clasp her new-born babe in her arms. But these signs of life were gone in a moment like the passing of a fitful breeze; and her rough nurse, stooping down to look more closely at her white face, saw that the young foreigner was dead.

For some minutes Chiara stood gazing at the dead girl, and the living child on her bosom, without moving. She had dispatched a boy to fetch the nearest doctor, but he was gone to a patient some miles away, and it would be two or three hours before he could reach the inn. All the house and all the village were asleep, except the watchman in the bell-tower, who struck the deep-toned bell every quarter. It had not occurred to her to summon any helper; she had known what was coming, and had made all necessary preparations. But she had not counted on any risk to the life of the young mother; and this made all the difference in the world.

The poor, blubbering girl said, "Indeed, my lady, I wouldn't hurt a fly, much less a king, and I cannot abide the French, nor frogs neither, for that matter."

But my lady was inexorable, and took a girl who could neither read nor write, to make up for her alarm about the progress of education towards addition and subtraction; and afterwards, when the clergyman who was at Hanbury parish when I came there, had died, and the bishop had appointed another, and a younger man, in his stead, this was one of the points on which he and my lady did not agree. While good old deaf Mr. Mountford lived, it was my lady's custom, when indisposed for a sermon, to stand up at the door of her large square pew,--just opposite to the reading-desk,--and to say (at that part of the morning service where it is decreed that, in quires and places where they sing, here followeth the anthem): "Mr. Mountford, I will not trouble you for a discourse this morning." And we all knelt down to the Litany with great satisfaction; for Mr. Mountford, though he could not hear, had always his eyes open about this part of the service, for any of my lady's movements. But the new clergyman, Mr. Gray, was of a different stamp. He was very zealous in all his parish work; and my lady, who was just as good as she could be to the poor, was often crying him up as a godsend to the parish, and he never could send amiss to the Court when he wanted broth, or wine, or jelly, or sago for a sick person. But he needs must take up the new hobby of education; and I could see that this put my lady sadly about one Sunday, when she suspected, I know not how, that there was something to be said in his sermon about a Sunday-school which he was planning. She stood up, as she had not done since Mr. Mountford's death, two years and better before this time, and said--

"Mr. Gray, I will not trouble you for a discourse this morning."

But her voice was not well-assured and steady; and we knelt down with more of curiosity than satisfaction in our minds. Mr. Gray preached a very rousing sermon, on the necessity of establishing a Sabbath-school in the village. My lady shut her eyes, and seemed to go to sleep; but I don't believe she lost a word of it, though she said nothing about it that I heard until the next Saturday, when two of us, as was the custom, were riding out with her in her carriage, and we went to see a poor bedridden woman, who lived some miles away at the other end of the estate and of the parish: and as we came out of the cottage we met Mr. Gray walking up to it, in a great heat, and looking very tired. My lady beckoned him to her, and told him she should wait and take him home with her, adding that she wondered to see him there, so far from his home, for that it was beyond a Sabbath-day's journey, and, from what she had gathered from his sermon the last Sunday, he was all for Judaism against Christianity. He looked as if he did not understand what she meant; but the truth was that, besides the way in which he had spoken up for schools and schooling, he had kept calling Sunday the Sabbath: and, as her ladyship said, "The Sabbath is the Sabbath, and that's one thing--it is Saturday; and if I keep it, I'm a Jew, which I'm not. And Sunday is Sunday; and that's another thing; and if I keep it, I'm a Christian, which I humbly trust I am."

But when Mr. Gray got an inkling of her meaning in talking about a Sabbath-day's journey, he only took notice of a part of it: he smiled and bowed, and said no one knew better than her ladyship what were the duties that abrogated all inferior laws regarding the Sabbath; and that he must go in and read to old Betty Brown, so that he would not detain her ladyship.

American Rescue Plan Expands Stimulus Check Eligibility to Non-Citizens and Mixed-Status Families

Washington, D.C. - In a significant move to provide financial relief to millions of individuals and families, President Joe Biden signed the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 into law, initiating another round of stimulus checks. This time, the eligibility criteria have been expanded to include non-citizens who pay taxes as residents in the United States and hold a valid Social Security number.

Non-Citizen Eligibility: A Shift in Policy

The American Rescue Plan marks a departure from the previous stimulus package, the CARES Act, which excluded non-citizens from receiving stimulus payments. This time around, lawful permanent residents and qualifying resident aliens who file taxes using a Social Security number are eligible for the $1,400 stimulus check. However, undocumented immigrants and individuals filing taxes with an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) remain ineligible.

Mixed Immigration Status Families Included

In a notable change, the American Rescue Plan includes mixed immigration status families for stimulus checks. This means that even if one member of a family is undocumented, other eligible family members, such as U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, and qualifying resident aliens, can still receive the payment. This provision recognizes the economic hardships faced by many mixed-status families during the pandemic.

Who Qualifies as a Non-Citizen?

To be eligible for the stimulus payment as a non-citizen, individuals must meet the following criteria:

  • Lawful permanent residents (green card holders)
  • Qualifying resident aliens (individuals admitted to the U.S. for permanent residence under specific immigration categories)
  • DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) participants
  • TPS (Temporary Protected Status) individuals
  • H1-B visa holders with a valid Social Security number

Exclusions and Special Cases

Certain non-citizens are not eligible for the stimulus payment, including nonresident aliens, foreign government-related individuals, teachers/trainees, foreign students, and professional athletes. Additionally, U.S. citizens living abroad may be eligible for a stimulus check, provided they meet specific criteria and file their taxes using a Social Security number.

Payment Methods and Claiming Missed Checks

Eligible recipients abroad will receive their payments via direct deposit or paper check based on the information on file with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Individuals who didn't receive the first two stimulus checks can claim them through the Recovery Rebate Credit on their 2020 taxes.

Impact on Individuals and Families

The expanded eligibility for stimulus checks under the American Rescue Plan is expected to provide much-needed financial assistance to millions of non-citizens and mixed-status families who have been disproportionately affected by the economic fallout of the pandemic. This inclusive approach underscores the Biden administration's commitment to supporting all residents, regardless of their immigration status, during these challenging times.

“Is this a sneer, sir?” asked the Colonel, drawing himself up to his full height.

“No, no, it ain't; no, upon my soul, I 'm quite serious. I never was less disposed for a jest in my life.”

“You could never have selected a less opportune moment for one, sir,” rejoined the other, gravely. “Am I to conclude, sir,” resumed he, after a second's interval, “that we have no difference of opinion on this affair?”

“None whatever. I agree with you in everything you have s-said, and everything you in-intend to say.”

“Your friend will then apologize?” resumed the Colonel.

“He shall,--he must.”

“Simply expressing his regret that an unguarded action should have occasioned a misconception, and that in lifting his arm he neither intended the gesture as a menace nor an insult. Is n't that your meaning?”

“Just so; and that if he had struck he would n't have hurt him.”

“Feu d'enfer! sir, what are you saying? or do you mean this for a mockery of us?” screamed the Colonel, in a fit of passion.

“You terrify me so,” cried Purvis; “You are so impeimpe-impetuous, I don't know what I 'm saying.”

The Frenchman measured him with a glance of strange meaning. It was evident that such a character was somewhat new to him, and it required all his skill and acuteness to comprehend it “Very well, sir,” said he, at last, “I leave the details entirely to yourself; speak to your friend, arrange the matter between you, and let us finish the affair as speedily as may be.”

“What is all this delay about?” muttered Norwood, angrily, as the other joined him; “is there any difficulty in stepping twelve or twenty paces?”

“None; but we've hit upon a b-better plan, and you've only to say that you 're sorry for it all, that you did n't m-mean anything, and that you never did b-b-beat a Frenchman, nor will you ever do so in future.”

“Why, what do you mean?” asked Norwood, in astonishment.

“That we 'll all go back and lunch at the 'Luna;' for there's no-nothing to fight about.”

Norwood pushed by him contemptuously, and with hurried steps walked up to where the old Colonel stood. “You are a French officer, sir,” said he, “and I rely upon your honor that, whether from the ignorance or inaptitude of that gentleman, no blame may attach itself to me in this business. I have no apology to offer, nor any amende save one.”

“Very well, sir, we are ready,” said the Colonel. “I will ask one of my countrymen to act for you, for I see you are in very indifferent hands.”

And now, like men who were well accustomed to the task, they set about the details of the duel; while Purvis, being at full liberty, slipped from the spot, and retired into the wood.

“You 've won the first fire, my Lord,” said a young Frenchman to Norwood. “The conditions are twelve paces--back to back--to torn at the word, and fire.”

Norwood bowed, and, without speaking, followed the other to the spot where he was to stand. As he waited thus, pistol in hand, he was directly opposite to the place wherein Purvis had taken refuge, and who, seeing Norwood in front of him, with a cocked pistol, and his finger on the trigger, uttered a scream of terror, and fell flat on the ground. Before the rest could discover the cause of the outcry, a shout from outside of “The Police!” “The Gendarmes!” was heard, and Dr. Grounsell rushed into the garden, followed by several dismounted dragoons. In an instant all were away. Norwood sprang over a low balcony into a vineyard; while in various directions the others scampered off, leaving Purvis alone upon the field.

But too happy to have fallen into the safe keeping of the authorities, Purvis accepted his captivity with a most placid contentment.

“She ain't here now.”

Mr. Brice's face displayed his disappointment. But the true lover holds a talisman potent with old and young. Mrs. Tarbox felt a sneaking maternal pity for this suddenly stricken Strephon.

“She's gone home,” she added more gently--“went at sun-up this mornin'.”

“Home,” repeated Brice. “Where's that?”

Mrs. Tarbox looked at her husband and hesitated. Then she said--a little in her old manner--“Her uncle's.”

“Can you direct me the way there?” asked Brice simply.

The astonishment in their faces presently darkened into suspicion again. “Ef that's your little game,” began Hiram, with a lowering brow--

“I have no little game but to see her and speak with her,” said Brice boldly. “I am alone and unarmed, as you see,” he continued, pointing to his empty belt and small dispatch bag slung on his shoulder, “and certainly unable to do any one any harm. I am willing to take what risks there are. And as no one knows of my intention, nor of my coming here, whatever might happen to me, no one need know it. You would be safe from questioning.”

There was that hopeful determination in his manner that overrode their resigned doggedness. “Ef we knew how to direct you thar,” said the old woman cautiously, “ye'd be killed outer hand afore ye even set eyes on the girl. The house is in a holler with hills kept by spies; ye'd be a dead man as soon as ye crossed its boundary.”

“Wot do YOU know about it?” interrupted her husband quickly, in querulous warning. “Wot are ye talkin' about?”

“You leave me alone, Hiram! I ain't goin' to let that young feller get popped off without a show, or without knowin' jest wot he's got to tackle, nohow ye kin fix it! And can't ye see he's bound to go, whatever ye says?”

Mr. Tarbox saw this fact plainly in Brice's eyes, and hesitated.

“The most that I kin tell ye,” he said gloomily, “is the way the gal takes when she goes from here, but how far it is, or if it ain't a blind, I can't swar, for I hevn't bin thar myself, and Harry never comes here but on an off night, when the coach ain't runnin' and thar's no travel.” He stopped suddenly and uneasily, as if he had said too much.

“Thar ye go, Hiram, and ye talk of others gabblin'! So ye might as well tell the young feller how that thar ain't but one way, and that's the way Harry takes, too, when he comes yer oncet in an age to talk to his own flesh and blood, and see a Christian face that ain't agin him!”

Mr. Tarbox was silent. “Ye know whar the tree was thrown down on the road,” he said at last.

“Yes.”

“The mountain rises straight up on the right side of the road, all hazel brush and thorn--whar a goat couldn't climb.”

“Yes.”

“But that's a lie! for thar's a little trail, not a foot wide, runs up from the road for a mile, keepin' it in view all the while, but bein' hidden by the brush. Ye kin see everything from thar, and hear a teamster spit on the road.”

“Go on,” said Brice impatiently.

“Then it goes up and over the ridge, and down the other side into a little gulch until it comes to the canyon of the North Fork, where the stage road crosses over the bridge high up. The trail winds round the bank of the Fork and comes out on the LEFT side of the stage road about a thousand feet below it. That's the valley and hollow whar Harry lives, and that's the only way it can be found. For all along the LEFT of the stage road is a sheer pitch down that thousand feet, whar no one kin git up or down.”

“I understand,” said Brice, with sparkling eyes. “I'll find my way all right.”

“And when ye git thar, look out for yourself!” put in the woman earnestly. “Ye may have regular greenhorn's luck and pick up Flo afore ye cross the boundary, for she's that bold that when she gets lonesome o' stayin' thar she goes wanderin' out o' bounds.”

"I hear Lady Tyrrell is quite the formidable figure," remarked Cecil, her voice layered with curiosity as she settled into the drawing-room the next morning.

"Formidable, indeed! Yet most engaging, in her own elusive manner," replied Frank, reclining with the nonchalance cultivated from his years of acquaintance with the whims and follies of gentlemen and ladies alike.

"Engaging, if only one has the taste for such complex allure," countered Julius, a shadow of something ineffable flitting across his countenance—a shadow that had not yet settled to cloud his usually bright demeanour, but one which certainly demanded notice.

Frank observed his older brother with an arched brow, sensing that unspoken history prickled beneath the surface of Julius's usually stalwart reserve, but chose to nimbly sidestep the matter at this juncture. "I hear she governs Sirenwood like a captain on the prow of a stately ship—every servant drilled in routine, every account meticulously balanced."

"She found it requisite to become prudent," opined Rosamond, lightly. "The place was nearly in shambles; the family is dependent on her vigilance."

"A mistress of a estate rather than a heart," Cecil noted with a slight smile, her glance drifting over to Julius, who seemed absorbed in merely observing the interaction.

"Perhaps such practicality to some appears enchanting," he acquiesced, thoughtfully. His tone suggested a conclusion half-relinquished, as if borne from the tether of an old recollection alighting once more in his mind, fresh as any present conversation.

"Lady Tyrrell has had no lack of admirers, Julius," Rosamond teased, her eyes twinkling with the untrammeled merriment of expressing what all others had only dared ponder. "Would you not number amongst them?"

"There are those whom admiration finds easy targets," Julius returned. "But admiration merely gets fogged with rumour and embellished with fancy until the true form can no longer be discerned."

At that, Frank shook his head slightly, as though waving away a cocktail party of entangled irony and reminiscence, wishing not to steep the morn any deeper in contemplation of ambiguous heartstrings or past dalliances. "Regardless, she holds Sirenwood now, and with a surety more subtle than most would credit."

"And what of Sir Harry?" inquired Cecil, lending weight to her question with an earnestness that never failed to solicit truthful discourse. "Has he indeed retired from the reckoning table?"

"Retired? Sir, never quite the recluse, though he lounges more than decides these days; Lady Tyrrell manages all practicalities," Frank said. "I hear he spends hours in their antiquarian library, often forgetting even the wineglass clutched limp in his hand till late."

"Cecil, you said you were planning a visit to Sirenwood later this week, did you not?" Rosamond asked, looking to her sister-in-law with genuine interest.

"I did intend a call," Cecil affirmed, though her voice held an edge of uncertainty—whether from the prospect itself, or from the tenuous web of untold stories she sensed hanging delicately untended, she did not profess.

"I shall accompany you then," Julius offered, his sentence short with a prompt finality that left no room for refusal, bringing the assemblage a ripple of curious satisfaction.

"Capital!" exclaimed Rosamond, beaming at what promised surely to be a most diverting visit maintained beneath the breadth of their collective unspoken speculation.

"You must assess Lady Tyrrell for yourself, Cecil," Frank said, settling back into his armchair and folding his hands with an air of benevolent conspiracy. "I am confident you shall not find her wanting."

Cecil merely smiled, fixating instead on the window where trailing branches splayed a cast of sun and shadow upon the floorboards, as if writing a language all their own—one seldom comprehended unless lived.

And so it was that their morning, touched as it had been with hidden meanings and reluctant admissions, settled back into its customary discourse, the conversation leisurely, yet charged with the allure of what lay ahead beyond the shadows of Sirenwood's storied halls. The prospect that awaited them promised not only answers but perhaps further enigmas to weave into the fabric of life’s rich tapestry in the quaint yet complex world they inhabited.

"But, papa ... everybody ... everybody goes!"

"Let everybody go, then," said Van Oudijck, testily. "I don't care for everybody."

"Oh ... you are so tiresome!" cried Doddie, stamping her foot. "I want to go!"

"And I say you shan't go! ... without my permission!"

Doddie's lower lip trembled. Her eyes, wide and shining with unshed tears, darted from her father's stern face to Theo, who sat by the window, seemingly engrossed in a book. But Theo felt the weight of her gaze, felt the plea for support radiating from his stepsister.

"She only wants to go to the band, father," he ventured, hesitantly.

Van Oudijck turned his head sharply, his bushy eyebrows drawn together in a formidable frown.

"And since when have you become privy to her desires, may I ask?"

"Oh, papa!" Doddie's voice rose in a wail, tears now spilling down her cheeks. "You're so unfair! You let Theo do whatever he pleases!"

"That is quite enough, Doddie!" Van Oudijck's voice was sharp, brooking no further argument. He rose from his chair, his imposing figure seeming to fill the room. "You will remain here this evening. That is final."

He turned on his heel and strode out of the room, leaving a heavy silence in his wake. Doddie, her face buried in her hands, sobbed quietly. Theo, his own face pale, rose from his chair and approached his stepsister cautiously.

"Don't cry, Doddie," he said, awkwardly patting her shoulder. "Perhaps ... perhaps if you apologize to father ..."

Doddie shook her head miserably. "He wouldn't listen," she mumbled into her hands. "He never listens!"

Theo sighed. He knew, from bitter experience, that his father could be unyielding when his authority was challenged. And Doddie, despite her youthful exuberance, could be astonishingly stubborn. It was a recipe for conflict, one that played out with distressing regularity in the Van Oudijck household.

He glanced towards the door through which his father had disappeared. He knew that his stepmother, his father's only true confidante, was expected back from Batavia that afternoon. Perhaps, he thought, her gentle influence might soften his father's stance.

"Look, Doddie," he said, forcing a cheerful note into his voice, "why don't we go and meet mother at the station? We can bring her back here, and then ... well, perhaps we can all talk to father together."

Doddie lifted her tear-stained face. "Do you really think so, Theo?"

"It's worth a try," he said, offering her a tentative smile.

And so it was that the two of them, their earlier disagreement momentarily forgotten, set off towards the station, their steps lightened by a sliver of hope. The afternoon sun, casting long shadows across the manicured lawns of the Dutch quarter, seemed to hold a promise of reconciliation.

As they walked, Theo found himself reflecting on the complex dynamics of his family. His father, a man of strict principles and unwavering authority, seemed to hold a special tenderness for Doddie, his only daughter. Yet, his affection often manifested as overprotectiveness, stifling Doddie's youthful desire for independence.

Theo, on the other hand, had always felt a certain distance between himself and his father, a distance widened by his own rebellious streak and his father's disapproval of his artistic pursuits. Yet, he longed for his father's approval, for a sign that he was not a disappointment to the man who had raised him.

Perhaps, he thought, this evening, with his stepmother's return and Doddie's heartfelt plea, a bridge could be built across the chasm that separated them. Perhaps, tonight, they could find a way to be a family, not just a collection of individuals bound by blood and circumstance.

Surrogacy legislation and regulation are crucially necessary at this juncture in society as the social stigma surrounding surrogacy diminishes. In recent years, the perception of surrogacy has shifted from a taboo practice to an acceptable means of building families, reflecting broader changes in societal attitudes toward fertility and reproductive technologies. This evolving perspective presents an opportune moment for legal frameworks to emerge that promote clarity and protection for all parties involved—intended parents, surrogates, and children. By formalizing surrogacy regulation, states can effectively address concerns related to exploitation and clarify the terms of agreements. This is not a pursuit of 'baby-selling' or 'reproductive prostitution' but rather the facilitation of services that allow individuals to partake in their reproductive rights, reinforcing the notion that surrogacy is a legitimate and dignified means of creating families.

The American Bar Association's advocacy for model surrogacy legislation, akin to Illinois' Gestational Care Act, underscores the importance of establishing robust legal standards that not only protect the interests of surrogates and intended parents but also enhance the legal landscape surrounding surrogacy. With the modern family structure adapting to include diverse definitions of partnerships and parental roles, such legislation provides clarity regarding parental rights, especially in interstate situations where surrogacy agreements may be contested across state lines. Establishing federal oversight, potentially through the Department of Health and Human Services, is also necessary for interstate surrogacy practices, ensuring consistency in legal interpretations and safeguarding the rights of all parties, regardless of their state of residency. Furthermore, as international couples increasingly seek American surrogates, it is imperative that U.S. legislation accommodates these dynamics, fostering inclusive environments for diverse families while abiding by legal and ethical standards.

The recognition of surrogacy not only aligns with changing cultural norms but also signifies a challenge to the traditional definitions of marriage and family units. Historical legal precedents, particularly Griswold v. Connecticut and Skinner v. Oklahoma, illustrate the evolving nature of marital rights and reproductive choices, acknowledging the right to privacy and the fundamental liberty of individuals to make decisions regarding procreation. As societal constructs transform, a fair legal approach is essential to adapt to these changes in personal relationships and marriage rights, establishing support for individuals who utilize surrogacy within their family planning. Positive surrogacy legislation does not advocate for surrogacy as a universal solution but instead serves to delineate acceptable practices, ensuring ethical considerations and the protection of all individuals involved. By formalizing and regulating surrogacy, society establishes a framework that honors the diverse and evolving fabric of American family life, recognizing the value of individual choices and the right to create families according to one's means and desires.

Bolstering U.S. Defenses Against the Twin Threats of Cyber and Biological Warfare

The United States has long stood as a beacon of strength and resilience, navigating through myriad challenges with an unwavering spirit. However, recent events have starkly showcased the nation's vulnerabilities to sophisticated threats that span the cyber and biological domains. The Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack and the unprecedented global COVID-19 pandemic serve as potent reminders of these contemporary dangers.

Amidst rising geopolitical tensions, it is increasingly apparent that terrorist organizations and hostile nations, including Iran and Syria, are poised to exploit these vulnerabilities. Such adversaries are likely to orchestrate multifaceted attacks that could severely disrupt American life, highlighting an urgent need for comprehensive preparedness.

Compounding these concerns, Microsoft recently uncovered a new wave of cyberattacks by Nobelium, a Russian-based group, targeting essential U.S. organizations. This revelation underscores the persistent cyber threats emanating from state-sponsored actors aiming to compromise national security.

In a forthcoming report that demands our immediate attention, the Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense starkly warns that all U.S. critical infrastructure sectors are at grave risk of biological incidents. Alarmingly, the report finds that none of the 16 designated critical infrastructure sectors has developed sufficient plans to address such threats.

The COVID-19 pandemic has cruelly highlighted the fragility of these sectors, revealing a distressing lack of preparedness for biological dangers. This glaring deficiency underscores the need for a strategic overhaul to safeguard national assets against these insidious threats.

Echoing these concerns, Tom Ridge, the first U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security and a former Republican governor of Pennsylvania, emphasizes, "Our enemies understand that biological and cyber warfare can significantly disrupt American life." Ridge's insights accentuate the critical nature of these threats and the imperative to fortify defenses.

Similarly, Tom Daschle, former Democratic Senate Majority Leader, cautions, "The federal government and private sector’s current state of unpreparedness is unacceptable." Daschle's statement reflects a bipartisan consensus on the urgency of bolstering national readiness against these perils.

History has demonstrated the devastating economic impacts of biological threats, with the 2014 avian influenza outbreak and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic serving as harrowing examples. The estimated economic onslaught of COVID-19 alone on the U.S. economy is a staggering $16 trillion, an amount that underscores the catastrophic potential of such crises.

Given these stark realities, it is incumbent upon us to advocate for better planning and preparation to shield our critical infrastructure from both biological and cyber threats. This includes investing in robust cybersecurity measures, enhancing the capacity of healthcare systems, and developing comprehensive contingency plans to ensure continuity of operations during crises.

Efforts to fortify our defenses must involve close collaboration between the federal government and the private sector. Leveraging their respective strengths and resources, this partnership can pave the way for innovative solutions and resilient frameworks capable of withstanding future threats.

It is imperative to emphasize that the cost of inaction far outweighs the investment required for preparedness. As we navigate the complexities of the 21st century, the need for a proactive and comprehensive approach to safeguard against biological and cyber threats has never been more critical.

In conclusion, let us heed the lessons of recent history and take decisive steps to reinforce our national security infrastructure. By doing so, we can protect the American way of life against the evolving landscape of threats that seek to undermine our safety, prosperity, and well-being. The time to act is now; the future security and prosperity of our nation depend on it.

The steady trickle of the brook mingled with the rustling leaves, offering an accompaniment to the meditations of the woodland. Mr. Arnold set about arranging his lunch with a measure of deliberation, though the browned crusts laid upon the old handkerchief did often threaten his composure. Miss Newell watched him with a wry smile pulling at the corner of her lips.

"Do let me assure you, my splendors are precise in their humble offerings," he remarked, elaborately.

She gave a gentle laugh, "I find myself concealed in doubt whether hunger will usurp sensibility."

Arnold addressed the afternoon with a light shrug. "Mrs. Bondy's talents for culinary irony remain unparalleled," he said, showing the remnants of sponge cake with exaggerated flourish. "Behold the artistry wherein she transforms flour and sugar into wistfulness."

Miss Newell, deeply endeared, lowered her gaze, a soft sigh attending. "Her aspirations, however noble, do not always mirror her achievements."

Arnold regarded her with a playful seriousness. "Fear not, my constitution remains unshaken by this confectionery conundrum."

"What a boon for those with valiant digestion," she countered, "though it is but trifling amusement for your resolve."

Whimsical ease settled over them, a certain brightness found in shared merriment. Miss Newell absently gathered a twig, tracing idle patterns into the soft earth. "Should you require assistance in the matters of culinary survival, summon me; I may attempt a better fate with the means given."

"An alliance formed in the fires of desperation," Arnold returned, a look of mirth in his eyes. "But for now, let destiny unfold in this dance of individual repast."

With another gurgle, the brook enticed the murmur of their steady dialogue. Arnold, having consumed enough to stave off immediate deprivation, leaned back upon his elbows and closed his eyes momentarily as the breeze stirred gentle fingers through the canopy above.

"Tis the toil that demands rest's sweet reprieve," he murmured as a prelude to the calm that must follow a midday meal.

Eyes tracing the slow drift of a cloud across the azure, Miss Newell did not attempt to stir those words left in the wake of respite. Quietly, she lent him the solace of companionship unburdened by speech, wherein their laughter lay already woven.

Her attention broke momentarily from the sky when a bird flitted close, spirit alive in song. Noting Mr. Arnold's steady breathing, eyes still closed, she allowed herself the quiet luxury of study. His face, bared to the sun and solitude, revealed lines of earnest labor bred by the land. Yet, there, softness lingered beneath his austerity, hidden by no more than a thistle's bramble.

The longing of dusk imposed its specter upon their idyll, the lengthening shadows hinting now at the day's impermanence. There arose in her a voice of practicality, which wrestled with leaving the warmth established between their kindred natures.

"Nicky Dyer," she said suddenly, "awaits my return. He’ll reprimand the languor that keeps me thus detained."

Arnold's eyes opened, the spell of ease reluctantly lifting. "Permit me then, to insist upon your indulgence of my company until the last cricket’s song."

And so, the moments unfolded beneath the eaves of tranquility, their sense of the hour dissolved, the boundary between names and faces softened in the expansion of silence. They remained thus engaged with the world’s subtle wonders, knowing full well their time shared would not go unscrutinized by the means of polite society.

But the forest whispered not acid, and the ravens asked no questions; as vespers drew near, they would part whole in an understanding which sought not possession. Happiness had no circumference; it was the span of a look upon what remained shared and what might yet be.

Finally, Arnold rose, brushing off his coat with a gesture of finality. "I return shortly to the yoke and its demands," he admitted.

Miss Newell stood to meet him, with a half-envious glance at the unperturbed waters. "A brief farewell, then," she agreed, though her heart lingered where warmth had quietly grown.

They began the short walk away from the gentle lull of the brook, the foliage closing behind even as the day settled into the quiet embrace of twilight.

Catastrophic Flooding Engulfs Jean Lafitte, Rivaling Hurricane Katrina's Devastation

Jean Lafitte, a small town in south Jefferson Parish, Louisiana, is grappling with unprecedented flooding in the wake of Hurricane Ida. As the storm's fury continues to unfold, hundreds of residents remain stranded, with floodwaters reaching heights of 10 to 12 feet, leaving them in a state of panic and desperation.

Police Chief Marcel Rodriguez describes the harrowing situation, saying, "This is worse than Katrina in some aspects. With communication lines down and roads impassable, search and rescue efforts are proving to be a monumental challenge.

Sergeant Jason Leorwald of the Jean Lafitte Police Department adds, "The conditions are severe, and it's impacting our ability to reach those in need. We're doing everything we can, but mother nature is not on our side right now."

Rescue teams are working tirelessly, navigating through the deluge in an attempt to reach stranded residents. Many of these individuals are trapped in their homes, which, in some cases, date back decades and were not built to withstand such extreme flooding. Shalina Chatlani, a reporter from the Gulf States Newsroom, shares, "The residents who stayed are in a panic mode, feeling completely cut off from the outside world."

Chief Rodriguez notes, "We thought we had learned from the past, but Ida has shown us that Mother Nature can still catch us off guard. As the floodwaters continue to rise and the storm rages on, the people of Jean Lafitte and the surrounding areas face an uncertain future. The next few days will be critical in determining the extent of the damage and the long road to recovery that lies ahead. The resilience of the community, tested time and again, will be put to the ultimate test in the aftermath of Hurricane Ida.

Gaston pressed on, undaunted by the dubiety in their eyes. "Yes, Frank Reade, Jr. A man of genius, a visionary. And I have seen his latest creation, gentlemen. The airship.

Age of the cyber-attack: US struggles to curb rise of digital destabilization

It’s been 40 years since Lisa Donnan has queued for gas. But last month the cybersecurity expert found herself joining the long lines of cars across the east coast of the US looking for fuel after the latest in a series of cyber-attacks had shut down the pipeline that provides fuel to 45% of the region.

“The last time I did that was in the Iran crisis,” she said. “My dad had to wait with me.”

The hack of the Colonial Pipeline was just one of a series of cyber-attacks that have hit the US and elsewhere recently. Hackers have taken down JBS, the world’s largest meat processor, disrupting the global meat market, closed schools in Iowa and hit hospitals in Ireland in what experts say is a dangerous escalation of a crime wave that has swelled from the small-scale blackmail operations of a few years ago to major assaults that threaten the livelihoods – and potentially lives – of millions.

Many of the recent attacks have been sourced to operations in Russia and US officials say that Russia’s responsibility for ransomware attacks carried out from its territory would be a central issue when Joe Biden meets Vladimir Putin in Geneva next Wednesday.

“One of the things that President Biden will make clear to President Putin, when he sees him, is that states cannot be in the business of harboring those who are engaged in these kinds of attacks,” the secretary of state, Tony Blinken, told Congress this week.

Eric Green, the senior director for Russia and central Asia in the national security council, said that one of the expected outcomes from the Geneva summit was a routine dialogue between senior US and Russian officials aimed at bringing greater stability and predictability to the relationship. One of the issues in the dialogue would be ransomware attacks.

“When we talk about strategic stability cyber will also certainly be on the agenda,” Green said in a recent discussion organised by the Centre for a New American Security. “The recent ransomware attacks remind us that the cyber domain is prone to misperceptions and that there are dangerous escalation risks.”

US officials say America will be pushing for Nato to expand its involvement in cyberdefence at the alliance summit in Brussels. But the unanswered question is how to respond to ransomware attacks by criminal groups for whom their host countries deny responsibility.

“Putin will deny interfering in US politics or conducting cyber-attacks, asserting that Washington has no proof, while rejecting the legitimacy of US concerns about what happens within Russia,” said Steven Pifer, former deputy assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs and now a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

“Biden should not waste time arguing. He should aim instead to ensure that Putin has a clear understanding of what conduct is out of bounds.”

The pressure for Biden to act is rising. There has been a 62% increase in ransomware globally since 2019, and 158% spike in North America, according to the 2021 SonicWall Cyber Threat Report. Alongside that rise, the nature of the crimes and their targets are also changing.

“We are seeing more attacks, more sophisticated attacks, bigger attacks and the scary thing is we are seeing them more on supply chains,” said Donnan. “It used to be about financial exfiltration, stealing money, and reputational damage. It’s now in a life-threatening environment. That is a dramatic change.”

Now a partner at the cybersecurity private equity investor Option3Ventures, Donnan says she doesn’t expect to see any let-up in attacks. Nation states including Russia, China and North Korea are getting more ambitious in their attacks and the criminal enterprises that operate under their wings are getting more brazen.

“The landscape is ripe and ready for attack from a perfect storm of hackers, nation states and the average cybercriminal,” she said.

Part of the recent surge is down to the pandemic, which has helped the hackers by accelerating the digitization of business and giving them more access points as people and businesses have moved to work remotely.

On top of that there has been an explosion in software development, much of which was not built with security in mind from the beginning, said Donnan. “We still have a culture of get to market, be first. We are designing code without security in mind,” she said.

Lastly there are few consequences to cybercrime. Cryptocurrencies are the preferred payment for ransoms and are as hard to track as the origins of the hack. With the authorities unlikely to crack the case anytime soon – if ever – for many targets not paying is a difficult choice. Joseph Blount, Colonial’s chief executive, told Congress last week that he decided to pay the $4.4m bitcoin ransom to get the pipeline back online after he saw “pandemonium going on at the markets”.

Politicians hit out at Blount for the company’s failure to stop the hack. But the government itself has also failed to stop numerous hacks and not paying the ransom can be more expensive than paying up and potentially leave companies open to further assaults. JBS paid $11m in bitcoin to its hackers, even though it had mostly fixed its problems, hoping the payment would prevent further issues arising from the attack.

In 2019 Baltimore was hit with a cyber-attack that seized control of parts of its government. The hackers demanded $760,000 in bitcoin but the mayor, Bernard “Jack” Young, refused to pay. The cost of rebuilding its systems has now reached $18.2m.

Publicly the FBI advises victims not to pay a ransom in order to discourage perpetrators from targeting more victims. But privately they will tell targets that they understand if they feel the need to pay.

In the Colonial case the FBI managed to seize the majority of the bitcoin payment – a hopeful sign that may discourage some attackers, according to experts – but the fact remains that most of these crimes go unpunished.

“It’s very difficult to prosecute, it takes a long time, it takes cooperation geopolitically because most of these attacks come from offshore,” said Donnan. “The government only has so many resources. It doesn’t take a lot of tools or brain capacity to do these things,” she said. “You can buy a tool kit on the dark web.”

One irony of the current wave of hacks is that the US is under attack by tools developed by its own National Security Agency (NSA). In 2016 an online group called the Shadow Brokers claimed to have infiltrated the Equation Group, the NSA’s own private hacking group, and obtained malware used by the US to target its enemies.

The Shadow Brokers claimed responsibility for the release of NSA software that facilitated May 2017’s WannaCry ransomware attack, which triggered more than 45,000 attacks in 99 countries and crippled parts of Britain’s National Health Service. Researchers believe that attack originated in North Korea.

In June 2017 the same cyber-attack tool developed by the NSA, called EternalBlue, was used to launch a series of attacks on Ukraine, affecting the government, banks and transportation systems and taking the radiation monitoring system at Chernobyl offline. That attack then spread around the world, hitting companies that had offices in Ukraine including FedEx, the advertising agency WPP, pharmaceutical company Merck and consumer goods maker Reckitt Benckiser.

The US, UK and other researchers blamed Russia for that attack, arguing it was not designed to make money but to damage Ukraine’s economy.

The escalation in cases comes even as spending on security is rising dramatically. The US is the number one country for cybercrime and also spends the most on cybersecurity.

In 2015 the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) announced it was hacked in 2015, one of the largest data thefts in history. Since then the US has spent $115bn on cybersecurity and the White House is asking Congress to commit roughly $10bn to civilian government cybersecurity next year – a jump of nearly 14%. Industry spent $41bn on cybersecurity in 2019 and is expected to have spent $53bn in 2020.

Even after all that money has been spent, said Donnan “we are still exposed because there is no consequence.”

But there are rewards.

Three years ago Paul Ferrillo, a partner at New York law firm Seyfarth Shaw who specialises in cybersecurity, says he was settling ransomware hacks for five bitcoin (about $6,000 per bitcoin then and currently around $36,000 each). “Now you are lucky if it’s 75 bitcoin or 100. I heard of one demand recently for $140m,” he said.

“If this is the new normal, they are winning,” he said. “These criminal actors are well-funded and smart whether they are state-funded or not. We need to be as smart as they are.”

Ferrillo said there was no silver bullet that would solve the crisis and that everyone from the government to the private citizen had to play a part. Companies have to get better at managing their data, storing backups offline and making sure it is harder to get into their systems.

He also wants to see more transparency from industry. Companies have often hidden hacks because they don’t want to look like “doofuses”, he said. “But when industry shares information, we all get smarter. We understand where we should look and how we should do better.”

But tackling this explosion in hacking will take action from everyone, he said, from government to private citizens. “Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility. We are all in this together,” he said.

Hurricane Ida Unleashes Fury on Mississippi and Louisiana, Leaving Devastation in Its Wake

Biloxi, Mississippi - Hurricane Ida, a formidable Category 4 storm, has unleashed its wrath upon the Gulf Coast, leaving a trail of destruction and heartbreak across Mississippi and Louisiana. In addition to the widespread destruction caused by Hurricane Ida, the city is also enduring a relentless heatwave, exacerbating the plight of its residents. The storm's impact has resulted in extensive power outages, leaving thousands of homes and businesses without electricity. The sweltering heat, coupled with the lack of air conditioning, has made conditions unbearable for many.

Residents Struggle Amidst Lack of Basic Necessities

The hurricane's aftermath has left residents in Mississippi and Louisiana facing severe conditions. Many lack access to electricity and tap water, relying on shared resources and the generosity of their neighbors. The situation has placed a significant strain on local communities, as they strive to provide assistance to those in need.

Uncertainty Looms Over Power Restoration

Authorities and Entergy, the local power company, have expressed uncertainty regarding the timeline for power restoration. Estimates suggest that it could take up to three weeks for electricity to be fully restored in the affected areas. This prolonged outage adds to the challenges faced by residents, who are already grappling with the aftermath of the hurricane.

Louisiana Governor Vows Assistance Amidst Slow Recovery

Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards acknowledged the slow pace of recovery efforts and pledged to deliver assistance to those affected. "We understand the frustration and anxiety that our residents are feeling," Governor Edwards stated. "We are committed to doing everything in our power to expedite the recovery process and ensure that our communities receive the support they need during this difficult time."

National Guard Mobilized for Rescue and Relief

In response to the devastation caused by Hurricane Ida, over 6,000 National Guard members from multiple states have been mobilized for rescue and relief efforts. These brave men and women are working tirelessly to assist local authorities in search and rescue operations, providing medical care, and distributing essential supplies to affected communities.

Ida's Impact Spans Multiple States

Hurricane Ida's destructive path extended beyond Mississippi and Louisiana, causing extensive damage and leading to flash flooding and tornadoes across several states. The storm made landfall as a Category 4 hurricane, packing winds of up to 150 miles per hour. Its impact was felt from Alabama to Florida, leaving a trail of destruction in its wake.

Federal Assistance Coordinated for Storm Recovery

President Biden and federal officials are coordinating closely with state and local authorities to provide storm assistance. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is actively engaged in relief efforts, deploying resources and personnel to support the affected communities.
