As Brady prepares for his 10th Super Bowl, his illustrious career continues to be a testament to his enduring talent and leadership on the football field.

There are houses in certain provincial towns whose aspect inspires melancholy, akin to that called forth by sombre cloisters, dreary moorlands, or the desolation of ruins. Within these houses there is, perhaps, the silence of the cloister, the barrenness of moors, the skeleton of ruins; life and movement are so stagnant there that a stranger might think them uninhabited, were it not that he encounters suddenly the pale, cold glance of a motionless person, whose half-monastic face peers beyond the window-casing at the sound of an unaccustomed step.

Such elements of sadness formed the physiognomy, as it were, of a dwelling-house in Saumur which stands at the end of the steep street leading to the chateau in the upper part of the town. This stree–ow little frequented, hot in summer, cold in winter, dark in certain section–s remarkable for the resonance of its little pebbly pavement, always clean and dry, for the narrowness of its tortuous road-way, for the peaceful stillness of its houses, which belong to the Old town and are over-topped by the ramparts. Houses three centuries old are still solid, though built of wood, and their divers aspects add to the originality which commends this portion of Saumur to the attention of artists and antiquaries.

It is difficult to pass these houses without admiring the enormous oaken beams, their ends carved into fantastic figures, which crown with a black bas-relief the lower floor of most of them. In one place these transverse timbers are covered with slate and mark a bluish line along the frail wall of a dwelling covered by a roof en colombage which bends beneath the weight of years, and whose rotting shingles are twisted by the alternate action of sun and rain. In another place blackened, worn-out window-sills, with delicate sculptures now scarcely discernible, seem too weak to bear the brown clay pots from which springs the heart’s-ease or the rose-bush of some poor working-woman. Farther on are doors studded with enormous nails, where the genius of our forefathers has traced domestic hieroglyphics, of which the meaning is now lost forever. Here a Protestant attested his belief; there a Leaguer cursed Henry IV.; elsewhere some bourgeois has carved the insignia of his noblesse de cloches, symbols of his long-forgotten magisterial glory. The whole history of France is there.

Next to a tottering house with roughly plastered walls, where an artisan enshrines his tools, rises the mansion of a country gentleman, on the stone arch of which above the door vestiges of armorial bearings may still be seen, battered by the many revolutions that have shaken France since 1789. In this hilly street the ground-floors of the merchants are neither shops nor warehouses; lovers of the Middle Ages will here find the ouvrouere of our forefathers in all its naive simplicity. These low rooms, which have no shop-frontage, no show-windows, in fact no glass at all, are deep and dark and without interior or exterior decoration. Their doors open in two parts, each roughly iron-bound; the upper half is fastened back within the room, the lower half, fitted with a spring-bell, swings continually to and fro. Air and light reach the damp den within, either through the upper half of the door, or through an open space between the ceiling and a low front wall, breast-high, which is closed by solid shutters that are taken down every morning, put up every evening, and held in place by heavy iron bars.

This wall serves as a counter for the merchandise. No delusive display is there; only samples of the business, whatever it may chance to be,--such, for instance, as three or four tubs full of codfish and salt, a few bundles of sail-cloth, cordage, copper wire hanging from the joists above, iron hoops for casks ranged along the wall, or a few pieces of cloth upon the shelves. Enter. A neat girl, glowing with youth, wearing a white kerchief, her arms red and bare, drops her knitting and calls her father or her mother, one of whom comes forward and sells you what you want, phlegmatically, civilly, or arrogantly, according to his or her individual character, whether it be a matter of two sous’ or twenty thousand francs’ worth of merchandise. You may see a cooper, for instance, sitting in his doorway and twirling his thumbs as he talks with a neighbor. To all appearance he owns nothing more than a few miserable boat-ribs and two or three bundles of laths; but below in the port his teeming wood-yard supplies all the cooperage trade of Anjou. He knows to a plank how many casks are needed if the vintage is good. A hot season makes him rich, a rainy season ruins him; in a single morning puncheons worth eleven francs have been known to drop to six. In this country, as in Touraine, atmospheric vicissitudes control commercial life. Wine-growers, proprietors, wood-merchants, coopers, inn-keepers, mariners, all keep watch of the sun. They tremble when they go to bed lest they should hear in the morning of a frost in the night; they dread rain, wind, drought, and want water, heat, and clouds to suit their fancy. A perpetual duel goes on between the heavens and their terrestrial interests. The barometer smooths, saddens, or makes merry their countenances, turn and turn about. From end to end of this street, formerly the Grand’Rue de Saumur, the words: “Here’s golden weather,” are passed from door to door; or each man calls to his neighbor: “It rains louis,” knowing well what a sunbeam or the opportune rainfall is bringing him.

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jerry Nadler Calls for DOJ Review of Kyle Rittenhouse Acquittal

KYLE RITTENHOUSE ACQUITTAL

House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jerry Nadler (D-N.Y.) called for a Department of Justice (DOJ) review of the Kyle Rittenhouse case following his acquittal last week on charges related to the shooting of three people during protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin, in 2020.

Nadler expressed his concerns during a recent interview, stating, "I think there should be an investigation. The notion that an armed, 17-year-old, vigilante can roam around and shoot people with immunity is frightening."

Rittenhouse was found not guilty on all charges, including homicide, after claiming self-defense during the incident. However, federal charges against him appear unlikely due to the nature of his alleged crimes.

Federal charges usually involve specific violations of federal law, but Rittenhouse is not accused of any. The charges against him have sparked debates over guns, vigilantism, and racial justice.

Rittenhouse, who was 17 at the time of the shootings, claimed he was present to protect property. However, prosecutors portrayed him as a "wannabe soldier." Rittenhouse testified in his defense, breaking down in tears during his testimony.

The trial's outcome and the judge's decisions have led to broader discussions on legal interpretations and self-defense laws. Circuit Judge Bruce Schroeder made headlines for his handling of the trial, including dismissing a gun possession charge against Rittenhouse.

Schroeder's decision to dismiss the weapon charge was based on the length of the gun's barrel compared to state law. Michael Cicchini, a Kenosha-based defense attorney, stated, "The Wisconsin age to possess a gun is 18, but the federal age to purchase a handgun from a licensed gun dealer is 21."

The Rittenhouse case has drawn extensive media coverage, with many questioning the role of vigilantes in law enforcement. Legal analysts have debated the boundaries of self-defense laws and the use of firearms.

Self-defense laws vary from state to state, with some requiring a defendant to prove they believed their life was in danger. Others only require the defendant to prove they believed they were in danger of great bodily harm or death.

In the Rittenhouse case, the jury found him not guilty based on his belief that he was in danger of great bodily harm or death when he shot the three individuals.

However, some critics have argued that self-defense laws are too broad and can lead to justifications for violence. The Rittenhouse case has only intensified these debates.

The dismissal of the gun possession charge against Rittenhouse has also raised questions about the legal interpretation of state laws. The interpretation of state laws can vary from judge to judge, leading to different outcomes in similar cases.

In the Rittenhouse case, Schroeder's interpretation of the law led to the dismissal of the gun possession charge. The decision has led to discussions on the need for clearer and more consistent interpretations of state laws.

In conclusion, the Rittenhouse case has sparked debates over guns, vigilantism, and racial justice. The dismissal of the gun possession charge and the jury's verdict have led to broader discussions on legal interpretations and self-defense laws.

Nadler's call for a DOJ review of the case highlights the ongoing controversy surrounding the incident and the need for further investigation into the matter. As these debates continue, the legal system will need to address the challenges surrounding self-defense laws and the use of firearms.

Felix Brandt, having sown the seeds of wonder in our young minds with his spectral narratives and exotic brews, became a fixture in our daily lives. Nikolaus Bauman, Seppi Wohlmeyer, and I, Theodor Fischer, found ourselves drawn to him as moths to a flickering flame. Our days, once filled with simple games of tag and the construction of miniature empires in the dust, were now punctuated by clandestine visits to the castle park, where Felix awaited us with steaming cups of his potent Turkish coffee and a fresh stock of fantastical tales.

One sweltering afternoon, as the Rhine sluggishly crawled past the village and even the bees seemed to hum with a drowsy languor, we found Felix unusually subdued. He sat upon his customary bench, a weathered oak affair that creaked beneath his weight, his brow furrowed and his gaze distant. Seppi, ever the bold one, nudged him playfully with his elbow. "Felix! What troubles you this fine day? Surely no ghost has stolen your tongue?" Felix managed a weak smile. "Nay, lads, no ghost, though perhaps something akin to it. I received a letter this morn, a letter from my sister in Schaffhausen. She writes of strange happenings in the town—whispers of a mechanical marvel, a clockwork contraption of immense size and complexity, said to predict the future." Nikolaus, ever the pragmatist, scoffed. "Predict the future? Preposterous! Such things exist only in fairy tales." But Felix held up a gnarled hand. "Hold your judgment, Nikolaus. My sister is a woman of sound mind, not one given to flights of fancy. She claims that this clock, built by a reclusive artisan named Herr Zimmerman, has become the talk of the town. Crowds gather daily to witness its pronouncements, and though few understand its workings, all agree that its prophecies are uncanny." Seppi's eyes widened. "Prophecies? What sort of prophecies?" Felix sighed. "Dire ones, it seems. Predictions of floods and famines, of wars and pestilence. The people of Schaffhausen are in a state of near panic, believing that Herr Zimmerman's clock has unveiled their impending doom." I, Theodor Fischer, felt a shiver crawl down my spine. Though Felix had taught us not to fear the supernatural, this felt different, more sinister. "But surely," I ventured, "such a thing is impossible. How can a mere clock predict the future?" Felix shrugged. "I know not, Theodor. But my sister's words weigh heavy on my heart. She begs me to come to Schaffhausen, to use my…experience, she says, to help calm the townspeople. She believes that my familiarity with the unseen world may offer some solace in these troubled times." He paused, his gaze settling upon each of us in turn. "And so, lads, I must leave you for a time. I must journey to Schaffhausen and see this clockwork prophecy for myself." A wave of disappointment washed over us. Felix was our confidant, our guide to the realm of the fantastic. Without him, the castle park would be a less enchanting place. But beneath our disappointment, I sensed a spark of excitement. A clock that predicted the future? It was a concept both terrifying and irresistibly alluring.

Florence, who was more pleased at what he heard than he would like to have acknowledged, promised to come forth from his hiding place and meet the world in a better spirit. And he did so; being really drawn back into the social circle by the attraction of Miss Weldon. At his second meeting with this young lady he was still more charmed with her than at first; and she was equally well pleased with him. A few more interviews, and both their hearts were deeply interested.

Now there came a new cause of disquietude to Edwin; or, it might be said, the old cause renewed. The going out of his affections towards Miss Weldon revived the whole memory of the past; and, for a time he found it almost impossible to thrust it from his mind. While sitting by her side and listening to her voice, the tones of Edith would be in his ears; and, often, when he looked into her face he would see only the fading countenance of her who had passed away. This was the first state, and it was exceedingly painful while it lasted. But, it gradually changed into one more pleasant, yet not entirely free from the unwelcome intrusion of the past.

The oftener Florence and Miss Weldon met, the more strongly were their hearts drawn toward each other; and, at length, the former was encouraged to make an offer of his hand. In coming to this resolutions, it was not without passing through a painful conflict. As his mind dwelt upon the subject, there was a reproduction of old states. Most vividly did he recall the time when he breathed into the ears of Edith vows to which he had proved faithless. He had, it is true, returned to his first allegiance. He had laid his heart again at her feet; but, to how little purpose! While in this state of agitation, the young man resolved, more than once, to abandon his suit for the hand of Miss Weldon, and shrink back again into the seclusion from which he had come forth. But, his affection for the lovely girl was too genuine to admit of this. When he thought of giving her up, his mind was still more deeply disturbed.

"Oh, that I could forget!" he exclaimed, while this struggle was in progress. "Of what avail is this turning over of the leaves of a long passed history? I erred--sadly erred! But repentance is now too late. Why, then should my whole existence be cursed for a single error? Ah, me! thou not satisfied, departed one? Is it, indeed, from the presence of thy spirit that I am troubled? My heart sinks at the thought. But no, no! Thou wert too good to visit pain upon any; much less upon one who, thou false to thee, thou didst so tenderly love."

But, upon this state there came a natural re-action. A peaceful calm succeeded the storm. Memory deposited her records in the mind's dimly lighted chambers. To the present was restored its better influences.

"I am free again," was the almost audible utterance, of the young man, so strong was his sense of relief.

An offer of marriage was then made to Miss Weldon. Her heart trembled with joy when she received it. But confiding implicitly in her uncle, who had been for the space of ten years her friend and guardian, she could not give an affirmative reply until his approval was gained. She, therefore, asked time for reflection and consultation with her friend.

Far different from what Florence had expected, was the reception of his offer. To him, Miss Weldon seemed instantly to grow cold and reserved. Vividly was now recalled his rejection by Miss Linmore, as well as the ground of her rejection.

"Is this to be gone over again?" he sighed to himself, when alone once more, "Is that one false step never to be forgotten nor forgiven? Am I to be followed, through life, by this shadow of evil?"

President Biden Rescinds Trump's Travel Ban on First Day in Office, Fulfilling Campaign Promise

In his first day in office, President Joe Biden issued an executive order to revoke the controversial travel ban imposed by his predecessor, Donald Trump, on noncitizens from 13 countries. The ban, colloquially known as the "Muslim ban," significantly limited legal immigration from countries deemed security threats and was first enacted in January 2017.

The policy initially targeted majority-Muslim countries but was expanded in February 2020 to include six more countries. The ban has been criticized for being discriminatory and has faced numerous legal challenges before being upheld by the Supreme Court in its third version. According to the Cato Institute, over 41,000 people have been denied visas due to the ban, with waivers being difficult to obtain.

Enrollment from affected countries in U.S. educational institutions and certain professions, such as healthcare, has seen a significant decline. Farhana Khera, executive director of Muslim Advocates, stated, "This ban was a symbol of discrimination and xenophobia. The damage it caused to families and communities is immeasurable."

The rescinding of the ban fulfills one of Biden's campaign promises on immigration policy. Critics argue the ban did not enhance national security and damaged the U.S.'s international relationships. Ramez Alghazzouli, a Syrian American, expressed his relief, saying, "I can finally breathe a sigh of relief knowing that my family and friends might have a chance to come to the U.S. again."

Former intelligence officials and ambassadors have criticized the ban for its focus on Islamist terrorism and the negative impact on U.S. national security. Elizabeth Neumann, former assistant secretary for counterterrorism and threat prevention at the Homeland Security Department, stated, "The ban sent a message that the U.S. was at war with Islam, which was counterproductive to our efforts to combat terrorism."

Ryan Crocker, a former U.S. ambassador, echoed this sentiment, saying, "The ban was not only un-American, but it also hurt our relationships with our allies and partners around the world."

Immigrant advocates urge further action from the Biden administration and Congress to dismantle Trump's immigration policies and barriers. Khera added, "While this is a significant step forward, there is still much work to be done to repair the damage caused by the previous administration's policies."

In conclusion, President Biden's executive order to rescind the travel ban is a significant step towards fulfilling his campaign promise on immigration policy. The ban, which has been criticized for being discriminatory and damaging to U.S. national security, has resulted in over 41,000 people being denied visas. The rescinding of the ban has been welcomed by immigrant advocates, former intelligence officials, and ambassadors, who urge further action to dismantle Trump's immigration policies and barriers.

FDA Amends EUAs for Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 Vaccines for Additional Dose for Certain Immunocompromised Individuals

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken a crucial step to protect a vulnerable segment of the population by amending the Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA) for the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines. This amendment allows for an additional dose of these vaccines for certain immunocompromised individuals, including solid organ transplant recipients or those with equivalent levels of immunocompromise.

"Today's action allows for a third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna COVID-19 vaccines for a specific group of immunocompromised individuals who may not have had a sufficient immune response to the standard two-dose regimen," said Acting FDA Commissioner Janet Woodcock, MD. "This is an important step in ensuring we're doing everything we can to protect those who are most vulnerable to COVID-19 during this pandemic wave."

Immunocompromised individuals, due to their reduced ability to fight infections, are at a higher risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. The additional dose is intended to increase their protection against the virus, but the FDA emphasizes that physical precautions, such as wearing masks and social distancing, should still be followed.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices is scheduled to convene to discuss further recommendations for this specific group. The third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine is authorized for individuals aged 12 and older, while the Moderna vaccine is authorized for those aged 18 and older. Both vaccines require an initial two-dose regimen, with the third dose to be administered at least 28 days after the second shot.

Dr. Woodcock highlighted the importance of healthcare providers playing a critical role in guiding their immunocompromised patients. "We encourage these individuals to have a conversation with their healthcare provider about their individual circumstances and whether an additional dose may be appropriate for them," she said.

In addition to the additional vaccine dose, the FDA also advises immunocompromised individuals to discuss monoclonal antibody treatment options with their healthcare providers in case they contract COVID-19. The EUA amendments have been issued to Pfizer Inc. and ModernaTX Inc. for their respective vaccines.

This amendment underscores the FDA's commitment to adapting its response to the evolving COVID-19 landscape and ensuring the safety and efficacy of vaccines for all Americans, particularly those most at risk.

A New Reality: Millions of Displaced Workers Face Career Shifts Amid Permanent Economic Transformations

As the coronavirus pandemic continues to upend the global economy, millions of Americans find themselves facing an uncertain future in the job market. Permanent shifts in work patterns, accelerated automation, and a transition to a different economy are reshaping industries and necessitating career changes and retraining for many.

Federal Reserve Chair Jerome H. Powell acknowledged this new reality during an interview with CNBC, stating, "It's clear that a significant portion of the work that's lost in this downturn is not coming back."

Susan Lund, Head of the McKinsey Global Institute, echoed Powell's sentiments, emphasizing the need for individuals to adapt. "The labor market will never look the same. Workers will need to be more flexible and adaptable than ever before," she said.

According to a recent survey by the W.E. Upjohn Institute for Employment Research, more than 40% of the unemployed are considering changing their occupations or fields of work. Brad Hershbein, a Senior Economist at the institute, explained, "People are recognizing that the job market is changing, and they need to change with it."

However, financial resources for retraining pose a significant challenge for many. Bill Gates, the founder-turned-philanthropist of Microsoft, emphasized the importance of addressing this issue. "We need to invest in education and training programs to help workers adapt," he said.

Automation is accelerating in industries such as retail and manufacturing, potentially reducing the need for human labor. Sumit Singh, CEO of online pet supply company Chewy, recently opened a fully automated fulfillment center requiring far fewer workers. Diane Pelkey, Chewy's spokeswoman, stated, "This is just the beginning of the automation wave in our industry."

Job postings indicate a decline in demand for various occupations, suggesting a shift in the job market. David Autor, an Economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, explained, "We're seeing a clear trend toward automation in many industries, and it's important for workers to be aware of this and prepare accordingly."

However, the unpredictability of which industries will thrive makes job transitions difficult. Stephanie Wissink, Managing Director at Jefferies, noted, "It's a challenging time for workers. Some sectors are experiencing growth, but it's hard to know which ones will continue to thrive."

Despite these challenges, initiatives like Michigan's 'Futures for Frontliners' program offer free tuition for retraining to front-line workers. Andrew Chamberlain, Chief Economist at Glassdoor, emphasized the importance of such programs, stating, "We need to ensure that workers have the resources and support they need to adapt to this new economy."

As the job market continues to evolve, it's clear that flexibility, adaptability, and a willingness to learn new skills will be essential for success. Powell summarized this new reality, stating, "The economy is changing, and workers need to be prepared for that change."

“You think that she is so very--very pretty?” said Miss Craven.

“She?--fate?--I’ll tell you what I think. I think that Harold Wynne has met with the greatest misfortune of his life.”

“If you believe that, I know that I have met with the greatest of my life.”

The corner of the hall was almost wholly in shadow. The settee upon which Mr. Airey and Miss Craven were sitting, was cut off from the rest of the place by the thigh hone of the great skeleton elk. Between the ribs of the creature, however, some rays of light passed from one of the lamps; and, as Mr. Airey looked sympathetically into the face of his companion, he saw the gleam of a tear upon her cheek.

He was deeply impressed--so deeply that some moments had passed before he found himself wondering what she would say next. For a moment he forgot to be on his guard, though if anyone had described the details of a similar scene to him, he would probably have smiled while remarking that when the lamplight gleams upon a tear upon the cheek of a young woman of large experience, is just when a man needs most to be on his guard, He felt in another moment, however, that something was coming.

He waited for it in silence.

It seemed to him in that pause that he was seated by the side of someone whom he had never met before. The girl who was beside him seemed to have nothing in common with Helen Craven. So greatly does a young woman change when she becomes frank.

This is why so many husbands declare--when they are also frank--that the young women whom they marry are in every respect different from the young women who promise to be their wives.

“What is going to happen?” Helen asked him in a steady voice.

“God knows,” said he.

“I saw them together just after they left you this morning,” said she. “I was at one of the windows of the Castle, they were far along the terrace; but I’m sure that he said something to her about her eyes.”

“I should not be surprised if he did,” said Edmund. “Her eyes invite comment.”

“I believe that in spite of her eyes she is much the same as any other girl.”

“Is that to the point?” he asked. He was a trifle disappointed in her last sentence. It seemed to show him that, whatever Beatrice might be, Helen was much the same as other girls.

“It is very much to the point,” said she. “If she is like other girls she will hesitate before marrying a penniless man.”

“I agree with you,” said he. “But if she is like other girls she will not hesitate to love a penniless man.”

“Possibly--if, like me, she can afford to do so. But I happen to know that she cannot afford it. This brings me up to what has been on my mind all day. You are, I know, my friend; you are Harold Wynne’s also. Now, if you want to enable him to gratify his reasonable ambition--if you want to make him happy--to make me happy--you will prevent him from ever asking Beatrice Avon to marry him.”

“And I am prepared to do so much for him--for you--for her. But how can I do it?”

“You can take her away from him. You know how such things are done. You know that if a distinguished man such as you are, with a large income such as you possess, gives a girl to understand that he is, let us say, greatly interested in her, she will soon cease to be interested in any undistinguished and penniless son of a reprobate peer who may be before her eyes.”

“I have seen such a social phenomenon,” said he. “Does your proposition suggest that I should marry the young woman with ‘a gray eye or so’?”

“You may marry her if you please--that’s entirely a matter for yourself. I don’t see any need for you to go that length. Have I not kept my promise to be frank?”

The mules were about to turn the matter over in their minds when Captain Binns sent the full force of the current through the wire and kept it going steadily. Thereupon the animals became panic-stricken. They began to rear and plunge; they turned around and dashed down the tow-path toward the boat. Then the line became taut; it jerked the boat around suddenly with such force that the stern of it broke through a weak place in the bank, and before the captain could turn off his battery the mules had dashed around the other side of the toll-collector's cabin, and then, making a lurch to the left, they fell over the bank themselves, the line scraping the cabin, the collector, three children and a colored man over with them. By the time the line was cut and the sufferers rescued the mules were drowned and all the water in the canal had gone out through the break. It cost Captain Binns three hundred dollars for damages; and when he had settled the account, he concluded to wait for the report of that committee before making any new experiments.

The report of the committee upon improved locomotion was submitted to the company during the following summer. It was a long and exceedingly entertaining document, and the following extracts from it may possess some interest:

THE REPORT.

"In reference to the plan offered by Henry Bushelson, which proposes to run the boats by means of his patent propeller, we may remark that the steam-engine with which the propeller is moved would sink the boat; and even if it would not, the propeller-blades, being longer than the depth of the canal, would dig about five hundred cubic feet of mud out of the bottom at each revolution. As a mud-dredge Bushelson's patent might be a success, but as a motive-power it is a failure; and his suggestion that the tow-path might be cut into lengths and laid side by side and sold for a farm, therefore, is not wholly practicable.

"The idea of William Bradley is that holes might be cut in the bottom of the boat, and through these the legs of the mule could be inserted, so that it could walk along the bottom, while its body is safe and dry inside. This notion is the offspring of a fruitful and ingenious intellect; and if the water could be kept from coming through the holes, it might be considered valuable but for one thin–omebody would have to invent a new kind of mule with legs about seven feet long. Mr. Bradley's mind has not yet devised any method of procuring such a mule, and unless he can induce the ordinary kind to walk upon stilts, we fear that the obstacles to success in this direction may be regarded as insurmountable.

"Mr. Peterman Bostwick urges that important results might be secured by making the canal an inclined plane, so that when a boat is placed upon it the boat will simply slide down hill by the power of the attraction of gravitation. This seems to us a beautiful method of adapting to the wants of man one of the most remarkable of the laws of Nature, and we should be inclined to give Mr. Bostwick the first prize but for the fact that we have discovered, upon investigation, that the water in the canal also would slide down hill, and that it would require about fifteen rivers the size of the Mississippi to keep up the supply. Mr. Bostwick does not mention where we are to get those rivers. He does, however, say that if it shall be deemed inadvisable to slope the canal, the boats themselves might be made in the shape of inclined planes, so that they would run down hill upon a level canal. There is something so deep, so amazing, in this proposition that your committee needs more time to consider it and brood over it.

The sun hung lazily in the sky, casting a warm glow over the sprawling estate where the Franklin family resided. As the family gathered on the veranda for their afternoon tea, the air was filled with a sense of ease and contentment. Mrs. Franklin, a woman of refined taste and impeccable manners, sat at the head of the table, her eyes scanning the latest edition of the Raleigh newspaper in search of the day's news.

Dolly, her eldest daughter, sat across from her, her expression thoughtful as she sipped her tea. "Do you not find it curious, Mother," she began, her voice tinged with curiosity, "how we are so quick to bestow pity upon the departed? Is it not more fitting to celebrate their lives, rather than mourn their passing?"

Mrs. Franklin looked up from her newspaper, a gentle smile playing on her lips. "Ah, my dear Dolly," she said, her voice soft and melodious, "you always had a way with words. Perhaps you are right. Perhaps we should remember the departed not with sorrow, but with joy for the time we shared with them."

Just then, Ruth, the youngest of the Franklin daughters, burst into a fit of giggles, her golden curls bouncing with each peal of laughter. "Oh, Mother," she exclaimed, her eyes sparkling with mischief, "you and your endless fascination with the bishop! Do you not tire of reading about his sermons and travels?"

Mrs. Franklin raised an elegant eyebrow in mock indignation. "Surely, my dear Ruth, you jest," she replied, her tone light and teasing. "The bishop is a man of great wisdom and learning. His words have the power to uplift and inspire."

As if on cue, Miss Billy Breeze, the family's closest friend and confidante, joined the lively conversation, her presence bringing a sense of calm to the spirited banter. "Now, now, let us not quarrel over such trivial matters," she chided gently, her eyes twinkling with amusement. "We must learn to appreciate each other's interests, no matter how diverse they may be."

Ruth, always quick to seize an opportunity for amusement, turned her attention to the family dog, Petie Trone, who sat at her feet, his tail wagging in eager anticipation. "And what of you, Petie?" she asked, her voice lilting with affection. "Do you have any opinions on the bishop's sermons, or are you content to chase squirrels in the garden?"

The mention of Petie brought a smile to Mrs. Franklin's face, her fondness for the four-legged companion evident in the way she reached down to pat his head lovingly. "Ah, Petie Trone," she murmured, "you are truly the heart and soul of this family. You bring us so much joy and laughter, even in the midst of our daily trials and tribulations."

And so, as the sun began its slow descent behind the rolling hills, casting long shadows across the estate, the Franklin family sat together in peaceful harmony, united by love, laughter, and the enduring bonds of family. With each passing moment, their hearts were filled with gratitude for the simple pleasures of life, knowing that as long as they had each other, they would always find solace and joy in each other's company.

A room of majestic proportions; furnished with every conventional luxury that wealth and good taste can command; lavishly provided with newspapers of the day and books of reference, to afford the inquisitive and the idle a boundless field of occupation; lighted by tall windows, which shed a faint and mournful light on the assembled multitude, and by gorgeous chandeliers, which cast a dazzling radiance over the assembled throng; may be one of the dreariest places of rest and shelter that can be found on the civilised earth. Such places exist, by hundreds, in those hotels of monstrous proportions and pretensions, which now engulf the weary traveller who seeks a moment's peace and quiet in the midst of his journey.

In the midst of this vast and aimless crowd, two women sat in a remote corner of the room, shrinking from the notice and observation of their fellow-travellers. One, a woman of mature years, with a face that wore the impression of suffering and sorrow, sat in repose, her eyes cast down, and her thoughts apparently lost in the depths of a past that was irretrievable. Her companion, a young girl of seventeen, with a countenance that was anything but handsome, and yet, at the same time, possessed of a certain quiet charm which was irresistible. Her eyes, bright and expressive, sparkled with a lively intelligence, and her lips, thin and small, curved upwards in a rare and captivating smile, which seemed to soften the sharp lines of her features, and to impart to her whole face a look of pathos and interest. The girl's dark hair was drawn tightly back from her forehead, and her delicate features were accentuated by a pair of large, dark eyes, that seemed to gleam with a deep and unspoken meaning.

The older woman, who sat beside her, was a study in contrast to her younger companion. A woman of commanding presence, with an aquiline nose that seemed to be a replica of that of some great Duke of Wellington, and a stern, unyielding jaw, that seemed to be cast in a mould of unbroken determination. Her hair, graying at the temples, was drawn back from her face, and her eyes, like two bright points of steel, seemed to flash with a fierce and unyielding spirit. Her features, as she sat in the midst of the swirling crowd, seemed to be carved out of some stern and unyielding stone, that seemed to defy all impressions of softness, or gentleness, or compassion. And yet, as one gazed at her, a subtle change came over her face, and her eyes, like two soft pools of water, seemed to overflow with a deep and hidden emotion.

The younger girl, whose dark eyes seemed to be turned upon her elder companion with an inquiring gaze, seemed to be a living embodiment of all that was soft and gentle and pitiful in the human heart. Her features, sharp and delicate as they were, seemed to be set with a gentle, almost pathetically shy, smile, which seemed to convey a deep and silent message to those who looked upon her, and her eyes, bright and expressive as they were, seemed to hold within them a deep and mysterious significance, which seemed to defy all interpretation. As one gazed at her, a sudden pang seemed to run over the heart, a pang of sorrow, and of sympathy, and of unutterable compassion. It was as if one had caught a glimpse of some deep and unutterable sorrow, which seemed to be hidden beneath the surface of her quiet and reserved countenance.

And yet, as one gazed at her, another and a more striking feature seemed to emerge, namely, the deep and affectionate bond which seemed to exist between her and her elder companion. The older woman's face, stern and unyielding as it was, seemed to be softened by a deep and hidden tenderness, which seemed to be revealed in every glance, every gesture, which she made towards the younger girl. Her eyes, like two bright points of steel, seemed to flash with a fierce and unyielding spirit, but they were also gentle and kindly, and seemed to shine with a deep and unutterable love. And as one gazed at the two women, sitting in the midst of the swirling crowd, a sudden thought seemed to strike one, a thought of some deep and hidden past, which seemed to be connected with this younger girl, and with this older woman, and with the mysterious and unutterable bond which existed between them.

Expiring vouchers significantly influence consumer behavior and market dynamics by shaping buyers' decisions through both psychological phenomena and economic considerations. Consumers facing imminent voucher expiration often feel compelled to make purchases even if favorable pricing is unavailable, reflecting what behavioral economists term loss aversion—the preference to avoid losses rather than acquiring equivalent gains (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Consequently, buyers may opt for a purchase from sellers who do not necessarily offer the lowest market price, driven primarily by the desire to avoid missing out on the perceived value of the voucher, rather than rational price comparisons. For instance, consumers frequently purchase goods that they ordinarily would not choose just to utilize expiring coupons from platforms such as Groupon, indicating irrational spending behavior arising from urgency rather than genuine need or preference.

Such behavioral responses, however, vary significantly across individuals with different risk attitudes. Economic theory suggests that risk-neutral buyers usually weigh voucher expiration less emotionally, assessing strictly economic value and usage needs before proceeding with a purchase. In contrast, risk-loving consumers may actively embrace the uncertainty and novelty introduced by expiring vouchers, leading them to experiment more willingly, even if it means purchasing less familiar items or from less competitive sellers. Empirical observations of retail environments support this theoretical distinction—risk-seeking consumer segments, for example young adult demographics, are frequently targeted by limited-time promotions because their impulsivity and preference for novelty enhance voucher effectiveness.

Additionally, experimental studies examining voucher-driven purchasing have observed notable differences from real-world market conditions. For example, lab experiments typically reduce informational asymmetry by openly presenting sellers' prices, whereas in real-world scenarios, consumers must actively conduct price comparisons and evaluations. Without clear visibility into price distributions, real-world consumers face search costs that might further weaken their resistance to suboptimal purchasing when under psychological pressure from expiring promotions. Further complicating real-world circumstances, strategic pricing manipulations like those regularly employed by companies such as Dell—with well-known practices of raising base prices immediately prior to discounts—exacerbate informational imbalances. Such manipulations capitalize on buyers' cognitive biases, making them perceive discounts as more attractive than their true economic value.

Loyalty factors, though potentially significant in real-world retail environments, remain limited in controlled experimental settings due to participants' lack of ongoing relationship or familiarity with sellers. Pre-experiment communication among participants might temporarily influence loyalty factors; however, loyalty remains peripheral to the primary economic and behavioral mechanisms investigated. Predictably, real-world firms strategically exploit voucher-driven behavior through targeted pricing strategies, recognizing that consumer biases and urgency lead to purchasing decisions that contradict rational economic expectations. Taken together, expiring vouchers significantly affect markets beyond straightforward price considerations, highlighting the necessity for firms to incorporate psychological insights into strategic pricing, while consumers must remain aware of psychological influences driving their purchasing decisions.

“Come on in,” he said, persuasively. “I know you are mad, and you have every right to be after yore hard work from break o' day till now; but nobody kin depend on women. Mandy's been makin' yore ma a hat all day. Flowery gewgaws an' grub don't go together.”

Paul came out. “Never mind,” he said. “It don't make no difference. Anything will do.” Father and son walked side by side into the fire-lighted kitchen. A clothless table holding a few dishes and pans stood in the center of the room. Just outside the door, on a little roofless porch, there was a shelf which held a tin basin, a cedar pail containing water, and a gourd dipper with a long, curved handle. And going to this shelf, Paul filled the basin and bathed his face and hands, after which he turned to a soiled towel on a roller against the weatherboarding and wiped himself dry, raking back his rebellious hair with a bit of a comb, while his father stood close by watching him with the gaze of an affectionate dog.

“That'll do, that'll do,” Ralph attempted to jest. “Thar ain't no company here for you to put on airs before. Set down! set down!”

Paul obeyed, and his father remained smoking in the doorway, still eying him with attentive consideration. Amanda brought from the fire a frying-pan containing the hot, bubbling mush, and pushed an empty brown bowl and spoon toward him.

“Help yoreself; thar's the milk in the pan,” she said. “If it is too sour you might stir a spoonful o' 'lasses in it. I've heard folks say it helps a sight.”

Paul was still angry, but he said nothing, and helped himself abundantly to the mush. However, he sniffed audibly as he lifted the pan and poured some of the thin, bluish fluid into his bowl.

“It wasn't my fault about the cow,” Amanda contended. “Scorchin' weather like this is the dickens on dumb brutes. Sook was a-pawin' an' switchin' 'er tail all the time I had hold of 'er tits. It must 'a' been a stingin' fly that got in a tender spot. Bang, bang! was all the warnin' I had, an' I found myself soaked from head to foot with milk. I've heard o' fine society folks, queens an' the like, washin' all over in it to soften their skins and limber their joints; but I don't need nothin' o' that sort. Yore ma's not back yet. She went over to see about the singin'-class they want her in. She had on 'er best duds an' new hat, and looked like a gal o' twenty. She was as frisky as a young colt. I ironed 'er pink sash, an' put in a little starch to mash out the wrinkles and make it stand stiff-like. They all say she's got the best alto in Grayson. I rolled 'er hair up in papers last night, an' tuck it down to-day. You never saw sech pretty kinks in your life. Jeff Warren come to practise their duet, an' him and Addie stood out in the yard an' run the scales an' sung several pieces together. It sounded fine, an' if I had ever had any use for 'im I'd have enjoyed it more; but I never could abide 'im. He gits in too many fights, and got gay too quick after he buried his wife. He was dressed as fine as a fiddle, an' had a joke for every minute. Folks say he never loved Susie, an' I reckon they wasn't any too well matched. She never had a well day in 'er life, and I reckon it was a blessed thing she was took. A tenor voice an' a dandy appearance are pore consolations to a dyin' woman. But he treats women polite--I'll say that for 'im.”

Paul had finished his mush and milk, and helped himself to the cold string-beans and fat boiled pork. His father had reached for a chair, tilted it against the door-jamb, and seated himself in it. He eyed his son as if the boy's strength and rugged health were consoling reminders of his own adolescence. Suddenly, out of the still twilight which brooded over the fields and meadows and swathed the mountain-tops, came the blending voices of two singers. It was a familiar hymn, and its rendition was not unmelodious, for it held a sweet, mystic quality that vaguely appealed.

“Bah!” spat LeNoir, “Dat beeg Macdonald I mak heem run like one leetle sheep, one tam at de long Sault, bah! No good!” LeNoir's contempt for Macdonald was genuine and complete. For two years he had tried to meet the boss Macdonald, but his rival had always avoided him.

Meantime, the pointer came swinging along. As it turned the point the boy uttered an exclamation--“Look there!” The song and the rowing stopped abruptly; the big, dark man stood up and gazed down the river, packed from bank to bank with the brown saw-logs; deep curses broke from him. Then he caught sight of the men on the bank. A word of command and the pointer shot into the shore, and the next moment Macdonald Dubh, or Black Hugh, as he was sometimes called, followed by his men, was climbing up the steep bank.

“What the blank, blank, do these logs mean, Murphy?” he demanded, without pause for salutation.

“Tis a foine avenin' Misther Macdonald,” said Murphy, blandly offering his hand, “an' Hiven bliss ye.”

Macdonald checked himself with an effort and reluctantly shook hands with Murphy and LeNoir, whom he slightly knew. “It is a fery goot evening, indeed,” he said, in as quiet a voice as he could command, “but I am inquiring about these logs.”

“Shure, an' it is a dhry night, and onpolite to kape yez talking here. Come in wid yez,” and much against his will Black Hugh followed Murphy to the tavern, the most pretentious of a group of log buildings--once a lumber camp--which stood back a little distance from the river, and about which Murphy's men, some sixty of them, were now camped.

The tavern was full of Murphy's gang, a motley crew, mostly French Canadians and Irish, just out of the woods and ready for any devilment that promised excitement. Most of them knew by sight, and all by reputation, Macdonald and his gang, for from the farthest reaches of the Ottawa down the St. Lawrence to Quebec the Macdonald gang of Glengarry men was famous. They came, most of them, from that strip of country running back from the St. Lawrence through Glengarry County, known as the Indian Lands--once an Indian reservation. They were sons of the men who had come from the highlands and islands of Scotland in the early years of the last century. Driven from homes in the land of their fathers, they had set themselves with indomitable faith and courage to hew from the solid forest, homes for themselves and their children that none might take from them. These pioneers were bound together by ties of blood, but also by bonds stronger than those of blood. Their loneliness, their triumphs, their sorrows, born of their common life-long conflict with the forest and its fierce beasts, knit them in bonds close and enduring. The sons born to them and reared in the heart of the pine forests grew up to witness that heroic struggle with stern nature and to take their part in it. And mighty men they were. Their life bred in them hardiness of frame, alertness of sense, readiness of resource, endurance, superb self-reliance, a courage that grew with peril, and withal a certain wildness which at times deepened into ferocity. By their fathers the forest was dreaded and hated, but the sons, with rifles in hand, trod its pathless stretches without fear, and with their broad-axes they took toll of their ancient foe. For while in spring and summer they farmed their narrow fields, and rescued new lands from the brule; in winter they sought the forest, and back on their own farms or in “the shanties” they cut sawlogs, or made square timber, their only source of wealth. The shanty life of the early fifties of last century was not the luxurious thing of to-day. It was full of privation, for the men were poorly housed and fed, and of peril, for the making of the timber and the getting it down the smaller rivers to the big water was a work of hardship and danger. Remote from the restraints of law and of society, and living in wild surroundings and in hourly touch with danger, small wonder that often the shanty-men were wild and reckless. So that many a poor fellow in a single wild carouse in Quebec, or more frequently in some river town, would fling into the hands of sharks and harlots and tavern-keepers, with whom the bosses were sometimes in league, the earnings of his long winter's work, and would wake to find himself sick and penniless, far from home and broken in spirit.

Debate Rages on in Washington D.C. Over Additional Stimulus Money for American Families, Child Tax Credit Payments in Limbo

BALTIMORE (WBFF/WKRC) – The debate in Washington D.C. over additional stimulus money for American families continues, with discussions centered around the Child Tax Credit (CTC) payments that were expanded under the American Rescue Plan.

Previous COVID-19 relief bills included stimulus payments of $1,200, $600, and $1,400 for eligible individuals, with the last signed into law by President Biden in March 2021. The American Rescue Plan took things a step further by expanding the federal Child Tax Credit, providing direct payments to families.

Under this expansion, families receive $300 for each child under 6 and $250 for each child ages 6 to 17 between July and December of 2021. For instance, a family with one child under 6 will receive $1,800 by December 2021 through the advanced payments.

Families not normally required to file a tax return could still benefit if they notified the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) by November 15, 2021. These eligible families will receive half of their total Child Tax Credit in a single payment on December 15, 2021. The potential one-time payments are up to $1,800 for each child under 6 and up to $1,500 for each child ages 6 to 17.

The future of the expanded Child Tax Credit is uncertain, with the Biden administration aiming to make it permanent. However, Democratic Senator Joe Manchin from West Virginia has expressed his desire to make changes to the CTC payments. Manchin is advocating for modifications that would limit the number of eligible children per family and cap the total amount of the payment.

Manchin's proposal comes as an attempt to address concerns over inflation and deficit spending. The Senator's stance is in contrast to the Biden administration's plans to make the expanded CTC a permanent feature.

President Biden's Build Back Better agenda, which includes extending the expanded Child Tax Credit through 2025, faces an uphill battle in the Senate due to the closely divided chamber. The ongoing negotiations among Democrats could impact the future of these payments and the financial assistance they provide to millions of American families.

Families eagerly await the outcome of these discussions, hoping for continued support during these challenging economic times. The uncertainty surrounding the Child Tax Credit payments adds to the financial stress felt by many households across the United States.

Both sides of the debate argue for the best interests of American families and the nation's economic recovery. As the negotiations continue, it remains to be seen what the future holds for the expanded Child Tax Credit and the relief it provides to millions of families.

You begin your journey toward better health by understanding the intricacies of cholesterol management and recognizing that every decision you make can positively influence your wellbeing. You learn that cholesterol, a fatty substance necessary for cell structure, can also contribute to heart disease when levels become unbalanced. Phytosterols, naturally occurring compounds in plants, bind to cholesterol in your digestive system and help excrete it, reducing overall cholesterol levels. Have you ever wondered how nature can offer solutions that work in tandem with modern science? Embracing these natural compounds gives you hope and reinforces the idea that proactive, informed health choices pave the way for a brighter future.

You soon discover that supplements like Vasacor play a valuable role in cholesterol management by lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels—the so-called "bad" cholesterol—and increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL), the "good" cholesterol. When you combine these phytosterol supplements with a balanced, lower-fat, high-fiber diet and regular exercise, you often see better results compared to relying solely on diet and exercise. This approach underlines the importance of a multifaceted strategy when addressing complex health issues. Can you imagine the enhanced benefits of utilizing both natural compounds and lifestyle modifications to boost your cardiovascular health? This integrated method provides not just hope but tangible progress toward your health goals.

As you continue exploring cholesterol management, you meet statins—medications known scientifically as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. These drugs work by inhibiting a key enzyme in the pathway of cholesterol synthesis, thereby reducing overall cholesterol production in your liver. While statins are powerful allies in reducing cholesterol levels, their use carries potential risks, including muscle breakdown—a condition called myopathy—and even possible kidney failure in severe cases. When faced with such risks, you naturally wonder: is the benefit of further lowering cholesterol worth the risk of these side effects? It becomes clear that a well-informed discussion with your healthcare provider is essential to weigh the benefits and drawbacks in light of your individual health profile.

Switching gears, you also learn about Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS), a condition that is far more debilitating than a simple bout of drowsiness. EDS leads you to experience severe fatigue during the day, impacting your energy levels and concentration, and even causing cognitive changes that impair daily activities. This condition challenges you to consider the quality of your sleep and the broader implications for your mental and physical health. Imagine needing excessive amounts of sleep and still feeling tired—this is the reality of EDS for many. Recognizing EDS as a serious health issue, rather than a minor inconvenience, inspires you to assess your lifestyle and seek appropriate interventions, as sound sleep is a cornerstone of overall health.

In the end, your journey emphasizes the interconnectedness of various health factors. By combining a holistic approach to cholesterol management—with options ranging from phytosterol supplements and Vasacor to lifestyle changes and, when necessary, statins—with vigilant attention to sleep disorders like EDS, you equip yourself with a comprehensive toolkit for improved health. Every step you take, every informed decision you make, builds a foundation for a healthier, more energized future. Isn’t it encouraging to know that with knowledge and thoughtful action, you hold the key to a better quality of life? Embrace this journey with optimism, for every positive change today contributes to a healthier tomorrow.

Kamala Harris to chair the National Space Council

CNN — The Biden administration will maintain the National Space Council and Vice President Kamala Harris will chair it, according to senior administration officials, adding another item to the vice president’s portfolio.

Harris confirmed her new role on Saturday, writing in a tweet, “As I’ve said before: In America, when we shoot for the moon, we plant our flag on it. I am honored to lead our National Space Council.”

Harris “intends to put her own personal stamp on the Council,” a senior administration official said. The official listed her personal priorities as STEM education, cybersecurity, supporting sustainable development of commercial space activity, diversity in the workforce and advancing peaceful norms and responsible behaviors in space, among others.

The National Space Council was led by Harris’ predecessor Vice President Mike Pence during the Trump administration. President Donald Trump had revived the council in 2017 by executive order and later, called for the creation of a “Space Force” that would create a sixth branch of the armed services.

Officials contend that for now, the National Space Council will operate under that same executive order from 2017 and haven’t made a decision whether changes are necessary but intend to review it.

As was the case for past space councils, the latest iteration will assist the President in generating national space policies and strategies and in synchronizing America’s civil commercial and national security space activities, officials said.

“In other words, the council’s basic objectives: national security, basic science, technological development, contributions to US economic growth and the commercial sector will all be maintained,” one official said.

Asked to identify the difference between Harris’ upcoming tenure and Pence’s, one official said: “I’ll just say without drawing too much of a contrast, I think her approach to this is just going to be to get the job done and use this to lead our space policy. And not really focus, perhaps, as much on big displays, but on getting the work done.”

Senior officials would not list where chairing the National Space Council lies among Harris’ other portfolio priorities, which now include leading diplomatic efforts to stem the flow of migrants in the Northern Triangle and the administration’s efforts to expand broadband high-speed internet.

“She’s got a lot on her plate, as was originally said, and this is just one more big task that she is taking on because it’s important. It’s important to the President, and the country,” the official said.

The vice president will swear in newly confirmed NASA administrator Bill Nelson on Monday.

Harris, as vice president, has engaged repeatedly with members from NASA – speaking with astronauts Shannon Walker and Kate Rubins virtually to mark Women’s History Month in March, as well as with astronaut Victor Glover in February.

The process of finding a civilian executive secretary, who would be appointed by the President, is still ongoing, official said.

There’s no official date for the first formal meeting of the National Space Council, but senior administration officials said Harris will get started soon.

Instagram User Claims to Have Witnessed Heated Argument Between Gabby Petito and Brian Laundrie in Wyoming Restaurant

An Instagram user (@NinaCelie) has shared a story about an encounter she and her boyfriend had at the Merry Piglett's Mexican Grill in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on August 27, 2021. According to Celie, they witnessed a heated argument between a couple they believe to be Gabby Petito and Brian Laundrie.

Celie's boyfriend, who has a "photographic memory," recalled the incident days later and recognized the couple from news reports. He described the man as "violently talking to the hostess" and "relentless" in his anger. The restaurant staff ultimately asked the couple to leave.

Celie's account aligns with the established timeline of Petito's disappearance. The last confirmed communication between Petito and her mother occurred on August 25th. Laundrie returned home alone in Petito's van on September 1st.

While Celie's story cannot be independently verified, it adds another potential piece to the puzzle surrounding Petito's disappearance. The FBI continues to seek information from anyone who may have seen the couple between August 27th and 30th, 2021.
