In public school, I felt as if I were a complete outcast, alone and unable to reach out to anyone around me; others made fun of me because I was poor, because I didn’t dress right, because I was different from them. I became cynical towards the world, and found myself completely apathetic toward schoolwork, having friends, and making goals for myself. I began to drink and smoke cigarettes at the age of thirteen, turning to alcohol as my mother before me, as I believed it was my only option to ameliorate the hopelessness of my dire situation. Even though I had been a bright, gifted student in elementary school, as my grades slipped I lost confidence in myself. When I went to PACE, at first I was skeptical; I couldn’t see how the school could help me, but instead worried I would become even more of a social pariah.

However, after a few months at PACE my natural outgoing self reappeared. I was able to confide in Mr. Michael, my counselor, about what was troubling me at home and my feelings. He always received my conversations in a positive, supportive manner, listening to what I said. For the first time I could remember, I actually had a voice. As we talked more and more, he helped me work through some of my problems and issues. I credit him as one of the biggest influences of my renewed interest in myself and in my schooling. I also grew more comfortable talking with my teachers. One teacher, Ms. Courtney, had such a funny and off-beat personality and was well-liked by many students. Ms. Courtney was a positive role model, and she showed me that I could be an individual, unique person and still be likable. The entire staff at PACE seeks to make compassion one of their utmost concerns; you just do not get that kind of an environment anywhere else. After a while I truly began to think of some of my teachers and mentors as extended family in a way; they cared about my triumphs, believed in my dreams, and gave me unconditional love and acceptance. They gave me what I didn’t have at home: someone to look up to.

Concentrating on my schoolwork was again possible because I didn’t feel like I was in a hostile environment as I had experienced in public school. I even made friends at PACE with a few of the girls. I found some like-minded individuals that did not judge me, but instead accepted me for who I was. I believe that the PACE environment helps to foster a feeling of sisterhood between young women, a feeling of belonging.

PACE tries to incorporate a sense of togetherness into their daily activities; for example, Spirited Girls, a class that PACE offered which resembled a life management skills class, gave you a journal to write down your thoughts and feelings in and the opportunity to share your entry with the rest of the class or teacher if you chose to do so.

The darkness of the night was still profound, the wind howling with a mournful sound, as Liem King and Than Khan followed the winding course of the small river Tjatjing, their footsteps quiet on the damp earth. The faint moon, now and then, cast a silver glow upon the rippling waters, but it was a feeble light, and served only to render the surrounding shadows more opaque.

As they walked, the low moaning sound, which had first attracted their attention, grew louder, and seemed to come from a point not far distant. The two Celestials exchanged a glance, their eyes gleaming with curiosity, and quickened their pace, their hands on the hilts of their krises. The sound, though low, was unmistakable, a mournful cry, like the wail of some lost spirit, and it sent a shiver down their spines.

The river Tjatjing, narrow and deep, wound its way through a dense thicket of mangroves, the trees towering above them, their branches creaking and swaying in the wind. The air was heavy with the scent of wet earth and decaying leaves, and the two men breathed it in deeply, their senses on the alert. Suddenly, the moaning sound ceased, and an oppressive silence fell, like a pall, over the scene.

Liem King and Than Khan stopped, their ears straining to catch the slightest sound, but there was nothing, only the wind rustling through the leaves, and the distant rumble of the surf. They looked at each other, their faces set, and moved cautiously forward, their eyes scanning the darkness. The river narrowed, and the trees grew closer together, forming a tunnel of foliage, through which the men made their way, their krises at the ready.

As they walked, the silence was broken by the sound of lapping water, and the creaking of wooden planks. Liem King and Than Khan exchanged a glance, and crept forward, their hearts beating faster. A boat, half-hidden in the shadows, rocked gently on the water, its occupants, if there were any, invisible. The two men approached cautiously, their senses on the alert, and peered into the darkness.

The boat, a small, native prau, was empty, but it had evidently been recently occupied, for a faint scent of tobacco and opium hung about it. Liem King and Than Khan looked at each other, their faces grave, and searched the surrounding trees, but there was no sign of life. The moaning sound, the boat, all seemed to point to some mysterious and sinister presence, lurking just out of sight.

Suddenly, a faint cry, like the cry of a bird, but human, pierced the night air, and Liem King and Than Khan started, their nerves on edge. The cry was repeated, louder, and the two men moved swiftly towards the sound, their krises flashing in the moonlight. As they ran, the cry grew louder, and they could distinguish words, a faint, despairing cry for help.

The trees grew closer together, and the undergrowth thicker, as the two men pushed their way through the thicket. The cry grew louder still, and they could tell that it came from a point not far distant. Suddenly, they burst through the trees, and found themselves on the edge of a small clearing. In the center of the clearing, a figure, bound and helpless, lay on the ground, a look of desperation in its eyes.

Liem King and Than Khan rushed forward, their krises raised, ready to strike, but as they approached the figure, they saw that it was a woman, a native girl, with a look of terror in her eyes. She struggled and cried out, as they approached, but Liem King and Than Khan quickly freed her from her bonds, and stood over her, their faces stern.

The girl looked up at them, her eyes wide with fear, and Liem King and Than Khan could see that she was trembling with terror. They spoke to her softly, in gentle tones, and slowly, she began to calm down, her sobs growing less frequent. As she looked up at them, Liem King and Than Khan saw that she was young, and beautiful, with a look of innocence in her eyes.

The girl, still trembling, told them her story, of how she had been kidnapped, by a band of smugglers, and brought to this place. She had managed to escape, but had been caught, and bound, and left to die. Liem King and Than Khan listened, their faces grave, and when she finished, they stood up, their krises still clutched in their hands.

As they stood there, they heard a sound, a faint rustling in the undergrowth, and they turned, their eyes scanning the darkness. The girl, still trembling, clung to Liem King's arm, and he patted her hand, reassuringly. The sound grew louder, and they could tell that it was the sound of footsteps, heavy and deliberate.

Liem King and Than Khan moved forward, their krises at the ready, and the girl clung to Liem King's arm, her eyes wide with fear. As they walked, the footsteps grew louder, and they could tell that they were being approached, by a group of men, their intentions unknown. The darkness seemed to grow thicker, and the air heavier, as they waited, their senses on the alert.

Suddenly, a group of figures, emerged from the trees, their faces sinister, and their eyes gleaming with malice. Liem King and Than Khan stood firm, their krises flashing in the moonlight, and the girl clung to Liem King's arm, her eyes wide with terror.

After this each took up a volume, and until teatime they read quietly.

From six to nine in the evening they again talked and read alternately. Their conversation was now retrospective; each revived memories of what she had endured in one or the other house of bondage. Never had it been their lot to serve 'really nice' people--this phrase of theirs was anything but meaningless. They had lived with more or less well-to-do families in the lower middle class--people who could not have inherited refinement, and had not acquired any, neither proletarians nor gentlefolk, consumed with a disease of vulgar pretentiousness, inflated with the miasma of democracy. It would have been but a natural result of such a life if the sisters had commented upon it in a spirit somewhat akin to that of their employers; but they spoke without rancour, without scandalmongering. They knew themselves superior to the women who had grudgingly paid them, and often smiled at recollections which would have moved the servile mind to venomous abuse.

At nine o'clock they took a cup of cocoa and a biscuit, and half an hour later they went to bed. Lamp oil was costly; and indeed they felt glad to say as early as possible that another day had gone by.

Their hour of rising was eight. Mrs. Conisbee provided hot water for their breakfast. On descending to fetch it, Virginia found that the postman had left a letter for her. The writing on the envelope seemed to be a stranger's. She ran upstairs again in excitement.

'Who can this be from, Alice?'

The elder sister had one of her headaches this morning; she was clay colour, and tottered in moving about. The close atmosphere of the bedroom would alone have accounted for such a malady. But an unexpected letter made her for the moment oblivious of suffering.

'Posted in London,' she said, examining the envelope eagerly.

'Some one you have been in correspondence with?'

'It's months since I wrote to any one in London.'

For full five minutes they debated the mystery, afraid of dashing their hopes by breaking the envelope. At length Virginia summoned courage. Standing at a distance from the other, she took out the sheet of paper with tremulous hand, and glanced fearfully at the signature.

'What do you think? It's Miss Nunn!'

'Miss Nunn! Never! How could she have got the address?'

Again the difficulty was discussed whilst its ready solution lay neglected.

'Do read it!' said Alice at length, her throbbing head, made worse by the agitation, obliging her to sink down into the chair.

The letter ran thus:--

'DEAR Miss MADDEN,--This morning I chanced to meet with Mrs. Darby, who was passing through London on her way home from the seaside. We had only five minutes' talk (it was at a railway station), but she mentioned that you were at present in London, and gave me your address. After all these years, how glad I should be to see you! The struggle of life has made me selfish; I have neglected my old friends. And yet I am bound to add that some of them have neglected me. Would you rather that I came to your lodgings or you to mine? Which you like. I hear that your elder sister is with you, and that Monica is also in London somewhere. Do let us all see each other once more. Write as soon as you can. My kindest regards to all of you.--Sincerely yours,

RHODA NUNN.'

'How like her,' exclaimed Virginia, when she had read this aloud, 'to remember that perhaps we may not care to receive visitors! She was always so thoughtful. And it is true that I ought to have written to her.'

How curious it is that a family, as close and candid as families may be, can find it needful and possible to hold secrets from one another, as though some fragile treasure threatened to dissolve under prying gazes or grow distorted in careless hands. The eldest daughter's first romance—a bright, glittering, incongruous marvel set amidst schooling, needlework, trivial quarrels and girlish ambitions—seemed precisely such a guarded and uncertain secret, yet the secrecy was futile, the veil worn all too thin. Eleanor's eyes held stories they no longer fully concealed, a new soft melody humming at her lips, a rosier colour dancing upon her cheeks when no other explanation could avail, betraying to each sister, no matter how young or heedless, that something entirely new and important had begun among them.

It is amusing to observe the pretended blindness which parents and elder sisters affect, attempting to deny or at least delay acknowledging this drastic innovation in the familiar order of things. They speak no word openly, as if speech alone could grant the event full authority, yet their careful silences and glances betray more knowledge than conversation ever would. A proposal once uttered, even in utmost secrecy or whispered in a moonlit garden shaded by boughs and quieted by nightingales, has an uncanny method of resonating throughout the house. Such a declaration touches the girls' hearts directly, invisibly, causing them to thrill with inexplicable hope or shiver with dread, though at the first, they barely comprehend its nature or its source. A new dignity clothes the lucky recipient, mingling strangely with her confusion and self-consciousness, drawing her nearer to their parents' serious, careful world and evolving her tastes, her choices, her accustomed merry talk.

Yet let none suppose wealth or poverty to be the true arbiters of this curious moment. Opulence, widely imagined the charmer that throws open the doors of life's greatest excitements and freedom, accomplishes precious little on romance's behalf. Nor, indeed, does proud poverty, in all its quiet resilience, render a young girl more aware of love's secrets, except, perhaps, by shortening childhood's sweet illusions and hastening the deeper intensities of feeling. Yet it is not money but youth itself, that tender, artless innocence, which romance most affects. Starched pinafores and braided hair soon give way to gowns and artful coiffures at the very first hint of romance; simple books and childish rhymes give place to sensitive poetry, sonnets and melancholy songs; childish laughter rang louder than ever, yet was somehow a degree more forced in Eleanor’s presence. Wealth had not shaped her impatience for womanhood, nor poverty caused her sobered contemplations, but falling in love itself had gently disenfranchised the happy carelessness of an earlier age.

As was ever the case in large families of girls, the younger sisters were to be sheltered with painstaking attention from all this sentimentality, from whispers of romance that might prove distracting or unsettling. Carefully, the reins were drawn; maternal caution placed upon lips honest but opaque words, ringing faintly hollow in the ears of bright listeners who could not yet clearly divine their father's sudden gravity or their mother's gentler advice, though they felt the significance plainly as their elders loosened bits of conversation just enough to incite—and frustrate—their curiosity. And yet, no sternest vigilance, no most guarded whispering between parents at nightfall, prevented news from trickling slowly, softly, gleefully down the little chain of sisters, from fourteen-year-old Abigail, sober-eyed and wise, to eleven-year-old delightful Flora, whose secret giggles betrayed immediate comprehension, to little Clara aged just eight, who tugged continually at skirts to ask why Eleanor's eyes glowed so prettily in candlelight, and why she wandered dreamily under the blossoming orchard alone.

There arose in consequence a confusing mixture of protection and teasing, envy tempered by pride. Eleanor stirred something marvellous, something inspirational, among her younger sisters—who gazed at her shyly, yet mischievously whispered behind closed doors; who wavered between great admiration for the lover who courted their sister so gravely and unabashed laughter at his stiff collar and solemn bowing. The very house itself seemed now to tremble and throb delicately, expectantly, upon the threshold of tremendous changes: new attachments, new rooms soon emptier, airy talk of wedding dresses and bridal preparations; and Eleanor herself, scarcely understanding her own restless sentiments, soon found herself wandering toward fond remembrance of simpler games in the nursery and wistful awareness of that curious, thrilling sadness of growing suddenly older, which nothing but this new heartbeat, charmingly troubling, could ever have produced.

Of these young women, one had an olive complexion, with the red blood mantling under it, and black hair, and glorious black eyebrows.

The other was fair, with a massive but shapely throat, as white as milk; glossy brown hair, the loose threads of which glittered like gold, and a blue eye, which, being contrasted with dark eyebrows and lashes, took the luminous effect peculiar to that rare beauty.

Their short petticoats revealed a neat ankle, and a leg with a noble swell; for Nature, when she is in earnest, builds beauty on the ideas of ancient sculptors and poets, not of modern poetasters, who, with their airy-like sylphs and their smoke-like verses, fight for want of flesh in woman and want of fact in poetry as parallel beauties.

They are, my lads.--Continuez!

These women had a grand corporeal trait; they had never known a corset! so they were straight as javelins; they could lift their hands above their heads!--actually! Their supple persons moved as Nature intended; every gesture was ease, grace and freedom.

What with their own radiance, and the snowy cleanliness and brightness of their costume, they came like meteors into the apartment.

Lord Ipsden, rising gently from his seat, with the same quiet politeness with which he would have received two princes of the blood, said, “How do you do?” and smiled a welcome.

“Fine! hoow's yoursel?” answered the dark lass, whose name was Jean Carnie, and whose voice was not so sweet as her face.

“What'n lord are ye?” continued she; “are you a juke? I wad like fine to hae a crack wi' a juke.”

Saunders, who knew himself the cause of this question, replied, sotto voce, “His lordship is a viscount.”

“I didna ken't,” was Jean's remark. “But it has a bonny soond.”

“What mair would ye hae?” said the fair beauty, whose name was Christie Johnstone. Then, appealing to his lordship as the likeliest to know, she added, “Nobeelity is jist a soond itsel, I'm tauld.”

The viscount, finding himself expected to say something on a topic he had not attended much to, answered dryly: “We must ask the republicans, they are the people that give their minds to such subjects.”

“And yon man,” asked Jean Carnie, “is he a lord, too?”

“I am his lordship's servant,” replied Saunders, gravely, not without a secret misgiving whether fate had been just.

“Na!” replied she, not to be imposed upon, “ye are statelier and prooder than this ane.”

“I will explain,” said his master. “Saunders knows his value; a servant like Saunders is rarer than an idle viscount.”

“My lord, my lord!” remonstrated Saunders, with a shocked and most disclamatory tone. “Rather!” was his inward reflection.

“Jean,” said Christie, “ye hae muckle to laern. Are ye for herrin' the day, vile count?”

“No! are you for this sort of thing?”

At this, Saunders, with a world of empressement, offered the Carnie some cake that was on the table.

She took a piece, instantly spat it out into her hand, and with more energy than delicacy flung it into the fire.

“Augh!” cried she, “just a sugar and saut butter thegither; buy nae mair at yon shoep, vile count.”

“Try this, out of Nature's shop,” laughed their entertainer; and he offered them, himself, some peaches and things.

“Hech! a medi--cine!” said Christie.

“Nature, my lad,” said Miss Carnie, making her ivory teeth meet in their first nectarine, “I didna ken whaur ye stoep, but ye beat the other confectioners, that div ye.”

The fair lass, who had watched the viscount all this time as demurely as a cat cream, now approached him.

This young woman was the thinker; her voice was also rich, full, and melodious, and her manner very engaging; it was half advancing, half retiring, not easy to resist or to describe.

The left hemisphere of the brain is responsible for analysis, while the right hemisphere of the brain is responsible for recognizing patterns. Evidence from numerous studies show that one hemisphere of the brain may be preferred over another in an individual, known as hemispheric preference. Cerebral lateralization affects the way an individual learns, especially through self-esteem and emotional states, which correlate with academic success. Researchers suggest that negative emotional states engage the right hemisphere of the brain more than the left hemisphere of the brain. Hemispheric preference also affects the way individuals learn. Modern schools are structured more toward educating individuals who are predominantly left-hemisphere preferred (mainly girls), and because of that, right hemisphere preferred individuals (mainly boys) are uncomfortable and have a tendency to act out. In order to help students achieve academic success, Beck describes three learning style inventories (LSI) to help teachers better educate all their students: the 4MAT System, Dunn’s LSI, and Renzulli and Smith’s LSI. Sonnier and Sonnier conclude that affective education is necessary to ensure a nurturing learning environment for students.

Inaccurate Initial Police Reports a Common Issue, Experts Say

PHILADELPHIA (AP) – The recent conviction of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd has brought renewed attention to the issue of inaccurate initial police reports, particularly in fatal encounters.

According to criminal justice experts, the omission of critical details in the initial police statement on Floyd's death is not an isolated incident. "Inaccurate initial police reports are a common issue," said Andre Johnson, Professor of Communication Studies at the University of Memphis. "It's a systemic problem that needs to be addressed."

Social media has played a significant role in highlighting discrepancies between initial police statements and video evidence. In the case of George Floyd, the initial police statement mentioned "medical distress" but failed to mention that Chauvin had pinned Floyd's neck for more than nine minutes. The statement was recirculated on social media after Chauvin's conviction, sparking outrage and calls for transparency.

Video evidence from bystanders has been crucial in revealing the truth in several high-profile cases, including Eric Garner's and Walter Scott's deaths. "Video evidence has been a game-changer in holding police accountable," said Johnson. "It's allowed us to see what really happened, rather than relying solely on police narratives."

The use of body cameras has become more widespread, with about 80% of large police departments now using them. However, storage costs are high, and footage release can be delayed. Nevertheless, video evidence has shown discrepancies in police narratives, sometimes leading to convictions, as in the case of Laquan McDonald.

In response to public outcry and demands for transparency, police and prosecutors have recently trended towards releasing body camera footage more swiftly. In Columbus, Ohio, body camera footage was quickly released after the fatal shooting of 16-year-old Ma’Khia Bryant, diverging from their usual protocol. Similarly, in Knoxville, Tennessee, body camera footage of Anthony J. Thompson Jr.'s shooting was released after public pressure, contradicting initial statements.

Minneapolis police spokesperson John Elder acknowledged that the initial statement on Floyd's death was inaccurate but was unable to correct it immediately. "We recognize that the initial statement did not fully capture the events that occurred," Elder said. "We are committed to transparency and will continue to work to ensure that our statements accurately reflect the facts."

In conclusion, the issue of inaccurate initial police reports is a systemic problem that requires attention and action. The use of body cameras and the release of footage can help to increase transparency and accountability. As the public continues to demand truth and justice, police departments and prosecutors must work to address these concerns and ensure that their statements accurately reflect the facts.

As the soldiers walked off, gesticulating as if at any moment they would throw their caps down and fight it out, in came my father, took up the letter, pulled out his glasses, and having read a little, called out--

“Charlie, here’s news for you.”

“GROVE END, UPDOWN, “May --, 18--.

“MY DEAR BROTHER,

“I was very glad to get your letter, for, guessing roughly, I should say it is not a day less than four years since I last heard from you. You hate the sea; yet you managed to cross the Channel once; can’t you cross it again and spend a few weeks with us?”

(My father shook his head.)

“I can give you some capital Burgundy, my cook knows her work, and though society here is rather drab-coloured, I can pick you out enough people to keep you well stocked with rubbers.”

(“He would have to entertain a corpse,” said my father. “The crossing would kill me--especially if it were calm--for then all the filth of the engine-room is tasted.”)

“And now to business,” continued the letter. “You want to place your son. Would he like to be a banker’s clerk?”

(“No,” said I; but my father took no notice.)

“One of my clerks is leaving me. His salary is £100. I will make it £150 for your son, if he will come. He can either live in lodgings or with us. He may prefer the former; but I think he will find our house more comfortable than any apartments he can get at Updown. The place will be vacant next week, and he can join when he likes.

“Richard was with me last month.”

(“Poor Dick!” said my father; “we haven’t met for twenty years!”)

“Do you know that he has changed his quarters, and purchased an estate at Shandon?”

(“Tom told me that Dick had retired on £40,000,” said my father, looking at me over his glasses.)

“He has grown very corpulent, and hankers after his old trade. A gain of £10 makes him giddy with joy; and he will forget, amid his transports, that he lost a hundred or more last account. His daughter Theresa has grown a fine woman. I shall be curious to see your son, who scarcely reached to my knee when I last saw him.

“My wife and Constance send all manner of kind messages.

“Believe me, dear Charles, “Your affectionate brother, “THOMAS HARGRAVE.”

“What is all this about?” said I.

“About?” cried my father: “why, about you.”

“What made you write? You didn’t tell me you had done so.”

“Because I wasn’t sure that anything would come of it. Why, this is from your uncle Tom. Didn’t you know you had such an uncle?”

“Of course I knew--but what made you write?”

“I’ll tell you,” answered my father, pulling off his glasses. “Last Monday evening I had a talk with Harris at the Club. Harris is a man I respect. I consider Harris,” said my father with emphasis, “an honest man. He spoke of you. ‘Major,’ said he, ‘I think Charlie is too fine a fellow to be allowed to run to seed in a place like this?’ ‘I’ll own, Harris,’ said I, ‘that it has sometimes struck me my son might be doing better.’ He then asked me, why I didn’t get you into some house of business in London. This sort of questions are very easily put. There’s no difficulty in asking a subaltern why he isn’t a field-marshal, or a poor man why he don’t invent something wonderful, and make a fortune. ‘The fact is,’ said I, ‘I have no interest in the City. I don’t think,’ I said, quite forgetting my brother Tom for the moment, ‘that I have a single friend in business.’ ‘Well, major,’ said Harris, ‘your boy and I are old friends: he’s a thorough Englishman and a gentleman, and has done nothing that I can see to deserve expatriation. I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I have a brother----’ ‘Faith Harris,’ said I, ‘I am truly obliged to you, but I can’t permit you to do for me what it is my duty, at all events, to try to do for myself. You’ve reminded me that I, too, have a brother who owns a private bank. By George!’”--(my father always swore like a gentleman)--“‘I’ll write to him! I have never asked either of my brothers a favour in my life; and I don’t suppose Tom will refuse me a first and last request.’ So, without saying a word to you, I sent a letter to Tom, asking his interest for you. I don’t know how it strikes you--but I never could have expected so handsome a reply after so long a silence. Why, he has answered me by return of post,” said my father, peering at the date.

White House Announces New COVID-19 Vaccination Policies: OSHA and CMS Mandates Protect Workers, Save Lives, and Boost Economy

The Biden Administration celebrated a significant milestone in the nation's fight against COVID-19: 70% of adult Americans are now fully vaccinated. This represents a dramatic increase from less than one percent when President Biden took office. Building on this progress, the Administration announced two major vaccination policies designed to further increase vaccination rates, protect workers, prevent hospitalizations, and save lives.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) will require employers with 100 or more employees to ensure their workforce is fully vaccinated or undergo weekly COVID-19 testing, with paid time for vaccination. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) will mandate that health care workers at Medicare and Medicaid participating facilities be fully vaccinated against COVID-19. These rules cover over 100 million workers in the United States.

These new policies aim to protect workers, prevent hospitalizations, and save lives. They are based on extensive scientific evidence showing the effectiveness of vaccines in preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. Economists unanimously agree that vaccination requirements will lead to a faster and stronger economic recovery. The rules also preempt any inconsistent state or local laws that limit employers' authority to require vaccinations, masks, or testing.

The impact of these vaccination mandates has already been demonstrated in participating organizations. Vaccination rates have increased by over 20 percentage points in some cases. The new OSHA and CMS requirements will provide further incentives for millions of Americans to get vaccinated. By increasing vaccination rates, we can strengthen our economy, save lives, and move closer to ending this pandemic once and for all.

"We're fixed for horses," said Billy, eyein' the string of fine animals, their coats shinin' like polished leather in the mornin' sun. "I reckon we'll make do."

"Don't you go gettin' any notions into your head now," I cautioned. "We ain't had no talk about equipment."

"I ain't," said Billy, standin' firm as the stone pilin's that held up the old cabin we'd just left. "I'm just sayin' we're set, that's all."

I watched him as he took a long pull from his water canteen, the sun glintin' off the droplets that clung to the hairs on his face. He had a way of gettin' under my skin, like a persistent burr that just wouldn't come loose.

"You're a hard man to please, Billy," I said, tuckin' my arms across my chest.

"I'm a hard man to live with," he shot back, his grin flashin' for a split second before it vanished into a scowl. "Now come on, we got work to do."

"What's the big hurry?" asked Jim, lopin' over to us with a long-legged stride.

"We got a long way to go, that's all," Billy said, his eyes flickin' towards the west.

"That's what the birds say, too," Jim drawled, lightin' a cigarette.

I watched the smoke curl up into the air, feelin' a sudden pang of unease. We'd been talkin' about movin' the herd for weeks now – and it was about time we made up our minds to do it.

Now we were gettin' set to move – or at least, as set as we were gonna get. I glanced over at the other boys, all of 'em loungin' against the wagon, lookin' like they was plumb disgusted with the whole operation.

Billy's eyes locked onto mine, him and I swappin' a look that spoke volumes. It said – among other things – that we wasn't gettin' anywhere.

We got our gear stowin' and loadin' up the wagon, and Jim came over with a frown creasin' his face.

"Listen, boys," he said, clappin' his hands together.

We all turned to him, expectant.

"We got a passenger," he said, flingin' back the bandana that covered his face.

"What's this, Jim?" I asked, mouth hangin' open.

"A woman," he said, his face straight as a board.

Billy's eyes narrowed, a low rumble startin' in his chest. I watched him take a deliberate step back, like he was preparin' for a fight.

"By thunder, Jim," he said, his voice in danger of breakin' into a shout, "what in tarnation –"

"Aw, shucks, Billy," Jim said, his voice calm as the evening air. "She's a fine woman, I promise you that. Traveled with a wagon bunch that went down the trail over a year ago."

"I don't care if she's a queen," Billy said, his face reddening, "she ain't comin' with us."

"Now hold up, Billy," I cautioned, not knowin' what was gettin' into Jim but willin' to bet my boots it wasn't good.

Later when he lay between two German featherbeds and Onufri brought him his book and a candle he asked him to take a seat by his bedside.

"Why are you such a deuced fool, Onufri?"

"If I am it is God's business, not mine, nor your highness'."

"Look here, Onufri. How would you like to have all common people black like those darkies?"

The servant spat out in horror and made the sign of the cross.

"For shame, sir. What harm have the common people done you that you should wish them a horrid thing like that? And where does your highness get these cruel thoughts? Surely not from your mother. For shame, sir."

"Idiot that you are, it's mere fancy, just for fun. There ought to be some difference between noble people and common. There is in some countries, you know." He told him about castes, the slave trade in America and passed to the days of chivalry, his favourite topic, until the retired hussar's head sank and a mighty snore rang out of his bushy moustache. Pavel flew into a passion.

"Ass!" he shouted, getting half out of bed and shaking him fiercely. "Why don't I fall asleep when you tell me stories?"

Onufri started and fell to rubbing one eye, while with his other eye he looked about him, as though he had slept a week. The stories he often told young Boulatoff mostly related to the days of serfdom, which had been abolished when Pavel was a boy of five. Onufri's mother had been flogged to death in the presence of her master, Pavel's grandfather, and the former hussar would tell the story with a solemnity that reflected his veneration for the "good old times" rather than grief over the fate of his mother.

That night Pavel dreamed of a pond full of calves that were splashing about and laughing in the water. He carried them all home and on his way there they were transformed into one pair, and the two calves walked about and talked just like Onufri and the transformation was no transformation at all, the calves being real calves and negroes at the same time. When he awoke, in the morning, and it came over him that the dream had had something to do with Onufri, he was seized with a feeling of self-disgust. He thought of the Polish woman and his treatment of her, and this, too, appeared in a new light to him.

Two or three hours later, when the countess returned from her morning walk Pavel, dressed to go out, grave and mysterious, solemnly handed her a sealed note from himself.

"Don't open it until I have left," he said. "I am going out for a stroll."

"What you said yesterday about my being hard-hearted and incapable of sympathy," the letter read, "left a deep impression on me. I thought of it almost the first thing this morning as I opened my eyes, and it kept me thinking all the morning. I looked deep into my soul, I overhauled my whole ego. I turned it inside out, and--well, I must say I have come to the conclusion that what you said was not devoid of foundation. Not that I am prepared to imagine ourselves as having anything to do with a woman whose family is a family of rebels and who has the audacity to pass our emperor without bowing; but she is a human being, too, and her sufferings should have aroused some commiseration in me. I envy you, mother. Compared to you I really am a hard-hearted, unfeeling brute, and it makes me very, very unhappy to think of it. My heart is so full at this moment that I am at a loss to give expression to what I feel, but you will understand me, darling little mother mine. I do not want to be hard and cruel, and I want you to help me.

The following morning, the sun cast its golden rays upon the small town of Abbeychurch, as the townsfolk prepared for the forthcoming activities of the week. The air was filled with a sense of anticipation, for it was the day of the annual children's feast after church, and every hand was busy in the making of preparations. Among the bustling activity, two girls, Elizabeth and Kate, found themselves in the quaint parlor of Mrs. Webbe's home, engaged in the task of creating two cushions for the desk and the imposing figure of the eagle that stood proudly in the corner.

'Yes, we have undertaken this task for the children's feast, Mrs. Webbe has tarried with her hands full of other matters, and since Kate understands the pattern better than I can,' Elizabeth mused, her needle deftly stitching a seam in the material.

'But what of Mrs. Hazleby, who insisted that she alone could handle such tasks?' Kate inquired, her eyes focused on her own piece of the project. 'Might she not be offended by our taking on this task without her consent?'

'Mrs. Hazleby is.. well,' Elizabeth paused, a wry smile playing on her lips, 'she is a woman of singular nature, and her feelings are often as unpredictable as the tides of the sea. Besides, the feast benefits from every hand that can be spared, and surely she will understand our intentions.'

As they worked, the sound of Mrs. Webbe's voice floated from the adjoining room, detailing the arrangements for the feast. She had taken great care to ensure that the smaller children would be properly fed, having consulted with the local schoolmistress about their dietary needs. 'We must see that they do not go hungry, nor feel overlooked,' she had insisted, her voice filled with determination.

Meanwhile, the sound of delicate laughter echoed from the entrance hall, heralding the arrival of three young guests. They were the daughters of the new clergyman, fresh from the north, and all three were eager to lend their assistance to the feast. 'We have brought some treacle tart recipes from our aunt, who is a most excellent baker,' the eldest of the three, a girl named Mellisa, informed Mrs. Webbe, her eyes sparkling with excitement.

'A most welcome addition, indeed,' Mrs. Webbe replied, her eyes twinkling in return. 'Let us hope that the feast shall be a resounding success, for the children's sake.'

Later in the day, as dinner planning began to take shape, Mrs. Webbe turned her attention to the seating arrangements for the upcoming dinner party. 'There are to be thirteen guests, and we must be mindful of the superstitions,' she explained to Elizabeth and Kate, who had joined her in the study. Colin L. Powell, Trailblazing Military Leader and Diplomat, Leaves Behind Complex Political Legacy

Colin L. Powell, the first Black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and a former secretary of state, died on October 25 at the age of 84 due to complications from Covid-19. Powell's passing has sparked widespread tributes from both Republicans and Democrats, highlighting his service, his breaking of barriers as a Jamaican-American, and his moral stances. However, his political legacy is more complex, as he navigated a changing Republican Party and ultimately distanced himself from it.

In November 1995, Powell announced that he was a Republican, but he never sought the presidency. According to Douglas Heye, former Republican National Committee communications director, Powell aimed to move the Republican Party closer to the spirit of Lincoln, promoting racial diversity and welcoming immigrants. However, Powell's vision contrasted sharply with the direction the GOP took under Donald Trump, emphasizing anti-immigrant rhetoric and populism.

Powell endorsed Barack Obama in 2008 and later Democratic candidates, distancing himself from the GOP, especially after the January 6 insurrection. He was criticized by some in the GOP as a "RINO" (Republican in Name Only) and diverged from the party due to its shift towards Trump's ideology.

Leon Panetta, former defense secretary, remembered Powell as a dedicated public servant who put country ahead of party. Powell's centrist approach to politics could eventually unify the increasingly polarized U.S. political landscape, according to Ari Fleischer, George W. Bush's former White House press secretary.

Anthony Cordesman, national security adviser to McCain and emeritus strategy chair at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that Powell's legacy is not just about his military or diplomatic service but also about his commitment to bipartisanship and civility in politics.

Madeleine Albright, former secretary of state, praised Powell's commitment to public service and his ability to bridge partisan divides. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) also paid tribute to Powell's service, acknowledging his contributions to the country's national security and diplomacy.

Donald Trump, however, criticized Powell as a "classic RINO" and for attacking Republicans. Powell's death has sparked a renewed debate about the future of the Republican Party and the role of moderate voices within it.

In conclusion, Colin L. Powell's political legacy is complex and multifaceted, reflecting his commitment to public service, his moral compass, and his efforts to promote bipartisanship and civility in politics. His passing is a reminder of the importance of dedicated public servants who put country ahead of party and of the need for a more centrist approach to politics in an increasingly polarized landscape.

IRS Issues "Plus-Up" Payments to 1 Million Americans

Washington – The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has distributed additional stimulus cash, known as "plus-up" payments, to people who lost income in 2020. These payments target individuals whose 2020 tax returns indicate they qualified for more than they initially received from the first two stimulus rounds.

Over the past two weeks, more than 1 million "plus-up" payments totaling $2.5 billion have been issued. The IRS has sent out more than 8 million supplemental payments this year.

Another 900,000 payments were made to low-income individuals who don't typically file tax returns but did so this year to claim their stimulus money.

The third stimulus payment, authorized in March, offers up to $1,400 per person and is expected to reach 85% of households. Families can receive $1,400 per dependent, including for adult dependents over 17, with the amount phasing out at higher income levels.

The latest aid package also increases the child tax credit, with periodic payments beginning July 15, based on 2019 or 2020 tax returns. Eligible parents will receive $3,600 for each child under 6 and $3,000 for each child under 18, with at least half being paid over the summer.

The child tax credit has been made fully refundable, potentially making 20 million more children eligible.

Eligibility for Plus-Up Payments

To be eligible for a "plus-up" payment, individuals must meet the following criteria:

  • Filed a 2020 tax return
  • Claimed the Recovery Rebate Credit on their tax return
  • Received less than the full amount of the first or second stimulus payment based on their 2019 tax return

How to Claim a Plus-Up Payment

Individuals who believe they are eligible for a "plus-up" payment should file a 2020 tax return as soon as possible. The IRS will automatically calculate any additional payment owed.

Other Stimulus Payment Updates

The IRS is continuing to process and issue the third stimulus payments. As of May 21, over 160 million payments have been sent out, totaling over $380 billion.

The IRS encourages individuals to use the "Get My Payment" tool on its website to check the status of their payment.

The girl looked undecidedly from him to us, but we had nothing to say.

I breathed--for the first time since I heard her, I thought. I opened my eyes. It was all black before them, they had been closed so long. I did not dare look at the Nice Boy. "No!" she cried vividly. "Don't say it again or I shall be displeased. Turn your eyes elsewhere. There is one here about whom I wish to consult you. Do you see the tall girl in black who is engaged with the miniatures?"

"His family’s doing well," she remarked softly, stirring her tea with a delicate clink of the spoon. "They say Mr. Simpson is making wise investments."

Tom nodded, though his mind lingered on the disparities marked by wealth. "They didn’t have it easy in the beginning," he conceded, "but things changed fast—too fast."
