Jack was accompanied to the gate in quite a friendly way by Comely. He smiled as he heard the click of the lock and bolts behind him, and thought a good deal about Joe Gumley as he made his way down the steep cliff path to the fishing village below. It was quite a small village: a few cottages clustered about a cobbled square, with others climbing the cliff, each with its little bit of garden.

The harbor was protected by a natural breakwater of rock running out to sea, and forming an excellent defense against the southwest gales. A few brawny fishermen were lounging about in jerseys and sou’westers, hands in pockets, pipe in mouth. Jack tried to enter into conversation with them, but found them strangely taciturn. They looked hard at him before answering his questions, used few words, and gave him very little information. Mr. Bastable laughed when, meeting Jack at luncheon, he learned how he had spent the morning.

"They’re not a talkative set," he said, "and were probably somewhat overcome by the presence of a king’s officer."

"But how did they know I’m a king’s officer, cousin? We fellows don’t go blabbing about: I didn’t tell ’em, and only Gumley and old Gudgeon know, besides you and my cousins."

"Perhaps it was Kate that told them. Ladies are great gossips, they say."

"I’m sure Kate doesn’t go gossiping with fishermen; do you, Kate?"

U.S. Ends Its Longest War: Troops Exit Afghanistan

Aug 30 (Reuters) – Nearly two decades after the United States first set foot in Afghanistan, triggered by the devastating attacks of September 11, 2001, the last of its troops left the country on August 30, 2021, closing the chapter on America's longest war. The exit marks not just an end but a reflection on a series of pivotal moments that shaped U.S. involvement in Afghanistan, leading to this consequential day.

The genesis of the U.S. presence in Afghanistan was rooted in the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 attacks. Orchestrated by al Qaeda from Afghanistan, where they were harbored by the ruling Taliban, these attacks prompted an immediate response. On October 7, 2001, the U.S. launched its first airstrikes against Taliban and al Qaeda targets, signaling the start of a conflict that would evolve immensely over the next 20 years.

One of the early turning points of the war was in December 2001, when Osama bin Laden, the mastermind behind 9/11 and then leader of al Qaeda, narrowly escaped U.S. bombing in the rugged terrains of Tora Bora, Afghanistan. His escape to Pakistan was a significant moment, underlining the difficulties and complexities the U.S. military would face in the region.

By May 2, 2003, the U.S. had declared major combat operations over, shifting its focus significantly towards Iraq. This pivot allowed the Taliban, which had been ousted from power, to regroup and gradually regain strength, leading to a resurgence that would challenge U.S. and NATO forces for years to come.

Acknowledging the resurgent Taliban and the deteriorating situation, President Obama, on February 17, 2009, made the decision to increase U.S. troop levels in Afghanistan. This surge saw troop numbers exceeding 100,000 in 2010, aimed at counter-insurgency operations and to stabilize the precarious situation.

A pivotal moment came on May 1, 2011, when U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden in Pakistan, more than a decade after the 9/11 attacks. This event was seen as a significant blow to al Qaeda and a moment of justice for the United States.

In response to the evolving dynamics on the ground, President Obama, on May 27, 2014, initiated a drawdown of U.S. forces, transitioning the primary role from combat to training and supporting the Afghan military, with plans for a complete withdrawal by the end of 2016.

The path to withdrawal took a more definitive shape under the Trump administration. On February 29, 2020, an agreement was signed with the Taliban, outlining the conditions for a U.S. troop withdrawal and the beginning of intra-Afghan peace negotiations.

However, the lead-up to the final withdrawal was marred by tragedy. On August 26, 2021, an ISIS suicide bomb attack at Kabul airport claimed the lives of scores, including 13 U.S. troops, underscoring the volatile and unpredictable nature of Afghanistan's security landscape.

In an official statement marking the end of the military mission in Afghanistan, U.S. General Frank McKenzie, head of U.S. Central Command, declared, "Tonight's withdrawal signifies both the end of the military component of the evacuation but also the end of the nearly 20-year mission that began in Afghanistan shortly after September 11, 2001."

As the United States turns the page on this chapter of its military history, the impact of its longest war - on both the Afghan population and American service members, their families, and the nation - will be felt for generations to come. The departure of the last U.S. troops does not just mark an end but also opens a new, uncertain chapter for Afghanistan amid fears of a Taliban resurgence and the future of its people's rights and freedoms hanging in the balance.

The sun had set, and the house was quiet, save for the crackle of the fire in the hearth and the distant hum of the crickets outside. Ezra sat in his favorite chair, the one Jinny had always insisted he use when he needed to rest, though now it felt as though he rested little these days. His eyes wandered to the mantel, where a small photograph of Jinny sat, her smile faint but warm, as though she could see him still, judging him, guiding him.

He often found himself in this state of quiet reflection, his mind wandering back to the words she had spoken to him in their simpler days, when life was not so burdened with the weight of loss and uncertainty. "Ef you're ever to git right with the Lord," she had said, her voice soft but firm, "you better start by bein' right with yerself." He had not understood then, but now, with the passage of time, the meaning of her words began to take shape in his heart.

Ezra reached for the book he had been reading, a worn volume with pages that felt thin and brittle to the touch. It spoke of Miss Myrtle Musgrove, a woman of uncommon grace and determination, who had taken it upon herself to teach the children of the village without once raising a hand to them in anger. The mere thought of her filled him with a strange mix of admiration and longing, as though she were the answer to a prayer he had not yet dared to make.

He closed his eyes for a moment, and in the darkness, he could almost see Jinny standing in the doorway, her hands on her hips, shaking her head at him with that knowing smile of hers. "Ef you're goin' to write to her," she would have said, "you'd best be sure you ain't jest chasin' arter a pretty face." Her voice was playful, but there was a seriousness in her tone that he could never forget.

The fire began to die down, casting long shadows across the room, and Ezra stirred, as though roused from a deep sleep. He picked up a piece of paper and a quill, the inkwell sitting cold and untouched beside him. His hand trembled slightly as he dipped the quill into the ink, hesitating before he began to write. The words came slowly, as though he were trying to capture not just his thoughts, but the very essence of his soul.

As he wrote, the memories of Jinny grew stronger, her presence more vivid in his mind. He could feel her beside him, her hand on his arm, her voice soft and encouraging. "Do right by her, Ezra," she would have said, her voice filled with that quiet wisdom that had always guided him. "Ef you can do right by her, you can do right by the Lord."

The letter, once begun, seemed to take on a life of its own, the words flowing from him as though they had been waiting to be set free. He wrote of his struggles, his doubts, and the way in which Miss Myrtle's story had touched him in a way he could not begin to explain. And as he wrote, he felt a strange sense of peace settling over him, as though the weight of his past was finally beginning to lift.

When the ink had dried, he folded the letter carefully and placed it beside the photograph of Jinny, as though seeking her approval one last time. "I ain't doin' this fer me," he said aloud, his voice steady despite the uncertainty that lingered in his heart. "I'm doin' it fer you, Jinny. To show you that I ain't jest a man of half-hearted faith."

The house fell silent once more, the night closing in around him as though it were a comforting shroud. Ezra sat for a time, his eyes fixed on the letter, his mind wandering to the distant village where Miss Myrtle Musgrove waited, unaware of the impact she had already begun to have on his life. And in that silence, he found a strange, tentative hope, a spark of something that felt almost like belief.

As the night wore on, the fire reduced to embers, and Ezra rose from his chair, his back stiff and his heart heavy. He knew the road ahead would be long and fraught with obstacles, both of his own making and those placed before him by the world. But for the first time in what felt like years, he could see a light in the distance, a flicker of something that might yet bring him peace.

And in that moment, as he prepared to face the dawn, Ezra felt a strange sense of obligation, not just to Jinny, but to himself. He had always been a man of little faith, but perhaps, with time and patience, he might yet learn to believe.

REvil Ransomware Group Hacked and Deactivated in Multinational Cyber Operation

In a significant blow to the notorious ransomware group REvil, a multinational cyber operation involving the FBI, investigative arms from various countries, and the U.S. Cyber Command successfully hacked and deactivated the group's operations. The takedown of REvil, known for its high-profile attacks including hacking the U.S. Colonial Pipeline, marks a major victory in the ongoing battle against cybercrime.

The operation, coordinated across borders, managed to exploit a vulnerability in REvil's backup system, effectively shutting down the ransomware group's infrastructure. According to reports, this tactic mirrored the techniques often used by REvil themselves to compromise their targets, demonstrating the irony of the group's own methods being turned against them. Oleg Skulkin from the Russian security company Group-IB noted, "It's almost poetic justice that the same tactics REvil used to target others were eventually used against them."

In an internet forum post, a leader of REvil known as 0_neday acknowledged the server compromise, confirming the group's deactivation. Notably, REvil's main spokesperson, known as Unknown, had disappeared from the internet in July, adding to the group's woes.

The cyber operation involved law enforcement agencies gaining access to and disabling REvil's servers from within, effectively crippling their ability to carry out further ransomware attacks. The success of this mission comes after REvil's high-profile hacks, particularly the one targeting the Colonial Pipeline, which caused significant fuel shortages and led to a state of emergency being declared across 17 U.S. states earlier this year.

Following the Colonial Pipeline incident, REvil further escalated its cyber activities by attacking software management company Kaseya, demanding a substantial ransom. The brazen nature of these attacks highlighted the urgent need for greater cybersecurity measures to protect critical infrastructure.

In response to the escalating threat posed by ransomware groups like REvil, the U.S. government has intensified efforts to treat these attacks on critical infrastructure as national security threats. By taking down REvil in a coordinated multinational operation, law enforcement agencies have sent a strong message to cybercriminals that such actions will not be tolerated and that those responsible will be held accountable.

As the global community continues to grapple with the growing threat of ransomware attacks, the successful operation against REvil serves as a pivotal moment in the fight against cybercrime. With cybersecurity experts and law enforcement agencies working together to dismantle these criminal networks, there is hope for a more secure digital landscape in the future.

The sun had barely risen above the horizon when Robert Coverdale emerged from the humble cottage that served as his home. The air was crisp and cold, with a faint tang of salt carried on the breeze from the nearby ocean. The village of Seahaven stirred slowly, its wooden houses clustered together like a family huddled against the encroaching mist. Robert pulled his coat tighter around him, the sleeves rolled up to reveal sturdy hands calloused from days of labor. His boots, though worn, were clean and well-mended, a testament to his Aunt Jane’s care.

As he walked along the narrow path leading to the shore, he passed by the tavern where his uncle, John Trafton, often spent his evenings—and often his wages. The signboard creaked in the morning wind, and the sound of laughter and clinking glasses drifted out through the open window. Robert’s expression darkened slightly at the sight, but he quickened his pace, determined to focus on the tasks ahead.

The fishnets were waiting by the water’s edge, ready to be cast into the deep, blue-green waters of the bay. Robert’s hands moved deftly as he prepared the lines, his mind racing with thoughts of the day’s catch. He knew that every fish he brought ashore was a step toward providing for his aunt and himself. Uncle John’s drinking had long since become a source of worry for Aunt Jane, and Robert was resolved to do whatever he could to ease her burdens.

As he worked, the sound of approaching footsteps drew his attention. He turned to see Aunt Jane coming down the path, her skirt tucked up modestly as she hurried toward him. Her face was drawn with worry, and her hands were clasped tightly in front of her.

“Robert, I’ve been looking for you,” she said, her voice tinged with urgency. “Uncle John—he’s been at the tavern since yesterday evening, and he’s yet to return. I’m afraid he’s taken to himself a bottle, and I don’t know what to do.”

Robert’s heart sank. He had long since grown accustomed to his uncle’s habits, but it never ceased to痛心. “I’ll go find him,” he said firmly, his tone leaving no room for argument. “But Aunt Jane, I have to tell you—I’ve made a decision. I won’t be selling any of our catch at the tavern today. Not as long as Uncle John is drinking up what little we have.”

Aunt Jane’s eyes filled with tears, but a faint smile tugged at her lips. “Thank you, Robert,” she whispered. “Your strength gives me hope.”

With a nod, Robert turned back to the water, his resolve as firm as ever. He knew the road ahead would be difficult, but he was determined to see it through. As he cast the nets into the water, the waves lapping against the shore seemed to echo his determination.

By midday, the sun had climbed higher, casting a golden glow over the village. Robert returned home with a respectable catch, his net heavy with fish. Aunt Jane waited at the door, her face etched with worry but also with a certain pride. “Where is Uncle John?” she asked, her voice trembling.

Robert hesitated before answering, his hands tightening on the fish he carried. “I found him at the tavern,” he said quietly. “He’s… not in a state to come home just yet.”

Aunt Jane sighed, her shoulders drooping. “I feared as much. But what are we to do, Robert? We need his help.”

Robert’s jaw tightened as he set the fish down on the table. “We’ll manage,” he said firmly. “I’ll sell the catch myself and use the money to buy provisions. And Aunt Jane, I’ve been thinking—I could take on more work, help with the nets or the sails for the other fishermen. Whatever it takes.”

Aunt Jane’s eyes filled with tears again, but this time, they were tears of gratitude. “You’re a good boy, Robert,” she said softly. “A true credit to your mother and father.”

As the afternoon wore on, Robert worked tirelessly, his hands moving with purpose as he prepared the fish for market. The quiet of the cottage was broken only by the occasional creak of the wooden floorboards and the soft murmur of the waves outside. Aunt Jane sat by the fire, her knitting needles clicking rhythmically, her mind a mix of worry and hope.

The evening brought with it a sense of quiet determination. Robert sat by the fire, his hands resting on his knees, his eyes fixed on the dancing flames. “Aunt Jane,” he said suddenly, his voice steady, “I’ve been thinking about the future. I want to make something of myself, to get out of this life, if only to give you a better one.”

Aunt Jane’s head snapped up, her eyes sharp with concern. “Robert, I don’t want you to leave. You’re all I have.”

“But I want to do this for you,” he insisted, his voice firm. “I want to give you a life where you don’t have to worry about where your next meal will come from. Where you don’t have to watch Uncle John destroy himself.”

Aunt Jane’s hands flew to her face, and she wept silently. “I never wanted you to grow up and see him like this,” she said, her voice breaking. “I only wanted to protect you.”

Robert reached out, his hand resting gently on her arm. “You’ve done enough, Aunt Jane,” he said softly. “You’ve given me a home, taught me right from wrong. I won’t let you down.”

As the night wore on, the two sat in silence, the weight of their circumstances pressing heavily upon them. But in Robert’s heart, a fire burned brightly, a resolve that would not be extinguished. He knew the road ahead would be long and difficult, but he was ready to face it, one step at a time.

The following morning, Robert rose before dawn, the air cool and crisp. He walked down to the shore, the village still asleep, and set to work with renewed determination. The fishnets were his livelihood, his ticket to a better future. And with each tug of the line, with each fish he pulled from the water, he felt a small but steady progress toward his goal.

Aunt Jane watched him from the cottage window, her heart heavy but also filled with a quiet pride. She knew that Robert was determined, that he wouldn’t give up. And as she watched him, she smiled, a small, knowing smile, and whispered a prayer for her dear boy.

I believe the main purpose of "Casablanca" is to entertain its audience. The film masterfully weaves a tale of love and loss against the backdrop of war-torn Morocco. We see the characters grapple with difficult choices, heartbreak, and the ever-present shadow of conflict. Isn't it fascinating how the war becomes more than a setting; it becomes a disruptive and terrible force that impacts each of their lives?

Rick, the protagonist, embodies this struggle as he wrestles with his past love for Ilsa. Ultimately, he makes a decision to let go, highlighting a powerful theme about moving on. "Casablanca" isn't just a shallow romance; it has emotional depth. The score, the acting, the story, all work in tandem to draw the viewer in. At the end of the day, we're left with a complete and compelling story. And yet, the beauty of "Casablanca" is that it offers a space for personal interpretation. What resonates with one viewer might strike another in a completely different way, and that's okay. For me, "Casablanca" was engrossing and engaging, a timeless classic that allows each viewer to find personal connections within its frames.

My experience tutoring a boy named Adrian opened my eyes to the subtle yet profound challenges of language barriers in schools. Adrian, despite speaking fluent English, struggled with reading. The culprit wasn't his grasp on the spoken word, but his unfamiliarity with the English alphabet. He knew words, but translating those words into written form through letters was an entirely different challenge. This revelation was a wake-up call to me – language barriers, especially those related to reading, can be anything but obvious, even in children who speak perfect English.

Adrian's predicament highlighted the crucial need for targeted solutions to help children grapple with English reading. In his case, I focused on tutoring him in reading with an emphasis on mastering the alphabet and improving pronunciation. It was like teaching him a new language within his own, a revelation that made me realize how important such specialized support can be. For children whose proficiency in English is limited, a blend of educational approaches is key. They often require a combination of visual aids, interactive lessons, and patient guidance to bridge the gap between their spoken language and written English.

A notable discovery was the potential of dual language systems as a beneficial strategy not just for non-English speakers, but for all students. This system encourages multilingualism and provides a richer educational environment where everyone can thrive. Some critics mistakenly believe that dual language education is a drain on resources. However, the reverse is often true—it fosters cognitive flexibility and enhances learning outcomes, something studies have consistently shown.

To ensure the success of dual language programs, having special aids or tutors who are bilingual is invaluable. They can provide nuanced support, understanding both the intricacies of the student's native language and the target language. It's not about requiring all teachers to be bilingual, which would be unrealistic, but rather implementing support systems that include bilingual personnel. This approach acknowledges the diversity of our classrooms and equips us to better serve our students.

In addressing language barriers in schools, we must remember that every child, regardless of their linguistic background, deserves an education that recognizes and nurtures their potential. Adrian's journey taught me that the path to overcoming these barriers is both nuanced and rewarding, requiring patience, creativity, and a commitment to inclusive education.

'Well, Paul, then. Your room is all ready for you, Paul, for, as I said to the minister, "I'll have it ready whether he comes on Friday or not." And the minister said he must go up to the Ashfield whether you were to come or not; but he would come home betimes to see if you were here. I'll show you to your room, and you can wash the dust off a bit.'

After I came down, I think she did not quite know what to do with me; or she might think that I was dull; or she might have work to do in which I hindered her; for she called Phillis, and bade her put on her bonnet, and go with me to the Ashfield, and find father. So we set off, I in a little flutter of a desire to make myself agreeable, but wishing that my companion were not quite so tall; for she was above me in height. While I was wondering how to begin our conversation, she took up the words.

'I suppose, cousin Paul, you have to be very busy at your work all day long in general.'

'Yes, we have to be in the office at half-past eight; and we have an hour for dinner, and then we go at it again till eight or nine.'

'Then you have not much time for reading.'

'No,' said I, with a sudden consciousness that I did not make the most of what leisure I had.

'No more have I. Father always gets an hour before going a-field in the mornings, but mother does not like me to get up so early.'

'My mother is always wanting me to get up earlier when I am at home.'

'What time do you get up?'

'Oh!--ah!--sometimes half-past six: not often though;' for I remembered only twice that I had done so during the past summer.

She turned her head and looked at me.

'Father is up at three; and so was mother till she was ill. I should like to be up at four.'

'Your father up at three! Why, what has he to do at that hour?'

'What has he not to do? He has his private exercise in his own room; he always rings the great bell which calls the men to milking; he rouses up Betty, our maid; as often as not he gives the horses their feed before the man is up--for Jem, who takes care of the horses, is an old man; and father is always loth to disturb him; he looks at the calves, and the shoulders, heels, traces, chaff, and corn before the horses go a-field; he has often to whip-cord the plough-whips; he sees the hogs fed; he looks into the swill-tubs, and writes his orders for what is wanted for food for man and beast; yes, and for fuel, too. And then, if he has a bit of time to spare, he comes in and reads with me--but only English; we keep Latin for the evenings, that we may have time to enjoy it; and then he calls in the men to breakfast, and cuts the boys' bread and cheese; and sees their wooden bottles filled, and sends them off to their work;--and by this time it is half-past six, and we have our breakfast. There is father,' she exclaimed, pointing out to me a man in his shirt-sleeves, taller by the head than the other two with whom he was working. We only saw him through the leaves of the ash-trees growing in the hedge, and I thought I must be confusing the figures, or mistaken: that man still looked like a very powerful labourer, and had none of the precise demureness of appearance which I had always imagined was the characteristic of a minister. It was the Reverend Ebenezer Holman, however. He gave us a nod as we entered the stubble-field; and I think he would have come to meet us but that he was in the middle of giving some directions to his men. I could see that Phillis was built more after his type than her mother's. He, like his daughter, was largely made, and of a fair, ruddy complexion, whereas hers was brilliant and delicate. His hair had been yellow or sandy, but now was grizzled. Yet his grey hairs betokened no failure in strength. I never saw a more powerful man--deep chest, lean flanks, well-planted head. By this time we were nearly up to him; and he interrupted himself and stepped forwards; holding out his hand to me, but addressing Phillis.

Louisiana alligator in Hurricane Ida attack found with human remains in stomach

Sept 14 (Reuters) - A 504-pound alligator believed to have killed a 71-year-old Louisiana man in Hurricane Ida floodwaters has been captured with what appears to be human remains in its stomach, the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff's Office said.

The 12-foot alligator's capture ended a two-week search by local and state agencies for Timothy Satterlee Sr, who had last been seen on Aug. 30 checking the storm damage outside his home in Slidell, about 35 miles (55 km) northeast of New Orleans.

The attack occurred the day after Ida, one of the most powerful hurricanes ever to strike the U.S. Gulf Coast, slammed Louisiana, causing devastating flooding in some areas outside a new levee and floodgate system protecting New Orleans.

An alligator "weighing a startling 504 pounds" was caught on Monday in a trap set by two Louisiana Department of Wildlife licensed nuisance hunters, according to a statement from St. Tammany Parish Sheriff's Office.

"Once the alligator was searched, it was discovered to have what appears to be human remains inside its stomach," the sheriff's office said. "Investigators will work with the St. Tammany Parish Coroner's Office to verify those remains belong to Timothy Satterlee."

Wildlife agents were scouring the area in air boats on Saturday when a drone they had deployed spotted a "rather large" alligator not far from the Satterlee home, said Captain Lance Vitter, a spokesperson for the sheriff's office.

The agents set traps, which proved successful on Monday. The agents then euthanized and cut open the alligator "and that's when they discovered the body parts," Vitter said. "It was the upper parts of a human body."

The Satterlee home is not far from an area frequented by tourists who visit for swamp tours promising sightings of alligators and other wildlife, Vitter said. Alligators do not usually attack humans unless the food they have stashed has been displaced, as can occur during major storms, he said.

Satterlee's wife saw a large alligator attack her husband after he had gone outside their raised home to check on the contents of their ground-level shed. The alligator had him in a "death roll" and had ripped off one of his arms, Vitter said, recounting the wife's statement to authorities. The wife, 68, intervened, and the alligator disappeared into the water.

Bleeding badly and starting to black out, the husband told her to get in their small boat and seek help, Vitter said. Vitter added that it would have been difficult for the wife to get her husband into the boat without his help and without it tipping over. She left him on their stairs.

The wife found help about one mile away and returned only to find her husband was no longer on the stairs, Vitter said. "She just never thought in her wildest nightmares that she would get back and he'd be gone."

Satterlee was a pillar of his community in Slidell, volunteering at the local school and cooking for storm victims, Vitter said, adding that he hoped finding the alligator would bring some closure for Satterlee's wife.

"Now that we have located the alligator at least she can get a death certificate," Vitter said.

The alligator was unusually large for the region, where those caught typically measure 7-1/2 to 8 feet in length and rarely exceed 300 pounds, Vitter said.

According to the Smithsonian's National Zoo & Conservation Biology Institute, male alligators can grow as heavy as 1,000 lbs (454 kg).

In exploring the dynamic between message and character within literature, one cannot overlook the instances where the author subordinates plot and protagonist to emphasize a particular message. This approach is evident in Ralph Ellison's "Invisible Man," where the author's focus on cultural impact takes precedence over intricate character development. Ellison's strategy is both commendable for its powerful socio-political commentary and criticized for potentially diminishing the literary quality of his work. By prioritizing the overarching message, Ellison draws readers into the thematic discourse of invisibility and identity, yet risks reducing his characters to mere vessels for conveying these ideas.

Ellison's depiction of the protagonist's electroshock therapy serves as a potent symbol of society's ruthless conformity and loss of individuality. This portrayal is not merely a narrative device but a profound critique of societal norms and their destructive impact on personal identity. Through this lens, the character's ordeal becomes a broader commentary on the human condition, resonating deeply with readers. However, as philosopher Emmanuel Levinas critiques, this prioritization of message over character can also signal a lack of respect for the 'Otherness' inherent in individuals. Levinas' philosophy calls for an engagement with the 'Other' that transcends utilitarian or instrumental treatment, suggesting that Ellison's focus may overlook the complexity and uniqueness of his characters.

Turning to Martin Heidegger's conceptualization of language and truth, we find a framework through which to further analyze this tension. Heidegger posits that language is not merely a tool for conveying truth but contains the essence of truth itself. In literature, this suggests that effective storytelling goes beyond mere exposition; it reveals truth through the interplay of narrative, character, and theme. Yet, in works that overemphasize message, there is a risk of stifling the discovery inherent in literature. This point is starkly illustrated by comparing Ellison's approach with Marlo Morgan's "Mutant Message Down Under." Morgan's tendency to over-explain her experiences detracts from the potential richness of symbolic interpretation, highlighting the importance of letting readers engage with and discover the narrative's deeper meanings.

Good literature, in its truest form, should reveal new aspects of humanity or provoke fresh perspectives. This unveiling of truth occurs through the careful balance between character development and thematic exploration. Literature achieves greatness not merely through its subject matter but in its ability to forge new connections between the reader and the world. The journey through stories allows for a personal encounter with the text, transforming the reading experience into a profound exploration of the self and the other.

In conclusion, the analysis of message versus character in literature invites a nuanced examination of how authors navigate the delicate balance between these elements. By employing philosophical frameworks to evaluate literary works, we can critically assess the effectiveness of an author's approach. Through contrasting examples, we underscore the principle that literature thrives on the interplay of message and character, each enriching the other to uncover underlying truths. Ultimately, masterful storytelling lies in its ability to stimulate thought and discovery, illuminating the human condition with both clarity and depth.

Green, under the influence of more liquor than his head could bear, and in the midst of companions whose sphere he could not, in consequence, resist, yielded in a new direction for him. Of gambling he had always entertained a virtuous disapproval; yet, ere aware of the direction in which he was drifting, he was staking money at cards, the sums gradually increasing, until from shillings the ventures increased to dollars. Sometimes he won, and sometimes he lost; the winnings stimulating to new trials in the hope of further success, and the losses stimulating to new trials in order to recover, if possible; but, steadily, the tide, for all these little eddies of success, bore him downwards, and losses increased from single dollars to fives, and from fives to tens, his pleasant friend, Bland, supplying whatever he wanted in the most disinterested way, until an aggregate loss of nearly a hundred and fifty dollars sobered and appalled him.

The salary of Martin Green was only four hundred dollars, every cent of which was expended as fast as earned. A loss of a hundred and fifty dollars was, therefore, a serious and embarrassing matter.

"I'll call and see you to-morrow, when we can arrange this little matter," said Mr. Bland, "on parting with Green at his own door. He spoke pleasantly, but with something in his voice that chilled the nerves of his victim. Green turned and saw the last man on the earth he desired to meet. His pleasant friend of the evening before had called to "arrange that little matter."

"Not too soon for you, I hope," remarked Bland, with his courteous, yet now serious, smile, as he took the victim's hand.

"Yes, you are, too soon," was soberly answered.

The smile faded off of Bland's face.

"When will you arrange it?"

"In a few days."

"But I want the money to-day. It was a simple loan, you know."

"I am aware of that, but the amount is larger than I can manage at once," said Green.

"Can I have a part to-day?"

"Not to-day."

"To-morrow, then?"

"I'll do the best in my power."

"Very well. To-morrow, at this time, I will call. Make up the whole sum if possible, for I want it badly."

"Do you know that young man?" asked Mr. Phillips, the employer of Green, as the latter came back to his desk. The face of Mr. Phillips was unusually serious.

"His name is Bland."

"Why has he called to see you?" The eyes of Mr. Phillips were fixed intently on his clerk.

"He merely dropped in. I have met him a few times in company."

"Don't you know his character?"

"I never heard a word against him," said Green.

"Why, Martin!" replied Mr. Phillips, "he has the reputation of being one of the worst young men in our city; a base gambler's stool-pigeon, some say."

"I am glad to know it, sir," Martin had the presence of mind, in the painful confusion that overwhelmed him, to say, "and shall treat him accordingly." He went back to his desk, and resumed his work.

It is the easiest thing in the world to go to astray, but always difficult to return, Martin Green was astray, but how was he to get into the right path again? A barrier that seemed impassable was now lying across the way over which he had passed, a little while before, with lightest footsteps. Alone and unaided, he could not safely get back. The evil spirits that lure a man from virtue never counsel aright when to seek to return. They magnify the perils that beset the road by which alone is safety, and suggest other ways that lead into labyrinths of evil from which escape is sometimes impossible. These spirits were now at the ear of our unhappy young friend, suggesting methods of relief in his embarrassing position.

Harry allowed me no time to feed on these horrors. Signing to me to dismount and leave Grey Sultan at the entrance, he led me through the long archway or tunnel. At the end we paused again, he watching, while I drew difficult breath. . . .

I saw a vast amphitheatre of granite, curving away on either hand and reaching up, tier on tier, till the tiers melted in the grey sky overhead. The lowest tier stood twenty feet above my head; yet curved with so lordly a perspective that on the far side of the arena, as I looked across, it seemed almost level with the ground; while the human figures about the great archway yonder were diminished to the size of ants about a hole. . . For there were human figures busy in the arena, though not a soul sat in any of the granite tiers above. A million eyes had been less awful than those empty benches staring down in the cold dawn; bench after bench repeating the horror of the featureless carvings by the entrance-gat–epeating it in series without end, and unbroken, save at one point midway along the semicircle on my right, where the imperial seat stood out, crowned like a catafalque with plumes of purple horse-hair, and screened close with heavy purple hangings. I saw these curtains shake once or twice in the morning wind.

The floor of this amphitheatre I have spoken of as an arena; but as a matter of fact it was laid with riveted sheets of copper that recalled the dead men's shelves in the Paris morgue. The centre had been raised some few feet higher than the circumference, or possibly the whole floor took its shape from the rounded hill of which it was the apex; and from an open sluice immediately beneath the imperial throne a flood of water gushed with a force that carried it straight to this raised centre, over which it ran and rippled, and so drained back into the scuppers at the circumference. Before reaching the centre it broke and swirled around a row of what appeared to be tall iron boxes or cages, set directly in face of the throne. But for these ugly boxes the whole floor was empty. To and from these the little human figures were hurrying, and from these too proceeded the thuds and panting and the frequent groans that I had heard outside.

While I stood and gazed, Harry stepped forward into the arena. "This also?" I whispered.

He nodded, and led the way over the copper floor, where the water ran high as our ankles and again was drained off, until little dry spaces grew like maps upon the surface, and in ten seconds were flooded again. He led me straight to the cages, and I saw that while the roof and three sides of these were of sheet iron, the fourth side, which faced the throne, lay open. And I sa–n the first cage, a man scourged with rods; in the second, a body twisted on the rack; in the third, a woman with a starving babe, and a fellow that held food to them and withdrew it quickly (the torturers wore masks on their faces, and whenever blood flowed some threw handfuls of sawdust, and blood and sawdust together were carried off by the running water); in the fourth cage, a man tied, naked and helpless, whom a masked torturer pelted with discs of gold, heavy and keen-edged; in the fifth a brasier with irons heating, and a girl's body crouched in a corner--

"I will see no more!" I cried, and turned towards the great purple canopy. High over it the sun broke yellow on the climbing tiers of seats. "Harry! someone is watching behind those curtains! Is i–E?"

Harry bent his head.

"But this is all that I believed! This is Nero, and ten times worse than Nero! Why did you bring me here?" I flung out my hand towards the purple throne, and finding myself close to a fellow who scattered sawdust with both hands, made a spring to tear his mask away. But Harry stretched out an arm.

In "Song of Myself," Walt Whitman's poetry breathes life into a complex philosophical query around war and equality. He affirms that every individual, regardless of their role or fate in war, possesses profound worth and deservingness. In his powerful meditation, Whitman underscores the inherent equality of all people, positing that victory in war is not an indicator of superior worth. Instead, he asserts that war, with its destructiveness and divisiveness, diminishes the unity and dignity of humankind. Through his poetic discourse, Whitman advocates for an enlightened understanding of equality, emphasizing that the merit of each individual is not quantifiable through military triumph. This stance is echoed when he writes about the steadfast equality of people on opposing sides, suggesting that both winners and losers are equally significant. His belief in absolute equality, where fame or victory has no bearing on an individual's value, is aBadge of his desire for societal progress and unity. Skeptics might argue that this perspective seems naïve and idealistic, but Whitman's goal is clear—to evoke rational thought and prevent the dissolution of civil society through war. His message, inspired by the principles of hard work, experience, and equality, is a potent call to re-evaluate the significance of warfare and foster understanding among all people. Thus, Whitman, through his poetic teaching, asserts that the value of equality exceeds any perceived glory derived from war.

As he advanced into the glade, any one familiar with his customary phlegmatic and unemotional manner would have seen at once that he was the bearer of no ordinary tidings.

"Thank Heaven I have found you!" were his first words, and there could be no doubt of the sincerity with which they were spoken.

"Murdered!" Drelincourt staggered back a pace or two, and then, putting forth his right hand, he caught hold of an oak sapling and gripped it hard. For a few seconds his body rocked like that of a man whose brain has been stunned and dizzied by some great shock.

"That is indeed a terrible discovery to have made," he went on, after a pause. "Kate dead! It seems incredible; altogether beyond belief."

"For all that, it is true."

"But what possible motive could any one have for the commission of such a crime?"

Roden's thin lips tightened. Evidently the question was one which he either would not or could not answer.

"When and by whom was the discovery made?" asked Mr. Drelincourt, after a brief pause.

"It was made by Lucille, nearly a couple of hours ago. She went as usual to take her mistress an early cup of chocolate, and--and found her dead in bed."

"Go on. Tell me all the particulars known to you."

"Mrs. Drelincourt had been stabbed to the heart, most probably while she was asleep."

"So! Has the weapon with which the deed was committed been found?"

"It had not when I left the Towers."

Drelincourt seated himself on the fallen trunk, and resting his elbows on his knees, he bent his eyes on the ground.

"As soon as the crime became known," resumed the other, "I sent off a groom on horseback to fetch Dr. Carew. On the way he met Mr. Ormsby and told him the news, and was ordered by him to at once communicate with the police."

"A very proper thing to do."

"Mr. Ormsby, accompanied by another gentleman, a stranger, had just reached the Towers before I left it."

"To come in search of me?"

"Exactly. It has taken me nearly an hour to find you. I hurried, first of all, to the Cot, but you were not there. Margery Trant had not heard you leave the house, and was unable to tell me in which direction you had gone. I set out to look for you, and it must have been instinct which directed my steps to this place."

He paused. A throstle in the wood piped a few notes and then ceased.

"Go on," said Drelincourt, without looking up. "You have something more to tell me."

"As I bent over Mrs. Drelincourt's dead body, I found this close by her pillow."

As he finished speaking, he drew from one of his pockets a white handkerchief bordered with a thin line of black, and having shaken it out, held it up to the light. On it were three or four crimson stains. "It is yours. Here are your initials in one corner," he said.

He had a softly modulated voice, but just now there was no more emotion either in it or his manner than if he had been discussing the state of the weather.

Drelincourt started to his feet, his face blanched to the lips. A moment or two he stared at the handkerchief as though it had for him a horrible fascination. Then the eyes of the two men met in a silence which seemed charged with hidden meaning.

It was a world to explore, as if one explored the entire Middle Age; it was also one unending, elaborate, religious function--a life, or a continuous drama, to take one's part in. Dependent on its structural completeness, on its wealth of well- preserved ornament, on its unity in variety, perhaps on some undefinable operation of genius, beyond, but concurrently with, all these, the church of Chartres has still the gift of a unique power of impressing. In comparison, the other famous churches of France, at Amiens for instance, at Rheims or Beauvais, may seem but formal, and to a large extent reproducible, effects of mere architectural rule on a gigantic scale. The [29] somewhat Gothic soul of Gaston relished there something strange, or even bizarre, in the very manner in which the building set itself, so broadly couchant, upon the earth; in the natural richness of tone on the masonry within; in its vast echoing roof of timber, the "forest," as it was called; in the mysterious maze traced upon its pavement; its maze-like crypt, centering in the shrine of the sibylline Notre-Dame, itself a natural or very primitive grotto or cave. A few years were still to pass ere sacrilegious hands despoiled it on a religious pretext:--the catholic church must pay, even with the molten gold of her sanctuaries, the price of her defence in the civil war. At present, it was such a treasure-house of medieval jewellery as we have to make a very systematic effort even to imagine. The still extant register of its furniture and sacred apparel leaves the soul of the ecclesiologist athirst.

In a hearing with U.S. senators, Joseph Blount, CEO of Colonial Pipeline, revealed that last month’s cyberattack, which significantly disrupted fuel supply in the Southeast U.S., was executed through a single stolen password. The breach happened via an outdated Virtual Private Network (VPN) system lacking multifactor authentication, a basic cybersecurity measure found in modern systems. Despite the complexity of the password, the lack of a second verification step like a text message allowed hackers easy access.

This breach has raised concerns about the vulnerability of critical U.S. infrastructure to cyberattacks, with recent incidents also affecting JBS, a major meatpacking company. The situation underscores the urgent need for improved cybersecurity measures across vital sectors.

The cybersecurity community often points out the inadequacy of single-factor authentication as this incident demonstrates, advocating for two-factor authentication as a standard practice. Despite the Colonial Pipeline's substantial $200 million investment in its IT infrastructure over the past five years, questions about its specific spendings on cybersecurity measures remained partially addressed, highlighting a potential area for improvement.

During the hearing, senators criticized the company’s preparedness and decision-making process, particularly its choice to pay a ransom to the hackers, a move against federal advice. However, Blount defended this decision as motivated by security concerns and the need for confidentiality.

Even after payment, the company is still dealing with the aftermath, with several systems offline and ongoing recovery efforts. The incident led to calls for stronger cybersecurity readiness to prevent future vulnerabilities. The U.S. Justice Department's recent success in recovering part of the paid ransom underscores the importance of collaboration between affected entities and federal agencies in addressing and mitigating cyber threats.

THE ancient Persians, who seem also to have been wonderful fellows to ride, had a pleasing system of deliberation, which has somewhat fallen into disuse in our modern Parliaments. According to the old historians, it was their practice to discuss all graver matters of policy when in a state of inebriety, giving their debate the advantage of being resumed and repeated next morning; also, should they inadvertently convene a meeting when sober, to reverse the process, and ascertain whether on getting drunk over it they arrived at the same result. The system was not without its merits, no doubt, one of the most prominent of which seems to have been that it entailed a double allowance of liquor. Mr. Sawyer was sufficiently a Persian to reconsider his decision of the previous night, when he woke next morning with a trifling head-ache, and a tongue more like that of a reindeer, as preserved by Fortnum and Mason, than the organ of speech and deglutition peculiar to the human subject.

He was a hard fellow enough; but no man can smoke cigars and drink hot-stopping the last thing at night, and get up in the morning without remembering that he has done so.

A plunge into his cold bath, however, a cup of warm tea, with a rasher of bacon frizzling from the fire, and well peppered, soon restored the brightness to our friend’s eye and the colour to his cheek. When he lit his cigar on his own well-cleaned door-step, and turned his face to the balmy breath of “jocund day,” under a soft November sky, dappled, and mellowed, and tinged here and there with gold by the winter sun, he felt, as he expressed it, “fit as a fiddle, and hotter upon Market Harborough than ever.”

He was a man of few words though, when he meant business, and only pausing for a moment at the Stable, and feeling the grey’s legs, which somehow always did fill after a day’s hunting, he took no living mortal into his confidence, not even the taciturn Isaac (of whom more hereafter); but started for a five-mile walk, to inspect the stables of a certain horse-coping worthy, with whom he had long been too well acquainted, and who generally had a good bit of stuff somewhere about the premises, provided only you could get hold of the right one.

Mr. Sawyer was not a man to order a horse out of the stable in the hunting season for any but the legitimate purpose of the chase. “Walking,” he said, “kept him in wind;” and off he started down a narrow lane that in summer was thick with blackberries and blooming with dog roses, and over a stile and across a fallow, and through a wood, at an honest five-mile-an-hour, heel-and-toe; every turn in the path reminding him, as he stepped along, of some feat of horsemanship or skilful shot, or other pleasing association connected with his country home. And this is one of the greatest advantages of hunting from home. After all, notwithstanding her irresistible attractions, we cannot follow Diana every day of our lives, and surely it is wiser and pleasanter to take her as we want her amongst our own woods and glades, and breezy uplands, and pleasant shady nooks, than to go all the way to Ephesus on purpose to worship with the crowd. Mixed motives, however, seem to be the springs that set in motion our human frames; and if Care sits behind the horseman on the cantle of his saddle, Ambition may also be detected clinging somewhere about his spurs.
