As for Jane, she loved and reverenced Draxy, very much as she did Reuben, with touching devotion, but without any real comprehension of her nature. If she sometimes felt a pang in seeing how much more Reuben talked with Draxy than with her, how much more he sought to be with Draxy than with her, she stifled it, and, reproaching herself for disloyalty to each, set herself to work for them harder than before.

In Draxy's sixteenth year the final blow of misfortune fell upon Reuben Miller's head.

A brother of Jane's, for whom, in an hour of foolish generosity, Reuben had indorsed a note of a considerable amount, failed. Reuben's farm was already heavily mortgaged. There was nothing to be done but to sell it. Purchasers were not plenty nor eager; everybody knew that the farm must be sold for whatever it would bring, and each man who thought of buying hoped to profit somewhat, in a legitimate and Christian way, by Reuben's extremity.

Reuben's courage would have utterly forsaken him now, except for Draxy's calmness. Jane was utterly unnerved; wept silently from morning till night, and implored Reuben to see her brother's creditors, and beg them to release him from his obligation. But Draxy, usually so gentle, grew almost stern when such suggestions were made.

"You don't understand, ma," she said, with flushing cheeks. "It is a promise. Father must pay it. He cannot ask to have it given back to him."

But with all Draxy's inflexibility of resolve, she could not help being disheartened. She could not see how they were to live; the three rooms over the store could easily be fitted up into an endurable dwelling-place; but what was to supply the food which the farm had hitherto given them? There was literally no way open for a man or a woman to earn money in that little farming village. Each family took care of itself and hired no service, except in the short season of haying. Draxy was an excellent seamstress, but she knew very well that the price of all the sewing hired in the village in a year would not keep them from starving. The Store must be given up, because her father would have no money with which to buy goods. In fact, for a long time, most of his purchases had been made by exchanging the spare produce of his farm at large stores in the neighboring towns. Still Draxy never wavered, and because she did not waver Reuben did not die. The farm was sold at auction, with the stock, the utensils, and all of the house-furniture which was not needed to make the store chambers habitable. The buyer boasted in the village that he had not given more than two thirds of the real value of the place. After Reuben's debts were all paid, there remained just one thousand dollars to be put into the bank.

"Why, father! That is a fortune," said Draxy, when he told her. "I did not suppose we should have anything, and it is glorious not to owe any man a cent."

It was early in April when the Millers moved into the "store chambers." The buyer of their farm was a hard-hearted, penurious man, a deacon of the church in which Draxy had been baptized. He had never been known to give a penny to any charity excepting Foreign Missions. His wife and children had never received at his hands the smallest gift. But even his heart was touched by Draxy's cheerful acquiescence in the hard change, and her pathetic attempts to make the new home pleasant. The next morning after Deacon White took possession, he called out over the fence to poor Reuben, who stood listlessly on the store steps, trying not to look across at the house which had been his.

The role of individuals in political change is a multifaceted concept analyzed through various theoretical frameworks, including Popkin's rational choice theory and Max Weber's theory of charisma. These theories provide diverse perspectives on how individual actions influence political movements and revolutions. While Popkin’s rational choice theory emphasizes the calculated decisions of individuals, Weber's theory of charisma underscores the emotive and transformational impact of leaders. Both perspectives, however, present limitations that may overlook the full spectrum of human agency in political change.

Popkin's rational choice theory propounds that individuals engage in political actions based on a cost-benefit analysis. This perspective posits that individuals weigh the potential personal gains against the risks involved in participating in political change. In the context of a small revolutionary group, individual decisions become particularly impactful as the efficacy and momentum of the movement largely depend on the calculated participation of each member. The departure or replacement of a single pivotal individual can dramatically alter the trajectory and timing of the revolution, often stalling progress and challenging the movement's cohesion.

However, rational choice theory may oversimplify the motivations driving individuals, especially during revolutions that are fueled by idealism, passion, and heroism. In such scenarios, participants may act against their immediate self-interest in a bid to achieve long-term communal goals. For instance, in a hypothetical revolution, an individual may choose to sacrifice personal safety for the broader objective of societal freedom, defying the traditional cost-benefit model of decision-making prescribed by rational choice theory.

In contrast, Max Weber's theory of charisma acknowledges the profound influence charismatic leaders exert on political change. According to Weber, charismatic leaders have the ability to inspire and mobilize individuals through personal magnetism and visionary rhetoric. This theory suggests that these leaders must adapt and evolve—either by adopting new leadership styles to sustain their influence or by institutionalizing their charisma into a more stable bureaucracy to create enduring change. A historical example of this could be seen in the transformation of revolutionary leaders who, after initially invigorating a movement, may establish the bureaucratic structures necessary to maintain post-revolutionary order.

Nevertheless, Weber's framework has its limitations. It often neglects the possibility that a charismatic leader might voluntarily step down to foster democratic principles or promote the greater good, rather than clinging to power. This omission limits the theory’s application to scenarios where leaders prioritize collective over personal agendas.

Both Popkin and Weber’s theories provide structural interpretations of individual roles in political change, which can inadvertently minimize the variation in human choices and the unpredictable nature of leadership dynamics. Rational choice theory’s structural approach fails to capture the emotive and altruistic dimensions of decision-making, while Weber’s focus on permanent leadership styles overlooks the complexity of surrendering power for systemic change.

In conclusion, both rational choice theory and the theory of charisma contribute valuable insights into the role of individuals in political change, yet they also embody inherent limitations. While Popkin’s theory emphasizes strategic decision-making, Weber highlights the emotional and transformational capacities of individuals. When analyzed within broader historical and structural contexts, these theories underscore the complexity of political change, where individual actions are as unpredictable as they are impactful. Understanding the nuances of these theories is imperative to fully appreciating the diverse pathways through which individuals can engender political transformation.

Here Mr. Anderson, his face a mask of forced resignation, interrupted.

"Very well, Eliza," he said, his voice tight. "You shall have your stage. But understand me, this is a singular concession, granted only because of the… the fervour you have displayed."

A spark of triumph flickered in Mrs. Anderson's eyes.

"Oh, John, you are a dear!" she cried, and bestowed a hasty kiss upon his cheek. "I shall make you the proudest man in the county!"

Mr. Anderson merely grunted, turning his gaze towards Al.

"Mr. Allston, I trust this… arrangement is entirely above board?" he asked, his tone laced with suspicion. "I have a profound unease regarding these theatrical ventures. I insist upon a meeting, at your earliest convenience, to discuss your… motives."

Al, though privately amused by the mayor's gruff demeanor, maintained a respectful countenance.

"Certainly, Mr. Anderson," he replied. "I shall be pleased to address any concerns you may have. But time presses, as I mentioned. Mrs. Anderson's swift departure is paramount."

As Al spoke, a commotion erupted from the darkened hallway beyond the parlor. Raised voices, punctuated by the clatter of what sounded like falling furniture, echoed through the house.

"What in tarnation is that ruckus?" Mr. Anderson muttered, his brow furrowed in annoyance.

Before anyone could answer, a figure stumbled into the room, propelled forward by a force unseen. It was Mr. Wattles, his face flushed with anger, his cravat askew. Behind him, a disheveled man, clearly the worse for drink, brandished a gleaming knife.

"I'll get you for this, Wattles!" the man snarled, his words slurred. "You think you can cast me aside like an old boot? I'll show you! I'll show you all!"

Al recognized the man immediately. It was Farley, Mr. Wattles's erstwhile advance agent, now clearly a man consumed by bitterness and drink.

Mr. Wattles stood his ground, though a flicker of fear danced in his eyes.

"Farley, put that thing away!" he commanded, his voice trembling slightly. "You're drunk and making a fool of yourself."

"A fool, am I?" Farley roared, taking a step closer, the knife glinting menacingly in the dim light. "You'll see who the fool is when I've… when I've…"

His words trailed off into incoherent mumbling, his drunken rage momentarily deflated. He swayed precariously on his feet, the knife wavering in his grasp.

Suddenly, the fight seemed to drain out of him. The menacing snarl dissolved into a pathetic whimper.

"Oh, Mr. Wattles," he sobbed, dropping to his knees. "Forgive me! I didn't mean it! I'm just… lost. Lost and alone. Please, don't turn me in to the authorities!"

Mr. Wattles, his anger seemingly evaporated by Farley's sudden collapse, sighed heavily.

"Get up, Farley," he said, his voice now weary. "You're a disgrace to yourself."

He extended a hand to help the fallen man to his feet.

"I won't have you arrested," he continued, "But you must leave this house immediately. And never darken my door again."

Farley, still weeping, clung to Mr. Wattles's hand.

"Thank you, Mr. Wattles," he choked out. "Thank you. I… I don't know what I would have done."

Mr. Wattles gently disengaged his hand.

"There's something else you should know, Farley," he said, his voice regaining its firmness. "I've already engaged a new advance agent. A Mr. Al Allston. He is far more capable than you ever were."

Farley’s bloodshot eyes widened in disbelief. He turned his gaze upon Al, who had watched the entire scene with a detached curiosity.

"That boy?" he scoffed, a sneer twisting his lips. "He’s barely old enough to shave! What does he know about advance work? This is preposterous!"

Texas Winter Storm Death Toll Could Be Much Higher Than The State’s Count, BuzzFeed Data Review Found – Houston Public Media

The February winter storm left thousands without power in subfreezing temperatures and caused serious damage to people’s homes, leaving some apartment tenants with nowhere to go.

While Texas officials have confirmed that 151 deaths were related to the freeze in February, the death toll could actually be four or five times higher, according to a BuzzFeed data review.

Using mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, BuzzFeed said it compared the number of deaths from all causes that were reported in Texas during and after the storm with the number of fatalities that are normally reported during ordinary conditions. That method is known as "excess fatalities" and has been employed during other disasters, like the COVID-19 pandemic, to estimate related death tolls.

"Our analysis, reviewed by three independent experts, suggests that between 426 and 978 more people than expected died in Texas in the week ending February 20 alone," the BuzzFeed report says. "Our best estimate is that 702 people were killed by the storm that week. Even the lowest end of the range is almost three times the number officials have acknowledged. Neighboring states that were hit hard by the winter storm but did not experience the widespread power outages seen in Texas did not show a spike in deaths."

The victims included medically vulnerable people with chronic conditions like cardiovascular disease, diabetes and kidney problems, BuzzFeed said.

The February winter storm left thousands without power in subfreezing temperatures and caused serious damage to people's homes, leaving some apartment tenants with nowhere to go.

In Harris County alone, at least 66 people died from the storm. The county also felt the brunt of electricity and internet service outages, and the ability to obtain food or groceries, according to a report from the University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs.

Texas lawmakers are currently considering legislation meant to prevent further blackouts, most of which are contained in Senate Bill 3. The bill touches on everything from regulating some retail electricity plans to establishing an energy emergency alert system, but some worry it won't do enough to make sure all of the state's natural gas infrastructure is winterized or that penalties won't be high enough to get gas companies to comply.

In Albert Camus' The Stranger and The Fall by Albert Camus, Meursault and Jean-Baptiste Clamence present contrasting perspectives on isolation and relationships, revealing distinct approaches to self and society. Meursault, the protagonist of The Stranger, embodies a passive detachment from conventional norms. He exists in a state of blissful ignorance, oblivious to his alienation from mainstream society. He is genuinely perplexed when others fail to comprehend his reactions, especially concerning his mother’s death or his lack of grief at the funeral. "Maman died today. Or yesterday maybe, I don't know." This indifference, though shocking to the reader and the court, stems from Meursault’s inability to feign emotions he doesn’t genuinely feel, marking a stark contrast to Clamence. Unlike Meursault, Clamence, the "judge-penitent" in The Fall, possesses a heightened awareness of societal perception and actively manipulates it. He strives to cultivate an image of moral superiority, an "elitist" persona intended to conceal his inner flaws. His acts of apparent kindness, such as helping blind people cross the street, are not motivated by genuine altruism but by a selfish desire for validation and the affirmation of his own virtue. Clamence’s behavior aligns with Nietzsche's concept of ressentiment, where he seeks to elevate himself by subtly demeaning others through acts of patronizing charity. Both men, ultimately, live self-centered lives; however, the difference lies in their approach to these lives. Meursault lives honestly according to his own interests and feelings and is indifferent to societal expectations. Clamence, in contrast, employs elaborate justifications and rationalizations to mask his true motives, creating a façade of moral righteousness.

In the realm of romantic relationships, the divergence between Meursault and Clamence becomes even more pronounced. Meursault’s relationship with Marie Cardona is uncomplicated, driven by physical attraction and the enjoyment of shared moments. He expresses no deep emotional investment or commitment, reflecting his general apathy toward societal constructs. Clamence, conversely, approaches relationships with a calculated strategy. He seeks to dominate his partners, losing interest once he has achieved control. He displays characteristics of Don Juanism, pursuing multiple relationships without experiencing genuine love or forming lasting connections. Each encounter is a conquest, a temporary amusement before he moves on to the next. He confesses, “How could I possibly love anyone? I, who haven't even managed to love myself properly?” This statement reveals the fundamental emptiness at the core of Clamence’s existence, a void he attempts to fill through fleeting encounters. He invests emotionally in each relationship, exploring its depths and nuances, but abandons it once he has exhausted its possibilities. The absurdity of Clamence’s life is underscored by these superficial, self-serving relationships, each a fleeting performance in his ongoing charade of moral superiority. His self-righteous actions ultimately lead to hypocrisy and, eventually, to a painful self-awareness of his own failings. He acknowledges the absurdity of his own existence and his inability to escape the cycle of judgment and self-condemnation. Meursault, on the other hand, remains steadfast in his indifference, unmoved by societal pressures or expectations, embodying a different kind of absurd hero: one who rejects meaning and embraces the present moment.

Prince Harry Calls for Social Media Reform, Decrying Misinformation and Extremism

In a powerful address, Prince Harry has issued an urgent call for social media reform, highlighting its detrimental impact on society and the spread of misinformation.

"Misinformation is a global humanitarian issue," Harry declared. "It affects every single one of us, whether we realize it or not."

The Duke of Sussex emphasized the tangible consequences of misinformation, citing the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol as a chilling example. "We've seen how misinformation can lead to real-world violence and division," he said.

Harry and his wife, Meghan Markle, have been actively consulting with experts on misinformation, recognizing its profound impact on individuals and communities. "We've been working with some of the world's leading experts on misinformation to understand the problem and find solutions," Harry explained.

The couple's personal experiences with online harassment have also fueled their passion for addressing social media issues. "Since my wife and I started our relationship, we've seen firsthand how powerful and damaging social media can be," Harry said. "We've been subjected to a wave of misinformation and hate speech that has been extremely damaging to our mental health."

Despite their decision to step down from their roles as senior working members of the British royal family and relocate to California, Harry and Meghan remain committed to tackling social media issues. "We're not quitting social media," Harry clarified. "We're just trying to make it a more positive and compassionate space."

Through their nonprofit organization, the Archewell Foundation, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are actively working to address social media concerns. Archewell has partnered with the Center for Humane Technology and established a fund for the UCLA Center for Critical Internet Inquiry.

"We're working with organizations that are developing new technologies and solutions to make social media a more positive and compassionate space," Harry said.

The Prince emphasized the importance of accountability, compassion, and a critical approach to our relationship with technology. "We need to hold social media companies accountable for the content that is shared on their platforms," he said. "We need to be more compassionate towards each other, and we need to be more critical of the information that we consume."

Harry expressed optimism about the possibility of improving the online space for future generations. "I believe that we can create a better online world for our children and grandchildren," he said. "But it's going to take all of us working together."

Alex Padilla Becomes First Latino to Represent California in U.S. Senate, as Security Measures Increase Ahead of Biden Inauguration

Former Los Angeles City Councilman Alex Padilla has been appointed by Gov. Gavin Newsom to fill the U.S. Senate seat vacated by Vice President-elect Kamala Harris. Padilla, who resigned as California secretary of state to assume his new role in the Senate, will be the first Latino to represent California in the U.S. Senate.

"It is an honor to serve the great state of California in the U.S. Senate," Padilla said in a statement. "I look forward to working with my colleagues to address the challenges facing our state and nation, and to fighting for the rights and opportunities of all Californians."

Padilla's appointment comes as security measures have been increased ahead of President-elect Joe Biden's inauguration, due to threats against the U.S. Capitol and state capitals. Charles Marino, CEO of Sentinel Security Solutions, discussed the enhanced security measures with NBC Southern California.

"We are taking a proactive approach to ensure the safety and security of everyone involved in the inauguration," Marino said. "We are working closely with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies to provide a comprehensive security plan that will protect everyone involved."

Gov. Newsom has also nominated Shirley Weber to succeed Padilla as secretary of state, potentially making her the first Black woman to hold that position. Padilla's deputy, James Schwab, will serve as acting secretary of state until Weber's confirmation.

"Alex Padilla's appointment to the U.S. Senate is a testament to his dedication to public service and his commitment to fighting for the rights and opportunities of all Californians," Gov. Newsom said in a statement. "I am confident that Shirley Weber will continue this legacy as secretary of state, and I look forward to her confirmation."

Padilla's background in both local and state government has prepared him well for his new role in the U.S. Senate. Before his political career, he earned a degree in mechanical engineering and worked for Hughes Aircraft.

"I have always been committed to public service, and I am excited to bring my experience and expertise to the U.S. Senate," Padilla said. "I look forward to working with my colleagues to address the challenges facing our state and nation, and to fighting for the rights and opportunities of all Californians."

Subbotsky's groundbreaking experiments have delved into the realm of non-rational reasoning, shedding light on the coexistence of multiple forms of reasoning in both adults and children. In one particular experiment involving adults, participants were asked to place a stamp in a box which, through manipulations by the experimenter, appeared altered. The results revealed a fascinating insight into phenomenalistic reasoning, as participants exhibited heightened caution when asked to place their driving license in the same box, indicating a behavioral shift towards this non-rational form of thinking. As Subbotsky observed, this experiment demonstrated that phenomenalistic beliefs in adults can manifest through behavior, not solely through verbal expression, highlighting the complex interplay between rational and non-rational modes of reasoning in the human mind.

Furthermore, Subbotsky noted a lingering 'residue' in the minds of adults, allowing for swift shifts to phenomenalistic reasoning when faced with perceived threats. This residue serves as a gateway for the emergence of non-rational beliefs, showcasing the malleability and fluidity of human cognition. In earlier experiments involving children, Subbotsky uncovered a similar reliance on cause-effect reasoning that diverged from scientific beliefs. The majority of children attributed the alteration of the postage stamp to the experimenter's manipulations, a stark contrast to the skepticism displayed by most adults. While children demonstrated susceptibility to phenomenalistic explanations, they did not resort to attributing the phenomenon to 'magic,' suggesting a nuanced progression towards non-rational thinking.

These studies suggest that both adults and children possess the capacity to swiftly revert to non-rational reasoning under specific conditions, emphasizing the intricate nature of cognitive processes. Subbotsky's subsequent investigations delved deeper into whether children's proclivity towards phenomenalistic thinking could potentially evolve into magical thinking, further blurring the lines between rational and non-rational thought processes. Through a meticulous exploration of human reasoning across different age groups, Subbotsky's experiments have illuminated the complex dynamics at play within the mind, underscoring the need for a comprehensive understanding of both rational and non-rational forms of cognition in the field of psychology and cognitive science.

The portrayal of a moral ideal, as my ultimate literary goal, as an end in itself—to which any didactic, intellectual or philosophical values contained in a novel are only the means. . . . Let me stress this: my purpose is not the philosophical enlightenment of my readers” .

Rand's characters are used as means to promote her own ends. Rand does her best to make the reader respect and appreciate Roark, because she knows that accepting him is to accept her philosophy. In fact, Howard Roark is not a man, he is a philosophy embodied . In short, she uses his humanity as a means to make us emotionally accept her philosophy. In opposition to her hero, Roark, Rand creates Ellsworth Toohey. He is less intelligent, less talented, and physically weaker than Roark. If that were not enough, Toohey is a master manipulator, and we are repeatedly shown how he uses others for his own ends. It is easy for the reader to choose which side he is on – whichever is opposed to a man like Toohey, which also happens to be Roark's side. In truth, Toohey's character is a masterful diversion. By making Toohey's manipulation explicit Rand hides the fact that she is being manipulative herself. Instead of real interactions, Rand sets up caricatures of people in order to emotionally connect us with her personal philosophy. By using Kant's ethical philosophy we are able to see what Rand is trying to do, and why this manipulation works. Instead of respecting humanity as an ends in itself, she is using it as a means.

Another important moral philosophy is Levinas's concept of our moral obligation to respect the alterity, the Otherness, of those around us. He says the Other, whoever they may be, is, “someone for whom I am answerable” . In fact, it is only in respecting the Other that we truly become part of the human family. This idea is explicitly understood and explained in a literary context by Flannery O'Connor, who says, “a story is a dramatic event that involves a person because he is a person, and a particular person—that is, because he shares in the general human condition and in some specific human situation. A story always involves, in a dramatic way, the mystery of personality.” We may be tempted to use these principles to judge how characters treat the Otherness of one another within a text, but I believe that we can more ably judge the literary value of a text by examining how the Otherness of the characters is treated by the author.

One text which deals powerfully with Otherness is Mark Twain's The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Finn was first published in 1884, some twenty years after the American Civil War. Twain seems to have realized that the Emancipation Proclamation may have granted blacks freedom from slavery, but that equality and respect have not accompanied that freedom. In 1884 most Americans still viewed blacks as different and inferior.

Stimulus Checks: A Lifeline for Struggling Households

As the country continues to grapple with the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic, the debate around the third stimulus package has been focused primarily on its impact on consumer spending. However, a recent analysis by Morning Consult highlights the lack of data-driven discussion on the package's impact on households' ability to pay bills. Traditional economic data, such as GDP and consumer spending, do not provide a complete picture of the distribution of savings among the population, leaving many households struggling to make ends meet.

The analysis used Morning Consult's proprietary tracking data on household finances to assess the impact of the proposed $1,400 stimulus checks. The findings suggest that targeting these checks towards low-income adults and parents could help prevent financial hardship and economic risks. While $1,400 may seem like a small amount to some, it could make a significant difference for many Americans who are struggling to pay bills and avoid financial hardship.

Fiscal spending during a recession aims to boost short-term economic activity and prevent financial harm to vulnerable households. However, financial delinquencies and defaults are seen as inefficient, and financial uncertainty hinders families' investments in their futures. The number of adults who experienced financial hardship in January remained relatively unchanged from December despite the second round of stimulus checks, highlighting the ongoing impact of the recession on low-income households.

The analysis also highlights the importance of targeting stimulus checks towards those who need them most. Financial difficulties are concentrated among low-income households, with many struggling to make ends meet. By targeting stimulus checks towards these households, policymakers can help prevent financial hardship and promote economic stability.

In conclusion, the third stimulus package has the potential to provide a much-needed lifeline for struggling households. By targeting stimulus checks towards low-income adults and parents, policymakers can help prevent financial hardship and promote economic stability. While the debate around the package's impact on consumer spending is important, it is equally crucial to consider the impact on households' ability to pay bills and avoid financial hardship.

Tragic House Fire in Sugar Land Claims Lives of Three Children and Grandmother

A devastating house fire in Sugar Land, Texas, has claimed the lives of three young children and their grandmother, leaving their mother and her friend critically injured.

The fire broke out on February 16, 2023, at around 2:15 a.m. at a residence on Sweet Gum Drive. The Sugar Land Fire Department responded promptly, but the blaze had already engulfed the home.

Jackie Pham Nguyen, the mother of the children, and her friend Mai Bui managed to escape the inferno but sustained severe burns. They were rushed to a local hospital, where they are currently receiving treatment.

Tragically, Nguyen's three children, 13-year-old Ethan, 11-year-old Emily, and 8-year-old Evan, along with her mother, Loan Le, 64, perished in the fire.

According to Doug Adolph, a spokesperson for the City of Sugar Land, the cause of the fire is still under investigation. However, he noted that the family had been using the fireplace for warmth due to power outages caused by the winter storm that had hit the area.

"We're still trying to determine the exact cause of the fire," Adolph said. "But we know that the family had been using the fireplace, and that's certainly one of the things we're looking at."

Nguyen, who is now facing the unimaginable loss of her children and mother, described them with love and admiration.

"Ethan was a bright and inquisitive boy who loved to play video games and build with Legos," she said. "Emily was a talented artist and a gifted musician. She played the piano beautifully."

"Evan was my little comedian," Nguyen continued. "He always made me laugh. He loved to play soccer and was always running around."

Nguyen also spoke fondly of her mother, Loan Le.

"My mom was the most loving and supportive person I knew," she said. "She was always there for me and my children. She will be deeply missed."

In the wake of this tragedy, two GoFundMe campaigns have been set up to honor Nguyen's children and support various charities. The campaigns aim to raise funds for tuition assistance at St. Laurence Catholic School, where the children attended, and to raise awareness for fire safety.

"We want to do everything we can to support Jackie and her family during this difficult time," said a spokesperson for one of the GoFundMe campaigns. "We also want to use this opportunity to raise awareness about the importance of fire safety."

Nguyen expressed her gratitude for the outpouring of support she has received from the community.

"I am so grateful for all the love and kindness that has been shown to me and my family," she said. "It means the world to us."

The Sugar Land Fire Department urges residents to take precautions to prevent house fires, especially during winter storms. These precautions include:

  • Never leave a fire unattended.
  • Keep flammable materials away from heat sources.
  • Have your chimney inspected and cleaned annually.
  • Install smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors in your home.
  • Develop and practice a fire escape plan with your family.

The Sugar Land community is deeply saddened by this tragic loss and extends its heartfelt condolences to the Nguyen family.

We do not keep Christmas now as we used to do in old Hanover. We have not time for it, and it does not seem like the same thing. Christmas, however, always brings up to me my cousin Fanny; I suppose because she always was so foolish about Christmas.

My cousin Fanny was an old maid; indeed, to follow St. Paul’s turn of phrase, she was an old maid of the old maids. No one who saw her a moment could have doubted it. Old maids have from most people a feeling rather akin to pity--a hard heritage. They very often have this feeling from the young. This must be the hardest part of all--to see around them friends, each “a happy mother of children,” little ones responding to affection with the sweet caresses of childhood, whilst any advances that they, their aunts or cousins, may make are met with indifference or condescension. My cousin Fanny was no exception. She was as proud as Lucifer; yet she went through life--the part that I knew of--bearing the pity of the great majority of the people who knew her.

She lived at an old place called “Woodside”, which had been in the family for a great many years; indeed, ever since before the Revolution. The neighborhood dated back to the time of the colony, and Woodside was one of the old places. My cousin Fanny’s grandmother had stood in the door of her chamber with her large scissors in her hand, and defied Tarleton’s red-coated troopers to touch the basket of old communion-plate which she had hung on her arm.

The house was a large brick edifice, with a pyramidal roof, covered with moss, small windows, porticos with pillars somewhat out of repair, a big, high hall, and a staircase wide enough to drive a gig up it if it could have turned the corners. A grove of great forest oaks and poplars densely shaded it, and made it look rather gloomy; and the garden, with the old graveyard covered with periwinkle at one end, was almost in front, while the side of the wood--a primeval forest, from which the place took its name--came up so close as to form a strong, dark background. During the war the place, like most others in that neighborhood, suffered greatly, and only a sudden exhibition of spirit on Cousin Fanny’s part saved it from a worse fate. After the war it went down; the fields were poor, and grew up in briers and sassafras, and the house was too large and out of repair to keep from decay, the ownership of it being divided between Cousin Fanny and other members of the family. Cousin Fanny had no means whatever, so that it soon was in a bad condition. The rest of the family, as they grew up, went off, compelled by necessity to seek some means of livelihood, and would have taken Cousin Fanny too if she would have gone; but she would not go. They did all they could for her, but she preferred to hang around the old place, and to do what she could with her “mammy”, and “old Stephen”, her mammy’s husband, who alone remained in the quarters. She lived in a part of the house, locking up the rest, and from time to time visited among her friends and relatives, who always received her hospitably. She had an old piece of a mare (which I think she had bought from Stephen), with one eye, three legs, and no mane or tail to speak of, and on which she lavished, without the least perceptible result, care enough to have kept a stable in condition. In a freak of humor she named this animal “Fashion”, after a noted racer of the old times, which had been raised in the county, and had beaten the famous Boston in a great race. She always spoke of “Fash” with a tone of real tenderness in her voice, and looked after her, and discussed her ailments, which were always numerous, as if she had been a delicate child. Mounted on this beast, with her bags and bundles, and shawls and umbrella, and a long stick or pole, she used occasionally to make the tour of the neighborhood, and was always really welcomed; because, notwithstanding the trouble she gave, she always stirred things up. As was said once, you could no more have remained dull where she was than you could have dozed with a chinkapin-burr down your back. Her retort was that a chinkapin-burr might be used to rouse people from a lethargy (she had an old maid’s tongue). By the younger members of the family she was always welcomed, because she furnished so much fun. She nearly always fetched some little thing to her host--not her hostess--a fowl, or a pat of butter from her one old cow, or something of the kind, because, she said, “Abigail had established the precedent, and she was ‘a woman of good understanding’--she understood that feeding and flattery were the way to win men.” She would sometimes have a chicken in a basket hung on the off pummel of her old saddle, because at times she fancied she could not eat anything but chicken soup, and she did “not wish to give trouble.” She used to give trouble enough; for it generally turned out that she had heard some one was sick in the neighborhood, and she wanted the soup carried to her. I remember how mad Joe got because she made him go with her to carry a bucket of soup to old Mrs. Ronquist.

"What do you think, Elihu?" asked old man Jenkins, his brow furrowed in concern, as he gazed down at his ailing heifer. "Can you do anythin' for her?"

Elihu Perkins shifted a piece of tobacco from one cheek to the other, his eyes fixed intently on the stricken animal. He puffed out a stream of smoke from his pipe, and let his gaze linger on the sick creature.

"Pears like it's the hemorrhage, Mr. Jenkins," he said at last. "She's been coughin' up blood somethin' fierce since morning, and now her eyes are sunken like an old stump. I've seen it before, but it's a hard thing to set to rights in animals, I reckon."

Mr. Jenkins' face fell, his lips thinning into a grim line. "But ye can save her, Elihu, can't ye?"

Elihu spat a wad of tobacco juice onto the ground, his eyes squinting with the effort of consideration. "I'll do what I can, Mr. Jenkins, but I won't promise nothin'. She's a mighty sick cow, and I'm beginnin' to think she's beyond help."

He paused, surveying the cow's withered frame. "It'smighty tough on you, Mr. Jenkins. Losin' a cow like that'd be a blow to any farmer. One that's as good a milker as your Bessie here is, the loss'll be felt for months."

"Don't you worry, Elihu," Mr. Jenkins said, his voice shaking with emotion. "I'll make out. I'll just have to get back to work right away and see how we can make up for her loss. But Harry here," he said, nodding towards the young boy who was watching the scene unfold with wide eyes, "he's got his schoolwork to think of. His ma says he's got a fine mind, and I aim to see he gets all the education he needs, no matter what."

Harry's face lit up with a look of pride at the mention of his schooling, but his eyes soon clouded with worry. "Ain't I gotta help Pa with the chores, though?"

Elihu nodded sympathetically. "You'll be needin' to, son. But I'll give your Pa a hand, and maybe between us we'll get the work done without you bein' too late for school. You just see that you get to the lessons, and don't you worry about us."

Harry nodded resolutely, then turned to his father. "I'll be right quick, Pa. I'll get the wood split and the water drawn, and—"

But Mr. Jenkins held up a hand, his expression stern. "No, Harry, not now. You get off to school. I'll handle the chores. I need your Ma to help Elihu with the cow. We can manage."

The young boy nodded, his face set with determination, and turned to make his way to the schoolhouse, his books clutched tightly in his hand. As he left, Mr. Jenkins turned back to Elihu, his expression unspoken.

Elihu met his gaze with a somber one, his eyes full of understanding. "I reckon it's a hard thing, losin' a cow like that. But I'll do what I can for her. Don't you worry, Mr. Jenkins."

Elihu squatted down beside the cow, his hands gently feeling her sides, his brow furrowed in thought. He clsed his eyes, as if prayin' for some sort of guidance, before beginning the task of administerin' his treatment.

Mr. Jenkins watched him, his eyes still filled with worry, his mind turned towards the future without his valuable heifer. Elihu's treatments might help, but deep down, he knew it was a mighty slim chance they'd succeed. The thought lingered, but he pushed it aside, refusin' to give up on the ailing animal just yet.

Cross-cultural studies concerning insomnia underscored marked variations in global health dissatisfaction, influenced by demographic, socioeconomic, and gender-specific factors. In an analysis conducted in New Zealand, researchers closely examined health disparities between Maori and non-Maori populations, demonstrating pronounced differences in insomnia prevalence and related dissatisfaction, and thereby highlighting the strength and relevance of studying ethnic health inequalities. Utilizing Multiple Logistic Regression analysis, the researchers effectively addressed their research questions by statistically modeling sociodemographic predictors, ultimately providing robust results concerning the prevalence and impact of insomnia on health dissatisfaction across different ethnicities. Meta-analyses further enhanced this body of research by aggregating findings from various countries, consistently showing notable gender differences; specifically, women were more predisposed to insomnia compared to men in 28 out of 31 countries studied. These variations were argued to be associated with socioeconomic and cultural norms, lifestyle choices, and demographic conditions prevalent within respective societies.

However, intriguing exceptions were observed within certain demographic contexts that challenged prevalent generalizations. Comparatively lower rates of insomnia among women were recorded in East Asian countries, diverging significantly from the global pattern. Research also revealed closely aligned insomnia rates among males and females within specific populations, notably those studied in Japan and Finland, suggesting cultural dimensions might influence manifestations and perceptions of insomnia. Yet, a methodological limitation emerged with respect to recorded lower insomnia rates among East Asian females; this limitation was attributed primarily to small sample sizes, a critical factor impacting representativeness and, consequently, generalizability of these findings. Despite methodological shortcomings, these cross-cultural insomnia studies significantly enriched the understanding of demographic variability and culturally embedded differences in sleep disturbance complaints and provided a nuanced lens through which the health dissatisfaction related to sleep disorders could be analyzed.

Nomura's study approached insomnia as conceptualized constructs represented as measurable variables, capturing intricate details concerning the frequency, intensity, and duration of insomnia episodes. Notably, Nomura investigated the relationship between insomnia and reported health dissatisfaction within Asian cultural contexts, establishing clear and statistically significant links between dissatisfaction levels and specific sociodemographic parameters. The findings indicated comparatively lower health dissatisfaction scores related to insomnia within Japanese culture when contrasted with Western populations, suggesting cultural variations in coping mechanisms and lifestyle practices that buffered psychological distress and dissatisfaction associated with sleep disorders. For instance, distinct sleep hygiene practices and culturally shaped acceptance of insomnia-related complaints potentially mitigated the adverse effects perceived within Japanese populations. Hence, while Nomura's findings substantiated the relevance of sociodemographic factors in influencing health outcomes, they also sparked discussion about cultural resilience strategies that moderated levels of dissatisfaction. Overall, cross-cultural insomnia studies provided comprehensive insights into demographic disparities, methodological considerations, and culturally dependent outcomes associated with sleep disturbances and health dissatisfaction across diverse cultures and populations.

Below him lay a succession of valleys opening into each other like gentle lakes, until they were lost to the southward. Westerly the distant range hid the bosky canada which sheltered the mission of San Pablo. In the farther distance the Pacific Ocean stretched away, bearing a cloud of fog upon its bosom, which crept through the entrance of the bay, and rolled thickly between him and the northeastward; the same fog hid the base of mountain and the view beyond. Still, from time to time the fleecy veil parted, and timidly disclosed charming glimpses of mighty rivers, mountain defiles, and rolling plains, sear with ripened oats, and bathed in the glow of the setting sun. As Father Jose gazed, he was penetrated with a pious longing. Already his imagination, filled with enthusiastic conceptions, beheld all that vast expanse gathered under the mild sway of the Holy Faith, and peopled with zealous converts. Each little knoll in fancy became crowned with a chapel; from each dark canyon gleamed the white walls of a mission building. Growing bolder in his enthusiasm, and looking farther into futurity, he beheld a new Spain rising on these savage shores. He already saw the spires of stately cathedrals, the domes of palaces, vineyards, gardens, and groves. Convents, half hid among the hills, peeping from plantations of branching limes; and long processions of chanting nuns wound through the defiles. So completely was the good Father's conception of the future confounded with the past, that even in their choral strain the well-remembered accents of Carmen struck his ear. He was busied in these fanciful imaginings, when suddenly over that extended prospect the faint, distant tolling of a bell rang sadly out and died. It was the Angelus. Father Jose listened with superstitious exaltation. The mission of San Pablo was far away, and the sound must have been some miraculous omen. But never before, to his enthusiastic sense, did the sweet seriousness of this angelic symbol come with such strange significance. With the last faint peal, his glowing fancy seemed to cool; the fog closed in below him, and the good Father remembered he had not had his supper. He had risen and was wrapping his serapa around him, when he perceived for the first time that he was not alone.

Nearly opposite, and where should have been the faithless Ignacio, a grave and decorous figure was seated. His appearance was that of an elderly hidalgo, dressed in mourning, with mustaches of iron-gray carefully waxed and twisted around a pair of lantern-jaws. The monstrous hat and prodigious feather, the enormous ruff and exaggerated trunk-hose, contrasted with a frame shrivelled and wizened, all belonged to a century previous. Yet Father Jose was not astonished. His adventurous life and poetic imagination, continually on the lookout for the marvellous, gave him a certain advantage over the practical and material minded. He instantly detected the diabolical quality of his visitant, and was prepared. With equal coolness and courtesy he met the cavalier's obeisance.

“I ask your pardon, Sir Priest,” said the stranger, “for disturbing your meditations. Pleasant they must have been, and right fanciful, I imagine, when occasioned by so fair a prospect.”

“Worldly, perhaps, Sir Devil,--for such I take you to be,” said the Holy Father, as the stranger bowed his black plumes to the ground; “worldly, perhaps; for it hath pleased Heaven to retain even in our regenerated state much that pertaineth to the flesh, yet still, I trust, not without some speculation for the welfare of the Holy Church. In dwelling upon yon fair expanse, mine eyes have been graciously opened with prophetic inspiration, and the promise of the heathen as an inheritance hath marvellously recurred to me. For there can be none lack such diligence in the True Faith, but may see that even the conversion of these pitiful salvages hath a meaning. As the blessed St. Ignatius discreetly observes,” continued Father Jose, clearing his throat and slightly elevating his voice, “'the heathen is given to the warriors of Christ, even as the pearls of rare discovery which gladden the hearts of shipmen.' Nay, I might say--”

The internet, with its vast array of content and interconnectedness, can be viewed as a modern, complex version of carnival. Just like a carnival, it combines elements from different cultures and metaphors, creating a unique and multifaceted entity that reflects the diversity of the real world. The internet mimics reality in various ways, from banal everyday occurrences to profound moments captured in short messages and images that can spark joy or outrage within seconds.

Within the digital realm, the internet establishes its own set of rules, often overturning traditional hierarchies and challenging societal norms. This can lead to a sense of disorientation as logic is upended, mirroring the chaotic and unpredictable nature of a carnival. Grotesque imagery and ambivalence are not experienced individually but rather communally, as people interact and react to content in real-time, blurring the lines between observer and performer.

Despite the freedom the internet provides, it is also plagued by constraints that restrict the full expression of ideas and opinions. This duality creates a bittersweet version of carnival, where playfulness coexists with bitterness, much like the conflicting emotions evoked by traditional carnivals. People's online experiences are shaped by their real-life exposure to binaries, influencing how they interpret humor and satire, sometimes to the detriment of meaningful discourse.

Ambivalence emerges as a central theme in the internet's digital carnival, as exemplified by authors like Sam Lipsyte, who navigate internal contradictions with humor and wit. The internet's departure from physicality distinguishes it from traditional carnivals, underscoring its purely digital nature. Visual content takes precedence online, highlighting the medium's reliance on images to convey meaning, challenging conventional interpretations of visual and literary media.

In conclusion, the internet functions as a modern-day carnival, weaving together visual and literary elements in a complex tapestry that defies easy categorization. Its blend of cultures, themes, and contradictions creates a space where the real and the virtual intersect, challenging users to navigate a maze of information and entertainment. Like a carnival, the internet can be enchanting and bewildering, offering a blend of joy and discomfort that reflects the intricate complexities of the human experience.

Dora had the same yellow curly hair, in tight, frizzly rings all over her head, like a boy's, a light complexion, and blue eyes, in a round, pug-nosed face; and she hung so entirely on Harold that I never doubted that she was his sister till, as we were sitting down to eat, I said, "Can't you come a little way from your brother?"

Eustace gave his odd little giggle, and said, "There, Dora!"

"I'm not his sister--I'm his wife!"

"There!" and Eustace giggled again and ordered her away; but I saw Harold's brow knit with pain, and as she began to reiterate her assertion and resist Eustace, he gently sat her down on the chair near at hand, and silently made her understand that she was to stay there; but Eustace rather teasingly said:

"Aunt Lucy will teach you manners, Dora. She is my sister, and we have brought her home to send her to school."

"I won't go to school," said Dora; "Harold would not."

"You won't get away like him," returned Eustace, in the same tone.

"Yes, I shall. I'll lick all the girls," she returned, clenching a pair of red mottled fists that looked very capable.

"For shame, Dora!" said the low voice.

"Harold did," said she, looking up at me triumphantly; "he beat all the boys, and had to come back again to Boola Boola."

I longed to understand more, but I was ashamed to betray my ignorance of my near relations, for I did not even know whether their mothers were alive; but I saw that if I only listened, Eustace would soon tell everything. He had a runaway chin, and his mouth had a look at times that made me doubt whether there were not some slight want in his intellect, or at least weakness of character. However, I was relieved from the fear of the vice with which the neighbourhood had threatened us, for neither of them would touch wine or beer, but begged for tea, and drank oceans of it.

We had not long finished, when Richardson brought me a note from Lady Diana Tracy, saying she had sent the carriage for me that I might at once take refuge from this unforeseen invasion.

I felt it out of all possibility that I should thus run away, and yet I knew I owed an apology for Harold's finding me and the old servants in possession, so I began to say that my old friend had sent the carriage for me.--I had been taken by surprise, their journey (one of the first across the Isthmus) had been so much quicker than I had expected, or I should have left the house free for them.

"Why?" asked Harold. And when I answered that the place was his and I had no business there, he did not seem to see it. "It is your home," he said; "you have always lived here."

I began explaining that this was no reason at all; but he would not hear of my going away, and declared that it was I who belonged to the place, so that I confessed that I should be very thankful to stay a little while.

"Not only a little while," he said; "it is your home as much as ever, and the best thing in the world for us."

"Yes, yes," responded Eustace; "we kept on wondering what Aunt Lucy would be like, and never thought she could be such a nice young lady."

"Not realising that your aunt is younger than yourselves," I said.

"No," said Eustace, "the old folk never would talk of home--my father did not like it, you see--and Aunt Alice had moved off to New Zealand, so that we could not go and talk about it to her. Mr. Smith has got a school in Auckland, you know."

I did not know, but I found that a year or two after the death of my brother Ambrose, his widow had become the second wife of the master of a boarding-school at Sydney, and that it was there that Harold, at ten years old, had fought all the boys, including the step-children, and had been so audacious and uncontrollable, that she had been forced to return him to his uncle and aunt in the "Bush." Eustace had been with the Smiths at Sydney until her move to Auckland, he had even been presented, and had been to a ball at Government House, and thus was viewed as the polished member of the family, though, if he had come as master, I should never have been drawn, as I was by Harold's free, kindly simplicity, into writing my thanks to Lady Diana, and saying that I could not leave my nephews so abruptly, especially as they had brought a little sister.

The air was thick with the hum of voices, the rustle of silken gowns, and the faint clink of crystal glasses. Leonora stood by the window, her reflection in the glass a mirror of her turmoil. She had always believed love to be an ethereal force, a divine spark igniting the soul. Yet, now, as she gazed at Marcantonio across the room, her heart did not soar with the passion of a thousand sonnets, but stirred with an uncertain flutter, as though a dove had taken up tentative residence there.

Was it love, this quiet warmth that nestled in her chest? Or was it merely acomplexContent of habit and familiarity? She recalled the grand visions of her youth—love as a noble knight on a charger, bearing a heart-shaped shield, his eyes alight with unwavering devotion. Now, she found herself captivated by a man whose eyes, though kind, held the weight of the world, and whose shield was the practicality of daily life. Was this the love she had once envisioned, or a shadow of its idealized form?

The ballroom buzzed with the sounds of a hundred conversations, each a thread in the tapestry of society. Dancers twirled in patterns as intricate as the social hierarchies they represented. Here, a marquis laughed heartily over a glass of champagne; there, a debutante curtsied with practiced grace, her eyes bright with the hope of a favourable match. Among them all, Leonora felt the weight of her own indecision, as though the very air pressed down upon her with the expectation of choice.

She thought back to the days when love was a distant constellation, its light reaching her only in the faintest glimmers of imagination. Now, it was a fire that warmed her, yet not with the fervor of a summer blaze, but the steady glow of a hearth. Was this enough? Did she dare to settle for the comfort of a real emotion when her soul craved the grandeur of the ideal? The question hung in the air, as tangible as the perfumed scent of the room.

As the evening progressed, the ballroom seemed to pulse with life, each beat of the orchestra’s music a heartbeat of society’sphony. Leonora observed the dance of masks—smiles that concealed, laughter that deceived, and eyes that mirrored the complexity of human relationships. In this masquerade, she saw the reflection of her own uncertainty. Was she ready to cast aside the fantasies of her youth for the reality of a man who, though imperfect, offered a love that was sincere and present?

The hour grew late, and the guests began to disperse, the ballroom’s energy waning like the final notes of a song. Leonora found herself alone by the window, the night air a cool balm on her heated cheeks. She closed her eyes, and in the darkness, she saw not the noble knight of her youth, but the familiar face of Marcantonio, his eyes gentle with a love that was, if not mythical, deeply human.

As the last strains of the orchestra faded, Leonora knew that her heart had spoken. It did not echo the grand declarations of her past imaginings, but it whispered a truth she could no longer deny. The ideal was beautiful, but the real was her reality. And in that quiet acceptance, she found a peace that transcended the confines of her romantic ideals. The chapter of her life was turning, and though the future held uncertainties, it did so with the promise of a love that was, above all else, real.

An inquest was held; some evidence was taken; and then it was adjourned for a week that the police might have time to make further investigations. They could not, as yet, learn that one suspicious person had known of the jewels.

Of all Miss Winter's friends, the one to make himself most busy was the Vicar of Nullington. An idle, easy-going man in general, Mr. Kettle could be aroused in a case like this: all his sympathies were with Miss Winter, and his curiosity was on the alert.

"After all," he observed to that young lady, one day when he was sitting with her to discuss details, "after all, the most mysterious part of the affair is not the sudden appearance of Hubert Stone on the scene. I daresay he could readily account for that, poor fellow, if he were living; perhaps he got in by the mail-train on the Sunday night, which you know passes at nearly one o'clock in the morning, and did not care to knock people up. No, the mystery lies in how the information, as to the hiding-place of the jewels, reached the cognisance of the rogue who stole them. And really, as Chief-Constable Wade justly observed, it would seem next to a certainty that the thief must be someone who had an intimate knowledge of the premises of Heron Dyke. You must see that, my dear, for yourself."

"I fear I do," sighed Ella.

"So far as people's recollection serves, Mrs. Toynbee mentioned simply that the bureau had been removed to your morning-room: Miss Winter's morning-room. Now, how should a common thief know which was Miss Winter's morning-room? It is only since the Squire died and your return that you have made it such."

"True," assented Ella.

"And altogether, taking one thing with another, I feel inclined to think it might have been no common thief who took them."

Ella lifted her eyes quickly. "Have you any suspicions?--of any one in particular?"

"No, my dear; no," he answered slowly; and, she thought, dubiously. "We can but wait. Perhaps Wade may ferret out more particulars."

But, on the same evening, when the Vicar was at home, safe within the four walls of his study, he dropped a word or two that nearly scared his daughter out of her senses. Somehow he had caught up a doubt in his own mind of Philip Cleeve.

"Oh, papa!" exclaimed Maria, in an accent of indignant horror.

"I don't say it was he, Maria; I should be very sorry to do that, or to breathe a syllable of this doubt to any one but you. Still, I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that things with regard to Philip do look somewhat suspicious--and Dr. Downes has long thought the same."

"Papa, papa!" she repeated.

"See here, child. In all the mysterious robberies that have taken place, and puzzled us for the past eighteen months, Philip has been present, beginning with Mrs. Carlyon's jewels. He was at her house the evening they were stolen; he was with Downes when he lost his snuff-box--he was with me when my purse disappeared. And, egad, if you come to that," added the Vicar, speaking rather unguardedly in his heat of recollection, "he was with Lennox and Freddy Bootle in London the night they lost things--the one his watch, the other his money."

Washington Post Staff Escapes Kabul Amidst Deteriorating Security

KABUL – Two days after the Taliban seized control of Kabul, Washington Post staff were offered a chance to escape on a chartered plane to Qatar. The journey to the airport, however, proved to be the most perilous part of their evacuation.

Security around Kabul's airport was rapidly deteriorating, with Taliban checkpoints springing up throughout the city. Washington Post reporter Aziz Tassal and his daughter had already experienced the brutality of the Taliban firsthand, having been beaten by fighters while trying to flee.

"They hit me with their rifle butts and kicked me," Tassal recounted. "They were saying, 'You're a spy, you're a spy.'"

The Biden administration was escalating evacuation plans, but could not guarantee safe passage to the airport. British troops assisted the Post group in bypassing a Taliban checkpoint, but the journey was far from over.

"We had to rent armored cars for our safety," said Tassal. "We saw desperate families and damaged vehicles along the way."

Upon reaching the military base, there were initial fears that no charter planes would land that day. However, an American military officer arranged for the group to leave on a U.S. military flight to Qatar.

The flight was packed with mostly Afghans, with seats removed to accommodate more people.

"It was a very emotional moment," said Tassal. "We were all relieved to be leaving, but we also knew that we were leaving behind a country in chaos."

The group also encountered desperate families and damaged vehicles on the road.

"We saw people trying to flee on foot, with their children and belongings," said Tassal. "We also saw cars that had been damaged by gunfire."

BY HEAVENS HE HAD BETTER NOT!

I must ask the reader to make the acquaintance of Major Grantly of Cosby Lodge, before he is introduced to the family of Mr. Crawley, at their parsonage in Hogglestock. It has been said that Major Grantly had thrown a favourable eye on Grace Crawley,--by which report occasion was given to all men and women in those parts to hint that the Crawleys, with all their piety and humility, were very cunning, and that one of the Grantlys was,--to say the least of it,--very soft, admitted as it was throughout the county of Barsetshire, that there was no family therein more widely awake to the affairs generally of this world and the next combined, than the family of which Archdeacon Grantly was the respected head and patriarch. Mrs. Walker, the most good-natured woman in Silverbridge, had acknowledged to her daughter that she could not understand it,--that she could not see anything at all in Grace Crawley. Mr. Walker had shrugged his shoulders and expressed a confident belief that Major Grantly had not a shilling of his own beyond his half-pay and his late wife's fortune, which was only six thousand pounds. Others, who were ill-natured, had declared that Grace Crawley was little better than a beggar, and that she could not possibly have acquired the manners of a gentlewoman. Fletcher the butcher had wondered whether the major would pay his future father-in-law's debts; and Dr. Tempest, the old rector of Silverbridge, whose four daughters were all as yet unmarried, had turned up his old nose, and had hinted that half-pay majors did not get caught in marriage so easily as that.

Such and such like had been the expressions of the opinion of men and women in Silverbridge. But the matter had been discussed further afield than at Silverbridge, and had been allowed to intrude itself as a most unwelcome subject into the family conclave of the archdeacon's rectory. To those who have not as yet learned the fact from the public character and well-appreciated reputation of the man, let it be known that Archdeacon Grantly was at this time, as he had been for many years previously, Archdeacon of Barchester and Rector of Plumstead Episcopi. A rich and prosperous man he had ever been,--though he also had had his sore troubles, as we all have,--his having arisen chiefly from want of that higher ecclesiastical promotion which his soul had coveted, and for which the whole tenour of his life had especially fitted him. Now, in his green old age, he had ceased to covet, but had not ceased to repine. He had ceased to covet aught for himself, but still coveted much for his children; and for him such a marriage as this which was now suggested for his son was encompassed almost with the bitterness of death. "I think it would kill me," he had said to his wife; "by heavens, I think it would be my death!"

A daughter of the archdeacon had made a splendid matrimonial alliance,--so splendid that its history was at the time known to all the aristocracy of the county, and had not been altogether forgotten by any of those who keep themselves well instructed in the details of the peerage. Griselda Grantly had married Lord Dumbello, the eldest son of the Marquis of Hartletop,--than whom no English nobleman was more puissant, if broad acres, many castles, high title, and stars and ribbons are any signs of puissance,--and she was now, herself, Marchioness of Hartletop, with a little Lord Dumbello of her own. The daughter's visits to the parsonage of her father were of necessity rare, such necessity having come from her own altered sphere of life. A Marchioness of Hartletop has special duties which will hardly permit her to devote herself frequently to the humdrum society of a clerical father and mother. That it would be so, father and mother had understood when they sent the fortunate girl forth to a higher world. But, now and again, since her August marriage, she had laid her coroneted head upon one of the old rectory pillows for a night or so, and on such occasions all the Plumsteadians had been loud in praise of her condescension. Now it happened that when this second and more aggravated blast of the evil wind reached the rectory,--the renewed waft of the tidings as to Major Grantly's infatuation regarding Miss Grace Crawley, which, on its renewal, seemed to bring with it something of confirmation,--it chanced, I say, that at that moment Griselda, Marchioness of Hartletop, was gracing the paternal mansion. It need hardly be said that the father was not slow to invoke such a daughter's counsel, and such a sister's aid.
